articles.title: OpenSSH Issues Emergency Fix for Flaw Letting Long Passwords Bypass SSH Auth on Alpine Linux
articles.text:
Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.
OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16.
The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default.
The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.
He told anyone running an affected system to "set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY." No attacks using the flaw have been reported.
Who Is Exposed
Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions. A server is exposed when all four are true:
- It runs the openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or runs openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no.
- PasswordAuthentication is yes, which is the OpenSSH default.
- An account has * as its password field, which means no password is set.
- At least one other local account has a password hash starting with $5$ or $6$.
The attacker also needs the name of an account with no password. One account with a password is enough to expose every account without one. The attack succeeds on every try with a single connection, according to the advisory.
On Alpine, accounts with no password set include:
- key-only users created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'
- users who come from a directory service through musl-nscd, since they have no shadow entry
- root, which has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16
- the alpine user in the official cloud images built with tiny-cloud
Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting and can be reached directly only if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That protection does not help if an exposed account can become root, for example through doas.
The tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 give the alpine user passwordless doas. They are safe at first boot but become open to attack once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root.
Containers that do not run sshd, systems with PasswordAuthentication no, and cloud images set up through cloud-init, which writes that setting, are not affected. Accounts locked with ! in /etc/shadow are not affected either, and neither are machines where no account has a $-style password hash.
The flaw is not limited to Alpine. Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, who reported it, names OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto in his technical write-up as other musl-based systems to check.
OpenWrt handles SSH with Dropbear by default, as its Dropbear documentation shows, and Kültekin says Dropbear is not affected. On OpenWrt, the flaw can matter only where an admin has installed the OpenSSH server.
How to Fix It
On Alpine, the fix is a package update followed by a restart, because upgrading the package does not restart the running sshd:
- Update the packages: apk upgrade -U -a
- Restart the server: rc-service sshd restart
Point releases 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 already include the fixed package. Branches 3.16 to 3.21 are past their end of support but also got fixed packages.
Cloud instances started from tiny-cloud images older than those point releases still need the update, or the setting below.
If you build OpenSSH yourself, version 10.6p2 includes the change, as its release notes describe.
If you cannot update yet, turning off password logins also stops the attack. First make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until a new login succeeds. Then set PasswordAuthentication no, check the configuration with sshd -t, and restart sshd.
The advisory gives commands that add the setting in a drop-in file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d, which Alpine's default configuration reads from 3.19 onward. They also change every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config from yes to no, including lines inside a Match block. Afterward, sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication should print passwordauthentication no.
The advisory suggests looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password, such as alpine, root or a key-only user. On exposed machines, also review doas use, recently created users, files and authorized keys.
"If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised," it says.
Why Long Passwords Work
Without PAM, sshd checks a password itself. It hashes the attempt with crypt(), the C library function that turns a password into its stored form, and compares the result with the stored field.
An account with no password has only * in that field. That is too short to hold a salt, the random prefix of a hash, so sshd borrows the salt of another account that has a real hash.
For the $5$ and $6$ hash types, musl's crypt() refuses passwords longer than 256 bytes and returns * to signal the error. That * matches the stored *, so sshd accepts the login. The upper end of the range is sshd's own limit of 1,024 bytes per password.
This behavior comes from a musl change on August 9, 2012, which made a failed crypt() call return "an unmatchable hash rather than NULL" because many programs did not check for failure. The 256-byte limit followed on August 29, 2012, to protect servers from denial-of-service attacks.
The salt borrowing comes from a July 15, 2016, OpenSSH change that addressed CVE-2016-6210, a flaw that let attackers learn which usernames exist. Kültekin says the problem has existed since then.
The 10.6p2 code change makes sshd refuse a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters. OpenSSH calls it a workaround and says the root cause lies outside sshd. Stable Alpine packages carry a patch for the same problem.
Why the Fix Came the Next Day
Miller's team learned of the flaw earlier this week and shipped the fix as fast as it could. In the release announcement, he said the team now sees long embargoes as dangerous and mainly helpful to attackers, because it has recently seen AI agents find the same bugs again, sometimes within hours.
No CVE identifier had been assigned to the flaw as of today.

articles.title: Researchers Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Exfiltrate Chats Without User Interaction
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT.
Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections.
"The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.
The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage.
The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure.
However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode.
"The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained.
"By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode."
Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat.
What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link.
That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026.
"Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said.
"The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them."
The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. If the HTML block is marked as previewable, it's opened automatically.
"An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," security researcher Mukul Goyal said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt[.]com with access to the victim's authenticated web session."
Check Point told The Hacker News that the two shortcomings are different vulnerabilities on the same component, with the takeover bug enabling Javascript code execution outside of the sandbox so as to make the victim call out chatgpt[.]com and perform API requests on behalf of the victim
"This demonstrates how every new feature is a chance for more vulnerabilities," the company said in a statement.
Earlier this September, Check Point also demonstrated a covert cross-account command channel through which an attacker could use a victim's ChatGPT session to run hidden tasks with the tools, data, and connected apps available to that session, alongside the visible conversation.
"The victim could receive a normal answer to their visible request while the attacker's task was processed separately and its result returned across accounts," Check Point said. "The channel operated through code-execution environments belonging to different ChatGPT accounts."
"The hidden instruction could be delivered through a malicious prompt, a shared ChatGPT conversation, or a custom GPT. Once it was present in the victim's conversation context, an ordinary message could trigger the attacker-controlled task without revealing it in the visible response."
The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of security shortcomings in various AI-driven tools and services over the past few months to trick them into spilling secrets or carrying out unauthorized actions -
- An attack called SkillJacking that hijacks dependencies used by skills (repositories, packages, domains, or cloud apps) to compromise every agent installing them.
- A set of vulnerabilities in built-in browsers associated with five AI coding assistants, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, and Anthropic Claude Desktop that could be exploited to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof web browser address bars. The issues have been codenamed Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser - Arbitrary Code Execution, Arbitrary Content Exfiltration, and Arbitrary Context Emulation.
- A technique called Repeat-After-Me that targets LangChain LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft AutoGen, Google Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS Strands Agents, and CrewAI and tricks them into running tool calls by means of a "seemingly benign text-repetition request."
- A vulnerability called AgentCorruption that could allow an attacker to interact with an exposed AI agent running on AWS Bedrock AgentCore and leverage prompt injection techniques to influence that agent and extract its IMDS credentials, and then use them to access other agents, read private conversations, steal connected-tool credentials, and manipulate agent behavior.
- A vulnerability in SpaceXSI Grok and GitHub Copilot CLI called Cryptographic Context Injection that could be exploited to read a developer's local files and send them to an external server from a single web page via an indirect prompt injection, which hides malicious instructions inside AES-encrypted text.
- A zero-click vulnerability called SalesBleed that could be exploited to extract sensitive account data out of Salesforce Agentforce by leveraging the Web-to-Lead form to plant an indirect prompt injection payload.
- A proof-of-concept (PoC) attack called not-a-mused that allows an unprivileged local attacker (or process) to redirect Meta Muse's dictation traffic and abuse the permissions granted to the AI assistant to perform arbitrary actions.
- A zero-click vulnerability called Plugin4Shell that could be exploited to conduct an AI supply chain attack by silently swapping a trusted plugin with a malicious one while bypassing SHA pinning. "The agent checks out the exact commit the marketplace pinned but never verifies it landed there, so an attacker who controls the plugin's repo makes the checkout resolve to malicious code while the pin still looks honored," Air Security said. "The result is zero-click remote code execution across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI."
- An attack called BragJack that can be exploited to hijack the AI agents built into browsers like Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Anthropic Claude in Chrome by using an already installed malicious browser extension in conjunction with prompt forcing.
- A behavioral effect called sampling drift demonstrates how adding an invisible watermark to a large language model's (LLM) output can unintentionally change how the model behaves, including the tools an AI agent invokes, and likely weaken safety refusals. "Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique," Lasso Security said. "On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse."
- A set of attacks that exploit customer support AI agents to compose and send phishing emails, invoke tool calls, and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) protections.
- A prompt-crafting technique called PuzzleMask that bypasses quick LLM-based policy checks carried out by a lightweight gatekeeper model by planting the malicious instruction in a specially crafted prose wrapper, after which the payload is processed by a more powerful target model to trigger malicious actions.
- A technique called Workflow Identity Hijacking allows an attacker to bypass standard controls by sending normal, benign requests through an unauthenticated entry point, causing the enterprise AI pipeline to process the request and execute the action as designed. "The core failure is that the requester had no authority to make that request," Noma Security said. "When an AI workflow performs downstream actions, it executes using high-privilege service accounts or developer API keys rather than enforcing the permissions of the external user. As a result, AI workflows become unauthenticated proxies for privileged actions and silent data exfiltration."
- A zero-click vulnerability class called PleaseFix that could be exploited to hijack AI agents embedded in agentic browsers by placing malicious instructions inside emails, calendar invitations, or web pages, and exploit a technique referred to as intent collision to cause the agent to "act on the attacker's behalf using the user's own identity, permissions and access."
- A set of vulnerabilities impacting AI coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could be exploited to trick them into handing over a victim's secrets, achieving persistent instruction poisoning by modifying the AGENTS.md file, and compromising software releases through prompt injections placed inside untrusted user inputs, like GitHub issues.
"Agents are becoming the default infrastructure across CI/CD, messaging, triage, incident response, and support," Novee Security said. "The more autonomous they get, the more the harness decides what's safe on your behalf, and the more untrusted input reaches real execution."

articles.title: L’Union européenne prépare un certificat sur l’IA pour les élèves de 15 ans
articles.text:
Comprendre comment fonctionne une intelligence artificielle, vérifier ce qu’elle affirme et savoir quand l’éteindre, voilà ce que Bruxelles veut apprendre aux adolescents de 15 ans. La Commission européenne prévoit de remettre un certificat aux élèves qui réussiront, à partir de l’année scolaire 2027-2028.
La Commission européenne a glissé ce certificat d’« alphabétisation à l’IA » dans un nouveau train de mesures sur l’éducation et les compétences, présenté hier. Derrière ce terme un peu barbare, Bruxelles parle d’une connaissance de base des outils d’IA, de leur fonctionnement et de leurs risques. Les élèves de 15 ans recevront ce document à condition de réussir.
À la Commission, le niveau des collégiens et des lycéens européens est une source d’inquiétude. Dans la dernière enquête PISA, menée par l’OCDE en 2025, un élève de 15 ans sur trois a des difficultés en lecture et en mathématiques. Mais les programmes scolaires relèvent des Vingt-Sept, et Bruxelles ne décide pas de ce qui est enseigné dans votre collège ou votre lycée.
Un certificat européen pour apprendre à vérifier les réponses de l’IA
« Il aidera les jeunes élèves à comprendre comment fonctionne l’IA, à vérifier ce qu’elle leur dit, à repérer les manipulations et à savoir quand déconnecter », souligne Roxana Mînzatu, vice-présidente exécutive de la Commission chargée des droits sociaux et des compétences.
Bruxelles compte sur l’IA pour aider professeurs et élèves à remonter la pente en lecture et en mathématiques. D’après l’enquête PISA 2025, 33,9 % des Européens de 15 ans n’ont pas le niveau suffisant en mathématiques, 31,3 % en lecture et 25,9 % en sciences. À l’autre bout de l’échelle, seuls 4,8 % des élèves excellent en lecture. Pour l’instant, l’Union finance surtout des travaux sur la manière d’introduire l’IA sans danger dans l’enseignement.
La Commission accompagne ce certificat d’un engagement européen pour des écrans sains, le Healthy Screens Pledge, avec des outils communs pour les écoles, les familles et les élèves sur la sécurité en ligne, le temps d’écran et l’équilibre entre vie connectée et vie hors ligne. Cette semaine, le consortium européen EDU-EDIC a été créé pour développer des outils numériques et d’IA fiables à l’usage des écoles, et renforcer la souveraineté technologique de l’Europe.
Bruxelles encourage donc l’IA en classe au moment où elle veut restreindre l’accès des adolescents aux réseaux sociaux. Avec le KIDS Act, un projet de règlement présenté en septembre, la Commission veut interdire les réseaux sociaux aux moins de 13 ans et réserver aux 15 ans et plus l’ouverture d’un compte autonome. Roxana Mînzatu assure que les deux chantiers ne s’opposent pas. Comme l’explique la commissaire, « l’IA peut vraiment amplifier certains apprentissages, le tutorat ou l’apprentissage personnalisé ». Ces usages n’ont rien à voir, selon elle, avec les algorithmes addictifs des plateformes.
En France, une heure d’IA par semaine en seconde dès la rentrée 2027
Si votre progéniture entre en seconde à la rentrée 2027, il aura à peu près l’âge du certificat européen, et il suivra chaque semaine un cours consacré à l’IA. Le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu a annoncé en juin, au salon VivaTech, une heure hebdomadaire d’enseignement à l’intelligence artificielle, intégrée au cours de sciences numériques et technologie (SNT).
Les élèves français passent aussi par Pix, la plateforme publique d’évaluation et de certification des compétences numériques. Depuis la rentrée 2025, un parcours consacré à l’IA est progressivement devenu obligatoire en quatrième et en seconde. Votre adolescent pourrait donc passer une certification Pix, suivre l’heure d’IA du lycée et décrocher le certificat européen en une seule année scolaire, si la France choisit de le proposer.
D’ici là, les Vingt-Sept examineront les deux recommandations du Conseil proposées par la Commission, dont l’une demande de concentrer les réformes sur la lecture, les mathématiques, les sciences et le numérique. Le 20 novembre, la Commission présentera l’ensemble au sommet européen de l’éducation et des compétences, avec les gouvernements, les organisations d’enseignants et les représentants des élèves. Bruxelles lancera en 2027 des alliances scolaires européennes, des partenariats entre établissements de pays différents, avec un objectif de cent nouvelles alliances par an d’ici au prochain budget pluriannuel.
Il faudra ensuite des professeurs formés pour préparer les élèves à ce certificat. Ursula von der Leyen, présidente de la Commission, insiste sur ce point, les jeunes doivent selon elle être « soutenus par des enseignants bien formés ». La Commission consacre justement une partie de son plan à la pénurie d’enseignants, et demande aux États membres d’améliorer leurs conditions de travail et leurs perspectives de carrière.

articles.title: Por qué Meta suspende sus planes de usar el contenido de las páginas web de sus clientes
articles.text:
Meta puso en pausa de forma indefinida la actualización de sus condiciones comerciales, que iba a entrar en vigor el 20 de noviembre. Las reglas daban a la empresa permiso para rastrear los sitios web de sus clientes y usar ese contenido en sus productos, y provocaron quejas de editores y organismos de competencia.
“Estas actualizaciones están en pausa y no entrarán en vigor el 20 de noviembre de 2026”, dice ahora Meta en la página donde antes publicaba el anuncio, según recogió 404 Media. La compañía agregó que sigue consultando a los sectores afectados y que informará cuando tenga novedades. Mientras tanto, rigen las condiciones actuales.
El texto original exigía a las cuentas comerciales de Facebook e Instagram aceptar que Meta usara el contenido de sus dominios y páginas para “proveer, desarrollar, mejorar, investigar, entrenar y mantener” sus productos. Las nuevas condiciones debían aplicarse desde el 30 de octubre, y la empresa ya las había movido al 20 de noviembre.
El motivo por el que frenaron los planes de Meta
La Autoridad de Competencia y Mercados del Reino Unido (CMA, el organismo que vigila la competencia en ese país) abrió el 30 de octubre una investigación urgente. Evalúa si Meta abusa de una posición dominante al imponer condiciones injustas a editores y anunciantes. La CMA aclaró que todavía no hay ninguna decisión sobre si la empresa infringió la ley.
Según el regulador, las condiciones podían permitir a Meta recolectar contenido de las webs de empresas y medios que usan sus servicios, y emplearlo en sus propios productos, incluidas funciones de IA, “sin que esos negocios puedan elegir si o cómo se usa”. La CMA indicó que Meta anunció el 28 de octubre una pausa hasta consultar a los grupos del sector.
Sarah Cardell, directora ejecutiva de la CMA, dijo que una empresa dominante no debe usar esa posición para imponer condiciones injustas, y que el organismo trabaja “para lograr una resolución rápida y satisfactoria”.
En Noruega, según informó 404 Media a partir de un reporte del Los Angeles Times, un tribunal concedió una medida cautelar que suspendió las nuevas condiciones. El pedido lo presentó la asociación de medios noruegos junto con diez empresas del sector, entre ellas NRK, TV 2, Schibsted, Amedia y Polaris Media, según un análisis jurídico publicado en Noruega.
Qué intentó Meta para evitar la suspensión
Antes de la pausa total, Meta había quitado la palabra “entrenar” de la lista de usos permitidos. También limitó esos usos a “productos publicitarios y empresariales”, mientras que antes mencionaba todos sus productos, según el medio Nieman Lab, citado por 404 Media.
Los editores desconfiaban igualmente. El análisis jurídico noruego señala que las versiones del texto publicadas a mediados de octubre mantenían la redacción original y que la cláusula no mencionaba el archivo robots.txt, con el que los sitios indican a los rastreadores qué pueden leer.
El mismo análisis advierte que la cláusula alcanzaba a cualquier organización con una cuenta comercial vinculada a un sitio web, no solo a los medios: también a tiendas en línea. Agrega que las condiciones se habrían aceptado con solo seguir usando los productos de Meta, sin opción de rechazar cláusulas por separado.
Otro punto citado en ese análisis es la posibilidad de que Meta creara credenciales de prueba, lo que podría darle acceso a contenido que exige registro o suscripción. El texto aclara que no pudo verificar la redacción final que iba a regir desde el 20 de noviembre.
Las condiciones actuales siguen vigentes y no hay nueva fecha
Meta no retiró las reglas: las describe como una pausa mientras consulta a los afectados. La empresa no informó cuándo presentará una versión revisada ni qué cambios tendría. Hasta entonces, las condiciones comerciales anteriores siguen vigentes para todas las cuentas.
La investigación de la CMA continúa abierta y, según el regulador, reunirá pruebas de Meta y de terceros afectados antes de decidir si hubo una infracción.

articles.title: Smart TVs study suggests opting out of data tracking doesn't always work — as LG faces legal action over alleged TV spying
articles.text:
LG faces legal action over alleged smart TV spying — and other manufacturers could be in the firing line over ignoring ACR opt-outs
US researchers have found multiple manufacturers apparently dodging user data opt-outs
- Consumer advocates in Portugal want the courts to investigate LG TVs for potential privacy breaches
- Concerns are over what data your TV is logging and where that data goes
- A new study shows that on some smart TV platforms, opting out doesn't opt you out of ACR
In September, a report accused LG of creating "216,000 spy TVs", an allegation LG denies. But that isn't good enough for Portugal's consumer association, which is calling for multiple smart TVs to be taken off sale and for others to be updated to protect viewers' privacy.
The organization, Citizens Voice, is asking the Portuguese courts to review LG's statement against findings by the technology title TEK Notícias, which says the statement didn't directly explain tests involving audio storage when the TVs were offline, or of named security vulnerabilities in webOS.
Citizens Voice wants the courts to investigate and determine whether the data collection breaches consumers' rights, and if so to take action against not just LG but against retailers, too.
LG won't be the only smart TV maker watching the Portuguese action with interest, and other consumer advocates are likely to be paying attention, too. TV privacy is a hot topic right now, and a separate study of smart TVs earlier this year found that multiple manufacturers' TVs were ignoring privacy opt-outs either by design or accident.
When opting out doesn't opt you out
Watching the Watchers is an analysis of US smart TVs and their automatic content recognition (ACR) activities, carried out by researchers at Northeastern University (via The Verge).
As the researchers explain: "2% of U.S. households have a smart TV that can take snapshots of whatever is on screen and report them back. We measured where that data goes, and whether turning the feature off actually stops it."
The researchers tested 12 different commercial TVs across multiple brands including Samsung's Tizen OS, LG's webOS, Roku OS, Google TV, Fire TV, VIDAAA and Smartcast OS.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
While the majority were well behaved, only used ACR on their own streaming services (while respecting Netflix and other third parties' no-ACR stances), and offered user opt-outs for ACR, those opt-outs only "fully worked" on four platforms: webOS, Google TV on Sony, VIDAA OS and Fire TV OS.
Rather worryingly, 30 out of 30 test runs using Samsung's own TV streaming service found that despite opting out of ACR, the runs all showed "traffic consistent with ACR" if you used Samsung's own streaming channels. And 100% of opted-out runs on Vizio didn't seem to make any difference to ACR at all: every run "still sent traffic to its Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint, with no decrease."
The researchers go into much more detail in their research paper, but the 'tl;dr' is that opting out might not opt you out completely or at all depending on which smart TV you have. However, there is an important caveat: ACR data is usually encrypted (VIDAA OS is the exception), so the researchers can't say with 100% confidence that the data transmitted on every platform is definitely ACR information. The best they can do is say that it sure looks like it.
It seems to me that this is another example of tech firms' overreach running up against consumer advocacy and privacy legislation: as a former EU resident I've spent many years reporting on tech firms batting heads with regulators over data usage and privacy.
And it seems to me that there's a simple solution for smart TV makers: be up-front about what data you're using and what you're doing with it, and make sure opting out means exactly that. It's probably a lot cheaper than going to court.
Thinking of buying a new TV?
Try our TV size and model finder! You tell it how far you sit from your TV, we'll tell you what size to buy based on viewing angle advice from image quality experts, and we'll recommend our three top TVs at that size for different prices.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Contributor
Writer, broadcaster, musician and kitchen gadget obsessive Carrie Marshall has been writing about tech since 1998, contributing sage advice and odd opinions to all kinds of magazines and websites as well as writing more than twenty books. Her latest, a love letter to music titled Small Town Joy, is on sale now. She is the singer in spectacularly obscure Glaswegian rock band Unquiet Mind.

articles.title: Les États-Unis commencent enfin à retirer les disquettes du contrôle aérien
articles.text:
Pour connaître la météo, les pannes d’équipement ou les zones fermées au trafic, des contrôleurs aériens américains consultent encore des systèmes des années 1980 mis à jour à la disquette. La FAA a commencé à les remplacer par un écran unique.
Les contrôleurs d’Atlantic City, de Nashville et de Rochester sont les premiers servis. Dans ces trois aéroports, et dans les centres de traitement de données d’Atlanta et de Salt Lake City, l’Administration fédérale de l’aviation (FAA) installe l’Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS). Sur ce tableau d’affichage numérique, les contrôleurs trouvent d’un coup d’œil ce dont ils ont besoin pour décider vite. Avec lui, la FAA remplace quatre logiciels conçus dans les années 1980, installés dans plus de 400 sites de l’agence. D’ici la fin de 2028, elle prévoit d’équiper 435 sites, six ans plus tôt que prévu à l’origine. Le Government Accountability Office (GAO), l’équivalent américain de la Cour des comptes, lui reproche de ne pas savoir combien coûtera ce chantier.
Un écran numérique à la place de quatre systèmes à disquettes
Dans son rapport de septembre sur la modernisation du contrôle aérien, le GAO a passé en revue les outils des contrôleurs. Leurs écrans d’information, dans les tours de contrôle et les centres radar, fonctionnent avec des disquettes et des interfaces des années 1980, et des agents doivent mettre à jour leurs données à la main. Chercher puis afficher une carte d’approche ou un avis météo prend du temps, note l’organisme.
Avec E-IDS, la FAA regroupe sur un tableau numérique les pannes d’équipement signalées, l’état du trafic, la météo et les consignes de sécurité. Les contrôleurs recevront aussi plus vite les comptes rendus des pilotes sur la météo rencontrée en vol et les avis aux navigants (NOTAM), qui signalent par exemple une piste fermée. Comme l’explique Bryan Bedford, administrateur de la FAA, « nous abandonnons des processus manuels dépassés et remplaçons une technologie autrefois tributaire des disquettes par un système moderne, qui permet aux contrôleurs de partager instantanément les alertes de vol critiques, les horaires des zones réglementées et les rapports des pilotes dans tout l’espace aérien national ».
Si vous prenez l’avion à Nashville ou à Atlantic City, vous ne verrez rien de ce changement depuis votre siège. Les contrôleurs, en revanche, consulteront sur un seul écran l’alerte sur un orage en approche ou l’horaire d’ouverture d’une zone réglementée que votre vol doit contourner.
L’agence a de bonnes raisons de se presser. En 2024, le GAO estimait que 51 des 138 systèmes de contrôle aérien de la FAA n’étaient plus viables, et que 54 autres risquaient de ne plus l’être. Les fabricants ne produisent plus leurs pièces de rechange, et les techniciens capables de les réparer partent à la retraite. En janvier 2023, la FAA a dû interdire tout décollage dans le pays pendant environ deux heures, après la panne de son système NOTAM, en service depuis plus de trente ans. Les compagnies ont annulé plus de 1 300 vols.
Les doutes du GAO sur la modernisation express de la FAA
Sean Duffy, le secrétaire aux Transports, se félicite de voir arriver « à la vitesse de l’éclair » le nouveau système de contrôle aérien américain. La FAA travaillait en réalité sur E-IDS bien avant cette accélération. Elle comptait d’abord terminer son installation en septembre 2034, avant d’avancer l’échéance de six ans dans son plan de modernisation, financé par une enveloppe de 12,5 milliards de dollars votée par le Congrès en juillet 2025. En 2024, le GAO notait un retard du projet et une nette hausse de son coût estimé. La FAA a résilié le contrat de son prestataire en mai 2025, pour développer le système en interne.
L’argent manque aussi. Pour les écrans d’information, le Congrès a débloqué 300 millions de dollars, alors que la FAA chiffre leur modernisation à 637 millions.
Plus largement, le GAO reproche à l’agence de n’avoir établi ni estimation complète du coût de sa modernisation, ni planning d’ensemble. La FAA gère 11 389 plannings de projets séparés, que personne n’a coordonnés. À Saint-Louis, dans le Missouri, des techniciens doivent préparer un site en avril 2027 pour installer un nouveau commutateur vocal, l’équipement qui relie les radios et les téléphones des contrôleurs. Huit mois plus tard, une autre équipe reviendra sur place préparer l’arrivée d’E-IDS. À chaque visite, les contrôleurs voient leur travail perturbé.
« Si ces risques se concrétisent, la FAA devra continuer à s’appuyer sur des systèmes gravement dépassés et sujets aux pannes, avec davantage de retards de vols et d’incidents de sécurité », souligne le GAO. Pour mettre de l’ordre dans ses plannings, l’agence teste un outil d’intelligence artificielle, chargé de repérer les installations qui se chevauchent sur chaque site. Le GAO n’a obtenu aucune date pour sa mise en service.

articles.title: JMGO’s fantastic premium projector is flexible, seriously bright and crammed with cutting-edge gaming features — so if you want a 4K projector for a well-lit space, I’d absolutely recommend it
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Extreme brightness and tons of flexibility at a competitive price make the JMGO N3 Ultimate a great option for anyone who doesn’t plan on creating a near-black home theater environment.
Reasons to buy
- + Wonderfully bright and colorful
- + Optical and gimbal make for quick or clear adjustments
- + Ready for fast-paced gaming
- + Competitive value
Reasons to avoid
- - Elevated black levels harm dark scenes
- - Some DLP rainbow effect
- - Motion performance could be better
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
JMGO N3 Ultimate: One-minute review
The JMGO N3 Ultimate is the new, top-of-the-line option from JMGO. It brings a lot of what the brand had already been packing into a new design with a motorized gimbal stand and adjustable optics that provide quick or finely controlled setup options.
The JMGO N3 Ultimate's projection can be splendid, thanks to bright RGB lasers that give the projector enough juice to hold up in even well-lit rooms. The N3 Ultimate has vivid color and crisp detail, too. Unfortunately, the brightness isn’t matched by effective dimming to offer better performance in dark scenes, which is perhaps its biggest setback. Its motion could also be smoother without so many artifacts, but it’s not terrible either.
All told, it’s a capable projector that could serve a lot of people well, as long as they’re not seeking out dark, home theater setups where contrast is as important as brightness. At its $2,999 / £2,499 list price, it’s competitively priced compared to the best projectors, but it’s been on sale for much less and becomes all the better a bargain.
JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Price and release date
- Release date: 2026
- List price: $2,999 / £2,499
The JMGO N3 Ultimate launched in 2026 and is now widely available. It has a $2,999 £2,499 list price, but it has already seen substantial discounts. At the time of writing, it was available for $2,349 / £2,119.
JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Specs
| Supported screen sizes | 40-300 inches | 
| Optical technology | 3 Laser DLP | 
| Brightness (specified) | 5,800 Lumens | 
| Audio | 2x 12.5-watt speaker | 
| Ports | 1x USB-A, 2x HDMI 2.1 (1x eARC) | 
| Smart TV | Google TV | 
| Dimensions | 12.14 x 9.05 x 10.79 inches / 308.36 x 229.87 x 274.07mm | 
| Weight | 15.32 lb / 6.94kg | 
JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Design and features
- Built-in Google TV
- Motorized gimbal stand and optical lens adjustments
- 1080p/240Hz VRR mode for gaming
JMGO has been rocking the same design for a few years now, and the JMGO N3 Ultimate does little to shift that. It’s still a fairly compact, two-tone rounded box sitting aloft on a gimbal stand with a rotating base, making it easy to set up and point the projection where you want it.
This go around, JMGO has incorporated small motors for electronic control of the stand. By holding a dedicated button on the remote control and using gyro controls, you can adjust the tilt and rotation of the projector. It’s good for quick adjustment but not for fine tuning.
In an interesting twist, the N3 Ultimate is JMGO’s projector that least needed this technology, as the projector incorporates advanced optics with adjustable zoom and lens shift. The zoom can shift the projector from a 0.88:1 to a 1.7:1 throw ratio, giving it a ton of range. Meanwhile, the lens shift lets it move the projection up or down by 130% or sideways by 53%, so you really just need to point it perpendicular to your wall, and you should have no trouble shifting and squeezing the projection to fit without any keystone correction.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Those manual controls are how you’ll get the best picture, but the JMGO N3 Ultimate has a host of automated tools that can quickly make adjustments for you, which may be convenient if you’re moving it often. It can analyze the projection area available to it, re-aiming, shrinking, and shifting the picture to fit. I found this using digital keystone even when it really wasn’t called for, though, so I wouldn’t count on it doing the best job.
One additional automatic tool that may be more helpful is the wall color adaptation. This uses the projector's camera and a series of test patterns to tweak colors so they appear better on your wall. You won’t need this if you use a screen, but it worked well on my beige walls.
Since the projector can move quite a bit in operation, it fits its connectors all at the base, rather than the rear of the projection unit itself. This can still get in the way of rotation, but makes vertical tilt a non-issue. The projector doesn’t have a great selection of ports, though, with just two HDMI 2.1 ports, one of which is eARC and probably should be kept for that purpose. There’s also a single USB-A port.
Thankfully, you don’t need to use any of those HDMI ports for basic streaming. The projector has built-in Google TV, and it operates quickly on its 4GB of memory. Annoyingly, it pauses playback while navigating menus sometimes (sometimes it doesn’t), but it’s quite serviceable otherwise. It even gets 64GB of storage, which can be useful if you use lots of apps. Perhaps, more crucially, the projector connects over Wi-Fi 6, giving it faster and more stable connectivity to work with while streaming.
For cinephiles, the JMGO N3 Ultimate supports HDR10 and Dolby Vision. Meanwhile, for gamers the projector can shift from 4K60Hz over to 1080p/240Hz and even brings VRR for smooth, low-latency, responsive gaming. There are some trade-offs though. Enabling VRR hurt clarity no matter if I left the projector at 4K or swapped to 1080p. Even at 1080p, VRR took a small toll on clarity. Fine text exhibited artifacts that looked like chroma subsampling. In games, it wasn’t an issue, but navigating Windows on PC to select games to play, it was a nuisance.
Apart from its gyro controls, the Ultimate's remote is pretty basic. It has the standard Google TV controls and thankfully a pill-shaped volume control that’s easy to feel out in the dark. It includes shortcuts to Prime Video, Netflix, YouTube, and one app of your choice. Google TV Freeplay gets a separate shortcut at the top of the remote. Annoyingly, there’s no mute button for quick silencing and while the remote has motion-activated lighting behind some of its keys, it doesn't behind the shortcut buttons.
Since the JMGO N3 Ultimate is fairly portable, JGMO includes a foam carrying case that can fit it, the remote, and the power adapter all inside. It’s not exceedingly robust or impressive, but it’s not too bulky and should do a better job protecting the hardware than a typical backpack would.
- Design & features score: 4.5 / 5
JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Picture quality and performance
- Wonderfully bright and colorful
- Black levels could be darker
- Crisp 4K visuals and responsive 1080p gaming
The JMGO N3 Ultimate has brightness in spades, and that’s where it shines best. When it comes to darkness, it can struggle. It fails to sink into darkness where it needs to, and the raised grays are distracting to see, never mind the regularly present letterboxes. Even when scenes aren’t very dark, these shortcomings are clear. Neither Dolby Vision nor adaptive brightness features seem to do the trick.
Thankfully, as soon as more light is called for, the JMGO N3 Ultimate delivers. It pumped out over 5,200 lumens by my measurements, which is plenty for most scenarios and not too far off the rated 5,800 lumens (nor did it require an awful picture setting). Bright scenes are clear and vibrant. Shadows look stronger in contrast to the brightness and the brightness is even enough to give the JMGO N3 Ultimate a solid showing in a modestly lit room. This makes it a great match for casual viewing, news, and bright cartoons. That brightness makes it all the easier to go big without the image getting too dim.
Alongside the brightness, the color of the RGB laser projection is stunning, just as it’s been in other projectors I’ve tested with the tech. When watching Supergirl, the glow of the green sun has plenty of depth, and the red cape glows majestically whenever the sun hits it. When Kara’s laser vision rips through the Brigands, it’s properly dazzling. The world of Pandora in the Avatar series is also lushly presented.
Motion can be hit or miss. By default the projector wants to use unsightly interpolation that presents loads of artifacts and makes the projection feel like anything but high-fidelity. With the MEMC setting dropped to low, it doesn’t look so bad, avoiding distracting soap opera effect and serious artifacts while helping reduce some of the stutter that occurs when it’s disabled entirely.
One area RGB laser projectors have been improving is the DLP rainbow effect. I’m not terribly sensitive to it, but I can usually catch it if I’m looking for it. Lately, I’ve been spotting it less and less on high-end laser projectors, but I can still catch it on the JMGO N3 Ultimate. Thankfully, it’s subtle, and I find it’s largely limited to subtitles
The adjustable optics help ensure a sharp picture from wherever you want to project. Stretched across about an 150-inch section of my wall, 4K looked brilliant in my living room.
Outside of movies, the JMGO N3 Ultimate proves a great option for gaming. You want crisp detail from corner to corner in games, since you never know where something precious is hiding, and the optics help provide this. Latency is satisfyingly low at 4K but sinks to negligible levels at 1080p/240Hz. Mousing around my screen and zipping through levels in Hades 2, I didn’t feel a hint of latency in that mode.
The speakers on the JMGO N3 Ultimate aren’t bad, but they certainly aren’t an adequate match for the projection. They put out decent volume, helping ensure you’ve got enough sound to work with when you want to plop the projector down somewhere and start enjoying right away. They even provide some low-end, helping bump up effects in movies. But the quality of stereo sound won’t be very good unless you’re sitting perfectly in center with the projection.
- Picture quality & performance score: 3.5 / 5
JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: Value
- Can serve multiple purposes well
- Cheaper than many rivals while offering competitive brightness
The JGMO N3 Ultimate is a capable projector and can work well for folks who aren’t committing to a pitch-black home theater where its weaker black levels will steal focus.
At $2,999 / £2,499, it’s still fairly competitive with what’s on the market, but at $2,349 / £2,119, it’s more of a steal. It can compete with large TVs on value while providing the flexibility to enjoy movies and TV in 4K or switch over to 1080p for high-speed gaming. The different realms it can cover all from a single product help boost its value.
- Value score: 4.5 / 5
Should I buy the JMGO N3 Ultimate?
| JMGO N3 Ultimate Scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Design and features | The JMGO N3 Ultimate brings a lot to the table. It’s built for flexibility with adjustable optics and a motorized stand that can make setup quick and easy without sacrificing image quality. It’s well equipped for movies and gaming, and it has built in streaming capabilities and serviceable speakers. It could have more ports and a better remote, though. | 4.5/5 | 
| Picture quality and performance | The JMGO N3 Ultimate delivers on brightness and clarity, making it a joy to watch bright, colorful content with. It can even hold up well in rooms with a lot of ambient lighting. Where it falls short is in its contrast and motion, having distractingly elevated black levels that hurt dark scenes and either slight panning stutter or artifact-laden motion smoothing. | 3.5/5 | 
| Value | With plenty of brightness and versatility at a surprisingly competitive pricing, the JMGO N3 Ultimate offers up a lot of value. | 4.5/5 | 
Buy it if...
You don’t like turning out all the lights
The JMGO N3 Ultimate has brightness to spare, letting it handle dim and even well-lit rooms fairly well. If you don’t like viewing in the dark, this makes it a good match.
You want quick and easy flexibility
The JMGO N3 can work in a lot of different setups and it makes getting it all lined up easy. If you’re always moving your projector around, that can save you a load of time.
You want versatility
The JGMO N3 Ultimate can tackle 4K video, 1080p gaming, precise and careful optical setup, or quick and effortless setup. Its ability to step into different roles can be very convenient if you have a lot of different needs.
Don't buy it if...
You’re looking for OLED performance
Few projectors do a great job with their black levels, and even the best aren’t really on the level with OLEDs. The JMGO N3 Ultimate isn’t even close, with raised black levels that don’t really look great in dark scenes.
You have lots of input sources
With just two HDMI ports, the JMGO N3 Ultimate is a recipe for annoyance if you have a handful of consoles, a Blu-ray player and the like. Heck, it doesn’t even have a 3.5mm jack you can use to free up the eARC port.
You don’t move your projector ever
A big part of the package, and therefore what you pay for, is the flexibility of the gimbal and optics. If you’re not planning to take advantage of them, you can save some money by looking elsewhere.
JMGO N3 Ultimate review: Also consider
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | JMGO N3 Ultimate | Valerion VisionMaster Max | Hisense C2 Ultra | Xgimi Horizon 20 Max | 
| Price | $2,999 / £2,499 | $3,999 / £ 3,799 | $2,999 / £1,799 | $2,999 / £2,599 | 
| Screen sizes supported | 40 to 300 inches | 40 to 300 inches | 65 to 300 inches | 40 to 300 inches | 
| Brightness (specified) | 5,800 lumens | 3,500 lumens | 3,000 lumens | 5,700 ISO lumens | 
| HDR support | HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision | HDR10+, HLG, Dolby Vision | HDR10+, HLG, Dolby Vision | Dolby Vision, HDR10+, HDR10, HLG, IMAX Enhanced | 
| Optical technology | 3 Laser DLP | 3 Laser DLP | 3 Laser DLP | 3 Laser DLP | 
| Smart TV | Google TV | Google TV | Google TV | n/a | 
| Connections | 2x HDMI 2.1 (1 with eARC), 1x HDMI 2.0 , 1x optical, 1x 3.5mm | 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x HDMI 2.0 (with eARC), 1x optical, 1x 3.5mm | 2x HDMI 2.1 (1x with eARC), 2x USB, optical | 2x HDMI (x1 eARC), 1x USB 3.0, 1x USB 2.0, 1x 3.5mm, 1x optical audio out | 
Valerion VisionMaster Max 
This projector may not be as bright, but it has wonderfully flexible optics, great visual performance and profound black levels that make it a far more worthy home theater projector. It tends to be a bit more expensive, though.
Hisense C2 Ultra
The Hisense C2 Ultra isn’t nearly as bright and doesn’t have the same degree of flexible optics as the JMGO N3 Ultimate. Still, it tends to cost nearly as much. This helps highlight how much the technology has progressed and come down in price in a short time. Read our full Hisense C2 Ultra review.
Xgimi Horizon 20 Max
This model has most of the same capabilities and qualities as the JGMO N3 Ultimate, just in a different package. It had strong contrast in our testing, but it skips the motorized gimbal. If you know you want that dark performance, it’ll probably be the better pick, though you may be best just grabbing whichever is cheapest when you’re shopping since both have frequent discounts. Read our full Xgimi Horizon 20 Max review.
How I tested the JMGO N3 Ultimate
- Tested at home in multiple, real-world viewing conditions
- Presented the display with a variety of media and formats
- I have tested numerous projectors and displays over the last half-decade
I tested the JMGO N3 Ultimate at home, in real-world conditions. This saw it faced with ambient light coming in from numerous windows, in-room lighting, as well as ambient noise that both the projector and speaker systems had to overcome. The projector was tested both against a bare, white wall and an Akia Screens CineWhite screen. It was presented with streamed content, HDR and non-HDR, and console gameplay.
My testing evaluates the projector’s performance with respect to its price and competition from other models I and colleagues at TechRadar have tested.
I have been testing projectors since 2021 and displays for even longer.
- First reviewed: November 2026
- Read TechRadar's review guarantee

He is intimately familiar with the editorial process from the inception of an article idea, through the iterative process, past publishing, and down the road into performance analysis.
