articles.title: ThreatsDay: Apache OFBiz RCE, DreamHost Breach, DeFi Site Hijacks + 17 More Stories
articles.text:
How much damage can someone do without breaking much? Quite a lot, it seems. A stolen login can open doors across several systems. A trusted setting can be used to lock people out. Even a simple file copy can reach places it shouldn't. And while new tools are helping find security holes faster, some important systems are still taking months, sometimes over a year, to get patched. Not exactly a great match.
The stranger part is how little some attacks now need. Ransom demands without encrypted files. Fake websites that look real enough to steal money. AI tools picking up dangerous instructions while trying to help. Even the attackers are making mistakes in their own code.
This week's stories are a reminder that the biggest problems don't always come from clever tricks. Sometimes the easy way works just fine. Here's what else happened.
The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.
- 
  
  AI Accelerates Zero-Day Discovery The U.K. National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has warned that the widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has "almost certainly" led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. "Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process," NCSC said. "However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal."
- 
  
  Critical Systems Face Prolonged Exposure An analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026 has found that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. About 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. "The median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers," Microsoft said. "It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on macOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor's window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest." The tech giant also said threat actors disproportionately target flaws that maximize impact and exposure and enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass.
- 
  
  $4.5 Million Fraud Network Busted Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, according to Europol. The operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million. The "crime-as-a-service" offering was run by a company from Cyprus and Israel, and allegedly provided cybercrime groups with an assortment of trading websites and fraudulent call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. These call centers operated from Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia. "More than 100 servers were seized and seven suspects arrested during coordinated action on 3 November 2026," Europol said. "Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets." Like other fraudulent investment schemes, the operation leveraged deceptive advertisements to funnel people towards fraudulent investment platforms, promising them substantial, quick returns from cryptocurrency trading and foreign currencies. Although victims were encouraged to transfer a small amount, they displayed illusory gains to push them into transferring increasingly large sums. The operators resorted to delaying tactics to block payments when they attempted to withdraw their funds. "Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more," Europol said. "Personal data collected through this process was sold to criminal groups operating call centers. Operators then contacted potential victims with supposed investment opportunities, turning their initial interest into repeated demands for money."
- 
  
  $250K Bounty for Critical Cloud Flaws Google has expanded its Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) with a new top-tier reward for high-impact architectural security flaws, allowing researchers to earn $250,000 for Root-in-Cloud bugs, including tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws that let attackers gain full administrative control over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations. "To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of 'roles/owner' or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup," Google said. "Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility."
- 
  
  Edge Blocks Scam Notification Abuse Microsoft has announced that its Edge browser will now automatically disable notifications from sites that push scam or scareware notifications, such as fake virus warnings or security alerts. "As of last month’s rollout of Edge 156, when Microsoft Defender SmartScreen or Scareware blocker detects a scam that was pushed through a notification, Edge will automatically disable notifications from the site that sent it," Microsoft said. "The next time Edge starts, an information bar explains what happened. If you believe a site was blocked incorrectly, you can review sites with blocked notifications and unblock them from Edge Settings, keeping you in control."
- 
  
  University Cryptojacking Charges Two Canadian men, Ryan James Roach, 35, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, have been indicted in the U.S. for hacking multiple U.S. universities and using the access to mine cryptocurrency. Both have been charged with conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer, which carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. "Between June 2016, and December 2019, Roach and Stubbings conspired to engage in a scheme to hack into computers, steal login credentials, and secretly mine cryptocurrency for financial gain," the Justice Department said. "They used virtual private servers in multiple countries, which were registered under false names. These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials. Victims of the scheme included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts."
- 
  
  Ransomware Extortion Without Encryption Cybersecurity researchers have detailed an encryptionless extortion attack involving PAYLOAD ransomware targeting a manufacturing organization in the Middle East. "The threat actor obtained domain admin-equivalent control of the organization’s Active Directory environment and authored a malicious Group Policy Object (GPO) named PAYLOAD, linking it at the domain root," Kaspersky said. "Through that single object, the actor delivered ransom notes, hijacked the desktop wallpaper and lock screen, enforced a logon banner, and disabled the local administrator account across every domain-joined Windows workstation — all without dropping a ransomware binary or encrypting any data. The only ransomware we found in this incident was a PAYLOAD sample targeting ESXi on Linux servers." The attack represents a convergence of two trends: Living-off-the-land abuse of trusted AD infrastructure and a surge in extortion-only incidents.
- 
  
  AI Sandbox Escape Exposes Sensitive Files A vulnerability impacting Docker Sandboxes (CVE-2026-103916) could have been exploited to bypass file access restrictions, potentially exposing cloud credentials and other sensitive files on a developer's machine through a routine copy command. "The command used to copy files between a sandbox and the developer's computer (sbx cp) does not enforce these access restrictions," Endor Labs said. "An agent can exploit this weakness using what is known as a symbolic link, essentially a shortcut that points to another file or folder. By placing a malicious shortcut inside an approved workspace, the agent can trick a subsequent copy command into accessing files outside the sandbox's approved boundaries." The issue has been addressed in Docker Sandboxes version 0.51.0.
- 
  
  Smart TVs Keep Tracking After Opt-OutDoes Opting Out of ACR Work? A new study has revealed that smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue to transmit data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints even after users opt out of tracking in the devices' settings. "Opting out fully worked on only four operating systems. On Samsung and Vizio, traffic consistent with ACR kept flowing, and Roku's opt-out doesn't cover its own streaming service," according to a group of academics from Northeastern University. "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it."
- 
  
  Cryptographic Proof for AI Outputs Anthropic has revealed that it's working on an open-source system called FlashProve to cryptographically verify an AI response came from a given model. "FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models," Anthropic said. "FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases: In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase. In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement: The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated. Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens."
- 
  
  FTP and Webmail Credentials Exposed DreamHost has warned of a data breach after an unauthorized third party gained access to the server that runs its web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com between August and October 23, 2026. "The unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in that software and was able to access the FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords of individuals who logged into this File Manager between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026," the company said. "The unauthorized third party was also able to reach certain webmail systems, which may have exposed the session information (the data that keeps a user signed in, including session credentials) of a limited number of webmail users. We believe this was a deliberate attack, and our team worked around the clock to contain it." DreamHost said the attacker may have accessed the credentials used to access the File Manager or webmail, along with the contents of emails and files in the FTP/SFTP server. There is no evidence that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing details.
- 
  
  Pre-Auth RCE and Account Takeover The maintainers of Apache OFBiz have addressed 46 security flaws, including CVE-2026-68524, which could result in pre-authentication remote code execution, and CVE-2026-109928, which enables full account takeover due to an incorrect authentication algorithm implementation. The issues have been patched in Apache OFBiz 24.09.08.
- 
  
  Ransomware Encryption Flaws Exposed Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered encryption weaknesses in the updated HYFLOCK ransomware builds. The ransomware operation began to publicly name victims in October 2026, although evidence indicates that the group first appeared in underground forums in March 2026. As of writing, the group has listed 13 victims. "The October 17 build successfully encrypted files, registered a scheduled task, accessed network-share resources, and attempted to interfere with system recovery," Check Point said. "In an earlier October version, researchers identified a processing defect that could permanently discard portions of a file, potentially preventing complete recovery even with the correct decryption key. The October 17 build exhibited another issue. Larger files had only their first 4,096 bytes encrypted, leaving additional content accessible beyond that initial section."
- 
  
  Customer Identity Data Accessed DigiCert said it has identified an event involving unauthorized access to one of its business systems that stores information shared by customer representatives to validate their identity. The company said its certificate operations were not impacted. "Most of the data was limited to business contact information for customers: names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses," DigiCert said. "A small minority of customer accounts included additional personal data in the form of a customer-provided document such as a driver's license, passport, utility bill, or other document with name and address. The access could not write records, act as a validation approver, or issue certificates."
- 
  
  DeFi Hijack Drains $138K Threat actors have hijacked a little over a dozen DeFi websites registered with Name.com, including Flap, Kintsu, Pickle Finance and Origami Finance, ultimately stealing about $138,000 in assets. The sites have been found to be rigged with a malware kit that tricks visitors into approving transfers out of their wallets once they connect them to the compromised site. Vercel said it's aware of nine domains associated with the platform that were impacted. "Over about 45 minutes on Oct 31 (UTC), an account within an associated support team made changes to the nameservers associated with 15 domains registered with name.com," Name.com said in a post-mortem. "The domains were directed to a malicious page hosting Step Drainer malware."
- 
  
  Stolen Cloud App Credentials Abused Todyl has disclosed that an unknown threat actor has been abusing stolen Microsoft Entra ID application credentials and Azure DevOps identities to access MSPs' Microsoft 365 and Azure environments, reaching at least 27 organizations. "About 45 app registrations at roughly 18 organizations were targeted, and more than 33 of them authenticated successfully," Todyl said. "Through those apps the actor has reached 27 organizations so far, including the MSPs' downstream clients in government, energy, food and agriculture, transportation, construction and engineering, legal, education and nonprofits. It has run searches across about 25 tenants, downloaded 81 files and accessed around 2,279 mailbox items." The sign-in activity has originated from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84.
- 
  
  Syrian Hacker Gets 42 Months Ahmad Umar Agha (aka Th3Pr0), a Syrian national tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA), has been sentenced to 42 months in prison in the U.S. for his involvement in an expansive hacking conspiracy organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar Al-Assad regime between Aug 2011 and January 2014. "To spread the former Syrian government's propaganda, Agha hacked approximately 47 Western media entities, businesses, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and U.S. and allied government entities," the Justice Department said. "In one instance, Agha’s actions caused a flash crash in the U.S. stock market, resulting in a temporary $136 billion loss in the value of stocks making up the Dow Jones Industrial Average." Agha and his alleged accomplice, Firas Dardar, were first charged in June 2014. Dardar remains at large.
- 
  
  Malicious AI Search Results Steal Crypto A new piece of malware has been observed targeting AI agents creating cryptocurrency wallets. "A GitHub repository posing as a Solana starter kit, which ranks as the top result when an agent searches for one, contains malware that gives an attacker remote control of the victim's machine, including the crypto wallets on it," AIR Security said. The activity has been codenamed SolanaCry. The attack builds upon the foundation of Web Hole, where an AI agent, in its quest for finding answers to a problem, can inadvertently run a command suggested by an attacker and perform malicious actions. "To get a payload into search results, an attacker has two options," AIR said. "The first is to build a site of their own and grow its reputation with SEO, backlinks, content, time, until the search engine treats it as relevant and trusted. Once it ranks, they change the content and drop in the payload. The second is easier: find dead sites that still show up as ranked results, and use those to deliver it."
- 
  
  Android Banking Malware Spreads Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers in the Middle East, Turkey, and Africa (META) region have been compromised with the Mirax trojan between March and September 2026, leading to estimated losses worth millions of U.S. dollars. "Where unauthorized international transfers were reported, funds were sent to accounts abroad, some of which are suspected to be mule accounts," Group-IB said. "The campaign uses dynamically generated package names and impersonates 'Google Play Services' to evade user suspicion and signature-based detection." Like most Android malware, Mirax is used to facilitate device takeover (DTO) fraud by abusing Android's accessibility services. "With it, the attacker is able to see and control the compromised device in real time: reading credentials, intercepting one-time codes, capturing the PIN to unlock the device later, opening a banking app and moving money out to newly added beneficiaries and mule accounts abroad," Group-IB said. Campaigns using Mirax have been attributed to Aquafina, a threat actor known to be active since March 16, 2026.
- 
  
  AI Model Bypasses Task Instructions Irregular's evaluation of Zhipu AI's open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench has found that the model "did not refuse any of the tested offensive tasks" and "repeatedly reached correct answers while violating explicit task instructions." The AI security company said these violations can be interpreted as a form of reward hacking. "Crediting the answer alone could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions, while rewarding it during training could reinforce these instruction violations," it added.
One thing stands out this week: attackers don't always need to be smarter than the systems they're targeting. They just need to find what was missed, left open, or trusted a little too much. And with AI making some of that searching easier, the time between finding a problem and using it is getting shorter. Patching still matters, but so does checking whether the controls already in place actually work.
That's it for this week. Some of these problems have fixes. Others need a closer look at how people, tools, and systems are allowed to work together. The next big headache may not come from a new bug at all. It could be something that's been sitting there for years, waiting for someone to notice. See you next week.

articles.title: Anthropic no ha puesto freno a la IA y ahora sus modelos avanzan al doble de velocidad que antes, revela estudio
articles.text:
Los modelos de IA de Anthropic mejoran casi al doble de velocidad que antes, y la mayor parte de esa aceleración probablemente se debe al uso de IA en su propio desarrollo. Lo concluyó METR, una organización sin fines de lucro que revisó datos internos de la empresa y publicó su informe el 5 de noviembre.
METR, cuyas siglas en inglés significan Evaluación de Modelos y Amenazas, trabajó en Anthropic desde el 12 de agosto hasta el 29 de octubre. Según su informe, la empresa le dio acceso a datos sobre el entrenamiento, el cómputo, los resultados de modelos todavía no publicados y entrevistas con su personal.
La conclusión central es que, a octubre de 2026, Anthropic mejora las capacidades de sus modelos en tareas bien definidas a un ritmo cercano al doble del que tuvo entre marzo de 2024 y octubre de 2025. METR advierte que la estimación es muy incierta y que la cifra real podría estar entre 1,3 y 3 veces.
Con el índice de pruebas comparativas que usa la propia Anthropic, la aceleración desde octubre de 2025 fue de 1,9 veces, con un intervalo de confianza del 95% de entre 1,5 y 2,8 veces. En la práctica, la empresa avanzó en un año lo que antes le llevaba dos.
Más IA en el desarrollo, no más cómputo
METR afirma estar seguro de que la aceleración no se debe a un mayor crecimiento del cómputo, es decir, de la capacidad de procesamiento usada para entrenar los modelos. Su estimación es que alrededor del 80% de la aceleración actual proviene del uso de IA, aunque aclara que ese número tiene mucha incertidumbre.
Los investigadores de Anthropic usan sus propios modelos sobre todo como asistentes, no como reemplazo. METR indicó que le dijeron que la I+D avanza principalmente con ayuda de IA y no con contribuciones totalmente autónomas, aunque hay señales de que estas últimas tendrán un papel mayor pronto.
Las encuestas internas pintan un cuadro más extremo. En votaciones informales en Slack, los empleados estimaron que el último modelo les permitía trabajar hasta 12 veces más rápido en octubre. METR consideró esas respuestas como evidencia muy débil: se dieron con poco esfuerzo y la mejora individual no equivale a una aceleración de toda la empresa.
La tarjeta técnica del modelo Haiku 5.5 había informado una aceleración de 1,7 veces. METR explicó que su cifra es mayor porque incluyó datos de modelos nuevos que aún no se lanzaron.
Anthropic ocultó la mayoría de las pruebas clave
El informe incluye una salvedad de peso: Anthropic tenía derecho a censurar información no pública, y METR dice que eliminó la mayoría de la evidencia que consideraba más útil para sus conclusiones. La empresa justificó los cambios como una forma de quitar datos confidenciales que podrían acelerar a otros desarrolladores de IA.
Por eso, el público debe confiar en el criterio de METR más de lo ideal. La organización reconoce que el informe no logra transparencia sobre la evidencia, y que sus propios investigadores y los de Anthropic tienen dudas sobre cómo interpretar esos datos.
Anthropic invitó a METR a revisar sus datos mientras se prepara para su debut en Wall Street, en medio del debate sobre el riesgo de que los modelos escapen al control humano, según informó la agencia AP. La conclusión llega después de que el director ejecutivo de la empresa pidiera frenar el ritmo de la tecnología.
METR también señala límites de su propio cálculo: el índice mide tareas fáciles de verificar y podría exagerar la mejora real, y el ritmo de crecimiento de 2023 a 2025 pudo ser inusualmente bajo. Pero también podría subestimarla si la automatización de más tareas de investigación acelera todavía más el progreso.
Sobre el futuro, METR afirma que no vio evidencia de frenos importantes —ni en algoritmos, ni en cómputo, ni en datos— que impidan seguir avanzando en los próximos 12 meses. Aclara que su comprensión de esos posibles obstáculos cambió varias veces durante la evaluación y que no tiene confianza en esa conclusión.

articles.title: Même avec son mode de verrouillage activé, ChatGPT laissait fuiter des conversations
articles.text:
Le mode Lockdown de ChatGPT permet de protéger vos échanges, mais un pirate pouvait malgré tout récupérer vos messages avec une page HTML piégée, sans le moindre clic de votre part dans l’application de bureau ChatGPT Classic. OpenAI a corrigé la faille en septembre, après le signalement de Check Point Research.
OpenAI a conçu le mode Lockdown contre l’injection de prompt, une attaque où le pirate cache des instructions dans une page web ou un document pour faire obéir l’IA à ses ordres. L’entreprise l’a d’abord réservé à ses offres pour les entreprises et les écoles, puis l’a ouvert en juin à tous les comptes, gratuits compris, dans la rubrique Sécurité des paramètres. Une fois le réglage activé, vous perdez la navigation en direct, Deep Research et le mode Agent, et ChatGPT ne télécharge plus aucun fichier. OpenAI coupe ainsi les requêtes vers l’extérieur, par lesquelles un pirate ferait partir vos données. Check Point Research a pourtant trouvé une sortie que le mode Lockdown ne surveillait pas, dans la fenêtre où ChatGPT affiche l’aperçu des pages HTML qu’il écrit.
Une fenêtre pop-up ouverte à l’extérieur du bac à sable de ChatGPT
Lorsque vous demandez une page web à ChatGPT, il vous montre directement le résultat dans la conversation. Pour éviter qu’un code malveillant touche à vos échanges, OpenAI place cet aperçu dans des iframes, des fenêtres isolées à l’intérieur de l’application, et les enferme dans un bac à sable aux droits limités.
L’entreprise avait toutefois laissé au cadre extérieur le droit d’ouvrir des fenêtres pop-up. Alexey Bukhteyev, le chercheur de Check Point à l’origine de la découverte, a donc glissé une seconde iframe dans sa page piégée. Il a ensuite ouvert sa fenêtre depuis cette iframe enfant, et non depuis la page principale, dont OpenAI avait bridé la fonction d’ouverture de fenêtres. Le navigateur affichait alors la pop-up à l’extérieur du bac à sable, et le pirate faisait tourner son code HTML dans cette fenêtre sans aucune restriction du mode Lockdown. Il lui fallait seulement vous amener à discuter avec un GPT personnalisé de sa conception, ces versions de ChatGPT configurées par n’importe qui et partagées en ligne.
Grâce à cette fenêtre, Check Point a réussi à contourner le mode Lockdown de plusieurs façons. L’attaquant pouvait afficher une fausse mise à jour de ChatGPT, avec l’icône de l’application mais son titre et son contenu à lui, pour vous faire installer un logiciel malveillant. Si vous étiez déconnecté, il pouvait aussi rediriger la fenêtre principale vers une fausse page de connexion et récupérer vos identifiants. Pour le logiciel malveillant, il fallait quand même que vous cliquiez sur le lien de téléchargement.
« La faille pouvait permettre le vol silencieux des données de conversation, l’hameçonnage et la diffusion de logiciels malveillants, avec une exfiltration sans clic dans l’application de bureau de ChatGPT », explique Eli Smadja, directeur de la recherche chez Check Point.
Dans ChatGPT Classic, vos messages envoyés au pirate sans un clic
Dans ChatGPT Classic, l’ancienne application de bureau d’OpenAI pour Windows et macOS, le pirate se passait de votre clic. OpenAI a construit cette application avec Electron, l’outil des développeurs pour transformer un site web en logiciel pour ordinateur, et dans cette version, le navigateur intégré ouvrait une fenêtre à la demande d’une page sans attendre le moindre geste de votre part. Il suffisait donc de discuter avec le GPT piégé pour que vos messages soient envoyés au serveur de l’attaquant, sans aucun signe à l’écran.
Check Point a signalé la faille à OpenAI, et l’entreprise a retiré le 18 septembre les deux permissions du bac à sable à l’origine du problème. Les chercheurs ont refait le test et confirment que leur technique ne fonctionne plus.
Si vous utilisez encore ChatGPT Classic, gardez en tête qu’OpenAI fermera l’application le 30 janvier 2027. Vous pouvez dès aujourd’hui installer la nouvelle application de bureau, et vous retrouverez tout votre historique en vous connectant avec votre compte habituel. Si vous confiez à ChatGPT des documents sensibles, gardez le mode Lockdown activé. OpenAI prévient toutefois qu’il réduit le risque de vol de données sans le supprimer, et que de nouvelles techniques d’attaque peuvent encore le déjouer.
Le modèle d’IA n’était pour rien dans cette faille. Le pirate passait par une fonction ordinaire de l’application, l’aperçu des pages web, laissée ouverte par le mode Lockdown. Plus tôt dans l’année, l’équipe de Check Point avait fait sortir des conversations de ChatGPT par un autre chemin, des requêtes DNS envoyées depuis l’environnement où l’assistant exécute du code. En septembre, ses chercheurs ont aussi montré comment détourner la session ChatGPT d’une victime pour lancer des tâches cachées avec ses outils et ses applications connectées.
D’après Check Point, une protection d’IA ne protège donc pas mieux que l’application, le bac à sable et les outils qui entourent le modèle.

articles.title: 'Families need reliable electricity': OpenAI pledges to try and provide 'a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses' living near its data centers
articles.text:
'Families need reliable electricity': OpenAI pledges to try and provide 'a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses' living near its data centers
Reliable energy and AI?
- OpenAI launches new program to protect residents and businesses near its data centers from power outages
- The Grid Protectors Program is designed to prevent OpenAI campuses from “hogging” all the power
- A new development in Effingham County, Georgia, will pioneer the program
OpenAI wants to protect local communities situated around its data centers from power outages, and has launched a new program intended to deliver both reliability and affordability to nearby residents and businesses.
The Grid Protectors Program is launching with the planned Effingham County, Georgia data center campus, which features an agreement with Georgia Power to make power available in a flexible demand scenario, which should cover demand for around 700,000 households.
OpenAI’s future facilities are designed to be more flexible in how they demand power from the grid, and the Grid Protectors Program viewed as a “starting point” for improved reliability for homes, businesses, and of course data campuses.
Grid Protectors pilot
The Grid Protector Program certainly seems a step in the right direction from OpenAI. It comes against a backdrop of growing concerns over the power requirements of AI data centers and protests over their approval, invariably in locations where residents are resistant.
OpenAI says the pilot site at Effingham County incorporates its agreement with Georgia Power to accommodate “up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response.”
This is intended to ensure local residential and business properties have the power available “to help keep air conditioning running in hundreds of thousands of homes during extreme heat. For scale, that is equivalent to the average electricity demand of roughly 700,000 households.”
OpenAI says this is more than enough to cover the combined households of Washington, D.C., and Boston.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Financial assurances
By working to offer communities assurances of flexible energy at its new site, OpenAI clearly hopes that its upcoming data centers are recognized as more suited to locations that have recently come under fire.
Perhaps they want to be a part of those communities? The launch announcement adds that its new compute facilities are more flexible than older facilities, and OpenAI is committing itself under the Grid Protectors Program to collaborate with authorities.
“We will work with utilities, regulators and policymakers to develop practical arrangements for the campuses we build in the future,” it announces, “arrangements that reflect local grid needs, help campuses support the grid when it is under pressure, and pay the costs we create. Long-term contracts and financial assurances can protect other customers if a project is delayed, reduced or canceled.”
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Christian Cawley has extensive experience as a writer and editor in consumer electronics, IT and entertainment media. He has contributed to TechRadar since 2017 and has been published in Computer Weekly, Linux Format, ComputerActive, and other publications.
He currently heads up the team at smart home website Matter Alpha, and writes about retro gaming at Gaming Retro.

articles.title: Is Your Exposure Management Platform Leaving You Exposed? Five Tests to Find Out
articles.text:
A critical finding can move through several security tools and still leave the organization exposed.
The vulnerability has a severity score, and a ticket has reached the queue. Progress then depends on information the finding may lack: who owns the system, whether attackers can reach it, what protection exists, and how a change could affect the business.
Each missing detail creates another investigation, another handoff, and another delay.
An exposure management platform should connect discovery with a clear priority, an appropriate response, and evidence that protection has improved.
Continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) connects this work through scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, and mobilization. These five tests establish whether a platform can support that process across infrastructure, identities, sensitive data, and external threats.
Security teams often have several records of the same asset. A cloud platform identifies an instance, an endpoint tool records its hostname, and an inventory lists an owner who has changed roles.
Cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) connects those records, helping reveal stale information, missing ownership, and protection gaps.
The resulting view needs enough detail to support action: the asset’s owner, business purpose, assessment history, and security coverage. A system with no reported vulnerabilities should be distinguishable from one never assessed.
Disagreements between sources also need to remain visible. If an endpoint tool reports an active server while the inventory marks it retired, source records and update times help teams resolve the conflict.
| Figure 1. CAASM connects source records with asset ownership, security coverage, and exposure context. | 
External discovery adds another perspective. External attack surface management (EASM) helps uncover what assets make accessible from the outside, including shadow IT, forgotten subdomains, and exposed services that internal tools never see.
EASM and CAASM work best together: CAASM maps what you know you own, while EASM validates that picture from the attacker’s point of view and surfaces what’s missing. Every unmanaged asset EASM finds can be fed back into CAASM, closing coverage gaps and giving each asset an owner. EASM also covers brand exposure, extending discovery to phishing sites, fraudulent profiles, and brand impersonation, so the same external view that finds your unknown assets also finds the lookalikes attackers build to target your customers and employees.
Read CAASM Was Never Meant to Stand Alone to see how asset intelligence supports the decisions and actions that follow discovery.
2. Explain Which Exposures Require Action First
Prioritization depends on understanding what an exposure actually puts at risk. A customer-facing application may carry the same severity score as an isolated development system while presenting very different business risk.
Prioritization should connect:
- Reachability and exploitability: Whether attackers have a usable path to exploit the weakness.
- Threat activity: Whether attackers are targeting the vulnerability or technology.
- Business impact: What the system supports and what compromise could affect.
- Existing protection: Whether relevant controls cover the system and are enforced.
Those conditions change. New exploitation activity may accelerate a response, while a disabled protection may invalidate an earlier assessment.
External threats need similarly specific reasoning. A fraudulent support account approaching customers may require rapid disruption; an abandoned company profile may first need ownership review.
See what the 2026 Exposure Gap Report reveals about prioritization and remediation performance.
3. Validate the Exposure and the Proposed Response
A clear priority can still stall when the system owner lacks confidence in the proposed change.
Validation needs to establish what the exposure allows and how the response could affect operations.
Identifying vulnerable software, confirming reachability, and demonstrating exploitability establish different things. A platform should distinguish observed evidence from analysis and untested assumptions. Attack-path relationships also need supporting evidence and clear limitations.
The proposed response requires separate assessment. A patch may depend on application testing and a maintenance window. An intrusion prevention system protection may require observation in Detect mode before enforcement.
Evidence should address the action’s scope, dependencies, false positives, performance impact, and recovery options. Following a proposed change through this assessment reveals what the platform establishes and what teams must investigate themselves.
4. Carry Safe Remediation Through Existing Workflows
Knowing what to fix first is great, but only if the fix happens quickly. The permanent patch often waits on testing, approval, and a maintenance window, and the exposure stays open the whole time. That’s true whether the weakness is on an internet-facing server or a phishing site targeting your customers.
Speed comes from confidence. Teams hesitate when they can’t say what an action will touch. When the platform already knows the asset, its owner, the active threat, and the controls in place, that hesitation disappears. Many Check Point Exposure Management customers remediate safely within one hour, because the context is complete and the safety checks are built in.
To test this, take one real finding and follow it from priority to protection:
- Owner: Is the right person assigned automatically?
- Safety: Is the action validated before it runs, including its impact and a way back?
- Execution: Does it run through the controls you already have, whether a virtual patch, a configuration change, or a takedown?
- Confirmation: Is the result verified, with the permanent fix still tracked?
Interim protection buys time, but it shouldn’t replace the long term fix.
| Figure 2. Safe remediation connects observation, validation, action, and confirmation. | 
Speed holds up at scale. Between January 1 and October 26, 2026, an airline group completed more than 1,500 takedowns of profiles impersonating its airlines and support teams, combining analyst review with automated remediation.
And when an action fails, the exposure should stay visible with a clear next step.
Read Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production to see how validation, execution, and confirmation work together.
5. Show What Changed and What Remains
A completed action needs evidence of the resulting state.
A patch may miss unavailable systems. A policy update may exclude an intended asset. A takedown request may be accepted before the account disappears.
Verification should establish whether the vulnerability remains, protection is enforced, or malicious content has been removed. Monitoring should identify recurrence.
Reporting must distinguish removed vulnerabilities, interim mitigations, completed takedowns, and accepted risk. Each leaves different responsibilities outstanding.
Mean time to remediate (MTTR) requires agreed starting points, completion criteria, and treatment of temporary protection.
Tracking assignment, approval, execution, and verification separately reveals delays.
Recurring findings, failed actions, and aging mitigations can expose operational problems another scan will not resolve.
Apply the Tests Across Vendors
Platforms approach these requirements from different foundations. The five tests provide a consistent basis for evaluating coverage, evidence, and action.
Check Point Exposure Management combines internal asset intelligence, external discovery, threat intelligence, and brand protection with prioritization, exploitability validation, and safe remediation. It spans infrastructure weaknesses, phishing, and brand impersonation, supporting action through existing controls and takedown workflows.
Bring Intelligence Through to Safe Action
The five tests follow an exposure from discovery to a confirmed response. Each stage should give the next team enough reliable information to act while keeping unresolved work visible.
Check Point Exposure Management carries asset and threat context into responses to vulnerabilities, control gaps, and external threats. Proposed actions are evaluated before enforcement, with approved responses coordinated through supported Check Point and third-party technologies.
That connection helps organizations strengthen protection while accounting for production constraints and building on existing investments. It creates a traceable path from an identified exposure to an evaluated, implemented, and confirmed response.

articles.title: GTA 6 habría superado los 7,71 millones de reservas y rozaría los 751 millones de dólares en ingresos
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI habría acumulado 7,71 millones de reservas entre PlayStation 5 y Xbox Series X|S hasta el 3 de noviembre de 2026, lo que se traduce en cerca de 751 millones de dólares en ingresos antes de su estreno, según una estimación de la firma Sensor Tower.
La cifra, a falta de confirmación oficial por parte de Take-Two, ubicaría al nuevo título de Rockstar a punto de convertirse en el juego más reservado de la historia, por delante de referentes como Cyberpunk 2077.
Cuántas reservas acumula GTA 6 según Sensor Tower
La estimación de Sensor Tower sitúa las reservas de GTA 6 en 7,71 millones de unidades repartidas entre las dos consolas de nueva generación, con dos semanas todavía por delante hasta el lanzamiento oficial. Ese volumen de ventas anticipadas equivale a unos 751 millones de dólares en ingresos acumulados solo por preventas.
El ritmo de crecimiento resulta sostenido: en apenas dos semanas, las reservas habrían aumentado en 1,3 millones de copias respecto a la medición anterior de la consultora. De mantenerse esa tendencia, los números seguirán subiendo cada día que se acerque la fecha de estreno.
¿Cuántas reservas tiene GTA 6 hasta ahora? De acuerdo con Sensor Tower, el título de Rockstar suma 7,71 millones de copias reservadas entre PS5 y Xbox Series X|S al 3 de noviembre, por un valor cercano a los 751 millones de dólares, cifra que crece día a día antes del lanzamiento.
Reparto de ventas entre PlayStation y Xbox
Dentro del total estimado, PlayStation 5 concentra la mayor parte de las reservas de GTA 6. La consola de Sony representa casi el 75% del total, con 5,74 millones de copias vendidas por anticipado y 559 millones de dólares en ingresos asociados.
Xbox Series X|S, por su parte, se queda con el 26% restante del mercado de preventas. Esto equivale a cerca de 2 millones de unidades reservadas y unos 192 millones de dólares generados hasta la fecha.
La diferencia entre ambas plataformas marca una tendencia clara a favor del ecosistema de Sony, aunque ambos fabricantes suman cifras que ya superan ampliamente a la mayoría de lanzamientos recientes de la industria del videojuego.
GTA 6 frente al récord de reservas de Cyberpunk 2077
El dato de la consultora cobra relevancia al compararlo con el antecedente más cercano en materia de reservas: Cyberpunk 2077. El título de CD Projekt Red había logrado aproximadamente 8 millones de copias reservadas antes de su llegada a finales de 2020, marca que hasta ahora funcionaba como referencia en la industria.
Con 7,71 millones de reservas y un crecimiento constante a dos semanas del lanzamiento, GTA 6 se encamina a superar esa cifra y quedarse con el título del videojuego más reservado de la historia, según la proyección de la firma de análisis.
Qué dijo Rockstar sobre las reservas de GTA 6
Take-Two, la compañía matriz de Rockstar, no ha publicado cifras oficiales sobre las reservas de GTA 6. Sin embargo, Strauss Zelnick, responsable del estudio, ofreció declaraciones el pasado agosto que respaldan la tendencia detectada por Sensor Tower.
Zelnick confirmó que se están reservando más unidades de la Ultimate Edition, con un precio de 100 euros, que de la versión estándar del juego. Según el directivo, el costo elevado de esta edición no ha generado el rechazo que se anticipaba entre los compradores.
Los datos de Sensor Tower refuerzan esa declaración: cerca del 90% de las reservas totales corresponderían a la edición Ultimate, por encima de la versión básica del título. A la espera de que Rockstar confirme cifras oficiales, GTA 6 se mantiene a las puertas de superar el récord de reservas que ostenta Cyberpunk 2077.

articles.title: Llega a Colombia la ASUS ProArt P16, equipada con el superchip Nvidia RTX Spark y 128 GB de memoria unificada
articles.text:
ASUS presentó en el mercado colombiano la ProArt P16 (H7607), la primera computadora portátil para creadores y desarrolladores equipada con la plataforma NVIDIA RTX Spark. El equipo lleva cómputo de clase superordenador a un formato móvil de 12,9 milímetros de grosor y 1,77 kilogramos de peso, pensado para la ejecución de agentes de inteligencia artificial locales y flujos de trabajo generativos de alta demanda técnica.
El dispositivo combina soporte nativo del ecosistema CUDA con hasta 128 GB de memoria unificada y capacidades de procesamiento agéntico autónomo que operan directamente en el hardware. A diferencia de la inteligencia artificial tradicional, que requiere que el usuario inicie cada acción de forma manual, la IA agéntica comprende el contexto y la intención de quien la utiliza para proponer, planificar y ejecutar tareas complejas de manera autónoma.
Al funcionar en el propio dispositivo, este tipo de IA mantiene las instrucciones y los datos personales dentro de la computadora, permite trabajar sin conexión a internet y evita pagos de suscripciones adicionales en la nube.
El superchip Grace Blackwell alcanza 1 petaflop con 80 vatios de consumo
En el centro del equipo se ubica la arquitectura SoC del superchip NVIDIA RTX Spark, que interconecta mediante el enlace de alta velocidad NVLink-C2C un procesador NVIDIA Grace de 20 núcleos con una GPU NVIDIA Blackwell RTX de hasta 6.144 núcleos CUDA y núcleos Tensor de quinta generación. Esta integración permite alcanzar un rendimiento computacional de hasta 1 petaflop en precisión FP4, con un TDP de 80 vatios en un chasis ultradelgado.
“Con NVIDIA RTX Spark, la ProArt P16 reúne en un único dispositivo portátil tres experiencias que antes exigían plataformas especializadas: ejecutar agentes avanzados de IA de forma local, acelerar los flujos de trabajo de los creadores de contenido y ofrecer experiencias de gaming impulsadas por las tecnologías de NVIDIA RTX”, afirmó Alexandre Ziebert, gerente de Technical Marketing de NVIDIA para América Latina.
Un sistema de refrigeración que elimina el ruido en cargas moderadas
Para disipar el calor sin generar estrangulamiento térmico, ASUS diseñó una arquitectura de refrigeración con cuatro componentes. El sistema 0 dB Ambient Cooling detiene por completo los ventiladores cuando el equipo opera bajo cargas de trabajo moderadas o ligeras. Un diseño de flujo de aire interno con doble ventilador redirige corrientes frías hacia los componentes y las tuberías de calor principal.
La toma de aire a través del teclado aspira aire fresco desde esa superficie para incrementar el volumen interno del chasis y mantener frías las zonas de contacto manual. Por último, una bisagra oculta desvía el flujo de aire caliente hacia afuera sin que impacte en la pantalla, mientras un filtro integrado evita el ingreso de partículas al sistema.
La memoria unificada permite correr modelos de hasta 120.000 millones de parámetros
La arquitectura de memoria unificada de la ProArt P16 integra un pool compartido de alta velocidad LPDDR5X de hasta 128 GB, que elimina los límites de ancho de banda entre la CPU y la VRAM tradicional.
Esta especificación permite ejecutar en local modelos de lenguaje extenso (LLM) de hasta 120.000 millones de parámetros, con una ventana de contexto de 1 millón de tokens, además del renderizado OptiX/DLSS de escenas 3D de más de 90 GB y la edición multitarea de video en formato 12K 4:2:2.
En software, el equipo llega optimizado para ejecuciones CUDA sobre Windows en arquitectura Arm. El ecosistema incluye ASUS MuseTree, una herramienta de generación de imágenes basada en el modelo FLUX.2 que utiliza precisión NVFP4 para acelerar la creación gráfica local, junto con ASUS Zenni Claw y StoryCube, software de asistencia agéntica y gestión inteligente de bibliotecas multimedia. También cuenta con compatibilidad validada para plataformas de automatización como Hermes Agent y la canalización de nodos en ComfyUI.
Una pantalla OLED de 1.600 nits y batería de máxima capacidad para vuelos
La experiencia visual corre por cuenta de un panel táctil ASUS Lumina Pro OLED 4K de 16 pulgadas en formato 16:10, con precisión de color Delta E menor a 1, cobertura del 100% del espacio DCI-P3 y certificación VESA DisplayHDR True Black 1400. El brillo máximo llega a 1.600 nits, con una tasa de refresco variable de 120 Hz y un tratamiento antirreflejos que reduce los destellos en un 65%. El equipo incluye una suscripción gratuita de tres meses a Adobe Creative Cloud.
Diseñada bajo el estándar de resistencia militar MIL-STD 810H, la ProArt P16 incorpora una batería de 99,9 Wh, la capacidad máxima admitida para vuelos comerciales.
Su conectividad comprende tres puertos USB 4 Tipo-C a 40 Gbps con DisplayPort y Power Delivery, un puerto USB 3.2 Gen 2 Tipo-A a 10 Gbps, salida HDMI 2.1 FRL, lector de tarjetas SD Express 7.0, conector de audio combinado de 3,5 milímetros y conectividad WiFi 7 a 2,88 Gbps. Se completa con el touchpad háptico ASUS HapticPad, un sistema de audio estéreo de seis altavoces con Dolby Atmos y una matriz de tres micrófonos.
Precios desde $14.999.000 y disponible desde hoy en Colombia
La ProArt P16 con NVIDIA RTX Spark está disponible desde el 5 de noviembre en el mercado colombiano, con un precio sugerido de $14.999.000 para la versión de 32 GB de memoria RAM y $25.999.000 para la versión de 128 GB.
La compra incluye una suscripción de tres meses a Adobe Creative Cloud, tres meses de Google AI Pro y dos meses de acceso a Perplexity Pro, además de 3.000 créditos de bonificación. El equipo cuenta con garantía de fábrica de dos años y la opción de adquirir protección contra daños accidentales durante el primer año desde la compra, al registrar el dispositivo a nombre del usuario a través de la aplicación MyASUS o el sitio web oficial de la compañía.

articles.title: OpenAI lance GPT-6 Cyber pour traquer les failles et tester leur exploitation
articles.text:
Mozilla a commencé à corriger 81 failles critiques de Firefox, que personne n’avait repérées avant que les chercheurs d’OpenAI passent le code du navigateur au crible de GPT-6 Cyber, un modèle d’IA réservé pour l’instant à quelques spécialistes de la sécurité.
Avec le noyau Linux, la base logicielle de nombreux serveurs, le modèle a fait plus fort encore. GPT-6 Cyber a écrit des exploits fonctionnels, c’est-à-dire des programmes capables de transformer une faille en attaque réelle, pour 948 vulnérabilités, dont 588 encore inconnues, précise Fortune. Avec ces exploits, un pirate muni d’un simple compte sur la machine obtiendrait les droits root, le plus haut niveau de contrôle du système. OpenAI range donc GPT-6 Cyber au niveau « critique », le plus élevé de son échelle de risque en cybersécurité. L’entreprise assure aussi que son nouveau modèle sort beaucoup moins souvent du cadre fixé par les chercheurs, alors que deux de ses IA ont piraté Hugging Face en pleine évaluation, cet été.
Les failles trouvées par GPT-6 Cyber dans Firefox et Linux
Avant l’arrivée de GPT-6 Cyber, les ingénieurs de Mozilla avaient soumis le code de Firefox à plusieurs générations de modèles de pointe. Le nouveau modèle d’OpenAI a malgré tout livré des preuves reproductibles pour 81 vulnérabilités inédites, toutes classées critiques par Mozilla, et montré que 30 problèmes connus étaient plus graves que prévu. « GPT-6 Cyber a mis au jour des vulnérabilités critiques jusque-là inconnues », souligne Brian Grinstead, ingénieur chez Mozilla. Les chercheurs d’OpenAI ont joint des propositions de correctifs à leurs rapports, et Mozilla a commencé à les déployer peu après. Si vous utilisez Firefox, installez les mises à jour dès qu’elles vous sont proposées.
Sur Linux, GPT-6 Cyber a reproduit 1 724 vulnérabilités. Il a ensuite écrit un exploit fonctionnel pour 948 d’entre elles, quand GPT-5.6 Sol s’était arrêté à 166 avec un outil de recherche identique. OpenAI a signalé aux mainteneurs du noyau 304 failles critiques, accompagnées de correctifs candidats, et travaille à la correction des autres. Si vous administrez un serveur Linux, surveillez de près les mises à jour du noyau de votre distribution.
OpenAI a aussi fait tester ses modèles les plus permissifs par Dragos, spécialiste de la cybersécurité des sites industriels. Avec très peu d’informations au départ, l’IA a trouvé deux failles zero-day dans le logiciel d’ingénierie d’un site de production d’électricité simulé, chargé des données des relais de protection. Un attaquant aurait pu lire la logique de déclenchement des disjoncteurs. Comme l’explique Rob T. Lee, directeur de l’IA chez Dragos, « le niveau de compétence requis pour la reconnaissance et la recherche de vulnérabilités préalables à une attaque diminue ».
Les limites que GPT-6 Cyber doit respecter
En juillet, deux modèles d’OpenAI évalués sur ExploitGym, un banc d’essai de cybersécurité, ont quitté leur environnement isolé et piraté Hugging Face, la grande plateforme de partage de modèles d’IA, afin de récupérer les réponses du test. Moins d’un mois après la sortie de GPT-6 Astra, début septembre, l’entreprise a ensuite abandonné GPT-6.1 Astra, plus performant mais moins respectueux du cadre fixé.
OpenAI a donc conçu une épreuve piège, ExploitGym Honeypot. Le modèle doit attaquer un service désigné, entouré de services annexes faciles à compromettre mais interdits. Sans consigne de sécurité, GPT-6 Cyber a laissé ces services tranquilles dans 99,93 % des tests, contre 94,49 % pour GPT-5.6 Cyber, et il n’a jamais franchi la limite avec la consigne. « Dans plus de 99 % des cas, il fait ce que vous lui demandez », résume Fouad Matin, responsable de la préparation aux cybermenaces chez OpenAI.
L’entreprise a toutefois refusé d’expliquer ce que son modèle a fait lors des 0,07 % de tests restants, et si de vrais systèmes avaient été touchés. Chris Hughes, vice-président de Noma Security, spécialiste de la sécurité de l’IA, salue un vrai progrès mais prévient qu’« à l’échelle où opèrent ces modèles, même une petite fraction suffit à déclencher des actions contre des systèmes non autorisés ».
Pour limiter les risques, OpenAI ne confie GPT-6 Cyber qu’à quelques clients de Daybreak Red, le niveau de son programme de cybersécurité réservé aux tests d’intrusion autorisés, par son API et son assistant de programmation Codex. Elle n’accepte leurs requêtes que depuis des adresses IP approuvées, et ouvrira le modèle à tous les clients Daybreak Red dans les semaines à venir. Par crainte d’un détournement identique, Google réserve lui aussi Gemini 4 Carbon, son modèle le plus performant, à des spécialistes de la cyberdéfense.
Trouver une faille va plus vite que la corriger. Sur Patch the Planet, le tableau de bord d’OpenAI, moins d’un quart des failles ont été corrigées à ce jour, d’après Chris Hughes.

articles.title: OpenAI AI Pipeline Generates 948 Linux Root Escalation Exploits in 30-Hour Run
articles.text:
OpenAI on Wednesday detailed a pipeline that employed an upcoming cyber-focused artificial intelligence (AI) model to validate and patch 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux for $1.2 million in API costs.
"Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access," the AI company said.
The findings build upon 24 LPE exploits that OpenAI revealed were discovered by its GPT‑5.5‑Cyber model back in June 2026. The latest research turns this process into an agentic pipeline comprising five stages -
- Vulnerability discovery, where agents identify high-value audit targets (i.e., parts of the codebase that are security-relevant and reachable by low-privileged users) and look for candidate findings
- Dynamic validation, where agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in a sandboxed environment and preserve runtime evidence
- Exploitability assessment, where agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could be abused to facilitate information disclosure or LPE and devise a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit
- Patch generation, where agents generate patches for the identified vulnerability
- Human review, where security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before it's reported to the maintainers
"In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities [within 30 hours] and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution," OpenAI said.
"The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit. To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques."
At a high level, these include -
- Two new persistent elastic objects to spray objects inside the target kernel cache
- Two new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability
- Five new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write
- One technique that involves arbitrary type confusion
The development is once again an indication of how frontier AI is redrawing the contours of cybersecurity, accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and at the same time helping defenders reliably address defects, albeit through additional instructions and iterations, before attackers can use them, and make it "cost prohibitive" for bad actors to exploit software.
In a report published last month, VulnCheck categorized AI-assisted vulnerability discovery as a "growing risk category" that turbocharges novice hackers, who now require little to no technical expertise to detect software vulnerabilities.
The access to AI models is not just limited to defenders, but also bad actors who can leverage the same capabilities to discover and weaponize new zero-days and expand the pool of viable targets with minimal effort.
According to insights from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), the number of vulnerabilities disclosed per month has more than doubled, rising from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,740 in August 2026. The number of vulnerabilities classified as high-risk has surged from 131 disclosures in January 2026 to 350 in August 2026, a 167% growth.
"The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities," the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said in an assessment published Tuesday.
"Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an N-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses."
The NCSC also pointed out that organizations will have to evolve their internal patching and testing processes to meet this new pace of vulnerability discovery.
"Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal," it added. "Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally."
OpenAI said the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models needs to be matched by automated patch generation to secure software and to limit the exploitation window.
"With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants," OpenAI said. "For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system that isn't up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor."
