articles.title: Qualcomm fecha acordo de infraestrutura 5G com a Starlink • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Qualcomm fecha acordo de infraestrutura 5G com a Starlink
Empresa vai fornecer componentes para implementar tecnologia terrestre do serviço Starlink Mobile nos EUA.
Resumo
- A Qualcomm fechou um acordo com a Starlink para fornecer componentes de infraestrutura 5G nos Estados Unidos.
- A empresa fornecerá hardware e software para implementar a tecnologia terrestre do serviço Starlink Mobile.
- As instalações começarão em 2027 e serão o “maior acordo de 5G” da Qualcomm até hoje.
A Qualcomm fechou uma parceria com a SpaceX para fornecer equipamentos essenciais de infraestrutura 5G do serviço Starlink Mobile nos Estados Unidos. A empresa, mais conhecida pela fabricação dos chips Snapdragon, será a fornecedora de hardware e software para a implementação da futura telefonia de Elon Musk.
As instalações começam já em 2027, no que será o “maior acordo de 5G” da Qualcomm até hoje, segundo a própria empresa. Agora, a fabricante passa a competir com empresas como Broadcom e Intel no mercado de chips voltados para torres de telefonia nos EUA. Além do país, a Qualcomm oferece componentes do tipo para o Japão e Vietnã.
Vale lembrar que a Starlink conseguiu aprovação da FCC, órgão análogo à Anatel nos EUA, para lançar uma constelação de até 15 mil satélites focada na rede mobile nos próximos anos. Por enquanto, a Starlink Mobile opera com 650 satélites na Órbita Baixa da Terra (LEO, na sigla em inglês), em parceria com a T-Mobile.
Qualcomm ajudará Starlink a expandir rede
A parceria com a Qualcomm sinaliza a expansão do serviço planejado pela SpaceX. Com a infraestrutura terrestre em operação, a rede poderá ser distribuída por todo o país, combinando o sinal de satélites e torres de telefonia. A estrutura pode dar à empresa de Elon Musk uma vantagem sobre futuras concorrentes, como AT&T, Verizon e a própria T-Mobile.
Segundo a Qualcomm, seus equipamentos vão permitir uma rede multibanda que pode operar em diferentes fases e ir além da implementação do 5G em terra. A ideia é contar com a tecnologia da empresa para retransmitir as ondas de rádio e o sinal de rede entre usuários do serviço.
Vivo e Starlink têm parceria no Brasil
Se nos EUA a empresa de Elon Musk desenha a expansão do serviço de telefonia, no Brasil há uma parceria recente com a Vivo, uma das principais operadoras do país. O acordo, confirmado em primeira mão pelo Tecnoblog, marca o lançamento do primeiro serviço de telefonia via satélite integrado a uma operadora no mercado brasileiro.
A Starlink já supera provedoras tradicionais de internet banda larga no Brasil. No mês passado, a Anatel revelou que a companhia de Musk registra mais acessos que a italiana TIM, além de ter sido a operadora que mais cresceu no mês de agosto, com 65 mil novas assinaturas.

articles.title: ChatGPT's new Images 2.6 update can bring your photos to life — so naturally I turned my cat into an animated GIF
articles.text:
ChatGPT Images 2.6 is here, and it can turn your photos into animated GIFs — so I tried it on my cat
More cat GIFs is never a bad thing
OpenAI has just released ChatGPT Images 2.6 across all subscription levels, including Free. It’s only a 0.1 upgrade to the previous Images 2.5, so it should come as no surprise that not that much has changed. In fact, there are only two new features, but they’re both worth your attention.
Firstly, you can now use ChatGPT to make animated GIF images, and second, you can now upload a persistent reference image, so you don’t need to keep uploading it when requesting a lot of different edits.
The first change is perhaps the most immediately interesting, but the second one could become more useful in the long run.
More cat GIFs, please
The Internet can never have enough cat GIFs, so naturally I decided to try the new feature on a photo of my cat, Chester. While Halloween has just been and gone, I thought I’d use that as inspiration for the sort of image I wanted to make of my cat. I used a fairly simple prompt: “Can you make a Halloween GIF of my cat to share with family?”
ChatGPT obliged without any objection, and transformed my cat into a feline wearing a Halloween-themed hat and cape and blinking slowly as a pumpkin flickered in the background. It’s especially fun for my family because there’s no way he’d ever let a human dress him up like this.
Once you’ve created your GIF it gives you a shareable link, so you don’t need to host it anywhere if you want to link people to it. Alternatively, you can download it or share it straight to X, LinkedIn and Reddit.
What ChatGPT produced was ok, but it was hardly going to set the Internet on fire, so I followed up with “That's cool, but it's not very active, can you make it more active please? Get creative.”
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
“Now we're talking!”, replied ChatGPT. “Your cat's gone full witch mode — casting a spell with a raised paw, conjuring a floating, glowing pumpkin, then giving a triumphant little meow before licking their lips. A proper bit of Halloween mischief!”
Indeed, the resulting GIF was much better, and Chester's movements looked realistic. I think this shows how important your prompt writing is — don’t be afraid to ask ChatGPT to get creative.
Time and time again
Of course, I might want to produce a GIF of this photo for a different occasion in the future so I asked ChatGPT: “Can you save the original photo as Chester so I can reference it again?”
After thinking for a second, it saved the photo as a reference image called Chester. It made a point that it was saving the original snap, not the Halloween versions, and said “In future chats, you can simply say something like: ‘Create a picture of @Chester dressed as a pirate.’ And I'll be able to use his original appearance without you needing to upload the photo again.”
I tested it with the prompt “Make a GIF of @Chester on the moon” and it provided one of Chester as an astronaut chasing a butterfly. How the butterfly was surviving on the moon, and how Chester was surviving when his ears poked through his space helmet, I don’t know, but I’ll go with it anyway.
Saving a reference image is a genuinely useful new feature. It might not be as flashy as the GIF creation, but I think it’s going to come in handy for the future. Overall I’m pretty happy with the Images 2.6 update. Nothing major has changed, but it’s nice to know I can now create a GIF from an image whenever I want, using ChatGPT’s natural language input method.
The best thing about Images 2.6 is how little effort it takes to get something fun out of it. I didn't need animation software, any technical knowledge or even a particularly clever prompt. All I needed was a picture of my cat and a willingness to let ChatGPT get creative. And now that Chester is saved as a reference image, I suspect this won't be his last starring role.

articles.title: Combined flaws let anyone into Alpine Linux and other distros by typing anything over 256 characters as a password — emergency fixes for OpenSSH and musl-libc issued for millions of systems, patch immediately
articles.text:
Combined flaws let anyone into Alpine Linux and other distros by typing anything over 256 characters as a password — emergency fixes for OpenSSH and musl-libc issued for millions of systems, patch immediately
Meanwhile, the parties involved are playing a game of hot potato with who's fault.
The internet is still reeling from the PHP engine vulnerability and all other security vulnerabilities found over the past few weeks, and we're not done. Today's special is quite spicy: you can get into Alpine, OpenWRT, and other Linux distros without needing a password, thanks to a combined bug with OpenSSH and musl libc. Just randomly type over 256 characters on the password prompt and you'll be let in through the SSHhole.
It works if you set an empty password for system users, which is the default on multiple distros. The bug is present, though not necessarily enabled, across Buildroot, Yocto, and Void Linux. OpenWRT uses Dropbear for authentication by default, but users can install OpenSSH instead.
The largest concern is by far Alpine, though, as it's pretty much the default choice for what could amount to millions of installs across Docker/Kubernetes/Proxmox containers and endless dependencies thereof, servers, cloud VMs, and embedded devices, among many others. Alpine comes with the requisite conditions set and password authentication enabled by default, which is why it needs immediate patching.
Broadly speaking, the vulnerability combination is: OpenSSH, musl, password authentication not explicitly disabled, not using PAM, and the one arbitrary user with a password set, using a SHA-512/256 hash. 
Patch your systems immediately, as per the project's advisory note. Meanwhile, the easiest mitigation is explicitly setting "PasswordAuthentication" to "no" in your OpenSSH configuration file and restarting the service.
While in practice the vast majority of Alpine and similar installs aren't reachable from the internet, any attacker inside a network, including but not limited to corporate setups, home labs, cloud networks, and VPNs, can let themselves in. Likewise, all it takes is one valid user account, not too hard to get in a large enough corporate environment, and then an attacker is inside the network. Scanning and testing the vulnerability is also trivial.
OpenSSH has already published a fix and an advisory post, as did musl author Rich Felker. Both parties seem to believe the other is at fault, but looking from the outside, blame is shared.
If you've ever looked in the /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow files, you may have noticed a single asterisk as a placeholder for the password hash for accounts with no password — meaning "no password should work." The SSHhole website has all the details, but the snafu happens both when musl's crypt() function returns "*" as an error condition instead of a null value as per usual conventions, and then OpenSSH uses it to compare to a password hash, when it shouldn't. An overly long input then triggers the chain of mistakes.

articles.title: J'ai testé le Dyson Purifier Cool PC1, ce purificateur d'air m'a complètement soufflée par son design
articles.text:
| Dimensions (HxLxP) / Poids | 105 x 220 x 220 cm / 4.7 kg | 
| Débit d'air | 1.044 m3/h | 
| Surface couverte | 81 m2 | 
| Technologie de filtre | Charbon, HEPA | 
| Options | Ventilateur | 
| Télécommande | Oui | 
| Minuteur | Oui | 
Avec le Purifier Cool PC1, Dyson propose un appareil hybride conjuguant purification de l'air et ventilation douce. Reprenant le design emblématique sans pales de la marque, ce modèle connecté promet de traquer les polluants, tout en rafraîchissant l’intérieur.
Commercialisé à 399 €, le Dyson Purifier Cool PC1 est un appareil deux-en-un combinant les fonctions de purificateur d'air et de ventilateur. Sur le plan technique, il s'appuie sur la technologie Air Multiplier de la marque pour diffuser le flux d'air sans utiliser de pales apparentes.
Le système de purification repose sur un circuit scellé intégrant un filtre HEPA H13 couplé à un filtre à charbon actif, “une association conçue pour capturer les gaz et 99,97 % des particules fines”, dit le constructeur. Contrairement au récent HushJet HJ10 et son format cylindrique projetant l'air vers le plafond, le PC1 conserve la fameuse silhouette élancée en forme de boucle, qui diffuse l'air plus directement.
Comme toujours chez le fabricant britannique, le soin apporté au design ne passe pas inaperçu. Avec sa silhouette élancée et l'absence de pales apparentes, le Purifier Cool PC1 s'intègre harmonieusement dans n'importe quel intérieur. S'il s'avère plutôt grand, il a le bon goût d'être suffisamment léger pour être manipulé sans peine. Il est ainsi très facile de le déplacer d'une pièce à l’autre, ou même de lui faire grimper plusieurs étages en glissant simplement sa large boucle d'amplification sous le bras. La préhension est sûre et l'appareil se transporte très naturellement.
Sur la machine en elle-même, les commandes physiques sont réduites à leur plus simple expression avec un unique bouton d'alimentation. Pour contrebalancer cette sobriété, la base accueille un bel écran couleur. S'il est de petite taille, il reste parfaitement lisible et affiche en temps réel des informations, telles que la vitesse de ventilation ou le niveau de qualité de l'air ambiant.
La télécommande fournie est toujours aussi bien pensée. Très compacte, elle regroupe l'essentiel des commandes : allumage, réglage des 10 niveaux de puissance, activation du mode Auto, gestion de l'oscillation et direction du flux d'air. Détail toujours aussi pratique et emblématique de la marque, elle vient se fixer magnétiquement sur la partie supérieure de l'anneau, les touches orientées vers le bas pour ne pas dénaturer les lignes épurées de l'appareil.
Pour exploiter le plein potentiel du purificateur, il faut se tourner vers l'app MyDyson. L'appairage en wifi s’effectue alors pas à pas sans la moindre difficulté. L'interface, claire et exhaustive, reprend les commandes de la télécommande tout en offrant un suivi approfondi sous forme de graphiques de la qualité de l'air intérieur. C'est aussi par ce biais que l'on accède à l'état d'usure du filtre et aux options de programmation poussées. Il est possible de définir des plages horaires récurrentes selon les jours de la semaine ou utiliser une minuterie ajustable très précisément par paliers de 5 min.
Enfin, l'entretien au quotidien est un jeu d'enfant. L'absence de pales et de grilles de protection évite l'accumulation fastidieuse de poussière dans des recoins inaccessibles ; un simple coup de chiffon humide suffit pour nettoyer les surfaces de la boucle. Quant au remplacement du système de filtration, il s'opère en un tournemain : les deux demi-cylindres perforés situés à la base se déclipsent d'une simple pression pour donner un accès direct et immédiat au filtre HEPA et au filtre à charbon actif.
Dans notre laboratoire, le Purifier Cool PC1 a révélé un profil atypique. Malgré un débit d'air très impressionnant mesuré à 1044 m³/h, il ne se montre pas le plus expéditif pour assainir la pièce. Lancé à sa vitesse maximale, il lui faut 5 min pour éliminer 50 % des particules fines, et un peu plus de 10 min pour n'en laisser que 20 %.
Sur le mode automatique, le PC1 réduit la pollution de moitié en 4 min 53 s, se faisant là encore distancer par le HushJet et ses 4 min 17 s.
Le PC1 reprend néanmoins de superbes couleurs sur le mode nuit. Sur ce régime discret, il parvient à assainir 50 % de la pièce en 7 min et 58 s. C’est un chouia de plus que le HushJet.
Finalement, on aurait pu penser que le Purifier Cool PC1 serait plus rapide que le HushJet en raison de sa taille, mais dans les faits, il n'en est rien. Le PC1 s'appuie sur un filtre HEPA traditionnel et délivre un flux d'air très directif, pensé avant tout pour rafraîchir un utilisateur ciblé. De son côté, le HushJet profite d'une filtration électrostatique et projette l'air vers le plafond, générant ainsi un brassage circulaire bien plus prompt à assainir le volume total d'une pièce. La conception hybride du PC1 (qui cherche aussi à ventiler) reste donc logiquement légèrement en retrait devant les purificateurs conçus spécifiquement pour traiter de grands espaces à toute vitesse.
Le niveau sonore du Purifier Cool PC1 a été pensé pour s'intégrer sans aucun problème dans n'importe quelle pièce de la maison. Sur son réglage le plus faible ou en mode nuit, le murmure de la ventilation se fait très discret avec seulement 35 dB mesurés par notre sonomètre. Il se fera ainsi totalement oublier dans une chambre à coucher vous réunissant avec Morphée.
En revanche, lorsqu'on sollicite l'appareil à son maximum pour purifier ou ventiler vigoureusement la pièce, le souffle devient logiquement plus présent et atteint 48 dB. Sans être assourdissant, il se révèle un peu plus bruyant que le HushJet HJ10 (46 dB) ou le très silencieux Xiaomi Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 (43 dB).
L'efficacité énergétique est généralement un point fort des appareils dépourvus de fonction de chauffage, et ce modèle confirme la règle. Sa consommation reste extrêmement modérée : en mode nuit, il se contente d'un très léger 3,7 W pour fonctionner
Poussé dans ses retranchements à la vitesse maximale, le PC1 plafonne à 28,7 W. S'il se montre un peu plus gourmand que le HushJet (19,6 W) ou que le modèle de Xiaomi (19,2 W) sur le même exercice, cela reste une consommation tout à fait dérisoire, qui n'aura aucun impact significatif sur votre facture d'électricité à la fin de l'année.
Le Dyson Purifier Cool PC1 s'impose comme un appareil hybride redoutablement élégant, pensé pour s'intégrer dans les pièces de vie sans dénaturer la décoration ni mettre en danger les petites mains grâce à son absence de pales. S'il n'est pas le foudre de guerre espéré à pleine puissance pour purifier une pièce en urgence, il se rattrape par un mode nuit très véloce, une consommation électrique maîtrisée et une app compagnon parmi les meilleures du marché. Un choix de confort, idéal pour maintenir une excellente qualité de l'air au quotidien tout en profitant d'une brise rafraîchissante, à condition de ne pas être trop regardant sur le chronomètre lors des pics de pollution.
Le Dyson PC1 assume son positionnement hybride. S'il s'incline sur la vitesse de purification brute face aux redoutables Dreo Purifier 530S et Xiaomi Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6, il offre en revanche une ventilation directe rafraîchissante. De son côté, le récent Dyson HushJet innove davantage en projetant l'air purifié vers le plafond. Le PC1 conserve toutefois des atouts de taille justifiant son statut premium : un design iconique et sécurisant sans pales, un mode nuit extrêmement véloce et une app experte inégalée.

articles.title: Locaweb adjusts data center capacity planning as demand grows - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Rising demand puts Locaweb’s data center strategy to the test
Growing demand and hardware shortages are forcing service providers to rethink data center capacity planning. For Locaweb Serviços de Internet S/A, a cloud hosting and digital services provider based in Brasil, keeping up with customer needs means anticipating infrastructure requirements earlier and finding alternatives when equipment isn’t readily available.
That pressure is changing how Locaweb approaches infrastructure decisions. The company is working more closely with technology partners, including Dell Technologies Inc., to assess alternative hardware configurations and manage supply challenges without compromising its services, according to Gustavo Gomes Salviano (pictured, right), chief technology officer of Locaweb.
“I think that [growing demand] brings the infrastructure challenge again to the board,” he said. “Now we need to think more quickly and strategically in the infrastructure than we did before.”
Salviano and Diego Puerta (left), Brasil general manager at Dell Technologies Inc., spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier for theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories – Data Centers of the Future interview series, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed capacity planning, supply constraints and the engineering collaboration supporting Locaweb’s growth.
Data center capacity planning starts earlier
Locaweb began as a hosting and email provider for small businesses before expanding into e-commerce, marketplace and financial solutions. That broader portfolio has increased the range of services its infrastructure must support, according to Salviano.
“First of all is to anticipate the demands,” he said. “We anticipate … more than we’ve done before. But the second thing is … we are working with our engineers and our partners’ engineers, like Dell, to think about how can we solve the problem that we’re facing.”
Memory availability is among the concerns shaping those discussions, alongside costs and delivery schedules. Locaweb and Dell have discussed supply challenges since last year, considering how to secure the right configurations in time to meet demand, Salviano explained.
“Sometimes we are re-engineering our [infrastructure] needs [to] solve the problem of the time and the length of the time of the delivery, the supply chain,” he said. “It’s challenging us to think about our partners and how we can change that without taking any functionality from our products and from our customers.”
Connecting infrastructure decisions to business needs
Addressing those supply challenges requires more than ordering equipment earlier. Locaweb also needs to consider alternative configurations that can meet its customers’ requirements without compromising performance. The companies’ longstanding relationship helps inform those technical choices. Dell’s familiarity with Locaweb’s environment lets teams assess alternatives against the performance and capacity its services require, according to Salviano.
“When we talk about our needs, our technical needs, they’ll understand our products,” he said. “They know what runs there.”
Those infrastructure decisions are also becoming more important as Locaweb introduces AI capabilities into its business. The company is developing tools that allow nontechnical users to build solutions for their own operational needs. Those tools are helping employees improve business processes, with IT supporting their efforts, Salviano noted.
For Dell, helping customers establish the foundation for enterprise AI begins with understanding their business objectives, according to Puerta.
“It’s not an IT transformation; it’s a business transformation leveraging IT,” Puerta said. “It must come from the leadership. IT is the enabler because what AI is doing is amplifying the possibilities.”

articles.title: AMD "Medusa Point" With 10-Core, 20-Thread CPU Configuration Surfaces
articles.text:
Thursday, November 5th 2026
AMD "Medusa Point" With 10-Core, 20-Thread CPU Configuration Surfaces
AMD's "Medusa Point" APU has surfaced on Geekbench, showcasing a 10-core, 20-thread configuration divided into two clusters: four "Zen 6" cores and six "Zen 6c" cores. This suggests that AMD will continue its hybrid approach with two different core types. Each core is equipped with 32 KB of L1 instruction cache, 48 KB of L1 data cache, and 1 MB of L2 cache, while all cores share a single 16 MB L3 cache. The sample shows a base frequency of 2.0 GHz, and Geekbench lists the maximum frequency at just 1996 MHz, which is likely a misreading of early silicon rather than its actual boost clock. The instruction set confirms full AVX-512 support, including the AVX512-FP16 and AVX512-VNNI extensions, along with AVX-VNNI. The test system was paired with 64 GB (only 55.58 GB usable) of quad-channel DDR5 memory running at 5,188 MT/s.
"Medusa Point" is rumored to introduce a desktop-exclusive "RDNA 4" into mobile segment with the new "RDNA 4m" variant. Although we initially lack direct comparisons between the two, some instruction set extensions, such as WMMA and SWMMAC instructions, suggest support in the new "GFX1170" GPU, which is expected to be part of the GFX11 generation, also known as "RDNA 3." Currently, this is believed to be an upgraded "RDNA 3" with many RDNA 4 modules, enabling FSR 4 support even on the less powerful "Medusa Point" APU.In terms of performance, the "Medusa Point" sample scored 3,100 points in the single-core test and 18,313 points in the multicore test. Compared to the 16-core Ryzen AI Max+ 395, which averages roughly 2,742 single-core and 27,412 multicore points according to Primate Labs' preliminary data, the 10-core "Medusa Point" leads by about 13% in single-core performance, while trailing in multicore as expected given its lower core count. Since this is an early engineering sample with seemingly locked or misreported clocks, final retail silicon should deliver higher performance once AMD finalizes frequencies and firmware.

articles.title: If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
articles.text:
If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
At TechSparks 2026, the Founder and President of TDK Ventures said Indian deeptech founders should plan for international markets from the start, and use the country’s tough operating conditions to develop capabilities that customers elsewhere would value.
For years, India’s best scientists left for the US. Now they are staying, and more of them are choosing startups over corporate labs. For Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President of TDK Ventures, those two shifts are the biggest changes in Indian deeptech over the past five to 10 years.
“The best talent starts to go into the startups in deeptech, and they try things that they would not have tried 10 years or even five years ago,” Sauvage said in a fireside chat with Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, at TechSparks 2026.
TDK Ventures is the corporate venture capital arm of Japanese electronics company TDK Corporation. Set up in Silicon Valley in 2019, it opened its Bengaluru innovation hub in 2023, its first office outside the US. India is its second largest market by number of investments, Sauvage said.
The ecosystem he is betting on is growing. India is home to more than 4,200 deeptech startups, which raised $2.3 billion in 2025, up 37% from the year before, according to a Nasscom–Zinnov report.
During the session titled ‘Global by design: What Indian deeptech needs to become globally iconic’, he laid out what Indian founders need to get right to build companies that compete globally, from picking a first customer and the right investors to planning for scale before it becomes expensive to do so.
Where India has the right to win
Speaking on investing in SpaceTech, Sauvage named the US, China, and India as the three countries where he would consider investing as a VC. Space is one area where he believes India has a clear advantage, built on decades of institutional investment through the Indian Space Research Organisation. The government’s space promotion agency, IN-SPACe, projects that India’s space economy will grow from $8.4 billion to $44 billion by 2033, raising its share of the global market from 2% to 8%.
TDK Ventures co-led a $20.5 million Series A in Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Ethereal Exploration Guild (The Guild), which is developing a fully reusable medium-lift launch vehicle.
Sauvage also pointed to a shift in AI. The conversation, he said, has moved from tokens and compute to electrons and gigawatts, which means everything involved in delivering power to chips now matters. TDK Ventures invested in C2i Semiconductors, a Bengaluru startup founded in 2024 by former Texas Instruments engineers that builds power management technology for AI data centres. Germany’s Infineon Technologies announced the acquisition of C2i in August 2026 and completed it in October, about two years after the startup was founded.
Beyond individual sectors, Sauvage credited a cultural trait: jugaad, or resourcefulness under constraint.
“Think about the entrepreneurship journey. It means going from an idea with massive constraints and creating something that’s valuable and does a job. That sounds like jugaad to me,” he said.
That resourcefulness shows up in the numbers, he added. Capital efficiency among Indian portfolio companies is world class. “I’m from Europe, but don’t talk about Europe when we think about capital efficiency,” he said.
Let the first market shape the product
When asked what founders building from India for the world should think about first, Sauvage pointed to Exponent Energy. Founded in 2020 by former Ather Energy executives Arun Vinayak and Sanjay Byalal, the company offers 15-minute fast charging. In June 2026, TDK Ventures co-led a Rs 200 crore ($21.1 million) round in Exponent, taking the company’s total funding since 2020 to $65.7 million.
Exponent’s long-term goal was megawatt-scale fast charging for intercity buses. It could not start there. Instead, it began by supplying battery management systems (BMS) to three-wheeler makers, a fragmented market with more than 70 manufacturers at the time.
“There was no way a German startup would convince BMW to take their solution. No way a US startup would convince General Motors to take their BMS solution,” Sauvage said.
India’s fragmented market let Exponent deploy across many manufacturers in Bengaluru and beyond, giving it a base to build from.
Founders need superpowers, and so do their investors
Sauvage described founders as superheroes. Each needs a superpower: something they know or can do that no one else can. That is what draws investors in. But, like any superhero film, there are many battles before the end, and founders need allies.
“You want to make sure that the investors you pick as an entrepreneur bring the right superpower at the right time,” he said.
Corporate VCs can bring a go-to-market channel, an early anchor customer, a hard-to-access supplier, or help reducing scientific risk, depending on who they are. He urged founders to choose investors based on what they add that the cap table does not already have.
For TDK Ventures, that means drawing on TDK’s work in energy, sensing, passive components, and power supplies. Sauvage said electric motorcycle maker Ultraviolette now gets components typically reserved for TDK’s largest customers, while TDK is working with The Guild on future component requirements and roadmaps.
Alongside seeking venture-capital financial returns, he said, TDK Ventures looks for ways TDK’s capabilities, or “superpowers”, can accelerate and de-risk a founder’s journey towards building a globally significant company.
First principles over trade-offs
Sauvage traced several portfolio wins back to first-principles thinking. TDK Ventures invested in AI chip company Groq in 2020. During an interview with founder Jonathan Ross before investing, Sauvage noticed that every answer, from setting company values to hiring, firing, and designing the compiler, came back to first principles.
That approach produced a chip architecture designed around the compiler, which allowed for fully predictable, low-latency inference. Sauvage said he was convinced inference was the future before the ChatGPT moment, when he estimated the market for inference alone at more than $60 billion. In December 2025, NVIDIA signed a non-exclusive licensing deal for Groq’s technology, reportedly worth about $20 billion, and hired Ross and several members of his team.
He applied the same lens to engineering decisions that look like trade-offs. Ultraviolette, he said, uses first-principles engineering to pursue improvements in performance, weight and cost together. The company now sells its bikes in Germany, France, Switzerland, the UK, and other European markets, bringing its products into markets served by established manufacturers such as BMW. Ultraviolette recently raised $85 million in a round led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures.
Patience and impatience at the same time
Deeptech founders, Sauvage said, need both. “Overnight success takes 10 years,” he said, noting that Groq took 10 years and SpaceX took 17. At the same time, founders need urgency and a sense of contribution to society.
Before investing, he looks for four things: a founder with a superpower, a category-defining product, a large enough market, and evidence the company can win one customer and then the next while staying capital-efficient. Markets worth $1 billion to $2 billion can be too small for the venture returns TDK Ventures seeks, he said, because the firm looks for each investment to have the potential to return the entire fund.
He cited SPAN, a Silicon Valley company led by Indian-origin founder Arch Rao. SPAN began by redesigning the home electrical panel, a product largely unchanged for a century.
As AI infrastructure demand surged, SPAN extended its power-management technology into distributed compute through partnerships, which Sauvage said changed the company’s trajectory.
Longer cycles also explain why India needs more corporate investors now, he argued. Using a roughly four-year journey to success in SaaS and fintech as an illustration, Sauvage described an ecosystem that can recycle entrepreneurial experience about 2.5 times a decade, as founders and employees carry what they have learned into new companies. A ten-year deeptech journey allows only one such cycle over the same period. Networks of repeat founders and alumni-founded businesses, like those associated with PayPal and SpaceX, therefore take longer to develop. Corporate investors can help bridge that gap with technical expertise, suppliers and customer relationships.
“I want global companies, corporates, and their corporate VCs to know this is the time to invest in India for deeptech,” he said.
Build for scale before it gets expensive
Sauvage emphasised thinking about scale and international expansion early, because shortcuts taken to win the first market in India can become expensive to reverse later.
When TDK Ventures met Ultraviolette, the team was already deliberate about Europe while focused on winning in India first, with customers riding its bikes as far as the Himalayas.
His advice to founders: find what is specific to India that a global customer would trust. India’s wide temperature range, for example, could favour energy storage that performs across extremes, such as sodium-ion or thermal batteries.
“Try to think about what makes you being in India a proof point that because you’re successful in India, you will win everywhere,” he said.
For Sauvage, India’s deeptech opportunity rests on more than talent. The founders most likely to build iconic companies are those who treat India as a starting point rather than a boundary, pick investors who fill specific gaps, and design for international markets before shortcuts become costly to undo. It is a long game that demands patience and impatience at once, and in his view, the moment for global capital to back it in India has arrived.

articles.title: Prévu pour durer 2 ans, il en aura tenu 22 : le télescope Swift de la NASA s’est désintégré dans l’atmosphère
articles.text:
Le télescope spatial Swift de la NASA a effectué sa rentrée atmosphérique mercredi 4 novembre à 13 h 39, heure de Paris, au-dessus du nord de l’île de Sumatra, en Indonésie, où il était alors 19 h 39. L’agence spatiale américaine l’a confirmé à partir des données de suivi de l’US Space Force. Le satellite d’environ 1 450 kg est retombé pile au milieu de la fenêtre de deux heures que l’armée américaine avait annoncée le matin même.
 Space-Track has confirmed that Swift has reentered Earth’s atmosphere on November 4, 12:39 UTC ± 1 min and has been registered as decayed.
See more details here: https://t.co/pRkdzNQUSj https://t.co/UXeSaVwdwo
— The Aerospace Corporation (@AerospaceCorp) November 4, 2026
« La NASA s’attendait à ce que la majeure partie du vaisseau se consume lors de son passage dans l’atmosphère, mais certains composants pourraient avoir survécu à la rentrée », précise l’agence. Avant la chute, elle évaluait à environ une chance sur 2 100 le risque qu’une personne soit blessée par un débris quelque part sur Terre, un niveau plus élevé que le seuil d’une chance sur 10 000 retenu par les règles américaines de limitation des débris spatiaux, mais qui reste faible. Comme l’orbite de Swift était peu inclinée, les éventuels fragments ne pouvaient retomber qu’entre 20,6 degrés de latitude sud et 20,6 degrés de latitude nord. Aucune victime n’a été signalée et aucun débris retrouvé au sol n’avait été rapporté jeudi.
Un sauvetage inédit qui a tourné court
Swift ne disposait d’aucun système de propulsion pour corriger son orbite. Pendant le maximum solaire, l’activité du Soleil a dilaté la haute atmosphère et augmenté le freinage du télescope, accélérant sa chute bien plus vite que prévu. Pour tenter de le sauver, la NASA avait signé un contrat de 30 millions de dollars avec la start-up Katalyst Space, dont le vaisseau robotique LINK a décollé le 3 juillet pour agripper Swift et le remonter sur une orbite plus haute. Fin juillet, LINK a perdu le contrôle de son orientation après la panne de deux de ses roues de réaction, et la NASA a abandonné l’opération le 19 août. « Dès le départ, c’était une mission à haut risque et à fort potentiel », a rappelé Shawn Domagal-Goldman, directeur de la division astrophysique de la NASA, cité par Aerospace Corporation.
Le télescope a malgré tout repris ses observations pendant quelques semaines. Le 20 octobre, descendu à 275 km d’altitude, il ne parvenait plus à compenser le freinage de l’atmosphère et a basculé en mode de sécurité. L’équipe de l’université d’État de Pennsylvanie, qui l’exploitait, a alors mis fin à ses opérations selon la NASA.
Une mission de deux ans qui en aura duré vingt-deux
Lancé le 20 novembre 2004 depuis Cap Canaveral, Swift devait à l’origine fonctionner deux ans pour étudier les sursauts gamma, les explosions les plus puissantes connues dans l’Univers. Sa force tenait à sa réactivité : il pouvait pointer ses télescopes vers une explosion fugace en une minute environ et alerter les observatoires du monde entier pour qu’ils prennent le relais.
En près de 22 ans, il a observé plus de 2 000 sursauts gamma et plus de 1 400 supernovae, et ses données ont nourri environ 7 000 publications scientifiques, selon la NASA. L’agence le décrit comme un « outil polyvalent pour explorer l’Univers », qui a aussi permis d’étudier des galaxies alimentées par des trous noirs supermassifs, des comètes ou des astéroïdes du système solaire. Sa construction, son lancement et son exploitation auraient coûté au total environ 500 millions de dollars en tenant compte de l’inflation.

articles.title: La France teste un robot maçon capable de construire 60 m² de mur en une journée : il pourrait arriver sur les chantiers en 2027
articles.text:
La France teste un robot maçon capable de construire 60 m² de mur en une journée : il pourrait arriver sur les chantiers en 2027
Fin octobre, près de Paris, Bouygues Construction a mis au travail le WLTR, un robot qui monte des murs de briques sans échafaudage. La machine a déjà tourné sur une centaine de chantiers en Europe et doit arriver sur ses premiers projets français début 2027. Elle soulagera les équipes, sans régler à elle seule le manque de maçons.
Sur une base mobile verte, un bras articulé saisit un bloc de terre cuite, l'enduit de deux cordons de colle et le pose au millimètre près, avant de repartir chercher le suivant. Du 26 au 30 octobre 2026, la scène s'est répétée à Chilly-Mazarin (Essonne) sur Scale One. Bouygues Construction a inauguré le 6 octobre cette plateforme d'essais de 2500 m², où le géant du BTP teste en conditions réelles robots, matériaux et procédés avant de les envoyer sur ses chantiers. Le maçon robotisé y partage l'espace avec un humanoïde, un chien-robot de surveillance et une imprimante 3D à béton. Drôle de voisinage…
A robot bricklayer named WLTR could soon be the solution to the UK's bricklayer shortage. It matches the output of five bricklayers and one laborer per hour, and is operated by just one person pic.twitter.com/wsrl3KPRds
— Reuters Tech News (@ReutersTech) May 19, 2026
Robot WLTR : une cadence théorique de 60 m² par jour
Le WLTR, surnommé Walter, pèse 2,5 t et vient de République tchèque. Le briquetier Wienerberger a conçu les blocs, KM Robotics et GreenBuild se sont chargés de la machine. L'opérateur charge les plans sur une tablette et un laser à lignes croisées donne l'alignement, puis le robot monte la paroi jusqu'à 3,50 m sans échafaudage. Les briques Porotherm “Robot-Ready” ont des encoches latérales où vient se loger la pince, et on les assemble à la mousse adhésive Dryfix ou au mortier-colle à joint mince.
Côté cadence, la fiche technique annonce 7,5 m² par heure en moyenne, avec des pointes à 10 m². Les 60 m² par jour qui circulent sortent de là : un chiffre théorique, calculé sur 8 h parce que les droits syndicaux des robots, pourquoi pas ? Selon Wienerberger, une douzaine de machines tournent déjà et ont monté plus de 55 000 m² de murs sur plus de 100 projets, de la Tchéquie au Royaume-Uni. Chez Bouygues Bâtiment Industrie, Philippe Robinaud a annoncé un premier déploiement sur des projets pilotes au premier trimestre 2027.
BTP : la robotique face à une profession qui ne trouve plus de relève
Les maçons manquent partout en Europe. En France, le métier revient chaque année parmi les plus difficiles à recruter dans l'enquête Besoins en main-d’œuvre de France Travail, et il vieillit sans que les jeunes s'y pressent, rebutés par les charges lourdes et les mêmes gestes répétés dehors, quel que soit le temps.
	
La machine créerait même des postes qualifiés, puisqu'il faut toujours des opérateurs pour la superviser
Au Royaume-Uni, où le robot a bâti en 2025 un lotissement de 27 maisons à Durham, le promoteur Jan Telensky ne tourne pas autour du pot : “Il n'entre tout simplement pas assez de maçons dans le métier.” D'après lui, la machine créerait même des postes qualifiés, puisqu'il faut toujours des opérateurs pour la superviser. Elle prend surtout en charge le plus pénible. Elle soulève des blocs jusqu'à 90 kg, et avec l'échafaudage disparaissent les risques de chute. Le maçon devient dès lors pilote. Deux personnes suffisent : un opérateur, plus un assistant qui alimente les palettes.
Productivité du robot maçon : des promesses à relativiser
Combien de maçons remplace-t-il ? Cela dépend beaucoup de qui répond. Auprès de Reuters, Jan Telensky parlait de cinq maçons et un aide. Le fabricant GreenBuild évoquait jusqu'à 200 m² par jour. Le groupe autrichien PORR, lui, a constaté sur un chantier tchèque une productivité parfois comparable à celle d'un seul maçon expérimenté. Les chantiers publiés tournent plutôt entre 5 et 7 m² par heure. On est donc loin des 200 m².
Le WLTR est à son aise sur les murs longs et droits, percés de peu d'ouvertures. Attention, il ne pose pas le premier rang ; cette assise de départ, les maçons la règlent à la main, au mortier hydrofugé et au laser, car la machine ne rattrape pas les défauts de la dalle. Il lui faut aussi ses briques dédiées, et les colles ont leurs exigences, puisque les avis techniques imposent de poser à 5 °C minimum, sans pluie ni gel. Des travaux visent à adapter sa pince au béton cellulaire et aux blocs de béton, ce qui lui ouvrirait bien plus de chantiers.
D'ici là, Walter reste un équipier de plus sur les bâtiments qui s'y prêtent, pas un remplaçant. Encore faut-il former ceux qui le pilotent.

articles.title: SpaceX no convenció a las operadoras con la telefonía de Starlink, así que Elon Musk se está creando su propia operadora móvil
articles.text:
Durante los últimos meses, Elon Musk ha estado llamando a la puerta de las grandes operadoras de EEUU. Su oferta era sencilla: usar sus redes de telefonía para ofrecer un servicio de telefonía móvil vía satélite con Starlink. Todas le dijeron que no. Cualquiera se habría rendido. Pero Musk ha hecho lo que solo Musk es capaz de hacer: montarse su propia operadora y hacerles la competencia a quienes le dieron con la puerta en las narices.
En pocas semanas ha comprado frecuencias, ha hablado con los dueños de las antenas y ha fichado a un proveedor de tecnología 5G para poner en marcha la red de telefonía por satélite que otros no quisieron montar.
El portazo de las telecos. El rechazo más claro llegó con los resultados del tercer trimestre. El consejero delegado de T-Mobile, Srini Gopalan, descartó cualquier acuerdo de operador móvil virtual (OMV) con SpaceX. Este tipo de acuerdos de OMV consiste en alquilar la red de otro operador y vender el servicio bajo su propia marca, por lo que Starlink se convertiría en un operador virtual con servicios de conectividad por satélite.
Gopalan aseguraba que "el satélite es una versión inferior del FWA con aún más limitaciones, como el tamaño del haz". El FWA (Fixed Wireless Access) es un modo de acceso a internet fijo mediante red móvil lo cual contribuiría a expandir la oferta actual de Starlink. Dan Schulman, de Verizon, fue igual de tajante asegurando que "no veo absolutamente ningún beneficio" en ofrecer una plataforma OMV a un proveedor de comunicaciones por satélite.
Si no te dejan la red, compras las frecuencias. Con la negativa de las telecos a darle acceso a sus redes de telefonía, Musk fue a por el recurso más escaso: el espectro. SpaceX pagó a EchoStar unos 17.000 millones de dólares entre efectivo y acciones. El paquete incluía frecuencias en la banda de 2 GHz, pensadas para hablar con móviles desde el espacio.
En octubre llegó la segunda pieza clave de la estrategia que estaba construyendo Musk. SpaceX acordó comprar a Grain Management hasta 14 MHz emparejados en la banda de 800 MHz. Son ondas bajas, que atraviesan paredes y llegan al interior de los edificios. Según SpaceX, con esas bandas Starlink Mobile podría ser "el primer operador de red en desplegar espectro satelital y terrestre". La Comisión Federal de Comunicaciones (FCC) de EEUU aún debe aprobar la operación.
Torres y chips para la red de tierra. No obstante, pese a que SpaceX ya tiene los satélites y la capacidad de enviar las señales de telefonía, todavía necesita algo fundamental: las antenas para distribuir esa señal. Bloomberg adelantó que SpaceX buscaba acceso a, al menos, 80.000 antenas en EEUU. Según la Wireless Infrastructure Association, serían la mitad de las 158.500 torres que había el año pasado.
Para equipar esos sitios, SpaceX acaba de firmar una alianza con Qualcomm por la que el fabricante suministrará sus plataformas Dragonwing para decenas de miles de estaciones base terrestres de Starlink Mobile, con despliegue a partir de 2027.
Boost Mobile, o cómo comprar clientes. Teniendo satélites, espectro de frecuencias, antenas y la tecnología necesaria para construir su red de telefonía, a Musk solo le faltaba una cosa: clientes que paguen las facturas. The Washington Post informó de que SpaceX estaba negociando la compra de Boost Mobile, que sería la puerta de entrada a un mercado de la telefonía valorado en 235.000 millones de dólares Si todo le sale bien, Musk controlará la cadena entera: satélites, red terrestre y tienda.
Lo paradójico es que pocas telecos pueden decir lo mismo, porque las operadoras no tienen satélites propios. En Europa, Telefónica, Orange y Vodafone se unieron contra Starlink y, como detallaba Forbes, aún no han elegido socio espacial. Los operadores virtuales, en cambio, dependen de una red ajena, justo lo que a Musk le habían negado niegan y ahora va a construir por su cuenta.

articles.title: Le Bluetooth passe à 7,5 Mbit/s : ce que ça va changer pour vos casques et écouteurs
articles.text:
Le Bluetooth franchit une nouvelle étape avec l'adoption officielle du High Data Throughput (HDT), une technologie capable d'atteindre 7,5 Mbit/s. De quoi ouvrir la voie à un standard commun pour l'audio sans perte et haute résolution. Mais les premiers appareils compatibles ne sont pas encore là.
Ce mercredi 4 novembre, le Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG), l'organisme chargé de faire évoluer la norme, a officialisé l'adoption du High Data Throughput, ou HDT. Une évolution qui doit permettre aux futurs appareils Bluetooth de transmettre davantage de données, avec des perspectives particulièrement intéressantes pour l'audio sans fil.
Nous évoquions déjà cette technologie mi-octobre, lorsque le Bluetooth SIG avait présenté son calendrier au Japon. Cette fois, le HDT est officiellement intégré à la spécification Bluetooth Core 7.0, même si sa prise en charge reste facultative pour les fabricants.
Jusqu'à 7,5 Mbit/s, et de nouvelles possibilités pour l'audio
Pour résumer, le HDT introduit une nouvelle couche physique de transmission pour le Bluetooth Low Energy (LE). Il promet un débit maximal de 7,5 Mbit/s, contre 2 Mbit/s avec le mode actuel. Un débit près de quatre fois supérieur donc, même si la comparaison ne vaut que pour le LE : le Bluetooth Classic, sur lequel reposent notamment LDAC et aptX, atteint déjà 3 Mbit/s bruts.
Pour comprendre l'intérêt de cette évolution, un flux audio stéréo de qualité CD non compressé représente environ 1,4 Mbit/s, contre 4,6 Mbit/s en 24 bits/96 kHz. Le HDT pourrait donc ouvrir de nouvelles possibilités pour l'audio sans perte et haute résolution, sans dépendre des solutions propriétaires actuelles.
Le Bluetooth SIG met également en avant une meilleure efficacité énergétique : en transférant davantage de données en moins de temps, la radio pourrait rester moins longtemps active et réduire sa consommation.
Attention toutefois : les 7,5 Mbit/s représentent un débit maximal de transmission, pas un débit audio garanti. Le HDT prévoit cinq paliers, à 2, 3, 4, 6 et 7,5 Mbit/s, permettant d'adapter la connexion aux conditions radio. Les deux modes les plus rapides sont même facultatifs pour les fabricants. À 4 Mbit/s, par exemple, un flux stéréo 24 bits/96 kHz non compressé ne pourrait pas être transmis tel quel. Le choix du codec restera donc déterminant.
Pas de mise à jour miracle pour les appareils actuels
Si la technologie est désormais adoptée, le standard audio qui doit en tirer parti reste attendu en 2027. Il faudra donc patienter avant de voir arriver les premiers casques, écouteurs et smartphones capables de l'exploiter pleinement.
Le HDT nécessite par ailleurs des composants compatibles aux deux extrémités de la connexion. Les appareils actuels ne devraient donc pas pouvoir en profiter par une simple mise à jour logicielle. Et puisque cette fonction est facultative, la mention Bluetooth Core 7.0 ne suffira pas à garantir sa présence.
Les bénéfices pourraient également dépasser l'audio. Le Bluetooth SIG évoque les applications de réalité étendue, les appareils intégrant de l'IA et les objets connectés. Le fabricant de puces Nordic Semiconductor imagine notamment des montres capables de synchroniser leurs données beaucoup plus rapidement ou des lunettes intelligentes échangeant davantage d'informations avec un smartphone.
L'étape technique est donc franchie, mais pour le moment difficile de dire combien de fabricants adopteront réellement le HDT et jusqu'à quel débit leurs appareils pourront monter.

articles.title: Menos gasto en inteligencia artificial: la medida de Apple para controlar sus costos internos
articles.text:
Apple está reduciendo el presupuesto que algunos de sus empleados pueden destinar al uso de herramientas de inteligencia artificial, en una estrategia para controlar sus gastos operativos. La compañía bajó el límite diario para determinados ingenieros de 300 a 200 dólares y evalúa nuevas restricciones que podrían dejar las asignaciones en apenas 100 dólares por jornada.
La decisión contrasta con los esfuerzos de la empresa por incorporar la inteligencia artificial en sus procesos de desarrollo de software y otras actividades internas. Aunque Apple busca que sus trabajadores utilicen estos sistemas para mejorar su productividad, también intenta evitar que el costo de los modelos más avanzados se convierta en un gasto difícil de sostener.
Según fuentes consultadas por Bloomberg, que solicitaron mantener el anonimato por tratarse de conversaciones internas, los nuevos recortes afectarían a determinados equipos de ingeniería. Otros departamentos ya tienen límites diarios de 100 dólares y la compañía habría considerado reducir algunas asignaciones hasta los 25 dólares.
Los empleados que necesiten un presupuesto superior para cumplir con sus responsabilidades podrán solicitar una excepción a los directivos de la empresa.
Por qué Apple está reduciendo el presupuesto para usar IA
Las asignaciones económicas que Apple entrega a sus trabajadores cubren el consumo de tokens, unidades de texto y otros datos que los modelos de inteligencia artificial procesan para responder a las solicitudes de los usuarios.
Los proveedores de estos servicios suelen cobrar según la cantidad de tokens utilizados. Por eso, las tareas que requieren un procesamiento más complejo pueden elevar considerablemente los costos. Entre ellas se encuentran la generación de código, la revisión de programas y la detección de errores durante el desarrollo de software.
Además, los modelos más avanzados suelen tener tarifas superiores a las de las versiones más económicas. Esto significa que un empleado que utiliza inteligencia artificial de manera intensiva puede consumir rápidamente el presupuesto asignado por la compañía.
Apple busca que sus trabajadores incorporen estas herramientas a sus actividades cotidianas, pero pretende que lo hagan con un mayor control sobre los recursos utilizados. Algunas divisiones están recibiendo indicaciones para recurrir a modelos menos costosos o utilizar sistemas de inteligencia artificial que funcionan directamente en los dispositivos, sin depender tanto de servicios externos.
Apple aumenta sus gastos en inteligencia artificial
La reducción de los presupuestos individuales se produce mientras Apple incrementa sus inversiones en investigación y desarrollo. Durante el ejercicio fiscal 2026, la compañía registró un aumento del 32% en este apartado, impulsado principalmente por los mayores costos de infraestructura y tecnología vinculada con la inteligencia artificial.
Los gastos operativos de la empresa también crecieron un 22% y alcanzaron los 75.500 millones de dólares, equivalentes al 16% de sus ventas netas totales.
Estas cifras muestran el desafío que enfrenta la compañía: necesita invertir en nuevas tecnologías para competir en el mercado de la inteligencia artificial, pero al mismo tiempo debe controlar los recursos que utiliza para desarrollar sus productos y modernizar sus operaciones.
Los empleados de Apple tienen acceso a diferentes plataformas, entre ellas Claude, de Anthropic; ChatGPT, de OpenAI; y Gemini, de Google. La variedad de servicios disponibles permite elegir herramientas según las necesidades de cada equipo, aunque también implica administrar distintos costos de utilización.
Otras tecnológicas también controlan el gasto en IA
Apple no es la única compañía que comenzó a limitar el dinero destinado al uso de inteligencia artificial por parte de sus empleados.
Microsoft también estableció restricciones sobre los presupuestos internos para estas herramientas. Tesla fijó un límite semanal de 200 dólares, mientras que Uber estableció asignaciones mensuales de hasta 1.500 dólares para determinadas herramientas de programación asistida por IA.
Meta, por su parte, implementó presupuestos de consumo y promueve el uso de sistemas desarrollados dentro de la propia empresa.
El movimiento refleja un cambio en la industria tecnológica. Después de una primera etapa en la que las compañías impulsaron la experimentación con inteligencia artificial, ahora buscan medir cuánto cuesta realmente incorporarla a sus operaciones y qué beneficios concretos aporta.
En el caso de Apple, todavía no está claro cuánto dinero permitirá ahorrar la reducción de los presupuestos. El resultado dependerá de los nuevos límites y de cuánto utilicen estas herramientas los empleados que necesitan modelos avanzados para realizar sus tareas.

articles.title: Android permitirá backup automático de fotos e vídeos no Windows • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Android permitirá backup automático de fotos e vídeos no Windows
Novidade do Android usará a ferramenta Quick Share para permitir que fotos e vídeos sejam enviados automaticamente para o Windows.
Quando o assunto é backup de fotos, normalmente pensamos em serviços nas nuvens, como o Google Drive, o OneDrive e o Dropbox. Mas usuários do Android poderão ter, em breve, a opção de transferir fotos e vídeos automaticamente de seu celular ou tablet para um computador com Windows.
Ainda não há um anúncio oficial a respeito. A novidade foi descoberta por veículos como o Android Authority nas notas de lançamento do sistema operacional para novembro de 2026, no tópico que aborda o Google Play Services versão 26.43.
Mesmo sendo curta, a nota deixa claro que o backup envolverá o Quick Share, ferramenta que já permite compartilhamento de arquivos entre dispositivos Android e PCs. Mas esse compartilhamento é manual. O recurso que o Google está preparando envia fotos e vídeos do Android de modo automático para o computador. Ao que tudo indica, arquivos de áudio também poderão ser enviados.
Os detalhes sobre como o backup automático funcionará ainda não foram revelados pelo Google, mas uma análise feita pelo Android Authority em abril, quando o recurso foi descoberto, indica que a configuração começa pelo Quick Share instalado no Windows, requer que o celular ou tablet esteja fisicamente próximo para o “pareamento” e exige o uso de uma Conta Google.
Ainda não há previsão para a disponibilidade geral, muito menos uma lista de aparelhos compatíveis. Mas, como o recurso foi mencionado em notas de lançamento recentes do Android, é de se presumir que a sua chegada oficial ocorrerá em um futuro próximo, embora de modo progressivo — há boas chances de que comece pelos celulares Google Pixel.
Se faz sentido? Bom, backup local ainda é backup. Pelo menos para quem tem um HD ou SSD específico para esse fim, um recurso que automatiza o backup do conteúdo gerado no celular certamente será bem-vindo. Essa também é uma forma de ter acesso rápido às suas fotos e vídeos, é claro.

articles.title: Scientists report on 'extremely rare reoccurring perturbations' caused by the Artemis II rocket — and they could have broken GPS
articles.text:
NASA's Artemis II rocket tore 5,000km holes in the atmosphere — causing GPS disruptions powerful enough to force self-driving cars to 'change lanes'
Something to keep an eye on
- Researchers report on 3 huge 'perturbations' caused by Artemis II
- The rips in the ionosphere could affect GPS systems
- Further study is needed to assess the impact of the rocket launch
The April 2026 Artemis II mission marked the first time humans have been in lunar space since 1972, and scientists are still picking through the masses of data collected along the way. New research set to be published in Geophysical Research Letters has now revealed some unprecedented tears the rocket launch ripped in our upper atmosphere.
Known as the ionosphere, this layer is bombarded with solar radiation, causing it to be packed with free electrons and positively charged ions — a mix which means it has a strong influence on radio waves, such as signals sent by Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) satellites, including the Global Positioning System (GPS).
The study team found that Artemis II triggered three separate disturbances in the ionosphere, all directly above North America, and measuring more than 5,000 kilometers (3,106 miles) in size. These pulse waves were caused by the initial rocket launch, and then by upper-stage orbital engines firing directly in the upper atmosphere.
It's a more powerful barrage of atmospheric disruption than we've seen from any previous rocket launch, including those launched by SpaceX, and it gives scientists important context on human-made 'space weather' — disturbances in the atmosphere that have the potential to interfere with ground infrastructure.
GPS disruption on the ground
While it's worth noting that this study didn't directly measure any disruption in GNSS or GPS systems — it's something the team hopes to follow up on later — the sort of disturbances recorded here have the potential to cause significant, if temporary, shifts in our navigation systems.
"A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes," study author and earth scientist Charles Lin, from National Cheng Kung University, in Taiwan, told Space.com. "It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."
"Though space launches often induce ionosphere disturbances, the Artemis-II Lunar mission for the first time produced extremely rare reoccurring perturbations over the same geographic region on three different occasions," write the researchers, while also suggesting it "will be essential to assess" future impacts from rockets on the ionosphere.

The impact of the ionosphere disruptions on GPS and GNSS are what the researchers are planning to look at next, including to what degree errors might have been introduced, and how long they lasted for. The results are likely to be vital in planning future rocket launches and maneuvers.

articles.title: Weathsimple touts AI banking as feds aim to end bank switching fees
articles.text:
It’s been a wild day in the finance world so far, but there’s some positive news out there, too. Wealthsimple has been busy, unveiling new AI, trading, and banking features, while CEO Michael Katchen said the federal government could ban fees for switching financial institutions.
To start, Wealthsimple revealed a dozen new features at its Wealthsimple Presents: Something Good Is Going To Happen (ironic name, all things considered) product showcase. These include Penny, an AI assistant that can handle everyday money and trading tasks; a faster, fully customizable app experience; and advanced tools for active traders.
AI banking assistant
Wealthsimple says that Penny can assist with everyday financial tasks like sending e-transfers and wires, providing spending insights, and flagging duplicate credit card charges. It can also manage expenses and pay invoices. For more self-directed investors, Penny can also help buy and sell stocks, ETFs, and other asset classes. Interestingly, Wealthsimple notes that Penny can understand broader prompts and take action on them.
For example, you could tell it to “Max out my RRSP by March” — and it will map out next steps like checking with securely connected financial institutions, setting up recurring investments, and adapting if a client’s situation changes.
Alongside this, Canadians will also be able to securely connect their Claude or ChatGPT accounts to their Wealthsimple accounts, select the level of access, and critical accounts will receive an extra check. This will be available in early 2027.
Here are some of the other features that Wealthsimple announced:
- Wealthsimple Pay: Instantly send up to $100,000 to other Wealthsimple users (available now)
- Temporary virtual cards: A first for Canadian consumers—the new temporary virtual cards will be available to all Wealthsimple prepaid card and credit card holders. A user can hold up to five cards at a time, and each has unique details, a custom expiry, and a spending limit (available end of 2026).
- Wealthsimple’s Business credit card: Any business can apply for the credit card with no FX fees and 1 per cent cashback on all purchases (available early 2027).
- WealthSimple Pro: serious traders can now consolidate all of their trading to Wealthsimple, bringing positions, watchlists, and level 2 market data into the app (available late November).
- Even faster trading: Mobile trades now take two steps instead of eight, and four seconds instead of 21.
It soon won’t cost you to switch banks
According to a post on X from Wealthsimple CEO Michael Katchen, the federal government is moving closer to banning exit fees.
This year alone, Canadians have been charged $73 million in exit fees to move their savings to Wealthsimple.
Today the federal government moved to ban these fees at federally regulated banks, an important first step toward fulfilling the promise made in Budget 2025 to ban investment and registered account transfer fees.
Thank you @FP_Champagne for your leadership. Now it’s time for provincial governments and the rest of the financial industry to follow.
Wealthsimple has never charged an exit fee. We earn the privilege of managing our clients’ money by giving them reasons to stay, not charging them to leave.
Every financial institution in Canada could decide today to end this tax on choice. You don’t need regulation to do the right thing.
https://t.co/yCXfGwWcYy
— Michael Katchen (@mkatchen) November 4, 2026
Interestingly, Katchen said that its customers have been charged $73 million to move their savings over to Wealthsimple.
Katchen says this is an “important step” toward fulfilling a promise made in Budget 2025 to ban investment and registered account transfer fees.
According to a federal government review of bank transfer fees, the average fee to transfer your account to a different institution ranges from $50 to $150 per account, with partial transfers costing between $25 and $75.

articles.title: India targets creating homegrown GPUs within 2 years and plans to commercialize indigenous SHAKTI and VEGA RISC-V processors — sees AI boom as a potential repeat of the Y2K opportunity for its IT industry
articles.text:
India targets creating homegrown GPUs within 2 years and plans to commercialize indigenous SHAKTI and VEGA RISC-V processors — sees AI boom as a potential repeat of the Y2K opportunity for its IT industry
India targets a homegrown GPU within 24 months as it expands its chip industry and AI ambitions
India wants to develop its own graphics processing unit (GPU) within the next two years as the country steps up efforts to build a domestic semiconductor industry and reduce its dependence on foreign chip suppliers, reports ETGovernment. The target was outlined by S.Krishnan, secretary of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), in a November 4 interview. "Under India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, we intend to target the development of an indigenous GPU chip. We should have a GPU chip of our own. This will not happen overnight. It is a project that will require approximately 24 months, and we intend to work towards that objective," Krishnan said.
The proposed GPU is part of a wider plan to establish an Indian hardware and software ecosystem, with Krishnan describing five layers needed to support AI development. These include: energy, accelerator chips, computing infrastructure and servers, AI models and applications. Indian companies such as VVDN, Kaynes and Avalon are already manufacturing servers, while the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) has developed its Rudra server range, whose systems are designed to support AI workloads, after which the government transfers the technology to local manufacturers. Krishnan also sees AI as a potential repeat of the opportunity India's IT industry experienced during the Y2K (the year 2000 bug) transition. "AI could create a similar opportunity, although the nature of the work will be different," he said.
The comparison is big for a country whose IT-enabled service sector employs about 6 million people. A NITI Aayog paper estimates that roughly two million existing jobs could become redundant as AI adoption changes the industry, but around 4 million more jobs could emerge. Krishnan argues that Indian companies could benefit from helping businesses worldwide integrate into their AI operations, just as they benefited from the demand for software services around the turn of the century.
The country has already attracted major interest with ASML, partnering with Tata Electronics to equip India's first commercial semiconductor fabrication facility in Dholera, Gujarat. The planned facility is expected to use 300mm wafers and eventually reach a capacity of 50,000 wafers per month. Intel also announced a strategic partnership with Tata Group covering semiconductor manufacturing and packaging for the Indian market. However, the proposed GPU remains an early-stage target. Krishnan did not identify a manufacturer, chip supplier, or builder for the project. India is also looking to bring its own homegrown SHAKTI and VEGA processors to commercial markets. Both are based on the open-source RISC-V architecture, allowing local developers to build processors without relying on proprietary CPU designs. Notably, these are CPU designs, separate from the GPUs now being targeted by MeitY.
That said, it is not the first time India has attempted to build its own GPU production unit. In 2019, India's IT Madras released a software development kit that allowed developers to begin building applications before the processors were commercialized. The project included several processor classes aimed at different markets, from embedded devices and micro-controllers to workstations and server workloads. The effort has continued since then, with the Aries 3.0 development board, which uses the C-DAC’s VEGA ET301 processor, being introduced in 2024. The 32-bit chip runs up to 100MHz and includes 26KB of SRAM and is intended for relatively simple applications such as sensors, wearables, and Internet of Things devices, rather than desktop PCs or graphics-intensive workloads.
However, there are signs that the SHAKTI and VEGA platforms are nodding beyond development boards and into practical applications. At the September 26 SEMICOM India event, the government highlighted projects using the processors, including an autonomous water-cleaning robot around SHAKTI and a digital telescope using VEGA. Another VEGA-based project was designed to monitor forest environments. The government's Design -linked Incentive (DLI) program is already supporting more of that work. MeiyT says 24 companies received assistance under the scheme, and subsequently raised venture capital or other private investment. Their projects include microcontrollers, drone flight controllers, smart meter chips and CCTV cameras.
India's semiconductor market is currently valued at just about $50billion and is expected to approach 100 billion by 2030, according to a report by the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA). The government wants local companies to capture more of that growth domestically rather than remain dependent on imported components.

- bit_user The article said:India is also looking to bring its own homegrown SHAKTI and VEGA processors to commercial markets.Wow! An article by Lucian Armasu! That takes me back! I always appreciated his articles, but he never seemed to read the comments.
The article said:Both are based on the open-source RISC-V architectureSince the author of this article is relatively new, I'll repeat my usual nag about this.
Open source describes an implementation. I can write a web server and then I can take the source code for it and release it as open source.
RISC-V is an ISA (instruction set architecture) and system architecture specification. Calling it open source would be like saying HTTP is open source. That's sort of nonsensical, because a specification doesn't really have source code.
So, what's the correct way to qualify RISC-V? Well, the RISC-V Foundation's own website says:
The RISC-V instruction set architecture (ISA) offers a highly customizable open standard platform, enabling developers to build, port, and optimize software applications, extensions, and hardware. Its simplicity and modularity enables efficient design and optimization, fostering innovation and reducing development time and cost. 
If merely calling it an "open standard" feels a bit weak, you can add that it's "royalty-free". Together, these two qualifiers indicate that anyone can access the specification and anyone can implement it without having to obtain a license or pay royalties to the RISC-V Foundation.
Why is it important to use an established ISA? Simple: a conformant implementation is automatically supported by a wide ecosystem of software and tools. If you develop your own ISA, then you face a massive software effort on top of all the work needed to develop competitive hardware! Being an open and royalty-free standard that's hosted in Switzerland means the implementer isn't beholden to a foreign company or potentially hostile government.

articles.title: Sony Electronics Introduces MDR-3R USB-C Wired Headphones
articles.text:
Thursday, November 5th 2026
Sony Electronics Introduces MDR-3R USB-C Wired Headphones
Sony Electronics Inc. today announced the MDR-3R, new USB-C-compatible wired headphones with a design inspired by the original MDR-3 model that debuted alongside the original Walkman TPS-L2 player. Introduced in 1979, the Walkman and MDR-3 helped create a new way of enjoying music freely on the go. Nearly half a century later, as listening styles have become more diverse, the value of wired headphones is being rediscovered for their simplicity, ease of use, and freedom from charging or pairing.
The MDR-3R inherits the MDR-3 concept of headphones designed to let people enjoy music freely both indoors and outdoors. It retains the original design, which reflects the heritage of portable audio culture, while adding modern usability features such as seamless USB-C connectivity, a built-in microphone for calls, and an in-line remote control. Reflecting the shared 1980s inspiration of the Walkman era and Netflix's Stranger Things, Sony will also launch a Stranger Things Edition at the same time.Faithful recreation of the MDR-3 design
The MDR-3R has been redesigned for modern use while preserving the experience value of freely taking music out into the world, which the original MDR-3 helped popularize.
The MDR-3R carries forward the original MDR-3 aesthetic design and comes with iconic blue and orange ear pads, allowing users to customize the look to suit their mood or preferences. The packaging and instruction manual also inherit the design of the original model.
The new headphones also maintain the MDR-3's lightweight, open-ear design, providing lasting comfort even during extended listening.
Updated functionality and connectivity for modern lifestyles
With USB-C support, the headphones connect smoothly to compatible devices such as smartphones. No charging, pairing, or updates are required—just plug them in and enjoy music or videos instantly.
They also feature a microphone for calls and an in-line remote for convenient operation.
Rich sound that brings out the appeal of music
Drawing on the original design specifications, the MDR-3R has been re-engineered with the same 23 mm driver units as the MDR-3 to reproduce sound quality close to the original. While staying true to the original sound signature, subtle refinements have been made to suit modern listening preferences. Its natural, well-balanced sound—a signature carried forward through generations of Sony headphones—brings out the full appeal of every track.
MDR-3R Stranger Things Edition
Bringing together the portable music culture of the Walkman era and the world of Netflix's Stranger Things, the MDR-3R Stranger Things Edition celebrates the spirit of the 1980s. Inspired by Max's signature headphone style and the mysterious Upside Down, this special edition features exclusive design details, including an engraved Stranger Things logo, red and black earpads, and custom packaging that extends the experience beyond the headphones themselves.
Environment in Mind
Our products also take the environment into consideration. Recycled plastic is used in a portion of the product, while plastic-free packaging further reflects how Sony strives to reduce the environmental impact of our products.
Pricing and availability
MDR-3R is available from now with a suggested retailed price of $59.99 USD/ $99.99 CAD / €59 / £49.
MDR-3R Stranger Things Edition is available for pre-order now with a suggested retailed price of $79.99 USD/ $129.99 CAD / €69 / £59.
