articles.title: University of Utah retains operational sovereignty with Redtail - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
University of Utah retains operational sovereignty as Redtail expands research access
Operational sovereignty gives universities authority over how shared computing resources are allocated, managed and secured.
The University of Utah’s Redtail AI factory supercomputer brings advanced computing capabilities to a statewide community. Supporting researchers, students, administrators and external partners through that infrastructure requires more than computing capacity, according to Manish Parashar (pictured), chief AI officer of the University of Utah.
“In research, we are always trying to balance research security with doing open research for societal good,” he said. “Depending on where you are, you might want to lean in one direction or the other. Having that capability to turn the knob becomes so important.”
Parashar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin for the “Sovereign AI: From Strategy to Reality” video series, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed university control of computing infrastructure, research governance and the investment needed to support Utah’s expanding ambitions. (* Disclosure below.)
Operational sovereignty starts with university expertise
Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. helped architect and deploy Redtail as a turnkey system. The university’s Center for High Performance Computing operates it, drawing on expertise that also supports separate regulated research environments, Parashar explained.
“They have admin access, they’re doing the allocations, they are doing the onboarding,” he said. “They’re doing the management and monitoring … the optimization [and] … the right sizing.”
The interview examined Utah’s approach through theCUBE Research’s Five Pillars of Sovereign AI framework: Territorial, Legal, Technological, Operational and Financial. The university retains operational and legal responsibilities, while financing rests on partnerships with the state and donors, according to Parashar.
“Our overall ecosystem is a hybrid,” he said. “There’s things that are on-prem, there are things that are cloud-hosted, and we always will look at it as a hybrid system. Not everything has to be territorially in a single data center or in the state.”
Redtail also gives the university a way to accommodate growing demand for protected computing by freeing up capacity in existing facilities. Current environments support sensitive and regulated research, including healthcare projects, and expanding their capacity is a priority, Parashar noted.
“How do we move into a facility that has not only the capacity, but is also compliant with emerging controls that are coming out? We want to grow that out, and that’s our focus right now,” he said. “And what happens is with the Redtail, a lot of our open research moves to that and that frees up capacity in our data center and other places where we can grow out this regulated environment.”
Statewide ambitions require sustained investment
The university’s One-U Responsible AI initiative connects research with broader societal needs. Its work spans innovation, public-sector collaboration and regional challenges such as air quality, Parashar explained.
“Being open there becomes very, very important because you want to bring the best ideas, the best data — and most often, it is citizen data that’s coming in — and be able to then see how we can most effectively use AI to address this very regional challenge,” he said. “We don’t want to lose ideas; we don’t want to lose the data that’s coming in. We want to assimilate it and make sure the outcome and the warnings that come out of that — the notifications — are as broadly disseminated as possible.”
Financial sustainability must accommodate rising demand as well as technology refreshes. Expansion planning began before the Redtail contract was signed, and the university is approaching federal agencies, including the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation, about investing in the existing ecosystem, Parashar noted.
“We are talking to the state and showing them value — very quickly — and convincing them that investing in this is good for the state [and] it’s good for its citizens,” he said. “We are [also] talking to additional philanthropic donors.”
The university’s statewide mission extends beyond providing access to computing resources. Training, workforce development and shared expertise are also part of the ecosystem that operational sovereignty must support, according to Parashar.
“It’s not that we need everything to be tightly controlled. We don’t want everything to be completely open,” he said. “We want to make sure we have the ability to right-size it depending on what we are working on.”

articles.title: Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost
articles.text:
KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla.—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.
With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP.Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.
Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.
A new Northstar
The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts, 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.
Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine, and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.
“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”
The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.
Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.

articles.title: Compartir internet desde el celular puede poner en riesgo tus datos: cuatro consejos para evitar intrusos
articles.text:
Compartir internet desde el celular permite conectar computadoras, tabletas y otros dispositivos a la red cuando no hay una conexión WiFi disponible. Esta función, conocida como hotspot o punto de acceso móvil, puede ser especialmente útil durante viajes, traslados o jornadas de trabajo fuera de casa. Sin embargo, si no se configura correctamente, también puede facilitar que personas desconocidas utilicen la conexión sin autorización.
El problema no se limita al consumo inesperado de datos móviles. Una red portátil sin protección adecuada puede exponer información personal y facilitar accesos no deseados a la conexión. Por eso, antes de activar esta herramienta, conviene revisar algunos ajustes de seguridad y establecer límites sobre qué dispositivos pueden conectarse.
1. Crear una contraseña segura para compartir internet
El primer paso para proteger una red portátil es establecer una contraseña difícil de adivinar. Cuando se activa el punto de acceso móvil, el teléfono crea una red inalámbrica a la que pueden conectarse otros equipos mediante una clave.
Si la contraseña es demasiado sencilla, como una secuencia de números, una fecha de nacimiento o el nombre de una persona, terceros podrían descubrirla y utilizar la conexión sin permiso.
Lo recomendable es combinar letras mayúsculas y minúsculas, números y caracteres especiales. También conviene evitar claves que se utilicen en otras cuentas o servicios, ya que una contraseña repetida puede aumentar los riesgos si llega a quedar expuesta.
En los ajustes del teléfono es posible modificar el nombre de la red y su contraseña. Cambiar ambos elementos ayuda a evitar que otras personas identifiquen fácilmente el dispositivo y reconozcan una clave que ya hayan utilizado anteriormente.
2. Comprobar el protocolo de seguridad de la red
Otro aspecto importante es revisar el tipo de cifrado que utiliza el punto de acceso móvil. Este mecanismo protege la información que circula entre el teléfono y los dispositivos conectados.
Entre los estándares disponibles, WPA3 ofrece una protección más reciente que WPA2. Si el celular y los equipos que se conectarán son compatibles, es preferible utilizar WPA3. Cuando esa opción no esté disponible, WPA2 sigue siendo una alternativa válida frente a redes abiertas o sin contraseña.
Para comprobar esta configuración, el usuario debe ingresar a los ajustes de conexión o de punto de acceso personal. La ubicación exacta de esta opción puede variar según el fabricante y la versión del sistema operativo.
También es importante revisar periódicamente qué dispositivos están conectados. Si aparece un equipo desconocido, lo recomendable es desactivar el punto de acceso, cambiar la contraseña y volver a habilitarlo únicamente para los dispositivos autorizados.
3. Desactivar el punto de acceso cuando no se utiliza
Mantener activada la función de compartir internet durante horas, incluso cuando nadie está conectado, puede representar un riesgo innecesario. Una red disponible permanentemente ofrece más oportunidades para que otros intenten acceder a ella.
Por eso, una medida sencilla consiste en apagar el punto de acceso apenas termine de utilizarse. Tanto Android como iOS permiten administrar esta función desde sus respectivos menús de configuración.
Algunos teléfonos también incluyen opciones para desactivar automáticamente el punto de acceso cuando no hay dispositivos conectados durante determinado período. Esta alternativa evita que la red permanezca habilitada por descuido.
Además de reducir las posibilidades de accesos no autorizados, apagar la función contribuye a disminuir el consumo energético del equipo.
4. Vigilar el consumo de datos y la batería
Compartir internet exige que el teléfono mantenga activos sus componentes de conexión inalámbrica y móvil. Esta actividad puede elevar el consumo de batería, especialmente cuando hay varios dispositivos conectados o se realizan tareas que requieren una conexión constante.
Por eso, conviene revisar el porcentaje de batería antes de utilizar el celular como módem portátil durante períodos prolongados. También es recomendable evitar que el equipo permanezca expuesto al calor mientras comparte internet.
Otro control necesario es el consumo de datos móviles. En Android y iPhone existen apartados que permiten consultar cuántos gigabytes se utilizaron y qué aplicaciones consumieron más información. Los operadores también ofrecen aplicaciones y plataformas de soporte para comprobar el saldo disponible.
Esta revisión permite detectar un gasto inusual que podría estar relacionado con dispositivos conectados sin autorización o con actividades que consumen grandes cantidades de datos, como las descargas y la reproducción de videos.
Cómo proteger la conexión al compartir internet
Utilizar el celular como módem portátil no implica necesariamente poner en riesgo la información personal. La seguridad depende, en buena medida, de mantener una contraseña robusta, elegir un protocolo de cifrado adecuado y controlar los equipos que utilizan la red.
Desactivar el punto de acceso cuando no se necesita y revisar periódicamente el consumo de datos también ayuda a evitar gastos inesperados y a preservar la batería. Son medidas sencillas que permiten aprovechar esta herramienta sin dejar abierta la conexión a personas desconocidas.

articles.title: Trop cher, trop fragile ? L’iPhone Duo pourrait bien faire le bonheur de Samsung
articles.text:
Apple espérait faire sensation avec son premier smartphone pliant, mais les débuts de l’iPhone Duo sont loin de se dérouler comme prévu. Entre premières déconvenues et concurrence bien installée, la firme de Cupertino pourrait bien avoir offert à Samsung une occasion en or de renforcer sa position sur le marché.
Le marché des smartphones pliants est plus que jamais scruté par les professionnels et les technophiles. Alors qu'Apple comptait faire de l'ombre à Samsung avec son très attendu iPhone Duo, lancé le 23 octobre dernier, le scénario semble prendre une autre direction. Entre premières critiques, problèmes techniques et facture salée, le nouveau venu laisse une partie des fans perplexes. Un retournement de situation qui tombe plutôt bien pour Samsung.

Le lancement d’Apple fait-il les affaires de Samsung ?
En Corée du Sud, les ventes du Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 ont bondi de plus de 20 % du 23 au 29 octobre, selon les médias locaux. En septembre, l’annonce du Duo avait déjà coïncidé avec une hausse de 10 %. Mais aucun chiffre mondial ni preuve d’un transfert d’acheteurs vers Samsung : Apple a peut-être simplement réveillé l’intérêt pour le format pliant.
Son démarrage reste cependant agité. Des usagers ont signalé des fissures sur l’écran interne dès les premières heures. Apple reconnaît un problème touchant, assure-t-il, peu d’appareils et propose des remplacements. Ce "CrackGate" alimente aussi des soupçons non confirmés de contrôles qualité allégés. Les tests révèlent une pliure qui peut se marquer davantage, sans démontrer une faiblesse générale de la charnière.
Les livraisons se compliquent également. John Ternus, nouveau patron d’Apple, ne sait pas quand l’approvisionnement se stabilisera. Entre fabrication complexe et flambée du prix des composants, la situation est délicate. Samsung en profite d'ailleurs pour chambrer son rival dans une série de publicités.
Le confort et le prix font pencher la balance
Même format passeport, même écran intérieur de 7,6 pouces, la ressemblance s’arrête vite. L’iPhone Duo, plus lourd de 53 g, impressionne par ses finitions en titane et sa pliure bien dissimulée sous une dalle mate. Mais en plein jour, ses couleurs paraissent moins éclatantes que sur l’Amoled, certe brillant, du Z Fold 8.
Les coins arrondis et asymétriques de l’écran externe d’Apple gênent parfois la lecture vidéo. Samsung préfère une façade rectangulaire, proche du 16/9. Sur le Duo, la caméra selfie placée dans un coin reste discrète, mais celle cachée sous l’écran intérieur crée un cercle réfléchissant. Ajoutez des apps mal adaptées, quelques bugs et une barre d’outils encombrante, et l’interface de Samsung sous Android paraît plus aboutie.
Dernier argument, et pas des moindres : le tarif. L’iPhone Duo démarre à 2339 € en France et frôle les 3850 € pour 2 To de stockage. Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 bénéficie de promotions, parfois autour de 1500 €, et de solides offres de la part des opérateurs. Apple marque donc des points sur le luxe et le design, mais pour un usage quotidien, les années d’expérience de Samsung semblent continuer de payer.

articles.title: Motorola présente le smartphone le plus cher du marché : le Signature 27 arrive le 16 novembre prochain
articles.text:
Neuf mois après la sortie de son premier smartphone ultra haut de gamme, le Signature, Motorola accélère un grand coup et s'apprête à lancer le Signature 27. Un smartphone encore plus ambitieux sur la partie technique, qui s'affichera à un tarif qui donne envie de se pincer pour s'assurer qu'on ne rêve pas.
Dans mon test du Motorola Signature, en février dernier, j'estimais que si le smartphone était d'excellente facture, il ne boxait pas dans la bonne catégorie. Lancé à 1299€, il était tout simplement beaucoup trop cher pour ce qu'il était. Une critique partagée par l'ensemble de la presse spécialisée, avec laquelle le constructeur a pourtant décidé de faire la paix. Pour preuve, le présent Signature 27 débarquera le 16 novembre prochain au prix exorbitant de 1899€. Non, ce n'est pas une faute de frappe.
Un design radical au service d'un téléobjectif 200 mégapixels
Après le raffinement esthétique du Motorola Signature, le modèle 27 passe presque pour un prototype mal fagotté. La faute à un camera plate qui regroupe maintenant les différents capteurs pour les mettre en valeur, de façon un peu chaotique si je peux me permettre. À l'ancienne, Motorola mise tout sur la photo donc, et espère nous convaincre d'investir 600€ de plus que pour le Signature sur la promesse d'un téléobjectif 200 mégapixels encore très mystérieux. Oui, à ce jour, on ignore encore de quel capteur il s'agit, et la fiche technique tait étrangement l'ouverture de l'objectif — ce qui est rarement bon signe.
Cet objectif reluisant s'accompagne d'un capteur grand-angle (Sony LYTIA L910) de 50 mégapixels, d'un ultra grand-angle de 50 mégapixels également, et d'une dernière optique à l'avant, pour les selfies, de 50 mégapixels également. Rien de foncièrement différent au Signature donc. Pour autant, Motorola en est sûr : il tient là son photophone ultime, qui a décroché la palme d'or des tests spécialisés de chez DxO Mark.
Parmi les autres nouveautés de ce modèle, on retiendra aussi des haut-parleurs conçus et tunés par Bang & Olufsen, dont Motorola s'enorgueillit de décrocher le tout premier partenariat pour de la téléphonie.
Un écran à la luminosité record ?
L'écran du Moto Signature 27 affiche une diagonale tout à fait standard de 6.78", mais la marque assure qu'elle tient là le nec plus ultra du marché en matière de luminosité, avec 12 000 nits annoncés. Je me dois de citer directement le communiqué de presse, qui m'a arraché un immense sourire : « Motorola le présente comme l’écran de smartphone le plus lumineux parmi les modèles commercialisés à partir de 1 799 € en Europe et dans la région META en novembre 2026 ». Je vous laisse revenir vers moi lorsque vous en aurez trouvé un autre. À part le récent OPPO Find X10 Pro Max, aucun autre smartphone n'ose une tarification aussi disproportionnée (en dehors des pliants, bien entendu).
Je note par ailleurs que l'écran 1,5K rétrograde à 120 Hz par rapport à son prédécesseur, qui offrait une fréquence plafond de 165 Hz.
Concilier performances et autonomie
C'était attendu : le Motorola Signature 27 est équipé de la puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, que je mettais justement à l'épreuve cette semaine dans le REDMAGIC 12 Pro (vendu 1000€ moins cher). Une puce ultra premium, qui assure au smartphone de truster les classements des mobiles les plus performants du marché. Deux modèles seront commercialisés le 16 novembre prochain : l'un avec 12 Go de RAM, l'autre avec 16 Go de RAM. Le stockage est quant à lui de 256 ou de 512 Go.
La capacité de la batterie du nouveau Signature fait un gros bond en avant, avec pas moins de 7000 mAh au compteur. C'était 5200 mAh sur le Signature du début d'année. De quoi promettre une autonomie très généreuse. La recharge, elle, ne bouge pas : 90W en filaire, et jusqu'à 50W sans fil avec le chargeur qui va bien.
Enfin, côté logiciel, le Motorola Signature 27 sera livré avec Android 17, et promet sept ans de mises à niveau. On parle à la fois des versions majeures d'Android, et des correctifs de sécurité, naturellement. À ce prix, il serait malvenu de proposer moins. Par ailleurs, Motorola assure que son smartphone dernier cri sera compatible avec la ROM alternative GrapheneOS dès son lancement, ce qui est une excellente nouvelle.
Motorola Signature 27 : prix et disponibilité
Annoncé aujourd'hui, le Motorola Signature 27 sera disponible à la précommande à partir du 16 novembre prochain dans les coloris Coal Smoke (gris foncé) et Capulet Olive (vert olive). Il devrait être commercialisé tout début décembre à partir de 1899€ pour 12 Go de RAM et 256 Go de stockage. Le tarif du modèle 16+512 Go ne nous a pas été communiqué à temps pour la publication de cet article, mais devrait être rendu public rapidement.
Nous avons donc sous les yeux le smartphone le plus onéreux du marché actuel et, très franchement, je suis extrêmement curieux de le prendre en main. Lancer si rapidement un successeur au Signature, à un tel prix, tout en apportant sur le papier si peu de nouveautés, ça intrigue au moins autant que ça inquiète.

articles.title: Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth
articles.text:
Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth
Startups often prioritise funding, sales and expansion while overlooking the operational foundations needed to sustain growth. The article explores why strong processes, reliable data and governance are essential to building scalable businesses.
Growth rarely announces itself. It arrives as a signed term sheet on a Friday evening, a large client wanting to go live in three weeks, or an investor doubling a commitment.
But the win is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the Monday after.
That Monday tells you whether you have built a company or simply had a good quarter.
When operations become a competitive advantage
In most startups, operations sit in the back seat. It is the team that asks for approvals, slows down contracts, and says “not yet” when sales say “yes”. Founders tolerate it the way one tolerates a seatbelt.
I have never accepted that framing. Bain & Company’s long-running research on growth found that 85% of the barriers to profitable growth are internal, with revenue outgrowing talent at the top of the list. Companies rarely lose to the market. They lose to their own machinery, and that machinery is operations.
Build it before you need it
Early on, operations feel optional. A small team, a founder who knows everything, a spreadsheet that works. Why design controls for a business that fits in one room?
Because by the time you feel the need, you are already late. Operations built in the middle of a growth spurt is built under pressure: rushed hires, patched processes, controls bolted on after something breaks. Worse, it takes bandwidth from growth itself. The team that should be closing the next client is busy repairing the last one. You slow down precisely when you meant to accelerate.
Nobody lays the tracks after the train has left the station.
This is not a case for bloat. It is a case for sequencing. Build the backbone one stage ahead of where you are, lean and proportionate, so the organisation absorbs growth instead of buckling under it.
The companies that scale most smoothly are rarely the ones scrambling when growth arrives; the reporting, controls and people for the next stage are already in place. Investors notice the difference.
In due diligence, a clean data room and a well-documented control environment often say more about a company's readiness than its growth curve does.
Run on data, not opinions
Operations is also where a company's data lives, or should. Every onboarding, approval, and report generates information. Most startups treat it as exhaust. The better ones treat it as instrumentation. When operations own clean, consistent data, leadership stops arguing about whose number is right and starts debating what to do about it. You see a bottleneck forming before a client complains. And automation and AI, which nearly every board is now asking about, only work on data you can trust.
Automate a messy process and you simply get the mess faster.
If your founders and your operations team are looking at different numbers, you do not have a data problem. You have an operations problem.
Never pay for the same lesson twice
The same discipline applies to mistakes. A mistake made once is a lesson; made twice, it is a choice.
Every error in a growing firm should leave something behind, whether a changed control, a clearer owner, or a better checklist.
The corollary matters as much. If the same method keeps producing the same disappointing result, the problem is rarely effort. It is the method. Operations should be the function that notices, asks why, and has the licence to change how the work gets done. Processes are not scripture. They are hypotheses, and good operators keep testing them.
Bring operations in before growth is sold, not after
For founders and boards redrawing their organisation charts this year, one test is telling. Do operations hear about a new product, market, or client after it is sold, or while it is being designed? If it is after, operations will always be firefighting, and firefighters rarely get to build anything.
Put operations where growth is planned, not at the end of the line where growth is processed. Give it a seat in strategy reviews, a voice in pricing and launches, and a mandate to say "here is how", not just "not yet".
Three questions are worth asking every quarter:
● If our business doubled next quarter, what would break first?
● Which decisions still need the founder, and should they?
● Would our records survive an investor's due diligence this week?
Will your growth last, or was it just a good quarter?
There is an old military line: amateurs talk strategy, professionals talk logistics.
India's startup story so far has been told in the language of strategy: rounds, valuations, category creation. The next chapter will be about sustaining growth rather than merely achieving it, and it will be told in the language of execution and governance. Momentary growth is an event. Sustained growth is a capability. And capability, in the end, is what operations builds.
(Sandesha Jaitapkar is the COO at Artha Group)

articles.title: France's new 'internet tax', which was meant to stop tech giants from sending huge amounts of data to your smartphone, has been killed off
articles.text:
France's new 'internet tax', which was meant to stop tech giants from sending huge amounts of data to your smartphone, has been killed off
Pper-gigabyte "internet tax" lasted only five days
- French deputies voted 11 to 10 to tax content providers €0.055 for every gigabyte sent to French internet subscribers
- Backers claim €10 billion a year in taxes, but the government disputes both the figure and whether traffic can be measured fairly
- Five days later, the Assembly rejected the budget's whole revenue section 458 to 0, wiping out the tax with it
France's lower house had voted to charge content companies for every gigabyte they deliver to French internet users - but the measure lasted only five days before it was shot down unanimously.
Deputies rejected the revenue half of the 2027 budget by a vote of 458 to 0, LCP reported.
Every amendment adopted during three weeks of debate fell with it, including the per-gigabyte levy; this means that what now goes to the Senate is the government's original bill, which never contained it to begin with.
How a gigabyte would have become a tax bill
The amendment, tabled by Socialist deputy Laurent Lhardit, would have required content providers to pay €0.055 (roughly $0.06) per gigabyte delivered to customers of French internet providers.
It passed at the opening of the 9 am sitting on Friday, October 30, with just 35 of the National Assembly's 577 deputies taking part: 11 voted for, 10 against and 14 abstained, according to the official session transcript. Both the government and the finance committee's general rapporteur, Philippe Juvin, opposed it. Its authors said it would raise around €10 billion ($11.2 billion) a year.
The mechanics are spelled out in the amendment itself: Internet providers, along with any company selling internet access to households or businesses, would count the data flowing to their customers and attribute it to whoever sent it, under the supervision of telecoms regulator Arcep and France's tax authority.
Senders would be identified by company name and their Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) registration number, and no record of what the data contained or where it went could be demanded.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The move has not only found obvious opposition within French politicians after its surprise initial approval in a nearly empty chamber, but has found surprisingly vocal critics at home: VideoLAN, the nonprofit behind VLC, warned the levy would cost it more than €1 million a year, MacGeneration reports, though Lhardit replied that the caps would protect it. The founder of a national ISP, Free, Xavier Niel, dismissed the deputies on X as "ignorant incompetents."
OVHcloud founder Octave Klaba, whose company raised some server prices by up to 87% this autumn over memory costs, calculated that on a 100Gbit/s transit port costing around €6,300 a month, the tax on his assumed traffic would reach €1.02 million a month. He put OVHcloud's exposure at €23 million to €70 million a year.
Even the operators who would have done the counting were unenthusiastic. The French Telecoms Federation, which represents Orange, Bouygues Telecom and SFR, does not reject the idea that big platforms should contribute more to networks, according to Freenews, but it is worried about the technical and administrative load of a scheme whose revenue would go to the treasury rather than to networks, and would rather see commercial negotiations with the platforms.
The solemn vote on the revenue section was due on Tuesday, November 3, but it slipped because 758 amendments were still unexamined at midnight on Monday, NosParlementaires noted. It came on Wednesday evening instead, and no group voted for the amended text, essentially killing the entire proposal in its tracks before the French Senate got involved.
To reappear, the tax would need a senator to refile it and a chamber controlled by the center-right Les Républicains to back it, which Next considered unlikely.
The idea itself is not going away: The Socialists put a €0.10-per-gigabyte version in the program they presented this summer, ahead of next year's presidential election. There is, however, international pressure and considerations that would ensure this never actually happens, even as countries vie to attract the most AI infrastructure investments, and this could be the biggest dealbreaker for multiple players.
Beyond France, it runs against the tide. Brussels spent years fielding telecom operators' demands that Big Tech chip in for network upgrades, the so-called "fair share" fight, and in January the European Commission's Digital Networks Act proposed only a voluntary cooperation mechanism rather than mandatory network fees.
Then there is Washington: Donald Trump has long threatened tariffs on countries that tax US tech firms, and in June 2026 he warned of 100% tariffs on any country implementing a digital services tax on American companies. A per-gigabyte levy whose biggest payers would be Google, Meta, Amazon, and Netflix would be hard to present as anything other than that.
For now, the proposal stands killed; nothing has changed on anyone's phone or internet bill, and, seemingly, for the 2027 budget at least, nothing will. But the idea could show up in other forms in the near future.

articles.title: En 2007, EEUU tuvo la disparatada idea de fabricar cemento quemando montañas de alfombras viejas: el experimento funcionó, hasta que llegó la factura
articles.text:
Estados Unidos tenía un problema que se medía en millones de toneladas: cada año, una montaña de moquetas y alfombras usadas terminaba en los vertederos. En el año 2007, un grupo de investigadores encontró una salida tan extraña como prometedora: utilizarlas para alimentar los hornos de las cementeras. Lo sorprendente es que consiguieron demostrar que funcionaba. Lo que vino después fue una lección sobre la distancia que separa una buena idea de un negocio rentable.
Millones de toneladas de alfombras. A comienzos de los años 2000, Estados Unidos generaba anualmente entre 1,8 y 2,3 millones de toneladas de residuos de moquetas, buena parte de los cuales terminaba en vertederos. El problema estaba en su composición: fibras sintéticas, adhesivos, tejidos de soporte y materiales minerales, una mezcla diseñada para resistir años de uso, pero extraordinariamente difícil de separar y reciclar.
Para los investigadores del Instituto Tecnológico de Georgia, aquella montaña de residuos planteaba una pregunta: ¿y si en lugar de recuperar cada componente se aprovechaba su contenido energético?
La ocurrencia tenía más sentido del que parecía. Las moquetas contienen fibras de nailon, polipropileno y otros polímeros derivados del petróleo que liberan energía al quemarse. Sus bases también incorporan carbonato cálcico, utilizado como materia prima en la fabricación de cemento. Esa combinación convertía a los hornos cementeros en candidatos interesantes: podían aprovechar la energía de los plásticos y admitir los componentes minerales.
Los ensayos preliminares atribuyeron a determinadas mezclas un poder calorífico de unos 23 megajulios por kilogramo, inferior al del carbón convencional, pero suficiente para estudiar su uso como combustible complementario.
Primero había que comprobar qué salía por la chimenea. Entre noviembre de 2003 y febrero de 2004, investigadores de la Agencia de Protección Ambiental estadounidense (EPA) realizaron 62 ensayos con alfombras y moquetas de polipropileno y dos tipos de nailon, introduciendo cargas de unos 400 gramos en un horno experimental.
Las pruebas demostraron que podían arder, aunque también revelaron diferencias según el material: las fibras de nailon aumentaban las emisiones de óxido nítrico y la alimentación por lotes producía picos transitorios de monóxido de carbono. El experimento no demostraba que quemar moquetas fuera ambientalmente inocuo, pero sí que existía una posibilidad técnica que merecía estudiarse a escala industrial.
El salto a una cementera de verdad. La prueba decisiva llegó en las instalaciones de Lehigh Cement en Evansville, Pensilvania, donde los investigadores quemaron alfombras trituradas junto con el combustible habitual. El material llegó a representar entre el 10% y el 15% del aporte energético, con una alimentación de unas dos a dos toneladas y media por hora.
Los resultados fueron alentadores: el horno pudo utilizar las alfombras sin que las emisiones medidas superasen los límites autorizados durante el ensayo. Los registros de óxidos de nitrógeno y dióxido de azufre permanecieron por debajo de los máximos permitidos, aunque el segundo mostró valores aparentemente superiores durante la combustión conjunta.
El primer enemigo fue una máquina que no dejaba de atascarse. El ensayo industrial tenía previsto utilizar unas 1.000 toneladas de alfombras, pero únicamente consiguió introducir alrededor de 200 toneladas en el horno. El motivo: el sistema de alimentación, originalmente diseñado para astillas de madera, que se atascaba cuando recibía aquel material fibroso y heterogéneo.
Las moquetas tampoco eran fáciles de preparar: había que triturarlas, mantenerlas secas y manipular grandes volúmenes de residuos. Además, el carbonato cálcico presente en su composición provocaba un desgaste considerable en las superficies de corte.
Y entonces llegó la factura. El informe final, publicado en febrero de 2007, reveló que el mayor obstáculo no estaba en la combustión, sino en el dinero necesario para transportar y preparar las alfombras. Los investigadores calcularon que su valor energético equivalía a unos 1,2 centavos de dólar por libra, pero el coste real de preparación y suministro alcanzó los 4,3 centavos: 1,5 por embalado y carga, otros 1,5 por trituración y 1,3 por transporte.
Dicho de otra forma, solo trasladar el material costaba 550 dólares por camión para un recorrido de unos 161 kilómetros. Es decir, el coste total multiplicaba por más de cinco la previsión inicial de 0,8 centavos por libra y superaba ampliamente el valor del combustible obtenido.
Una solución que funcionaba, pero no salía a cuenta. La investigación, dirigida por Matthew Realff desde Georgia Tech y financiada por el Departamento de Energía estadounidense, concluyó que las alfombras eran técnicamente adecuadas como combustible alternativo, pero económicamente inviables en las condiciones estudiadas. Una planta más cercana a los puntos de recogida, mejores equipos de trituración o un combustible convencional más caro podían modificar las cuentas, aunque también había que invertir en sistemas de almacenamiento y alimentación.
El experimento dejó así una paradoja: Estados Unidos disponía de millones de toneladas de residuos aprovechables y de hornos capaces de utilizarlos, pero no de una cadena logística que permitiera hacerlo de manera rentable. En 2007, los investigadores no descubrieron que las alfombras fueran un mal combustible, más bien descubrieron que llevarlas hasta el horno costaba más de lo que valía quemarlas.

articles.title: 14 millions de plaques d’immatriculation piratées en France : Auto-Planning confirme une cyberattaque massive
articles.text:
Le site spécialisé FrenchBreaches révèle que des pirates ont mis en vente une énorme base de données dérobée à Auto-Planning. Cette entreprise française permet aux centres de contrôle technique de gérer leurs rendez-vous en ligne et d’envoyer des rappels par SMS à leurs clients. Une plateforme concurrente, baptisée Auto Contrôle Paris, est également touchée par les mêmes cybercriminels.
Plus de 200 millions de lignes de données
Les hackers, qui se font appeler « Operation GlassLodge » sur les forums criminels, affirment avoir dérobé plus de 200 millions de lignes de données. Selon les estimations de FrenchBreaches, le fichier concerne près de 18 millions de personnes et 13,9 millions de plaques d’immatriculation. Certaines données ne sont pas récentes et remonteraient à 2008.
Les échantillons contiennent les noms et prénoms des automobilistes, leurs adresses e-mail et numéros de téléphone, leurs plaques, la marque et le modèle de leurs véhicules, ou encore la date et l’heure de leurs rendez-vous. Près de 92 millions de rendez-vous sont recensés dans les répertoires, assurent les pirates. Ils affirment aussi détenir 36 545 factures au format PDF. Ces documents sensibles pourraient contenir des relevés d’identité bancaire (RIB), ce qui ouvre la voie à des arnaques ou à des tentatives d’usurpation d’identité. Les cybercriminels ont réclamé 33 333 dollars de rançon à Auto-Planning, menaçant de divulguer toutes les données sur la toile. Rien n’indique que l’entreprise a répondu à la demande du gang.
L’entreprise a vite reconnu l’attaque. C’est également le cas d’Auto Contrôle Paris. Conformément à leurs obligations légales, Auto-Planning et Auto Contrôle Paris ont prévenu la CNIL (Commission nationale de l’informatique et des libertés), le gendarme des données personnelles en France.
À lire aussi : Des frigos à plus de 100°C – après les supermarchés, des pirates s’attaquent aux congélateurs du don du sang
Fausses amendes et faux contrôles techniques
Une plaque d’immatriculation, croisée avec un nom, un numéro de téléphone et une date de rendez-vous, représente une sérieuse menace pour tous les Français concernés. Avec ces informations, un escroc peut envoyer un SMS d’arnaque très crédible. Il peut vous demander de confirmer votre prochain contrôle technique en payant des « frais de réservation » fictifs, ou de régler une fausse amende de l’ANTAI en citant votre véritable plaque.
Une plaque associée à une identité peut aussi aboutir à une usurpation d’identité. La victime risque alors de recevoir des contraventions pour des infractions qu’elle n’a pas commises. Le croisement d’une adresse et d’un modèle de véhicule pourrait aussi aider des malfaiteurs à repérer une voiture en particulier, un modèle de luxe par exemple, ou un domicile laissé vide.
Ce n’est pas la première fois que des plaques d’immatriculation se retrouvent entre les mains de cybercriminels. Fin octobre, un pirate surnommé ChimeraZ affirmait déjà avoir volé une base de près de 850 000 plaques françaises, associées au nom, au téléphone et à l’adresse de leurs propriétaires.

articles.title: Chinese AI lab Moonshot reportedly looked at European data centers to access Nvidia chips, report claims — Kimi-maker primarily interested in inferencing capacity, but also asked about training clusters
articles.text:
Chinese AI lab Moonshot reportedly looked at European data centers to access Nvidia chips, report claims — Kimi-maker primarily interested in inferencing capacity, but also asked about training clusters
Chinese AI labs are attempting to export their data since they cannot import Nvidia GPUs.
Moonshot AI, the Chinese lab that made Kimi, is reportedly looking towards Europe to gain access to the latest Nvidia Blackwell AI GPUs. According to CNBC, the company is in talks with at least one European data center to lease clusters with 8,000 or more GPUs for inferencing, and that it’s also interested in securing compute capacity for training.
While Chinese companies are banned from acquiring Nvidia Blackwell and other AI GPUs that offer the same or better performance containing U.S. technologies, a loophole has so far allowed them to gain access to compute by renting them from data centers abroad. The U.S. House is attempting to patch it and passed the Remote Access Security Act, but it must still go through the Senate and the White House before it can turn into law. In the meantime, Chinese AI labs are exploiting the loophole and training their models on foreign data centers that have acquired Nvidia chips.
The U.S. and China have been locked in an AI arms race, with the latter’s open-weight models behind frontier U.S. models by just a matter of months. More importantly, these models, like Kimi K3, are significantly easier to run and could even be much cheaper to use. These advancements happened despite Washington’s efforts to make it harder for Chinese AI labs to acquire hardware that uses American technologies through export bans. But even though President Donald Trump eventually made a 180-degree turn and allowed Nvidia H200 chips for export to China, Beijing has taken steps to protect its domestic AI chip industry by blocking H200 imports at the border, meaning these companies must look elsewhere if they want to access the latest, most powerful AI GPUs to train their models.
Moonshot also has a limited window if it wants to secure compute capacity outside of China — Nvidia has reportedly told its data center clients to limit their business and avoid serving more than 49% of their capacity to Chinese outfits. This could be a harbinger of things to come, especially as reports like these could spotlight the bipartisan bill and increase pressure to advance the legislation sooner rather than later.

articles.title: Big Canadian documentary about BioWare to premiere next year
articles.text:
An upcoming Canadian documentary will chronicle the history of BioWare, the legendary Edmonton-based game developer that was shut down on Oct. 21.
As reported by Deadline, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story will chronicle the history of the iconic Canadian studio, which was founded in 1995 by University of Alberta medical doctors Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip. According to Deadline, this doc began shooting two years ago, so it will cover “the final chapter” of BioWare, although it’s unclear how deep into the weeds of all of that it will actually get. For context, a relatively small team of about 50 people were still left at BioWare working on a fifth Mass Effect game, which has since been cancelled.
Commissioned by Edmonton-based Super Channel, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story is written and directed by Edmonton native Akash Sherman (Singhs in the Ring) and co-produced by Edmonton-based Fennessey Films and Score G Productions.
Per Deadline, the film will feature founders Muzyka, Zeschuk and Yip, Casey Hudson (creative director on Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and the Mass Effect trilogy), The Game Awards creator Geoff Keighley, Canadian gaming host Victor Lucas (The Electric Playground), former EA CEO John Riccitiello, Lucasfilm Games VP Douglas Reilly, Canadian-American actress Jennifer Hale (star of KOTOR and the Mass Effect trilogy) and BioWare developers like Drew Karpyshyn (KOTOR and Mass Effect writer), Mark Darrah (veteran Dragon Age producer) and James Ohlen (lead designer on Baldur’s Gate and KOTOR), among others.
A release date hasn’t been confirmed, but Deadline reports that the film will premiere sometime next year following a “major film festival run” and a world premiere next year. Naturally, a lot of people will be anticipating this, given the global mourning from fans and developers alike.
Parent company EA, which is now co-owned by the Saudi regime, reportedly shut down BioWare to prioritize a new Star Wars: Battlefront game after taking on billions in debt due to the acquisition being a leveraged buyout.

articles.title: Celular com a 2ª melhor câmera do mundo chega ao Brasil • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Celular com a 2ª melhor câmera do mundo chega ao Brasil
Motorola Signature 27 tem preço a partir de R$ 10.999, com Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 e memória RAM de 12 GB.
A Motorola lança nesta quinta-feira (05/11) um novo smartphone ultrapremium no Brasil: o Motorola Signature 27 tem preço a partir de R$ 10.999. Ele tem a melhor câmera de smartphone lançado em 2026 e a segunda melhor do mundo. Além disso, é o primeiro aparelho com Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, tela com pico de brilho de 12.000 nits e bateria de 7.000 mAh.
O modelo já está em pré-venda por R$ 10.999, na versão de 256 GB. A configuração de 512 GB era a única do antecessor no lançamento. Agora ela sai por R$ 11.999, ou seja, R$ 3.000 a mais que o Motorola Signature original, que estreou em março por R$ 8.999. Com isso, a fabricante passa dos R$ 10 mil entre os seus celulares de formato tradicional. Só os dobráveis custam mais: o Razr 70 Ultra sai por R$ 12.999 e o Razr Fold, por R$ 15.999.
A chefe de marketing do laboratório DXO Mark, especializado em testes de fotografia, revelou que o Signature 27 conquistou o segundo lugar entre as melhores câmeras do planeta neste ano. Além disso, traz o melhor sistema de câmera lançado em 2026. De acordo com Aurélie Singer, o produto traz uma série de avanços, com destaque para a fidelidade do tom de pele registrado pelo smartphone.
Aurélie enfatizou que o produto tem bom desempenho tanto em fotos quanto em vídeos, e em todos os sensores. O Signature 27 obteve 173 pontos no DXOMARK, atrás apenas do Huawei Pura 80 Ultra (175 pontos), lançado em 2025. Logo atrás da Motorola estão: iPhone 18 Pro (172), Vivo/Jovi X300 Pro (171), Oppo Find X9 Ultra 170) e Vivo/Jovi X300 Ultra (170).
A teleobjetiva periscópica tem 200 MP, zoom óptico de 3x e zoom híbrido de até 100x. Já a câmera principal usa o sensor Sony LYTIA L910, de 50 MP. Ela traz a tecnologia LOFIC, que amplia a captura de informação em cenas com grande diferença de luz, como shows e paisagens urbanas à noite.
Completam o conjunto uma ultrawide de 50 MP com modo macro e uma câmera frontal de 50 MP. O celular grava vídeos em até 8K com Dolby Vision. A empresa promete fotos e os vídeos com Ultra HDR no Instagram, graças a uma parceria com a Meta.
A Motorola diz que o aparelho é o primeiro do mundo com um Action Sensor dedicado. Trata-se de um sensor de visão baseado em eventos (EVS, na sigla em inglês), criado pela Sony, que registra o movimento de forma independente das câmeras. Segundo a fabricante, o sensor ajuda a congelar cenas em alta velocidade no modo Action Shot.
O Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 foi anunciado pela Qualcomm em setembro. Segundo a Motorola, os ganhos em relação ao Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 são de até 37% na eficiência energética da CPU, até 35% no desempenho da NPU e até 44% no desempenho da GPU. O antecessor usava o Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, uma versão menos potente.
O SoC funciona em conjunto com a memória RAM LPDDR5 de 12 GB.
Para controlar o aquecimento, o sistema ArcticMesh usa gel térmico com microdiamantes e uma câmara de vapor 40% maior que a do modelo anterior.
A tela de 6,8 polegadas usa a tecnologia Extreme AMOLED Duo, que empilha dois painéis AMOLED para aumentar o brilho e reduzir o consumo. O pico é de 12.000 nits, o maior do mercado segundo a fabricante, considerando os celulares lançados até outubro. A Motorola afirma que o painel consome até 34% menos energia e dura até 121% mais do que a tela AMOLED do Signature anterior.
A bateria passa de 5.200 mAh para 7.000 mAh, com tecnologia de silício-carbono, e promete até 62 horas de uso misto. O carregamento com fio é de 90 W, com carregador incluso na caixa. O sem fio chega a 50 W, mas exige um carregador vendido à parte. A bateria maior tem um custo: o Signature 27 tem 7,99 mm de espessura e pesa 227 g. O antecessor, que tinha a espessura como um dos destaques, media cerca de 7 mm e pesava 186 g.
Na lista de itens que reforçam o posicionamento ultrapremium estão o áudio assinado pela Bang & Olufsen; as certificações IP68, IP69 e IP69K contra água e poeira; o padrão militar MIL-STD-810H; e o vidro Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3.
O aparelho terá sete atualizações do Android e sete anos de atualizações de segurança. Na parte de IA, o Gemini Intelligence promete executar tarefas com várias etapas em diferentes aplicativos, e a Motorola Qira integra celulares e computadores da Motorola e da Lenovo.
O modelo também será o primeiro da Motorola compatível com o GrapheneOS, sistema operacional de código aberto focado em privacidade. A empresa diz que mais detalhes serão divulgados no futuro.
O Motorola Signature 27 já está em pré-venda no site da Motorola, nas cores Pantone Coal Smoke (cinza-chumbo) e Pantone Capulet Olive (verde). Confira os valores informados pela Motorola:
| Armazenamento | RAM | Preço | 
|---|---|---|
| 256 GB | 12 GB | R$ 10.999 | 
| 512 GB | 12 GB | R$ 11.999 | 
Nas operadoras, quem fez o pré-registro tem um voucher de R$ 1.000. Na Claro, o aparelho sai a partir de R$ 7.799 em 21x sem juros, no plano Multi 200GB. Na Vivo, sai a partir de R$ 7.199, no plano Vivo Total Família 4/5. No varejo, a Amazon, Magalu, Mercado Livre, Inter Shop e Bradesco Shop oferecem parcelamento em até 21x.
A fabricante também oferece um pacote com a capa magnética Moto Snap Case por R$ 99 e o relógio Moto Watch Ultra por R$ 2.899.

articles.title: Bazzite 45 Launches With Start of Linux EAC V2 Support and Wider Handheld Compatibility
articles.text:
Thursday, November 5th 2026
Bazzite 45 Launches With Start of Linux EAC V2 Support and Wider Handheld Compatibility
Shortly after the official Fedora 45 launch, Bazzite 45 has launched, with a rebase to Fedora 45, Gnome 51.1, and KDE Plasma 6.8.2. The new Bazzite version lists updated OGC Linux kernels—7.2.15 for AMD and Intel, and 6.18.60 for NVIDIA users—and additional hardware support, including for the Acer Predator Atlas 8 and ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X20, but also for more peripherals, including the Logitech TrueForce racing wheel hardware. The Mesa driver version has also been updated to 26.2.6, InputPlumber has been updated, and CoolerController has been moved to the official docker container, while XWaylandVideoBridge has been removed in the name of stability and squashing KDE bugs. The rest of the actual updates are minor back-end changes, save one. 
As per the announcement post on the Universal Blue Discourse page, as of Bazzite 45, Bazzite has become accepted by Epic Games as a signing key provider, and the development team behind Bazzite has added a Linux EAC V2 readiness checker to Bazzite 45. The checker automatically updates the latest Linux EAC V2 requirements and compares the requirements to the current kernel and BIOS configurations—specifically kernel and module signing, Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, measured boot, IOMMU, kernel lockdown, kexec, and BPF LSM. If there are any incompatibilities, the user will be notified by the readiness checker.Some of the other, more notable small improvements made behind the scenes include an updated extest library for proper Steam Input support in the new Steam 64-bit client and an implementation of Chunkah, which, alongside other changes that have reduced build time and increased reliability, have reduced Bazzite image updates to as little as 100 MB. 
In the coming weeks, the Bazzite team will be testing the Linux kernel 7.3.1 and focusing on implementing HDMI 2.1 and VRR, changes that will soon be in the unstable Bazzite channel for those wanting to be on the bleeding edge or wanting to test new features.

articles.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
articles.text:
Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.
The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.
One connection, works every time, needs no retries
There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
When all the conditions are met, the consequences are high.
“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,” Alpine maintainers said Thursday. “It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.”
When logging into a passwordless account, the attacker can gain access by inputting more than 256 characters in the password field.
Security firm Checkpoint said that the use of the SHA256 or SHA512 functions “matters because sshd borrows that account’s salt. Without it, the attack fails.” Company researchers said their testing also showed that the account must be active, not just hold a hash. Checkpoint further reported that root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit password setting, though reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still become root.

articles.title: AI architecture gaps keep agents stuck in demo mode - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Oracle wants to pull stalled AI agents out of demo mode and into production
Companies want AI agents faster than they can build the AI architecture to run them. Most can put together a convincing demo. Far fewer can move agents into production without exposing data, hurting uptime or blowing their budgets.
That gap is pushing database providers to rethink what a data platform for agents has to deliver. Nearly 70% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents, yet very few get them into production, according to Çetin Özbütün (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, data warehouse and autonomous database, at Oracle Corp.
“AI is very easy to demonstrate, but when you try to bring it into production, enterprises usually encounter four different deployment difficulties,” Özbütün said. “The first of them is around security. It’s very hard to securely provide access to AI agents, and that’s one of the top challenges.”
Özbütün spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI architecture and the challenges of moving agents into production. (* Disclosure below.)
Building an AI architecture agents can trust
Security is the first hurdle. AI agents are finding vulnerabilities at unprecedented levels, and customers often can’t patch their databases before attackers exploit those flaws, Özbütün noted. Oracle’s Autonomous AI Database encrypts data at rest and in transit by default, and users can’t turn those protections off.
“As soon as the vulnerability is found, before it’s released anywhere else, we bring it into production in Autonomous AI Database,” Özbütün said.
Resiliency is the next test, because agents run around the clock and put heavy, unpredictable demands on the data platform. Oracle commits to 99.995% availability with no exclusions. That figure is measured by whether a client can connect and run queries, not by whether the underlying infrastructure is running, Özbütün explained.
“We patch our systems on a weekly basis, for example,” Özbütün said. “All of our patches are online patches, so the database is up and running, accepting new connections, accepting new requests while we’re running the patch.”
The same always-current approach applies to Oracle’s Deep Trust AI architecture, in which the database enforces the security profiles that customers define. New capabilities such as the expanded Deep Data Security features show up in Autonomous AI Database as soon as they’re announced, ahead of on-premises releases, according to Özbütün.
“You do nothing as the user or administrator of Autonomous Database to get this functionality,” Özbütün said. “As soon as a new functionality is available, like Oracle Deep Data Security, it becomes available for you to use on day one.”

articles.title: Nvidia, Municipal Leaders Frame AI as Critical Urban Infrastructure - EE Times
articles.text:
BARCELONA, Spain — At the Smart City Expo World Congress, executives from Nvidia and municipal officials from Europe and the U.S. made the case for AI as an indispensable component of civic infrastructure.
With a keynote by Paolo Guglielmini, Nvidia’s VP for EMEA, and an executive panel moderated by Michael Lake, CEO of Leading Cities, the summit emphasized the need for local governments to establish centralized computing facilities—termed “AI factories”—to turn vast volumes of urban data into civic operational decisions, maintain sovereignty over sensitive municipal data, and retain technical talent rather than see it move to private technology centers.
Municipal data gap and architecture
In a keynote titled “From AI Factories to Intelligent Cities,” Guglielmini described what he called a structural bottleneck in modern municipal governance: the disparity between the raw data cities collect and the fraction they analyze to guide civic operations.
“Your organizations, your city’s municipalities, and regions have never had so much data available to you,” said Guglielmini, pointing to continuous streams from water utilities, air quality monitors, traffic sensors, mobile devices, GPS trackers, and satellite imagery. “But the gap between the data that’s available and the data that we use for decision-making has never been this great.”
To close that operational gap, Guglielmini proposed a five-layer architectural model for civic technology: energy, compute hardware, foundational infrastructure, software models, and end-user applications. He noted that while cities invest heavily in hardware, much of the economic value is created at the application level.
“Economic opportunity will happen where compute resides,” Guglielmini said. “Talent will stay where compute infrastructure is built. The lion’s share of startups created today are AI-native startups, and entrepreneurs and innovators will always follow where infrastructure is built.”
Addressing the technical friction within city halls, Guglielmini said legacy administrative systems often hinder modernization. “Very often, the organizations you are within have a lot of legacy,” Guglielmini said. “We have data that is nested. We have silos. We have applications built over tens of years. AI is perfect to build that layer on top that harnesses the power of data.”
From digital twins to language agents
To illustrate how localized computing can translate into municipal operations, Guglielmini detailed three distinct deployments across European regions.
In the Doubs department in eastern France, regional authorities built digital replicas of more than 500 public buildings, according to Guglielmini. Rather than relying solely on structural geometry, the digital mock-ups integrate real-time utility records, maintenance histories, and environmental metrics. “This is not about pure geometry,” Guglielmini said. “These are mock-ups that are enriched with data maintenance, data records, and utility records. Simulating cities and urban planning into the future has never become so affordable, so quick, and so valuable.”
In Palermo, Italy, municipal authorities established a center of excellence that uses a real-time AI model to process feeds from cameras and multiple types of sensors. The system combines urban monitoring with traffic management, emergency response dispatching, and municipal waste tracking. “Palermo went off and built a center of excellence that is incredibly capable of fusing sensor data from a multiplicity of facets and really shorten the time to emergency response,” Guglielmini explained.
In Barcelona, municipal technology developer 1 Million Bots deployed an agentic service platform built on “Laia,” a specialized language model developed at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. The model was trained specifically to handle regional administrative procedures in Spanish and regional languages, including Catalan, Galician, and Basque.
“Laia is a model that is highly specialized and highly sovereign for the Spanish language, and for all the [languages] that are important to address the largest possible population of your citizens,” Guglielmini said. He emphasized that local hosting keeps public data secure: “The city is in control of the applications, in control of the data, and in control of the permitting and permissions of who gets to see that data.”
Moving from pilot projects to reality
Following the keynote, Michael Lake, president and chief executive of Leading Cities, convened an executive panel titled “By the City, for the City: Making AI Work.” Lake organized the discussion around three core principles: Purpose, Power, and Proof.
“Technology doesn’t fail because it’s bad,” Lake said. “Technologies and communities fail because the system that it needs to survive is not ready for it.”
Charbel Aoun, director of smart cities and spaces for EMEA at Nvidia, criticized municipalities’ tendency to treat AI as a series of disconnected software pilot projects rather than integrating them into their operations—a pattern panel members characterized as “death by a thousand pilots.”
“Most of the pilots end up being a lessons-learned paper,” Aoun said. “What we need to prove is the value and the adoption.”
Aoun argued that cities should treat computing capacity as foundational civic infrastructure, comparable to electrical grids or water lines. “AI is becoming critical infrastructure,” Aoun noted. “If we achieve that point, then we need to learn from the broadband mistake and from previous mistakes. Cities can own it, rent it, or partner, but they need an AI factory foundation.”
U.S. cities focus on productivity and public safety
Panel members from American cities described pragmatic approaches designed to establish public trust and streamline labor-intensive municipal tasks.
Mayor Keith A. James of West Palm Beach, Fla., said his administration chose public records processing as its first application. Municipal staff members handle extensive paperwork under strict legal timelines, making document retrieval a natural fit for automation.
“Cities tend to be very labor-intensive or paper-intensive,” James said. “You want to show the residents the AI working, and you want to begin with realistic applications. Our project involves public records requests. It helps our residents because we respond efficiently, and it takes some of the burden off our staff.”
In Tampa, Fla., Mayor Jane Castor said public safety departments have led municipal technology adoption because of immediate operational demands. Tampa recently deployed an automated drone response system linked directly to its real-time crime center, allowing aerial units to reach emergency scenes ahead of ground vehicles.
To prevent department silos, Tampa is also deploying “Iris,” a software platform that consolidates data from water quality, wastewater, solid waste, purchasing, and permitting into a single executive dashboard.
Castor emphasized that clear boundaries are vital to maintaining public confidence. “You have to share information with your community so that trust is there,” Castor said. “They shouldn’t feel like there’s a surveillance state in your community.”
European AI strategies in universities and communities
European municipal leaders highlighted frameworks that link technology deployment directly to academic institutions and geographic equity.
First Deputy Mayor Jakub Mazur of Wrocław, Poland, detailed how his administration replaced ad hoc software trials with a citywide strategy anchored by the Wrocław University of Science and Technology and its 25,000 students. The city deployed an AI-assisted enrollment system that handles 95% of school placements for local families, while encouraging technical graduates to remain in the regional economy.
Mazur stressed that decisions affecting citizens must remain accountable to elected officials, not automated systems.
“We need to own it because the city is responsible for data and the decision-making process,” Mazur stated. “We are democratically elected; we can be voted out. The algorithm cannot be voted out.”
For Rome, Italy, Deputy Mayor Valeria Baglio outlined a strategy focused on neighborhood-wide inclusion. Rather than concentrating digital investments in tourist-heavy central districts, Rome’s strategy extends digital public services across outer residential areas.
Rome’s initiative operates through “CTE Roma“, or Houses of Innovation, a municipal network linking city government, regional universities, startup incubators, and living labs. “We are working to bring digital services closer to residents across all districts, so that innovation isn’t just focused around central stations or downtown hubs,” Baglio said.
Building infrastructure for long-term value
To conclude his keynote, Guglielmini said that building municipal computing infrastructure doesn’t necessarily require a multi-gigawatt capital investment right away. He urged city officials to consider a modular rollout approach.
“Your AI journey can start from something very small—something portable and powerful,” Guglielmini said, noting that numerous European technology enterprises began operations using compact desktop supercomputing units. “Adding the right level of ambition is fundamental, but getting started with a use case that is really transformational for your communities and thinking about it in modular terms is fundamental to get going.”
Looking ahead, Guglielmini said he expects the next decade of urban technology to focus less on experimentation and more on deploying permanent, on-the-ground computing assets to support urban productivity and growth.
“Infrastructure build-out for the next 10 years is going to mean building intelligence that is at your fingertips to help you run your cities more effectively and economically,” Guglielmini said. “Focus on the use cases that are most transformational for where you are, bring together the right ecosystem, and look at the resources you have available to build compute capacity that serves your community.”

articles.title: J’ai essayé le premier MacBook avec écran tactile, et c’est un grand oui
articles.text:
Alors que sur Windows, il n’existe pratiquement plus de PC au delà des 1000 euros qui n’intègre pas une dalle tactile, jusqu’ici, Apple ne voulait rien entendre sur ses MacBook. C’est désormais fini avec le dernier MacBook Proled, premier ordinateur siglé de la pomme à intégrer une dalle tactile.
Cette dernière n’est d’ailleurs pas la seule nouveauté à l’horizon. Comme son nom l’indique, le nouveau MacBook Pro intègre également une dalle OLED, abandonnant ainsi la technologie Mini-LED. Dernier changement et pas des moindres, à l’instar de l’iPhone 15 Pro, le MacBook dit adieu à la fameuse encoche et s’équipe d’un poinçon de forme oblongue sur la partie supérieure de l’écran pour laisser passer la webcam.
Nous l’avons pris en main dans sa version 16 pouces en amont de sa commercialisation, voici nos premiers retours.
Un ajout qui a un coût
Avant de passer à nos premières impressions, glissons tout de même un mot sur la question du prix, car le MacBook Pro se décline désormais en deux gammes. D’un côté, le MacBook Pro avec Écran PROLED, celui que nous testons ici, et, de l’autre, le MacBook Pro classique si l’on peut dire. Celui-ci démarre à 2299 euros, mais ce tarif vous permet d’obtenir une puce M6 un peu faiblarde, comparée au M5 Pro mis de série sur la version OLED. Il nous faut donc comparer les prix avec cette puce.
Résultat, cela donne un MacBook Pro Mini-LED à 2899 euros avec la M5 Pro, modèle de base (15 cœurs CPU, 16 cœurs GPU), et 3299 euros pour la version avec écran OLED. Le tout en 14 pouces. On monte respectivement à 3399 euros et 3899 euros en 16 pouces. L’option OLED coute donc en moyen entre 400 et 500 euros selon la taille de dalle. Précisons que ces versions n’intègrent pas le verre nanotexturé, une option qui vous coutera 165 euros.
Avec une telle différence de prix, la question de l’utilité de l’écran OLED, mais aussi des différents ajouts apportés sur cette version, se pose donc davantage. Nous allons donc tenter de débroussailler tout ça.
Le tactile : une vision vers le futur du MacBook déjà bien intégrée
Intéressons-nous d’abord à la nouveauté la plus brûlante : l’écran tactile. D’aucuns trouvent que cette nouveauté ne sert à rien tant le pavé tactile du MacBook est déjà très performant, d’autres considèrent qu’Apple rattrape enfin un retard important sur le reste de l’industrie. Qu’en est-il vraiment ?
En tant qu’utilisateur régulier de PC Windows ou encore de l’iPad Pro en usage façon laptop, ce passage à l’écran tactile m’a paru tout naturel. Quel plaisir de pouvoir scroller sur un long article à la main plutôt que de devoir utiliser sa souris. Ou encore de venir cliquer avec ses doigts sur une coche plutôt que de chercher son pointeur de souris sur l’énorme dalle de 16 pouces ici présente.
D’autant que, contrairement aux soucis de jeunesse d’un certain iPhone Duo avec iOS, la première mouture du tactile sur macOS est très soignée. Basiquement, tous les raccourcis que vous connaissez avec le pavé tactile fonctionnent ici avec l’écran. On balaye d’un geste distrait toutes les fenêtres en un clin d’œil, on passe d’un écran à l’autre avec le geste à trois doigts, et on vient réajuster une fenêtre ou encore la réduire en cliquant simplement. Tout cela est très fluide et bien intégré.
Nous avons simplement relevé deux soucis pour l’heure. Le premier est assez évident et peu dépassable : nous nous retrouvons avec un écran plein de traces de doigts. À éviter donc si vous y êtes complètement allergique.
Deuxième problème : le tactile fonctionne davantage comme un pointeur de souris que comme du tactile sur un iPhone. Résultat, certains usages qui peuvent paraitre naturels ne fonctionnent pas. Exemple : pour drag and drop un dossier, il n’est pas possible de juste l’attraper et le déplacer. Il faut rester appuyé un certain temps avant de déclencher l’action attrapée. Autre exemple : lorsqu’on lance un jeu vidéo où le tactile parait plutôt indiqué, comme Balatro, par exemple, cela ne fonctionne pas vraiment comme attendu, avec des micro-lags ici ou là avant chaque action, ce qui oblige à revenir au pavé tactile.
Après quelques jours à le manipuler, l’intégration du tactile sur MacBook Pro est tellement bien finie et agréable, qu’elle ouvre nécessairement la voie à une généralisation de la fonction à terme. Apple va sans aucun doute faire redescendre cette option vers les gammes inférieures. On peut imaginer que le prochain MacBook Air sera servi en premier, puis que, d’ici deux ans, par exemple, un Macbook Neo finisse par le proposer en option. Une chose est sûre : Apple ne s’est pas enquiquiné à rendre tout cela aussi propre pour ne le proposer qu’en option à 400 ou 500 euros.
L’OLED apporte vraiment quelque chose
Le passage à la technologie Tandem OLED est-il un plus par rapport à l’ancien Mini-LED ? D’après nos mesures, réalisées à l’aide Portrait Displays et du logiciel Calman Ultimate, l’ajout le plus intéressant concerne la luminosité.
Comme vous pouvez le voir dans le tableau ci-dessous, le Pic lumineux manuel est certes un cran en dessous de ses prédécesseurs, mais le pic lumineux HDR monte à une valeur très rare dans le monde du PC, avec 1939 cd/m². De quoi damer le pion au Macbook Pro 16 pouces M5 Pro classique et ses 1017 cd/m². En pratique, cela devrait se montrer particulièrement agréable et sympa lorsque vous visionnez un film en Dolby Vision par exemple.
Concernant la colorimétrie, dans les grandes lignes, disons que le MacBook Pro PROLED conserve les qualités de ses prédécesseurs, à savoir une calibration proche de la perfection. Le delta E 2000 moyen, qui mesure la dérive des couleurs, demeure excellent tant en sRGB (0,8) qu’en P3 (0,6), des valeurs très proches des anciens MacBook Pro, à 0,2 ou 0,1 près, soit une différence invisible à l’œil nu.
On note tout de même une bascule sur la balance des blancs. Si les MacBook Pro Mini-LED se plaçait très proche du standard des 6500 K, le passage à l’OLED fait le choix d’une balance légèrement plus froide avec 6782 K. Cela rappelle les écrans OLED des iPhone qui réalisent le même choix et offre ainsi une continuité si vous êtes utilisateurs-rices d’iPhone.
Shortcode P3 + gris
En sRGB, l’écran reste très performant, avec une courbe de couleurs très plate et un maximum à seulement 2, donc à peu près imperceptible.
Shortcode sRGB
En HDR, comme vous pouvez le voir, le Delta E ITP moyen grimpe nécessairement un peu plus haut plutôt que sur un Delta E 2000, mais le score de 4.1 demeure très honorable, malgré quelques pics dans les rouges, les bleus et les magentas.
Shortcode HDR + gris
Dynamic Island : un peu gadget en l’état, mais plaisant visuellement
Dernière nouveauté à aborder et pas des moindres : le MacBook Pro PROLED intègre donc une Dynamic Island inspirée de l’iPhone 18 Pro. Et en l’état, celle-ci reprend tout le langage de design que l’on connaît sur l’iPhone. On retrouve les petites animations en haut de l’écran qui indiquent que de la musique est en cours d’écoute, qu’un appel FaceTime est en cours, ou encore les fameux points orange et vert pour avertir que le microphone ou la caméra sont utilisés.
Il est également possible d’ouvrir des sous-menus lorsqu’on clique sur la Dynamic Island et ainsi accéder à des réglages. C’est le cas sur FaceTime, par exemple. Chaque option peut être manipulée à l’envi à la souris ou au doigt en fonction de votre préférence. Nous avons toutefois rencontré quelques bugs sur cet usage précis.
En conclusion : une superbe intégration, mais rien d’indispensable
À l’arrivée, que pensez de cette nouvelle dalle, à la fois tactile et OLED, le tout percé de la nouvelle Dynamic Island ? D’abord, il faut saluer une intégration quasi parfaite. Tant la partie logicielle du tactile, a part quelques bugs mineurs, que la calibration matérielle de l’écran, sont assez irréprochables. La Dynamic Island est peut-être l’élément le plus faible et le moins intéressant de l’ensemble, puisque l’étendue de ses usages nous parait pour l’heure un peu chiche. À voir comme d’habitude avec le temps si des développeurs d’apps tierces s’en emparent intelligemment.
En revanche, si l’exécution est quasi parfaite, il ne nous semble pas pour l’heure que cette nouvelle dalle soit indispensable au MacBook Pro. C’est sans doute ce que pense Apple également, qui continue de commercialiser sur son site les MacBook Mini-LED avec un prix inférieur de 400 à 500 euros selon les options. Si vous escomptez vraiment vous servir du tactile, vous pouvez donc vous lancer avec plaisir dans cette nouvelle mouture. Si, par contre vous appartenez à la cohorte des sceptiques sur cette nouveauté, penchez plutôt pour un Mini-LED et prenez une version plus musclée du MacBook avec l’argent économisé.
