articles.title: 'Zelda Ocarina of Time' es el juego más influyente de la historia y sólo ha necesitado un lavado de cara para volver a ser perfecto
articles.text:
En Xataka no solemos hablar de notas de videojuegos. En lo personal, tampoco me gusta demasiado porque prefiero leer un texto y formar una opinión sobre el mismo.
Nuestros compañeros de Vidaextra y 3DJuegos hace tiempo que dejaron de poner notas, al igual que otros medios como Eurogamer y demás, pero entre todos los que sí acompañan la valoración de un análisis de un numerito hay cierta unanimidad en algo: el remake de 'The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time' es perfecto.
Hasta el punto de que se acaba de colar como uno de los juegos mejor valorados de la historia. Otra vez.
Venciendo al enemigo del tiempo
Analizar un remake, además uno que es tan extremadamente fiel como este, es complicado. ¿Lo tratas como un juego nuevo? ¿Valoras que cambie algo o que, por el contrario, no cambie nada? ¿Analizas simplemente las mejoras de calidad de vida y el cambio visual?
Por suerte, no es tarea mía responder a esa pregunta y lo mejor es que eches un ojo a los análisis. Mis compañeros de Vidaextra y 3DJuegos ya han contado lo que tienen que contar sobre el juego y parece evidente que es un título que ha salido de lo más redondo, pero hay algo más: el 96 en Metacritic.
Metacritic es lo que es: un agregador de notas. Está bien para ver de un plumazo la opinión de parte de la prensa especializada, pero no deja de ser eso, una web en la que aparecen las notas. Sin embargo, hay compañías que le dan mucha importancia, como una PlayStation que, al menos antes, fijaba metas de puntuación en Metacritic para sus estudios.
Y, en el caso del remake de 'Zelda Ocarina of Time', ese 96 de nota media tras 87 análisis es una absoluta barbaridad que lo eleva al "Olimpo" de las notas.
Se ha llevado una cantidad bárbara de notas perfectas, con una media a la par de 'Half Life', 'Skyrim', 'Gran Turismo', 'Tekken 3', 'Baldur's Gate 3', 'Uncharted 2' o 'Metal Gear Solid 2', pero también con la misma puntuación que 'The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker' o de 'The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom'.
Curiosamente, por muy buenas notas que tenga está tres puntos por detrás del que sigue siendo el mejor juego de la historia... según las notas de Metacritic: 'The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time', el de 1998.
Es el único juego con un 99 de media (con "sólo" 22 reviews) y tiene todo el sentido al ser no sólo uno de los juegos más influyentes de la historia, sino un juego fundacional.
Fue tan adelantado a su tiempo que, añadiendo ciertas mejoras de calidad de vida y ese lavado visual, el remake mantiene el tipo perfectamente. Es evidente que ha salido muy bien, pero ahora el morbo es ver qué pasará cuando salgan los análisis de 'GTA VI'. 'GTA V' tiene un 97 en Metacritic y 'GTA IV' un merecidísimo 98.
Al final, el título de "mejor juego del año" ya se verá en la gala de los GOTY, pero no falta tanto para descubrir cuál de los dos es el que más notas perfectas consigue. Pero bueno, sea como sea, en el caso de 'Ocarina of Time', Alberto Pastor de 3DJuegos resume la experiencia de una forma espectacular: un juego que ha sobrevivido el paso del tiempo.

articles.title: 'We can't get it back' — even Sam Altman worries about who will control AI's future
articles.text:
'We can't get it back': Sam Altman warns of the two ways AI could go 'really wrong' — and one involves losing control of our future
OpenAI's CEO is optimistic about AI even while outlining doomsday scenarios
Sam Altman spends much of his time explaining how AI could transform the world for the better and pushing back against doomsayers. Nonetheless, the OpenAI CEO has some fairly unsettling ideas about how AI development could lead to a disaster, or disasters plural. He outlined a couple of these nightmares during an episode of the Figuring Out With Raj Shamani podcast in disturbing detail.
The two dystopias stem from almost opposite problems: either humanity losing control of increasingly powerful machines, or one group seizing control of most of the technology.
"One is that there’s a loss of control to AI, and we intentionally or accidentally sort of cede control of the future to systems that are unbelievably more capable than we are, and we can’t get it back," Altman said. "And the other is like, one person or company or country gets way too powerful relative to everybody else."
The first scenario is less the tired cliché of a robot uprising and more of a soft surrender of humanity's choices to AI until it's impossible to take back any agency from the AI software. The other is a more modern, if still clichéd, speculative-fiction scenario: an overwhelmingly powerful technology controlled by one person or corporation, leaving everyone else at their mercy. They are both endlessly discussed by people in the industry and policymakers, but having Altman issue the warning is still notable.
Altman, through OpenAI and ChatGPT, is one of, if not the central face of AI to those who have heard the bare minimum about the technology and its flaws. Altman believes those capabilities could bring extraordinary benefits, but his comments suggest he's not sanguine about the looming chaos that AI carries as well.
Handing over decisions
Advanced AI taking over because people cede control has only become a real-world concern in recent years as the technology moved beyond simply answering questions and into decision-making territory. AI agents can already interact with websites and complete complex assignments, and developers are working toward systems that require less and less human supervision. The more responsibility those systems receive, the greater the consequences if their objectives diverge from what people actually intended.
It's important to remember that what we call AI now relies on probability prediction in different forms. While very powerful and leveraging huge amounts of data, it can't actually make judgments like a human, and doesn't have to be malicious to be harmful. That's why models tend to opt for the disastrous choice of using nuclear weapons as a strategy when simulating how to run a nation.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Humans might not understand or approve of how an AI pursues an objective, even if humans issued the task. And if the AI model has enough power and is embedded in enough critical systems, people might not be able to redirect or stop it. After all, an AI system told to reduce gridlock on the road might logically conclude the solution is to remove the roads, or send an order to any Wi-Fi-enabled car to stop operating. That particular scenario is very unlikely, but the fact that it's not actually impossible is unnerving enough.
We're all familiar with the more human problem of technological and industrial monopolies Altman extended to AI in his other apocalyptic warning. Plenty of people have sounded the alarm about how there is already too much power in too few hands with too little regulation. Altman's hands being among them doesn't mean he won't criticize the fact.
"I think it’s actually much better for the world for there to be multiple AI efforts with slightly different approaches that are competing with each other and putting out different ways," Altman said. "I also have this like dislike of too intense power concentration. I think that’s not what works, so I’m hopeful we don’t do that.”
Altman's disdain is in some tension with his company's ambitions and actions. Claiming OpenAI is already dominant in several respects, such as AI infrastructure, is an illustration of the dominance he says he worries about.
"I think we have the most users and the best stack from chips to data centers to models to other things that come around that sort of put abundant intelligence into people’s hands. I think we have the best brand and the values that people who are going to use this technology want," Altman said. Nonetheless, he claimed, "we want everybody else to succeed, and I think people can feel that from us.”
Optimistic doomsaying
Despite those warnings, Altman remains fundamentally optimistic about where AI is taking humanity. Asked about his children growing up in a world increasingly shaped by the technology, he expressed confidence that people would find ways to adapt. His outlook suggests that he sees AI's risks as serious challenges to manage rather than reasons to abandon its development.
"I don’t know what the future’s going to look like, but I am comfortable that I have enormous trust in people to figure out how to adapt and thrive and make society better for all of us," Altman said. "I think the world will most likely keep getting much better."
That optimism extends to OpenAI's future plans to apply AI to scientific exploration. He pointed to recent mathematical achievements as evidence that the technology might be approaching a point where it can contribute meaningfully to fundamental research.
"I am extremely excited to see how far we can push AI to discover new science," Altman said. He envisions "a machine that can help us understand the world better, discover the deepest insights in physics, figure out new medical treatments, a new source of energy, things that I think we can’t even imagine but that better scientific understanding will enable. I am extremely excited for us to go build that machine."

articles.title: Discord is rebuilding its desktop app in Rust to fix its memory problem
articles.text:
Software Pigs Do Fly: PC memory is becoming an increasingly unattainable hardware product these days, which means software developers will need to adapt. Discord, one of the worst offenders when it comes to excessive RAM use, is apparently going to tackle this long-standing issue by giving up on inefficient web-based development frameworks.
Microsoft is finally doing something about Windows 11's abysmal performance on lower-end systems, and third-party software developers are following suit. Discord's CTO has recently confirmed that the popular messaging platform is soon getting a brand-new desktop client. Unlike past web-based versions, it should deliver much better performance thanks to the adoption of the Rust programming language.
Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy said the company has been adopting Rust since 2018, using the general-purpose, memory-safe language in several parts of its infrastructure and products. Some parts of the current client are written in Rust as well, but converting the whole app is apparently going to take longer.
 – Stanislav (@svishnevskiy) November 4, 2026
The Electron-based app is going away, Vishnevskiy confirmed, and so is React Native on mobile. Electron apps can exploit the pervasiveness of JavaScript and other popular web technologies, but they are extremely taxing on performance compared to C, Rust, or other native code. Every Electron app ships with its own copy of Chromium, which means memory usage is always going to be higher than with native alternatives.
Vishnevskiy shared a screenshot from his system's Task Manager in which the "Discord Phoenix" app is humming along at around 290 MB of RAM. Electron-based Discord is notorious for being a massive memory hog, wasting gigabytes of DRAM and forcing developers to resort to some questionable tricks to try and improve performance and efficiency.
The new Rust client will hopefully solve both issues. Discord's mobile version will retain its current native UI, Vishnevskiy said, but will share the same Rust code now being adopted for the desktop release. The company wants to put a beta version in users' hands soon, although no specific timeframe has been given at this point.
Discord's push to make its app more efficient could not have come at a better time. AI data center plans are ravaging the chip supply chain, and PC DRAM products are now at the bottom of most manufacturers' priority lists. According to TeamGroup CEO Chen Ching-wen, customers will soon be unable to purchase any quantity of DDR4 or DDR5 RAM no matter how much money they have.

articles.title: Container orchestration for AI: Latest trends at KubeCon - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
What to expect during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA: Join theCUBE Nov. 10-12
Kubernetes has emerged as the default container orchestration standard, a foundational platform layer across the enterprise. Will Kubernetes also play a central role in positioning the next generation of AI workloads for production?
This is the question on the minds of the cloud-native community as it gathers this month for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA in Salt Lake City. With the rise of AI agents that have progressed from answering user questions to executing code and running business systems, customers are increasingly interested in controlling what autonomous agents are allowed to do.
“That brings us to OpenShell, an open-source secure agent runtime that Red Hat is helping develop alongside Nvidia and, of, course, the broader community,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante, during a pre-event interview. “The approach puts enforcement into the environment where the agent operates, setting boundaries around what it can access and execute rather than relying on a model alone to follow the rules. We think this is a central question for the next chapter of cloud native: how do enterprises give agents enough freedom to be useful without giving up control?”
During KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, Nov. 10-12, theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with executives from Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp., among others. TheCUBE will examine the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production. (* Disclosure below.)
Container orchestration for AI
OpenShell, while still an early-stage project, is actively being developed for Kubernetes environments. The activity reflects growing customer interest in using containerized environments for applications, according to theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty.
“Fifty-one percent of organizations report that 51–75% of their applications now run in containers, representing a sharp rise from just a few years ago,” Nashawaty said. “Organizations now run the majority of their applications in containers which is a sharp rise that reflects the accelerating cloud-native transformation central to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.”
OpenShell was accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project in September. One component of OpenShell allows agents to run in isolated sandboxes with limits on the files they can reach, an approach actively supported by the cloud-native community within the Kubernetes ecosystem.
“It builds on top of some core Kubernetes special interest groups,” said Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, during an interview with theCUBE. “The Agent Sandbox is one of them so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes APIs.”
Kubernetes-native security
Cheslock’s point about security highlights the growing concerns and recent publicity surrounding AI agents and their ability to break out of isolated environments and compromise systems. Rapid enterprise adoption and integration of AI are increasing the risk profiles for organizations, a topic that will be on the agenda for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.
“Our research data reveals that 41.3% of organizations cite increased vulnerability risk as the top security challenge, introduced by faster CI/CD cycles and a tension that cloud-native teams are increasingly turning to Kubernetes-native tooling to resolve,” Nashawaty said.
Enterprise reliance on cloud-native tools and open-source software requires confidence that these technologies are safe to use inside enterprise infrastructure. In May, Red Hat and IBM Corp. unveiled Project Lightwell, a $5 billion commitment to help enterprises secure open-source software.
“For the last year, especially since the Mythos moment, [security] has been the first thing that we’ve talked about in every customer conversation I’ve had,” said Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights for hybrid platforms at Red Hat, in conversation with theCUBE. “We’re trying to make sure that customers can feel secure and understand and use these tools. There’s even more effort being put on security than ever, which has always been a focus of Red Hat. If we don’t make sure that layer is as locked down and reliable and trusted as possible, everything else becomes secondary.”
Tools for multicloud
At this month’s KubeCon gathering, theCUBE will explore how various practitioners are using Kubernetes to ensure workload portability across multicloud environments. Companies such as Vultr and ScaleOps are building Kubernetes-based tools that can support a range of platforms, reflecting enterprise computing trends.
“With our AppDev research finding that 94% of organizations now operate across two or more cloud providers, the demand for consistent, developer-friendly Kubernetes-based platforms has never been more pressing,” Nashawaty explained.
KubeCon also offers an opportunity to assess the progress of key technology projects under the CNCF umbrella. One of the major contributors in this arena has been Google LLC, which contributed the open-source service mesh Istio, serverless building blocks via Knative and Kubernetes itself. KubeCon is an annual reminder of how large the CNCF ecosystems has become, according to Red Hat’s Miniman.
“They’ve got a big ecosystem. I can give example after example of who created these technologies,” Miniman told theCUBE. “Oh yeah, the GitOps stuff came out of Intuit, and the platform engineering stuff came out of Spotify. Just find your focus and go in there, because there is no way you can cover all of it.”
TheCUBE event livestream
Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA from Nov. 10-12. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.
How to watch theCUBE interviews
We offer various ways for you to watch theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also get all the coverage from this year’s events on SiliconANGLE.
TheCUBE podcasts
SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.
SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.
Guests
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, theCUBE will speak with Red Hat leaders and other industry executives about the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production.

articles.title: Amazon agora oferece AppleCare na compra de iPhones no Brasil • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Amazon agora oferece AppleCare na compra de iPhones no Brasil
Garantia estendida da Maçã fica disponível automaticamente para celulares da marca vendidos no e-commerce.
A Amazon anunciou que vai oferecer o serviço AppleCare de forma automática na compra de iPhones na plataforma. A novidade foi anunciada junto à chegada dos iPhone 18 Pro e iPhone 18 Pro Max ao e-commerce. Apresentados em setembro, os aparelhos chegaram ao Brasil com preços a partir de R$ 11.999.
A novidade vale para qualquer modelo de iPhone vendido e entregue pela Amazon, garantindo 24 meses de cobertura global. O suporte permite acesso a substituições e peças originais da Maçã, além de especialistas da própria empresa nas Apple Store e lojas autorizadas.
A varejista é o primeiro e-commerce a disponibilizar o AppleCare, em parceria com a Assurant. O serviço já era oferecido para iPhones no país por meio da operadora Vivo e do banco Itaú. No site da Apple, também é possível contratar a garantia estendida, mas a opção está restrita a Mac, iPad e Apple TV.
Com a proteção estendida, os clientes podem acessar o suporte oficial da Maçã 24 horas por dia, além de contar com especialistas próprios da Apple em lojas oficiais e credenciadas. A ativação é automática e via IMEI, com reparos feitos por profissionais autorizados, garantia de peças originais e mais benefícios.
Apesar de chegar na Amazon, o AppleCare ainda tem algumas restrições por aqui. Antes da novidade, o serviço só ficava disponível para iPhones por meio de seguros feitos junto à Vivo ou ao Itaú. Agora, serviços como atendimento especializado direto pelo aplicativo e facilidade no acesso ao conserto do dispositivo não exigem pagamento de uma assinatura, por exemplo.
De acordo com a diretora de telefonia e serviços da Amazon Brasil, Gabriela Giannico, a ideia é “oferecer aos consumidores brasileiros confiança e segurança em cada etapa: compra, entrega e proteção a longo prazo”.
O AppleCare da Amazon funciona em parceria com a Assurant, que também está por trás do serviço oferecido pelo Itaú, disponível desde 2022 para clientes do programa iPhone para Sempre.
Segundo a Amazon, além do AppleCare em si, clientes também podem parcelar a compra do iPhone em até 12x sem juros no site ou app.

articles.title: Sony revives the original Walkman headphones, adds USB-C
articles.text:
Color us nostalgic.
Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player.
Originally called the “MDR-3L2,” the first Walkman headphones were known for their sleek, adjustable gray plastic headband, which extended via metal sliders and ended in signature orange, circular ear cushions. The lightweight, on-ear headphones are a contrast to the bulky headsets that are popular these days, which use wide, cushioned headbands for long-term comfort and large earcups that can support big drivers and are often heavily padded for noise isolation.
The new MDR-3R (note the slightly different name) headphones look just like the originals and come with orange and blue ear cushions.
New headphones are often wireless these days, but the MDR-3R continues the wired tradition of the MDR-3, with an essential twist: a USB-C connector.
“The MDR-3R has been redesigned for modern use while preserving the experience value of freely taking music out into the world, which the original MDR-3 helped popularize,” Sony’s announcement says.

articles.title: Freedom Mobile to upgrade all plans to Canada/U.S./Mexico data
articles.text:
Freedom Mobile is giving all monthly mobile data plans access to Canada/U.S./Mexico data coverage at no extra cost.
In an announcement sent to MobileSyrup on Nov. 5, the carrier said it would update eligible customers’ data plans starting on Dec. 8. In a follow-up email to MobileSyrup, Freedom noted that some “more niche plans, such as pay-per-use data plans,” will eventually get converted as well, but it won’t happen on Dec. 8.
“There are no changes to customers’ monthly price or recurring data allotment. Instead, customers will benefit from a simpler experience, using their included data seamlessly across Canada, the United States and Mexico without daily roaming fees or the need to swap SIM cards while travelling,” Freedom said.
Notably, Freedom has offered plans with Canada/U.S./Mexico data for a while now, as well as other roaming benefits like Roam Beyond data and unlimited talk and text in over 120 global destinations.
However, for customers on older Freedom plans that might not have the Canada/U.S./Mexico coverage, this is a major win. It also aligns with some of Freedom’s other benefits, like the carrier’s ‘Price Freeze Promise,” which pledges not to increase customers’ wireless rates as long as they keep their plan.
This comes after Freedom said it was “gearing up to switch on its wireless network in Manitoba” last month as it continues a push to expand its Canadian network.

articles.title: UPERFECT GR14BU portable monitor review: A 120 Hz 3K OLED touch display at a killer price
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
Although it has some flaws, the GR14BU excels in value pricing, features, and performance.
Reasons to buy
- + Bright, colorful display
- + 3K resolution and touch support
- + 120 Hz panel
- + Value pricing
Reasons to avoid
- - Kickstand and overall design don’t support portrait mode
- - Cheap OSD buttons
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
As the portable monitor category matures, a number of new players have entered the market to claim their share of the pie. One company that we haven’t had a chance to sample yet is UPERFECT. But the company is coming out of the gate swinging with the first review sample that it sent our way: the GR14BU.
As its name suggests, the GR14BU is a 14-inch portable monitor, but it doesn’t have a run-of-the-mill 60 Hz 1080p IPS panel like you’ll find on most of the best portable monitors in this segment. Instead, it features an OLED panel with a dense 2880 × 1800 (3K) resolution and a 120 Hz maximum refresh rate. On top of that, the GR14BU also supports touch input in Windows 11.
On paper, it’s a promising product with a street price of under $300. That’s roughly three times the price of a garden-variety 14-inch IPS panels, but is it worth the premium?
Design of the UPERFECT GR14BU
At first glance, the GR14BU impresses with its black aluminum frame that wraps around the 14-inch panel. The sleek design is enhanced by the glossy glass, which is typical for OLED panels.
Things take a downward turn from there, however. While the GR14BU features an integrated kickstand, which is much appreciated on a portable monitor, it’s tiny and is mounted directly in the middle of the back panel of the monitor. Because of this position, the GR14BU can only be used in landscape mode. Even if you could somehow prop the monitor up in portrait mode, this would be hindered by the two USB-C ports and HDMI port on the right side of the monitor, and the five OSD buttons on the left side.
Speaking of the OSD buttons, they feel cheap and wobble around like buttons you might find on a cheap plastic stopwatch you’d find at Dollar Tree. They’re shockingly bad for a device with a $399 MSRP. The five buttons are: Power, OSD, Up, Down, and Back.
UPERFECT included a plethora of cables and adapters in the box, which should satisfy all your connectivity needs. Our review unit included two USB-C-to-USB-C cables, one micro-HDMI to HDMI cable, two 180-degree USB-C to USB-C adapters, one 180-degree micro-HDMI to HDMI adapter, and one USB-C wall adapter.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
One thing to note as we discuss cables and adapters is that when connecting the GR14BU to my test system using a single USB-C to USB-C cable, the monitor was locked at 20 percent brightness and would not go any higher. However, when using the second USB-C to USB-C adapter connected to the USB-C wall adapter, the GR14BU would automatically boost brightness to its maximum level.
UPERFECT GR14BU Specifications
| Panel Type / Backlight | OLED | 
| Screen Size / Aspect Ratio | 14 inches / 16:10 | 
| Max Resolution & Refresh Rate | 2880 x 1600 @ 120 Hz | 
| Response Time | 1 ms (GtG) | 
| Typical Brightness | 500 nits | 
| Contrast Ratio Typical | 100,000:1 | 
| Ports | 2x USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode), 1x micro-HDMI | 
| Speakers | 2 x 1-watt | 
| Touch Support | Yes | 
| Dimensions | 12.2 x 8.5 x 0.28 inches | 
| Weight | 1.3 pounds | 
| Warranty | 1 year | 
OSD on the UPERFECT GR14BU
The OSD on the GR14BU is no-frills, offering just the basic controls that you’d expect to find on a portable monitor. Without even accessing the main OSD, pressing the Up button brings up the volume controls, with a subsequent press of the Up button raising the volume, while pressing the Down button lowers the volume. Likewise, pressing the Down button separately invokes the Brightness menu.
Pressing the dedicated OSD button brings up the full menu, where you can access picture and color settings. Pressing the Up and Down buttons navigates you through the OSD; pressing the OSD button again executes a menu item, while the Back button takes you back one level in the OSD.
Display Performance on the UPERFECT GR14BU
The GR14BU features a 14-inch display with a dense-for-its-size 2880 x 1600 resolution, in a 16:10 aspect ratio. That pixel-dense panel is backed by a 120 Hz refresh rate, which is twice that of most portable monitors, along with multi-touch support in Windows 11.
UPERFECT claims that the GR14BU has a maximum brightness of 500 nits, but we measured a maximum of 368.6 nits when plugged in at 100 percent. While well short of the manufacturer’s claim, this is clsoe to peers like the Asus ZenScreen OLED MQ16AH (369.4 nits) and ViewSonic ColorPro VP16-OLED (369.8 nits).
Our instrumented tests also showed similar color performance to the Asus and ViewSonic. The GR14BU measured 132.2 percent coverage of the DCI-P3 color space, while sRGB coverage came in at 186.6 percent.
In real-world scenarios, I found the panel to be sufficiently bright in my well-lit home office, and even enough to overcome most reflections when sitting outside in overcast conditions. Colors looked vibrant, with especially punchy reds and greens while looking at nature footage on YouTube. As with all OLED monitors, black levels were impeccable, which I particularly took note of while watching the latest teaser trailers for Avengers: Doomsday.
For my usual productivity tasks, I was really disappointed that I couldn’t use the GR14BU in portrait mode, which is probably the biggest miss for me. I like having that versatility to switch between portrait and landscape modes at will.
I also tested out the 120 Hz refresh rate at native resolution for gaming. I played Battlefield 6 with the GR14BU hooked up to my desktop computer via HDMI and had no trouble until there was heavy action on the screen. It was then that frame rates momentarily dipped into the 90 fps range, and I noticed a bit of screen tearing. The GR14BU doesn’t support any kind of Adaptive-Sync technology, like FreeSync or G-Sync.
UPERFECT includes a pair of tinny speakers integrated into the GR14BU. There is quite a bit of audio distortion once you get past 75 percent, but if you keep the volume at a moderate level, the quality is passable. There’s no bass, and music sounds flat (I tried various genres, ranging from Jay-Z to Susanne Sundfør to Jai Wolf). You’re better off relying on your laptop’s built-in speakers than relying on the pair included on the GR14BU.
Bottom Line
I came in expecting a lot from the UPERFECT GR14BU, given its specs. However, there are plenty of caveats. The GR14BU has a bright and colorful 3K OLED panel, along with a 120 Hz refresh rate. It even includes an integrated kickstand and internal speakers.
However, the kickstand doesn’t allow the monitor to be used in portrait mode, and the 120 Hz maximum refresh rate doesn’t have the backing of Adaptive-Sync. There are also some quality lapses, like the woefully cheap OSD buttons.
However, much of this can be overlooked considering the price. The GR14BU can be had right now for $299 from Amazon, making it an incredible value given the specs. For comparison, we recently reviewed the Asus ZenScreen OLED (MQ16FC), which has a 16.1-inch 1200p OLED non-touch display with a 60 Hz refresh rate. The GR14BU outclasses the MQ16FC in color performance, brightness, and specs while only commanding a $30 premium and including touch. That’s an impressive feat, despite its design and build deficiencies.
Brandon Hill is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware. He has written about PC and Mac tech since the late 1990s with bylines at AnandTech, DailyTech, and Hot Hardware. When he is not consuming copious amounts of tech news, he can be found enjoying the NC mountains or the beach with his wife and two sons.

articles.title: Aina AI Ring: Rs 47,000 Wearable Brings AI Agents Closer
articles.text:
Aina launches Rs 47,000 ring to bring AI agents to your fingertips
As AI agents become capable of handling everyday tasks, Aina is betting that a smart ring can make interacting with technology simpler. But can it offer enough utility to justify a Rs 47,000 price tag?
What if booking a cab, sending a message or managing a meeting required nothing more than a flick of your thumb? Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based startup Aina believes the next phase of artificial intelligence will be less about asking machines questions and more about letting them anticipate what people need. At a private launch event in Bengaluru, the startup unveiled an AI-powered smart ring that combines a colour display, voice commands and gesture-based controls. Priced at $499 (Rs 47,000), the device is available for pre-order at a limited early-bird price starting at $399 (Rs 37,700), with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. Unlike conventional smart rings, which largely focus on health and fitness tracking, Aina wants its device to become an everyday interface between users and AI agents. The premise is simple: AI agents are getting smarter, but using them still involves unlocking phones, navigating apps and approving individual actions. Aina wants to reduce that friction. Its proposition revolves around a question displayed during the launch presentation: What if AI didn't wait to be asked?
An AI ring that anticipates your next move
To simplify these interactions, Aina has built its ring around three features: Cues, Voice and Remote.
Cues uses contextual information, including routines and connected applications, to anticipate what users might want to do next. For instance, if someone regularly books a cab around the same time each morning, the ring could suggest booking a ride without waiting for an explicit request. At the launch event, Aina demonstrated a ride-booking interaction that illustrated how everyday transactions could be completed through minimal gestures.
The ring can be operated using a five-way joystick-like control, allowing users to approve or reject suggestions with their thumb without reaching for a smartphone. Aina says its context-aware intelligence can learn users' routines and anticipate relevant actions over the next 15 minutes, drawing on information from the iPhone, Mac and connected services. The company showcased integrations involving Uber, Apple Music, Spotify, phone calls, calendar meetings, smart home controls and email actions.
The second interaction method, Voice, allows users to dictate notes, set reminders, send messages and issue commands. Aina also showcased use cases involving WhatsApp and Telegram, alongside Mac dictation through Wispr Flow. The third feature, Remote, turns the ring into a controller for connected devices. According to the company, users can manage music, phone calls, smart home appliances and meeting controls without picking up another device.
What goes into the $499 ring?
According to specifications presented at the Bengaluru launch, the ring weighs less than 13 grams and features a titanium body, full-colour display, haptic feedback and directional audio. The company claims up to 18 hours of battery life and plans to offer the device in four colours: Eclipse Black, Amber Gold, Mercury Silver and Slate Titanium, across seven sizes. Aina also highlighted a five-way control mechanism called the Shifter, which works alongside its gesture-based interface.
The startup says the ring will come with an open developer platform, allowing third-party developers to build new interactions and integrations. It also showcased support for AI agent platforms including Muse, Grokbot and Instinct. The company currently supports iOS and Mac, with further integrations expected to be announced later. Whether its open platform translates into a substantial developer ecosystem will become clearer once the device reaches customers.
From Ultrahuman to Aina
Aina was founded by Apoorv Shankar, who previously served as vice-president of hardware at Bengaluru-based wearable technology company Ultrahuman. Shankar founded Aina in May 2025 as a human-computer interaction lab, focusing on how people could interact with intelligent software beyond conventional screens and keyboards. The startup raised $5.5 million in seed funding in July 2026, as previously reported by YourStory. The round was led by Redstart Labs and 360 ONE Asset, with participation from MIXI Global Investments, Antler, Blume Founders Fund and angel investors including CRED founder Kunal Shah and Razorpay co-founders Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar. The funding was earmarked for commercialising its AI-first hardware interface and expanding its engineering and product teams.
Aina says it spent around 15 months developing the technology and began testing the ring with a limited group of users in October 2026.
Can a ring replace everyday smartphone interactions?
Aina's launch comes as technology companies experiment with new ways of bringing AI into daily life. While smartphones remain the dominant interface for digital services, the rise of AI agents is prompting startups to rethink how people give instructions, approve actions and receive information. Aina's approach is to make that interface smaller and more contextual, with users retaining control over whether suggested actions are executed.
However, at $499, the ring is a premium purchase, particularly when smartphones and smartwatches already perform many of the functions it promises. Its usefulness will depend on how accurately its AI anticipates user needs, how reliably it works with third-party services and whether the thumb-based controls become intuitive enough for daily use. Battery life, voice recognition and application support will also matter when the product moves beyond controlled demonstrations. For now, Aina's claims remain to be tested at scale, with commercial deliveries planned for January 2027.

articles.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time : ça y est, tout le monde fait déjà n’importe quoi avec l’ocarina
articles.text:
Sorti ce jeudi 5 novembre sur Nintendo Switch 2, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time fait revivre l’un des épisodes les plus emblématiques de la saga. Cette nouvelle version profite de graphismes entièrement remaniés, de cinématiques doublées, de musiques orchestrales et de contrôles modernisés, sans perdre ce qui faisait le charme de l’original. Le remake ajoute aussi une fonction inédite : la possibilité de jouer de l’ocarina pour de vrai.
Dans le jeu, l’ocarina sert notamment à faire passer le jour à la nuit, à se téléporter ou à appeler Epona, la jument de Link. Les boutons de la manette suffisent, mais vous pouvez aussi fredonner ou chanter la mélodie devant le micro de la console, voire jouer d’un vrai instrument : Link la reproduit avec le sien. Les fans s’en sont emparés dès la sortie, transformant cette fonctionnalité en véritable terrain de jeu.
Comme le jeu se contente d’une mélodie ressemblante, rien n’oblige les plus mélomanes (ou les moins, on ne sait pas trop) à jouer ou chanter juste. Si certains prennent le sujet très au sérieux et jouent des airs d’ocarina très fidèles, d’autres ont déjà détourné la fonctionnalité pour en faire… n’importe quoi.
L’ocarina de Zelda: Ocarina of Time est déjà détourné
Les réseaux sociaux étant des outils formidables pour transformer une chose toute simple en usine à mèmes, les premières vidéos détournant cette fonctionnalité n’ont pas tardé à fleurir sur Reddit, X et Bluesky. Quelques notes improbables et une séquence de gameplay suffisent à faire d’Ocarina of Time un défouloir pour les amateurs de détournements. Beaucoup ont ainsi vite testé les limites de la reconnaissance sonore : le jeu identifie une mélodie criée dans le micro, jouée sur un vrai instrument ou même diffusée par un autre écran.
La situation est d’autant plus cocasse que l’ocarina occupe une place importante dans l’identité d’Ocarina of Time. Ses mélodies font partie des souvenirs les plus marquants de nombreux fans de Zelda, et voir cette mécanique emblématique détournée pour jouer n’importe quoi revient donc à prendre un élément sacré avec l’intention de ne surtout pas se tenir tranquilles.
La Switch 2 n’a sans doute pas fini d’entendre des versions très libres du Chant d’Epona.

articles.title: J'ai pris en main le Motorola Signature 27 : a-t-il de quoi inquiéter le Galaxy S26 Ultra ?
articles.text:
Après avoir officialisé son Signature 27 en septembre dernier, Motorola s’est décidé à le présenter ce jeudi 5 novembre. Nous avons pu prendre en main le nouveau smartphone haut de gamme de la marque, et il a de sérieux atouts à faire valoir face à ses concurrents comme le Galaxy S26 Ultra, l’iPhone 18 Pro ou encore le Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, pour ne citer qu’eux. Voici notre premier avis sur le Motorola Signature 27, en attendant notre test complet.
Un grand smartphone haut de gamme
Avec sa diagonale d’écran de 6,8 pouces, le Motorola Signature fait clairement partie des grands gabarits. Pour autant, il reste très agréable à utiliser à une main. Le smartphone est très fin pour sa taille et il garde un bon équilibre malgré son bloc caméra plus épais que le reste du téléphone. Le châssis est un mélange d’aluminium et de céramique qui fait très « premium » et le dos profite de deux finitions assez différentes.
La première finition se trouve sur le modèle noir charbon. Il s’agit d’un tissu texturé qui propose un bon « grip » une fois en main et qui fait un peu penser au kevlar que l’on retrouvait sur certains Motorola Razr. Le modèle vert olive du téléphone opte quant à lui pour une finition plus douce au toucher.
Côté ergonomie, on retrouve les boutons d’alimentation et de volume sur la tranche droite, un bouton dédié à l’IA sur la tranche gauche, ainsi qu’un système de haut-parleurs stéréo (en haut et en bas) conçu en partenariat avec Bang & Olufsen, et plus Bose comme sur le Motorola Signature.
Côté batterie, Motorola a mis les petits plats dans les grands en intégrant une batterie de 7000 mAh, compatible avec la charge filaire 90W et la charge sans fil 50 W. Aucun chargeur n’est fourni dans la boîte, il faudra donc en avoir un compatible.
Un écran Tandem OLED qui met une claque
L’écran est l’une des évolutions les plus impressionnantes de ce modèle. Le Signature 27 embarque une dalle Extreme AMOLED Duo de 6,8 pouces (LTPO 120 Hz, Dolby Vision). La grande nouveauté repose sur l’adoption de la technologie Tandem OLED (deux dalles OLED superposées), comme sur le dernier MacBook Pro. De quoi obtenir un contraste parfait et des couleurs éclatantes.
Motorola annonce une luminosité maximale pouvant atteindre 12 000 cd/m2 en mode automatique. Oui l’écran est impressionnant, mais cette prise en main ne nous a pas permis de le mettre à l’épreuve. Le 01lab s’en chargera pour notre test complet du Motorola Signature 27.
Performances et refroidissement : le chaud et le froid
Le Motorola Signature 27 embarque une puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 (ouf !) gravée en 2 nm, couplée à 16 Go de RAM LPDDR5X et jusqu’à 1 To de stockage UFS 4.1. On ne se fait pas beaucoup de soucis sur la capacité du téléphone à tout faire tourner comme une horloge, mais une telle puissance dans un smartphone aussi fin semble avoir demandé pas mal de travail au niveau du refroidissement.
Motorola a donc agrandi son système de refroidissement (qui était un des points faibles du précédent modèle). On retrouve donc une nouvelle chambre à vapeur, du métal liquide, du cuivre et un nouveau gel thermique. Là encore, nous verrons lors de notre test si ce système de refroidissement « ArcticMesh » tient ses promesses lorsque l’on repousse le téléphone dans ses retranchements.
Quatre modules photo
Pour son bloc caméra arrière, le Motorola Signature 27 muscle son jeu par rapport au modèle précédent. On retrouve ainsi :
- Un capteur principal de 50 Mpx (Sony LYTIA 910) avec stabilisation optique (OIS).
- Un téléobjectif périscope 200 Mpx offrant un zoom optique 5x et un zoom numérique jusqu’à 100x.
- Un ultra grand-angle 50 Mpx.
- Un capteur de mouvement dédié pour capturer les sujets en mouvement de la manière la plus nette possible.
Côté vidéo, le téléphone est capable de capturer jusqu’en 8K à 30 i/s.
Quelques photos prises avec le Motorola Signature 27. – © 01net
Et côté logiciel, ça donne quoi ?
Motorola promet 7 ans de mises à jour de l’OS et de sécurité pour son Signature 27. L’interface est assez épurée, ce qui n’est pas pour nous déplaire. On retrouve évidemment des fonctionnalités IA, avec notamment les outils de chez Google comme Gemini Gemini Omni pour la génération et l’édition de vidéos à partir de prompts, et Lyria pour la création musicale. Rambler, la dictée vocale survitaminée par l’IA du clavier Gboard est également de la partie.
Le téléphone est également compatible avec le système d’exploitation GrapheneOS, ce qui devrait plaire à ceux qui accordent beaucoup d’importance à la confidentialité et la sécurité.
Prix et date de sortie : on n’était pas prêts
Le Motorola Signature sera vendu au prix conseillé de 1899 € sur le site de Motorola. Vous avez bien lu. À titre de comparaison, l’iPhone 18 Pro Max est vendu à partir de 1629 € et le Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra à partir de 1469 €. Il sera également disponible chez Orange à partir de 839 € TTC si vous souscrivez un forfait 200 Go.
Les précommandes débutent le 16 novembre et se terminent le 2 décembre, date de lancement officielle du Motorola Signature 27.
De belles promesses à confirmer dans notre test complet
Cette première prise en main du Signature 27 nous a confirmé les ambitions de Motorola. Le produit est très prometteur, mais il faudra éclaircir ou confirmer certains points, comme l’autonomie, la qualité de l’écran ou encore les performances thermiques, lors de notre test complet afin de savoir si le Signature 27 a les épaules pour rivaliser avec les cadors du marché.

articles.title: Le Bluetooth, c'est fini : Sony ressuscite son mythique casque Walkman en version USB-C
articles.text:
Le Bluetooth, c'est fini : Sony ressuscite son mythique casque Walkman en version USB-C
Sony ressuscite le MDR-3, son casque emblématique lancé en 1979 avec le premier Walkman, dans une version filaire USB-C qui mise sur la nostalgie et la simplicité.
Le regain d’intérêt pour les produits audio filaires, synonymes de praticité (pas d’appairage Bluetooth, pas de batterie) et de déconnexion dans un monde où le numérique nous sollicite en permanence, ne se limite plus aux écouteurs. Pour preuve, Sony vient de dévoiler un casque filaire vintage baptisé MDR-3R, directement inspiré du légendaire MDR-3. Celui-ci avait été commercialisé pour la première fois en 1979 avec le baladeur cassette TPS-L2, le tout premier Walkman de Sony.
Sony MDR-3R
Sony MDR-3R : un casque vintage fidèle à l’original de 1979
Au-delà des plus jeunes générations attirées par le rétro, Sony s’adresse également aux nostalgiques ayant connu ce casque à l’époque. Le design du MDR-3R est en effet pratiquement impossible à différencier de celui du modèle original, tant du côté de ses dimensions que de sa structure en aluminium, en passant par son arceau ajustable flexible et ses aérations acoustiques à l’extérieur des coques. Malgré la présence d’un câble, il se veut pratique en déplacement, notamment en raison de sa compacité et de son poids plume de seulement 38 g.
Le MDR-3R est par conséquent très spartiate, loin des standards élevés des casques Bluetooth actuels. Sony ne s’est volontairement pas écarté de cette conception dépassée, tant pour rendre hommage au produit original que pour ne pas faire grimper la facture.
USB-C, télécommande et microphone : le MDR-3R s’adapte aux usages actuels
Malgré cela, Sony s’est attelé à adapter le MDR-3R aux modes d’écoute actuels. De fait, il troque la terminaison mini-jack 3,5 mm de son ancêtre contre un connecteur USB-C pouvant être branché sur n’importe quel smartphone, tablette ou ordinateur d'aujourd'hui.
À noter que le câble n’est pas amovible au niveau des oreillettes. Une telle conception aurait permis à Sony de proposer un câble mini-jack 3,5 mm optionnel pour ceux qui souhaiteraient également utiliser le MDR-3R avec des sources analogiques, mais cela ne semble malheureusement pas au programme.
En tant que produit nomade adapté à son époque, le MDR-3R intègre une télécommande sur son câble, qui permet de gérer facilement la lecture (play/pause, passage des pistes) et le volume. En complément, celle-ci intègre également un microphone permettant de répondre aux appels téléphoniques. Autant de petits raffinements que le MDR-3 ne possédait évidemment pas.
Un retour rétro à 70 €, décliné en édition Stranger Things
S’appuyant sur les caractéristiques techniques du modèle d’origine, le MDR-3R conserve les transducteurs de 23 mm du MDR-3. Néanmoins, Sony aurait modernisé leur signature sonore pour répondre aux attentes des auditeurs d’aujourd’hui. Il en résulterait une restitution "naturelle et harmonieuse", et potentiellement des basses plus profondes.
Bien sûr, le MDR-3R demeure un casque supra-auriculaire dont les petites coques sont séparées de l’oreille uniquement par de très fins coussinets en mousse. Il ne faut donc pas s’attendre à la moindre isolation acoustique et, par conséquent, à une extension correcte dans le bas du spectre.
Dans la boîte, on retrouve à la fois des coussinets orange et bleu, à l’image du modèle emblématique. Sony a d’ailleurs poussé la nostalgie très loin, puisque le casque est livré avec le même packaging et le même manuel d’utilisation que celui commercialisé en 1979. Le MDR-3R est aussi décliné dans une édition spéciale Stranger Things, célèbre série Netflix dans laquelle le personnage de Max utilise à plusieurs reprises le combo Walkman TPS-L2 + casque MDR-3.
Le MDR-3R et le MDR-3R Stranger Things seront disponibles dès ce mois de novembre aux prix respectifs de 70 € et 80 €. À ce tarif, il existe bien sûr des casques Bluetooth bien plus performants chez Xiaomi ou CMF notamment, mais le MDR-3R s’impose avant tout comme un objet lifestyle, aussi bien capable de ravir les fans de néo-rétro que les nostalgiques des années 80.
Maintenant, il ne manque plus à Sony que de rééditer ses emblématiques Walkman CD ou cassette, plutôt que d’utiliser cette marque pour lancer des baladeurs numériques à 5000 €, dont le recours à des composants plaqués or suffit à justifier une bonne partie du tarif.

articles.title: La peur d'un blocage des réseaux sociaux propulse cette application gratuite au sommet des téléchargements
articles.text:
Portée par les manifestations d'octobre et la panne d'Orange, Bitchat grimpe dans les classements français. Cette messagerie gratuite, lancée par Jack Dorsey, permet de communiquer sans Internet ni réseau mobile.
Les applications comme WhatsApp ou Signal ont besoin d'une connexion Internet pour transmettre des messages. Bitchat propose une autre approche : faire communiquer les smartphones directement entre eux, sans passer par les infrastructures des opérateurs. Gratuite et open source, cette application disponible sur Android et iOS connaît depuis quelques semaines un regain d'intérêt en France.
- Maillage Bluetooth hors ligne
- Relais automatiques multi-sauts
- Chiffrement privé de bout en bout
Une messagerie propulsée par les manifestations et les inquiétudes autour des réseaux sociaux
Disponible depuis juillet 2025, Bitchat a été développée à l'initiative de Jack Dorsey, cofondateur de Twitter. Jusqu'alors relativement confidentielle en France, elle a commencé à gagner en popularité dans le sillage des manifestations du 17 octobre 2026 contre la vie chère, marquées par des violences et des pillages.
Le 19 octobre, Gabriel Attal a proposé de bloquer temporairement certains réseaux sociaux dans les zones touchées par des émeutes. Deux jours plus tard, le ministre de l'Intérieur Laurent Nuñez a également évoqué la possibilité de suspendre leur utilisation en cas de pillages importants. Ces déclarations ont alimenté les inquiétudes, même si aucune coupure des plateformes n'avait alors été décidée.
Sur les réseaux sociaux, des appels à installer Bitchat ont commencé à circuler en prévision des mobilisations des 24 et 31 octobre. L'objectif était notamment de pouvoir continuer à échanger en cas de saturation des antennes mobiles ou d'indisponibilité d'Internet.
La panne nationale d'Orange du 21 octobre a ajouté un argument assez concret à cette démarche. Pendant près de dix heures, une partie des abonnés de l'opérateur a rencontré d'importantes difficultés pour appeler, envoyer des SMS ou accéder à Internet depuis son téléphone.
Le résultat s'est rapidement vu dans les classements. Le 22 octobre, Bitchat occupait la première place de la catégorie « Réseaux sociaux » sur l'App Store français. Le 30 octobre, elle conservait cette position et atteignait le 22e rang de l'ensemble des applications gratuites. Sur Android, elle avait également grimpé à la neuvième place de la catégorie « Communication » le 23 octobre.
Comment Bitchat permet de communiquer sans Internet
Contrairement aux messageries traditionnelles, Bitchat utilise principalement le Bluetooth Low Energy pour établir des communications locales entre smartphones. Elle repose sur un réseau dit « maillé », dans lequel chaque appareil peut recevoir et transmettre les messages des autres.
Le principe ressemble à une chaîne humaine : un premier téléphone transmet un message à son voisin, qui le relaie à son tour vers un troisième appareil. Cette succession de relais permet d'étendre les communications au-delà de la portée Bluetooth d'un seul smartphone, sans connexion Internet ni antenne mobile.
L'application ne nécessite ni création de compte, ni adresse e-mail, ni numéro de téléphone. Les échanges peuvent se faire sous pseudonyme, dans des conversations privées ou des salons publics. Les messages privés bénéficient d'un chiffrement de bout en bout, tandis que les discussions publiques restent accessibles aux participants du réseau.
Bitchat peut également utiliser le protocole décentralisé Nostr lorsqu'une connexion Internet est disponible. Celui-ci permet notamment d'accéder à des salons géographiques et de communiquer avec certains contacts éloignés.
Reste que le fonctionnement hors ligne impose plusieurs contraintes. Sans suffisamment d'utilisateurs à proximité, le réseau maillé perd rapidement son intérêt. Les murs, la distance ou les interférences peuvent aussi empêcher la transmission des messages. Impossible, donc, de compter sur le Bluetooth seul pour joindre systématiquement un correspondant à plusieurs centaines de kilomètres.
La confidentialité mérite également quelques précautions. Le chiffrement des messages privés ne garantit pas un anonymat complet : le livre blanc du projet reconnaît que certains identifiants diffusés par Bluetooth peuvent permettre de reconnaître un appareil.
Bitchat représente ainsi davantage une solution de communication locale et de secours qu'un remplacement universel de WhatsApp ou Signal. Encore faut-il l'avoir installée avant une éventuelle coupure et pouvoir compter sur d'autres utilisateurs équipés.
- Maillage Bluetooth hors ligne
- Relais automatiques multi-sauts
- Chiffrement privé de bout en bout
Son succès français rappelle surtout qu'une messagerie indépendante des opérateurs peut trouver son public bien après son lancement, lorsque l'actualité vient soudainement lui donner une utilité concrète.

articles.title: Papelera de WhatsApp: dónde está y cómo liberar espacio sin borrar chats importantes
articles.text:
WhatsApp cuenta con una función de administración de almacenamiento que permite identificar y eliminar archivos pesados sin necesidad de borrar chats, conocida como la papelera de reciclaje.
La herramienta reúne fotos, videos, notas de voz, documentos y stickers que ocupan memoria en el teléfono. Su revisión permite localizar los elementos de mayor tamaño, las copias repetidas y los archivos reenviados muchas veces, con la posibilidad de conservar los mensajes y los chats que contienen información útil.
Dónde encontrar la papelera de WhatsApp
El acceso se encuentra dentro de la configuración de la aplicación. En iPhone, el recorrido comienza al tocar la foto de perfil; en dispositivos Android puede aparecer como “Ajustes”. Después, hay que ingresar en Almacenamiento y datos y seleccionar “Administrar almacenamiento”.
Desde esa sección, WhatsApp muestra cuánto espacio ocupa la aplicación en el dispositivo y organiza los contenidos por chat o canal. Permite revisar archivos grandes y elementos que han sido reenviados con frecuencia.
Cómo liberar espacio sin eliminar los chats en WhatsApp
El usuario puede elegir una conversación determinada dentro de “Administrar almacenamiento” y revisar las fotos, videos, documentos y audios asociados. Allí es posible ordenar los elementos por fecha o tamaño, seleccionar uno o varios archivos y presionar el ícono de eliminación.
Borrar contenido multimedia desde esta pantalla no elimina el historial completo del chat ni expulsa al usuario de un grupo. La conversación seguirá disponible en la lista de chats, con sus mensajes de texto y el resto de los archivos que no hayan sido seleccionados.
Antes de confirmar la eliminación, conviene comprobar si el material está marcado como destacado o si contiene datos que podrían ser necesarios más adelante.
Por qué se llena el almacenamiento de la aplicación de WhatsApp
Los videos suelen concentrar la mayor parte del espacio, sobre todo en grupos con actividad constante o en conversaciones donde se comparten grabaciones de alta definición.
Además, los documentos, las notas de voz extensas, los GIF, los stickers y las fotografías pueden aumentar el volumen de datos que almacena la aplicación.
El problema se agrava cuando está activada la descarga automática de archivos. En ese caso, el teléfono guarda de forma inmediata material recibido mediante datos, WiFi o itinerancia. Para limitar esa acumulación, se puede ingresar en Almacenamiento y datos y definir qué tipo de contenido se descargará con cada conexión.
Qué riesgos existen al vaciar la papelera de WhatsApp
La principal precaución es que WhatsApp no ofrece una papelera interna para recuperar archivos eliminados desde la administración de almacenamiento. Una vez que se confirma la acción, el contenido se borra de los archivos multimedia de la aplicación, pero podría persistir una copia en la galería o en otra carpeta del dispositivo.
La recuperación de mensajes y archivos depende de una copia de seguridad creada antes de la eliminación. Si el respaldo no incluía el contenido o si fue reemplazado por uno posterior, no habrá una vía para restaurarlo desde WhatsApp.
Por eso, es conveniente verificar los elementos uno por uno y realizar una copia de seguridad antes de una limpieza amplia, en especial si se trata de documentos laborales, fotos familiares o audios importantes.
Cómo evitar que se sature el almacenamiento del dispositivo
La limpieza de WhatsApp puede complementarse con una revisión de la galería del teléfono, donde quedan duplicados de fotos y videos descargados desde la aplicación.
Eliminar contenido repetido, desinstalar aplicaciones que no se utilizan y trasladar material a servicios como Google Fotos o iCloud son alternativas para ampliar el almacenamiento disponible.
Asimismo, es útil comprobar el tamaño de las copias de seguridad. Los respaldos de chats pueden incluir una gran cantidad de archivos multimedia y ocupar espacio tanto en el teléfono como en la nube.

articles.title: Real-time data pipelines drive Oracle's multicloud database push - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Oracle’s multicloud approach: Put the database wherever AI pipelines already run
Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are learning that real-time data pipelines matter as much as the models. An agent working from a stale subset of corporate records delivers far less than one wired into live, mission-critical data.
That shift is changing how companies decide where their databases run. Oracle Corp. has pushed its database modernization strategy into other clouds, and customers are moving databases next to the applications and AI pipelines they are building, according to Nathan Thomas (pictured), senior vice president of product management for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at Oracle.
“Customers are defining their AI pipelines, I think from an enterprise business perspective, with an eye towards trust, with an eye towards security,” Thomas said. “They are really looking at, ‘How do I get the mission-critical data into those pipelines?'”
Thomas spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how real-time data pipelines help improve agentic AI performance. (* Disclosure below.)
Building real-time data pipelines where the apps already live
Oracle offers its database on its own cloud, on-premises through Cloud@Customer and inside Amazon Web Services Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Azure and Google LLC’s Google Cloud. Customers rarely ask which cloud to pick, since existing relationships and the location of their applications usually settle the question, Thomas explained.
“They’re usually saying, ‘Hey, I’ve already got a relationship. Let’s put the database where my apps are and where my AI pipelines are,'” Thomas said.
Running the same Exadata hardware everywhere also takes the sting out of migration. AI projects are adding value to database migrations, and a like-for-like hardware move avoids most of the refactoring that once made them so painful, he noted.
“I’m coming from on-prem on an Exadata. I can move into the cloud on an Exadata,” Thomas said. “It’s the same hardware, same environment, same tools, same management, same performance.”

articles.title: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
articles.text:
Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools. Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI. Google didn’t see the backlash coming, but now that it’s here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what’s changing.
The gist of the new policy, according to Google’s blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts.
When Google revealed its new policy, the company’s VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times, which interpreted the situation as Google will “turn off search” if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate. Google’s approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.
The company clarified in a tweet that it will allow schools to disable Gemini apps while leaving search active for students. If they don’t want any AI, they can leave it all off. Essentially, Google is giving schools that want to completely block AI the ability to go all the way, even removing search from student accounts.
A Google spokesperson tells Ars that the company has not made any changes to the new policy it announced this week. However, the vagueness of Google’s blog post and public statements didn’t fully explain what it plans to do. articles.title: The New York Times reportedly in talks to buy Letterboxd for $330 million | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The New York Times Company has reportedly “entered exclusive negotiations” to acquire Letterboxd for $330 million, according to a report from The New York Times itself.
Letterboxd, an online platform for movie lovers that could be compared to Goodreads for movies, has grown dramatically in recent years. Letterboxd reported 3 million users in January 2021, a figure that grew to 28 million by April of this year. More than half of its users are under 35.
Letterboxd was previously reported to be seeking a new owner. According to the Times, film studios A24 and Sony were interested in the acquisition, but A24 was priced out.
Letterboxd is free, but users can access advanced features with a paid subscription. Its projected earnings for this year are estimated at $15 million, which is only about 4.5% of what the Times is supposedly offering to buy the company for.
The New York Times Company declined to comment on the acquisition to its own paper (lol). Personally, we wouldn’t be surprised if these anonymous tips were coming from inside the house, so we’re inclined to take this report pretty seriously.

articles.title: Intel leaker claims Nova Lake desktop chips have 5.1 GHz clock limit beyond 90°C — high clock speeds could demand significant cooling for next-gen chips
articles.text:
Intel leaker claims Nova Lake desktop chips have 5.1 GHz clock limit beyond 90°C — high clock speeds could demand significant cooling for next-gen chips
According to the leaker, the chips will top out at 5.1 GHz if their core temperature isn't kept below 90°C.
According to new information from reasonably reliable Intel leaker Jaykihn, Intel's upcoming Nova Lake desktop CPUs will have an unusual limiter applied. He claims that the next-gen desktop parts from Intel will "universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1 GHz when above 90°C." That doesn't mean the parts will top out at 5.1 GHz, which would be disastrous, but it does mean that you're going to need some darn good cooling to reach high clock rates on Nova Lake desktop CPUs.
Let's be clear about what he's saying. He's not saying that Nova Lake CPUs can't go above 5.1 GHz. He's also not saying that Nova Lake CPUs have their thermal limit at 90°C. While Jaykihn doesn't provide any clock rate information, he does imply that the chips will go above that, possibly quite significantly, as long as the thermals are kept in check, and he does say that the "Tjmax" value of Nova Lake is 100°C. Notably, that's a drop from 105°C in Arrow Lake, although prior-gen Raptor Lake CPUs had the same 100°C peak.
The mechanism that this most clearly resembles is Intel's own Thermal Velocity Boost. TVB, if you're not familiar, is the feature that allows high-end Intel CPUs to hit their highest clock rates. Put simply, TVB simply says that if the chip isn't overheating, it can go 100-300 MHz higher than its rated Turbo Boost Max speed. It's a little confusing, because these TVB clock rates are often quoted as the "Max Turbo Frequency"; Intel even does this itself. But TVB clocks are not the same as standard turbo clocks, and a lot of users who don't have exotic cooling probably never actually see these speeds in practice since they do require optimal conditions.
Does this mean that the practical limit of Nova Lake desktop CPU clocks is 5.1 GHz? Well, that depends on how hard these parts are to cool. Remember, we're dealing with chips fabricated on a 2nm-class process; in this case, it's reportedly TSMC's N2P for the compute tiles, while the peripheral chiplets are all on Intel's own 18A or 18A-P. This has consequences, as N2P is reportedly much denser than 18A, but it also lacks back-side power delivery, which means that the thermal resistance of the individual dies is considerably lower. Combined with much lower power consumption from a real node step, it may turn out that Nova Lake is actually quite easy to keep cool.
Ultimately, that is going to depend in part on how much Intel decides to push the "fMax", or maximum frequency. Rumors have put AMD's Zen 6 desktop Ryzen processors above 6 GHz for peak clock rates; if that's true, Intel could be looking at as much as a 20% clock rate disadvantage at 5.1 GHz. Obviously, as noted above, the chips are expected to have a higher fMax than that, but it remains to be seen how easily users can keep the parts cool enough to make use of the extra clock rate headroom given this new limit. Both Intel's flagship Core Ultra 9 285K and the Red Team's extant Zen 5-based Ryzen 9 9950X can reach 5.7 GHz before overclocking.
For tuners, a frustrating detail is that this 5.1 GHz hard clock limit apparently "cannot be raised." That means folks doing system tuning on Nova Lake will be strongly encouraged to undervolt to reduce the thermal output of their processors and help them maintain high performance. That's unusual, as historically Intel allows users to adjust the thermal throttle point of their processors when overclocking. That may potentially still be the case on processors unlocked for overclocking, of course; Jaykihn is reporting based on leaks and engineering samples rather than final released products.
Even if Nova Lake doesn't scale clocks much over Arrow Lake, it could still be quite a bit faster than the previous generation. Recall that the new chips will come with new core architectures and new technologies, including APX core extensions and bLLC, Intel's long-awaited response to AMD's 3D V-Cache. Forecasts are indicating that gaming performance could be as much as 33% faster than Arrow Lake, which would be huge. However, this 5.1 GHz limit could be a downer for people who are interested in the rumored 52-core version of Nova Lake. We'll find out how much it matters when the Core Ultra 4000 series launches either very late this year or very early next year, although we wouldn't expect the 52-core flagship or bLLC versions until next summer.

articles.title: Razer Basilisk V4 Pro: Loveable and flawed in equal measure
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Despite being a sizeable upgrade over its predecessor, the Razer Basilisk V4 Pro is a frustratingly flawed addition to the company’s lineup.
Reasons to buy
- + Comfortable shape and satisfying clicks
- + HyperScroll wheel is very useful
- + Loads of customizable buttons
- + Excellent build quality
- + Even better battery life
Reasons to avoid
- - HyperScroll wheel is loud and mushy
- - Button placements aren’t ideal for fingertip grip or smaller hands
- - Hefty weight won’t suit everyone
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Razer Basilisk V4 Pro two-minute review
One of the first gaming mice I ever used was a Razer Basilisk, and I enjoyed it so much I wore the grippy rubber sides down until they were completely smooth. I’ve moved over to much more lightweight pointers in the years since, but with Razer launching the Basilisk V4 Pro, has the company done enough to tempt me back and resurrect that fond old love affair?
Spoiler alert: not completely. Because while the Basilisk V4 Pro is an excellent upgrade over its predecessor, it also comes with a few drawbacks that prevent it from being a total must-buy. It’s a great gaming mouse and might be ideal in the right (large) hands, but don’t go into this expecting perfection.
Let’s start with the positives. Razer has kept the Basilisk’s familiar ergonomic form factor, which is best suited to palm grip users, and its comfortable sculpted shape fits snugly into your hand. The build quality is also good, with solid plastics throughout and grippy textured finishes on the sides. And while it’s still a fairly hefty 100g, that’s still 10% lighter than the 112g Basilisk V3 Pro.
Battery life has increased to 200 hours in 2.4GHz mode at a 1,000Hz polling rate, or 275 hours on Bluetooth LE — up from 140 hours and 210 hours on the Basilisk V3 Pro. Note that that’s with the RGB lighting disabled. My review unit arrived with 66% battery, and in my testing (using it in 2.4GHz mode with a 1,000Hz polling rate and the RGB switched on), that dropped to 0% after 45 hours, so you can probably expect just under 70 hours on a full charge when using these settings. That’s a sizeable drop on 200 hours, but you’ll get much more juice if you dim the RGB lights.
Compared to the Basilisk V4 Pro’s predecessor, Razer has outfitted the latest version with a couple of extra buttons: one on the top-left corner of the left click and another next to the side buttons. That means you’ve now got 14 customizable controls on this device, making it a sort of halfway solution between a regular mouse and the button-crazy Razer Naga V3 Pro.
One of those buttons — the additional on one the side — could be assigned to Razer’s “Perfect 180” feature, the company suggested. This instantly spins your in-game character around 180 degrees, and if you think that sounds like cheating, you might have a point — even Razer admitted to us that they thought it could get banned in competitive games. Still, until that happens…
Razer also told us it had made the left and right click buttons sound less “ticky,” and they do have a satisfyingly soft and quiet actuation, one that’s a little less piercing to the ears than those on the Viper V4 Pro. They’re not silent, but they’re pleasing in use.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Sandwiched between those buttons is Razer’s HyperSpeed scroll wheel that, while not strictly a gaming feature, might be one of the Basilisk V4 Pro’s best aspects. You can set it to spin freely or ratchet (with two strength options) in Razer’s Synapse app, but its real party trick is its Smart-Reel feature. If you’ve set it to ratchet, a quick spin of the wheel automatically flips it into free-spin mode; put the brakes on and it moves back to ratcheting. It’s a great way to rapidly move through documents and spreadsheets without having to manually change modes.
But while I liked the HyperScroll wheel, I didn’t love it. Every time it switches modes (from free spinning to ratcheting, say), there’s a loud and slightly disconcerting crunching sound that starts to grate after a while.
Pushing it in to click the scroll wheel also feels very soft and mushy — it’s imprecise compared with Razer’s own alternatives like the Viper V4 Pro, which is much crisper to click. It’s a welcome feature on the mouse, but it’s clearly inferior to the MagSpeed wheel you’ll find on the Logitech MX Master 4.
This was something I found time and again with the Basilisk V4 Pro: I’d often be pleased with one feature, only to observe a downside to it after I’d used it a little more. I was happy to see an extra side button that I could program to my needs, for instance, but then started to notice it getting in the way and messing up my two-side-button muscle memory.
Or take the RGB lighting as another example: it looks lovely (especially on the Spectrum Cycling setting), but considering you never look at the mouse when using it, and your hand covers it up anyway, it felt a little pointless. Perhaps Razer could have done away with it and eked more battery life out of the Basilisk.
Ultimately, the Basilisk V4 Pro hasn’t converted me back to its temptingly sculpted form factor. It offers a capable combination of features, buttons and comfort, and for many gamers — especially those with larger hands — it’ll be an attractive option. It’s still one of the best gaming mice around, despite its drawbacks.
But for every two steps forward, there’s one step back that tempers its progress, whether that’s the imperfect HyperScroll wheel, the hard-to-reach buttons for all but palm grip users or the questionable, battery-draining RGB. I went into this looking to rekindle my love for an old flame, but in the end, I found myself stuck in the Basilisk’s friend zone.

The Razer Basilisk V4 Pro is priced at $169.99 / £169.99 / $289.95 AUD and is available now from Razer’s website and third-party retailers. Its price has crept up by $10 / £10 / $10 AUD versus the Basilisk V3 Pro 35K.
