articles.title: Building a Culture for a Kubernetes-Based Platform in a Bank
articles.text:
In a banking environment, open source can earn trust by running real workloads, as Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin explained in their talk Building Cloud Native Culture in a Bank at KubeCon & CloudNativeCon Europe. Deploying Kubernetes was the easy part; the hard part was culture: community of practice, shared knowledge, rituals, ownership. Teams try things, keep what works, and improve bottom-up.
Open source was not an obvious choice in their banking environment, Cusin mentioned. They received questions about support and accountability. Instead of trying to convince people with theory, they started running real workloads. Over time, trust was built by operating the platform day after day:
Open source stopped being seen as a risk. It became the foundation.
They treated their first version of Kubernetes like a project. "We delivered it, we got a good adoption", Cusin said. But the operation was incredibly hard. Not because the technology was broken, but because they hadn’t built the culture around it yet:
Nobody knew who to call, responsibilities were blurry, and teams were consuming the platform without really contributing to it. Every incident felt like a fire drill.
They realized deploying Kubernetes was the easy part. The hard part was building the culture with a community of practice around it. The shared knowledge, the rituals, the ownership model, Cusin explained:
Without that culture, no platform survives its own success.
They invite people to experiment, for instance by having a yearly competition where everybody can submit their ideas and the one that wins, actually gets implemented. Many of their improvements came from the bottom up, Paramonova argued.
They used open source as a compass, something that helped them orientate a subject, Cusin explained:
When Kubernetes appeared, we recognized it immediately. Strong Kubernetes, transparent governance, and real production users. The compass pointed; we followed. And now we are watching OpenStack the same way.
A compass doesn’t force you in one direction. It helps you recognize the right opportunity when it arrives, Cusin said.
They tried things, and some of them didn’t work. They kept the ones that did. The act of trying, of deliberately designing how teams interact, creates the culture we have today, Cusin said. Structure first, the culture follows.
Every organization is different; every regulated environment has its own constraints, Paramonova said. You need a compass during your journey. It’s something that will guide you when everything else is uncertain. For us, it was open source, she concluded.
InfoQ interviewed Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin after their talk.
InfoQ: How did you gain trust from your development teams?
Stéphane Cusin: Over time, trust emerged from a combination of transparency and reliability. When developers see that the platform consistently helps them deliver applications safely and efficiently, adoption follows naturally.
Marcy Paramonova: Trust was not something we could establish by presenting a roadmap or writing good documentation, though both matter. It came from running things. From being present when something broke. From being honest about what was not yet ready.
Cusin: Today, our culture is centered around ownership, automation, transparency, and continuous improvement. Teams are empowered to move quickly, but they do so within a framework of shared standards and platform capabilities. The result is not only greater efficiency, but also greater consistency, reliability, and visibility across the organization.
InfoQ: How did Kubernetes transform how your organization builds software?
Cusin: Kubernetes gave us a common platform and a common operating model. In the first version of our platform, we gave teams flexibility. We exposed many Kubernetes capabilities directly and allowed teams to customize their deployment model extensively. In practice, that often resulted in different patterns emerging across teams.
One of the lessons we learned as platform engineers is that developers do not come to a platform looking for more infrastructure choices. They come to a platform to deliver software.
In our current platform, Kubernetes is no longer the product. Kubernetes is the implementation detail. The product is a simple, secure, and standardized software delivery experience.
We provide opinionated deployment patterns, standardized Helm charts, and common platform capabilities. As a result, when an engineer moves from one team to another, the deployment experience is largely the same. They do not need to relearn how applications are packaged, deployed, monitored, or operated.
Paramonova: The transformation I experienced most directly was organizational. Kubernetes gave teams a common language. It created shared abstractions that made collaboration across different parts of engineering much more natural.
Before, a lot of knowledge was siloed by team or by technology stack. Kubernetes did not erase those silos overnight, but it gave everyone a shared foundation to build on. That changed conversations, and changed what was possible.

articles.title: Groundcover automates Kubernetes sizing. Engineers set the bounds.
articles.text:
Groundcover automates Kubernetes sizing. Engineers set the bounds.
On Tuesday, groundcover launched Autonomous Infrastructure in beta to continuously adjust CPU and memory requests for Kubernetes (K8s) Deployments based on production data.
Built on technology from Wand, the K8s resource optimization platform groundcover acquired in September, the beta uses data already collected from groundcover’s eBPF sensor to inform resource allocation decisions, while giving engineers a direct view into how those decisions could affect infrastructure costs and workload performance.
Shahar Azulay, CEO and co-founder of groundcover, tells The New Stack about the balance the company is trying to get right: “The goal isn’t simply to reduce resource requests as much as possible. It’s to find the right balance between efficiency and stability across the entire environment.”
That can mean reducing requests for workloads consuming far less than they’ve been allocated, but it can also mean increasing requests when a workload needs additional resources to operate reliably. The objective is not simply a smaller infrastructure footprint. It’s an environment that continuously receives the resources it needs, without paying for capacity it doesn’t.
How to get there? Azulay says teams need “a continuous feedback loop that uses real production telemetry to identify when workloads are over- or under-provisioned and safely adjust them.”
Does nobody know a good way to right-size K8s workloads?
It’s not for lack of trying. There are already a lot of different ways to tackle the burden of right-sizing K8s workloads.
For example, scheduled rightsizing applies changes at chosen intervals, so it may not respond between scheduled updates. In-place resizing can change resources on running pods, although some changes require container restarts. Automated tools can also generate and apply recommendations within policies engineers set.
When asked why he thinks K8s rightsizing continues to trip people up, Azulay tells The New Stack the challenge lies in striking the right balance between cost efficiency and application stability:
“Resource requests are typically set at deployment time, when teams are making their best estimates before a workload has experienced real-world production traffic,” he explains. “The challenge is that workloads are constantly changing, but resource configurations often aren’t.”
“The challenge is that workloads are constantly changing, but resource configurations often aren’t.”
After initial deployment, teams may simply let sleeping workloads lie, i.e., they don’t revisit original resource requests for reconfiguration. While workloads may keep spinning along just fine, this approach means teams risk unknowingly leaving them over- or under-provisioned—with costly consequences.
For organizations running hundreds or thousands of workloads, keeping those configurations accurate becomes an ongoing engineering task. Teams must analyze utilization, identify opportunities, test new settings, and revisit them as traffic and application behavior change. Even with the expertise, they may not have the time to do it continuously.
Azulay describes over-provisioning as “the safer choice because nobody wants to risk performance issues or outages.” But that extra peace of mind can come with unnecessary infrastructure costs; in a 2025 study published in Applied Sciences, researchers found that optimizing K8s resource allocation improved a combined performance-and-cost score by approximately 50% compared to the conventional maximum resource allocation approach.
Under-provisioning carries different risks. Requests help Kubernetes schedule pods, and CPU requests influence how CPU time is shared under contention; setting them too low can leave workloads short of CPU time. Limits work differently: CPU limits cause throttling, while exceeding a memory limit can trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) kill. Low memory requests can also increase eviction risk when a node is under memory pressure.
There’s also a relationship between workload requests and the cost of the cluster itself. Node autoscalers such as Karpenter can provision or remove nodes based on the resources workloads request, but they don’t determine whether those requests accurately reflect what each application needs. If workloads consistently request too much, the autoscaler may maintain more capacity than necessary. Right-sizing those requests gives the node autoscaler a more accurate basis for allocating infrastructure.
What if the answer to done-right right-sizing is sitting in your production data?
Groundcover thinks so. That’s why its new Autonomous Infrastructure draws on the groundcover eBPF sensor, which is already collecting telemetry across applications and infrastructure. The beta uses that production history to recommend CPU and memory requests for Kubernetes Deployments. Brand-new Deployments remain in a learning state until enough data is available.
But the approach isn’t simply to observe a spike in resource consumption and increase requests afterward. By the time a reactive system responds, the performance impact may already have occurred. Instead, groundcover’s optimization engine analyzes workload behavior over time, including usage patterns and resource contention, to anticipate capacity requirements and prepare workloads for expected changes in demand.
That distinction matters for workloads with recurring traffic spikes. The goal is to have enough resources available when demand arrives, without permanently allocating for peak consumption.
When engineers open the beta, they get a direct view of how much CPU and memory each workload requests versus what it uses, plus the number of under-provisioned workloads and estimated monthly savings if they apply changes. Groundcover’s product page says dollar estimates use default list prices that administrators can adjust with their own prices and discounts. These estimates do not establish that a cloud bill will fall by the same amount; realizing savings also depends on whether freed capacity lets teams reduce billed infrastructure.
An important part of the experience is that customers can see those opportunities before enabling autonomous optimization. Because groundcover already collects the necessary telemetry, existing customers can evaluate potential savings without deploying a separate monitoring agent or conducting another data-collection exercise. They can inspect recommendations, understand their expected impact, and decide which workloads, if any, to optimize.
Rather than setting resource requests at deployment time and letting them run on autopilot, engineers can use Autonomous Infrastructure to put real-time telemetry to work and continuously adjust resources based on production behavior. And because groundcover already collects the necessary telemetry, teams running a supported sensor version don’t need a separate agent or a new data-collection period for existing Deployments with sufficient history.
Why the answer lies in the context
When asked how real-time production data can improve K8s right-sizing, Azulay tells The New Stack it comes down to understanding how workloads affect one another in production.
While some resource optimization tools size each workload on its own, he claims that approach doesn’t tell the whole story.
“Kubernetes workloads don’t operate in isolation. They share nodes, compete for available resources, and can directly affect one another’s performance.”
Instead, to find the optimal balance between efficiency and stability, Azulay says engineers need tools that consider the entire environment:
“Kubernetes workloads don’t operate in isolation. They share nodes, compete for available resources, and can directly affect one another’s performance.”
For example, lowering CPU requests changes how a workload shares CPU under contention and can let the scheduler pack more workloads onto a node. A recommendation based only on one workload’s usage can therefore miss contention effects across the node.
This is one limitation of approaches that rely primarily on historical utilization for each workload. Two applications with similar CPU consumption may require different resource allocations depending on their traffic patterns, neighboring workloads, and the contention they experience. Applying the same sizing formula to both can leave one over-provisioned and the other vulnerable to performance problems.
To right-size each workload without bruising others, Azulay tells The New Stack resource optimization tools must not only evaluate real-time resource consumption against what’s being requested but consider the traffic patterns, workload behavior, and available resources across the node:
“True optimization requires understanding both individual workload behavior and the broader environment in which those workloads operate.”
Azulay says Autonomous Infrastructure uses that broader context. Leaning on Wand’s optimization engine, the beta uses node-level contention to inform right-sizing recommendations and make adjustments that consider the entire environment.
“It also looks beyond application containers to account for injected sidecars, such as Istio, Linkerd and Vault agents, which can be overlooked sources of resource waste,” Azulay says.
The integration with groundcover also connects resource optimization to the observability workflows engineers already use. Rather than receiving an isolated recommendation from a separate optimization tool, engineers can investigate workload behavior using the logs, traces, metrics, and infrastructure context available in the same platform. That helps them understand why a change was recommended and evaluate its impact on the environment.
The result is a connection between observing infrastructure and acting on what the data reveals. Production telemetry informs optimization decisions, and engineers can use that same observability context to understand what happens afterward.
But are engineers ready to automate right-sizing?
Letting a tool like Autonomous Infrastructure take over K8s right-sizing can sound like a convenient solution. As Azulay tells The New Stack, many teams simply don’t get around to reconfiguring resource requests because of time and resource constraints — and engineers aren’t always sure the changes will improve efficiency without impacting stability.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean engineers are ready to go all in on automated right-sizing, at least for now. In Kube.today’s 2025 community poll on Kubernetes resource management, 56.5% of respondents selected manual tools such as kubectl and dashboards as their primary approach. That result reflects the poll’s respondents, not Kubernetes practitioners as a whole.
Groundcover’s own research, administered by Atomik Research, underlines engineers’ uncertainty about going fully autonomous. In the survey of 500 U.S. technology professionals, 87% say AI or automation is already integrated into observability workflows, but only one-third (34%) call it “fully operational and trusted.”
For those hesitant to hand over the reins for resource optimization, groundcover’s beta might offer some relief.
Per groundcover, Autonomous Infrastructure is “opt-in at every level.” By default, automation is off; groundcover’s launch blog describes opting in a cluster and then enabling individual Deployments.
While the beta may use production telemetry to autonomously adjust resource requests, engineers still set the parameters, defining minimum and maximum bounds for CPU and memory requests. The beta changes requests only, leaving limits unchanged. A declared limit caps the recommendation; a workload constrained by that limit appears as “Bounded.” Groundcover says every policy change is versioned and an audit log records who assigned each workload to a policy and when. A resource used by an HPA or KEDA utilization-based autoscaler is left unchanged. The beta uses in-place resizing when possible and falls back to a rollout when necessary.
For engineers who may be wary of giving a resource optimization tool full access to decide and execute K8s right-sizing, these constraints can ease the transition. Plus, they can easily keep a pulse on what the beta is doing, with groundcover’s view showing how many workloads are managed autonomously in each cluster and namespace.
“…engineers aren’t being asked to trust a black box.”
Perhaps more importantly, engineers aren’t being asked to trust a black box. They can review the reasoning behind recommendations, inspect the expected effects, and choose precisely where to enable autonomous changes. The automation is designed to remain understandable and reversible.
Who will get right-sizing right?
Groundcover says the Autonomous Infrastructure beta is available at no additional cost to its customers running the groundcover sensor on Kubernetes, with a supported sensor version required. The beta covers Deployments and their sidecars; support for other workload kinds is on the roadmap. The company is inviting design partners and plans demonstrations at booth #111 during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, Nov. 9–12, 2026, in Salt Lake City.
The question for the next generation of Kubernetes optimization tools may be less about how aggressively they can reduce resource requests and more about how intelligently they can manage them. That means anticipating demand, accounting for contention across the environment, and making changes engineers can understand and trust.
For groundcover, bringing optimization into the same platform that collects and analyzes production telemetry is a step toward that model: infrastructure that doesn’t just report what’s happening, but uses that understanding to continuously improve how it runs.

articles.title: Nvidia's RTX Spark GPU priority control is quietly showing up on regular GeForce PCs
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Nvidia built a new GPU priority control for its RTX Spark laptops, allowing owners to keep games running smoothly while an AI agent churns away in the background. Now, the same setting is showing up in the Nvidia App on some standard GeForce RTX PCs, too. Nvidia hasn't said a word about bringing the feature to those systems, however. 
 
 
The option, called GPU App Prioritization, sits under System > Advanced in Nvidia App version 11.0.9.585. Reddit user Warkratos first spotted it and posted screenshots on r/nvidia. They showed several presets for splitting GPU priority between the app in focus and whatever is running in the background.
By default, the foreground app gets 80% priority, while background tasks receive the remaining 20% Favoring the foreground increases that split to 90/10, while a custom setting reportedly allows users to go as far as 95/5. That means someone playing a game while exporting a video or running a local AI model could decide which workload gets the bigger slice of GPU resources.
That's essentially the same as the Resource Management control Nvidia added to its RTX Spark laptops on October 28. At the time, the company pitched it as a way to give background AI agents more or less access to the GPU. On those machines, the feature also only works when hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling is enabled in Windows.
On GeForce cards, however, availability appears to vary considerably. One RTX 5090 owner confirmed that the option appeared after updating. Another user with an RTX 5070 Ti, the same app version, and hotfix driver 621.12 found no such option.
Nvidia's release notes for the update don't mention the feature at all, listing new DLSS overrides and game optimization profiles instead. For now, it's unclear whether this is a staged rollout, something tied to specific drivers, or simply a setting that slipped out before Nvidia intended to announce it.
Anyone curious can update the Nvidia App and check under System > Advanced. Nvidia hasn't confirmed whether the GeForce implementation requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling, but given that the RTX Spark version does, it's worth making sure the feature is enabled in Windows' graphics settings, too. Just keep in mind that nobody has independently tested how much of a difference the setting actually makes yet.

articles.title: Nuevo GTA 6 hace que Xbox cree una consola en forma de cocodrilo: se llama Xbox Series X-BITE y se va a sortear
articles.text:
La Xbox Series X-BITE es la respuesta de Microsoft a la expectativa generada por Grand Theft Auto VI. La compañía presentó una edición especial que esconde una consola Series X funcional dentro de la figura de un caimán de tamaño real, inspirada en la fauna de Florida.
El anuncio llega semanas antes del lanzamiento del videojuego de Rockstar Games, previsto para el 19 de noviembre de 2026. Aunque no hay un referencia textual al juego, debido al acuerdo de marketing entre PlayStation con Rockstar y Take-Two Interactive, en la presentación hay varios detalles que dejan claro el motivo de esta edición especial, que no estará a la venta.
Cómo es la consola de Xbox con forma de cocodrilo
La Series X-BITE representa a un caimán que parece haber tragado una videoconsola. La pieza supera los 1,50 metros de largo desde el hocico hasta la cola.
El reptil tiene ojos de color verde cuya pupila está inspirada en el logo de Xbox. En su cuerpo se puede ver iluminado el logo de Xbox Nexus, y entre las fauces del animal reposa un control inalámbrico personalizado con marcas que simulan mordeduras.
Para fabricar la pieza, Xbox trabajó junto a John Nolan Studio, un estudio especializado en animatrónica y diseño de criaturas que participó en producciones como The Witcher y Jurassic World: Dominion. El equipo combinó modelado 3D y escultura para reproducir la textura de la piel del animal e integrar los componentes de la consola en su interior.
Existe una única unidad de la Series X-BITE y no estará a la venta. Xbox aclaró que se trata de una fabricación personalizada y que ningún animal real fue utilizado durante su elaboración.
Cómo participar en el sorteo para tener la Xbox en forma de cocodrilo
La dinámica para ganar la consola se desarrolla a través de las redes sociales de Xbox. El período de inscripción comenzó el 3 de noviembre a las 9.00 hora del Pacífico y se extiende hasta las 23.59 del 10 de noviembre de 2026, también hora del Pacífico.
Existen tres formas de participar: a través de X, Instagram o TikTok. En cualquiera de las tres plataformas, el mecanismo es el mismo: seguir la cuenta oficial @XBOX, compartir una de las publicaciones designadas para el sorteo y escribir manualmente el hashtag #XbiteSweepstakes en el repost.
El hashtag debe tecleado a mano: las publicaciones que no lo incluyan de esa forma quedan automáticamente descalificadas. Además, la cuenta utilizada para participar debe tener su configuración en modo público mientras dure el concurso.
Cada persona puede sumar hasta tres entradas en total, con un límite de una por cada red social. El uso de dispositivos automatizados para participar está prohibido.
Cómo se va a elegir al ganador
El concurso está abierto a residentes legales de los 50 estados de Estados Unidos, Washington D. C. y Puerto Rico, mayores de 18 años al momento de inscribirse. No se requiere ninguna compra para entrar ni para aumentar las posibilidades de ganar.
El sorteo aleatorio se realizará alrededor del 11 de noviembre de 2026, a cargo de GMR Marketing, entre todas las entradas elegibles recibidas durante el período habilitado. El ganador será notificado por mensaje directo en la red social utilizada para participar y tendrá 48 horas para responder con su nombre completo, teléfono y correo electrónico.
Luego de ese primer contacto, deberá confirmar su elegibilidad y proporcionar una dirección de envío dentro de las 24 horas siguientes. Si no cumple con los plazos, pierde el premio y Xbox intentará notificar a un suplente, con un máximo de cinco intentos antes de declarar el premio vacante.

articles.title: Ocient raises $100 million as agentic AI drives growth in large-scale analytics - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Ocient raises $100 million as agentic AI drives growth in large-scale analytics
Ocient Inc., the maker of a speedy data analytics platform, today said it has raised $100 million in a Series C funding to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business.
That business is fueled by growing demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers seeking to analyze massive datasets without sampling. The new round brings the Chicago-based company’s total funding to $260 million.
Ocient said it expects revenue to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling revenue the previous year. The company said the new financing will accelerate delivery of its OcientAIQ Solutions, which enable AI agents and human analysts to query petabyte-scale datasets.
Chief Executive John Morris said much of the growth is coming from new customers in national security and telecommunications, particularly organizations using the platform to consolidate cybersecurity information.
“They’ve been accustomed to having to sample data coming off the network,” Morris said. “They don’t have anything that can handle the ingest rates, nor that can store at an affordable price tens of petabytes of data.”
Ocient’s original business focused on high-performance analytics, but the emergence of AI agents has expanded its potential market. Increasingly, software agents rather than human analysts are querying its systems, driving higher utilization and creating demand for more comprehensive datasets.
The OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration. Its architecture minimizes data movement and uses forward error correction instead of conventional replication to provide data protection with reduced storage overhead.
“The architecture is designed not to move data around constantly as most architectures do, and to have nothing replicated,” Morris said.
The company competes with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and open-source analytics implementations, although its technology frequently complements existing platforms rather than replacing them, the CEO said.
Cybersecurity has emerged as a particularly promising market. Ocient provides the underlying data infrastructure that enables security tools and AI agents to analyze network activity across complete historical datasets, potentially identifying threats that conventional sampling would miss.
However, Morris said the company isn’t positioned as a cybersecurity tool. “We don’t do the detection algorithms and the sort of things that the companies in that space do,” Morris said.
Government and defense customers account for a substantial portion of Ocient’s business. The company recently established a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve those markets.
Morris said the new funding should be sufficient to help Ocient reach breakeven, although he declined to provide a timetable. Ocient plans to direct much of the investment toward hiring sales and customer delivery personnel while continuing engineering development.
The company is also seeing increasing demand for on-premises deployments as customers seek greater control over costs and sensitive information. “Most of our opportunities now are on-prem because they’re either repatriating for cost reasons or for data sovereignty and data protection issues,” Morris said.
The company is also looking to expand geographically, particularly in Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, while pursuing additional cybersecurity customers.
The round was co-led by Boka Capital Ltd. and OCA Ventures LLC, with participation from previous investors Greycroft Partners LLC, In-Q-Tel Inc., Blue Bear Capital LLC, Buoyant Ventures Management LLC, PSP Partners LLC’s PSP Growth fund and Pritzker Group Venture Capital LLC.

articles.title: MAHA lost bigly in the midterms—is it at death's door?
articles.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump (L) listens as U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during an election rally on October 23, 2026 in Fort Myers, Florida.
Credit:
Getty | Alex Wong
U.S. President Donald Trump (L) listens as U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during an election rally on October 23, 2026 in Fort Myers, Florida.
Credit:
Getty | Alex Wong
As Democrats blew away their Republican rivals in an unprecedented midterm sweep Tuesday, the Make America Health Again movement also got bowled over, raising questions about the fate of the motley movement.
MAHA—which has centered around anti-vaccine activist and current Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—saw many of its favored candidates and allies lose, while vocal adversaries of Kennedy won. And the coalition was splintering under stress even before the voting started; in recent months, supporters have accused Kennedy and the Trump administration of inaction and betrayals in their two years in power.
Now hobbled in Washington, shedding supporters, and showing little to no influence in voting booths, is MAHA on its deathbed? Or will it be reborn—possibly into a new group? Could it be assimilated into a blue platform—after sloughing off the more repulsive, conspiratorial aspects of Kennedy’s ideology? These are the questions circling in the aftermath of Tuesday’s bloodbath.
In a social media poll Wednesday afternoon, Mary Talley Bowden—a dejected MAHA activist, anti-vaccine advocate, and doctor reprimanded for prescribing ivermectin to treat COVID-19—polled her followers about what should come next. She offered three options: Start a third party, join the Democrats, or overthrow the GOP. As of publication time, joining Democrats trailed at just 3 percent of the votes. The remaining votes were roughly split between overthrowing the GOP—whatever that means—and forming a third party, which had a small lead at 49 percent.
Cracking coalition
That MAHA could fade out entirely or fracture into negligible shards seems like a very real possibility. Its collection of disparate groups and varied agenda items has always made its cohesiveness seem tenuous. A Politico poll in June revealed that people who identified as MAHA had different ideas of what the movement’s priorities are (or should be), as well as different political leanings, and sometimes opposing ideologies.
Some within the movement embrace (or at least accept) Kennedy’s fringe beliefs, such as his zealous anti-vaccine views, his rejection of germ theory, and his false claim that 5G is damaging our brains and causing cancer. Some also believe, like Kennedy, in chemtrails and want all mRNA vaccines banned. There are members who support his plan to ban water fluoridation and also seem fine with his false claim that Lyme disease was created by the US military as a military weapon.
Others, meanwhile, have been attracted to MAHA by the more reasonable, non-absurd issues Kennedy touts. Those include improving the quality of Americans’ food and diets, reducing their exposure to environmental contaminants, and limiting the influence of industry and corporate interests on Americans’ health, particularly limiting the sway of pharmaceutical and chemical companies.
With various priorities, Kennedy and MAHA leaders have spent the past two years finding ways to disappoint their members. Some like Bowdon are angered that Kennedy has yet to ban mRNA vaccines. In February, Kennedy sparked particularly intense backlash among supporters for embracing Trump’s decision to increase domestic production of the pesticide glyphosate—a pesticide many in the MAHA movement wanted banned. Kennedy further fueled feelings of betrayal in September by appearing at a MAHA-branded summit that had hefty corporate sponsorships, including from behemoths such as Walmart, Anthropic, OpenAI, Grail, and UnitedHealth.
“MAHA was supposed to expose the revolving door between money, industry and government, not build its own,” Robert Malone, a fringe scientist and previous Kennedy ally, wrote in a scathing response to the summit.
Signs of dying
Going into the midterms on Tuesday, the number of disenchanted MAHA members had mounted. In October, Tiffany Cianci, a former Kennedy supporter, published a MAHA scorecard, which lists 42 promises that Kennedy and leaders made to the MAHA members and then largely broke. The scorecard reports 37 promises broken, five partially fulfilled, and zero kept. One of the “partially kept” promises was removing synthetic dyes from foods, particularly children’s foods. Kennedy announced an effort to do that—with much ballyhoo—but later admitted that the FDA did not ban or even have an agreement with food companies to remove the dyes. Instead, Kennedy said he has an “understanding” with food companies. The dyes remain in foods.
In a press release, Cianci wrote that the scorecard revealed “an abysmal string of broken commitments and betrayals.” It also contained a direct quote from her, saying: “I believed deeply in the promise that MAHA represented, particularly the possibility of confronting chronic disease and building a healthier future for America’s children. But belief was never supposed to mean blind loyalty.”
The press release included quotes from several other prominent MAHA leaders, all expressing disappointment with Kennedy and the Trump administration. Later in October, Calley Means, a top ally and senior advisor to Kennedy, resigned from his position, reportedly “disillusioned” and frustrated by delays in food policy changes sought by MAHA.
Another prominent figure to fall out with Kennedy was Vani Hari, an online influencer who goes by “food babe” and has previously identified as a “MAHA Mom.” As voting results were streaming in Tuesday night, Hari posted a comment on social media that she had given Politico months earlier, saying: “Women don’t come out to vote for glyphosate and war,” referring to the pesticide Kennedy had embraced and the Iran war.
Midterm devastation
In the wake of the blue sweep, it’s clear that more than half of the 24 MAHA-endorsed candidates lost their races Tuesday. That includes Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Texas and Zach Lahn, who ran for governor of Iowa. Lahn in particular was considered a “dream MAHA candidate,” and his campaign was seen as a test of MAHA’s political influence. Kennedy himself headlined a political rally for Lahn last week, calling it “the most important election going on in this country.” Lahn lost to his Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, who flipped the seat with an 11-point spread, turning the office blue for the first time in 20 years.
Alex Clark Voetberg, who hosts a wellness podcast called Culture Apothecary for Turning Point USA, echoed Hari, pointing to the glyphosate betrayal as a reason for the defeats. “MAHA moms stayed home and it could’ve swayed some of these races that were unbearably close. Should’ve listened to our warnings on protecting glyphosate—but you needed Bayer for the war,” Clark Voetberg wrote on social media.
Otherwise, MAHA also lost allies, such as Senator Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who founded a MAHA caucus in the Senate. Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) lost his seat in the House despite reports that Kennedy allegedly intervened in the race to help him win. Meanwhile, critics of Kennedy notched wins, including Representative-elect Richard Pan, a physician from California; Senator-elect Annie Andrews, a pediatrician from South Carolina; and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist with a medical degree from Michigan.
Many congressional Democrats are already raring to hold Kennedy to account and remove him—and several of the newcomers are eager to help make it happen. In August, Andrews laid out her plans for health priorities to South Carolina Democrats, saying, “I believe we need to fully fund the CDC and the NIH, and I believe we need to impeach and remove RFK Jr.”
On Wednesday afternoon, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) wrote on social media: “The time is now. RFK Jr. must resign or be fired. End of discussion.”
MAHA and Kennedy
If Kennedy is removed from office, the outlook for MAHA in its current form seems even murkier. On the one hand, Kennedy’s removal may make it easier for those in the movement to shed the divisive, abhorrent aspects of his ideology and focus on broadly popular issues—healthy foods, environmental contaminants, and industry influence. Such a move may help MAHA cement itself as a sustainable political fixture. But some of the most vocal figures in the MAHA realm are doggedly loyal to Kennedy, throwing such a transition into doubt.
Zen Honeycutt, an anti-vaccine activist and founder of Moms Across America, is one of those Kennedy loyalists. Honeycutt drew attention before the election for reaching out to Democrats on common causes. Her group endorsed several blue candidates, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, and Rep. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire (all of them won their races).
“We expect Democrats and Republicans to work together,” Honeycutt told Politico earlier this month. “Health is not a political issue. You know, poison is not partisan. Cancer is not choosy.”
The sensible comment might suggest Honeycutt doesn’t care which party or politician follows through with MAHA’s goals, just as long as they’re achieved. But this is not actually Honeycutt’s position. Her intentions were made clear in exchanges on social media with Bowden, who harshly criticized Honeycutt for crossing party lines, particularly for talking with Ocasio-Cortez. “You understand she’s trying to use you?” Bowden wrote.
Honeycutt explained that she was working to smooth Kennedy’s path in Washington, not hand power to Democrats, who she said had been “fascist in mandating vaccines.” She instead turned the criticism to Bowden, saying the MAHA infighting and mudslinging was what was hurting the cause and handing Democrats wins.
On Wednesday, Honeycutt reaffirmed her allegiance to Kennedy, warning Democrats that impeaching him would be “extremely unwise.” She reposted a comment from one of her followers, writing: “I’m willing to give Dems a chance with their new power before I judge. I’m an independent. Kennedy is my red line. If they cross it I want them to get absolutely fucked in 2028.”
Still, there are some inklings that part of MAHA could be absorbed into blue platforms—whether the leaders of the movement in its current form like it or not.
Earlier this month, Brinda Adhikari, a journalist and co-host of the podcast Why Should I Trust You?, argued that MAHA wasn’t dying but remaking the Democratic Party to be more like its old self. In a Substack post titled How MAHA Is Making Democrats Democrats Again, Adhikari pointed to a health policy document from House Democrats with a section, led by Ocasio-Cortez, titled “Reclaiming MAHA and Protecting American Families.”
Adhikari wrote that some of the issues touted by MAHA are a natural fit for the Democratic Party. She stretched back to Rachel Carson’s seminal Silent Spring in 1962 and the progressive environmental activism that elevated issues of health, pesticides, toxic chemicals, and corporate influence over public health. “These were once bread-and-butter Democratic issues,” Adhikari wrote. “But somewhere along the way, Democrats lost some of their identity as the party leading these fights.”
Adhikari and Democrats credit Kennedy with redirecting attention to these issues, which have broad support among voters.
“Americans’ concerns about chronic disease and food safety, especially that which is linked to corporate influence over environmental regulation and public health, are legitimate and long overdue for a serious legislative response,” the House Democrat’s policy document reads. “The Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has galvanized a significant segment of the Republican Party and attracted many previously apolitical and non-traditional voters, yet many of the concerns raised by the movement are bipartisan in nature.”
A KFF poll in May found that 75 percent of Americans want stricter regulations on food additives—a prominent MAHA priority—and 64 percent want stricter regulation of pesticides in agriculture, another key MAHA agenda item.
But Kennedy and the Trump administration have not only failed to deliver on these issues, but they have also spoiled the movement, using “the legitimate concerns of American consumers about food safety to spread misinformation about vaccines, public health, and science,” the policy document reads. “Their rhetoric has systematically led to the erosion of trust in public health, the science community, and decreased vaccination rates, leading to fatal outbreaks in some cases.”
Possible political shift
Democrats intend to reclaim the popular health and environmental issues, free of Kennedy’s corrosive anti-science rhetoric. The document outlines plans to restore regulations that protect clean water and air damaged by the Trump administration, advance policies to keep toxic substances out of food, and further Food is Medicine policies, which provide produce prescriptions to American families to improve nutrition and health.
Adhikari predicts a political shift. “I increasingly think MAHA’s most unexpected legacy may be pushing Democrats back toward their own roots: challenging corporate power, fighting dangerous chemicals in our food supply, and holding toxic polluters accountable,” she wrote.
MAHA leaders tied to Kennedy and the anti-vaccine movement, like Bowden and Honeycutt, are unlikely to get behind such a shift. This could cause MAHA’s political power—however strong it actually is—to fracture. MAHA leaders have claimed repeatedly that their followers have the ability to sway elections. If MAHA hadn’t been betrayed or at least disappointed by Kennedy and Trump in the last two years, MAHA could have prevented Tuesday’s Republican wipeout, they have said.
But the polling data doesn’t support the idea that keeping MAHA in its current form maximizes its political power. While MAHA does have significant support among voters—41 percent of US adults say they support MAHA—that support is primarily tied to the health, environmental, and food safety issues, which are popular among non-MAHA supporters, too. Further, just 4 percent of MAHA supporters cited vaccines and medical choice—Kennedy’s key issues—as their reason for supporting the movement, the KFF poll revealed.
Beyond MAHA’s primary issues, both voters overall and MAHA supporters specifically said MAHA issues weren’t top of mind this election; instead, both groups named the cost of healthcare as a bigger issue than those prioritized by MAHA (the MAHA movement is not associated with the issue of health care reform). A separate KFF poll on election day found that 50 percent of voters thought that the Democratic Party was better able to handle healthcare, while only 30 percent of voters said the same of the Republican Party.
For now, it’s unclear exactly how—or if—MAHA will influence the political landscape going forward. It could break apart, live on through revamped Democratic policies, or try to form a new political party entirely. And, apparently, there’s also the possibility it will try to overthrow the GOP.
Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes.

articles.title: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday.
First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user.
While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.
The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it.
As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)
The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)
The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end. When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.
Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.

articles.title: DreamHost admits major cyberattack saw hackers steal customer data and access inboxes
articles.text:
DreamHost admits major cyberattack saw hackers steal customer data and access inboxes
A software vulnerability allowed threat actors to obtain login credentials
- DreamHost discloses breach exposing FTP/SFTP credentials and some webmail account session data
- Attackers exploited a vulnerability in the company’s File Manager service to access customer accounts
- DreamHost reset affected passwords, offered credit monitoring, and urged users to strengthen account security
Popular web hosting provider DreamHost has confirmed threat actors walked away with login credentials to its customers’ hosting accounts, as well as webmail accounts.
It is now urging organizations to take steps to protect themselves, as it works to tighten up on security and make sure these things never happen again.
In a copy of a data breach notification letter sent to affected organizations, DreamHost said that roughly two weeks ago it discovered unauthorized third-party access to the server that runs its web-based File manager at files.DreamHost.com.
Access to the manager was compromised during August 2026, the company further said, adding that the threat actors walked in by exploiting a vulnerability in that software.
Payment data secure
The flaw, which the company did not detail or describe, granted the attackers access to FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords of logged-in individuals. Furthermore, they were able to reach some webmail systems and grab session information - including credentials - of a “limited number” of webmail users.
Cybercriminals having access to login credentials means that whatever information is stored inside File Manager and the webmail should also be considered compromised. Furthermore, it means the emails can be used to disseminate spam, launch phishing attacks, or even engage in highly disruptive Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks that could be almost impossible to detect.
DreamHost did not discuss the identity of the attackers, and did not say if they reached out with an extortion attempt. “We believe this as a deliberate attack, and our team worked around the clock to contain it,” is all it said on the matter.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The investigation is still ongoing so the information is inconclusive, but DreamHost said there is currently no evidence that the attackers accessed control panel login information or customer billing details. The company allegedly doesn’t store full payment card numbers and only retains a secure token representing the payment card information. This token cannot be used to make purchases elsewhere.
“However, our investigation is ongoing, and if we discover any significant additional information, we will update this post,” DreamHost said.
DreamHost’s response
In response to the incident, DreamHost said it “took steps” to stop the attackers from further accessing its systems, and to address the exploited vulnerability.
Active sessions of users who may have been affected have been terminated, and their passwords were reset. Therefore, if you try to log into your DreamHost account and see that the password was reset, consider your data breached. DreamHost claims to have implemented “additional security measures” to prevent such incidents from happening again, although it did not say exactly what was done.
“DreamHost also is working closely with outside legal advisors and security and forensics experts to ensure the incident is properly addressed,” it said.
In the meantime, it urged customers to review their statements and notify the police of any suspicious activity, as well as to obtain and monitor their credit card reports. The company also advised users place a fraud alert on their credit report. Detailed steps on what customers can do to defend themselves can be found on this link.
Finally, DreamHost offered all affected individuals one year of free credit report monitoring and identity theft protection services through Equifax which is more or less standard practice in these situations.
So far, no threat actors claimed responsibility for the breach, and the data has not yet leaked to the dark web.
This is not the first cybersecurity incident DreamHost has experienced. In 2012, attackers gained access to one of its database servers, potentially exposing customer FTB and shell-access passwords. The company responded by resetting affected passwords, although it reported no evidence of significant malicious activity against customer accounts. Five years later, in 2017, the company suffered a major Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack against its DNS infrastructure, resulting in widespread connectivity issues for customers.

articles.title: Congresswoman calls for artificial superintelligence ban after Democrats' seismic midterm sweep — demands regulation of 'out of control' industry and pause on advanced AI
articles.text:
Congresswoman calls for artificial superintelligence ban after Democrats' seismic midterm sweep — demands regulation of 'out of control' industry and pause on advanced AI
The announcement follows Democrats taking both the House and Senate from the GOP during the U.S. midterms.
Just one day after the Democrats swept the U.S. midterm elections, Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) called for an agenda to pause advanced AI development. The Arizona representative said on X that the “out of control” industry needs to be regulated, and she even went as far as calling for the ban of artificial superintelligence. Many issues about AI data centers also went on the ballot during the November 3 election, with the majority of Americans voting against them. However, it should be noted that the backlash that AI data centers are facing are driven by concerns about utility hikes, noise pollution, and other impacts of power-hungry campuses, not just artificial intelligence in general.
Rep. Ansari was elected to the House in 2025, representing Arizona’s third congressional district. She’s also a member of the House Oversight Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation, as well as the Subcommittee on Economic Growth, Energy Policy, and Regulatory Affairs. While she doesn’t have a subcommittee or committee leadership position yet, these subcommittee memberships should give her some avenues to influence the U.S. Congress’ response to the White House’s AI policies, especially now that her party holds the majority in both the House and Senate.
The calls to regulate artificial intelligence aren’t new, with Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling for various actions against the tech companies focusing on artificial intelligence since last year. The independent senator has initially called for a halt on AI data center construction to ensure that the technology benefits “all of us, not just the 1%,” which followed up about half a year later with a bill that proposes 50% public ownership of U.S. AI firms and a $ 1,000 dividend for every American. He also proposed a 20-year prison sentence for anyone who develops artificial superintelligence, putting it nearly on par with the unauthorized development of nuclear weapons. Other Senate leaders are also confronting Big Tech companies and accusing them of misleading the public when it comes to the benefits that AI delivers to the communities they’re in.
However, these moves go against President Donald Trump’s artificial intelligence agenda, which the administration sees as a race against China. He recently sat down with some of the top executives of the biggest AI companies for lunch at White House, where they promised to “self-police” AI development after news that OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s LLMs have been wreaking havoc on the internet. It was also after this moment that Trump decided that AI is suffering from a branding problem and renamed the technology “Super Intelligence.” Some comments on her X post also showed resistance to her call — a user claiming to have stage 4 terminal lung cancer asked her to reconsider, saying that AI-powered medical research could save his life, while Elon Musk shared her post and wrote: “It’s a Brave New World.”
Nevertheless, the White House also acknowledged the unpopularity of AI data centers and took steps to reduce their impact on the electricity costs for the average residential and commercial user by asking hyperscalers, utility providers, and even state governors to sign the “ratepayer protection pledge.” Trump even went as far as mandating AI data centers to pay energy dividends to the local community, but it seems that his moves were deemed too little, too late by most voters.
