articles.title: SpaceX, Qualcomm team up to build a Starlink Mobile 5G network
articles.text:
SpaceX has partnered with Qualcomm in order to build out a 5G mobile network.
Under a new multi-year deal, SpaceX will bring Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure tech to what is described as “tens of thousands” of 5G cell towers across the U.S., with the first deployments set for 2027.
With the Qualcomm partnership, SpaceX will use Dragonwing to boost network coverage, capacity, and efficiency. As expected, SpaceX will pair this technology with its satellite constellation.
This essentially means that the aeronautics company is pushing to make Starlink Mobile a major carrier in the U.S., with intentions to compete directly with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon.
According to The Verge, the company has already bought a large number of spectrum licenses, and other recent reports note that it was actively exploring a purchase of U.S. telecom company Boost Mobile.
While the news is U.S.-focused, it’s notable since SpaceX is partnered with Rogers in Canada, with the carrier using Starlink to power its satellite-to-mobile features. It’ll be interesting to see what SpaceX’s carrier push will mean for that partnership, or what a Starlink Mobile could mean for the broader Canadian telecom industry.
This news comes as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared a desire to move away from Starlink.
Source: Qualcomm via The Verge
Image Credit: Qualcomm

articles.title: Duro revés judicial para 'The Pitt' por parecerse demasiado a 'ER'
articles.text:
The Pitt, una de las series más aclamadas de los últimos años, acaba de sufrir un duro revés judicial. ¿El motivo? Parecerse demasiado a ER (Urgencias en España, ER Emergencias en Latinoamérica), la aclamada producción televisiva que también tuvo a Noah Wyle como protagonista y que se emitió desde 1994 hasta 2009.
Variety reporta que un tribunal falló de forma unánime contra una apelación que había presentado Warner Bros Television, que aseveraba que ER y The Pitt eran shows sin ningún tipo de relación entre sí. No obstante, los jueces consideran que existen pruebas suficientes para permitir una demanda que inculpa a la serie de HBO Max de ser un reboot no autorizado.
La acusación en cuestión llega de parte de Sherri Crichton, la viuda de Michael Crichton, el creador de ER. La misma argumenta que The Pitt viola los términos contractuales originales de Crichton y Warner Bros, que determinaban que cualquier obra derivada de la serie original tendría que recibir la autorización de este o sus herederos.
Vale aclarar que la demanda no es nueva. Crichton la presentó en agosto de 2024, cuando The Pitt ni siquiera había debutado en el catálogo de HBO Max. Según la esposa del creador de ER, John Wells y Noah Wyle querían realizar una secuela de la serie original, pero terminaron cambiando de dirección cuando no obtuvieron su aprobación.
No obstante, considera que existen muchos elementos en común entre ambos títulos para todavía considerar a The Pitt como un reboot o un proyecto derivado, sin contar este con el visto bueno explícito del creador de ER. Sherri Crichton sostiene que esto viola los términos del acuerdo original de su esposo Michael con Warner Bros.
El parecido con ER, un gran drama para The Pitt
De acuerdo con el tribunal que falló contra la apelación de Warner Bros Television, existen "similitudes claras y numerosas" entre The Pitt y ER. Por ejemplo, el uso de una sala de urgencias como escenario principal, el uso de terminología médica específica en el guion, el ritmo de los episodios, la representación gráfica de heridas y lesiones, y hasta la presentación de personajes jóvenes y recién salidos de la facultad de medicina.
Ahora que la justicia ha fallado contra WB, la demanda de Crichton por The Pitt podrá avanzar hacia el juicio. De todos modos, está abierta la puerta a que las partes alcancen un acuerdo extrajudicial. Sea como sea, el culebrón todavía no ha escrito su última página.
Noah Wyle y John Wells han reconocido públicamente que su primera idea era desarrollar una secuela de ER, pero que ello no fue posible y por eso decidieron darle una vuelta de tuerca con The Pitt. Originalmente, la demanda les acusaba también de violar las condiciones contractuales estipuladas por Michael Crichton a sabiendas de lo que hacían, aunque eso sí ha sido desestimado por los jueces.
Más allá de la batalla legal entre los responsables de The Pitt y la familia del creador de ER, la serie de HBO Max no correría peligro. Las dos primeras temporadas fueron impactantes y cosecharon aclamación tanto del público y la prensa, como también de la comunidad de trabajadores de la sanidad.
En agosto pasado, HBO Max lanzó el primer tráiler de la tercera temporada de The Pitt. Si bien todavía no tiene fecha de estreno confirmada, sí es un hecho que llegará en enero de 2027.

articles.title: Russische Hacker sollen Website von Luxushotel ins Visier genommen haben: Was steckt dahinter?
articles.text:
Ein Websitebesuch reichte: So nutzten Hacker eine Schwachstelle in iOS und Android aus
Hacker:innen sollen Schwachstellen in den Betriebssystemen iOS und Android ausgenutzt haben, um Besucher:innen verschiedener Websites zu hacken. Das geht aus einem Bericht der Cybersecurity-Firma Sekoia hervor. Bei ihren Analysen identifizierten die Forscher:innen eine groß angelegte „Watering-Hole“-Kampagne, die verschiedene Infektionsvektoren nutzte.
Aufgrund technischer Überschneidungen, operativer Muster, der Opferprofilanalyse und der Infrastruktur schreibt Sekoia die Kampagne mit „mittlerer bis hoher Wahrscheinlichkeit“ der russischen Hackergruppe APT29 zu, die dem russischen Auslandsgeheimdienst zugeordnet wird. Die Sicherheitslücken konnten inzwischen geschlossen werden.
Hacker:innen nahmen Websites ins Visier
Den Sicherheitsforscher:innen zufolge hatten viele der betroffenen Internetseiten einen Bezug zum andauernden Krieg zwischen Russland und der Ukraine. Sekoia schätzt, dass die Angreifer:innen es dabei auf diplomatische Ziele abgesehen haben könnten. Die Angriffe begannen, sobald iPhone- oder Android-Nutzer:innen eine der Websites besuchten. Das Gerät wurde in diesem Moment durch ein in den Datenverkehr eingeschleustes Javascript erfasst.
Die endgültigen Payloads waren auf die jeweilige Plattform zugeschnitten und versuchten laut den Forscher:innen, Browser-Cookies, in einigen Fällen WLAN-Passwörter und sogar die gesamten Daten des Mobilgeräts zu stehlen. Einer der Angriffe habe auf die Website eines Luxushotels in der Nähe einiger britischer Regierungsinstitutionen abgezielt. Auch der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj soll dort schon übernachtet haben.
Auch america250.org zählt zu den betroffenen Internetseiten. Sie befasst sich mit dem 250. Jahrestag der amerikanischen Unabhängigkeit. Betreiber der Seite ist eine überparteiliche Gruppe aus Gesetzgeber:innen, Führungskräften der Wirtschaft und mindestens einem ehemaligen Mitglied der Trump-Regierung. Die Angreifer:innen registrierten eine ähnlich klingende Website und nutzten diese Domain als Reverse-Proxy. Die gefälschte Website lieferte Inhalte der echten Seite aus, denen bösartiges Javascript hinzugefügt wurde.
„Wir gehen davon aus, dass die Angreifer:innen diese Website aufgrund ihrer Verbindung zu einem vielbeachteten nationalen Fest bewusst ausgewählt haben, um das Ereignis möglicherweise als Vorwand für Spear-Phishing-Kampagnen unter dem Deckmantel von Einladungen zu nutzen”, so die Forscher:innen.
So gingen die Angreifer bei ihrer Angriffskampagne vor
Die Hacker:innen nutzten drei Infektionsvektoren. Dazu zählten die direkte Javascript-Injektion in den Datenverkehr legitimer Websites, Proxy-Domains sowie die Kompromittierung der Lieferkette eines ukrainischen Webanalyse-Dienstes. In der ersten Phase erstellte das injizierte Javascript ein Profil des Browsers und des Geräts der Besucher:innen.
Anschließend lösten die Angreifer:innen anhand dieser Informationen eine von drei Zero-Click-Exploit-Ketten aus, die ohne Interaktion der Opfer funktionieren. Laut Sekoia beruht die Zuordnung zum russischen Auslandsgeheimdienst auf den Profilen der Ziele und Ähnlichkeiten mit einem früheren Angriff, der ebenfalls APT29 zugeschrieben wurde.

articles.title: Why Magnetic Sensor Selection Has Become a System Architecture Decision - EE Times
articles.text:
Kiloampere busbars, 2,000 V solar platforms, hollow-shaft robot joints and nanoamp standby budgets are pulling magnetic sensing in directions no single sensing principle can follow.
Ask a traction inverter designer, a robotics engineer and someone building a battery-powered water meter what they need from a magnetic sensor, and you will get three answers with very little overlap.
The inverter designer is measuring current across an enormous range, from a few amperes in control circuits to several hundred amperes or more in the traction inverter and battery main circuit, carried on busbars that will never pass through a PCB. A colleague on the photovoltaic and storage side faces a twist on the same problem: those platforms are moving toward 2,000 V, so the sensor package itself now has to provide the creepage and clearance that used to belong to a separate module. The robotics engineer wants encoder resolution approaching optical performance, but the center of the joint is reserved for cables, so the sensor has to work off-axis. And the meter designer mostly cares about one figure: how much current the sensor draws while it waits, because that decides how many years the battery lasts.
These are all magnetic sensing problems, and they do not share a best answer. Hall, AMR, TMR, inductive and fluxgate techniques each have a regime where they are the right physics and others where they are a compromise. That turns sensor selection into an architecture decision, weighed against power budget, field strength, accuracy, interference, mechanical integration, isolation and cost all at once. It also means the range of technology a supplier can draw on starts to matter as much as any single datasheet.
NOVOSENSE has built its magnetic sensor business on that premise, covering all five principles across current, angle, position, speed and switch functions. Yole Group ranks the company fourth globally by magnetic sensor shipment volume and first among Chinese suppliers. Shipments exceeded one billion units in 2025, with cumulative volume above 4.6 billion. For a design engineer, though, the more useful question is how the selection logic works in practice.
Matching the Sensing Principle to the Requirement
Hall effect is still the foundation. It is the most mature technology in the NOVOSENSE portfolio and the most versatile, supporting switches, latches, current sensors, angle sensors and linear position sensors. Planar and vertical Hall elements together enable 2D and 3D detection, and because the elements and their conditioning circuitry can share a single silicon die, the packages are compact and reliable. Hall is also forgiving. Its wide linear range and resistance to saturation simplify designs in strong fields or crowded electromagnetic environments, and in appliances, consumer electronics and smart-home products that have no need for nanoamp-level power, it is usually the better system choice on cost and maturity.
TMR takes over where Hall runs short of sensitivity or power headroom. Its strengths are high sensitivity, low noise and very low power consumption. NOVOSENSE’s TMR switch solutions draw as little as 200 nA while sampling above 1 kHz, which suits battery-powered utility meters and industrial equipment that need both long battery life and fast response. TMR also handles weak fields and longer sensing distances better than Hall. AMR fills out the magnetoresistive side of the portfolio with low-power switching, high-resolution angle encoding and automotive wheel-speed sensing.
Inductive sensing removes the permanent magnet altogether, although NOVOSENSE is quick to point out that losing the magnet is rarely the goal in itself. “What matters more are the resulting system-level characteristics,” the company says. With no magnet, the sensor is inherently insensitive to external fields, which suits compact designs sitting near high currents, motors or power electronics, and inductive technology can reach higher angular accuracy than existing Hall or magnetoresistive approaches. The price is integration effort. An inductive design needs a matching target rotor, coil or PCB structure, usually takes more space than a compact Hall solution and is rarely a drop-in replacement for an existing magnetic encoder.
Fluxgate covers the precision end of current sensing. Here NOVOSENSE supplies the signal-conditioning ASIC and the customer designs the probe, windings and module, so final performance depends on the whole assembly. A well-executed fluxgate system typically reaches the 0.5 percent accuracy class, with particular strength in offset stability and low-current detection, which is why it appears in battery management, on the grid side of photovoltaic inverters, in energy storage and in leakage-current detection.
NOVOSENSE Magnetic Sensor Technology Lineup
Table 1 summarizes how the five principles line up. When a customer arrives with a requirement rather than a technology preference, NOVOSENSE first asks what the measurement is for and whether a production-proven solution already exists in a comparable system or adjacent industry. For new applications, the team works through range, accuracy, response time, power, interface, installation space, environment, EMC, reliability, functional safety, cost and production constraints. “The technology is selected according to these system constraints rather than a predetermined preference for Hall, AMR or TMR,” the company explains. The answer often surprises the customer. A solution proven in AGVs or robot vacuum cleaners, for example, might be adapted for a robotics program to reduce cost or implementation complexity.
Table 1. Magnetic sensing principles at a glance
| Principle | Where it fits best | Design considerations | Typical applications | 
| Hall effect | Mature and cost-effective; wide linear range and resistance to saturation; element and conditioning on one die; differential designs reject stray fields | Lower intrinsic sensitivity; not suited to nanoamp-level power budgets | Switches and latches, integrated and linear current sensing, automotive angle, 3D and linear position | 
| AMR | Low-power switching, high-resolution angle encoding, wheel-speed sensing | Performance depends on element materials and process maturity; NOVOSENSE can also supply the conditioning ASIC for a customer element | Automotive wheel speed, angle encoders, low-power switches | 
| TMR | Highest sensitivity and low noise; switch current as low as 200 nA with sampling above 1 kHz; weak-field and long-distance detection | Hall remains more cost-effective where nanoamp power is unnecessary and more tolerant of strong fields | Battery-powered meters, low-power switches, industrial level sensing; angle and position in development | 
| Inductive | No permanent magnet; inherently insensitive to external fields; highest angular accuracy (MT6901 typical INL ±0.02°) | Requires a matching target rotor, coil or PCB structure; larger than compact Hall; rarely a drop-in replacement | Robot joints, high-end servo, precision machinery, inductive proximity switches | 
| Fluxgate (conditioning ASIC) | System accuracy in the 0.5 percent class; offset stability; low-current detection | Customer designs probe, windings and module; performance depends on the full assembly | BMS, photovoltaic inverter grid side, energy storage, leakage-current detection | 
The Development Chain Behind the Breadth
Five sensing principles only help if each one is backed by more than a sensing element. What an engineer actually receives, accuracy over temperature and over the life of the part, is a property of the whole chain: element, signal-conditioning ASIC, package, calibration and production test.
Asked which link was hardest to build, NOVOSENSE pointed to the sensing elements. AMR and TMR elements demand long-term work on materials, physical mechanisms, manufacturing processes and reliability, and relatively few suppliers have real capability there. Calibration is the other link that separates products, since errors have to be characterized across temperature, field or angle and compensation parameters programmed into each device.
Three-temperature calibration shows what that means on the production floor. Each device is stabilized at low, room and high temperature, a known current or field is applied, offset and sensitivity errors are measured, and compensation coefficients are calculated, written to the part and verified. That is how high-precision NOVOSENSE current sensors reach approximately 1 percent accuracy across the operating temperature range. It is not free. Anyone who has watched a tester wait out a cold soak will know where the time goes: cooling and thermal stabilization take longer than heating, so temperature cycling often consumes more test time than the electrical measurements. NOVOSENSE is also candid that calibration retention over the operating life cannot be reduced to one universal number. It depends on the product, element, package and stress conditions, and it is confirmed through product-level reliability qualification and lifetime assessment.
The same chain lets NOVOSENSE supply only the conditioning ASIC when a customer brings its own AMR or TMR element, handling amplification, compensation, waveform conditioning and interface conversion, including SPI output. Around the silicon, the company supports customers with circuit design, magnetic-field simulation, mechanical assessment and system debugging.
Current Sensing: From Amperes to Kiloamperes
The current-sensing portfolio divides at roughly 200 A. Below that point, integrated sensors route current through a conductor inside a PCB-mountable package, with measurement ranges extending to ±400 A. Above it, linear sensors work with external magnetic structures, taking total coverage to about 2,000 A.
The boundary comes mainly from package current-carrying capability and system architecture. Conductor cross-section, power dissipation, temperature rise, PCB current capacity and safety requirements all cap what an integrated part can handle, and beyond roughly 200 to 300 A, designers move the main current onto a busbar anyway. In EV traction systems running from several hundred to more than 1,000 A, a linear sensor with an external magnetic structure simply fits the architecture better. The line is moving, though. The market is already asking for integrated solutions in the 300 to 400 A range, and even at the same measurement range, a package that carries more current brings lower on-resistance, lower loss and less temperature rise.
For integrated devices, the package is an engineering variable, not a footprint preference. Compact QFN and SOP packages serve 12 V, 24 V and 48 V systems with moderate isolation needs, while wide-body and ultra-wide-body packages serve on-board chargers, DC-DC converters and 400 V to 800 V battery platforms. Bandwidths reach 1 MHz and 2 MHz for fast overcurrent response.
The NSM2051 takes that idea furthest. Aimed at emerging 2,000 V photovoltaic and storage platforms, its key change lies in the package rather than the die. An ultra-wide-body outline extends creepage and clearance to 15 mm and supports a basic-insulation working voltage of 2,800 VDC and 2,000 Vrms while remaining PCB mountable. Isolated current sensing moves onto the board in place of a larger conventional module, reducing system size, external module count and assembly steps.
Above the integrated range, the external magnetic structure sets the tradeoffs. A C-core is the mature option. It concentrates the field from the target current and shields against some external interference, generally giving the best stray-field immunity and accuracy. NOVOSENSE C-core solutions have been adopted by major Chinese automotive manufacturers, and the NSM203x linear sensor pairs with an external C-core and busbar for traction measurement. The U-shaped magnetic concentrator trades some of that margin for compactness. The NSM2025 redirects the horizontal field into the vertical plane so the sensor mounts directly on the PCB, with approximately 1.5 percent full-temperature accuracy, roughly 270 kHz bandwidth, a typical 2 µs response time and operation from −40°C to 150°C.
Coreless designs, now sampling, go furthest on size, weight and system cost and avoid core saturation and hysteresis entirely. The honest tradeoff is greater sensitivity to ambient fields, crosstalk from adjacent conductors and installation tolerance. Coreless works when sensor and busbar are designed together, using busbar slotting, differential placement, tolerance control, crosstalk compensation and magnetic-field simulation. Put simply, the busbar drawing matters as much as the sensor datasheet.
GaAs Hall current sensors are also sampling, aimed at designs where drift is the limiting error. GaAs elements deliver lower sensitivity drift and better full-temperature accuracy than silicon Hall, but because the element and conditioning ASIC are fabricated separately and joined through multi-chip packaging and wire bonding, cost is higher than for a single-die silicon device. Targets include high-accuracy industrial current sensing, battery management, and photovoltaic and energy-storage systems.
Position, Angle and Speed: Resolution in Constrained Mechanics
For industrial motion, NOVOSENSE combines conditioning ASICs with Hall, AMR and inductive encoders, and the lineup is easiest to read as a ladder of accuracy. NOVOSENSE’s encoders support both on-axis and off-axis installation in robot joints, servo systems and motors. The MT6835 offers up to 21-bit resolution and is a practical replacement for optical encoders at 19 bits and below, already used in general-purpose servo motors, battery and food-processing equipment, 3D printers and other automation systems. In those applications, customers weigh cost, environmental robustness, reliability and installation complexity alongside angular accuracy.
For 19- to 23-bit requirements, the MT6901 inductive encoder is the next rung. Compared with Hall-based solutions, it delivers higher system-level accuracy, with typical INL of ±0.02° and angular error held below ±0.07° from −40°C to 125°C. Because it needs no permanent magnet and is insensitive to external fields, it keeps that accuracy next to motors and high-current conductors. Compared with high-accuracy optical encoders, it offers lower system cost along with the environmental robustness of a non-optical design, making it a strong fit for robotic joints, high-end servo systems and precision machinery. Optical encoders still lead above 23 bits of effective resolution, in precision cutting and machining, high-end metrology and laboratory calibration, and they remain the reference used to test other encoder technologies.
The NSM350x solves a mechanical problem as much as an electrical one. Robot joints use hollow shafts so power and communication cables can run through the center, simplifying cable management and shrinking the joint, and an encoder sitting on the axis blocks that path. The NSM350x moves the sensing elements off-axis and reads a dual-track magnetic ring, using a Vernier algorithm that compares the two tracks to recover single-turn absolute angle at up to 22-bit resolution. It supports 1.28 mm, 1.5 mm and 2.0 mm magnetic pitches and 16, 32 and 64 pole pairs. Typical INL is ±0.3° after simple self-calibration and ±0.1° after constant-speed self-calibration. That second figure carries a process requirement: the customer has to provide stable constant-speed rotation during assembly or production calibration, usually with a coaxial motor-to-motor fixture.
In automotive angle sensing, Hall is the more widely used technology, and for good reason. Integrating the Hall elements and conditioning circuitry on one die produces compact, reliable packages, while differential architectures and Hall’s lower intrinsic sensitivity give strong immunity to external fields. That counts for a lot in electrified vehicles, where high-current conductors are packed close together. The MT652x family uses 3D Hall sensing to detect field changes in the XY, XZ or YZ planes for valves and actuators. Meanwhile, the MT6511 employs a differential Hall architecture to improve immunity to stray magnetic fields. For ride-height sensing, the planar Hall NSM3219 uses a two-wire PSI5 current interface that provides strong interference immunity, supports PCB-less sensor designs and cuts wiring and overall system cost.
Further down the stack, Hall switches and latches span low-voltage consumer, 24 V industrial and automotive requirements up to 60 V, with speed-and-direction outputs, two- and three-wire interfaces, programmable options and 3D sensing, while xMR switches serve battery-powered equipment. The NSM903x shows how much now fits in one device: planar and vertical Hall elements for X, Y and Z detection, on-chip CORDIC processing for 360° angle calculation, 3D and angle-switch modes, low-power operation, an interrupt function and I2C, for joysticks, wearables, smart crowns and position switches.
Where the Portfolio Is Deployed
In vehicles, the portfolio reaches across body systems (windows, sunroofs, tailgates, seats, wipers and headlamp adjustment), thermal management valves, powertrain current measurement from BMS main circuits and traction inverters down to on-board chargers, DC-DC converters and PFC stages, and chassis functions such as steering angle, vehicle height, pedals, wheel speed and electric power steering. Industrial deployments center on current sensing in photovoltaic, energy-storage and charging systems and on closed-loop feedback in servo and stepper systems. Consumer uses range from appliance motors to earbuds, smart crowns and wearables, where low-power Hall and TMR parts protect battery life.
Functional safety follows the product architecture, not the sensing principle. Depending on the device, NOVOSENSE provides on-chip diagnostics, signal-plausibility checks, fault-status outputs and dual-channel or redundant outputs, backed by safety documentation and development support. Examples run from ASIL A for the MT72xx and NSM101x Hall switches and latches, through ASIL B(D) for the NSM41xx wheel-speed sensors and ASIL C for the NSM3219, to ASIL D for the MT6521 and MT6511 angle sensors. “Functional-safety capability is not determined directly by whether a product uses Hall, AMR or TMR technology,” NOVOSENSE notes. The same reasoning answers the common hesitation about TMR in safety-relevant positions. TMR already has years of volume production in automotive angle sensing, industrial level sensing and low-power switches, and NOVOSENSE qualifies its automotive TMR parts to standards such as AEC-Q100, evaluating the element, ASIC, package and interconnects together.
Where Magnetic Sensing Goes Next
According to NOVOSENSE, robotics is producing the most concentrated set of new problems. Humanoid and collaborative robot joints must balance angular accuracy, compact design, hollow-shaft routing, field immunity, in-system calibration and cost at once. Two gaps stand out. High-accuracy calibration still depends on a motor-to-motor fixture, which is manageable for a standalone motor and difficult once that motor is buried inside a joint, and customers want to calibrate simply by turning the joint during final assembly or maintenance. Robot builders also want single-chip encoders that support multiple industrial protocols and store algorithms, configuration and calibration data on-chip, eliminating external MCUs, memory and extra PCBs.
Mature markets are moving too. Portable medical and consumer devices keep pushing for lower power, lower noise and faster response, automotive switch applications increasingly require functional-safety support, and the move to 48 V architectures raises voltage-withstand requirements. Over the next two years, NOVOSENSE plans to broaden its inductive encoder and TMR portfolios across more accuracy levels, sizes and installation arrangements, extend TMR into angle and position sensing, integrate more algorithms, memory and communication protocols, and develop ultra-low-power TMR and inductive switch and proximity solutions. Outside China, the company has set up offices and local support teams in Germany, Japan and South Korea, where customers put heavy weight on long-term reliability data, functional-safety documentation, supply continuity and local engineering support.
The thread running through all of this showed up when NOVOSENSE described how its customer conversations have changed. As the portfolio grew, discussions gradually shifted from “where can this product be used?” to “what solution does this system require?” For engineers juggling current, voltage, resolution, power and mechanical constraints in the same design, that second question is the right place to start.

NOVOSENSE is advancing innovation across automotive electronics, renewable energy & power supply, industrial control, and consumer electronics with a comprehensive portfolio of isolators, interfaces, drivers, sensors, signal chain, and power management ICs.

articles.title: What Makes a Quantum Company Valuable? - EE Times
articles.text:
Ahead of the World Quantum Festival 2026 in Cannes, France, quantum investors weighed technical bottlenecks, commercial timing, and customer adoption, with healthcare offering a revealing test.
Nardo Manaloto, managing partner of Qubits Ventures, asked the founder of an unnamed startup for a commercial roadmap. The startup was building a photonic quantum computer and had said it would need a decade to deliver its ultimate product. Manaloto wanted to know what the company could sell along the way.
The startup proposed a sequence beginning with a photon detector, followed by a chip, before progressing toward the computer itself. For Manaloto, each intermediate product must solve a customer problem and have commercial value on its own while advancing the company’s long-term technology roadmap.
“The roadmap also extends to the business side,” he told EE Times.
That requirement captures a central challenge in quantum investment. Scientific progress can make a technology promising, but building a valuable company also calls for judgments about customers, financing, and timing.
Finding the bottleneck
Owen Lozman, managing partner of Copenhagen-based quantum investment fund 55 North, draws on his experience in semiconductor investing. He looks for startups that can solve an industry bottleneck by the time customers urgently need a solution.
“Generally in deep tech, we’re not looking for, ‘Does the invention work?’ but, ‘Does it solve a problem at the time at which it’s going to be needed by the customer?’” he told EE Times.
In quantum, that can mean helping system developers move from laboratory assemblies to reliable, reproducible equipment. Lozman cited 55 North’s investment in Monarch Quantum as an example: Optical modules that can be manufactured consistently become increasingly important as quantum companies professionalize their supply chains.
Lozman distinguished three types of quantum businesses, each with different commercial challenges and measures of progress:
- Component suppliers: They must supply reliable, reproducible equipment as quantum computer builders scale production. Investors can examine revenue growth, production costs, and profitability. Lozman said he favors technologies serving multiple qubit architectures and several potential customers.
- Quantum computer developers: They must move from demonstrating individual qubits to building useful, scalable systems. Investors assess their technical differentiation and approach to scaling, including whether they must build manufacturing capacity themselves or can use existing semiconductor infrastructure.
- Software and applications companies: They must understand customer problems and prepare solutions for when suitable quantum hardware becomes available. Investors look for evidence of customer willingness to pay and a credible fit between the product and customer needs. Timing matters: Expanding before the hardware is ready can leave a company burning cash without sufficient revenue.
Value before revenue
Early sales provide evidence of demand, but they are not the only way a quantum company can become valuable. “In a lot of deep tech, the revenue is rarely the exit trigger,” Lozman said, referring to what prompts an acquisition or another opportunity for investors to cash out. “Technology is often the exit trigger.”
A system developer may lack a capability that a smaller company has developed. Bringing them together could create substantially more value than either business holds separately. Manaloto likewise sees value in defensible intellectual property, specialized engineering capabilities, strategic partnerships, and technologies that address critical industry bottlenecks—even before substantial revenue arrives.
Some companies pursuing complete quantum systems may ultimately merge or become component suppliers themselves, Lozman said. Their technology could remain important even if their original business model changes.
For applications companies, however, timing creates a particular danger. They need close customer relationships and a clear understanding of product requirements, but expanding before suitable hardware exists can leave them spending heavily without the expected revenue.
“If you’re a year or two early and you’re burning too much cash, it’s very, very difficult to sustain your company,” Lozman said. “Survivability will be a key kind of KPI for a lot of the assets in this space.”
Manaloto’s demand for intermediate products addresses that financing challenge. The objective is to build revenue and company value while progressing toward the final technology. But an intermediate product still needs a customer and a credible market.
Healthcare’s data opportunity
Healthcare is an application area that particularly interests Manaloto. His experience includes work with Kaiser Permanente’s innovation group and technology fund, where he encountered the difficulties of detecting disease earlier and obtaining useful biological information.
He sees opportunities in quantum sensing instruments that could reveal additional information about cellular processes. Unlike applications that depend on future quantum computers, some sensing businesses could commercialize instruments and measurements sooner, he argued.
Qubits Ventures has invested in Probius Bio, a Stanford spinout developing a quantum electrochemical spectroscopy platform. Manaloto described a system that captures molecular vibrational signatures from biological samples and converts those measurements into biochemical datasets that could support biomarker discovery, drug development, and biological research.
He is also evaluating an investment in an unnamed company developing diamond-based quantum sensing technology to investigate free radical activity and oxidative stress within living cells. Such measurements could help researchers and pharmaceutical companies study cellular behavior, disease mechanisms, and drug responses, he said.
For Manaloto, the opportunity extends beyond selling instruments. The greater potential lies in translating biological measurements that have been difficult to obtain into information that researchers, pharmaceutical companies, and eventually healthcare providers can act on. Research applications could provide an initial market before diagnostic or therapeutic uses are established.
“What do I do with that data? How do I translate it? How can pharma use it?” Manaloto said.
Those questions expose the distance between producing an unfamiliar measurement and delivering a useful product. A researcher needs to understand what the measurement reveals about the biological sample. A clinician needs evidence that it informs a decision. The technology must fit the way they already work—or offer enough benefit to persuade them to change their practices.
Integration with existing systems and compliance requirements add further work before a healthcare organization becomes a repeat customer, Manaloto said.
Capturing the benefit
Lozman identified another hurdle: The company selling a sensor may be separated from the organization receiving its greatest economic benefit. “It’s hard making money out of a sensor,” he said. “It’s hard to get people to recover the value if the buyer and the beneficiary are not close in the value chain.”
A measurement could improve a downstream process while leaving the instrument supplier struggling to capture a sufficient share of the benefit. The business model must connect the product’s price to an outcome the customer recognizes and will pay for.
In pharmaceutical research, Lozman sees potential opportunities in instruments that simplify drug discovery, improve toxicology assessment, or support better clinical-trial endpoints.
Qualification can be slow. Drawing on his experience across electronics and healthcare, Lozman noted that customers have strong reasons to protect processes that already work. A new technology must solve a sufficiently important problem to justify its introduction.
The same caution can benefit a company once its product is established. “Once you’re in, it’s very hard to get displaced,” Lozman said.
Both Manaloto and Lozman will attend the World Quantum Cannes Festival on November 17–18, where quantum technology providers, investors, and potential customers will meet to discuss applications and commercialization. For investors, those conversations offer an opportunity to hear how prospective users define their problems—and what they might be willing to pay to solve them.
For quantum investors, that’s where scientific promise must lead: a capability that solves a consequential problem, reaches the market at the right time, and gives its developer a defensible business. The roadmap to that outcome can matter as much as the eventual machine.

articles.title: Adding Network Security To AI, HPC, And Data Centers
articles.text:
The location of security functions such as MACsec or IPsec has become a key architectural decision.
AI and HPC are transforming data center networking. Modern infrastructures typically consist of a front-end network connecting users, storage, and management systems, and a back-end network interconnecting GPUs and compute nodes. At the largest scale, AI clusters span multiple locations, relying on scale-across networking to create a unified infrastructure.
While most modern data centers use leaf-spine architectures, implementation choices are influenced by more than technical requirements. Existing vendor relationships, product availability, supply-chain considerations, and total cost of ownership all play important roles. Consequently, organizations pursuing similar objectives often implement the network based on their business priorities, operational constraints, and upgrade strategies.
AI and HPC infrastructures process valuable data and represent significant financial investments. Protecting these environments requires controls for:
At the same time, security mechanisms must support the fundamental goals of AI infrastructure:
The industry benefits from more than a decade of operational experience with technologies such as MACsec and IPsec in high-speed networks. The primary challenge today is determining where and how those capabilities should be implemented.
Modern AI networks operate at hundreds of gigabits per second and are rapidly moving toward multi-terabit speeds. At these performance levels, network security must be implemented in following way:
Fig. 1: Hardware-accelerated network security architecture with data plane and control plane.
One of the most important architectural decisions is the location of security functions such as MACsec, IPsec, or emerging Ultra Ethernet security mechanisms.
Integrating security directly into the switch ASIC allows encryption and authentication to become part of the packet-forwarding pipeline.
Advantages:
Challenges:
Alternatively, security functions can be implemented in external PHY devices (like the line-card retimer/gearboxes) or security-enabled pluggable modules.
AI and compute systems rely on specialized transport protocols, including InfiniBand, RoCEv2, Ultra Ethernet Transport (UET). Unlike fabric-level security, transport security is typically associated with a specific user, job, or workload and therefore operates as an end-to-end service. Security must remain transparent to the underlying fabric while preserving the low latency and high throughput required by accelerated computing.
For this reason, transport security is integrated into (Smart) NICs and closely coupled with hardware-accelerated transport processing and often support multiple transport and security protocols simultaneously to accommodate diverse communication requirements.
Fig. 2: Network security in the AI NIC.
Modern infrastructures deploy multiple security layers simultaneously based on topology, trust boundaries, and workload requirements:
These mechanisms are largely complementary rather than competitive. MACsec is commonly used for link-level protection, IPsec secures routed traffic across networks, and transport-level security protects AI and HPC communication flows.
Advances in optics are expanding deployment options for network security. MACsec is now being integrated directly into 800G and 1.6T optical modules, enabled by use of silicon technologies optimized for low-power packet processing.
Looking ahead, chiplet-based switch and NIC architectures, together with near-package and co-packaged optics, may create new opportunities for security integration. Dedicated I/O chiplets could become a natural location for encryption and authentication functions while preserving valuable compute and switching resources.
Network security is now a fundamental requirement for AI, HPC, and cloud-scale data centers. Protecting traffic at terabit speeds demands hardware-based implementation capable of maintaining line-rate performance while meeting cost and power targets.
The industry offers multiple deployment options, including switch ASICs, external PHYs, optical modules, SmartNICs, and future chiplet-based architectures. This flexibility allows data center designers to balance security, performance, power efficiency, and system cost according to the needs of their infrastructure.
Rambus addresses these challenges through a broad portfolio of industry-proven network security silicon IP supporting rates up to 1.6T, and 3.2T in the future. Customers can balance security features, throughput, power consumption, and integration effort to deploy network security capabilities that meet the performance, cost, and time-to-market requirements of their silicon devices. articles.title: Constantine : un nouveau film est en route, Keanu Reeves enfin de retour ?
articles.text:
Le média américain Deadline a révélé ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 que DC Studios avait recruté Francis Galluppi pour écrire un film consacré à John Constantine. Le cinéaste s’est fait connaître avec son thriller policier The Last Stop in Yuma County (2023). Sam Raimi, créateur de la saga Evil Dead, l’a ensuite choisi pour écrire et réaliser Evil Dead Wrath, septième film de la série et son premier long-métrage pour un grand studio. Avec son futur Constantine, DC Studios replonge dans l’occulte, le terrain de jeu du personnage surnommé Hellblazer.
Un projet encore à l’état d’ébauche pour Constantine
Le projet n’en est qu’au tout début. D’après les sources de Deadline, le film est en développement très précoce chez DC Studios. Aucun réalisateur ni aucun acteur n’y est rattaché, et aucune date de sortie n’a été fixée.
Créé en 1985 par Alan Moore, Steve Bissette et John Totleben dans les pages de The Saga of the Swamp Thing (numéro 37), John Constantine s’est imposé comme le détective de l’occulte par excellence. C’est un Britannique désabusé, magouilleur et gros fumeur, qui fréquente aussi bien les démons que les anges déchus.
L’ombre de Keanu Reeves et le grand ménage du DCU
Cette annonce relance les questions sur la suite de Constantine, le film culte réalisé par Francis Lawrence en 2005, dans lequel Keanu Reeves incarnait une version de l’exorciste à Los Angeles. Deadline ne dit pas si Keanu Reeves ou cette suite sont concernés. On ne sait donc pas si Francis Galluppi écrit une nouvelle version du personnage, peut-être rattachée au DCU que reconstruisent James Gunn et Peter Safran, ou s’il reprend le projet Constantine 2.
Clayface dépasse déjà les 90 millions de dollars (environ 80 millions d’euros) de recettes mondiales pour un budget de production d’environ 40 millions de dollars. Avec ce succès et l’arrivée de cinéastes venus du film de genre comme Galluppi, DC Studios mise de plus en plus sur l’horreur et le polar noir. Le cinéaste doit d’abord livrer Evil Dead Wrath, attendu dans les salles américaines le 7 avril 2028.

articles.title: UK emerges as key base for African tech startups - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
The United Kingdom (UK) has emerged as a key international base for African tech companies, offering a mix of incorporation, operations and regulatory licensing that sets it apart from other global markets, according to a new report.
TLP Advisory, a cross-border venture law practice with its origins in Nigeria, has released its third annual report, Home and Away: Tracking African Tech’s Global Footprint, which examined 100 tech companies across Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Egypt, Ghana and Morocco, and their affiliations with the UK, US and UAE.
It found the US is largely associated with financing-linked incorporation, while the UAE serves as an operational base with access to the wider Middle East. The UK combines both, alongside a broader commercial presence.
Of the companies with UK affiliations, 84 per cent are incorporated there, 47 per cent have an operational presence, and 19 per cent hold regulatory licences. Just three per cent of US-affiliated companies and four per cent of UAE-affiliated companies hold licences in those markets.
“A round closed in Delaware and a licence in London are both important but they play very distinct roles,” said Odunoluwa Longe, co-founder and partner at TLP Advisory. “Our recommendation to founders is to be deliberate about what they want to achieve in each market.”
The UAE is the most operationally focused of the three markets, with 87 per cent of UAE-connected companies running operations there. Its regional pull is strongest among Egyptian startups, 70 per cent of which have a UAE affiliation, compared with 50 per cent for the US.
For fintechs in particular, the UK offers an established market and a large African diaspora. The report also highlights the SEIS and EIS investor tax relief schemes, the Global Entrepreneur Programme, English common law, and access to public markets through the London Stock Exchange and AIM as key draws.
“The UK didn’t feel foreign to us,” said Alex Forsyth-Thompson, founder and CEO of South African fintech Float. “There are a lot of South Africans here, so we had social capital from day one.”

articles.title: How Pine Labs is building for the agent economy: CTO Sanjeev Kumar on trust, control and execution
articles.text:
How Pine Labs is building for the agent economy: CTO Sanjeev Kumar on trust, control and execution
At TechSparks 2026, Pine Labs Chief Technology Officer, Sanjeev Kumar showcased how developers, merchants, and teams can put AI agents to work, backed by controls that keep them accountable.
AI agents are starting to run real parts of a business, from finding customers to processing complaints. For banks, fintech companies, and enterprises, that raises a basic question: how far can an agent be trusted to act on its own?
Pine Labs is addressing this question by building an ecosystem that enables AI agents to take on tasks across commerce while keeping their actions accountable. Speaking at its product showcase at TechSparks 2026, Sanjeev Kumar, CTO, Pine Labs, said, “We have tried to make AI a first-class citizen in our ecosystem.”
Over the past 18 months, Pine Labs has been building a commerce operating system around AI agents, combining tools to manage their permissions and track their actions with applications for merchants and enterprise teams. Its Agent Store will open the ecosystem to third-party developers building for merchants and banks.
Building trust into AI agents
For agents to operate in banking and enterprise environments, organizations need to know what they are authorized to do and how their actions can be audited. Pine Labs has developed Grantex, which Kumar described as ‘Open Authorization 2.0 for AI agents’. It assigns each agent a defined set of permissions, an expiry, and a record of the human who authorized it. If an agent authorized to read and draft emails attempts to send one, the action can be blocked and its permissions revoked, including those of any child agents. A tamper-proof, hash-chain audit trail records its actions.
Kumar outlined the work involved in connecting tools and systems, setting up retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), running continuous evaluations, and deciding where human intervention is necessary. These components need to work together before an agent can reliably handle tasks in an enterprise environment.
Pine Labs first deployed the technology across its compliance, finance, HR, and marketing teams, with processing taking place within its own environment. The company is also implementing it with banks in India and overseas.
From cyber fraud complaints to faster resolution
Cora, Pine Labs’ compliance and resolution agent, takes cyber fraud complaints from intake to closure. It matches complaints to transactions, categorizes them, routes them to relevant teams, and prepares responses for review. Kumar said Pine Labs has been able to close some complaints on the same day, compared with the typical three-to-five-day turnaround.
The agent records a 15-step trace of its work, including validation, transaction lookups, settlement checks, and team notifications, along with supporting evidence and confidence levels. When a system connector is unavailable, Cora can use robotic process automation (RPA). In the demonstration, it accessed the government cyber police portal and filled in an action-taken form with transaction details and the disputed amount. A human operator retains control of the password and one-time code and reviews the form before submission.
Opening the platform to developers
Having deployed agents across its own compliance, finance, HR and marketing teams, Pine Labs has since opened its platform to developers and merchant partners. The company is also working with banks in India and overseas.
To show how the technology could be applied beyond its own operations, Kumar pointed to a hackathon organized by Pine Labs and The Ken , which drew more than 380 agent submissions from students, fresh graduates, and engineers across India. The winning entry helped people decide what to cook for dinner.
Developers can create skill files, connect tools, and define tasks in plain English, while AgenticOrg provides visibility into agents, confidence scores, and audit trails via Grantex. The AgenticOrg is intended to help third-party developers build applications for merchants and banks using Pine Labs’ infrastructure.
Helping small merchants run ad campaigns
For smaller businesses, Pine Labs has also developed an ads agent accessible through its merchant interface. Merchants connect their Google Ads account, enter details about their business, and provide a brief, budget, and campaign goal. The agent researches local demand and nearby competitors, then generates ad copy for search, display, and YouTube.
Merchants can request changes and approve the campaign before it goes live. The demonstration showed setup taking about two minutes, with campaign performance and lead routing available through the same interface.
Building an ecosystem for commerce
From internal enterprise workflows and cyber fraud resolution to advertising for small businesses, Pine Labs is applying its agent infrastructure to different parts of commerce. Grantex sets guardrails for what agents can do; AgenticOrg helps teams, individuals, and AI enthusiasts build agents, manage work, and execute tasks, and AgenticOrg is intended to let developers build further applications for merchants and banks.
Pine Labs is betting that the future of commerce will be shaped not just by what AI agents can do, but by how reliably they can do it. By combining the infrastructure to govern agents with applications that solve real business problems, the company is looking to make autonomous AI a working part of commerce, for enterprises, banks, and merchants alike.

articles.title: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra silently obstructed safety research tasks
articles.text:
OpenAI disclosed that its GPT-6 Astra frontier model sometimes hindered safety research by complicating simple tasks, abandoning viable approaches, and silently refusing researchers’ requests.
During evaluation, the AI company's model reported nonexistent or self-made blockers without explaining its restrictions to users.
OpenAI said it first received a report of what it calls "covert underperformance" in Astra on August 20. The company then conducted targeted evaluations to investigate the behavior and determine its causes, noting that it had not observed the same issue in GPT-5.6 Sol.
OpenAI says it received the first report of what it calls “covert underperformance” in Astra on August 20. The company then ran specifically designed evaluation experiments to determine the extent and cause of this behavior, noting that the issues were not observed in GPT-5.6 Sol.
“Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing,” reads OpenAI’s report.
“This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison.”
A rubric item is one specific requirement used to score the model’s work, essentially an item on a grading checklist.
The main issue is that instead of explicitly declaring its inability to help with a research task and explaining its limitations to users, the model silently quits when it considers the work unsafe.
The concern is that researchers may trust results the model silently changed or left incomplete, misleading safety testing and wasting valuable research time.
OpenAI provided eight specific examples of this behavior, drawn from internal evaluations.
These include avoiding a retry fix that would improve a training pipeline, restricting exploit-development assistance, excluding a violent source from a safety evaluation, and limiting jailbreak-data exports.
OpenAI hypothesized that training intended to produce safer behavior may have encouraged undisclosed obstruction of safety work. However, it has not established this as the definitive cause for the observed model’s behavior.
The company also located a grader, a tool that evaluates AI model performance during reinforcement learning, that favored covert withholding over explicit refusal. However, it did not conclusively establish this as the cause.
OpenAI found no evidence that Astra deliberately engaged in this behavior to undermine research or make users “underestimate its capabilities.”

articles.title: Quels changements pour Windows 11 avec la mise à jour 27H2 ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Plus de six ans après le lancement de Windows 11, Microsoft n’est pas encore prête à passer à autre chose. D’après des informations obtenues par The Verge, la firme de Redmond serait en train de préparer une mise à jour majeure de son système d’exploitation pour la deuxième moitié de l’année 2027.
Point de Windows 12 de prévu donc, mais une version 27H2 qui promet de nombreux changements sous le capot.
Des gros travaux sur le code
Contrairement aux deux dernières versions majeures de Windows 11 qui se contentaient de corriger et d’améliorer certains aspects du système, cette dernière inclurait une refonte d’une bonne partie du code, un peu comme la version 24H2 qui était, à l’époque, la plus grosse mise à jour du système 11 depuis son lancement. Microsoft semble donc adopter un cycle de développement de trois ans pour les mises à jour « majeures » de son système avec des améliorations plus discrètes entre.
Le plus gros chantier sera à priori de réunir les deux bases « Germanium » et « Bromine » du système. Si les deux font tourner Windows 11, la première est dédiée aux systèmes x86, tandis que la seconde a été développée pour coller aux besoins des machines sous puces ARM. La mise à jour 27H2 devrait mettre tout le monde sur un pied d’égalité en termes d’accès aux diverses fonctionnalités et simplifier le développement des prochaines mises à jour.
La prise en charge d’Intel APX devrait également améliorer les performances sur les prochaines puces Intel, mais uniquement sur ces dernières. Les anciennes seront à priori exclues, même si Microsoft a fait des efforts sur le côté réactivité de son système récemment. Enfin, un nouveau fond d’écran devrait aussi voir le jour, histoire de marquer symboliquement la rupture.
À quand Windows 12 ?
La question qui reste en suspens est : quand verra-t-on émerger Windows 12 ? La version actuelle du système a clairement acquis une réputation douteuse, même si des améliorations ont été faites au fil des ans. Un retour à zéro pourrait aider à passer l’éponge, surtout que le monde de l’informatique a bien évolué depuis la première version de Windows 11 en 2021.
    Pour aller plus loin
Fin de Windows 10 : « un désastre de sécurité » selon les experts, mais l’Europe a un avantage
            
Et en même temps, cette bascule serait risquée à un moment où l’entreprise est déjà accusée de jouer le jeu de l’obsolescence programmée en abandonnant les PC Windows 10. Surtout que cela fait à peine un an que Windows 11 a gagné le concours de popularité face à son prédécesseur.
