articles.title: Gamers go to ridiculous lengths to "improve" GTA VI with Nvidia's DLSS 5
articles.text:
While the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI won’t be available on PC this month, some gamers are making ridiculous preparations to use their PC graphics cards to apply Nvidia’s DLSS 5 technology to the console exclusive.
On an explicitly unmoderated GTAVI subreddit, user RevolutionaryBus8208 lays out a proposed setup, which runs a PlayStation 5 through a 4K capture card to a PC. From there, the video signal is run through Veyra, an open source tool that can apply DLSS 5’s AI-powered “neural rendering” to video content. The result—which also uses DLSS frame generation to increase the 30 fps source to a 90 fps output—is then piped back to a 4K TV, theoretically adding some of the benefits of a beefy PC graphics card to a console-exclusive game.
To demonstrate the potential of this setup, RevolutionaryBus8208 used Veyra to upscale the Grand Theft Auto VI Extended Look trailer posted in August. The resulting DLSS-ified version looks a bit better in places, with sharper background elements, subtler shadows, and more believable light scattering on some surfaces. But it also seems a bit washed out compared to the original video’s deeper blacks and arguably suffers from an unnaturally smooth “soap opera effect” in some scenes.
There ain’t nothing for free
While the upscaled version causes some occasional graphical artifacts and glitches from the frame generation process, it’s still an interesting proof of concept that shows just how far DLSS 5 has come from some of the early horror-show memes that circulated on the Internet earlier this year.

articles.title: CEO da Nvidia é chamado ao Congresso dos EUA após alerta sobre possível espionagem chinesa
articles.text:
Os líderes republicanos de três comissões influentes da Câmara dos Representantes dos Estados Unidos solicitaram que Jensen Huang, CEO da Nvidia, participe voluntariamente de uma reunião a portas fechadas com parlamentares. O objetivo é esclarecer a relação do executivo com uma empresária ligada a uma companhia investigada pelo governo estadunidense por suspeita de ajudar a China a obter chips de inteligência artificial (IA).
O pedido foi feito nesta quinta-feira (5) pelos deputados Brian Mast, John Moolenaar e Rick Crawford, responsáveis, respectivamente, pela Comissão de Relações Exteriores, pelo Comitê Seleto sobre o Partido Comunista Chinês e pelo Comitê Seleto de Inteligência.
Os parlamentares querem que Huang compareça em 18 de novembro para falar sobre suas interações com Alice Huang, executiva da empresa Megaspeed, sediada em Singapura. Também pretendem questioná-lo sobre as políticas de segurança da Nvidia para evitar espionagem por parte de governos estrangeiros.
“É fundamental que o Congresso determine até que ponto a segurança nacional dos Estados Unidos foi colocada em risco”, escreveram os deputados no pedido.
O porta-voz da Nvidia, John Rizzo, não confirmou se o CEO aceitará o convite. Em declaração, afirmou que a empresa conta com equipe de segurança de excelência que acompanha Huang quando necessário.
Relação com executiva entrou no radar das autoridades
- O pedido dos parlamentares ocorre após reportagem do The New York Times, publicada na semana passada, revelar que Jensen Huang mantinha relação próxima com Alice Huang. Segundo o jornal, agências de inteligência estadunidenses identificaram essa relação por meio de vigilância sobre a executiva;
- A situação despertou preocupação dentro do governo dos Estados Unidos pela possibilidade de que ela estivesse obtendo informações comerciais ou de segurança nacional durante seus contatos com o CEO da Nvidia;
- Alice Huang é cidadã chinesa e ocupou o cargo de diretora-gerente da Megaspeed durante os primeiros oito meses de existência da empresa, em 2025. Posteriormente, retirou seu nome dessa função nos documentos corporativos. A companhia também passou a contar com um diretor de Singapura que trabalha em Xangai (China);
- O governo estadunidense investiga a Megaspeed desde o fim de 2024. Naquele período, um funcionário do Departamento de Comércio visitou um centro de dados da empresa na Malásia e considerou o local suspeito. Os equipamentos da Nvidia encontrados no endereço ainda estavam embalados, o que levantou dúvidas sobre se estavam sendo enviados para lá ou retirados do local.
Registros comerciais obtidos pela plataforma ImportGenius indicam que uma empresa ligada à Megaspeed na Malásia comprou pelo menos US$ 4,8 bilhões (cerca de R$ 26,2 bilhões) em equipamentos avançados de IA que continham chips e tecnologia da Nvidia entre junho de 2024 e fevereiro de 2026.
A suspeita das autoridades é de que a Megaspeed tenha ajudado a China a contornar restrições comerciais estadunidenses e obter acesso aos componentes da fabricante.
A Nvidia afirma cumprir a legislação e diz não haver evidências de que seus chips estejam sendo contrabandeados para a China. Na semana passada, Rizzo também afirmou que as interações de Huang com Alice não eram incomuns ou inesperadas. Segundo o porta-voz, reuniões com clientes fazem parte do trabalho de um CEO, e Huang conversa com milhares de executivos de empresas clientes todos os anos.
Leia mais:
- SpaceX levanta R$ 216 bilhões para comprar chips de IA da Nvidia
- China chama acusações de espionagem contra CEO da Nvidia de falsas
- Startup chinesa tenta contornar restrições dos EUA para acessar chips da Nvidia
Pedido representa mudança de postura entre republicanos
A iniciativa dos três parlamentares também chama atenção por representar mudança de postura de lideranças republicanas, que, em grande parte, acompanharam o presidente Donald Trump em abordagem menos intervencionista em relação ao setor de tecnologia.
Huang construiu relação próxima com Trump nos últimos dois anos e os dois conversam frequentemente sobre assuntos relacionados à tecnologia.
O movimento ocorre ainda depois das eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos, que evidenciaram a preocupação de parte do eleitorado com os impactos da indústria tecnológica. Entre os temas estão o potencial da IA para eliminar empregos e a construção de grandes centros de dados em comunidades locais.
O sentimento contrário às grandes empresas de tecnologia favoreceu, em grande medida, candidatos democratas. A iniciativa republicana pode ser um sinal de que o partido não pretende deixar esse tema exclusivamente nas mãos de seus adversários políticos.
Nvidia já havia sido questionada sobre vendas de chips
O episódio também se conecta a uma investigação anterior do Congresso. Em abril de 2025, John Moolenaar e o Comitê Seleto sobre o Partido Comunista Chinês abriram apuração sobre as vendas de chips da Nvidia na Ásia. Nos meses seguintes, porém, o governo Trump recuou de restrições às vendas de componentes da empresa para a China.
Huang também acompanhou Trump em sua primeira viagem diplomática ao Oriente Médio. Na ocasião, o presidente anunciou grande venda de chips para os Emirados Árabes Unidos e a Arábia Saudita.
A Nvidia ainda doou mais de US$ 20 milhões (cerca de R$ 109,2 milhões) para a construção do salão de festas da Casa Branca e prometeu investir US$ 500 bilhões (aproximadamente R$ 2,73 trilhões) na fabricação de produtos nos Estados Unidos.
Em junho, Huang já havia recusado um pedido para prestar depoimento ao Senado feito pela senadora Elizabeth Warren, democrata de Massachusetts (EUA) e principal representante da minoria no Comitê Bancário. Na semana passada, após a publicação da reportagem sobre a relação do executivo com Alice Huang, a parlamentar voltou a cobrar seu comparecimento.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”
Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.
“The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center, and it’s something that people can say, ‘I don’t want this in my community,’” she explained. “I think there’s an underlying bigger issue, which is how people feel about AI in general.”
Meta believes it could turn around the negative consumer sentiment around AI if it’s able to demonstrate the value, not only of the data centers coming to local communities, but also in the technology itself.
“The stakes of who builds the technology that cures cancer, that gives access to education, that is also a very fundamental difference … Mark [Zuckerberg, Meta CEO] is very ‘long human,’ and he’s betting on humans more than machines,” Powell McCormick explained. “And that’s what we mean when we say the future is for everyone. That people should not be left behind. But the way to ensure that is that this technology is democratized, that people have access to it in a very fair and transparent way,” she said.
The exec also touted Meta’s experience in building data centers, saying that the company has been doing so for 20 years, as it takes a lot of compute power to offer the products it does in the social networking space. Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.
But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.
“I think it’s going to be harder,” Powell McCormick said, describing what the future of building data centers looks like. “It has been hard, I should say, but I also think that it’s becoming clear what models work, and the states want those models that work.”
Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.
Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.
Going forward, she expects data center projects to come under more review and be weighed against whether the constituents actually want them.
Meta has pinned its hopes on its AI investments, particularly its consumer AI agent Muse scaling far beyond the 10 million users it has today, to become a business that one day serves billions. But even if that’s not the case, it believes that its investments in data centers will not be for nothing, as the compute itself will be valuable.
“We’re getting calls every day to lease that compute [we’ve built], and so one way or another, we’re seeing a path to monetization,” Powell McCormick said.

articles.title: I've tested Apple's new iMac with M6, and more power for the same price is a winning combination
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The M6 iMac is the best all-in-one computer you can buy right now — and Apple hasn't raised the price. It delivers plenty of power for work or play thanks to its better-equipped chip, and it still comes in seven fun shades wrapped in a modern, sleek design that fits just about anywhere. Pair that with 16GB of RAM to start, a USB-C keyboard and mouse or trackpad, and up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports, and you've got an excellent desktop for a family, a business, or a creator.
Reasons to buy
- + Yes, it's still the best all-in-one computer
- + Sleek, modern build in several fun shades
- + Vibrant 24-inch 4.5K Retina display
- + Excellent performance from the M6 chip
Reasons to avoid
- - No major changes to design
- - Nano-texture costs extra
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
At a glance: Apple iMac 24-inch (M6) Review
Apple's iMac with M6 is the latest generation of its all-in-one desktop. Like the M4, M3, and M1 before it, it keeps the modern, colorful design and slim build and includes a keyboard and mouse (or trackpad). Out of the box it's running macOS 27.2, and it's a capable desktop for creative work, productivity, and everyday tasks.
Good news: Apple hasn't increased the starting price. For $1,499, you get an M6 chip with a 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, and Dual 16-core Neural Engine, plus 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. A $1,699 configuration upgrades to a 12-core CPU and GPU and 512GB of storage. Nano-texture glass, additional Thunderbolt 4 ports, and Ethernet are also available as options.
Apple's Mac mini with M6 is the closest alternative, and lets you choose your own display, keyboard, and mouse. There's also the more powerful Mac Studio with M5 Max or M5 Ultra, alongside plenty of Windows desktop options.
Apple iMac (2026, M6) scorecard
How the Apple iMac (2026, M6) scored in our review
| Group 1 Data |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product | Value () | Design () | Performance () | Overall () | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple iMac (2026, M6) | 4.5 | 4.5 | 5 | 4.5 | 
Apple iMac 24-inch (M6) Review: Value for money
Apple's iMac with M6 isn't a revolution, but rather a lesson in squeezing more value out of a familiar package without raising the price. And I want to underscore the latter, as the iMac starts at $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$2,399 for the entry-level configuration, which is the same price as the M4 iMac — although Apple did increase the price of the M4 model earlier this year. For that price, you get a well-equipped Mac desktop that gives you everything you need to get started right out of the box.
That starts with the iMac itself, which is a modern, slim, colorful unit that won't take up much real estate, while giving you the canvas of a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display. Even without nano-texture glass — if you choose not to upgrade, as with my review unit — it's a colorful, vibrant, and rich experience that works well for everyday tasks and more creative work alike.
And, of course, there's the new M6 chip. It's a meaningful performance upgrade that keeps everything running smoothly, whether you're juggling everyday apps, working across multiple browser tabs, or getting stuck into more creative tasks. The addition of the Dual 16-core Neural Engine is another important part of the equation, helping accelerate AI-powered features, and giving this iMac more room to grow as Apple Intelligence continues to evolve. It's not just about getting a faster Mac today, but having a capable desktop that should feel ready for what's next, too.
Ultimately, it's excellent value for someone buying a new desktop Mac, whether it's their first iMac or an upgrade from an older machine. If you already have the M4 iMac, though, there's less reason to rush out and upgrade. This is a speed bump rather than a reinvention, but getting more performance for the same price is still a win.
If you currently have an older iMac or an aging Mac, and want a desktop that gives you everything you need out of the box — including a great display — there’s really no better value in Apple’s lineup.
Apple iMac 24-inch (M6) Review: Design
- Familiar, colorful all-in-one design
- Immersive 24-inch 4.5K Retina display
- You can still get it with nano-texture glass
Apple's iMac is still instantly recognizable as the latest generation of its iconic all-in-one. The new iMac with M6 looks just like the iMac with M4, M3, and M1 that came before it. It's still plenty colorful, and offers an expansive 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, all in a remarkably thin build that takes up minimal space wherever you decide to place it.
On the front, the 24-inch screen is surrounded by a white bezel, with the bottom featuring a chin in whichever color you've chosen. I'm testing the Purple model, just like last time, which is a light, likely Wonka-approved take on the shade. The rear and sides feature a darker, matte aluminum version of purple that really pops, while the giant Apple logo remains front and center on the back.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
For connectivity, the left side has a headphone jack — yes, the iMac has a proper audio jack — while the rear houses the power connection, which magnetically snaps into place. It's convenient, though not a quick-release connection like MagSafe on the MacBook Air or MacBook Pro. Around back, you'll either get two Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports or four, depending on the configuration. I'm testing the higher-end option with all four, and the power adapter also features a 2.5Gb Ethernet port.
Not much else is different here, especially since Apple introduced this design way back with the M1. If purple isn't your shade, there are six other color options: Orange, Blue, Yellow, Green, Silver, and Pink. You'll also get a color-matched keyboard and Magic Mouse or Magic Trackpad in the box, along with a matching USB-C to USB-C cable.
The display is really good, with a 4480 x 2520 resolution and up to 500 nits of brightness. Using it as my daily Mac, I've found it to be a great screen for just about everything. Colors pop, there's plenty of detail, and the resolution scales nicely whether I'm checking email, browsing the web, replying to messages, putting together presentations in Keynote, scrolling through Photos, or hopping on a FaceTime call.
It's equally enjoyable for watching content, whether that's a full-screen YouTube video or something playing in a window while I work. And for more creative tasks, there's plenty of detail and color to work with when editing photos or videos.
I do miss the optional nano-texture glass on my review unit, particularly when dealing with natural light or other reflections. But if you're placing the iMac in a space without a ton of direct sunlight or reflective surfaces, I think you're largely all right with the standard glossy finish.

| Screen | 24-inch 4.5K Retina display with 4480 x 2520 resolution at 218 ppi and 500 nits brightness | 24-inch 4.5K Retina display with 4480 x 2520 resolution at 218 ppi and 500 nits brightness. Optional nano-texture glass. | 
| Storage | 256GB (starting, but configurable up to 1TB) | 256GB (starting, but configurable up to 2TB) | 
| Ports | Two Thunderbolt 4/USB-C ports, headphone jack | Four Thunderbolt 4/USB-C ports, headphone jack | 
| Wireless | Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be), Bluetooth 6, and Thread connectivity | Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be), Bluetooth 6, and Thread connectivity | 
| Camera | 12-megapixel FaceTime camera with Center Stage and Desk View functionality | 12-megapixel FaceTime camera with Center Stage and Desk View functionality | 
| Weight | 4.42 kg/9.74 lbs | 4.44 kg/9.79 lbs | 
| Dimensions | 54.7 x 46.1 x 14.7cm / 21.5 x 18.1 x 5.8 inches | 54.7 x 46.1 x 14.7cm / 21.5 x 18.1 x 5.8 inches | 
Apple iMac 24-inch (M6) Review: Performance
- Apple's M6 chip brings a welcome performance boost over M4, M3, or M1
- Everyday multitasking feels effortless, even with 16GB of RAM
- Improved Neural Engine makes AI and creative tasks feel snappy
As I hinted at above, the main change with Apple's iMac for 2026 is the processor. Apple's all-in-one computer is jumping from M4 to M6, and there are still two main configurations to choose from. For most folks, the entry-level iMac should be more than enough. Priced at $1,499 / £1,499 / AU$3,499, you get an M6 chip with a 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, and Dual 16-core Neural Engine, alongside 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.
For $1,699 / £1,699 / AU$3,699, you can step up to an M6 with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, along with the same Dual 16-core Neural Engine, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. That extra horsepower should come in handy for more creative tasks and on-device AI functionality.
It's also worth noting that neither configuration comes with a price increase over the previous generation. Both feature improvements to Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, now sitting at Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, along with Thread connectivity to help with the smart home.
I've been testing the step-up model with the fully specced M6 chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. Out of the box, setup was a breeze, and the iMac is running macOS 27.2. Here's a pro tip: as part of the onboarding process, you can choose to set up your new Mac using an iPhone or iPad, which speeds things up a bit.
From there, you're presented with a welcome screen; hit Enter, and you're ready to start using your iMac however you'd like. And, as has been the case with most Macs since Apple made the jump to its own chips — Apple Silicon — everyday performance isn't really an issue. In my daily use, I've had no trouble running Safari and Google Chrome, both with more than a dozen tabs open, alongside Messages, Mail, Photos, Pixelmator Pro, and Slack, all without skipping a beat. Thanks to the M6 chip, multitasking is effortless, and everything feels zippy and responsive. That's particularly impressive given that this configuration has just 16GB of RAM.
One key advantage of the M6 is its Dual 16-core Neural Engine, compared with the single Neural Engine in earlier iMac models. This helps power Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features, and I've found some of the multimodal capabilities particularly snappy. For instance, I can ask Siri to create a calendar event based on an invitation displayed on my screen in Mail or Gmail, and even have it invite other people. You can type your request into Spotlight or use the built-in microphones to get started.
Similarly, as part of the latest updates to Apple Creator Studio, Generative Fill within Pixelmator Pro works quite snappily here. It's also easy enough to ask it to try again if the result isn't quite right. You can also use Siri AI within Numbers, Pages, and Keynote for a little extra assistance. I've found myself making good use of the big screen, too, starting with a photo edit in the Photos app using tools like Expand or Clean Up before sending it into Pixelmator Pro to refine things further. The Super Resolution functionality is particularly handy for boosting overall image quality.
Previously, my iMac with M4, which was specced with a beefier 32GB of RAM, scored 3,646 in single-core and 14,724 in multi-core testing with Geekbench 6.3. The iMac with M6 surpassed those results, scoring 4,553 in single-core and 20,038 in multi-core with Geekbench 6. That's roughly a 25% improvement in single-core performance and a 36% jump in multi-core performance over the M4.
We also ran Geekbench 7, where the M6 iMac scored 3,931 in single-core and 21,374 in multi-core testing. While those results aren't directly comparable to my previous Geekbench 6.3 scores, they further demonstrate the kind of performance this machine can deliver.
It's an impressive leap over two generations of Apple Silicon, and one that matches my real-world experience over the past few days. The iMac with M6 feels zippy, responsive, and ready for a challenge, even with just 16GB of RAM inside.
The iMac remains the centerpiece of Apple's all-in-one desktop lineup. Unlike the Mac mini or Mac Studio, you're getting a complete system that's ready to go right out of the box. That means a screen, speakers, ports, keyboard, and mouse are all included, making it an excellent choice for someone buying their first desktop Mac, upgrading from an older model or even a PC, or a business looking for a straightforward, all-in-one solution.
The iMac has always served a lot of different use cases, and Apple's latest iteration doesn't change or revolutionize that. But a speed-bump upgrade can still be a worthwhile one, especially when it brings more performance without increasing the price. You're getting more computer for the same money, and that's always welcome.
Should I buy the Apple iMac with M6?
✅ You want an excellent all-in-one computer
No price increase, improved performance, a sleek and colorful design, and a great display make the iMac with M6 an easy recommendation. It's an excellent all-in-one package that has plenty to offer without costing more than the previous generation.
✅ You're already in the Apple ecosystem
It goes without saying, but the iMac plays really well with iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and iCloud. You'll feel right at home with familiar apps, a shared clipboard between devices, the ability to mirror your iPhone on the iMac, and even the convenience of having calls ring on your desktop.
✅ You want a colorful, good-looking desktop
I said it with the M4, but I really love the look of the iMac. You get your pick of colors, and the result is a sleek desktop that weighs less than 10 pounds and doesn't look like a hunk of junk. It can fit just about anywhere.
❌ You need a bigger screen
Unlike a Mac mini, Mac Studio, or even a MacBook you plug into a display, the iMac with M6 only comes in one size: 24 inches. So if you need something larger or want flexibility, you'll want to look elsewhere
❌ You need the most powerful Mac
Apple already makes the M5 Max and M5 Ultra, both in desktop and laptop form, so if you need more power for more intensive tasks — be it creative work or running AI models — you'll want to look at those
How I tested the Apple iMac with M6
I've spent the past five days putting the Apple iMac with M6 through its paces. After unboxing it, I set it up in two different spaces — my kitchen island and my desk — to get a sense of how it fits into different environments. I downloaded a range of apps for work and play, including Google Chrome, Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Slack, and Geekbench.
I used it as my daily work machine, juggling browser tabs, messages, and creative projects, while also running benchmarks and more demanding tasks. Outside of work, I played games, took calls, watched movies, and listened to music to get a feel for its overall performance and entertainment experience.
First reviewed November 2026.
Jacob Krol is the US Managing Editor, News for TechRadar. He’s been writing about technology since he was 14 when he started his own tech blog. Since then Jacob has worked for a plethora of publications including CNN Underscored, TheStreet, Parade, Men’s Journal, Mashable, CNET, and CNBC among others.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables. In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.

articles.title: The MacBook PROLED XDR (M5 Max) is more than its touchscreen
articles.text:
I’ve only used the MacBook PROLED XDR for a couple of days, so I definitely need to put it through the wringer far more, but here are some initial thoughts about Apple’s first-ever touchscreen laptop.
First, I reviewed the M5 Max with an 18-core CPU/32-core GPU with 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. This variant clocks in at $6,499 in Canada, quite a bit more than the base PROLED model with M5 Pro, which starts at $3,999. For most people, the M5 Pro is already overkill, but the M5 Max does offer a notable performance increase that could be worthwhile for professional users.
Touching your screen
Apple has finally released its first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen. Back in 2010, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs publicly dismissed the idea of a touchscreen MacBook. At the time, Jobs said that vertical touch surfaces don’t work for MacBooks because you’re holding up your arm for an extended period of time to use it, leading to arm fatigue. “After an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off,” said Jobs.
I was introduced to the touchless Mac world back in 2019 with my first iMac, and since then I’ve completely switched over from a Windows laptop to various MacBooks, and honestly I completely forgot touch screen laptops existed.
I kind of agree with Jobs’ sentiment that touch screen isn’t really for laptops, and the novelty of a touch screen laptop has definitely worn off. And since I’ve been reviewing the PROLED, I haven’t found many reasons that require me to touch my screen. Require is definitely the key word here, as sometimes I find myself touching the screen just for the ease of it. While keeping my arm stretched for a long period would get tiring, I don’t think anyone is really using a laptop that way.
I’m only ever raising my arm to touch the screen for little moments. I’ve been using vertical tabs with Safari on the macOS 27.3 beta, and sometimes reaching out to press on a tab is an easy touch.
Also, when you’re lying down on a bed with the MacBook PROLED, it’s super easy to just use your thumb or finger to swipe up or down or turn the page when you’re reading. I like that the display is also very sturdy, so when you are touching the screen, there’s no movement.
Otherwise, it’s nice that you can touch the Dynamic Island to turn on Siri AI or Spotlight, but the existing CMD+Space shortcut is also super easy to do. It’s cool that the Magic Trackpad and the screen have the same gestures, so you sort of feel at home touching the display if that’s what you’ve decided to do. I’ve done a bit of photo editing with the PROLED, and haven’t found a need to touch the screen yet with this either.
PROLED XDR
What’s most impressive about the new MacBook Pro isn’t the touchscreen, but its beautiful new screen. The laptop has up to 2,000 nits of brightness in peak HDR and SDR brightness, both P3+Adobe RGB, and an insane 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, so everything is genuinely beautiful to look at.
Anime looked so great on this display, my weeb soul was so happy. It was one of the best ways to watch some of my favourites like Jujutsu Kaisen and Demon Slayer. Games like Control, Hades and Slay the Spire looked absolutely phenomenal as well. The screen is just so crisp; blacks are pitch-black, whites are bright, and colours are spectacular. Shows and games look so beautiful that I can imagine myself just pulling out the laptop to consume content. I’ve also been using the new M6 MacBook Pro, and no shade at that MacBook (I really like the M6), but this screen is fantastic.
And the screen’s brightness controls the brightness of the logo on the back as well. However, there doesn’t appear to be a way to fully turn off the logo glow without also darkening the display, closing the lid, or turning the laptop off. We’ve reached out to Apple to double check this though.
I also remember thinking that a Dynamic Island wouldn’t matter much, but I was very wrong. I love the Dynamic Island and whenever I went back to the M6 I was so displeased with the notch. Getting phone calls, when I order Uber Eats, or when I listen to music I’ll see Live Activities, which are useful and expand when with a touch and the animation is so smooth. I like that Siri and Spotlight expands from is it as well.
More than just the screen
Of course, this MacBook Pro with an M5 Max chipset is far more than a beautiful screen. I played some Control and Hades II and the games ran without a hitch. However, I did realize that the laptop gets pretty hot. I played Control for about 10 minutes, and it started to get too warm to keep on my lap.
I had ray tracing and HDR turned on, and the game ran and looked beautiful, but it just got warm. I also edited about 15 photos with Adobe Photoshop on the MacBook Pro, and tasks went smoothly, and it was easy, but the laptop did get noticeably warm here — not hot, but doing the same amount of photo editing on the M6 MacBook Pro, the laptop stayed quite cold to the touch.
This isn’t isolated to the PROLED MacBook or the M5 Max, with MobileSyrup EIC Jon Lamont’s MacBook Pro with M5 Pro also getting quite warm under similar usage.
I haven’t really had the laptop long enough to talk about battery life, I haven’t used a lot of AI features or done any video editing yet; so I’ll definitely follow up with more details in the coming weeks.
I’m not sure if the MacBook PROLED XDR needed a touchscreen. Maybe Steve Jobs was right, and a touchscreen is meant for iPhones and iPads, but not MacBooks. Either way, it’s here, and it works cleanly with gestures. However, the PROLED XDR offers such a beautiful screen, and if you’re someone who works in art or needs perfect colour accuracy and an extremely high dynamic range, then this is a good choice.
And despite not being too excited about the touch screen, whenever I switch back to the M6 MacBook Pro, I find myself touching the screen every once in a while, missing the PROLED XDR.
The MacBook PROLED costs $3,999 to start and is available starting Nov. 6, 2026.

articles.title: This $79.98 TP-Link wireless router with Wi-Fi 7 tech is back down to its lowest-ever price — Archer BE3600 unlocks multi-gigabit networking, ideal for gaming or 4K streaming with 33% off
articles.text:
This $79.98 TP-Link wireless router with Wi-Fi 7 tech is back down to its lowest-ever price — Archer BE3600 unlocks multi-gigabit networking, ideal for gaming or 4K streaming with 33% off
Give your wireless network a quick upgrade
There's a budget-friendly TP-Link router on sale and it's back down to the lowest ever price we saw it at over Amazon's sales event last month. Right now, the TP-Link Archer BE3600 wireless router is down to $79.98, a 33% saving compared to its list price.
● Check out this deal on Amazon
You won't be surprised to find that this is one of the best Wi-Fi routers you can pick up on a budget, but that's before this discount. You'll see in our TP-Link Archer BE3600 review why this is such a good deal, as this router adds Wi-Fi 7 support to your network cheaply and easily, albeit with a few caveats. Those aside, you're still getting strong performance for 2.4 and 5 GHz with this router.
This TP-Link Archer BE3600 router is one of the best-value routers you can buy right now, offering some Wi-Fi 7 support and 2.5G LAN accessibility.
The BE3600 is not a flashy gaming router, but a no-nonsense option with a standard design that looks very much how you'd expect. It's a flat, rectangular box with four antennas that help deliver good wireless coverage. It has one 2.5 Gbps WAN port to hook it up to your internet connection, as well as an extra 2.5 Gbps and three additional 1 Gbps ports for your home devices.
You've also got one USB 3.0 port, which you can use to connect a printer or external hard drive to use across your network. As far as configuration is concerned, TP-Link's setup is easy to complete using the router's admin page through your browser.
On paper, this is a Wi-Fi 7 router, but there's a compromise you'll need to be aware of. Unfortunately, it doesn't support the full Wi-Fi 7 spec, as it's missing the 6 GHz band. While that is a downside, you do get excellent performance at 2.4 GHz, which is still the dominant Wi-Fi band and one that'll prove useful for any legacy devices you have, especially at close range.
The price is what sells this router, because you'll struggle to find specs and speeds this cheap from other brands. If you're settling for an ISP-issued router, or you need a secondary repeater to cure some Wi-Fi not-spots, then this TP-Link Archer BE3600 (also known as the BE230) is worth considering for its $79.98 sale price. This limited-time deal might not be around for too long, however, so pick it up while you can.

articles.title: Más problemas para One UI 9, que rompe el WiFi y las redes móviles de varios Samsung Galaxy
articles.text:
Si tu Samsung Galaxy ha comenzado a tener problemas severos de conectividad, es posible que la culpa sea de One UI 9. Usuarios de dispositivos del fabricante coreano están reportando inconvenientes en varios modelos tras instalar la más reciente versión de la capa de personalización de software, que trae la actualización a Android 17.
El presunto fallo en One UI 9 está provocando fallos en el WiFi de los equipos afectados. Según recoge Android Authority, este es el inconveniente que más se repite entre el público, pero no golpea a todos de la misma forma. Algunos usuarios hablan de que ya no pueden conectarse a su red doméstica, pero que en otras conexiones guardadas funciona todo con normalidad. Otros, en tanto, mencionan que el WiFi funciona bien en redes 2.4 GHz, pero no así en las de 5.0 GHz.
Pero la cosa se vuelve todavía más complicada, pues otros usuarios de móviles Samsung Galaxy están teniendo problemas con las redes móviles tras instalar One UI 9. En algunos casos se menciona que falla la conexión con la cobertura celular y que no hay forma de cargar apps o sitios web hasta usar una red WiFi. En otros, directamente no se reconoce la SIM.
Al momento de redacción de este artículo, Samsung no se ha pronunciado respecto de los problemas de conectividad que están azotando a los móviles Galaxy. La causa concreta de los fallos todavía es un misterio, pero que todos los dispositivos afectados hayan comenzado a sufrirlos tras actualizar a One UI 9 genera señalamientos lógicos contra el software.
Móviles Samsung Galaxy experimentan fallos de conectividad severos con One UI 9
Entre los dispositivos actualizados a One UI 9 que se han registrado fallos de WiFi, redes móviles y tarjetas SIM, están estos modelos:
- Galaxy S24,
- Galaxy S24 Plus,
- Galaxy Z Fold 7,
- Galaxy A56,
- Galaxy A52s
- Galaxy A36.
En ninguno de los casos reportados hasta el momento se ha logrado una solución permanente, lo cual es una preocupación adicional porque implica que sí o sí hay que esperar una intervención de Samsung para que se resuelva.
Si la causa de los problemas está en un bug de One UI 9, como todo apunta, no sería el primer inconveniente de gravedad que están experimentando los dispositivos recientemente actualizados. A finales de octubre se supo que el software estaba arruinando la autonomía de los Galaxy S24 y S25 en todas sus variantes. Usuarios impactados reportaron que sus teléfonos se quedaban sin carga tras apenas 3 horas y fracción con la pantalla activada.
Estaremos atentos a cualquier novedad sobre los nuevos fallos de conectividad. Si Samsung confirma que se trata de un problema en One UI 9, seguramente veremos pronto un parche para enmendarlo. Aun así, no podemos aventurar tiempos reales de demora para una solución.

articles.title: Turning Conv2D Into A Practical GPU Compute Pattern
articles.text:
A reusable optimization mindset for engineers building GPU compute kernels.
Convolution is one of the foundational operations in modern machine learning, but it is also a useful example of a broader engineering idea: many apparently specialized tensor operations can be reorganized into well-understood compute patterns that are easier to implement, optimize, and scale.
This article explains a practical way to implement 2D convolution by treating it as a structured form of matrix multiplication. The goal is not to promote a specific product or benchmark result, but to show a reusable optimization mindset for engineers building GPU compute kernels.
Key idea: A 1×1 convolution is effectively a matrix multiply, and larger K×K convolutions can be expressed as a sequence of matrix-like accumulations with careful attention to cache behavior and loop ordering.
Conv2D is everywhere in inference pipelines, image models, and feature extraction stages. Yet the implementation challenge is often less about the mathematical definition and more about the execution strategy: how data is laid out, how work is grouped, and how memory traffic is controlled.
A useful approach is to avoid treating convolution as a completely unique primitive. Instead, interpret it as a compute pattern closely related to matrix multiplication. This can reduce implementation complexity and create a clearer path for optimization.
A standard Conv2D operation can be described as applying a learned filter tensor across an input tensor to produce an output tensor.
C = A * B
Where:
A is the input tensor of size N × H × W × C_in
B is the weight tensor of size H_filter × W_filter × C_in × C_out
C is the output tensor of size N × H_out × W_out × C_out
In practice, one of the most important simplifications comes from looking at the data in a way that matches the compute engine rather than the original mathematical notation.
A 1×1 convolution is the cleanest place to see the matrix multiplication analogy. At each spatial position, the input contributes a feature vector of length C_in. The weights map that vector into an output vector of length C_out.
If the input tensor is already stored in NHWC order, each spatial feature vector is naturally arranged in a way that can be interpreted as rows of a matrix, without requiring explicit data rearrangement.
Practical takeaway: For NHWC input, a 1×1 convolution can be treated directly as a matrix multiply from C_in to C_out, producing output in NHWC order with no transposition step.
This matters because unnecessary data movement is often one of the fastest ways to lose performance. When the original layout already matches the desired access pattern, the implementation can stay simple and efficient.
Once the filter grows beyond 1×1, each output element depends on multiple spatial locations. A 3×3 convolution, for example, combines nine separate spatial contributions. Conceptually, this becomes a set of matrix-like products that are accumulated together.
That means the problem is no longer just “do matrix multiplication,” but “do repeated matrix-like accumulation while minimizing memory waste.”
For a 3×3 filter, there are nine C_in × C_out contributions per output location. A naive implementation can achieve good arithmetic utilization, but it may repeatedly flush and reload input data through the cache hierarchy. That is where execution order becomes critical.
One of the most useful lessons in convolution optimization is that equivalent mathematics can produce very different memory behavior.
A straightforward ordering may process each filter position as if it were a separate matrix multiply and accumulate the result. While this is simple, it can cause the same input region to be fetched repeatedly into L1 cache and potentially L2 as well.
Reordering loops can improve locality, reduce refetch traffic, and increase effective cache reuse. In other words, the arithmetic stays the same, but the memory system sees a much friendlier pattern.
Optimization principle: When a kernel is already compute-valid, one of the highest-value changes is often to restructure loop nesting to improve data reuse before attempting low-level instruction tuning.
The following sample illustrates the core structure of the convolution loop nest. The details are implementation-specific, but the pattern is broadly recognizable: load weights, compute input coordinates, read vectorized input values, synchronize local memory, and accumulate partial products.
1	VEC_TYPE out_vec = 0.0;  // accumulator for results, with _N_STRIDE length
2	while ((idx_x += 2) < K_STEPS * 2) {
3	  for (int fh = 0; fh < F_H; ++fh) {
4	    for (int fw = 0; fw < F_W; ++fw) { 
5	     int idx_in2 = 
6	          IDX_FROM_4D(fh, fw, F_W, idx_x * 4 + load_in2_k_offset, CI, load_in2_n_offset, CO); 
7	     ((__local float *)localBuf)[local_idx] = (load_in2_n_offset >= CO) ? 0 : in2[idx_in2];
8	 
9	      const int hi = h * STRIDE_H + fh * DILATION_H - PAD_TOP;
10	      const int wi = w * STRIDE_W + fw * DILATION_W - PAD_LEFT;
11	 
12	      idx_y = IDX_FROM_3D(b, hi, IN_H, wi, IN_W);
13	      input1_8.lo = (float4)read_imagef(in1, samp, (int2){idx_x, idx_y});
14	      input1_8.hi = (float4)read_imagef(in1, samp, (int2){idx_x + 1, idx_y});
15	      barrier(CLK_LOCAL_MEM_FENCE);
16	      batch8_F32_MM(input1_8, (__local float16 *)localBuf, (float2 *)&out_vec,
17	                    (float2 *)&out_vec);
18	      barrier(CLK_LOCAL_MEM_FENCE);
19	    }
20	  }
21	}
This kind of kernel is useful to study because it highlights where performance usually lives:
Real convolution kernels are shaped not only by filter math, but also by parameters such as padding, stride, and dilation. These affect both correctness and performance.
Zero padding is the most common approach and is the one reflected in the source implementation. A typical boundary-safe pattern checks whether the computed input coordinate falls within valid image bounds before issuing the read.
1	float8 input1_8 = 0;
2	if ((hi >= 0) && (hi < IN_H) && (wi >= 0) && (wi < IN_W)) 
3	{
4	  input1_8[i] = { ... }
5	}
This is correct and easy to reason about, but a branch inside a hot loop can be expensive. One alternative is to move boundary handling outside the innermost loop by redirecting out-of-range reads to a dummy zero-filled line or buffer. That trades branch cost for setup logic and is often worth testing.
Important: Boundary checks are not just a correctness concern. Their placement in the loop nest can have a measurable effect on throughput.
Filter size and stride also shape performance in less obvious ways.
These effects are often indirect rather than absolute. A larger filter does not automatically make a kernel faster, and a larger stride does not automatically make it slow. But both influence the balance between arithmetic work and memory traffic, which is exactly where many Conv2D kernels are won or lost.
The most transferable value in this Conv2D implementation is not a single micro-optimization. It is the method behind it.
This approach tends to produce implementations that are easier to reason about and easier to evolve. It also creates a stronger foundation for future acceleration, because many hardware platforms already invest heavily in dense linear algebra patterns.
When turning Conv2D into a matrix-like GPU kernel, several mistakes come up repeatedly:
Caution: A mathematically elegant implementation is not always a performant one. Equivalent formulations can behave very differently on real hardware.
If you are designing or reviewing a GPU convolution kernel, it helps to think in three layers:
Strong kernels usually come from aligning all three layers, not from over-optimizing only one of them.
Conv2D is often presented as a special-purpose deep learning primitive, but from an implementation perspective it can often be understood as structured matrix multiplication plus careful accumulation across spatial neighborhoods.
That framing is powerful because it simplifies design decisions. It encourages reuse of proven compute patterns, reduces unnecessary data motion, and puts optimization effort where it usually matters most: locality, loop order, and bandwidth efficiency.
For engineers working on GPU inference and tensor kernels, that is the bigger lesson. Good performance does not begin with heroic low-level tuning. It begins with choosing the right interpretation of the problem.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Grey secures CBN approval to operate as IMTO - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Grey, the Y Combinator-backed cross-border payment platform, has received approval from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) to operate as an International Money Transfer Operator (IMTO) in the country.
Grey enables individuals and businesses to easily own and manage multi-currency accounts in USD, GBP, and EUR, supporting transfers to more than 170 destinations. It also offers access to virtual cards.
Disrupt Africa reported in September the startup was now enabling direct payout to Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon and Rwanda, and the CBN approval now allows Grey to facilitate inbound international money transfers into Nigeria, covering person-to-person, business-to-person and business-to-business payments.
Grey said the licence gives it a stronger foundation to grow its remittance operations in Nigeria, expand its links to international payment corridors, and serve individuals and businesses receiving funds from abroad.
“Securing CBN approval to operate as an IMTO is an important step for Grey in Nigeria. It strengthens our ability to facilitate inbound international transfers and reflects our long-term commitment to building reliable financial infrastructure for individuals and businesses operating across borders,” said Idorenyin Obong, CEO and co-founder of Grey.
The Nigerian approval adds to Grey’s existing regulatory credentials in North America. The company is registered as a Money Services Business (MSB) with FinCEN in the United States, and with FINTRAC in Canada, where it is also registered as a payment service provider under the Retail Payment Activities Act.

articles.title: MacBook Pro with M6 review - brilliant combination of speed, performance and battery efficiency - Tech Guide
articles.text:
- RATING
The MacBook Pro continues to prove itself as the ultimate pro laptop for users who work hard and play hard. With the new M6 chip on board it adds even more power, performance and efficiency to your workflow.
Apple’s new MacBook Pro with M6 is a workhorse laptop that is now even more powerful and versatile with greater access to Siri AI and Apple Intelligence to really supercharge your workflows.
Tech Guide received the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 for our review. It is also available in a 16-inch version.
This is Apple’s annual upgrade of the MacBook Pro with its latest silicon. In this case the M6 which includes an advanced 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core and a 12-core GPU that offers up to 30 per cent faster graphics and up to 25 per cent faster AI workloads than the M5.
That’s a remarkable upgrade from last year’s device.
Customers tend to hold onto laptops for a lot longer than they do their smartphones so it could be several years between upgrades.
With that in mind you can imagine the improvement a customer will see with the MacBook Pro with M6 if they’re upgrading even from the M4 and other earlier laptops.
Apple released the MacBook Pro with M1 back in 2020 and that’s probably served users well since then.
So for those customers, upgrading to the MacBook Pro with M6 would be an absolute game changer.
For example, on-device AI on the new MacBook Pro with M6 is 13 times faster than on the M1.
Design-wise the MacBook Pro with M6 is identical to the previous model.
This is a move we applaud because the current design works.
The MacBook Pro is not that heavy (1.55kg) or too thick (1.55cm) and it’s still very easily portable.
It has a stunning 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display with 1,600 nits of peak HDR brightness and a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
Everything you view on the screen, including your videos and photos, looks amazing.
Same thing with the applications you’re working on or the content you’re creating.
You will never tire of the quality of this amazing display.
But one difference there is from last year’s model is the price.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 started, when it was released in 2025, at $2,499.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $3,199.
But you are getting a better computer that’s faster and more power efficient.
For our review we put it to the test with some video and photo editing which gave us instant results and renders.
Our go-to video editing application is Final Cut Pro and editing videos with the MacBook Pro with M6 is effortless.
And the biggest improvement is when it comes to exporting the video, which could be up to 10GB in size.
Before, it would take several minutes but with the MacBook Pro with M6 it took less than a minute.
Here are some other improvements you can expect with the MacBook Pro with M6:
– Up to 13x faster time to first token performance for LLM prompt processing compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
– Up to 11.7x faster render performance with ray tracing in Blender compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
– Up to 3.3x faster image-processing performance in Affinity compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.2x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
– Up to 2.5x faster project build performance when compiling code in Xcode compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
With this much performance and power at your back, the MacBook Pro with M6 is also an incredible gaming computer as well.
Another welcome addition to the MacBook Pro with M6 is Wi-Fi 7 – finally! Wi-Fi connectivity is now faster and up to speed with today’s mesh routers
It also has Bluetooth 6 on board.
It also has two Thunderbolt 4 ports on the left side and another Thunderbolt 4 port on the right. There’s also an HDMI port and a memory card slot, plus a headphone jack.
And it uses the same brilliant MagSafe charging connection.
Another top feature of the MacBook Pro with M6 is its battery life runs for up to 24 hours on a single charge.
That’s 14 hours more than Intel-based MacBook Pros.
And the MacBook Pro with M6 charges faster as well and can get to 50% in just 30 minutes with a higher-wattage USB-C power adapter like the 96W Power Adapter.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is available now and is priced from $3,199.
The 16-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is also available now and starts at $4,799.
VERDICT
The MacBook Pro continues to prove itself as the ultimate pro laptop for users who work hard and play hard. With the new M6 chip on board it adds even more power, performance and efficiency to your workflow.

articles.title: Why AI’s biggest challenge lies beneath the model
articles.text:
Why AI’s biggest challenge lies beneath the model
At TechSparks 2026, Michael Cronin of Couchbase explained why fragmented data infrastructure remains a major barrier to enterprise AI adoption and why companies need to fix their data systems before scaling AI applications.
AI models are becoming increasingly accessible, but turning them into products that work reliably remains a challenge, particularly when enterprises are dealing with fragmented data infrastructure.
At TechSparks 2026, Michael Cronin, Vice President, Sales, Asia-Pacific, Japan & India, Couchbase, joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video, YourStory, for a discussion on moving AI beyond experimentation, production failures, governance challenges, customer experience, and India's growing role in AI innovation.
AI’s missing link: the data layer
Over the decades, large enterprises have adopted different databases and point solutions to address specific problems. While each solved an immediate need, the result has often been a fragmented data layer, with multiple systems that struggle to work together.
Cronin sees this fragmentation as a major barrier to AI adoption. Citing industry estimates, he said 70–80% of AI development projects never reach production, while an MIT study found that 95% fail to become profitable.
Couchbase’s operational data platform is designed to address this challenge by helping enterprises consolidate their data infrastructure.
Rather than trying to fix everything at once, Cronin advised companies to start small.
“My advice to founders and enterprises that are struggling with the fragmentation of the data layer is to pick your most critical use cases first,” he said.
Cronin cited the example of Tesco, the UK retailer with a large global Capability Center (GCC) in Bengaluru. Its multiple systems were affecting customer experience, particularly during busy shopping periods such as Black Friday and weekends.
Tesco began consolidating its data layer, starting with a single instance and use case before extending the effort across its technology stack.
The consolidation enabled the retailer to handle millions of transactions per second with sub-millisecond latency. According to Cronin, the example shows how companies can begin addressing fragmentation through a single use case before expanding the changes across their operations.
AI moves at machine speed. Can data keep up?
The pressure to develop AI products has led many enterprises to prioritize models and applications. However, pilots often run on small datasets in controlled environments, leaving organizations unprepared for the demands of production.
Cronin pointed to the growing scale of machine-generated traffic.
“Eighteen months ahead of schedule, machine traffic has overtaken human traffic on the internet. That’s the AI scale. That’s the machine speed scale that enterprises need to operate on,” he said.
When AI applications encounter real-world workloads, fragmented data systems can prevent them from operating reliably at scale.
The growing use of AI agents adds to the challenge. As agents become more autonomous and take on decision-making responsibilities, enterprises need to ensure they can access the right data while working within appropriate governance frameworks.
Fragmented systems can make communication and governance more difficult, limiting the ability of agents to operate autonomously.
Cronin also urged enterprises to reconsider how they allocate their AI investments. While models are evolving rapidly, enterprise data remains a critical asset.
“The models are rentable. Today’s best model is yesterday's newspaper. The true asset for the enterprise is the data,” he said.
More API layers aren't the answer
As enterprises began recognizing that fragmented data was holding back their AI initiatives, many responded by adding APIs and connectors to link existing systems.
Cronin cautioned that this approach could introduce further complexity rather than solve the underlying problem. Each additional connection brings latency, risk, and another potential point of failure.
Instead, he recommended consolidating the data layer so applications and AI agents can communicate with it more directly, bringing data closer to customers.
According to Cronin, many enterprises, including large GCCs in India, are now reassessing their architecture to address data fragmentation. Without these changes, further investment in AI development could lead to the same problems.
Consolidating data can also improve customer experience by helping systems manage growing demand, remain available and respond quickly.
As customers expect more from AI-powered services, having data available at the edge is becoming increasingly important.
India: From back office to innovation leader
Cronin observed that business cultures vary across the Asia-Pacific region, but fragmented data infrastructure remains a common challenge for AI adoption.
At the same time, India is becoming an important centre for AI innovation and decision-making.
He noted that 80% of Couchbase's top 50 global accounts have a significant presence in India, with much of their AI innovation and leadership based in the country.
Couchbase is also expanding its presence in India, with its Asia-Pacific headquarters moving to Bengaluru. Its Indian enterprise customers include Air India, Airtel, BigBasket, and Mahindra Finance.
According to Cronin, India’s role in global business has moved beyond cost savings, with innovation, leadership, and important business decisions increasingly taking place here.
He cited Air India's next-generation entertainment platform, which is being built on Couchbase. The platform aims to provide passengers with personalized shopping and entertainment experiences even when an aircraft is offline.
For Cronin, the project shows how Indian enterprises are using technology to improve customer experiences under real-world operating conditions.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft a corrigé une importante faille dans Paint, mais pas chez tout le monde
articles.text:
Il y a quelques semaines, Microsoft dévoilait l’existence d’une importante vulnérabilité dans son application de dessin Paint. Identifiée sous la référence CVE-2026-83844, cette brèche dévoilée le 13 octobre et dont le niveau de gravité a été classé comme importante par Microsoft est de type « lecture hors limite ».
Concrètement, il s’agit d’une faille qui, en cas d’exploitation, permettrait à un pirate de procéder à une attaque sans clic. Bien que l’exploitation de cette faille soit considérée comme complexe, elle permettrait à un pirate d’exécuter du code à distance sur la machine ciblée.
La bonne nouvelle, c’est que Microsoft a déjà corrigé le trou dans la raquette. La mauvaise, c’est que la firme de Redmond a visiblement quelques soucis quant au déploiement de son patch correctif.
Une mise à jour qui se fait attendre sur le Microsoft Store
D’après le bulletin de sécurité de Microsoft, la faille a été corrigée dans la version 11.2609.401.0 de Microsoft Paint. Pourtant, de nombreux utilisateurs et administrateurs IT qui ont a priori activé l’installation automatique des mises à jour rapportent que la mise à jour corrective ne leur est pas proposée dans le Microsoft Store sur leur machine.
Même lorsque l’option pour installer automatiquement les mises à jour est activée, aucune mise à jour ne leur est proposée et la version de Microsoft Paint dont ils disposent reste bloquée sur un numéro de version antérieure au correctif. Vous pouvez vous-même le vérifier en ouvrant Paint, puis en cliquant sur le bouton des Paramètres.
Par ailleurs, aucun outil tiers utilisé pour trouver le paquet de mise à jour au format MSIX ne leur aurait permis d’accéder à l’installation de cette mise à jour.
L’absence de mise à jour pose également un autre souci. En entreprise, les outils de sécurité tiers utilisés signalent Paint comme vulnérable à cause de l’absence de ce correctif.
Le principal problème dans cette histoire, c’est que les mises à jour des applications Microsoft ne sont pas gérées par Windows Update. Par conséquent, l’installation des mises à jour de sécurité mensuelles n’a aucun effet quant à la protection contre cette vulnérabilité. Comme toutes les applications de Microsoft, Paint est mis à jour séparément depuis le Microsoft Store.
Un bug dans le déploiement
L’hypothèse la plus probable pour expliquer ce problème est qu’un bug s’est glissé dans le processus de déploiement de la mise à jour par Microsoft, bloquant de fait l’accès à celle-ci.
Il est par ailleurs possible que ce problème de mise à jour ne concerne que certaines régions. Sur notre PC, la mise à jour de Paint n’était pas installée bien que l’option pour installer automatiquement les mises à jour soit activée.
Ceci étant, en se rendant directement dans la section Téléchargements, et en lançant manuellement une recherche de mises à jour, celle-ci nous a bien été proposée et s’est installée automatiquement.

articles.title: Vos enceintes connectées KEF peuvent désormais se transformer en satellites home cinéma
articles.text:
Vos enceintes connectées KEF peuvent désormais se transformer en satellites home cinéma
KEF accélère dans le home cinéma en permettant à sa barre de son XIO d’accueillir ses fameuses enceintes connectées LSX II, LSX II LT et Coda W comme enceintes surround sans fil. De quoi renforcer l’immersion sonore, sous certaines conditions.
KEF fait enfin évoluer sa barre de son XIO avec une mise à jour logicielle qui permet d’y associer des enceintes arrière issues de son catalogue. L’ajout de véritables canaux derrière la position d’écoute permet de considérablement renforcer l'immersion en home cinéma, puisque les effets arrière sont désormais diffusés directement vers l’auditeur, et non plus seulement reproduits par traitement virtuel ou réflexion acoustique.
La fonction est disponible avec les LSX II, LSX II LT et Coda W. Pour les propriétaires de ces enceintes actives connectées, l’intérêt est de pouvoir les réutiliser comme canaux arrière dans un système construit autour de la XIO. Il n’est pas nécessaire de les relier à la barre par un câble audio traversant la pièce, car la transmission passe par un récepteur sans fil KEF KW2 RX.
Bien sûr, pour KEF, cette nouvelle fonction est aussi un moyen d’inciter les possesseurs d’une barre de son XIO à investir dans des enceintes connectées, et inversement. L’adaptateur KW2 RX était jusqu’alors réservé à l’association d’un caisson de basses KEF KC62, KC92 ou KUBE, sans la contrainte des câbles.
La transmission sans fil passe par un récepteur KEF KW2 RX optionnel
Si la mise à jour est gratuite, tant pour la barre que pour les enceintes, cette configuration nécessite d’investir dans un récepteur KW2 RX, vendu 179 €. Heureusement, un seul adaptateur suffit pour associer une paire d’enceintes actives compatibles, mais il faudra malgré tout passer à la caisse, alors que de nombreuses enceintes connectées pouvant faire office de satellites communiquent directement avec la barre de son.
La configuration s’effectue depuis l’application KEF Connect, qui guide l’utilisateur dans l’association des enceintes. La barre de son transmet le signal au récepteur KW2 RX sur une bande radio de 2,4 GHz, avec une latence de 57 ms et une résolution allant jusqu’à 24 bits/48 kHz. Celui-ci se connecte aux entrées mini-jack 3,5 mm ou optique des enceintes. À noter que cet adaptateur doit être alimenté sur secteur à l’aide d’un câble USB-C inclus, ce qui complique un peu la mise en œuvre.
KEF ne détaille pas les formats sonores pris en charge, mais en l’absence de canaux latéraux et verticaux sur ses enceintes actives, il est probable que la hauteur des effets Dolby Atmos et la cohérence entre l’avant et l’arrière de la scène sonore soient limités. Pour l’heure, KEF ne prévoit pas non plus la possibilité d’ajouter une seconde paire d’enceintes actives, en frontal ou sur les côtés de la position d’écoute.
KEF LSX II
Une compatibilité vouée à s’étendre d'ici la fin de l'année
KEF prévoit d’élargir progressivement la liste des enceintes compatibles. Les LS50 Wireless II rejoindront le dispositif en décembre 2026, tandis que les LS60 Wireless et LS LUXE sont annoncées pour courant 2027.
Pour les utilisateurs déjà équipés en KEF, cette évolution permet donc de faire évoluer leur installation en conservant leurs enceintes, plutôt que de repartir sur un système surround séparé. Elle reste néanmoins réservée aux modèles compatibles et implique l’achat du KW2 RX.

articles.title: Qualcomm busca fuera del móvil lo que le quita la crisis de la memoria: coches, IA y antenas para SpaceX
articles.text:
Qualcomm lleva años diversificando negocio, pero por encima de todo, sigue siendo esa empresa de los procesadores Snapdragon para los móviles Android. No en vano, la propia compañía celebra un 'fiestón' cada año en Hawái para presentar sus procesadores para móviles (y también portátiles) más potentes de cara a los próximos meses, pero este año la cosa se ha enfriado debido a la sonadísima crisis de memoria.
Y, en un escenario en el que los envíos globales de móviles ha caído en picado, Qualcomm ha decidido reorientar el transatlántico. ¿Los objetivos más jugosos? Coches, antenas para SpaceX y la IA, cómo no.
En corto. Como tantas otras, Qualcomm ha presentado resultados financieros. En su caso, como en el de Apple, corresponden al último trimestre de su ejercicio fiscal y la cifra clave es la de 10.442 millones de dólares ingresados en este periodo, con unas ganancias operativas de 2.769 millones de dólares. Mucho dinero, pero un 7% menos que lo alcanzado en el mismo periodo del año anterior.
El beneficio por acción también fue un 28% inferior y el de las ganancias operativas también cayó un 27%. Y, aunque los ingresos superaron por "poco" los 10.140 millones de dólares que esperaba Wall Street, es evidente que hay cierta preocupación debido a que una de las patas principales del negocio se ha quedado coja.
Luces y sombras. Dentro del análisis presentado por la compañía podemos ver que la división de automoción ha aumentado un 89% hasta alcanzar los 1.990 millones de dólares. Es un subidón importante que, sin embargo, no consigue tapar que la división de chips para móviles "sólo" facturó 5.137 millones de dólares. Esto implica un 26% menos que en el mismo periodo del año anterior y refleja que la situación es la que es.
Lógico. Hemos venido hablando durante todo este año (y ya a finales del pasado, incluso) sobre cómo la crisis de memoria RAM y almacenamiento iba a provocar que el mercado de móviles se contrajera. Al principio teorizábamos con que las compañías volverían a apostar por modelos con menor cantidad de RAM, pero lo que ha terminado pasando es que la RAM se ha mantenido en su mayoría, pero los precios del dispositivo han aumentado.
También algo más drástico, como que se están fabricando y enviando menos móviles en una clara contracción del mercado. La International Data Corporation, una consultora especializada en tecnología y una de las fuentes más potentes junto a Canalys y Counterpoint, ya apuntó en agosto que los envíos mundiales de móviles iban a caer casi un 17% este año.
También señaló que el precio de la DRAM y la NAND había subido más de un 300% interanual y que el precio medio de un móvil había aumentado hasta un 28%. Esto hace no sólo que menos gente compre móviles y que los móviles sean también más caros, sino que Qualcomm está viendo que sus márgenes se reducen. Antes, el procesador era el componente más caro en un móvil, pero ahora es la RAM.
Playas prometedoras. El margen operativo de la división de Chips han caído del 29% de un año antes al 24%, y se estima que en el trimestre actual se quede entre el 20% y el 22%. Esto lleva a buscar soluciones, y aquí apuntan en tres direcciones:
- Coches. Ya hemos dicho que han crecido y esperan que sea una pata fuerte de cara al ejercicio de 2027.
- Centros de datos. Prevén más de 650 millones en este trimestre para los chips de centros de datos, con un objetivo de llegar a los 5.000 millones para el año fiscal completo. Para ello, tienen acuerdos como el de Amazon para chips de inferencia de IA.
- Antenas para SpaceX. Este mismo 4 de noviembre, Qualcomm anunció que iba a suministrar equipos de radio, unidades de banda base y software para la futura red 5G terrestre de Starlink Mobile en Estados Unidos. Desplegarán miles de torres a partir de 2027 y la propia Qualcomm (que ha fabricado chips 5G para Apple) describe la operación como "su mayor acuerdo 5G hasta la fecha". También es la base de la futura infraestructura 6G para la IA.
Girando el barco. El problema de esto es que las cosas están muy en el aire. Los chips y los coches son mercados que Qualcomm tiene asegurados, pero los ingresos tanto de SpaceX como de los centros de datos dependen de que se construyan esos centros de datos, de que no pinche la burbuja, de que los planes de SpaceX vayan como está previsto y de que las Big Tech como Amazon sigan apostando por esos chips de inferencia de Qualcomm en lugar de ir a por otro fabricante que aparezca con una solución más interesante.
Al margen de esto, es un ejemplo más de cómo la situación con la IA ha trastocado los planes de una compañía. A veces para mal (Qualcomm y los móviles), a veces para bien (Nvidia abandonando el gaming para centrarse en las GPU de IA o Micron dejando el segmento de consumo para producir únicamente RAM también para la IA).

articles.title: OnlyOffice rajoute un assistant IA à sa suite bureautique mobile
articles.text:
Les applications Documents de la suite OnlyOffice pour iOS et Android reçoivent un assistant IA qui résume, crée des fichiers et remplit les formulaires PDF. L’éditeur annonce aussi 44 failles corrigées dans ses solutions.
Après OnlyOffice 10.0, déployé en octobre, c’est au tour des applications mobiles d’être mises à jour. L’IA est à l’honneur sur iOS et Android.
Ce que l’IA sait faire sur mobile, et les 44 failles corrigées en parallèle
L’assistant est accessible depuis la section Documents, là où l’on range ses fichiers. Il est possible de lui poser une question sur un fichier sans l’ouvrir, de lui demander un résumé ou de chercher une information précise. Cet assistant accepte aussi des fichiers et des images en pièce jointe, par exemple pour l’interroger sur leur contenu, sans avoir à copier un texte ou à décrire une image. Sur iOS, les fichiers stockés dans le cloud de l’entreprise sont aussi acceptés.
Dans les éditeurs de texte, de feuilles de calcul et de présentations, un chat IA propose des fonctions adaptées à chaque outil. Il devient plus simple d'effectuer diverses actions comme rédiger ou résumer, analyser ou nettoyer des données, suggérer un graphique, préparer des notes de discours ou encore générer une image. La réponse s’insère directement dans le document. Sur Android, un onglet IA dédié rassemble l’assistant et les réglages des fournisseurs.
L’assistant crée aussi des fichiers à partir d’une simple description. Il génère des présentations structurées, avec du texte et des images, et sur iOS des documents texte et des feuilles de calcul. La génération s’effectue en arrière-plan ; il est donc possible de continuer à travailler dans l’application en parallèle. Pour les formulaires PDF, l’IA repère les champs à compléter et renseigne les dates, les coordonnées ou les numéros de téléphone. Elle peut aussi ajouter une signature ou une image, et sur Android, puiser les coordonnées dans l’appareil.
Les IA de Grok et DeepSeek s’ajoutent à celles de Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google et Ollama. Sur iOS 26 et versions ultérieures, la dictée vocale est traitée directement sur l’appareil. Sur Android, les réponses de l’IA peuvent être lues à voix haute, dans la langue détectée automatiquement. Côté serveur, les administrateurs des éditions Enterprise et Developer peuvent configurer les fournisseurs et les modèles autorisés, sans que chaque utilisateur ait à saisir sa propre clé API. Ils peuvent d’ailleurs désactiver l'IA pour un éditeur ou pour tout le serveur.
En parallèle, OnlyOffice annonce 44 failles corrigées dans plusieurs composants : conversion de documents, éditeur PDF, macros, WOPI (le protocole qui permet à une plateforme de stockage d’intégrer l’éditeur), fonctions d’IA et configuration du serveur. Ces brèches concernaient des risques d’accès non autorisé aux fichiers, d’élévation de privilèges, de compromission de sessions de coédition et d’exécution de scripts malveillants.
OnlyOffice conseille aux installations auto-hébergées de passer manuellement en 10.0.2.
Si la suite OnlyOffice est avant tout destinée aux entreprises, elle propose une version gratuite pour les particuliers qui permet de créer des documents de type Word, Excel, PowerPoint ainsi que des formulaires. Ergonomique à souhait, elle joue aussi la carte de l'auto-hébergement et de la sécurité.

articles.title: OpenSSH flaw lets attackers log into password-disabled Linux accounts
articles.text:
A newly disclosed flaw involving OpenSSH and musl, dubbed "*sshole," allows attackers to log in to certain Alpine Linux and other musl-based Linux accounts configured to block password authentication simply by entering an oversized password.
The flaw only affects OpenSSH servers running on Linux distributions that use the musl C library, including Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, and Yocto, under certain authentication configurations.
Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library.
Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts.
However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.
To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins.
The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit.
This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.
To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.
Kultekin says exploitation requires the following conditions:
- OpenSSH is running on a musl-based Linux system, such as Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, or Yocto.
- PAM authentication is disabled, as it is by default in Alpine Linux's openssh-server package.
- SSH password authentication is enabled.
- At least one account has an asterisk (*) as its password hash.
- Another account has a valid password hash.
The researcher warns that Alpine Linux's official AWS and Azure cloud images have an affected default 'alpine' account with passwordless 'doas' privileges, which could allow attackers to gain root access.
Systems using glibc, including Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora, and those using PAM authentication are not vulnerable to this attack.
Kultekin says he discovered the vulnerability using AI agents that ran about 17,600 authentication tests with different OpenSSH configurations, malformed password hashes, and oversized passwords.
The vulnerability has been fixed in OpenSSH 10.6p2, and Alpine Linux administrators are advised to update their OpenSSH packages using apk upgrade openssh.
Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH.
Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.
On Alpine Linux, the following command can reveal successful SSH password logins:
grep "Accepted password" /var/log/messages
If the logs show a successful password login for the alpine account, administrators can check whether that account has password authentication disabled:
grep '^alpine:' /etc/shadow
If the account's password field contains *, but SSH logs show a successful password login, it could indicate that the vulnerability was exploited.
