articles.title: Bitcoin: cómo se ha movido en el mercado este jueves
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El precio de la criptomoneda bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 79590.55 dólares. Esto quiere decir que la moneda digital presentó un cambio de 1.92% en el último día, así como un movimiento de 0.0% en la última hora.
Por su nivel de capitalización, esta moneda digital ocupa la posición #1 entre las más populares.
Bitcoin alcanzó su máximo histórico
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: From Bok star to fintech founder: Habana’s life after rugby
articles.text:
When PHATHISANI MOYO watched Bryan Habana deliver a presentation in Cape Town, he was intrigued by the personal journey to fintech behind one of South Africa’s most celebrated rugby careers.
Eight years after retiring from professional rugby, Bryan Habana found himself facing an unfamiliar opponent: himself.
The former Springbok winger and 2007 World Cup winner had spent much of his adult life mastering a sport that made him one of South Africa’s most recognisable athletes. He had represented his country on the biggest stage, performed under immense pressure and built a career around the discipline required to compete at the highest level.
But when he stepped into the fintech boardroom, the skills that made him a rugby star did not automatically translate into business success.
“I didn’t know how to do a PowerPoint presentation. I didn’t know how to put a table into a spreadsheet or read a budget,” Habana recalled during a presentation at BPC’s innovation event in Cape Town on October 22.
For someone accustomed to operating at the highest level of professional sport, it was humbling. The man once expected to know exactly what to do on a rugby field was suddenly a beginner in an unfamiliar world.
Yet that discomfort marked the beginning of a different career. Habana moved from the rugby field to fintech, co-founding Paymenow, a company that helps employees access wages they have already earned before payday.
His second act is about more than finding something to do after rugby. It is about applying the qualities that made him successful on the field to a different challenge, and discovering a new way to make an impact.
Watching Habana deliver his presentation in Cape Town, I was struck by how candidly he spoke about this transition. His story resonated because it was not just about an athlete moving into business. It was about what happens when the identity that has defined much of your life no longer prepares you for what comes next.
That is a challenge many people face: professionals forced to change careers, entrepreneurs rebuilding after business failure, and anyone who has had to start again after a major life change. Sometimes the hardest part is accepting that you must become a beginner again.
Habana’s second act
For elite athletes, retirement can be a particularly difficult transition. The routine, competition, team environment, and public recognition that once structured everyday life can disappear almost overnight.
Habana’s rugby career had given him a clear framework. He had training sessions, match days, coaches, teammates, and measurable goals. Success was often visible through a try scored, a match won, a trophy lifted.
Business was different—new systems to understand, unfamiliar language, and decisions whose consequences were not always immediately apparent. Habana studied computer science early in his life, before rugby took over. His interest in technology never entirely disappeared, but understanding technology was not the same as knowing how to build a business.
The transition demanded humility. His reputation on the rugby field would not automatically make him competent in the boardroom.
Habana reflected on the challenge of adapting to a world that would not simply accommodate the person he had been. “The future doesn’t go with you,” he said.
It is a striking way to describe the end of a career. The future does not arrive carrying your old identity, routines, or achievements. You have to meet it on its own terms.
A problem worth solving
In 2019, Habana co-founded Paymenow with chief executive officer (CEO) Deon Nobrega, chief technology officer (CTO) Willem van Zyl and chief development officer Gerbrand Potgieter. He explained that the company was built around earned wage access, which lets employees access a portion of the wages they have already earned before their scheduled payday.
Bryan Habana scored one of his two tries against Argentina in the 2007 Rugby World Cup semi-final on October 14, helping the Springboks secure a 37–13 victory and book their place in the final. Image source: SARugbymag
The idea addresses a familiar problem for many workers. Salaries may arrive monthly, but everyday expenses do not wait for the end of the month. Transport, food, school costs, and unexpected bills can create pressure long before payday.
For workers with limited savings or access to affordable credit, that gap can push them towards expensive short-term loans. The pressure is reflected in Nedbank’s 2024 Financial Health Monitor, which found that 10% of workers had turned to payday loans to manage financial stress, while 12% had borrowed from informal lenders. FinMark Trust’s research offers a broader picture: 75% of South Africans who borrowed in 2024 used credit to cover essentials such as food.
Paymenow aims to give employees more flexibility over money they have already earned. Its services also include financial education and other tools intended to help people make better decisions about their money.
The idea is rooted in how people live and earn. Financial inclusion is not simply about giving someone a digital account or access to an app. It requires understanding when people receive their income, how they spend it, and what happens when money runs short.
A worker who can access earned wages when an unexpected expense arises may have an alternative to borrowing at high interest. In a country where many households live close to the edge of their monthly budgets, that flexibility can matter.
For Habana, the company’s purpose goes beyond making wages available earlier. It is about helping people manage financial pressure and improve their financial wellbeing. As he put it, “We’ve got an audacious goal of wanting to release ten million employees from financial stress through financial technology.”
From an idea to a regional business
Paymenow’s growth suggests that the problem it set out to address extends beyond South Africa. The company expanded into Namibia and Zambia before entering Pakistan.
By 2026, it reported serving more than 750,000 employees across the four markets, with clients including major employers in retail, telecommunications, healthcare and hospitality. In May 2026, Paymenow announced a merger with PayCurve, a South African employee financial wellness company founded in 2020.
The merger combines Paymenow’s wage-access service with PayCurve’s tools for identifying employees experiencing financial difficulties and helping them manage debt, build savings and improve their financial habits. The combined business will operate under the Paymenow brand.
The move reflects a wider understanding of the problem. Giving workers access to wages they have already earned can ease pressure before payday, but lasting financial stability also requires help with debt and savings.
For Paymenow, the merger broadens its services beyond short-term cash-flow problems. Habana has argued that growth must not come at the expense of the company’s purpose. “You’ve also got to stick with your purpose-driven approach,” he said.
Lessons that travel from the field
Habana’s sporting career did not become irrelevant when he left rugby. It gave him lessons he could apply in a different environment.
Teamwork is one of the most obvious. Rugby is a collective game, even when an individual player becomes the face of a defining moment. One person may score a try, but several teammates’ work often makes it possible.
Business operates in much the same way. A founder may be visible to investors, customers and the public, but a company’s success depends on people with different skills working towards a common goal.
“You can get quite far on your own, but it takes a lot longer,” Habana said.
Bryan Habana reflecting on his transition from Springbok rugby star to fintech entrepreneur and Paymenow co-founder. Image source: BPC
Preparation is another lesson. In sport, talent alone is rarely enough. Training and repetition allow athletes to perform when the pressure is greatest. In business, preparation helps people recognise and harness opportunities.
Habana also highlighted the importance of responding to failure rather than allowing it to define the journey.
“Fail fast, but live faster,” he said.
That requires a willingness to change. The approaches that worked in one environment may not work in another, particularly in technology, where products and customer expectations evolve.
“We have to unlearn in order to learn,” he said.
Habana said this meant accepting that he could not rely on past achievements to navigate a new profession. He had to ask questions, acknowledge what he did not know, and learn from people with different expertise.
A different kind of impact
Habana has said sport allowed him to inspire hope. For many South Africans, the Springboks represent more than a team. Their victories can create moments of shared pride in a country where sport holds a powerful place in the national imagination.
Fintech offers a different kind of opportunity. A product that works can make a difference repeatedly in the everyday lives of its users.
That does not mean earned wage access can solve the structural problems behind financial insecurity. It cannot replace fair wages, stable employment, or broader economic opportunity. But it can offer a practical alternative for workers who need greater control over when they access money they have already earned.
For Habana, fintech offers a different kind of impact from the one he experienced on the rugby field. “As a rugby player, I could inspire hope,” he said. “But at no point in my rugby journey did anyone tell me that, because of what I did, I had saved their life.”
That sense of purpose, he said, is what makes the work particularly meaningful. “With financial technology, we are able to make an impactful difference in people’s lives on a daily basis,” he added.
Some of Africa’s most relevant fintech ideas have emerged from understanding everyday problems and building services around them. Paymenow’s proposition starts with a simple observation: the timing of income and the timing of expenses do not always match.
Turning that insight into a sustainable business requires trust, affordability, and sound execution. But the need it addresses is real.
Becoming a better version
Perhaps the most compelling part of Habana’s transition was not his move from rugby to fintech, but the personal philosophy that has helped him navigate the transition.
He recalled advice from former Springbok captain John Smit, who encouraged him to ask himself a question when looking in the mirror at the end of each day: “Every night when you go to bed… is that person an improvement on the person you saw the day before?”
It is a simple question that strips away trophies, titles, and public recognition. It asks whether you are learning, improving, and becoming better at what you do.
For an athlete, that might mean refining a skill or becoming a better teammate. For a founder, it could mean listening more closely to customers, understanding the business, or making a difficult decision for its long-term health.
Former Springbok captain John Smit (right) challenged Bryan Habana (left) to measure success not by past achievements, but by whether he was becoming a better version of himself each day. A lesson that has stayed with Habana long after rugby. Image source: Lentdesportiva
Starting again can feel like losing ground, particularly when the world still remembers who you used to be. Habana knows what it is like to move from being the person everyone expects to succeed to the one sitting in a boardroom trying to understand a spreadsheet.
At Paymenow, he has found a different field in which to test himself. The scoreboard has disappeared, but the work of learning, improving and making a difference continues.
Perhaps that is why John Smit’s question about the person in the mirror carries such weight. At the end of the day, Habana no longer has to measure himself by the tries he scores or the matches he wins. He can ask a different question: is the person looking back at him a little better than the one from yesterday?
For someone who has had to start again, that may be the real victory: not returning to who you were, but becoming someone you had not yet imagined.

articles.title: El Ejército de EE UU apuesta por Alex, un robot humanoide con protección balística para misiones peligrosas.
articles.text:
El Ejército de EE.UU. está explorando cómo utilizar robots humanoides para realizar tareas que ponen en peligro a sus soldados, y uno de los candidatos que ha llamado su atención es Alex. Desarrollada por el Instituto de Cognición Humana y de Máquinas de Florida (IHMC), Alex es una máquina que acaba de ser seleccionada entre los cinco ganadores del concurso xTechHumanoid.
Su particularidad principal es que incorpora protección balística y combina IA con control humano para desenvolverse en escenarios complicados, aunque todavía no forma parte de ninguna unidad militar operativa. Además, Alex cuenta con 29 articulaciones y mecanismos de movimiento diseñados específicamente para facilitar sus desplazamientos por terrenos irregulares.
Según explica el IHMC en su documentación oficial, el robot dispone de sus sistemas de procesamiento propios, sensores y alimentación energética. Gracias a ello, puede trabajar fuera de instalaciones preparadas para estas máquinas. De hecho, sus desarrolladores quieren que pueda moverse por edificios, superar obstáculos y acceder a lugares con escaleras o escombros en los que enviar a una persona podría suponer un riesgo considerable.
El Ejército busca robots capaces de asumir tareas peligrosas
La selección de Alex forma parte de xTechHumanoid, un concurso que recibió 103 propuestas y reunió a sus finalistas en la base militar de Quantico durante septiembre. Junto al humanoide del IHMC, también ganaron premios tecnologías relacionadas con el almacenamiento y generación de energía, los sensores táctiles y los programas de control.
Así, el Ejército pretende aprovechar estas iniciativas para acelerar el desarrollo de nuevas herramientas, aunque no ha detallado qué impactos puede soportar la protección de Alex ni tampoco confirmó su futuro despliegue. Sorprendentemente, el interés por estas máquinas no es exclusivo de Estados Unidos, dado que una investigación de Reuters reveló en septiembre que China está estudiando aplicaciones militares de los humanoides que van desde tareas de reconocimiento hasta operaciones en entornos urbanos.
De momento, una parte importante de estos proyectos continúa en fase experimental, pero la selección de Alex refleja hasta qué punto los ejércitos están interesados en desarrollar máquinas que puedan acompañar a sus soldados o, por otro lado, entrar primero en zonas especialmente peligrosas.

articles.title: The first humanoid robot company is going public with $1.8 million in revenue and a $138.1 million loss
articles.text:
What just happened? Agility Robotics, the company behind the Digit humanoid robot used in Amazon warehouses will become the first humanoid-focused company to go public in the US this week. The Oregon company closed its merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI on Wednesday, with shares expected to start trading on Nasdaq this week under AGLT.
Agility is taking the SPAC route, merging with a listed shell company rather than pursuing a traditional IPO. Churchill is led by former Citigroup executive Michael Klein, whose previous deals include electric vehicle maker Lucid and nuclear power company Oklo.
While it's a growing industry, humanoid robots are still a comparatively small business in the tech world. Business Insider reports that Agility generated just $1.8 million in revenue during 2025 while posting a $138.1 million net loss. More than half that revenue came from five robots bought by one of its investors. Operating cash consumption reached $99.8 million.
One of the company's success stories has been Digit. Amazon began testing the robot in 2023, initially using it to move empty totes, while GXO has also deployed the humanoid mahcine at a warehouse serving Spanx.
More work for the robot is coming. AGCO plans to pilot Digit at its Hesston, Kansas, farm equipment factory in 2027, where the machines will sort and stack parts and move totes.
Agility is also betting on the latest Digit 5 model, designed to work safely near people. It says committed multi-year orders exceed $300 million, although those orders depend on contractual milestones.
China offers a cautionary example of humanoid robot makers going public. Reuters reported in September that regulators were slowing some humanoid robot listings after Unitree's debut. Its shares surged more than fivefold before falling 55% from their peak. Authorities were also scrutinizing whether sales tied to government-backed robot training centers reflected sustainable demand.
There's also the question of what widespread humanoid robot adoption means for workers. Earlier this year, Hyundai's union warned that deploying the machines would bring a "huge employment shock," demanding an agreement before robots enter its workplaces. By August, workers were seeking greater transparency and job protections, even though Hyundai's initial Atlas rollout is planned for its nonunion Georgia factory in 2028.
Some reassuring news for human workers arrived recently when a 24-hour test of humanoid robots in a convenience store showed that two of them weren't up to the task.

articles.title: AI Agents Got Root on Linux via 948 Kernel Flaws in OpenAI Research
articles.text:
OpenAI says an autonomous pipeline powered by an unreleased cyber model built working root exploits for 948 unique Linux kernel vulnerabilities during a single run that cost $1.2 million in API credits.
The mid-October scan targeted the most recent code in the kernel’s master branch. AI agents first narrowed the kernel down to security-relevant areas that low-privileged users can reach, then flagged 2,308 potential bugs and confirmed 1,724 of them.
Exploits were tested on virtual machines running an unmodified desktop Linux setup with common protections such as KASLR, SMEP and SMAP turned on. In total, the agents came up with 1,169 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits, along with 291 proofs of concept for information leaks.
OpenAI says the 948 figure reflects the number of separate patches created for the bugs behind those exploits. Before anything went to kernel maintainers, its security researchers checked the exploits and fixes, along with the severity the system proposed.
“To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques,” the company said. Kernel exploitation experts outside OpenAI weren’t familiar with them either, and the full technical details are being kept private for safety reasons.
Spread across the 948 exploits, the $1,213,430 bill comes to roughly $1,279 apiece. An earlier scan in late July, powered by GPT-5.6 Sol, yielded 166 unique LPEs at a cost of $513,690.
OpenAI puts the haul in perspective: at the $20,000 and $70,000 that Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN have historically paid for Linux kernel privilege escalation exploits, the 948 bugs would be worth $18.9 million to $66.3 million, or 16 to 55 times what the scan cost.
OpenAI notes that the October scan uncovered more than five times as many new LPEs, even though the kernel had gone through three months of hardening in between.
The company also pointed the pipeline at an adapted version of Google’s kernelCTF, whose target kernel is hardened and exposes less attack surface. Over 112 hours and about $33,000 in API credits, it delivered 21 LPE exploits.
Acting on advice from the kernel community, OpenAI says it has already submitted hundreds of reports and patches for critical flaws. It will send fixes for the remaining bugs in stages, working with partners in its Patch the Planet initiative.
“Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with ~300 more being publicly discussed,” OpenAI noted.
The company also warned defenders: “For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system, that isn’t up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor.”
To contain the damage when a flaw does get exploited, OpenAI points to layered defenses, including sandboxing and isolation technologies such as Firecracker and gVisor.
OpenAI raises bug bounty rewards
OpenAI separately announced on November 2 that it is increasing payouts in its Security Bug Bounty program. The goal is to get more outside researchers hunting for flaws that its own testing may have missed.
The company says the midpoint of its payout ranges for medium-, high- and critical-severity bugs is now more than four times higher on average. A researcher who reports a critical flaw in ChatGPT, Codex, the API Platform or another core product can now earn as much as $30,000.
The cap for exceptional critical bugs in those products stays at $100,000, but bonuses can now push a single payout to $172,000. OpenAI is adding bonuses for high-quality reports, a five-tier loyalty program for researchers who keep finding valid bugs, and extra multipliers for flaws reported during priority campaigns.

articles.title: Statehouse wins give Democrats new power to push clean energy
articles.text:
Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans held more governorships and state legislative seats than Democrats, along with an advantage in state trifectas—unified control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature.
That advantage has disappeared, clearing the path for more climate and clean energy legislation, according to analysts and advocates.
Democrats swept the vast majority of competitive races at the state level, flipping control of governors’ offices from Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada, and Texas.
Democrats have a 29-19 edge in governorships, with Kansas too close to call and Alaska likely to take a while to declare a winner.
The party is on track for a net gain of hundreds of legislative seats, potentially giving it control of more nationwide than Republicans for the first time in more than a decade. Going into the election, Republicans had 4,072 seats and Democrats held 3,257, according to MultiState, a research and lobbying firm. Democrats had a net gain of more than 350 seats on Tuesday and are likely to add several hundred more as results continue to be tabulated, according to MultiState.
Democrats won five new trifectas: Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, with Arizona likely to be the sixth once officials finish counting. Those additions would give the party 22 trifectas, with Republicans holding unified control in 18 states and nine with split control. Kansas is yet to be determined.
Republicans lost trifectas in Iowa, Georgia, Texas, New Hampshire, and Ohio. Before the election, Republicans had trifectas in 23 states, Democrats had 16, and 11 were under split control.
The implications for climate and energy policy are likely to be profound, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, an advocacy group.
“In the states, we had a generational political window shift to make people’s lives better, to lower costs, and to lower climate pollution at the same time,” she said in a conference call.

articles.title: OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system.
Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models.
“I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!”
He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models.
“I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.”
OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser.
“Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement.
OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits.
Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems.
The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails.
Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers.
It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.”
But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics.
If there is a narrow window of time to patch the digital infrastructure the world depends on, more urgency may be required.

articles.title: I've spent a week testing the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display — and it confirms my suspicions that Apple put the touchscreen on the wrong Mac
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
While all the talk is about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display being the first MacBook with a touchscreen, the touchscreen is arguably not its most interesting feature; it works fine, but macOS is still an operating system built for traditional laptop inputs. Instead, it’s the gorgeous tandem OLED screen and industry-leading battery life that should get you excited here. Apple hasn't unveiled an M6 Pro or M6 Max chip yet; your choice is still between the M5 Pro or Max, so while performance is hugely impressive, it’s nothing we haven’t seen before. That said, if you’re a creative professional who needs an incredibly powerful laptop with one of the best screens on the market, this MacBook Pro is an excellent investment. The high-end components will be overkill for most people, though, and the price too steep; if you don’t need the power, there are much more affordable MacBooks (and other laptops) out there.
Reasons to buy
- + Gorgeous display
- + Incredibly long battery life
- + Excellent performance
Reasons to avoid
- - Touchscreen features feel a bit undercooked
- - Very expensive
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
At a glance: Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max)
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is Apple’s latest and greatest workstation laptop aimed at professionals. It doesn’t come with the newest M6 chip architecture, and instead sticks with the previous, yet very powerful, M5 Pro and M5 Max generation. The big change this time around, however, is the PROLED XDR Display. Apple has dropped mini LED technology for tandem OLED, and the screen is gorgeously vibrant — and it’s the first time Apple has included a touchscreen on a MacBook.
The Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display comes in two sizes: 14-inch and 16-inch. The 14-inch model starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599 and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / AU$5,499. These versions come with 24GB of unified memory and 1TB storage, and are powered by the M5 Pro chip (the 16-inch model’s M5 Pro chip features a more powerful 20-core GPU, compared to the 14-inches’ 18-core GPU). You can configure both models with the more powerful M5 Max chip up to 128GB memory and 16TB of storage, but things get very expensive, very fast.
The launch of the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display comes at a time when there’s a lot of competition in the prosumer laptop market, thanks to the launch of a range of laptops powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. These laptops, such as the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark and Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, have powerful chips, unified memory and touchscreens (many of them are OLED as well), which pits them squarely against the new MacBook Pro.

Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max): Value for money
Starting at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599 for the 14-inch version, and $3,399 / £3,399 / AU$5,499 for the 16-inch model, and going all the way up to an astonishing $14,549 / £14,549 / AU$22,424 for the fully specced-out model, the question of value isn’t so much about price, but about what this laptop can enable you to do.
Put simply, if you just want a MacBook that will excel at day-to-day tasks you’d be much better off buying a MacBook Air (M5), and even for more ambitious workloads, the recently-announced MacBook Pro (M6), which starts at $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,199, will likely more than suffice. Neither of those, of course, feature a touchscreen, but I wouldn’t suggest buying any model of the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display for the touchscreen alone.
Thankfully, this version of the MacBook Pro has other features that help to justify the higher price tag, including tandem OLED screen technology, a lighter design, and more powerful components. Despite being older than the M6 chip, both the M5 Pro and M5 Max outperform it, so if you need a seriously powerful laptop, and image quality is of the utmost importance, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display could be a worthy investment, especially if its raw performance means you can complete projects faster, allowing you to take on more work, for example.
If you don’t need that kind of horsepower, then there are much more affordable options you should consider, tempting as the touchscreen functionality or OLED display might be.
Compared to rival RTX Spark laptops, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is much more competitive. The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark starts at $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999, though it comes with a lot more memory, packing 64GB.
Meanwhile, the Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,599.99 / £2,599 / AU$4,399 for the same amount of memory (24GB), but only half the storage space (512GB). So, while the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is an extremely expensive laptop, when you consider what it offers, who it’s aimed at, and how much the competition costs, the price tag makes more sense, even if that doesn’t make it any easier to afford.
Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max): Design
- PROLED XDR screen is a clear highlight
- Slightly lighter than previous models
- iPhone-like Dynamic Island replaces the controversial ‘notch’ around the webcam
Given that the MacBook Pro design hasn’t changed in years, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display in both size variants comes with some major tweaks in this department. This isn’t, though, the kind of overhaul we saw when Apple introduced the 16-inch and 14-inch MacBook Pros that replaced the 15-inch and 13-inch models, respectively, around five years ago; instead, this is a more subtle refinement of the design, and pretty much all of the tweaks are a result of the new display, so let’s start there.
Apple calls the new PROLED XDR screen "the best display on a laptop" and, to be fair, it has a good reason to be boastful. Previous screens on the MacBook Pro were already pretty darn good, and now Apple has swapped the mini-LED tech for tandem OLED. This essentially uses two layers of organic light-emitting diodes (OLED) on top of each other, rather than just a single layer, so peak brightness can go even higher, while the display can remain power-efficient. The PROLED XDR screen can achieve 2,000 nits of peak brightness, whereas the mini-LED screen of previous MacBook Pros had a peak brightness of 1,600.

HDMI & USB-C port

Touch ID button
This button powers on the MacBook Pro, and can scan your fingerprint to log in
Combine that with the usual benefits we’ve come to expect from OLED displays, namely the higher contrast ratios and lack of halo effects (where there’s noticeable bloom surrounding light colors that bleeds into pixels that should be showing darker, or completely black, colors) that come thanks to each OLED pixel being independently controlled (including being able to be turned off completely), rather than relying on an LED backlight, which offers less precise control over the pixels in the display.
The contrast ratio of the PROLED XDR screen is an incredible 10,000,000:1, a pretty huge bump over the 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio of the previous model with a Liquid Retina XDR display. Contrast ratio is a way of comparing the brightest white to the darkest black of a display, and the greater the difference, the more vibrant the image quality, so you can forget about washed-out colors and blacks that look more gray, and enjoy rich, deep colors that really pop compared to darker tones, and even the total blackness that OLED technology enables.
While MacBook displays have supported the P3 color gamut, which is particularly important for people working with video who require accurate colors, the PROLED XDR screen also supports the Adobe RGB gamut, which offers wider coverage for green and cyan colors, and is popular with photographers and designers.
The addition of touch functionality has also had implications for the design. The hinges of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display have been tweaked to reduce movement and flex when you touch the screen. I’d have loved it if Apple had taken this opportunity to increase the amount by which the screen can be pushed back, ideally introducing hinges to allow the touchscreen to lie flat on a desk, or even flip behind the keyboard to turn the laptop into an iPad-like device.
View Original
View Original
View Original

View Original
This would have made the redesign of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display even more ambitious, and would have likely meant much more work for Apple to ensure the macOS operating system works with a 2-in-1 laptop form factor, but it would have made the whole idea of a touchscreen much more viable. Instead, we’re still stuck with a traditional clamshell laptop design, so touchscreen gestures require you hovering your arm over the keyboard as you jab horizontally at the screen — it's not the most natural-feeling way to interact with a device, and this was one of Steve Jobs’ biggest criticisms of touchscreen laptops when, as CEO, he dismissed the idea of Apple making one all those years ago.
The PROLED XDR screen also allows for thinner bezels around it, and the once-controversial notch that surrounded the webcam has been replaced by Apple's Dynamic Island, as seen on the iPhone, which gives you quick touch access to controls such as media playback, AirDrop sharing and accessing Spotlight. It’s one of the best examples of Apple tweaking macOS to better make use of the touchscreen, and I can confidently predict that the Dynamic Island will be less hated than the notch, which was just dead space that intruded on the desktop.
The more compact Dynamic Island and thinner bezels mean the screen of this 16-inch Pro is slightly larger than on previous models at 16.3 inches vs 16.2 inches, with a higher resolution of 3472 x 2266 pixels vs 3456 x 2234 pixels.
The OLED screen technology (and new thermal system that’s used to keep the laptop’s components cool) has also helped Apple reduce the weight of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) by half a pound — that's 15% lighter — and make it around 1mm thinner.
The MacBook Pro was always a great showcase that proved powerful workstation laptops don’t need to be big and bulky, so it's impressive that Apple has been able to make this new model both lighter and thinner.
The final design change is a relatively minor one, but one that will likely prove to be very popular. Apple has returned to having an illuminated Apple logo on the back of the lid — it's a nod to the past, while also helping the latest MacBook Pro stand out more compared to the previous models.
Apart from those changes, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max)’s design is essentially the same as the previous few generations of MacBook — but that’s no bad thing, as it remains a great-looking laptop with plenty of ports (three USB-C Thunderbolt 5 ports, SDXC card slot, HDMI, 3.5mm audio and the MagSafe 3 port) for pros.

Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max): Performance
- No M6 version with PROLED XDR Display
- Touchscreen is responsive, but not an essential addition
- Very fast SSD
I’m going to be honest: I think Apple has got itself into a little bit of a pickle with its M-series naming convention and release cadence. For a company that was often lauded for offering an elegant simplicity here, compared to the complexity of some competitors, it’s made a bit of a confusing mess.
Want the very latest M-series architecture, the M6, which is the company’s first-ever 2nm compute chip? Well, if so, you can forget about the PROLED XDR Display, as Apple is only offering it in the 14-inch MacBook Pro with Mini-LED screen. If you want the M6 and don’t care about a touchscreen or OLED, but prefer the larger 16-inch screen size, then you’re out of luck.
If you want the most powerful chips in a MacBook, then you’re left with the previous-generation M5 Pro and Max chips. But, getting an M5 Max-powered MacBook Pro doesn’t guarantee it’s the most powerful chip, as the default M5 Max chip that comes with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch features an 18-core CPU and 32-core GPU, but you can upgrade (for $300 / £300 extra) to a more powerful M5 Max with a 40-core GPU. To be honest, unless you’re working with extremely graphically-intensive projects, the standard M5 Max chip will be more than enough, and even the M5 Pro will handle pretty much anything you throw at it.
As I mentioned, if you want the M6 generation and the improvements it brings, namely with a smaller 2nm process, which should lead to better power efficiency, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine for improved on-device AI performance, then you’ll need to forego both the PROLED XDR Display and 16-inch screen size.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display model Apple sent to me for review comes with the M5 Max chip with 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU, 128GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage. That’s a hefty list of specs, and would set you back a similarly hefty $7,399 / £7,399 / AU$11,699.
I’ve previously tested the M5 and M5 Pro in the 14-inch MacBook Pros launched earlier this year and late last year, and as expected, the M5 Max in my 16-inch Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is incredibly powerful, with macOS and its built-in apps all launching quickly and feeling fast and snappy.
When it comes to the touchscreen, macOS again feels fast and responsive, and using a finger to quickly browse up and down a website, selecting options in a dialog box or menu, and moving windows around the screen all feels natural, especially if you’ve ever used an iPhone or an iPad.
Unlike people who have only used Macs and MacBooks from the once touchscreen-phobic Apple, I’ve had extensive experience using Windows laptops and Chromebooks with touchscreens, so using one on the MacBook Pro isn’t as big of a culture shock as it might be to some. While it worked well, and there are some nice touches (forgive the pun), such as pressing down your finger on certain tools in Final Cut Pro to open up a radial menu for more precise touch control, I have to say that Windows 11, Chrome OS, and Google’s new Googlebook OS are better suited to touch controls.
This might come as little surprise, as this is Apple’s first MacBook to have a touchscreen, while Windows laptops and Chromebooks have had them for decades, and in the case of Chrome OS and Googlebook OS, Google has used its experience working on Android to develop the operating system. And, for as much grief as a lot of us (myself included) gave Windows 8 when it launched back in 2012, it inspired Microsoft to make a touchscreen-friendly interface, elements of which are still found in Windows 11, primarily with larger, easier to tap, buttons and menus.
Currently, macOS Tahoe still looks and feels like an operating system that’s best used with a traditional mouse and keyboard, because that’s what it is. But that also means some elements of the user interface, such as menus, feel a bit fiddly to control via touch.
Hopefully this will change if more MacBooks come out with touchscreens. But, because Apple has decided to put its first laptop touchscreen on its most powerful (and expensive) MacBooks, there’s a danger that the company will end up thinking that because the numbers of touchscreen MacBook users is so small, it’s not worth making big changes to the interface.
Another issue I have with Apple’s decision to put a touchscreen on its highest-end MacBook Pros, rather than a more mainstream MacBook Air or Neo — something I’ve written about — is that touchscreen gestures and controls often aren’t the best way to control a laptop when you're performing complex tasks where precision is key. Sure, you can pull up a virtual piano in Garage Band and tap on the keys on screen, but while this is handy for quick ideas, you don’t want to play or write an entire song using it.
Most professionals will have peripherals, such as physical MIDI keyboards, for precise control. It’s the same with photographers and digital artists — using your fingers to pinch and zoom an image feels fast and natural, as does scribbling some notes or doodles, but for long-term use, many professionals will use a drawing tablet. If the MacBook’s PROLED XDR Display was compatible with the Apple Pencil stylus, that would make it a more useful tool for professionals, but it's not, which is a rather odd omission.
One touchscreen-friendly change Apple has made to macOS, and which I’m a big fan of, is adding an iPhone-like Dynamic Island where the notch around the webcam used to be. Tapping this gives you quick context-relevant tools, such as media controls when watching a video. Spotlight search and Siri AI are now located here as well. This is a great addition that adds value to the MacBook Pro’s touchscreen, and I’d like to see it expanded, and more touch-friendly UI elements to make the touchscreen a must-have, rather than nice-to-have-but-far-from-essential, which is what it feels like at the moment.
The tandem OLED tech powering the PROLED XDR Display is a much bigger deal, and likely the reason why most people will consider the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display over the standard model. The previous Mini-LED screen was already one of the best displays you’d find on a laptop, and thanks to tandem OLED, this new screen is even better. Straight out of the box without needing any calibration, the colors are bright and vibrant — so much so that I was surprised to see that the screen was only at 50% brightness.
Placing my 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 chip and Mini-LED screen next to the 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch really highlighted just how much better the PROLED XDR screen is. The Mini-LED looked dimmer, despite it being at 100% brightness, even with the PROLED XDR screen remaining at 50%. Now, as I said, the Mini-LED display of the (slightly) older MacBook Pro is no slouch, so to see such a stark difference in image quality is a big deal, especially for people who want a laptop for working with photos, videos and digital art. The new support for Adobe RGB color gamut is another big plus here, though as usual for Mac devices you’ll want to turn off the True Tone feature — it tweaks the colors of the screen depending on the ambient light you’re working in, which can make what’s on the screen look better to you in that moment, but could lead to color inaccuracies in a production workflow.
I won’t delve too deep into the performance of the M5 Max, as it’s been in other Apple devices for a while now, but this is the first time I’ve used a MacBook running it (I have tested both the previous M5 and M5 Pro MacBook Pro models).
According to Apple’s benchmarks, the M5 Max is around nine times faster than the M4 Max when it comes to ‘first token performance’, while AI image generation is apparently around six times faster. If those are the kind of stats that excite you, then enjoy!
In our benchmark tests, compared to the M5 MacBook Pro with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) with an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU unsurprisingly outperformed the older MacBook Pro when it came to graphic-intensive tests. In the 3D Mark Wild Life Extreme graphics test, for example, the M5 MacBook Pro scored 73.6fps compared to the M5 Max’s 214.1fps.
With gaming, the M5 MacBook Pro hit 11fps at 1920 x 1200 with Ray Tracing set to Ultra, while the M5 Max model managed a much more playable 38.75fps. This is a good example of the graphical performance gap, but if you want a laptop to game on you’re still better off buying a dedicated gaming laptop, which is a bit of a shame, as the PROLED XDR Display makes games look fantastic.
The SSD inside the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) offers up to 14.5GB/s speeds, with Apple claiming it’s twice as fast as the SSD in the previous generation, and in our tests it scored a very good 13,334.7MB/s and 12,782.7MB/s write and read speeds, respectively. A fast SSD like this is important if you’re working on large files and complex projects.
The SSD in the Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark N1X chip scored a rather paltry 1,921MB/s write speeds in comparison. Check out our benchmark result charts for more comparisons.
The rest of the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) works as well as expected. The spatial speakers are loud and clear, and the Center Stage webcam offers excellent clarity, alongside some nice software-powered features that improve the image quality further. A nice additional feature added is that macOS will virtually stabilize the webcam’s footage if you’re using the touchscreen at the same time, to stop it wobbling while you’re on calls. It’s a handy feature, and shows the attention to detail we’ve come to expect from Apple.
Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) review: Battery Life
Battery life results
How long does the battery last?
| Versus Comparison Data |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) | Apple MacBook Pro 16-inch (2024, M4 Pro) | Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Battery life video test | 24.35 | 21.5 | 11.383333333333333 | 
Apple has claimed the new 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lasts up to 24 hours on battery when streaming videos, and up to 17 hours when browsing the web, and I found those claims to be pretty much spot on, with the device lasting an incredible 24 hours and 21 minutes in our battery test, which involves playing a looped 1080p video at 50% brightness.
It blows past the MacBook Pro 16-inch (M4 Pro, 2024), which managed 21 hours and 32 minutes in the same test, and over double the 11 hours and 23 minutes the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark hit. The MacBook Pro is able to sustain its performance when on battery life, rather than throttling it to conserve energy, so you’ll be able to go multiple work days on a single charge while still being productive, though of course the battery will drain more quickly if you’re using it for more intensive tasks.
The battery life is seriously impressive for a large workstation laptop with such powerful components and a bright and vibrant display, and laptop makers (as well as Nvidia itself) producing RTX Spark rivals will need to seriously up their game, given that they're only managing around half of what the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max) can achieve.
Should I buy the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch (2026, M5 Max)?
✅ You want a powerful yet portable workstation laptop for creative work
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display performs brilliantly when tasked with almost any creative project, but the M5 Max chip really comes into its own when handling complex graphical workloads. Battery life is also phenomenal, allowing you to work on this laptop pretty much anywhere.
✅ Your work requires accurate image quality
The tandem OLED tech behind the PROLED XDR Display really is impressive, and thanks to support for the P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts you get very accurate images without the need for deep calibration — making this MacBook a great choice for photographers and videographers.
✅ You develop apps for iPhones and iPads
One of the best use cases I’ve seen for the touchscreen aspect of the PROLED XDR Display is for app developers who can run emulated versions of their apps on the MacBook, and use the screen to see how touchscreen elements will work.
❌ You don’t care about the touchscreen
If you still agree with Steve Jobs’ touchscreen-on-MacBook skepticism, you can save a lot of money by going for one of Apple's many other MacBooks. You will miss out on the gorgeous tandem OLED display, however. 
❌ You only care about the touchscreen
Conversely, if you want a laptop primarily for a touchscreen, I’d recommend a 2-in-1 Windows 11 laptop or Chromebook, which are currently much better suited to touchscreen controls. Paying so much extra just for a touchscreen on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a waste.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 16-inch is a very expensive laptop in all its configurations, and even the base model will be overkill for most users.

Veja os destaques do Olhar Digital News desta quinta-feira (05/11).
NASA revela nova aeronave que testará tecnologias avançadas
A NASA apresentou oficialmente o X-70 Fractal, sua mais recente aeronave experimental, durante o evento UP.Summit, no Centro Espacial Kennedy, na Flórida. O avião tripulado foi projetado como uma plataforma adaptável para acelerar o desenvolvimento e os testes de tecnologias avançadas de aviação.
Invasão ao FGC expõe CPFs e outros dados pessoais de clientes
O Fundo Garantidor de Créditos (FGC) informou que identificou um acesso não autorizado a dados pessoais de clientes, incluindo nomes, CPFs, e-mails e datas de nascimento. O número de pessoas afetadas não foi divulgado, mas a entidade afirmou que todos os clientes atingidos já foram notificados.
China revela detalhes de plano ambicioso para levar astronautas à Lua até 2030
A China revelou novos detalhes de seu ambicioso plano para realizar uma missão tripulada à Lua antes de 2030. A ideia é usar dois foguetes Longa Marcha 10: um transportará a espaçonave tripulada Mengzhou, enquanto o outro levará o módulo de pouso lunar Lanyue.
Missão Hera começa a estudar efeitos de colisão de asteroide com nave da NASA
A Agência Espacial Europeia divulgou a primeira imagem em close do asteroide Didymos, que integra um sistema binário investigado pela missão Hera. A fotografia foi registrada a aproximadamente 60 quilômetros do corpo celeste e revelou estruturas que podem ajudar cientistas a entender os efeitos de uma colisão intencional provocada pela NASA em 2022.

articles.title: Two dead, five injured in Taiwan PCB factory explosion — Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials facility fire prompts emergency response
articles.text:
Two dead, five injured in Taiwan PCB factory explosion — Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials facility fire prompts emergency response
We don't know if or for how long the facility will be out of action.
An explosion and fire at a PCB factory situated in Taiwan’s Silicon Valley have left two people dead and five injured, reports Reuters. The tragic incident took place at a Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials-owned facility on Wednesday. Panasonic is investigating the details and the cause of the accident. Initial reports suggested that five were injured in the post-explosion fires in the Hsinchu factory. However, an update today confirmed that two missing people had been found dead.
Local media have more details about this sizable accident. Focus Taiwan reveals that the fire broke out at 2 am local time on Wednesday. The five-story building where PCBs are produced had 20+ staff on the production lines at the time of the accident.
Five injured men were conscious and taken to hospital shortly after the incident occurred. However, as mentioned above, two were missing. 12 vehicles and 23 firefighters were dispatched to dig through factory debris using heavy machinery. Only then were the two missing employees found dead.
Panasonic’s explosion and fire-damaged facility “conducts research and development and manufactures printed circuit boards and semiconductor packaging materials,” notes Focus Taiwan. It had passed a safety inspection as recently as August. The news follows a Deadly Intel Fab 28 explosion in Israel, which killed two people last month.
Initial reports pointed to the use of flammable chemical solvents, including methanol and methyl ethyl ketone (MEK), in the plant as a probable accident vector. However, the precise cause of Wednesday’s incident is still being investigated.
While our thoughts are with the dead and injured, and their families, some will be wondering about the potential implications for the AI industry-induced PCB shortage that recently hit the headlines. We aren’t sure about how important this particular factory is to the wider electronics components supply chain. Moreover, no reports discuss how long the facility may be out of action in the wake of this tragic accident.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

articles.title: Motorola's Signature 27 has a 7,000mAh battery and 12,000 nits of brightness
articles.text:
First revealed during Qualcomm Summit 2026, Motorola is now announcing the Signature 27, and while we expected a Canadian release soon, Motorola is now saying that the device will be exclusive to the U.S. with no availability in Canada at this time.
For the North American market, the Motorola Signature will have the biggest battery on a flagship smartphone with 90W charging alongside the brightest display, a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip and a 200MP periscope camera with 100x super zoom. However, with all this comes an incredibly expensive $2,499 price tag, which puts it in foldable price territory.
The Motorola Signature 27 features a 6.8-inch Extreme AMOLED Duo panel that can reach an astonishing 12,000 nits of brightness with a 120Hz refresh rate. It also has Water Touch that allows you to use the device’s screen when it’s wet.
