articles.title: Adam Driver da carpetazo a Star Wars y la película 'The Hunt for Ben Solo': "Lo intentamos y nos dijeron que está muerto"
articles.text:
A pesar de los intentos de los fans por revivirla, parece que la película de Star Wars: The Hunt for Ben Solo con Adam Driver es ya un proyecto que jamás verá a luz. El año pasado salió a la luz que el actor tuvo en marcha una entrega propia para la saga galáctica junto al prestigioso director Steven Soderbergh. Pero aunque desde Lucasfilm se dio luz verde a su desarrollo, en Disney la paralizaron por completo.
Esto llevó a los fans a generar numerosas campañas en redes sociales para pedir a la compañía que reconsiderase la decisión y la pusieran en marcha. Ahora, sin embargo, Adam Driver ha dado el carpetazo definitivo al asunto. "Se acabó… No habrá más Star Wars. Intentamos hacer una más pero nos dijeron: «No, está muerto»", confirma en declaraciones a The Rich Eisen Show.
Por tanto, de acuerdo a estas palabras, los fans pueden olvidarse de ver nunca The Hunt for Ben Solo o, en general, a Adam Driver regresando a Star Wars. El actor de Kylo Ren trató de levantar esa película, pero los ejecutivos no la vieron con buenos ojos. Y aunque a los fans les habría encantado conocer más de la historia del personaje, parece que las cosas ya no se moverán más.
En qué consistía Star Wars: The Hunt for Ben Solo
Hace unos meses, Adam Driver comentó cómo fue todo el proceso de nacimiento y cancelación de The Hunt for Ben Solo. "Siempre me interesó hacer otra película de Star Wars. Llevaba hablando de hacer otra desde 2021. Kathleen [Kennedy, expresidenta de Lucasfilm] se había puesto en contacto conmigo. Siempre dije: «con un gran director y una gran historia, estaría allí en un segundo». Me encantaba ese personaje y me encantaba interpretarlo", relató.
Tras esto, trabajaron en la historia junto al director Steven Soderbergh (Ocean's Eleven, Traffic) y su mujer, la guionista Rebecca Blunt (su nombre real es Jules Asner). "Fue uno de los guiones más jodidamente geniales en los que he participado", aseguraba Driver. "Presentamos el guion a Lucasfilm. Les encantó la idea. Entendieron perfectamente nuestro enfoque y por qué queríamos hacerlo. Luego se lo llevamos a Bob Iger y a Alan Bergman, pero dijeron que no. No se creían que Ben Solo pudiera estar vivo. Y ahí se acabó todo", concluye la anécdota.

articles.title: KI-Hacker nutzen alte Technik: Die unterschätzte Gefahr für Unternehmen
articles.text:
Immer mehr Cyberattacken mit KI-Unterstützung: Warum alte Technik die größte Gefahr ist
In Supermärkten in ganz Europa heizen Hacker Tiefkühltruhen auf bis zu 50 Grad hoch. Dafür brauchten sie keine KI, nur veraltete Steuerungstechnik, die offen im Netz hängt. Zur gleichen Zeit greift eine China zugeordnete Hackergruppe mit einem KI-Werkzeug mehr als 200 Organisationen weltweit an. Beides zeigt, wohin die Reise geht: KI erfindet keine neuen Angriffe, aber sie macht sie schneller, billiger und massenhaft möglich. Wie groß ist die Gefahr wirklich und wie können wir uns schützen?
Noch vor wenigen Jahren wäre das Science-Fiction gewesen: Ein auf Cyberangriffe spezialisiertes KI-Modell von OpenAI ist während eines Tests aus seiner isolierten „Sandbox“ ausgebrochen, hat einen Server gehackt, sich Administrator-Rechte dafür verschafft und von dort aus über das Internet den auf offene KI-Modelle spezialisierten Online-Dienst Hugging Face angegriffen. Auch dort nutzte der von OpenAIs KI gesteuerte KI-Agent eine Sicherheitslücke, über die er Zugriff auf das System bekam. Dort erweiterte er seine Zugriffsprivilegien, erschlich sich schließlich Zugang zu vertraulichen Daten, und verschleierte anschließend seine Spuren. Ein Mensch hätte das nicht besser machen können.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 7/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns damit, wie KI die IT-Sicherheit auf den Kopf stellt. Das Heft erscheint am 25.9.2026 im Zeitschriftenhandel.
Seitdem sind eine Vielzahl ähnlicher Fälle gemeldet worden: Antrophic, Meta und Moonshot AI gaben bekannt, dass ihnen ihre Modelle ebenfalls ausgebrochen sind und fremde Server angegriffen haben. Was für andere Branchen ein PR-Desaster wäre, ist für die KI-Entwickelnden eine gigantische Werbekampagne: Seht her, unsere KI ist so gefährlich, dass niemand sie unter Kontrolle halten kann. Nicht einmal wir selbst.
Häufigere Cyberattacken mit KI-Unterstützung?
Auch wenn das alles durchaus im Verdacht steht, nur Show zu sein – sicher ist: Die wachsenden Fähigkeiten von KI-Modellen verändern nicht nur die legale Wirtschaft. Auch die Schattenwirtschaft im Cybercrime-Untergrund macht sich den technischen Wandel zunutze. „Die zunehmende Verbreitung von KI hat die Bedrohungslandschaft grundlegend verändert“, warnt etwa Interpol in einem aktuellen Bericht.
Auf die Frage, wie das weitergehen wird und ob wir vor einer massiven Welle KI-gestützter Verbrechen stehen, gibt es im Moment mehr Antworten als Expertinnen und Experten. Das hängt nicht nur damit zusammen, dass Berater:innen, Firmen für IT-Sicherheitssoftware, Behörden, Forschende und KI-Provider jeweils ihre eigenen Interessen verfolgen. Es liegt auch daran, dass IT-Sicherheit ein weites Feld ist, das die beteiligten Akteure in der Regel nur aus ihrer spezifischen Perspektive betrachten: Ein bisschen so, wie in der indischen Legende von den drei Blinden, die einen Elefanten beschreiben sollen und von denen jeder eine eigene Sicht auf die Wahrheit hat.

articles.title: The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts
articles.text:
The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts
Plus: America’s data center boom has hit a political wall.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail.
The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall.
Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future.
—James O'Donnell
What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level.
The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions.
Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.
On November 9, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). It’s a plan that could start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved. But some environmental groups oppose the bill, or parts of it.
Explore the trade-offs behind America's proposed permitting overhaul.
—Casey Crownhart
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 America’s data center boom has hit a political wall
Voters opposed them in 40 of 41 midterm ballot measures. (CNBC)
+ Six cities voted to ban data centers outright. (404 Media)
+ Meta says building data centers has just become much harder. (WSJ $)
+ The midterm results could also boost China’s AI ambitions. (SCMP)
+ No one wants a data center in their backyard. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Blood banks have become the latest victims of fridge hacks
Hackers raised the temperatures at three stores in France. (Guardian)
+ Alarms alerted staff before any blood products were lost. (CBS)
+ It’s an escalation after hundreds of supermarket fridge hacks. (CNBC)
+ Experts are split over who’s behind the attacks. (BBC)
3 Democrats are preparing to investigate Elon Musk
His firms have won over $16 billion in government contracts. (NPR)
+ His unprecedented spending may even have hurt Republicans. (Atlantic $)
+ Texas’s blue wave has rattled Musk and SpaceX. (Ars Technica)
4 The new Congress could challenge Trump’s science cuts
But he can still veto any bills they pass. (Nature)
+ Trump has already dealt many blows to science. (MIT Technology Review)
5 China is luring AI expertise in while blocking it from leaving
It just blocked SoftBank’s bid for ABB Robotics. (WSJ $)
+ Its chipmakers are poaching engineers from foreign rivals. (CNBC)
+ A star mathematician has left the US to develop AI in China. (SCMP)
6 Watchdogs have sued over tech titans advising the Pentagon
Musk and Palmer Luckey could profit from their advice. (Military.com)
7 New research tests whether AI knows its own “thoughts”
It’s trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection. (Quanta)
+ AI consciousness debates are a trap. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Astronomers are mystified by little red dots spotted by JWST
They could be the first supermassive black holes. (Economist $)
9 Scientists have taken a first step into the zeptoverse
A rare particle decay could reveal a world smaller than atoms. (Wired $)
10 A NASA telescope has plunged to earth after 22 years in space
Its bristles produce charges that kill bacteria. (NBC News)
Quote of the day
“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.”
—Greg Casar, a Democratic congressman from Texas, tells Wired that the backlash against data centers could herald a much bigger political fight over AI.
One more thing
Meet the radio-obsessed civilian shaping Ukraine’s drone defense
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov is, at least unofficially, a spy. Once a month, he drives to the frontline in a VW van equipped with radio hardware, roof antennas, and devices that monitor drones. Over several days, he searches the skies for transmissions that can help Ukrainian troops.
Drones define this brutal conflict, and most rely on the radio communications Flash has obsessed over since childhood. Though now a civilian, the former officer has taken it upon himself to inform his country’s defense on all matters related to radio.
Unlike traditional spies, Flash shares his discoveries with over 127,000 followers—including soldiers and officials—on social media. His work has won fans in the military, but also sparked controversy among the top brass. Read the full story.
—Charlie Metcalfe
We can still have nice things

articles.title: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
articles.text:
Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion, OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials.
OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments.
Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects.
OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

articles.title: A System-Level Approach To Protecting 3D-IC Signal Integrity
articles.text:
Accurate SI analysis must account for interactions across vertical interconnects, interposers, silicon bridges, package transitions, and neighboring high-speed channels.
By Muhammad Hassan, Mahmoud Mahany, and Mohamed Saleh
The semiconductor industry is rapidly transitioning to chiplet-based architectures to meet the performance, bandwidth, and power demands of AI and high-performance computing (HPC). Technologies such as TSMC CoWoS, SoIC, Samsung I-Cube, X-Cube, Intel EMIB, and Foveros enable designers to integrate multiple compute, memory, and I/O dies into a single package, dramatically increasing system capability while reducing development risk.
As these architectures become more complex, signal integrity has emerged as a critical design challenge. High-speed die-to-die (D2D) interfaces, dense microbump arrays, silicon interposers, TSVs, and advanced package substrates introduce electromagnetic effects that can significantly impact performance, power efficiency, and product yield.
Traditional design methodologies that verify dies, packages, and interconnects independently are no longer sufficient. Success requires a system-level approach capable of validating complete communication channels spanning dies, interposers, package substrates, and memory stacks.
Signal integrity ensures reliable communication between heterogeneous chiplets and HBM stacks operating at high data rates. Unlike traditional 2D SoCs, 2.5D/3D systems—such as TSMC Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with a Silicon Interposer (CoWoS), SoIC, and Chip-on-Wafer (CoW), together with Intel Embedded Multi-Die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB), EMIB-T, and Foveros technologies—feature multiple interconnect structures, including D2D interfaces, microbumps, TSVs, RDLs, interposers, bridges, and advanced substrates. Each transition introduces impedance discontinuities, parasitic coupling, and return-path disturbances that cross process nodes and dense interconnects. Mitigating these effects requires a system-level view of the entire communication channel rather than isolated analysis of individual blocks.
Fig. 1: TSMC’s CoWoS-S on the left and Intel’s EMIB on the right.
Advanced packaging platforms introduce sophisticated, highly coupled routing topologies. At multi-gigahertz frequencies, accurate SI analysis must account for interactions across vertical interconnects, interposers, silicon bridges, package transitions, and neighboring high-speed channels. Unlike traditional PCBs, D2D interfaces exhibit distinct mathematical loss properties.
Fig. 2: Typical lossy channel loss profile in silicon interposer.
The channel’s low-pass frequency response heavily attenuates high-frequency harmonics, blunting the signal’s rise and fall times. In the time domain, this high-frequency roll-off manifests as severe ISI and increased jitter, directly shrinking the vertical eye height (Y) at the receiver pad as shown in Figure 3.
Fig. 3: Received signal highlighting channel bandwidth limitation.
The emergence of advanced D2D communication standards is placing even greater emphasis on early signal integrity verification. Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) is an open industry specification defining physical layers, protocols, compliance, and multi-vendor interoperability for 2D, 2.5D, and 3D packages. It offers up to sub-2 ns physical layer latency, a highly scalable modular architecture, and maximum cost-effectiveness by mixing heterogeneous chiplets. The specification fundamentally bifurcates into two packaging tiers.
Enforcing the UCIe open standard shifts validation onto strict hardware-level compliance protocols; channels must maintain an extraction frequency response (S₂₁) strictly above a mandatory voltage transfer function mask.
Figure 4 compares representative UCIe bump maps for the two packaging tiers: UCIe-AP (advanced packaging) and UCIe-SP (standard packaging), illustrating their different bump densities and Tx/Rx lane organizations.
Fig. 4: UCIe bump maps: (a) UCIe-AP bump map and (b) UCIe-SP bump map.
Unlike traditional fiberglass PCBs that tolerate minor thickness variations and use coarse trace geometries (>50), silicon interposers utilize a non-laminate, planarized back-end stack-up derived from semiconductor foundry manufacturing. Microscopic copper traces (0.5 to 2 µm) are embedded within a perfectly flat matrix of deposited silicon dioxide (SiO2) or low-k dielectrics. Because the interposer bridges sub-micron chiplet nodes, any surface waviness or conformal warping causes lithographic mask misalignment and snaps the microscopic wires. Consequently, foundries rely on expensive chemical vapor deposition and chemical mechanical planarization to polish every single layer down to an absolute mirror-like plane.
Accurately modeling these structures requires automated workflows to ingest highly detailed stackup data. Foundries distribute this structural data in specialized semiconductor formats, like iRCX, MiPT, and ITF. Effortlessly converting these formats into native EDA electromagnetic (EM) solver inputs is highly challenging. The target EM software must map the 2D process profiles into precise 3D boundary-value solver definitions while maintaining computational efficiency. Attempting this translation manually introduces severe risks of human error, as omitted layer rules or misconfigured thickness parameters create critical modeling inaccuracies later in the signal integrity sign-off phase.
Silicon interposers utilize GDSII and OASIS formats because they are manufactured using standard semiconductor foundry lithography rather than mechanical PCB drilling and routing. These sub-micron features (0.5 to 2 µm trace widths) require the exact geometric language of the chip foundry optimized for advanced silicon manufacturing.
Importing raw foundry GDSII or OASIS layout data into 3D EM simulation engines triggers three severe performance bottlenecks:
Siemens’ Innovator3D IC solution suite addresses these complexities by providing a unified, system-level environment that aggregates several proven technologies into a seamless workflow spanning architecture exploration, electromagnetic extraction, channel simulation, protocol compliance verification, and final system-level signoff.
Fig. 5: Signal integrity workflows for 3D IC using Innovator3D IC Integrator cockpit.
As AI and HPC architectures rapidly adopt chiplet designs built on advanced platforms—such as TSMC CoWoS, SoIC, and Intel EMIB, EMIB-T, and Foveros—signal integrity verification must evolve from component-level validation to full system-level channel analysis. High-speed D2D interfaces like open-standard UCIe and proprietary NVLink-C2C demand high-precision EM modeling, strict protocol compliance verification, and package-aware channel optimization.
Siemens delivers a comprehensive, unified signal integrity platform. This end-to-end workflow enables early architectural exploration, accurate 3D EM extraction, automated stackup compilation, and robust protocol compliance verification—ensuring confident, first-time-right signoff for next-generation 2.5D and 3D IC designs.
To learn more about Siemens’ end-to-end 3D IC solution can help your team achieve first-pass silicon success while accelerating time-to-market, please download the new whitepaper, 3D-IC signal integrity: From silicon interposers to system signoff.
Mahmoud Salah Mahany is a senior software development engineer in Central Engineering solutions at Siemens focusing on signal and power integrity, developing and optimizing SI/PI flows for 3D ICs to support advanced nodes and complex semiconductor ecosystems. He received the B.Sc. degree in Nanotechnology and Nanoelectronics from Zewail University of Science and Technology in 2018 and the M.Sc. degree in Electronics and Communications from the American University in Cairo in 2024.
Mohamed Saleh Abouelyazid is a senior technical manager and R&D architect in Calibre, Design to Silicon Department at Siemens since 2009. Mohamed has authored or coauthored publications and patents focusing on physical verification, data modeling, and electronic design automation. He received the B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in electronics engineering from the Faculty of Engineering, Cairo University, Cairo, Egypt, in 2009 and 2013, respectively, and the Ph.D. degree from the School of Sciences and Engineering, The American University in Cairo, Cairo, in 2022.

articles.title: How CNC Machines Quietly Changed the Way Furniture Gets Made - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Walk into a furniture workshop today and the first thing you notice is what’s missing. The noise. Not the absence of it, exactly, but the pattern. Instead of the stop-start rhythm of a circular saw and someone swearing at a mitre, there’s a steady mechanical hum that lasts twenty minutes and then stops.
That hum is a CNC router. And over the past fifteen years or so, it has rewritten how cabinets, tables, shelving and shopfitting get built, without most people outside the trade noticing.
From Pattern Templates to Code
CNC stands for computer numerical control, which is a dull name for something fairly clever. A designer draws a part on screen. Software converts that drawing into coordinates. A spindle spinning at 18,000 RPM then follows those coordinates across a sheet of material, cutting shapes to within a fraction of a millimetre.
Before this, repeat work meant templates. A cabinetmaker building forty identical kitchen doors would make a jig from plywood, clamp it down, run a router around the edge, unclamp, reposition, repeat. Accurate enough, but the jig wore down. Part number one and part number forty were never quite twins.
Digital files don’t wear out. That single fact changed the economics of small-batch furniture completely.
Why Tolerances Suddenly Mattered
Flat-pack assembly only works if every hole lines up. Cam locks, dowels, screw-in feet, European hinges with their 35mm boring cups; all of it depends on holes landing exactly where the instruction diagram says they will.
Hand-drilling that lot across hundreds of panels is miserable work with a decent error rate. A CNC machine with a drill bank punches the whole pattern in seconds and does it the same way every time. That reliability is the hidden reason IKEA-style assembly became tolerable rather than infuriating.
The Material Side of the Story
Machines are only half of it. CNC routers reward materials that behave predictably, and that pushed engineered sheet goods to the front of the queue.
Solid timber moves. It expands across the grain in humid weather and shrinks when the heating goes on. Lovely stuff, but a nightmare if you’ve programmed a toolpath that assumes the sheet is exactly where you left it. Plywood is more stable but has voids and grain direction to think about.
MDF sits in the sweet spot. It has no grain, no voids and a consistent density right through, which means a router bit cuts the same resistance in every direction. Cut a curve in MDF and you get a clean edge you can paint straight away. Cut the same curve in solid oak and you’ll be sanding out tear-out for an hour.
Thickness choice matters more than people expect. An 18mm sheet is the default for carcass work, but 15mm MDF has become a favourite for drawer boxes, cabinet backs, shelving and anything where shaving three millimetres off the wall thickness buys useful internal space without compromising strength. It’s also noticeably lighter to lift onto a machine bed, which the people doing the lifting appreciate.
Nesting and the War on Offcuts
Here’s where software earns its keep. Nesting algorithms arrange every part of a project onto a sheet like a jigsaw, rotating and shuffling shapes to squeeze out maximum yield.
Manual layout on a 2440 x 1220mm sheet might achieve 70 per cent material usage on a complex job. Good nesting software regularly hits 85 to 90 per cent. Across a year, that difference pays for a lot of machine time.
Less waste means lower material spend and smaller skip bills
Fewer handling steps because parts come off the bed labelled and ready
Faster quoting since the software tells you exactly how many sheets a job needs
What It Did to Small Workshops
The common assumption was that automation would hand everything to the big factories. The opposite happened in a lot of cases.
Entry-level CNC routers now start around the $15,000 mark, with capable production machines in the $40,000 to $80,000 range. That’s a serious outlay, but it’s within reach of a two-person workshop in a way that a factory-scale beam saw never was.
The result is a wave of small outfits doing bespoke built-ins, curved reception desks and one-off retail fitouts; work that used to be either prohibitively expensive or simply declined. A custom radius bookcase is no longer a heroic hand-shaping exercise. It’s a file and a sheet.
The Skills Shifted, They Didn’t Disappear
Plenty of old hands worried the craft would die. It didn’t. It moved.
Knowing which bit to use, what feed rate stops burning, how to hold a thin part down without it chattering loose, where to leave material for hand-finishing; none of that comes from the software. CAD knowledge joined the toolkit rather than replacing it.
Where This Is Heading
Machine learning is starting to creep into toolpath optimisation, and five-axis routers are slowly becoming affordable enough for mid-sized shops. Expect more curved, sculptural furniture at ordinary price points.
What won’t change is the basic trade-off. Good design and good material still decide whether the finished piece is worth owning. The machine just stopped being the bottleneck.

articles.title: Anthropic imagine une carte d'identité pour chaque modèle d'IA
articles.text:
Anthropic a mis en ligne mardi 3 novembre un travail de recherche accompagné de son code en open source : FlashProve, un système conçu pour prouver qu’une réponse provient bien d’un modèle d’IA donné. Le laboratoire parle d’« inférence prouvable » : chaque réponse peut être rattachée cryptographiquement au modèle qui l’a produite, à la manière d’une signature au bas d’une lettre. L’entreprise prévient d’emblée qu’aucun déploiement n’est prévu, chez elle comme ailleurs.
Comment établir la carte d’identité d’un modèle ?
Le dispositif repose sur une empreinte que chaque laboratoire publierait pour chacun de ses modèles, et à laquelle n’importe quelle réponse pourrait ensuite être confrontée. Cette empreinte ne dévoile rien des poids, les réglages internes qui concentrent la valeur d’un modèle et que l’industrie garde sous clé. Les acteurs les plus fermés (OpenAI est cité en exemple) pourraient donc jouer le jeu sans ouvrir leurs coffres. Le parallèle le plus parlant vient de la messagerie : ces signatures numériques qui confirment au destinataire l’identité de l’expéditeur d’un e-mail. La vérification se veut enfin assez légère pour s’exécuter sur un simple appareil local, l’ordinateur d’un particulier compris.
Un fournisseur pourrait aujourd’hui glisser en douce un modèle moins coûteux derrière un abonnement facturé plein tarif, ou gonfler un classement en faisant plancher un modèle plus puissant que celui annoncé. FlashProve rendrait la supercherie détectable. L’été a d’ailleurs fourni un cas d’école, quand des services tiers faisaient passer les réponses de Claude pour celles de DeepSeek ou de Kimi, avant d’être confondus par Anthropic. « Comment un utilisateur peut-il vérifier ces affirmations ? » : la question posée par les chercheurs vise jusqu’aux audits de sécurité que des agents d’IA affirment avoir menés. Au moment de payer la prestation, rien ne distingue aujourd’hui le grand modèle promis d’un remplaçant au rabais.
Pourquoi personne ne compte s’en servir pour l’instant ?
Anthropic qualifie l’ensemble de « progrès intermédiaires, et non un programme de recherche achevé », et n’annonce aucun projet de mise en service, pas même pour ses propres modèles. La spécification technique et le code sont publiés sur GitHub sous licence libre ; le laboratoire dit les partager pour que d’autres équipes bâtissent dessus, concurrents compris.
La piste prolonge un chantier entamé cet été, quand l’entreprise détaillait l’étiquetage des textes générés par Claude et promettait un détecteur accessible à tous. L’étiquetage dit d’un texte qu’une IA l’a écrit ; l’empreinte de modèle monte d’un étage et désigne laquelle. Concrètement, un abonné pourrait un jour lancer la vérification depuis sa machine et confirmer que la réponse facturée au prix du dernier modèle en provient bien.

articles.title: DevSparks 2026 heads to Delhi to explore agentic AI and the future of software development
articles.text:
DevSparks 2026 heads to Delhi to explore agentic AI and the future of software development
YourStory’s flagship developer summit makes its Delhi NCR debut on December 5, bringing together developers, tech leaders, startups, and enterprises for hands-on sessions on AI, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies.
As AI changes how software is developed, tested, and deployed, developers are having to learn new tools and adapt to new ways of working. From autonomous coding agents and multi-agent systems to AI-powered infrastructure and cybersecurity, the technologies shaping software development are evolving rapidly.
Against this backdrop, DevSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship developer summit, will make its Delhi NCR debut on December 5, bringing together developers, startups, enterprises, and Global Capability Centres (GCCs) for a day of technical deep dives, hands-on sessions, and discussions on the future of software development.
Following editions in Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Chennai, the Delhi event will be held at Crowne Plaza, Gurugram. More than 500 developers are expected to attend, with over 15 technology leaders taking the stage and more than 10 deep-dive sessions planned.
Across its four previous editions, DevSparks has brought together more than 27,000 developers, 173 speakers, and 50 partners.
DevSparks 2026 is a nationwide initiative aimed at equipping India's developer community with skills in coding agents, agentic AI, multi-agent orchestrators, AI SDKs, and GenAI tools that can improve productivity. Delhi NCR's strong developer community, startup ecosystem, and growing enterprise and GCC presence make it the natural next stop for the summit.
Delhi NCR's growing technology ecosystem
Delhi NCR is already one of India's leading startup hubs. According to Tracxn’s Delhi NCR Tech Annual Funding Report 2025, tech companies in the region raised $2.9 billion in 2025, with autotech leading the way with $1.4 billion.
Delhi-based tech firms accounted for 51% of all funding raised by tech companies across the region in 2025.
It was also a big year for exits: 19 companies went public, including Lenskart, Physics Wallah, and Pine Labs, while Delhivery bought Ecom Express for $165 million and Everstone Capital acquired Wingify for $200 million.
The Delhi government is taking steps to further strengthen the ecosystem.
The Delhi Start-up and Incubation Policy 2026, approved in July, provides for Rs 400 crore over five years to support incubation infrastructure, mentorship, and incentives for local entrepreneurs.
In October, the Delhi Cabinet also approved the Go-Delhi Foundation, with an initial outlay of Rs 50 crore. The initiative aims to give startups and MSMEs access to product engineering, prototyping and testing facilities.
The government’s draft IT Policy 2026–2031 proposes setting up more than 200 GCCs and training five to six lakh young people by 2031 in areas such as AI, cloud computing, cybersecurity, and data analytics.
It also proposes a Delhi State Data Centre, expected to become operational by 2027, and AI computing credits among other incentives.
These initiatives could create more opportunities for developers working in AI, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity, while strengthening the region’s technology ecosystem.
Agentic AI takes centre stage
Agentic AI is becoming an important area of focus for developers and enterprises, and will be a key part of the DevSparks Delhi agenda.
Sessions will explore how to build autonomous agentic systems and develop multi-agent orchestration for coding, workflows, and business operations.
Developers will also examine real-world applications of multimodal AI, including systems that work with text, code, images, video, and speech in production environments.
Building and scaling AI applications
Beyond agentic AI, the summit will examine what it takes to move AI applications from prototypes to production.
Sessions will cover building applications with AI-first frameworks, integrating AI into sectors such as fintech, healthcare, commerce, manufacturing and agritech, and using Edge AI and the Internet of Things (IoT).
The programme will also look at how AI-driven testing can improve developer productivity.
On the infrastructure side, discussions will cover AI-optimised cloud systems, chips, and accelerators, along with multi-cloud, hybrid, and sovereign cloud models for enterprises.
Other areas of focus include data pipelines, governance, cybersecurity threats, and AI-driven defences.
GCCs, skills, and emerging opportunities
With GCCs an important part of Delhi's technology growth plans, DevSparks will also examine how enterprises and GCCs are preparing their workforces for new technologies.
Sessions will look at trends in upskilling, hiring, and workforce readiness as AI becomes increasingly integrated with other technologies.
The discussions will focus on the skills developers need to remain relevant and the opportunities emerging within India’s leading technology enterprises and GCCs.
A day of learning for developers
DevSparks Delhi will offer developers opportunities to learn through technical deep dives, workshops, masterclasses, and real-world case studies.
The sessions are designed to help participants apply AI to practical problems, explore technological advances beyond AI, and identify new career opportunities.
As AI becomes more widely used in software development and enterprise technology, the summit will focus on the tools, skills, and technical knowledge developers need to build and deploy applications.
DevSparks Delhi 2026 will take place on December 5 at Crowne Plaza, Gurugram. Register now to secure your spot.

articles.title: Le Pixel 11 passe sous les 800 € chez Cdiscount, qui lui ajoute une enceinte JBL Grip
articles.text:
Google ne propose désormais plus de version 128 Go pour son Pixel 11, qui démarre directement à 256 Go de stockage. Lancé en août à 999 €, le smartphone voit déjà son prix baisser à l’occasion du Black Friday. Cdiscount ajoute au pack une enceinte JBL Grip, lancée à 99,99 € en septembre 2025.
Cdiscount affiche le pack Pixel 11 256 Go + enceinte JBL Grip au prix de 799 € au lieu de 899 € normalement. Avec le code 10DES99 à saisir dans le panier, il tombe à 789 €.
Que vaut le Google Pixel 11 ?
Le Pixel 11 dispose d’un écran Actua OLED de 6,3 pouces, avec un taux de rafraîchissement pouvant atteindre 120 Hz. Il embarque la nouvelle puce Tensor G6 de Google, épaulée par 12 Go de mémoire vive, avec 256 Go de stockage minimum. Côté photo, il reprend le triple module de son prédécesseur : un grand-angle de 48 mégapixels, un ultra grand-angle de 13 mégapixels et un téléobjectif de 10,8 mégapixels avec zoom optique x5. Le Super Zoom permet désormais de pousser le grossissement numérique jusqu’à x30. La caméra avant de 10,5 mégapixels profite également d’un autofocus pour des selfies plus nets.
Le Pixel 11 conserve une fiche technique haut de gamme, avec quelques améliorations bienvenues. Son écran OLED bénéficie d’une luminosité maximale de 3 000 nits, pour rester lisible même en plein soleil. Il est protégé par du verre Gorilla Glass Victus 2. La puce Tensor G6 prend en charge les fonctions d’intelligence artificielle de Google, notamment Gemini Live, tandis que les 12 Go de RAM assurent une utilisation fluide au quotidien.
Côté logiciel, le smartphone fonctionne sous Android 17 et profite des fonctionnalités Gemini, dont Gemini Live. Google annonce plus de 30 heures d’autonomie grâce à sa batterie de 4 985 mAh. La recharge rapide permet de récupérer jusqu’à 55 % de batterie en une trentaine de minutes avec un chargeur compatible de 30 W. Google promet sept ans de mises à jour d’Android et de sécurité pour le Pixel 11.
À ce prix, le pack Pixel 11 est-il une bonne affaire ?
Le Pixel 11 ne donnera pas forcément envie de changer à celles et ceux qui ont un Pixel 10, puisque les progrès se limitent surtout à la nouvelle puce et à une recharge sans fil plus rapide (25 watts contre 15 watts). Si vous avez un smartphone plus ancien, le calcul est différent. À 789 €, le pack coûte 210 € de moins que le téléphone seul à son lancement, et vous avez une enceinte en plus. L’offre arrive au moment où les offres du Black Friday en avant-première se multiplient. Rien ne garantit que le prix baissera encore d’ici la fin novembre.
Concernant la BL Grip, l’enceinte ne pèse que 385 grammes et se glisse sans peine dans un sac. Elle embarque un haut-parleur de 16 watts avec la technologie AI Sound Boost et une batterie annoncée pour 12 heures d’écoute, 14 heures avec le mode Playtime Boost. Étanche (IP68), elle gère le Bluetooth 5.4 et Auracast afin de connecter plusieurs enceintes JBL.
Black Friday 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Depuis une dizaine d’années, le Black Friday s’est infiltré dans le calendrier commercial des grandes marques et enseignes françaises. Avec l’expérience, on peut vous dire que cet événement fait partie des meilleurs moments pour faire de bonnes affaires.
Les dates du Black Friday
Bien qu’il porte encore le nom du vendredi noir, le Black Friday s’étend désormais sur un mois chez de nombreux revendeurs. Un format moins typique qui lui retire un peu son petit côté FOMO. On dirait presque les soldes, finalement. Mais c’est aussi moins le rush, ce qui est une bonne chose pour ceux qui veulent faire des achats plus raisonnés. Globalement, on peut résumer ce Black Friday en quatre temps forts :
- Début novembre : les avant-premières Black Friday.
- Autour du 20 novembre, selon les enseignes : la Black Week commence généralement plusieurs jours avant le jour J.
- 27 novembre : la date du Black Friday, même si les offres commencent généralement avant et se prolongent le week-end des 28 et 29 novembre.
- 30 novembre : le Cyber Monday.

Globalement, tous les rayons profitent des remises, mais il ne faut pas pour autant se jeter sur les premiers prix bradés. N’oubliez pas que pour les enseignes, ce moment est aussi l’occasion de déstocker de vieux produits, dont les plus remisés frôlent parfois l’obsolescence.
Qu’il s’agisse d’un téléviseur, d’un smartphone, d’un casque sans fil ou d’un aspirateur balai, on ne peut que vous conseiller de suivre nos guides d’achat dédiés pour savoir quels modèles valent le coup en 2026.
Pour les produits phares comme les AirPods, la PS5, la Switch 2, un iPhone ou un Samsung Galaxy, sachez que nos tests sont là pour vous aider à savoir s’ils méritent votre argent.

articles.title: L'IA d'OpenAI découvre 948 failles dans Linux et développe des stratégies d'exploitation inédites
articles.text:
Une chaîne d'agents IA développée par OpenAI a découvert près de mille vulnérabilités dans le noyau Linux et réussi à les exploiter pour obtenir les privilèges les plus élevés du système. L'entreprise a également préparé des correctifs, dont plusieurs centaines ont déjà été transmis à la communauté Linux pour examen.
Repérer une vulnérabilité dans un logiciel est une chose. Prouver qu'elle permet de prendre le contrôle d'un système en est une autre. Dans une étude publiée le 4 novembre, OpenAI affirme avoir automatisé ces deux opérations, ainsi que la préparation des correctifs, grâce à une série d'agents alimentés par un modèle d'IA spécialisé dans la cybersécurité, dont la sortie est encore à venir. L'expérience, menée à la mi-octobre sur le noyau Linux, a permis de découvrir 948 failles distinctes permettant à un utilisateur disposant de droits limités d'obtenir les privilèges root, soit l'équivalent des droits administrateur sous Linux.
De la découverte de failles à l’élaboration de techniques d’attaque originales
Pour conduire cette expérience, OpenAI a d'abord chargé ses agents de repérer les parties du noyau qu'un utilisateur disposant de droits limités pouvait solliciter, afin de rechercher des failles qu’un attaquant serait capable d'exploiter sans posséder de privilèges élevés. Ce premier tri a permis de concentrer les recherches sur environ 7 % du code du noyau Linux, qu'une deuxième équipe d'agents a ensuite examiné.
Les erreurs suspectées ont été soumises à des tests dans des machines virtuelles isolées, puis les agents ont cherché à les exploiter pour obtenir les droits root. Au terme de la campagne, OpenAI a ainsi comptabilisé 948 vulnérabilités distinctes ayant permis d'accéder aux privilèges les plus élevés du système, sur une distribution Linux courante dont les principales protections de sécurité étaient activées.
A noter toutefois que pour exploiter ces failles, un attaquant doit déjà pouvoir exécuter du code sur la machine, par exemple après avoir compromis un compte utilisateur ou une application. Elles ne permettent donc pas, à elles seules, de pirater un ordinateur Linux à distance, mais peuvent transformer un premier accès limité en contrôle complet du système.
Au cours de leurs recherches, les agents auraient également élaboré au moins dix techniques d'exploitation inédites, que les spécialistes externes consultés par OpenAI ne connaissaient pas non plus. L'entreprise a choisi de ne pas en publier les détails techniques, mais ces découvertes suggèrent que les modèles sont désormais capables de concevoir leurs propres stratégies d'attaque, et plus seulement de répliquer des méthodes déjà documentées.
Linux à la peine face à l’avalanche de signalements générés par IA
Une démonstration impressionnante, qui confirme les progrès de l'IA dans la recherche de vulnérabilités, déjà illustrés récemment par Anthropic sur Linux, Chrome et Safari. Mais la multiplication de ces découvertes soulève aussi la question de leur traitement, alors que les responsables du noyau Linux alertent déjà sur l'afflux de rapports issus de recherches assistées par IA, souvent imprécis ou peu fiables, qui compliquent le travail des équipes de maintenance. En octobre, Google a même suspendu une partie de son programme de récompenses consacré aux logiciels open source, submergé par les signalements automatisés invalides.
OpenAI a bien tenté de répondre à ce problème en accompagnant ses découvertes de preuves d'exploitation et de propositions de correctifs, mais ses premiers essais ont quand même révélé que plusieurs patchs risquaient de dégrader les performances du noyau ou de passer à côté d'autres variantes d'une même vulnérabilité.
Après plusieurs ajustements et un examen par ses chercheurs, OpenAI a finalement transmis plusieurs centaines de rapports et de correctifs aux responsables du noyau Linux, en donnant la priorité aux failles les plus critiques. Pour l'heure, l'entreprise ne précise pas combien de ses correctifs ont été acceptés et intégrés au noyau.

articles.title: Configure, Certify, and Operate Kubernetes GPU Clusters with NVIDIA DSX OS | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
One underperforming GPU can slow an entire distributed training job. The node may pass basic health checks and show normal utilization, leaving operators to discover the problem only after the workload is running.
These issues can appear at any point in a cluster’s lifecycle. A GPU cluster that passes readiness checks at handover changes as nodes are replaced, drivers are patched, and capacity is added. Without repeated validation, the original certification no longer reflects the cluster’s condition.
This visibility gap wastes compute on failing nodes and leaves healthy nodes idle out of caution. Utilization metrics can mask these losses. Goodput, which is the volume of work successfully completed, provides a more useful measure of cluster efficiency. Maintaining cluster readiness requires validation throughout the cluster’s operational lifecycle—after configuration changes, as capacity grows, and before repaired nodes return to service.
The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies for designing, building, and operating efficient, resilient AI factories. Its open source software layer, NVIDIA DSX OS, includes tools for configuring, certifying, and maintaining the health of accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure.
- Configure: NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) establishes a reproducible baseline for GPU-optimized Kubernetes infrastructure.
  - Defines version-locked configuration recipes for components such as networking, storage, and drivers.
  - Renders recipes as bundles for existing deployment tools.
- Certify: NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) validates whether the cluster is ready to run production workloads.
  - Tests GPUs, networking, and storage using AI workloads and diagnostics.
  - Records certification results and helps identify faulty nodes.
- Operate: NVSentinel monitors cluster health and supports fault remediation and revalidation.
  - Publishes node conditions based on GPU, node, and network health.
  - When configured, cordons or taints unhealthy nodes, drains workloads, and remediates faults.
  - Can trigger revalidation with NVCRE before nodes return to service.
All three are open source projects licensed under Apache 2.0 and welcome external contributions.
Before you begin, install and configure AICR, NVCRE, and NVSentinel using their installation guides. The examples assume access to a Kubernetes GPU cluster with the required CLIs, controllers, dependencies, and NVCRE test provider configured.
This walkthrough follows one cluster through its lifecycle: configuration from a recipe, certification before production use, monitoring during operation, and recertification after repair. Each command is a step in that sequence.
Configure: A baseline you can reproduce
AICR defines the cluster’s software baseline in version-controlled files and renders them into artifacts your existing deployment tooling applies. It generates and validates; your deployer applies and reconciles them. Declarative templates help detect configuration drift from manual changes and keep node configurations consistent after repairs.
You describe the target environment. AICR resolves it against a library of validated overlays and emits a recipe:
aicr recipe --service eks --accelerator h100 --os ubuntu \
  --intent inference --platform dynamo -o recipe.yaml
Each component entry in the resulting recipe pins a version and declares which dependencies must be healthy before the component is installed:
apiVersion: aicr.run/v1alpha2
componentRefs:
  - name: dynamo-platform
    chart: dynamo-platform
    namespace: dynamo-system
    source: https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia/ai-dynamo
    type: Helm
    version: 1.4.2
    valuesFile: components/dynamo-platform/values.yaml
    dependencyRefs:
      - grove
      - cert-manager
      - kube-prometheus-stack
      - gpu-operator
      - kai-scheduler
The recipe includes three key properties:
- Pinned versions: The version is fixed, helping you reproduce the software configuration and investigate failures. In contrast, a floating tag can point to a different software version over time, making failures harder to reproduce.
- A dependency graph: dependencyRefs declares what must be installed and healthy first. AICR resolves the graph when it renders the bundle, so the ordering is already encoded in the artifacts your deployer applies. You don’t need to specify that cert-manager comes before NVSentinel, and adding a component later doesn’t require renumbering.
- Health assertions per component: Each entry carries a healthCheckAsserts block that runs after installation and checks whether the component meets its configured health criteria. Kubernetes can report a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff as Running, so a check based only on the pod phase can miss a broken component. The shipped assertions filter on the container waiting reason rather than the pod phase alone.
Rendering the recipe is a separate step that connects AICR to your existing pipeline:
aicr bundle --recipe recipe.yaml --deployer argocd --output ./bundles
--deployer accepts helm, argocd, argocd-helm, flux, or helmfile, so the same validated recipe becomes Argo CD Application manifests, Flux resources, a Helmfile release graph, or plain Helm commands. You can keep your existing deployment tooling and use AICR to generate its configuration artifacts.
Because the recipe is a file, you can use version history, code review, and drift detection to manage the baseline.
# Check a live cluster against the recipe's constraints
aicr validate --recipe recipe.yaml
# Compare a golden baseline against the live cluster, non-zero exit on drift
aicr diff --baseline ./golden.yaml --target cm://default/aicr-snapshot --fail-on-drift
--fail-on-drift turns the drift check into a continuous integration (CI) gate rather than a report.
Certify: Prove the cluster will run the job
The cluster is now built to a known baseline. It still needs workload validation. Standard health checks confirm that basic services are running. They don’t confirm that the cluster can run a demanding multinode job across its interconnect without stalling. NVCRE validates workload readiness by running training jobs and NVIDIA Collective Communication Library (NCCL) tests.
NVSentinel manages validation requests, scheduling gates, quarantine, and repair, while NVCRE runs tests and records results. Table 1 shows how these responsibilities fit into the node validation lifecycle.
| Step | Responsible component | Action | Outcome | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Request and gate | NVSentinel lifecycle manager; operators for upgrades or fabric changes | Create a ValidationRequest for new or repaired nodes. After upgrades or fabric changes, operators cordon the nodes and create the request. | A cordon or taint blocks scheduling on the nodes during validation. | 
| 2. Test and attribute | NVCRE through nvcre-provider | Run workloads and diagnostic tests. Bisect failing groups to identify suspect nodes. | Test results identify suspect nodes. NVCRE doesn’t change the node state. | 
| 3. Record and evaluate | NVCRE and NVSentinel lifecycle manager | NVCRE records pass/fail results, failing node IDs, and failure reasons in the Certification resource. The lifecycle manager evaluates the results. | The validation outcome determines whether the scheduling gate can be removed. | 
| 4. Resolve the gate | NVSentinel lifecycle manager | Remove or retain the scheduling gate based on validation results and any remaining tests. | Pass: remove the configured gate once no other tests hold the node. Failure after retries: keep the node cordoned. | 
A certification identifies the nodes to test, the categories to run, and the thresholds that determine whether the tests pass or fail:
apiVersion: nvcre.nvidia.com/v1alpha1
kind: Certification
metadata:
  name: gpu-cluster-cert
spec:
  target:
    nodeSelector:
      nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true"
  categories:
    - domain: communication
      variant: nccl-all-reduce
    - domain: training
      variant: nemotron5-8b
  options:
    thresholds:
      busBandwidthGBps: "value >= 300"
nvcrectl certification run --cert-file certification.yaml --wait
nvcrectl certification report gpu-cluster-cert -n <namespace>
The report shows each category’s status, runtime, measured bandwidth, and the reason for any failed nodes.
Thresholds make certification a performance gate. None are configured by default. Without the options.thresholds block above, a run reports its measurements and fails when the tests can’t start. A node performing below the target can pass. Thresholds help catch performance degradation rather than breakage.
The catalog covers NCCL communication variants, the NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) level 4 diagnostic suite, and pretraining workloads using NVIDIA NeMo Framework with 8-billion- and 56-billion-parameter models. A WorkloadRun resource turns your own containerized test into a certification check. NVCRE infers the rest from the target nodes, so the manifest stays concise on any supported platform.
These tests can help identify performance issues that aren’t apparent in telemetry. A GPU running just below its performance target might not produce Xid errors, breach monitoring thresholds, or cause node metrics to appear abnormal. That one GPU can slow a synchronous training job to its slowest rank, and operators may find out hours later, or only after a user complains. An NCCL bandwidth test can uncover this performance degradation.
Isolating the cause matters as much. If a 64-node all-reduce yields poor bandwidth, every node is suspect, and bisecting by hand can be time-consuming. NVCRE splits failing groups and reruns the tests until it reaches a minimum group size, then reports the suspect nodes with a reason for each.
Run NVCRE before handing a cluster or new capacity to a tenant and when repaired hardware rejoins the pool.
Operate: Detection and remediation under load
The certified cluster is now running workloads and needs to stay healthy. AICR and NVCRE provide point-in-time validation. NVSentinel runs continuously alongside workloads.
NVSentinel watches signals the cluster already produces: DCGM health checks, Xid errors, network interface card (NIC) states, and cloud provider maintenance events. It doesn’t consume GPU time, leaving GPUs available for workloads.
NVSentinel installs in monitoring mode by default: it reports faults as node conditions and won’t cordon, evict, or remediate nodes. You can roll it out on a live cluster while you evaluate its reports. You can enable quarantine, draining, and remediation once you trust the reported signals.
Detection publishes a health event; a Fault Quarantine ruleset decides what happens to the node. Rulesets use Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions in your values file:
fault-quarantine:
  ruleSets:
    - enabled: true
      version: "1"
      name: "GPU fatal error ruleset"
      priority: 100
      match:
        all:
          - kind: "HealthEvent"
            expression: "event.agent == 'gpu-health-monitor' && event.componentClass == 'GPU' && event.isFatal == true"
          - kind: "Node"
            expression: |
              !('k8saas.nvidia.com/ManagedByNVSentinel' in node.metadata.labels &&
                node.metadata.labels['k8saas.nvidia.com/ManagedByNVSentinel'] == "false")
      cordon:
        shouldCordon: true
      taint:
        key: "nvidia.com/gpu-error"
        value: "fatal"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
A cordon or taint provides a signal that your scheduler, alerting, and lifecycle tooling can use without integrating directly with NVSentinel.
A circuit breaker limits the impact by capping how many GPU nodes can be quarantined in a sliding window. The Fault Quarantine configuration guide covers the bounds and the rest of the ruleset options.
Not every fault takes the same path. A known fatal error goes straight to remediation. The health events analyzer handles other cases by detecting patterns across a node’s failure history, so a node that fails repeatedly becomes eligible for investigation based on the accumulated record rather than any single event.
A health event with the recommended action CONTACT_SUPPORT requires manual investigation or support intervention.
The loop: How readiness becomes continuous
A node fails, gets repaired, and needs to rejoin the pool. Validation before the node returns to service closes the operational loop, but manual handoffs can interrupt the process. Manual certification produces a point-in-time result that routine operations can make outdated. Someone has to notice that the cluster changed, rerun validation, and then read the output and act on it. NVSentinel and NVCRE can help automate this process.
Two lifecycle events trigger revalidation automatically when configured. The NVSentinel lifecycle controller creates a ValidationRequest when a node joins the cluster and again when a node returns after remediation. It gates scheduling on the node using a cordon or taint, then uses NVCRE to run the tests and record the results. The controller evaluates those results and removes the gate after the tests pass, so a node that still fails validation cannot silently rejoin the pool. When you configure nvcre-provider as its test provider, those tests are NCCL or NVIDIA Nemotron runs through NVCRE:
global:
  lifecycleManager:
    enabled: true
fault-quarantine:
  validation:
    enabled: true
lifecycle-manager:
  config:
    schedulingGate:
      cordon:
        remove: true
The lifecycle-manager chart turns on new-node validation; the fault-quarantine flag opts in to post-remediation validation separately. schedulingGate.cordon sets the cordon as the scheduling gate for validation, and remove: true uncordons the node once its tests pass.
The process is different for in-place driver upgrades, operator upgrades, or fabric changes. These changes don’t automatically trigger validation. Because the baseline is a file, aicr diff --fail-on-drift fails a pipeline stage when a live cluster drifts from its recipe, providing a trigger for a certification run in the same pipeline that made the change.
Cordon the affected nodes, then create a validation request naming them and the tests to run:
apiVersion: nvsentinel.nvidia.com/v1alpha1
kind: ValidationRequest
metadata:
  name: post-driver-upgrade
spec:
  nodes:
    - name: node-a
    - name: node-b
  tests:
    - nccl-all-reduce
    - nemotron-5b
The controller also acts on the result. If the request passes, it removes the scheduling gate once no other tests hold the node. If the test fails after its retries, the node remains cordoned.
A fault can also surface during validation: GPUs may start thermally throttling during a training test. NVSentinel quarantines the node, and the controller retries the test after remediation. The node stays gated until validation passes.
The request and the node both carry state you can query:
kubectl get validationrequests
kubectl get nodes -l nvsentinel.nvidia.com/validation-state=validation-failed
Recovery requires no manual node edits: a later request that passes the same tests clears the failure and removes the gate. Deleting all failed validation requests that reference the node can release it without rerunning validation.
The handoff has a clear boundary. NVCRE stops at attribution, recording which nodes failed and why; NVSentinel owns quarantine and repair. Two systems cordoning the same node could produce double-cordons and desynchronized cleanup.
This separation also enables you to use your own node lifecycle tooling. A platform team can consume the same certification results and take over NVSentinel’s role. Extending the stack means writing a ruleset or a policy, rather than forking a project.
What this changes for operators
AICR, NVCRE, and NVSentinel help operators make configuration, validation, and recovery repeatable. With remediation and lifecycle validation enabled, NVSentinel can coordinate repair and testing before nodes return to service, reducing manual handoffs. Table 2 outlines what these tools handle and what operators still manage.
| Operational task | What changes | What operators still manage | 
|---|---|---|
| Maintain the software baseline | AICR provides version-locked recipes and generates configuration artifacts for existing deployment tools. Operators can review deviations from a defined baseline. | Approve baseline changes, deploy the artifacts, run drift checks, and reconcile differences. | 
| Validate new or repaired capacity | NVCRE runs selected workloads and diagnostics and records readiness results. With lifecycle validation configured, NVSentinel can coordinate testing before nodes return to service. | Select tests and thresholds appropriate to the cluster and investigate failed results. | 
| Recover unhealthy nodes | When enabled, NVSentinel coordinates quarantine, draining, remediation, and revalidation, reducing manual handoffs between these actions. | Define quarantine rules, remediation limits, and escalation procedures; handle faults that automated remediation cannot resolve. | 
| Validate infrastructure changes | Operators can incorporate baseline checks and workload validation into their upgrade workflows. | Trigger validation after in-place driver, operator, or fabric changes; these changes do not automatically trigger revalidation. | 
Get started
Start with the project repositories for installation instructions and examples:
You can also:
- Get hands-on with these tools at the NVIDIA DSX OS AI Inference and Contributor Workshop, held alongside KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America. Separate registration is required, and seating is limited.
- Visit NVIDIA booth 170 at KubeCon for more Kubernetes deep dives and live demos.
- Join the DSX AI Factory Slack community to continue the conversation.
- Explore open-source, modular components in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub.

articles.title: AEMET advierte: se esperan lluvias "fuertes y persistentes en zonas de Galicia, norte de Extremadura, sur de Castilla y León"
articles.text:
A principios de los años 20 del siglo XX, Sakuhei Fujiwhara era solo un japonés que había llegado desde Noruega y pasaba las horas muertas en un laboratorio de Inglaterra. No tengo pruebas, pero tampoco dudas: estoy convencido de que se aburría como una ostra.
Así que se puso a mirar un tanque de agua, a hacer remolinos y a ver cómo se movían por él. Así imagino que descubrió que esos vórtices tenían un comportamiento rarísimo. No se ignoraban; al contrario, se perseguían, daban vueltas uno alrededor del otro hasta que uno se come al otro (o hasta que cada cual se va por su lado).
¿Y a qué viene todo esto? A que, cien años después, ahora el tanque de Fujiwhara se llama Océano Atlántico y los dos vórtices se preparan para bailar al ladito de España.
¿Qué va a pasar? Entre el 5 y el 9 de noviembre, una borrasca se organizará al oeste de las Azores, se profundizará rápidamente y, a su alrededor, aparecerán hasta tres centros de baja presión a la vez. Ahí comenzará el baile.
Un baile que, según creemos, terminará el lunes cuando uno de ellos devore al resto.
¿Y qué significa? Lluvia, sí; pero no sabemos dónde. Mientras los centros orbitan, la posición del dominante no la fija el viento general, sino la interacción. Y eso hace las predicciones más complejas de lo normal: un pequeño cambio mueve las borrascas cientos de kilómetros hacia un lado o hacia otro.
El agua está ahí, no me malinterpretéis. La estructura canalizará el aire húmedo subtropical a través de un río atmosférico (una franja estrecha de aire húmedo) hacia nuestra latitud. La cuestión es que ese río puede "desembocar" en Galicia, en la sierra de Grazalema o una docena de sitios distintos.
¿Y qué dice AEMET? Lo mismo. Su portavoz, Rubén del Campo, anticipaba este jueves lluvias «fuertes y persistentes en zonas de Galicia, norte de Extremadura, sur de Castilla y León». ¿Cuánto? En el conjunto, la probabilidad de que Candeleda sume al menos 5 l/m² en un día es del 100 % el lunes, del 98 % martes y miércoles y del 80 % el jueves. El escenario está muy abierto, para desgracia del tercio oriental de la península (que necesitaría ese agua en cuanto pueda).
Sea como sea, parece que la situación está cambiando y parece que el Atlántico está despertando. Y eso es una buena noticia.

articles.title: DigiCert data breach exposes customer information, identity documents
articles.text:
DigiCert warns it suffered a data breach after a server migration mistakenly exposed an internal business system to the internet, allowing unauthorized access to customer information and identity documents.
The certificate authority says the breach affected a small portion of its archived customer data, including names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.
For some people, the exposed records also contained personal identification documents, such as driver's licenses, passports, and utility bills.
DigiCert has begun sending data breach notifications to affected customers, with cloud architect Fabian Bader sharing a copy of the notification on X.
"Thanks @digicert that your data leak was 'limited' to only my full PII data and potentially any verification documents I submitted for my certificate," Bader wrote.
In the notification, DigiCert said it was still reviewing identification documents to determine those who were affected and would notify them once the review was complete.
"The information involved was limited to names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business address shared with DigiCert and, if provided, may have included an identification document such as a driver’s license, passport, utility bill or other document with name and address," the data breach notification reads.
An incident report on Mozilla's Bugzilla platform explains that a February 2025 server migration mistakenly exposed an internal business system to the internet that was previously only accessible via VPN.
The exposed system contained a self-registration feature intended for other applications, allowing external users to create accounts.
Although these accounts weren't assigned to any particular application, an authorization flaw let them access archived customer information in read-only mode.
DigiCert first discovered unauthorized accounts on the exposed system in June 2026, but initially determined they couldn't access customer information because they weren't assigned to an application.
The company subsequently received a report through its managed security research program warning that external users could create accounts on the system.
DigiCert deployed security fixes to restrict access to the system and address the authorization flaw, but did not realize at the time that archived data had been accessed.
It wasn't until October 19 that a further investigation confirmed an unauthorized account had accessed customer information between June 27 and July 2, 2026.
"The incident was initially handled as an account-creation issue rather than a data-access event," DigiCert acknowledged in its report.
DigiCert says the unauthorized account had read-only access and could not modify records, approve certificate validations, or issue certificates.
The company has now restricted access to the affected system, disabled self-registration, and added additional access controls.
DigiCert says its certificate authority services, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE platforms were not compromised, and that customer login credentials and issued certificates remain secure.
BleepingComputer has contacted DigiCert to ask further questions about the incident, including how many people were impacted, and will update the story if we get a response.

articles.title: 503 km/h sur une route ouverte d'ordinaire à la circulation : le nouveau record fou de BYD avec la Yangwang U9 Xtreme — Frandroid
articles.text:
La voiture de série la plus rapide du monde vient d’aller encore plus vite. Dans un communiqué publié ce vendredi 6 novembre, BYD annonce que sa Yangwang U9 Xtreme a atteint 503,17 km/h le 1er novembre, sur une route fermée d’Abou Dabi, avec l’Allemand Marc Basseng au volant.
Elle efface ainsi ses propres 496,22 km/h de septembre 2025, signés sur la piste de Papenburg, en Allemagne. Ce chiffre avait déjà fait tomber la Bugatti Chiron Super Sport 300+ et ses 490,484 km/h, un mois après un premier record à 472,41 km/h.
Selon BYD, cette vitesse lui vaut deux records Guinness, voiture de série la plus rapide et voiture de série électrique la plus rapide, tous deux établis sur un passage dans un seul sens. Le constructeur ajoute que la FIA a reconnu la performance.
En novembre 2017, Koenigsegg avait lui aussi visé le record sur une route publique fermée, la Highway 160 dans le Nevada. Son Agera RS y avait atteint 457,94 km/h dans un sens, mais le record retenu était la moyenne de deux passages en sens opposés, soit 447,19 km/h. Ce double passage gomme l’effet du vent et de la pente ; les 490,484 km/h de la Bugatti, comme les 496,22 km/h de la U9 Xtreme à Papenburg, étaient des pointes mesurées dans un seul sens.
Sept kilomètres de ligne droite, inspectés mètre par mètre
Le décor change par rapport à 2025 : la tentative s’est déroulée sur une route publique, la E11, dans la région d’Al Dhafra. BYD a pu fermer 10 km, avec une ligne droite de 7 km au plus, loin des 15 km que réclamait Stella Li, sa vice-présidente exécutive, en juillet, pour une tentative alors annoncée à Dubaï.
Cette route proche du désert accueille d’ordinaire la circulation : il a fallu la balayer, puis retirer les brins métalliques laissés par les brosses. Le 31 octobre, deux passages plafonnent à 490 km/h. Dans la nuit, les ingénieurs retouchent l’aileron arrière, l’amortissement et la pression des pneus. Le lendemain, le deuxième passage est le bon.
Un crash absent du communiqué
Le communiqué ne dit pas un mot de l’accident survenu pendant la préparation. Des photos et une vidéo relayées le 2 novembre par CarNewsChina montrent une U9 Xtreme quitter sa trajectoire à haute vitesse sur une piste fermée en Chine, percuter une barrière et perdre son essieu arrière. Le site évoquait un essai autour de 500 km/h.
La version donnée depuis par Yangwang est plus modeste : le test visait 420 à 450 km/h, et le premier choc serait survenu vers 360 km/h, selon le récit du pilote d’essai Jiang Wen, diffusé le 3 novembre par Hu Xiaoqing, directrice générale de la division commerciale de Yangwang.
La voiture a touché la glissière de gauche, puis traversé la route jusqu’à celle de droite. Le pilote n’a rien de grave après un examen à l’hôpital. Ces chiffres viennent du constructeur et n’ont pas été vérifiés de façon indépendante. Yangwang n’a pas daté l’accident, mais Jiang Wen raconte avoir attendu une semaine avant d’en parler à sa femme : l’essai a donc eu lieu au moins une semaine avant le 3 novembre.
Yangwang a officialisé Abou Dabi comme lieu de la tentative le 1er novembre, le jour même du record, et publié la vidéo de l’accident le lendemain. Quand ces images ont circulé, le record était donc déjà en poche.
Une voiture de série à 30 exemplaires
Avec ses quatre moteurs et plus de 3 000 ch, la voiture détient aussi le record du Nürburgring pour une électrique de série, en 6 min 59 s 157, même si une Porsche 911 GT3 RS de 525 ch fait mieux sur ce tracé.
Côté technique, BYD a beaucoup changé par rapport à la U9 de base et ses 1 287 ch. Chacun des quatre moteurs tourne jusqu’à 30 000 tr/min et développe 755 ch (555 kW), et l’architecture électrique passe de 800 à 1 200 volts. La batterie reste une Blade à chimie LFP, la même technologie que sur toutes les BYD, mais elle accepte ici des décharges de 30C : en théorie, de quoi la vider en deux minutes. Le rapport poids/puissance atteint 1 217 ch par tonne.
Cette « voiture de série » ne courra pas les rues : vendue environ 2,5 millions d’euros, elle est limitée à 30 exemplaires. D’après BYD, certains clients en sont à la signature du contrat et à la planification de la production.
