articles.title: Valve support wins praise after restoring games a Steam user deleted during depressive episodes
articles.text:
In context: Steam has long let players permanently remove games from their accounts. One user ended up using that option far more than they wanted to as a result of years of depressive and manic episodes. Plenty of the games they deleted were ones they'd played and loved, so they eventually asked Steam Support if any could be brought back. Less than 14 hours later, an agent replied to say the games had been restored. 
 
 
The user, who goes by 3lizardintrenchcoat on Reddit, shared the support ticket on r/Steam in late November 2025. In it, they admitted the request felt "insane and over the top" before asking whether some of the paid games they had deleted over the years could be brought back.
They also offered an easier fallback in case that wasn't possible. All they wanted was a list of every game they'd ever played on the account, free ones included. As they pointed out, Steam's purchase history only shows games that are still active and that were paid for, so it couldn't fill in the gaps on its own.
An agent named Lucy replied early the next morning, confirming a restore to the user's library. If anything still seemed to be missing, she offered to send over the full list of previously owned games, too.
The story got a second life this week after the Waste.gg account posted a screenshot of the exchange on X. That post described it as a restore of the user's "entire game library" and has since crossed 2.2 million views. Strictly speaking, though, the reply only mentions "your game" in the singular, so exactly how many titles came back hasn't been confirmed.
 – Waste.gg (@skinwaste) November 3, 2026
Valve's support team has racked up a few of these moments lately. Back in June, it sent a new dad a free Steam Deck OLED carrying case after his newborn threw up on the original. He had only asked whether he could buy a new one. Gestures like that arguably carry a bit more weight coming from a store that, since 2024, reminds buyers at checkout that a purchase only gets them a license.
Even so, Steam's "permanent" removal tool has never been quite as final as its name suggests. Anyone who remembers a removed game can search for it through Steam Support, choose "It's not in my library," and restore the old license in a couple of clicks. But Steam doesn't provide players with a list of the games they've removed. That's the exact gap this user ran into before support stepped in.

articles.title: CBN sets $11.16m capital rule for foreign stablecoin issuers
articles.text:
New rules from Nigeria’s Central Bank (CBN) will require foreign-currency stablecoin issuers, including companies behind dollar-pegged tokens such as USDT and USDC, to maintain at least ₦15 billion ($11.16 million) in paid-up capital to operate in Africa’s largest cryptocurrency market.
The rules, released Thursday evening, will require foreign stablecoin issuers to establish licenced entities in Nigeria and comply with local capital, reserve, and operational requirements or risk losing market access. The CBN also set a ₦10 billion ($7.44 million) minimum capital requirement for issuers of naira-backed stablecoins.
The regulations come nearly three months after the CBN opened the second cohort of its regulatory sandbox in August, creating a dedicated track for stablecoin issuers and other virtual asset companies to test their products under its supervision for the first time.
The new framework creates a formal licencing system for stablecoins, digital tokens that are intended to maintain a fixed value against fiat currencies such as the US dollar or naira. Businesses and individuals in Nigeria use tokens to move money across borders, settle transactions, and access the dollar.
The new rules come as major issuers push to expand their presence in the country. In August, Tether, the El Salvador-based company behind USDT, sought to hire an Expansion Manager in Nigeria. This week, Circle, the US company that issues USDC, appointed Gillian Darko, a former strategy executive at stablecoin infrastructure company Yellow Card, as its Vice President and Head of Africa.
The move underscores Africa’s growing importance to global stablecoin companies, even as regulators seek greater control over how dollar-backed digital assets are distributed and used within their borders.
Under the CBN’s new regulations, foreign-currency stablecoins can only be offered, distributed, or made available to Nigerians through a locally incorporated and licenced issuer. Foreign regulatory approvals will not exempt the companies, such as Tether and Circle, from meeting Nigeria’s requirements.
Issuers must also maintain reserves backing their tokens, establish arrangements for customers to redeem them, and submit regular reports to the regulator. The CBN will require monthly reserve attestations and may impose additional capital or liquidity requirements on issuers considered a risk to the financial system.
Existing operators will have 180 days from the date the regulations take effect to apply for a licence, although the CBN has yet to specify when that period will begin. Companies must register with the regulator within 30 days and begin submitting supervisory reports within 60 days.
“Failure to submit within that period shall require cessation until the required licence or authorisation is obtained,” the CBN said.
Foreign-currency stablecoin operators will also face scrutiny over their Nigerian incorporation, licencing, and distribution arrangements. Companies seeking to continue operating while their applications are reviewed must obtain explicit regulatory permission.
The new rules also ban algorithmic stablecoins, digital currencies that rely primarily on adjustments to token supply to maintain their value without sufficient reserve backing. Unlike conventional stablecoins backed by fiat currencies or other valuable assets such as gold, their dependence on algorithms makes them more vulnerable to sudden losses in value and harder to regulate.
With this framework, the CBN seeks greater oversight of non-security virtual assets used for payments, including stablecoins, as they play an emerging role in how businesses and merchants move money across borders and source foreign exchange (FX), and how fintechs access dollar liquidity to pre-fund international payments and settlements.

articles.title: Ethereum: cuál es el precio de esta criptomoneda este día
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda digital #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
Ether es un token que se utiliza específicamente en la blockchain ethereum para pagar transacciones. Este token es responsable de impulsar casi todo lo que ocurre en la red, misma que puede ser usada por cualquier persona para crear y ejecutar contratos inteligentes, que son programas de software que se ejecutan de manera autónoma y sin la intervención del usuario.
De acuerdo con el portal de Binance, la moneda digital solana actualmente cuenta con 122.2M de unidades creadas.
La cotización de ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 2387.35 dólares, lo que significa que la criptomoneda tuvo un cambio de 3.17 % en el último día.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0 % con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #2.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum y su última actualización
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: En Japón, un hombre se encuentra con un Toshiba Libretto 50 con Windows 95 que era un ordenador portátil de lujo a su salida en 1997
articles.text:
Cuando un hombre visitó una tienda de electrónica de segunda mano en Akihabara (uno de los barrios tecnológicos más conocidos de Tokio), nunca pensó que se toparía de frente con una joya casi única. Se trataba de un Toshiba Libretto 50 con Windows 95 que estaba a la venta por unos 140 euros, pero lo más curioso es que este pequeño portátil llegó a costar más de 1.700 euros cuando salió al mercado en 1997.
Toshiba presentó el Libretto 50 el 7 de enero de aquel año, y en su momento llamó mucho la atención por sus dimensiones. Medía 21 centímetros de ancho, 11,5 de fondo y 3,4 de grosor, y pesaba unos 850 gramos que lo colocaban muy por debajo de los portátiles convencionales de aquella época que podían pesar varios kilos. Así, hablamos de un sistema Windows completo en un dispositivo que casi cabía en la palma de tu mano.
En su interior había un procesador Intel Pentium de 75 MHz, 16 MB de memoria RAM y un disco duro de 810 MB. También tenía una pantalla en color de 6,1 pulgadas con resolución de 640 × 480 píxeles, además de un pequeño teclado con 80 teclas. Y aunque estas características resultan bastante modestas actualmente, el ordenador podía ejecutar programas como Word 95, Excel 95 o Internet Explorer 3.
Tener un ordenador tan pequeño en 1997 no salía precisamente barato
El Libretto 50 se comercializó en Japón por entre 228.000 y 248.000 yenes, dependiendo de la versión elegida. Al cambio aproximado que recoge la publicación original, hablamos de unos 1.590 a 1.730 euros, una cantidad considerable para un portátil de aquella época. Eso sí, Toshiba tuvo que desarrollar un sistema de refrigeración que aprovechaba la propia placa base para disipar el calor, además de utilizar paneles de magnesio de apenas 0,7 milímetros para conseguir un equipo tan compacto.
La autonomía tampoco era especialmente elevada, ya que su batería ofrecía entre una hora y media y dos horas de funcionamiento, aunque podía llegar a las cuatro horas con una batería de mayor capacidad. Y para utilizar determinados accesorios, como una disquetera externa o conectar otros periféricos, había que recurrir a adaptadores y módulos adicionales.
Pese a su elevado precio, Toshiba decidió llevar el ordenador fuera de Japón unos meses después. En junio de 1997 anunció su comercialización internacional y, en Estados Unidos, el Libretto 50 llegó con un precio anunciado de 1.999 dólares. La compañía también fabricó una versión más rara, llamada Libretto 50M, con pantalla táctil y destinada a la aseguradora japonesa Meiji Life, aunque este último modelo no llegó a venderse al público general.

articles.title: Multipliés par dix en un an, les vols de câbles sur les bornes électriques risquent de faire grimper le prix de vos recharges
articles.text:
Vols de câbles sur les bornes de recharge : 15 % du réseau touché et un risque de hausse des tarifs pour les conducteurs
Les vols de câbles sur les bornes de recharge explosent en France, avec plus de 1 000 stations dégradées fin octobre 2026.Une situation qui contraint les conducteurs de voitures électriques à toujours prévoir une solution de secours sur la route, tout en faisant peser le risque d’une hausse des tarifs.
Arriver devant une borne avec moins de 10 % de batterie et découvrir une station de recharge totalement hors d’usage devient une mésaventure de plus en plus courante pour les conducteurs de voitures électriques. La faute à des câbles volés pour récupérer et revendre le cuivre qu'ils contiennent. Ce phénomène prend une telle ampleur qu’il inquiète aujourd’hui les opérateurs, les automobilistes et jusqu’aux bancs de l’Assemblée nationale. Le pire serait une répercussion de ces dégradations sur le prix du kWh facturé aux usagers.
Quelques kilos de cuivre dérobés pour des millions d’euros de dégâts, une riposte politique bientôt enclenchée ?
Selon l’association Charge France, les vols de câbles ont été multipliés par dix en un an, touchant un millier de sites fin octobre 2026, soit plus de 15 % des bornes de recharge rapide déployées en France. Il faut dire que le cuivre (revendu aux alentours de 13 € le kilo) peut être récupéré sans risque d’électrocution, étant donné que le courant ne circule dans le câble que lorsqu’une voiture est branchée.
Si le butin ne dépasse pas quelques dizaines d’euros par câble, le préjudice global atteint 14 à 21 millions d’euros, totalisant 637 à 800 plaintes déposées en 2026. Comme les assureurs refuseraient de couvrir ces pertes, les opérateurs pourraient répercuter la facture sur leurs grilles tarifaires. D’autant que les exploitants comme Ionity doivent aussi financer de coûteux systèmes de sécurité pour se protéger, allant des caméras et alarmes aux câbles équipés de traceurs GPS ou d’encre indélébile.
Face à ces dégradations qui peuvent “rendre certaines stations indisponibles pendant plusieurs semaines et compromettre les déplacements des automobilistes”, la députée Olga Givernet (Ensemble pour la République) a interpellé le ministère de l’Intérieur le 3 novembre 2026. Dans sa question écrite au gouvernement, elle juge que “la multiplication de ces vols appelle une réponse publique renforcée” et que les pouvoirs publics “doivent également veiller à la fiabilité de l’accès à la recharge”.
L’élue propose ainsi d’examiner si “les installations les plus stratégiques pourraient bénéficier d’une protection renforcée au titre des dispositifs applicables aux infrastructures critiques”, via une directive européenne de 2022. Une piste soutenue par Charge France, qui rappelle qu’au Portugal, ce statut et une condamnation à neuf ans de prison ont éradiqué le problème, alors que des peines de deux ans ferme viennent d’être prononcées à Toulouse et Troyes.
Une réponse ferme des pouvoirs publics devient urgente, la fiabilité du réseau étant indispensable pour rassurer les automobilistes réfléchissant à sauter le pas en abandonnant leur voiture thermique pour l’électrique.

articles.title: Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market
articles.text:
Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States.
The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor.
“When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. “Because they’re paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.”
Agility is one of many startups attempting to commercialize humanoid robots. But the company has stood out from the competition through its lead in deploying and operating Digit humanoid robots with multiple customers, including the warehouses of logistics company GXO, the South Carolina factory of German automotive manufacturer Schaeffler, and the automotive production lines of Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. As Agility’s very first customer, GXO announced it would expand deployments of Digit robots beyond a warehouse in Georgia to additional facilities in North Carolina and Tennessee.
The filings accompanying Agility’s journey toward becoming a publicly traded company—based on a merger with a special purpose acquisition company—also provide a rare look at the business prospects and potential unit economics of humanoid robots. Most of its startup competitors remain privately held companies that have not been nearly as forthcoming.
Another exception has been China’s humanoid robotics company Unitree, which opened its books when it went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange STAR Market in August 2026.
Robot rental or ownership
Agility described the “illustrative unit economics” for both its “robots-as-a-service” subscription business and an “ownership model,” which would involve corporate clients purchasing robots outright, in an S-4 registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on September 4.
With the subscription model, customers would pay a one-time cost of about $25,000 per robot for delivery and deployment to a work site, along with a recurring monthly fee of $8,500 for software and maintenance.
Customers can also purchase the robot’s hardware outright for a one-time payment of $200,000, along with another one-time cost of $20,000 for delivery and deployment. But that still comes with an annual subscription fee of $36,000 for software and maintenance, or about $3,000 per month.
In exchange for renting or purchasing the robots, customers would get access to the latest Agility robot, known as Digit 5, starting in 2027. The bipedal robot has swappable end-effector “hands,” can lift up to 50-pound loads, and can perform more than 20 hours of work in a 24-hour period with the help of a fast-charging battery system.
The fast-charging battery technology provided by the UK-based company Nyobolt requires just nine minutes to deliver 90 minutes of robot runtime. “We worked with them for well over a year to design the pack that goes in our robot,” Hurst told Ars. “So the battery pack is fully custom and is ours, and we have the exclusive agreement with Nyobolt around using their [battery] chemistry in humanoid robots.”
The Digit 5 also comes with an onboard safety system that enables it to detect humans moving nearby and take appropriate actions, like standing still or squatting to minimize the risk of harm. That could unlock more opportunities to deploy Digit 5 beyond the confines of isolated work cells within warehouses and factories, said Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at Agility, in a previous conversation with Ars.
During a presentation for analysts and investors on October 6, Agility’s chief financial officer, Michael Beer, described the Digit subscription model as allowing customers to replace $200,000 in annual labor costs with $100,000 in annual robot costs, while buying a Digit robot outright could replace $1.1 million in labor costs with about $400,000 in robot costs over five years.
Agility’s business costs and revenue
Meanwhile, Agility described its own annual operating costs per robot as being $15,000 to provide the necessary software and maintenance, along with a one-time cost of $15,000 for Agility to initially deploy each robot.
The robotics company also estimated each Digit v5 humanoid robot as initially costing Agility $150,000 based on the bill of materials. Each robot is estimated to have a useful operational lifespan of about five years.
But Agility anticipates that bill of materials cost falling to $75,000 per robot once it ramps up to annual production of 1,000 robots, and eventually $30,000 per robot if the company can produce 10,000 robots per year. The company plans to gradually ramp up production at its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Oregon.
When balancing such business costs versus revenue, Agility anticipates that it could earn about $500,000 per robot on an annual basis through the subscription model, and about $400,000 per robot each year if a customer purchases the Digit robots outright while paying ongoing software and maintenance fees.
The subscription revenue calculations disclosed in Agility’s S-4 filing were based on an unidentified customer’s $300 million order covering 1,000 Digit 5 robots over a three-year subscription contract.
However, such a customer order does not mean Agility is guaranteed to earn $300 million, because the contract requires the robotics company to deliver on certain “contractual milestones, product features and specifications.”
The robotics company’s financial disclosures also bluntly state that “Agility has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future.” In 2025, the company earned just $1.8 million in revenue against $140 million in operating loss, which shows it’s still in the early stages of building a sustainable business.
Future risks and prospects
Agility said it continues to devote “substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot,” while continuing to expand the RoboFab manufacturing facility. On October 21, Agility also announced plans to build a new facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, for supporting Digit robot deployments and further developing the robot’s software and AI.
Beyond the challenges of building its own business, Agility’s financial disclosures also cautioned that “competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying rapidly, with well-funded entrants including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon, and NEURA Robotics, among others, actively developing competing humanoid systems.”
Many of those companies have advantages, such as “significantly greater brand recognition, customer relationships, and financial, technical, manufacturing, and other resources,” Agility’s S-4 filing acknowledged. It also listed business risks involving uncertain AI-driven robotic performance in the real world, safety issues in sharing workspaces with human workers, changing regulations, and cybersecurity threats.
Still, Agility co-founder Hurst described a large potential market with “millions of unfilled roles” involving manual tasks that would typically require higher-cost but relatively low-skilled human labor. Within the next year, Hurst expects multiple Agility customers to be sharing videos of the Digit robots “just very boringly doing their work” to the point where “all of the excitement and hype and novelty of humanoids has worn off.”
“It’ll look a bit like the dawn of the automotive market, and different companies will have different niches—some companies will build the Ford F-150 and some companies will build a Mazda Miata,” Hurst told Ars. “There’s going to be a bunch of different niches for multi-purpose human-centric machines like these.”
Although Hurst sees Agility’s path eventually leading to a general-purpose autonomous robot in the future, he has consistently dismissed the idea of any company immediately deploying humanoid robots to riskier and less structured environments, like people’s homes. “Digit 5 is not going to walk into your living room and do dishes and stuff like that,” he said. “Nobody is.”
Whatever happens with Agility’s journey in the coming years, it will be instructive for anyone interested in the broader trajectory of the humanoid robot industry.
Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English.

articles.title: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal — combined company to supply scale-up and scale-in optics for AI data centers
articles.text:
Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal — combined company to supply scale-up and scale-in optics for AI data centers
The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2028.
Marvell Technology Inc. has signed a definitive merger agreement to acquire Lumentum for an enterprise value of $115 billion, combining two of the biggest players in the data center optics market into one company. According to a joint press release on November 2nd, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own, which the companies put at about $1,132 per share. This figure represents a 23.9% premium over the company's unaffected closing price on October 28, the last trading day before reports of the deal affected prices.
The agreement — which leaves Marvell's current shareholders with about 67% of the combined company and Lumentum's with about 33% — is reportedly the second-largest tech transaction deal ever after the SpaceX-xAI merger, according to Bloomberg. Both boards have approved the deal unanimously, and it is expected to close in the first half of 2028, pending regulatory and shareholder approval.
The acquisition represents another significant expansion of Marvell's optical infrastructure portfolio, following its $10 billion acquisition of Inphi in 2021 and its $3.5 billion upfront purchase of optical interconnect startup Celestial AI, completed in February 2026. All three mergers and acquisitions involved companies handling different parts of one of the most critical AI infrastructures: optical connectivity.
As AI infrastructure continues to scale, optical connectivity is becoming increasingly important for moving vast amounts of data between processors, racks, data centers, and even on the accelerator board itself. With the acquisition of Lumentum, Marvell, which already supplies optical DSPs, silicon photonics, and high-speed SerDes, is positioning itself as one of the industry's major suppliers of optical interconnect technologies, spanning scale-across and scale-out networking to emerging scale-up and scale-in connections.
Why AI infrastructure is moving towards optical connectivity
Modern AI data centers house thousands of interconnected accelerators exchanging enormous volumes of data. As data volume, speed, and travel distance scale, copper interconnects, the conventional medium for inter-rack connections, hit physical limits, becoming impractical at around one to two meters. The industry's solution has been a transition to optics, moving data as light instead of electrical signals.
First, optical transceivers and fiber optics replaced copper for inter-rack connections and beyond. Pluggable transceivers containing a laser chip, digital signal processor (DSP) chips, and several optical components convert the accelerator's electrical signals into light for transmission over fiber, then convert them back into electrical signals at the receiving end.
The industry is also looking to bring optics into the accelerator package itself with co-packaged optics and near-packaged optics. In conventional packages, signals from the logic chip have to travel inches along copper traces across the board to reach the transceiver. Co-packaged optics takes the optical engine out of the pluggable module and places it as a photonic integrated circuit (PIC) chip directly on the switch or accelerator package, shrinking the electrical path.
These shifts to optics have made optical interconnects one of the most critical AI infrastructure markets, driving several multi-billion-dollar deals and major partnerships among industry players across the different technologies and processes involved.
From silicon to lasers: What Marvell and Lumentum bring to the table
The optical interconnects market encompasses several critical technologies. On the electronics side, semiconductor chips such as high-speed serializer / deserializers (SerDes) and optical DSPs prepare and process electrical data signals. Electronics also include analog components such as drivers and transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs) that interface with the optical hardware. Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) use microscopic optical components such as waveguides, modulators, and photodetectors to manipulate light, encode information onto it, and convert received light back into electrical signals, combining all of this into a single chip.
Whether an optical engine sits inside a pluggable transceiver or directly on the board, it still needs a laser, either integrated into the assembly or supplied externally, which brings us to another specialized branch of semiconductor manufacturing: laser technology. Lastly, fiber optic cables and associated passive optical components transmit and distribute light while optical circuit switches redirect optical connections through a network.
Marvell already covers most of the electrical and electronics side, with a portfolio that includes custom AI accelerators, Ethernet switches, high-speed SerDes interfaces, DSPs, optical drivers, TIAs, and silicon photonics. Lumentum, on the other hand, supplies many optical components, including high-performance lasers, modulators, photodetectors, optical transceivers, and optical circuit switches. Combining these portfolios and processes allows Marvell to develop more complete solutions, designing and optimizing electrical and optical components as part of the same system.
Perhaps the most strategically important part of Lumentum's business is its expertise in compound semiconductors, particularly indium phosphide (InP), which is critical for laser and other optical chips. Unlike conventional silicon, which has an indirect bandgap and is inefficient at generating light, InP-based semiconductor structures can efficiently emit and detect light, making the material well suited for manufacturing high-performance lasers and other optical components used in high-speed communication systems.
Lumentum is also bringing its manufacturing experience to the merger. Unlike Marvell's predominantly fabless semiconductor business, Lumentum directly controls its front-end semiconductor fabrication processes, owning and operating specialized InP fabrication facilities, which its CEO Michael Hurlston described as the world's largest InP manufacturing footprint during the acquisition announcement. If the deal closes in 2028, Marvell will transition into a hybrid model, inheriting Lumentum's internal factories while keeping its chip side outsourced. The combined company would also gain access to gallium arsenide (GaAs) technologies.
A $115 billion bet and a long road to 2028
Over the years, Marvell — already one of the biggest custom ASIC suppliers, with clients such as Google, AWS, Meta, and Microsoft — has also strategically positioned itself as a major player in the optical interconnects market, supplying the largest optical transceiver manufacturers. In March 2026, Nvidia invested $2 billion directly in Marvell in a partnership that brings Marvell’s custom XPUs and scale-up networking into Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion ecosystem.
Marvell's biggest optics competitor, Broadcom, also supplies custom AI accelerators, networking silicon, and optical connectivity components, offering both the electronic chips and the optical components. Acquiring Lumentum would give Marvell a more comprehensive portfolio similar to Broadcom's. Nvidia’s separate $2 billion stake in Lumentum would also convert into Marvell shares, consolidating its two $2 billion bets into a single holding.
A key question is how vertical integration affects existing customers, as Marvell supplies optical module manufacturers, while Lumentum sells optical components to companies that also compete with its transceiver business. Merging operations could create concerns among customers that depend on the companies for critical components. Marvell CEO Matt Murphy addressed this issue during the company's November 2 investor conference call, stating that the company intends to maintain its existing component supply model. Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston also emphasized that supplying competitors is already an established part of the optical industry's business model.
Financially, Marvell expects the combined company’s total addressable market to reach about $550 billion by 2030 — roughly $60 billion more than the two companies’ standalone estimates combined. The companies also expect more than $1 billion in annual run-rate cost synergies, primarily from cost of goods sold. Combining Marvell’s current-quarter guidance with Lumentum’s latest results, the companies put the merged business at about $17.7 billion in annualized revenue.
According to Murphy, pairing Lumentum’s next-quarter guidance with analyst consensus for Marvell’s next quarter lifts that figure to more than $21 billion. Lumentum's recent performance shows the growing demand behind these projections. The company reported $1.26 billion in revenue for its first fiscal quarter of 2027, a 136.5% year-over-year increase. It also announced a second major near-packaged and co-packaged optics design win, which Hurlston said he expects to generate more than $5 billion in revenue.
However, the merger's huge valuation raises questions about whether future growth will justify the acquisition price. Investors reacted negatively to the announcement, with Marvell shares closing down 12.7% at $171.41 on November 2 and Lumentum falling 18.6% to $684.40. For now, the agreement is subject to a lengthy review, with an outside date of November 1, 2027, and options to extend to February 1, May 1, and finally August 1, 2028, if regulatory approvals are still pending. If the deal then fails on regulatory grounds alone, Marvell owes Lumentum $3.2 billion. However, if either board backed out or took a rival offer, Marvell would pay $5.8 billion, and Lumentum $2.9 billion.
Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: Cómo instalar la APK de XUPER TV en Android: una búsqueda que expone contraseñas y cuentas bancarias
articles.text:
La búsqueda de cómo instalar la APK de XUPER TV en un celular Android suele partir de una intención concreta: acceder desde el teléfono a películas, series, canales y transmisiones deportivas sin contratar una suscripción.
El problema es que esta plataforma no está disponible en las tiendas oficiales y obliga a descargar un archivo desde páginas externas. Detrás de la instalación de apps streaming no oficiales pueden ocultarse riesgos para contraseñas, archivos personales y cuentas bancarias.
ESET advierte que este tipo de plataformas puede abrir la puerta a programas que espían la actividad del dispositivo, roban información o incorporan nuevas aplicaciones sin que el usuario comprenda sus consecuencias.
Por qué una APK descargada fuera de la tienda oficial es peligrosa
Las tiendas oficiales de aplicaciones aplican controles técnicos y revisiones sobre el software que publican. Esos mecanismos no garantizan una seguridad absoluta, pero reducen la circulación de archivos modificados, engañosos o diseñados para extraer datos.
La búsqueda de XUPER TV puede conducir a portales que ofrecen varias versiones del mismo archivo, enlaces de descarga poco claros o supuestas actualizaciones. En ese recorrido, resulta difícil comprobar quién creó la aplicación, si fue alterada o si conserva el funcionamiento anunciado.
Qué señales alertan de riesgos al aceptar permisos de una APK
Una aplicación streaming necesita ciertos accesos para reproducir contenido y conservar ajustes básicos. La situación cambia cuando solicita facultades que exceden esa función, como conocer qué otras aplicaciones están abiertas, revisar el contenido almacenado en el dispositivo o modificar archivos del teléfono.
ESET identificó este tipo de pedidos en el análisis de Magis TV, ahora llamada XUPER TV, una plataforma que se promocionaba para ver series, películas y deportes sin pago mensual.
La firma la tomó como ejemplo de aplicaciones potencialmente indeseables. Los permisos excesivos no prueban por sí solos una conducta maliciosa, pero requieren cautela cuando no guardan relación con la función principal de la app.
De qué forma pueden quedar expuestas las contraseñas y las cuentas bancarias
El riesgo no se limita al archivo que el usuario descarga. Una aplicación con accesos invasivos puede actuar como puerta de entrada para programas de espionaje o troyanos bancarios.
Estas herramientas buscan datos de inicio de sesión, códigos de verificación, mensajes, historial de uso y otra información que puede facilitar el acceso a servicios financieros.
Asimismo, pueden aparecer notificaciones que imitan avisos legítimos de bancos, plataformas de pago o empresas de mensajería. El objetivo es dirigir a la víctima hacia una página falsa para que ingrese credenciales.
Qué información del teléfono podría quedar al alcance de ciberdelincuentes
Los accesos a la memoria del dispositivo pueden exponer fotos, videos, documentos y archivos de audio. En muchos teléfonos, ese espacio reúne comprobantes de transferencias, capturas de conversaciones, copias de documentos de identidad, notas personales o grabaciones.
Entre otros peligros, una aplicación que puede alterar el almacenamiento tiene la capacidad de modificar, borrar o incorporar archivos. Ese escenario puede afectar el funcionamiento del dispositivo y dificultar la detección de contenido dañino.
Los expertos señalaron que los permisos para leer y escribir datos fuera de la aplicación pueden ser aprovechados para robar información personal o introducir archivos maliciosos.
Por qué hay consecuencias legales por usar plataformas piratas
La descarga de aplicaciones que retransmiten contenido sin autorización puede implicar problemas vinculados con la propiedad intelectual. Las películas, series, señales de televisión y competencias deportivas cuentan con titulares de derechos que definen dónde y bajo qué condiciones se distribuyen sus contenidos.
Los expertos advierten que las emisiones sin licencia pueden derivar en bloqueos por parte de proveedores de internet o en acciones judiciales, según la legislación de cada país. Antes de instalar una APK, hay que revisar si la plataforma identifica a su responsable, informa condiciones de uso y ofrece canales de soporte.
La falta de datos sobre quién opera el servicio es otra señal para evitar instalarlo en un teléfono que concentra información personal y financiera.

articles.title: OpenAI president Greg Brockman says company could be IPO ready in 2027 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads.
In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so. Yes.”
“We’ve been very clear this year that we want to go public when we feel is the right time for us, and I feel extremely good about the business. I feel like we’ve made so much progress this year, and I’ve honestly never felt more confident in what we’re doing,” Brockman said.
He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share.
“We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.”
By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He explained that the growth wasn’t simply the result of something that happened in the quarter itself, but rather the culmination of investments the company had been making up to that point.
Now the majority of OpenAI’s revenue is coming from the enterprise business, which previously accounted for only around 30% of its total revenue.
“And it’s not that consumer [revenue has shrunk] … It’s been growing, but it’s the enterprise segment has really taken off,” he said, pointing to a recent partnership with JPMorgan Chase as one example of the type of client it’s now winning deals with.
Brockman also spoke more broadly about the lessons OpenAI learned from selling into the enterprise market as well. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul.
“A year ago, we weren’t even really in the enterprise game, right? We were really perceived as a consumer company, and a lot of the companies we’d start talking to would say, ‘Is OpenAI really committed to the enterprise?’” Brockman said. “But it’s so different today.”

articles.title: Cyberattack Hits French Blood Bank Site but No Blood Products Are Compromised
articles.text:
A cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.
The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).
The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday. Monitoring systems quickly detected the problem, allowing staff to take action in time so that “no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said that the attack had attempted to reset temperatures that normally are at minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit) to as high as 110 C (230 F).
The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the EFS statement said.
“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” the blood bank said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld, said in a statement it “is aware” of the cybersecurity incident.
“The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld’s direct control,” the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking “appropriate measures.”
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.
This week’s cyberattacks on refrigeration systems mirrored an episode in mid-October that targeted fridges and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.
One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as 250 million euros ($281 million), and crimp its operating income for the period by up to 100 million euros.
“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” CEO Franz Muller said. “As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today,” he said in a statement released with Delhaize’s quarterly earnings.
The company had earlier blamed “malicious actions by others” and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States.

articles.title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
articles.text:
A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
The midterms are over, and the next big fight could be over permitting reform.
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.
With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.
The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.
The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.
So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)
One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.
The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.
Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.
Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.
Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.
A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.
Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.
But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.
“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.
To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.
This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.
In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

articles.title: Vom Spinoff der TU München in den Halbleiter-Sektor: Dieses Startup prüft Chips per Diamantmikroskop
articles.text:
Mit Diamanten in den Chip schauen: Wie ein Münchener Startup Fehler in KI-Chips aufspürt
Lange spielte Deutschland bei der Entwicklung modernster Chips nur eine Nebenrolle. Doch KI-Boom, geopolitische Spannungen und die Abhängigkeit von Asien und den USA verändern die Lage. Es fließen Milliarden für neue Chipfabriken und Millionen für junge Technologieunternehmen. Deutschland investiert wieder kräftig in die Halbleiterindustrie.
Doch während Fabrikprojekte scheiterten, entstehen an Universitäten und Forschungsinstituten neue Unternehmen mit spezialisierten Technologien. Diese entwickeln Speicher, Materialien, Chipverbindungen und Maschinen für die Halbleiterproduktion. Bund und Länder unterstützen die ambitionierten Startups mit hohen Förderbeträgen. Hinzu kommen Millionen von Venture-Capital-Investoren. In diesem Sektor positioniert sich auch das Halbleiter-Startup Quantum Diamonds aus München. Die Firma will mit einer neuartigen Messtechnologie die Qualitätskontrolle in der Halbleiterindustrie verbessern.
Wie Quantum Diamonds Fehler in Chips sichtbar macht
Gerade leistungsfähige KI-Chips bestehen aus zahlreichen übereinanderliegenden Schichten. Fehler im Inneren lassen sich mit herkömmlichen Verfahren nur schwer erkennen. Das kostet Zeit und Geld und verringert die Ausbeute in der Produktion.
Das 2022 von Kevin Berghoff und Fleming Bruckmaier als Spinoff der Technischen Universität München gegründete Startup entwickelt sogenannte Quanten-Diamantmikroskope, die winzige Magnetfelder messen. Dafür nutzt es atomare Fehlstellen in synthetischen Diamanten. Vereinfacht gesagt: Die Sensoren machen elektrische Ströme innerhalb eines Chips sichtbar und lokalisieren Defekte, ohne den Halbleiter zu zerstören.
Erste Praxistests hat die Technologie bereits bestanden. Nach Unternehmensangaben wurde das Verfahren mit neun der zehn größten Halbleiterhersteller erprobt, darunter TSMC und Samsung. Seit April 2026 sind erste Systeme bei Eurofins EAG Laboratories in Kalifornien und Integrated Service Technology (iST) in Taiwan installiert. Damit ist die Technologie nicht mehr nur ein Forschungsprojekt, sondern wird bereits in der Industrie eingesetzt.
Die größte Herausforderung steht allerdings noch bevor: Bisher konzentriert sich die Technologie auf einzelne Chips. Künftig sollen ganze Wafer mit Hunderten oder Tausenden Chips schnell und zuverlässig geprüft werden. Das große Ziel allerdings ist laut Quantum-Diamonds-Gründer Berghoff aber „eine vollständige Qualitätskontrolle direkt in der Chipfabrik”.
152 Millionen Euro Investition: Quantum Diamonds bleibt in München
Für den Sprung in die industrielle Fertigung investiert Quantum Diamonds 152 Millionen Euro in einen Produktionsstandort in der bayerischen Hauptstadt. Der erste Abschnitt wurde im Juli 2026 eröffnet. Möglich macht das unter anderem eine Finanzierung über 91 Millionen Euro: 15 Millionen Euro stammen von Investoren wie dem Berliner Investor World Fund, weitere 76 Millionen steuern Bund und Bayern im Rahmen des European Chips Act bei.
Hinter der Förderung steckt auch eine industriepolitische Entscheidung. Quantum Diamonds hatte zwischenzeitlich einen Umzug in die USA erwogen. Der Bundesstaat Arizona lockte mit einem attraktiven Förderangebot. Dort bauen auch TSMC und Intel ihre Produktionskapazitäten aus. Mit einer Förderquote von rund 50 Prozent gelang es Bund und Bayern, das Startup in Deutschland zu halten.
Während große Fabrikprojekte von Intel in Magdeburg und Wolfspeed im Saarland scheiterten, könnten spezialisierte Zulieferer wie Quantum Diamonds für die deutsche Halbleiterindustrie an Bedeutung gewinnen. Das Münchner Startup entwickelt keine eigenen Chips, sondern Prüftechnik für deren Herstellung. Denn auch ohne eigene Chipfabriken kann Europa eine wichtige Rolle in der globalen Halbleiterindustrie spielen: mit Maschinen, Materialien und Produktionsverfahren, auf die große Chipproduzenten angewiesen sind. Voraussetzung ist allerdings, dass die neuen Technologien zuverlässig funktionieren und sich in die industrielle Fertigung integrieren lassen.
Die Erwartungen der Investoren sind hoch. „Quantum Diamonds hat das Potenzial, Europas nächstes ASML zu werden“, sagt Daria Saharova, Managing Partner beim World Fund. Der Vergleich ist ambitioniert: Der niederländische Konzern gehört zu den wichtigsten Ausrüstern der weltweiten Chipindustrie und liefert hochkomplexe Maschinen für die Chipproduktion. Davon ist Quantum Diamonds noch weit entfernt. Die Hoffnung des Investors: Das Münchner Startup könnte mit seiner Prüftechnik langfristig eine ähnlich wichtige Rolle in einem spezialisierten Bereich der Halbleiterindustrie spielen.
Wo deutsche Startups für die Chipindustrie ansetzen
Auch andere deutsche Startups arbeiten an Technologien für die Halbleiterindustrie. Das Aachener Startup Black Semiconductor entwickelt optische Verbindungen zwischen Chips, die Daten schneller und energieeffizienter übertragen sollen. Bund und Nordrhein-Westfalen unterstützen das Unternehmen mit 228,7 Millionen Euro, weitere 25,7 Millionen Euro kommen von Investoren.
Das Dresdner Startup FMC (The Ferroelectric Memory Company) arbeitet an Speichertechnologien, die unter anderem den Energieverbrauch von KI-Rechenzentren senken sollen. Dafür sammelte das Unternehmen 77 Millionen Euro von Investoren und 23 Millionen Euro an öffentlichen Fördermitteln ein. NextGO Epi aus Berlin wiederum produziert spezielle Galliumoxid-Wafer für energieeffizientere Leistungshalbleiter, etwa für Elektromobilität und Energietechnik.
Die jungen Unternehmen setzen damit an unterschiedlichen Stellen der Halbleiterindustrie an: bei Materialien, Speichern, Chipverbindungen und Prüftechnik. Sie konkurrieren nicht direkt mit den großen Chipproduzenten, sondern entwickeln Technologien, die deren Fertigung verbessern sollen.
Die Startups müssen einen messbaren Vorteil für den Chip-Sektor liefern
Doch Fördermillionen und technologische Durchbrüche garantieren noch keinen Erfolg. Die Startups müssen ihre Entwicklungen in die industrielle Produktion bringen, internationale Kunden gewinnen und sich gegen etablierte Wettbewerber behaupten. Gerade in der Halbleiterindustrie ist dieser Schritt teuer und langwierig.
Denn die großen Chipproduzenten setzen neue Technologien nicht einfach in ihren Fabriken ein. Maschinen und Materialien müssen umfangreiche Tests bestehen, zuverlässig funktionieren und sich in bestehende Produktionsabläufe integrieren lassen. Vor allem müssen sie einen messbaren Vorteil bringen: weniger Ausschuss, niedrigere Kosten oder eine höhere Leistung. Für junge Unternehmen bedeutet das hohe Investitionen, lange Entwicklungszeiten und eine enge Zusammenarbeit mit den Halbleiterherstellern.
Deutschland verfügt über starke Forschungseinrichtungen und wichtige Industrieunternehmen. Entscheidend ist nun, ob Unternehmen wie Quantum Diamonds, Black Semiconductor und FMC den Sprung von ersten Praxistests und Pilotprojekten in die industrielle Serienproduktion schaffen. Erst dann zeigt sich, ob aus den geförderten Technologien erfolgreiche Industrieunternehmen werden.
