articles.title: 2026 iPad mini review: Maximizing the mini
articles.text:
The iPad mini has long felt like a niche product. It has earned a reputation as a quality tablet for people who want something small, comfortable, and portable, but its small screen and comparatively limited processing power have restricted its appeal, making it best suited to watching media or playing games.
With the 2026 version, the iPad mini is more competitive than ever. Its chip is current, its speakers are better, and, most impressively, it trades its 8.3-inch IPS screen for an 8.5-inch OLED that can hold its own against other premium tablets. There isn’t much more you can ask of an iPad this small.
But at just $50 less than the larger, more powerful iPad Air (11-inch), the iPad mini still has a hard time making a case for itself.
Larger OLED screen
The most immediately noticeable change to the 2026 iPad mini is its display. At 0.2 inches larger than the 2024 iPad mini’s screen, the difference might not sound like much, but it has a meaningful impact on a tablet this small. Beyond providing a bigger view of photos, video content, and lengthy documents, the extra space makes it easier to work with multiple windows, giving you more room to view them and adjust their size and location.
I tested the mini in the “midnight” colorway. It’s also available in a lighter “starlight” hue.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
I tested the mini in the “midnight” colorway. It’s also available in a lighter “starlight” hue.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
One of our biggest complaints about the prior mini was its bezels, which felt large for a tablet of its size. This time, Apple managed to fit a larger screen in a slightly smaller tablet (7.69 × 5.22 × 0.21 inches and 0.56 pounds for the 2026 mini versus 7.69 × 5.3 × 0.25 inches and 0.65 pounds for the 2024 mini) by reducing the bezels by 24 percent. The result is a streamlined viewing experience that feels more modern and appropriate for a new Apple product.
And you’ll certainly want to watch content on the 2316 × 1512 OLED display, which packs 326 pixels per inch. OLED displays often lack the brightness of their LCD-LED counterparts, but the gap has narrowed in recent years. The new mini is brighter than its IPS-based predecessor, with Apple claiming full-screen brightness of up to 600 nits, compared to 500 nits on the previous model. It’s also much better suited to HDR content, with peak HDR brightness reaching 1,200 nits for highlights and a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1.
Since content consumption is arguably the mini’s strongest use case, it makes sense for Apple to focus on changes that enhance the viewing experience. Watching shows and movies feels as luxurious as possible on a screen this size, and the mini maximizes its display in nearly all the ways that matter.
I say “nearly” because the mini still has a 60 Hz refresh rate; 120Hz is limited to the iPad Pro. A 120 Hz refresh rate makes little difference when watching most shows or movies, but it can make some tasks, such as scrolling through long documents, look smoother. Still, the difference is less noticeable on a smaller screen.
Overall, the refresh rate didn’t feel like a drawback during regular use. Apple has gone a step further, noting that OLEDs typically have faster response times than IPS displays. That’s generally true when discussing gray-to-gray (GtG) response times. However, moving picture response time (MPRT) can be a better indicator of potential persistence-related motion blur, including during scrolling, because it measures how long an image remains visible on the display, contributing to blur as your eyes track moving content. GtG, by contrast, measures how quickly individual pixels transition between shades. Slower pixel transitions can create motion artifacts such as ghosting.
According to Blur Busters’ MPRT Indicator, the mini has an MPRT of about 17 ms, about what I’d expect from a 60 Hz IPS display. Anyone who needs a high-refresh screen will still want to look at the Pro series.
One feature the mini borrows from the iPad Pro but that other iPads lack is the option for nano-texture glass, which is designed to reduce glare. It costs an extra $100 and is only available on the 256GB and 512GB versions of the mini.
A current-gen processor
The 2024 mini debuted with a year-old chip, but this year’s model sports Apple’s latest mobile processor. The 2026 mini makes a considerable jump from the A17 Pro, a 3-nanometer, iPhone 15 Pro-era chip from 2023, to the A20 Pro, a 2-nanometer chip that debuted in the new iPhone 18 Pro.
The newer chip has 50 percent more memory bandwidth, which significantly boosts graphics performance. It’s also up to 60 percent faster.
I tested the 512GB version of the iPad Mini, which, like the 128GB and 256GB versions, features a seven-core integrated GPU. The 512GB model, however, gets a bump from five CPU cores to six and doubles the number of 16-core Neural Engines from one to two, promising better performance in on-device AI applications, such as image generation.
I don’t expect many people to run particularly intensive workloads on a tablet this small. Still, tasks such as photo editing, light video editing, and juggling many open applications felt smooth. The performance boost makes the iPad mini much more powerful than the standard iPad 11, which uses an A16 processor. The iPad Pro (M5) and the iPad Air (M4), however, remain better equipped for demanding workloads such as video editing and 3D rendering.
Siri AI is still in beta, so we won’t cover that in this review. But the tablet supports features under the Apple Intelligence umbrella, including various generative AI capabilities. Tasks like removing objects from photos, changing a photo’s perspective, or extending a photo’s borders should take roughly the same amount of time on the 512GB iPad mini as they do on the iPhone 18 Pro. In my experience, that’s usually about 20 seconds.
Better speakers
The mini is surprisingly loud. Its speakers are powerful enough to make TV dialogue easy to hear, even with my noisy heater running in the background.
The tablet has two woofers designed to deliver higher volume and stronger bass than the prior mini. A pair of custom-designed tweeters between the tablet’s glass and aluminum enclosure are intended to improve the clarity of higher frequencies.
You won’t get the deepest bass or the crispest high notes, but the speakers surpassed my expectations when playing music. I didn’t immediately feel the need to connect the iPad to dedicated speakers.
And the mini pulls this off without any visible speaker holes in its chassis.
No speaker holes here.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
No speaker holes here.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
That detail helped the mini earn the first IP67 rating for an iPad. The Ingress Protection rating means the device is “dust-tight” and “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water,” according to the International Electrotechnical Commission.
Other changes
The 2026 mini has the same 12 MP front and back cameras as its 2024 predecessor, but the front-facing camera has moved from one of the shorter sides to one of the longer sides. This took some getting used to for FaceTiming and selfies. Holding the tablet in portrait orientation now places you off-center in the frame, while holding it in landscape mode to FaceTime on the go quickly became uncomfortable. The new location was fine when I could sit down and prop the tablet on a stand.
The front-facing camera is in the top bezel.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
The front-facing camera is in the top bezel.
Credit:
Scharon Harding
Another addition is the back camera’s Adaptive True Tone flash, which Apple markets as a way to quickly scan documents. When the Camera app identifies a document, such as a piece of paper or a book, it automatically adjusts which of the camera’s LEDs light up to minimize shadows and produce clearer text.
When I used the tablet’s camera to photograph text on both a piece of paper and a book, it quickly used machine learning to identify them as documents. A pop-up appeared, offering the option to “Scan Document”; selecting it allowed me to automatically take a picture of just the document. It’s not a feature many people will use regularly, but when the need arises, it makes capturing a sharp, detailed image of text considerably easier.
Additional upgrades include a move from Wi-Fi 6E to Wi-Fi 7 and from Bluetooth 5.3 to Bluetooth 6. These capabilities come from the introduction of Apple’s N1 wireless networking chip, which also adds Thread support. Apple launched the N1 last year with the iPhone 17-series and iPhone Air.
The iPad mini also has the C2 cellular modem that Apple unveiled last month in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. For those who rely on cellular service, it’s reassuring that the tablet uses the same technology here as some of Apple’s best phones.
Although it’s not an upgrade, it’s impressive that the new mini has the same battery life as its predecessor, despite having a smaller chassis and a larger screen. The mini also gains support for fast charging.
iPad mini…to the max
With the 2026 model, the iPad mini feels less like a compromise. Its larger OLED screen, current-generation processor, more durable build, and better speakers make it feel more modern and competitive than the 2024 version.
These improvements come with a pricing predicament, though. Today, the iPad mini starts at $699 for the 128GB version, putting it just $50 below the 11-inch iPad Air (M4) at its lowest configuration. The 512GB mini I tested, which came with a more powerful A20 Pro chip, is $999. In 2024, the iPad mini started at $499, and the iPad Air 11-inch (M2) started at $599.
The mini’s OLED screen is a standout, but the Air remains a better choice for those seeking a balance between power and portability. Its more capable processor and still-excellent, larger IPS display make it more versatile. It also offers comparable battery life, though it lacks fast charging. Meanwhile, the Pro series remains the best option for demanding workloads and extensive multitasking. The Mini is much more capable of handling serious work, multitasking, and editing than it was before, but it still isn’t the best iPad for these purposes.
Despite narrowing the gap with other tablets, the mini is still a niche product. The biggest reason to pick it over other iPads is if you truly want the smallest device, primarily for content consumption. My preference for devices that are easy to handle without straining my smaller hands or weighing me down, combined with my appreciation of high-end displays, love of streaming, and interest in using secondary screens to boost productivity, confirms that this niche has an audience. Many of Apple’s improvements make the mini more enjoyable for these users.
Beyond comparisons with the rest of the iPad lineup, though, the mini makes the most of its small design. Apple fit just about everything it could into a device that’s somehow even smaller than its predecessor.
For anyone looking for an ultraportable tablet primarily for enjoying content on an excellent, high-end display, the mini is a markedly better device than it used to be.
The good
Fantastic screen that feels more premium with smaller bezels and OLED performance
Strong speakers for a small tablet
The first iPad with an IP rating
The bad
Refresh rate is lower than some other premium tablets
Only $50 cheaper than the bigger, more powerful iPad Air
Scharon is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica writing news, reviews, and analysis on consumer gadgets and services. She's been reporting on technology for over 10 years, with bylines at Tom’s Hardware, Channelnomics, and CRN UK.

articles.title: Dafne Keen confiesa lo más trágico de Hollywood siendo una niña: "Me ofrecían cocaína"
articles.text:
La actriz española Dafne Keen, estrella de la película Logan de Marvel y la saga X-Men, ha sorprendido con unas impactantes declaraciones sobre su paso por Hollywood. La madrileña, de 21 años, saltó a la fama mundial siendo solo una niña cuando protagonizó aquella cinta junto a Hugh Jackman. Y muy pronto tuvo que aprender lo que se cuece de verdad en la industria detrás de las cámaras.
En una entrevista concedida al podcast Inside of You, Dafne Keen ha confesado que incluso a esas edades ya le proponían consumir drogas. "Me ofrecían cocaína en las fiestas de fin de rodaje", revela, "yo era muy pequeña, tendría 11, 12 o 13 años". Por suerte, asegura, siempre rechazó esas proposiciones. "Vi lo que era y pensaba: 'No me interesa mucho'. Afortunadamente, les decía que no".
A su vez, ha confirmado que siempre ha tenido los pies en la tierra y ha sido bastante responsable con el consumo del alcohol. "Creo que nunca he estado lo suficientemente borracha como para tener resaca. Tengo mucho control con eso", cuenta la joven actriz. Incluso afirma que ha mentido en varias ocasiones diciendo que ya había bebido suficiente solo para poder mantenerse sobria. En definitiva, Dafne Keen parece querer alejarse de los excesos de Hollywood.
Quizá uno de los responsables de su visión responsable con respecto a la industria sea el mismísimo Hugh Jackman. Y es que, según cuenta, siempre la protegió mucho. "Fue increíblemente protector y maravilloso. Se aseguraba de que nadie abusara de mis horarios, de que me divirtiera en el rodaje y que no fuese consciente de las tensiones que pudiera haber detrás de escena", recuerda agradecida. "Lo sentía como una especie de figura paterna, de verdad", promete.
¿Volverá Dafne Keen como X-23 a Marvel?
Aunque Dafne Keen conquistó al mundo entero como X-23 en Logan, los problemas de 20th Century Fox con la saga X-Men y su posterior fusión con Disney truncaron la carrera de la actriz como la joven mutante. La compañía quería colocarla como una de sus grandes protagonistas, pero todo acabó cuando La Casa del Ratón adquirió el estudio.
En cualquier caso, Dafne Keen tuvo una nostálgica y emotiva aparición en Deadpool y Lobezno hace solo unos pocos años, regresando a su querido personaje. Y, a raíz de ese cameo, los fans han vuelto a pedir una y otra vez su retorno al UCM. Algo que ella misma abrazaría sin pensarlo. "Lo haría durante el resto de mi vida, al 100%", revelaba hace meses en una entrevista.
De hecho, su presencia en Avengers: Doomsday o Avengers: Secret Wars no está para nada descartada. Pero pase lo que pase, lo cierto es que a Dafne Keen no le ha faltado el trabajo en Hollywood. A lo largo de los años, la madrileña ha aparecido en series como La materia oscura, Star Wars: The Acolyte o, en solo unos días, en la tercera temporada de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo.

articles.title: Airbnb is working on an AI travel agent
articles.text:
Airbnb plans to roll out an AI agent in the first half of 2027 that will help users plan and book travel, the company said in its Q3 2026 earnings shareholder letter released today.
Airbnb is working on an AI travel agent
The travel company is planning an “AI-native” trip-planning experience that’s set to roll out next year.
“Today’s AI agents are good at simple, routine tasks, like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment,” Airbnb said. “But planning a trip on Airbnb is different.” The company argued that its experience matching hosts and guests, its current role in being part of reservations already, and a “new interface” built “specifically for travel” gives it an edge.
Here’s how Airbnb says that new interface will work:
We don’t think a traditional chatbot is the right way to plan a trip. We’re developing a custom-designed, AI-native experience that builds the interface around your question. Rather than a chat window, our agent draws on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what you’re looking for. Our agent will help guests explore options, make decisions with the people they’re traveling with, and take action directly in Airbnb.
Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said before that the company plans to launch an agent in 2027, telling the Skift Global Forum that it would have an interface that’s “much richer than a chatbot.”
In its shareholder letter, Airbnb also said that AI is “the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb” and has changed how it develops products and operates.

articles.title: Fitting AI Models To Edge Applications
articles.text:
Compression can shrink AI models, but efficient edge deployment starts with matching the architecture to the workload and hardware limits.
Key Takeaways:
Today’s AI industry faces two very different challenges. On one side, enormous AI data centers and AI factories are seeking more efficient ways to process high-parameter large language models (LLMs), with bandwidth and memory as the key bottlenecks. On the other side are smaller AI models running locally on edge devices, where there isn’t enough area, power, or memory for complex, higher-parameter LLMs.
“This has led to a gold rush with people raising huge amounts of capital to build mega data centers, but has also sparked innovation on the edge,” said Ed Plowman, CTO at Imagination Technologies. “People are trying to work out how they can cram an entire container of liquid into a very small cup, and that has been driven by the fact that compute resources are not the main problem at the moment. It’s bandwidth, and that’s why RAM has gotten so expensive. That triggered a whole bunch of researchers to look at what the key problems are and what we can do about it. That triggered innovations around quantization — reducing activations and weights simultaneously — to make the models even smaller but still maintaining the output capability of the model.”
AI models come in many shapes and sizes to fit a wide range of edge devices, from earbuds to phones, home appliances, industrial IoT, robotics, and automotive systems. Designers need to choose a model with the right number of parameters because an oversized model can slow the device down or cause it to overheat. On the flip side, if the model is too small, the product may not be smart enough.
The first step in right-sizing an AI model for an embedded application is to define its purpose. “You have to start from the point of view of what you want the model to do, but then there are a million and one things we can throw at it to make it smaller,” said Plowman. “Quantization and self-compression are very effective tools. Distillation is another approach, and it works better on transformers than on traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). All these things are starting to combine to get us to a point where the gold rush for bigger and bigger GPUs is less prevalent. The enablement in embedded systems and the progression towards quite intelligent models being able to run on truly embedded platforms is becoming more realistic.”
| Technique | How It Works | Key Characteristics | 
|---|---|---|
| Distillation | Trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher. | Transfers learned behavior into a smaller model. | 
| Pruning | Removes low-impact weights, neurons, heads, or layers. | Structured (whole units) or unstructured (individual weights). | 
| Quantization | Uses fewer bits for weights and activations. | Retains network structure; correction limits accuracy loss. | 
| Self-compression | Gradually reduces precision, potentially to zero bits. | Managed compression that can target proprietary hardware. | 
Fig. 1: Common ways to compress AI model
The model size must be considered alongside the system. “The hard part is designing a model that is sophisticated enough to solve the problem but small enough to fit the device,” said Magnus Gedda, CTO and chief product officer at Imagimob, an Infineon Technologies company. “On top of that, the model usually shares memory and compute with the rest of the application, so the available resources are smaller than the spec sheet suggests. Optimization techniques like pruning and quantization can shrink a model, but they are applied after design and usually after training, and they cost some accuracy. You need to pick an initial architecture that is the right size from the start so that its optimized version still fits the device and meets the performance target. Getting those three things to line up — problem fit, size, accuracy after optimization — is where most of the effort goes.”
Others agree that system-level efficiency is the central challenge. “Edge AI is ushering in a shift from ‘largest model wins’ to ‘experience per watt,'” said Steve Woo, distinguished inventor and fellow at Rambus. “Techniques such as compression, pruning, and lower-precision arithmetic help shrink models to fit local resources, but deployment remains difficult because memory capacity and bandwidth are often limiting factors. Getting a model onto the device is just the beginning. Making it run efficiently within tight power and latency budgets is where the engineering challenge begins.”
Choosing the wrong AI model can lead to extra work after deployment or a substandard product. “Once you have the optimized model, deployment is not that hard,” said Infineon’s Gedda. “The model is converted to C code, compiled for the target, and flashed to the device. The challenge is using the hardware to its full potential, so that inference is energy-efficient and low-latency. Edge hardware is extremely varied — MCUs, accelerators, NPUs, DSPs — and standards are somewhat lacking. So without the right tooling you end up with a generic, inefficient deployment, or a lot of manual work per target.”
These deployment constraints make model selection an application-specific exercise. The right architecture depends on the functions the device must perform and the workloads it must support.
Functions and workloads determine the correct model
Edge device and physical AI workloads vary considerably across sectors, from medical to industrial, automotive, home, or personal. The specific modalities of the collected sensor data are the primary driver for selecting the optimal AI model type and size.
“Right-sized inference for physical AI is critical,” noted Mick Posner, senior product marketing group director for chiplets at Cadence, in a recent blog. “Intelligent physical systems do not have a one-size-fits-all compute profile. Some workloads require always-on, low-power inference. Others require higher-performance multimodal processing across cameras, radar, lidar, audio, environmental sensors, and system-state data.”
Each hardware function and end-device feature needs to be considered and defined. “The best techniques for right-sizing AI models for edge AI are being able to categorize your functionality so that you don’t need a big model,” said Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA. “A 4-billion [parameter] model on a sensor is huge, even though we’re now talking 1 trillion [in the cloud]. Being able to bake that model into less than a billion parameters and have it in each of the sensors is doable. We need to define the highest-priority, must-have function, and train it well in an SLM (small language model). It could even be an ML (machine learning) model or a neural network model. It doesn’t need to be an LLM.”
After defining the must-have functions, designers can start building the AI core, then slowly add more features, including must-have, critical, or nice-to-have.
“Those are the three categories I see people defining in terms of how they do it architectural-wise, and where they fit in what intelligence,” said Balasubramanian. “Once you have determined those categories, the must-haves should be very close to the sensor. You can’t make everything must-have. You really need to prioritize and design it in a way that [the system] is able to be in a self-contained sensor loop with the local compute, local memory requirement, and sometimes even a local backup environment. Everything is cut up. You also need to have at least an hour or two of power envelope available so that the device doesn’t slow down or shut down.”
In the automotive sector, companies are increasingly deploying AI models for certain tasks and functions, though much of that industry is still using CNNs from about three or four years ago, Plowman noted. “They haven’t fully moved to transformers yet, or embraced the latest compression techniques. But certain external bodies have produced image segmentation object recognition systems, which use transformers.”
For IP providers tasked with optimizing these models, one challenge is that they may not get to see the actual model their customers are using. “The automotive guys train their own models, and they’re very secretive about them, for safety, security, and proprietary IP reasons,” said Plowman. “We don’t get to see them. We get a lot of proxies about what they look like or proxy functions that they want to accelerate, but it’s very rare that we get an entire model to play with.”
Fig. 2: IP modules for edge AI and physical AI. Source: Synopsys
For right-sizing, each IP block needs to be weighed against the model size. “Right-sizing a model for the edge is a systems problem, not a single-point optimization,” said Licinio Sousa, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “Techniques like quantization help the model fit, but real-time latency, power, cost, and functional safety all have to be balanced together. As AI models evolve faster than silicon development cycles, systems also need enough flexibility to support not only today’s workloads, but the models that come next.”
Once the model and system architecture are aligned, designers must determine which compression techniques can meet those constraints without sacrificing critical accuracy or performance.
Challenges of various compression techniques
Designers typically use a variety of compression techniques to right-size a model, and each has pros and cons.
For example, distillation enables drastic shrinking but potentially more loss. “You interrogate the model to find and see which bits of it light up,” said Imagination’s Plowman. “You do a similar exercise where you trim things off, but there is always loss from the teacher-student model. The student is trying to refine from the big model the essentials of what the teacher model knows. That’s why there’s potentially more inherent loss, but you retain much more of the reasoning capability. It drastically shrinks the size of the model, but there’s only so far you can go with that without going to quantization.”
Quantization makes models take a roundabout path to their destination instead of a direct one. “When applying an input to a network, there is a starting point for navigation,” said Plowman. “Then, depending on the values that you’ve given it, you need to navigate to an endpoint. Every time you do a layer you’re nudging the transform in a slightly different direction. With a full-width value such as FP32 or FP16, you’re going much more directly to a given point.”
Full-width values travel as the crow flies, while quantization is closer to city-block navigation. “We go up one, over one, up one, over one, but eventually you end up in exactly the same place,” said Plowman. “The trick with quantization is making those small, more angular steps mean the same thing as the direct navigation, but without the overhead power, memory, and other costs of the associated mathematics. It starts off with all the weights in the model, and it starts fitting them into buckets that match the quantization. There are lots and lots of different ways of doing the quantization. That’s a very brutal way of doing it.”
A gentler way is self-compression. “Self-compression techniques understand that, as a model is being trained, certain pathways will be very popular while others will be less popular,” explained Plowman. “You never know what this dimensional shape will look like. It’s random every time you retrain. You can maneuver the space to recreate certain desirable shapes you want every time, or get close to them, but there is an element of randomness. You get certain pathways that become critical as scaffolding for the rest of the system, but they’re not pathways that will matter in the end. We look for the sensitivity to those pathways, then quantize and quantize and quantize them down to zero bits. If nothing changes in the model and you still get the same outcomes, there was likely very small, or infinitesimally small, or no contribution from [those pathways].”
Fig. 3: A quantized transformer architecture. Source: Imagination
For quantization and self-compression, the complexity lies in managing the loss. “You need to make sure you’re not throwing away things that you really need, and that you’ve got good data coverage in the training set for the quantization flow,” Plowman observed.
For example, in automotive, engineers need to avoid losing long-tail data on edge cases or rare training samples that let an autonomous system navigate unusual road conditions.
Conclusion: Trending smaller
Small language models and other compact models suit resource-constrained edge devices, but they require system-level design and optimization to deliver the functions and features a specific product needs.
Ultimately, successful edge AI deployment starts with defining the workload and choosing an appropriately sized architecture — not simply shrinking the largest available model. Compression can help close the remaining gap, but its value depends on preserving accuracy while meeting the device’s power, memory, latency, cost, and safety requirements. As models and hardware evolve at different rates, flexible system design will be essential to support current applications and future workloads.

articles.title: Adding AI Image Generation to a Small Project Without Rewriting Your Code - Tech Guide
articles.text:
A few weeks ago I wanted to add automatic cover images to a side project, a little tool that turns blog drafts into shareable posts. Simple enough, I thought. Pick an image model, call the API, done by dinner.
It didn’t go that way. Rather than signing up with every provider and stitching the results together, I decided to tryToAPIs, an OpenAI-compatible gateway that puts text, image and video models behind one API and one key. That choice saved me some work, although I only understood why after seeing what the alternatives involved.
The Boring Part Nobody Warns You About
The trouble with adding AI features isn’t the generation itself. It’s everything around it. Every provider has its own request format, its own way of handling keys, its own rate limits and its own billing dashboard. Before settling on a gateway, I’d signed up for two services just to compare output. By Sunday afternoon I had two sets of credentials, two invoices to watch, and an awkward if provider == … branch I already knew I’d regret.
Then one of those services started throwing rate limit errors during a test run. My app didn’t handle them gracefully. It just stopped. That was when I stopped thinking of this as a model-picking problem and started treating it as a plumbing problem.
What a Gateway Actually Changes
The idea is simple. Instead of wiring your app directly to each provider, you point it at a single API that follows a familiar request format. The gateway handles the connections behind the scenes. If you’ve used the OpenAI SDK, much of the setup will look familiar, although individual models can still have their own parameters and response behavior.
You also get one place to manage usage and billing instead of several. I’m not going to pretend it’s magic. But for a small project where I didn’t want to maintain three separate integrations, it was worth an evening to try.
What the Switch Actually Involved
Less than I expected. The gateway used a familiar base URL and API key setup, so I didn’t need to redesign the rest of my application. For image generation, I used a straightforward HTTP request because the model returns an asynchronous task rather than an immediate image.
Here’s a simplified version of the submission code:
import os import requests response = requests.post( “https://toapis.com/v1/images/generations”, headers={ “Authorization”: f”Bearer {os.environ[‘TOAPIS_API_KEY’]}” }, json={ “model”: “gpt-image-2”, “prompt”: “Flat illustration of a desk with a laptop and a cup of tea, soft morning light”, “size”: “1:1”, “resolution”: “1k” }, timeout=30 ) response.raise_for_status() task_id = response.json()[“id”] print(task_id)
That submits the image request. The next step is to check the task status and retrieve the finished image. I kept that part separate so the app could handle jobs that took longer than expected.
A couple of things tripped me up, so they’re worth flagging.
First, model names. They don’t always match what you’d type when calling a provider directly, so check the model list before assuming. I wasted twenty minutes on a “model not found” error that turned out to be a naming mismatch.
Second, rate limits still exist. A gateway doesn’t make them vanish. I added a simple retry with exponential backoff and made sure failed requests wouldn’t bring down the whole process. If you’re hitting 429 errors, backing off and reducing concurrent requests is a sensible first step, whatever service you’re using.
What I Learned About Image Generation
For the images themselves I settled on the GPT Image 2 API, mainly because it handled two things I needed: generating from a text prompt and working from reference images. The second mattered more than I’d expected. Once the tool could take an existing graphic and use it as a visual reference, it became far more useful than a plain text-to-image box.
One thing to know is that image jobs can run asynchronously. You submit a task, get an identifier, then check its status until the result is ready. That’s fine, but it changes how you structure your code. My first version assumed an instant response, and I had to untangle it later.
Prompt wording also made more difference than I’d expected. Short, concrete instructions like “a flat illustration of a desk, soft light, no text” generally gave me more usable results than long, flowery descriptions. I wasn’t always happy with lettering inside generated images, so I started adding titles and labels myself afterwards.
When a Gateway Isn’t Worth Using
I should be upfront about this. If you only ever use one provider, and you’re happy with its pricing and reliability, a gateway adds another layer you may not need. You’d be solving a problem you don’t have.
It also pays to read the pricing page before moving anything serious. Some models are billed per token, others per request or generated image. The costs aren’t really comparable until you’ve worked out how you’ll use them. I’d suggest starting with one low-stakes feature and watching usage for a week before migrating anything important.
There’s also the question of dependency. A gateway simplifies provider management, but your application still relies on that gateway being available. Timeouts, retries and error logging remain your responsibility.
What I Would Do Next Time
For me, the win wasn’t a single model. It was having a consistent way to work with different models and one place to check usage instead of several. Switching still takes some testing, especially when models accept different parameters, but the integration is easier to manage.
If you’re building something similar, my advice is to resist the urge to over-engineer. Pick one feature, get a working call, add a basic retry, and only then think about fallbacks and cost tuning. The initial setup is the easy bit. It’s the habits you build around it that make it hold up.

articles.title: Closing the Identity Gap at the Service Desk
articles.text:
Organizations have invested heavily in securing employee logins. Multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access policies and other identity controls make it harder for attackers to gain unauthorized access. But these protections can be undermined if the process for recovering access isn't held to the same standard.
When an employee needs to regain access to their account, it’s often the service desk that provides the password reset or account recovery. Yet identity verification commonly still relies on knowledge-based questions, such as an employee's manager's name or department.
This creates a gap in identity security where a weaker route into an account can bypass stronger login security. And as social engineering attacks become more convincing, that gap is becoming increasingly dangerous.
Why Knowledge-Based Verification Can No Longer Be Trusted
Attackers can gather a surprising amount of information before making a call. LinkedIn profiles, company websites, social media and leaked data can reveal everything from job titles and colleagues to office locations and personal details.
Armed with this information, an attacker can answer verification questions correctly and appear to be a legitimate employee.
This becomes particularly dangerous when passing these checks is enough to authorize a password reset or recover an account. An attacker could gain access to that account without ever needing to compromise the employee's original credentials.
The risks of knowledge-based authentication are well established. NIST's digital identity guidelines no longer recognize security questions as an acceptable authentication method. Against the threat landscape in 2026, knowing information about someone is not proof of their identity.

Verizon’s Data Breach Investigation Report found stolen credentials are involved in 44.7% of breaches. 
Effortlessly secure Active Directory with compliant password policies, blocking 4+ billion compromised passwords, boosting security, and slashing support hassles!
AI and Social Engineering Make the Gap More Dangerous
Cybercriminal groups such as Scattered Spider have made the service desk a preferred target. Rather than trying to bypass MFA directly, attackers impersonate employees and convince service desk agents to reset passwords or register new MFA devices. A convincing phone call can be enough to gain access to an account.
Generative AI is making these attacks harder to detect and easier to scale. Attackers can use AI to create believable stories, generate natural-sounding conversations and even impersonate employees' voices. This makes it increasingly difficult for service desk agents to distinguish legitimate callers from attackers.
A 2025 Gartner survey found that 62% of organizations had experienced a deepfake attack involving social engineering or automated processes in the previous year.
Meanwhile, Verizon's 2026 DBIR found that social engineering through texts and voice calls had a 40% higher success rate than traditional email phishing.
Service desk agents can no longer rely on how convincing someone sounds. Identity verification needs to be based on secure, consistent checks rather than an agent's ability to recognize an impersonation attempt.
It's Not Just a Security Problem
Access recovery also comes at a cost. Account lockouts create service desk tickets which interrupt employees' work and put pressure on overworked IT teams. When someone loses access outside office hours, even a routine reset can mean hours of downtime.
There is a monetary cost as well; a single help desk password reset costs around $70. Multiply that by hundreds or thousands of requests, and the expense quickly adds up.
Secure self-service recovery can help employees regain access without contacting the service desk, while streamlined identity verification helps agents handle requests that still need support. With the right processes in place, organizations can reduce the workload without weakening security.
Closing the Gap: What Secure Service Desk Verification Looks Like
It’s unrealistic to expect service desk agents to become experts at spotting AI-enabled social engineering attempts. Training is still crucial, and agents should feel confident in refusing requests or escalating when something doesn’t sound right.
Alongside that, they need a reliable way to verify identities before making sensitive account changes. Verification should be a required step, not a judgment call based on how convincing someone sounds.
Solutions like Specops Secure Service Desk help organizations put this into practice through a straightforward four-step process:
- An employee contacts the service desk: An employee, ‘John Doe’, calls because he can't access his account. The agent starts a recovery request through Specops Secure Service Desk.
- The agent locates the account: Using John's details, the agent finds his account and initiates the verification process.
- Identity verification takes place: Specops Secure Service Desk supports a range of verification methods, including email, SMS, and third-party authenticators like Duo, so organizations can choose an appropriate method for the request whether the caller has access to a smartphone or not.
- The agent proceeds once verification succeeds: Only after John has successfully verified his identity can the agent carry out the requested action, such as resetting his password.
The goal is to make secure identity verification a consistent part of service desk workflows, without adding unnecessary friction for agents or employees.
Make Account Recovery as Secure as Login
Strong login security means little if attackers can bypass it with a convincing call to the service desk. Password resets and account recovery need verification that's just as robust as the authentication controls they protect.
By replacing knowledge-based questions with consistent, secure verification, organizations can reduce the risk of impersonation without making life harder for employees or service desk agents.

articles.title: The ex-Secret Service agent who flipped a hacker is now raising a second $250M cybersecurity fund | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO.
Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says.
Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his résumé, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing.
One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A.
Now Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade.
His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue.
Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.”
After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 résumés but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first.
The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.)
What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it.
By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “Operation Firewall.”
Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.”
Six years as CISO at the financial services company TIAA followed, and then two years at Home Depot starting in 2019. But in 2021, feeling burned out, he quit without anything lined up for the first time since age 16.
That chapter didn’t last long. The founders of Wiz, whose security software Ward had used at Home Depot, put him on a short list for a job at their company. Jeff Horing, a venture capitalist at Insight Partners, which had co-led Wiz’s $100 million Series A round in late 2020, interviewed Ward for the role, then offered him one at Insight instead.
It’s a good-news, bad-news story, given that Wiz was acquired last year by Google for $32 billion. When I asked him about it last week, Ward observed that the friend who took the Wiz job “made life-changing money,” but said it doesn’t bother him.
Regardless, he spent just three years at Insight, where he says he worked on Wiz, Abnormal Security, and Elisity, which IonQ agreed in October to buy for up to $1.3 billion. Then, at age 49, he thought about striking out on his own for the first time.
He says people told him it was a young man’s game. He left anyway and began cold-emailing limited partners. Ultimately, fewer than 20 LPs filled the fund, including Horing.
Ward started Brightmind in 2024 with Talpaz, a CrowdStrike corporate development executive whose deals overlapped with Ward’s during his time at Insight. Tayler Sipperly, another CrowdStrike corporate development alum, was the firm’s third employee.
The partnership ended this past spring. Asked what happened, Ward, using carefully worded legalese, cited “differences in opinions regarding operations and the future of Brightmind.” In August, Talpaz and Sipperly co-founded a new venture firm with Elia Zaitsev, CrowdStrike’s global CTO for the past three years. Called Cognition, it’s now reportedly targeting a $170 million first fund to back cybersecurity startups.
Brightmind’s first fund has made 14 investments to date, with one exit: that SNGL sale.
Some investors asked why Brightmind didn’t ride out that bet even longer. But Ward says he’s seen enough across his career that he feels confident in warning founders when they’re “going to race past the turn.”
In cybersecurity, he says, the best sales come between a startup’s third and seventh years. Indeed, he says his team tracks every security acquisition and what buyers are building versus buying. If Palo Alto Networks is likely to buy something, he says, CrowdStrike will experience “FOMO, then Zscaler is going to look over and go, ‘What did they just do? I should probably do the same thing.’”
Understanding how the pieces fit together is the trick, Ward explained, offering some hypotheticals. If CrowdStrike is building a product, he said, it’s unlikely to buy a portfolio company that makes something similar. Palo Alto Networks might love a company, but not if buying it would force its customers to switch away from something it bought five years ago.
“It’s very easy to go, ‘Good match,’ ‘terrible match,’” he said. “And that’s really what we spend a ton of time figuring out.”
He has timing on his side, at least. Early-stage cybersecurity startups are outraising their later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade, according to PitchBook, which counts $4.7 billion worth of seed-through-Series B deals through September.
That total is already ahead of the entirety of 2025, even though the number of deals fell to 248 from 358 last year. Seed rounds in particular are ballooning, per PitchBook. The average cybersecurity seed round jumped to $8.4 million in the first nine months of this year, from $5.54 million a year earlier.
Ward questions how much of that money is really going to AI security. By PitchBook’s count, 278 deals in the first half of 2026 were bucketed as such, but his team’s manual review found only 30 true ones. He doesn’t think Anthropic or OpenAI will “take over the security world,” but instead will do “just enough.”
For real-time protection, which he terms “zero second,” he favors cyber-specific models that run locally on a customer’s own systems, like that of Empirical Security. He also looks for startups that could trounce established companies that he considers vulnerable, name-checking 27-year-old Qualys and 24-year-old Tenable.
Ward says Brightmind’s second fund won’t be entirely cybersecurity, focusing about 20% on AI infrastructure deals. He expects a meaningful number of teams to come from Israel, too. (Roughly 40% of the debut fund’s startups are based in Tel Aviv.)
Asked about the founders he’s most comfortable backing, the response is immediate: second-time founders who stick together.
Brightmind is comprised of five people right now: COO Iva Messy, also a Seton Hall graduate, came from venture firms Felicis and Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) on the recommendation of Ward’s cousin, Carl Eschenbach, a former Workday CEO who is now back at Sequoia. Sven Wollschlaeger, a Midwesterner whom Ward calls one of the hardest-working people he’s known, spent three years alongside Ward at Insight and is a principal at Brightmind.
CTO Jamie Mneimneh, whom Ward first hired at Home Depot as a distinguished engineer, is the most technical person of the team. He built the cloud computing environment on AWS where the firm tests startups’ products. Mneimneh also built the AI agents that now source most of Brightmind’s deal flow, which is how the firm avoids hiring a bench of analysts and keeps management fees down, says Ward.
Taylor Cleveland, Ward’s chief of staff at Home Depot, joined the firm a few months ago.
For all the career changes, Ward says the real force driving him hasn’t changed. He grew up without money and still worries it could happen again, saying he’s being paid to produce a “3x net fund,” and he’s “not going to celebrate until we get that.”
Said Ward: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have a level of being very naive to like, not being qualified to do something. I’ve just always looked at people and been like, ‘Okay, you know more than me today, but tomorrow, it’s going to be a little less, and the day after that, it’s going to be less, and eventually, I’m going to catch you and surpass you, and I’m going to know more than you.’ That’s how competitive I am.”

articles.title: Blinkit Ambulance to charge Rs 2,500 for non-emergency cases
articles.text:
Blinkit Ambulance to charge Rs 2,500 for non-emergency cases
Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal noted that a growing share of bookings for its free ambulance service were for routine checkups, hospital visits and hospital-to-home transfers.
Blinkit Ambulance, the free service from the quick commerce company, will now start charging Rs 2,500 for non-emergency transfers.
“Emergency transfers–free, as always. Non-emergency transfers–₹2,500, charged after the trip. Broadly in line with what private ambulances charge. This money goes to the Eternal Foundation, which runs these ambulances and will help us scale them even further,” Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal said in a post on X.
Goyal noted that Blinkit Ambulance was started as a spirit of service, and in the last two years, it has served around 20,000 emergency cases and more than 42,000 cases in total. “We haven't charged a single rupee for any of them. And we want to keep it that way,” he remarked.
The reason for the change is that a growing share of bookings were for routine checkups, hospital visits and hospital-to-home transfers, the post noted. As Goyal remarked that every such booking requires a fully equipped emergency ambulance with paramedics.
“We hope that this charge will dramatically drop the usage of our Ambulances for non-emergency cases. 10-minute ambulances have saved and can save thousands of lives, and we need to keep them available for emergencies that need them the most,” Goyal said.
He also highlighted the challenge faced in providing free ambulance services is the availability of paramedics. However, he further added that they are planning to introduce Blinkit Ambulance to all major cities in the country in the next 2-4 years.

articles.title: SpaceX plans to build more data center compute than Google's entire lifetime capacity in just 1.5 years — analysts say target is realistic, SpaceX to build staggering 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone
articles.text:
SpaceX plans to build more data center compute than Google's entire lifetime capacity in just 1.5 years — analysts say target is realistic, SpaceX to build staggering 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone
Elon Musk's venture does appear to be moving much faster than its competitors.
A scant two weeks ago, Elon Musk made yet another bold claim: he was "highly confident" that SpaceX could build 10 GW of data center capacity in 2027 alone. The grandiose statement raised a few eyebrows, but in a detailed write-up, the analysts at Semiaccurate explain how that's actually doable... if the stars align. That +10 GW figure over the existing 3 GW would mean the company had built in as much data center capacity in 1.5 years as Google did in its entire existence, according to the post. The site notes that should this forecast ring true, that would make SpaceX the fastest-building hyperscaler on the planet, far outpacing every other player.
As proof of progress, the analysts point to how quickly the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 buildouts are progressing, estimated from aerial shots and available information. They note that Colossus 2's power generation capacity went from only 0.4 GW in January to a projected 2.4 GW by the time the year is out, at the rate that the relevant hardware is popping up. The site tallies up 9 GW of potential data center capacity across the sites it's tracking, including Colossus and Starbase facilities.
Notably, the facility includes 89 turbines capable of delivering approximately 2.5 GW, helped along by a total of 1377 Tesla battery Megapacks, all already on the campus. Due to emissions regulations, the facility will only eventually be allowed to operate roughly 1.24 GW of its own turbines.
Even with the 1.2 GW eventually coming in from the grid, there's a 300 MW shortfall to be filled by the batteries, which Semianalysis expects will top up with compute load variation and possibly external power. SpaceX has an agreement with the state of Mississippi that lets it temporarily operate the extra turbines, with a promised phase-out by July 2027.
As of September 25, Elon Musk had stated that Colossus 2 already had 550,000 GPUs working, presumably in the extant Macrohard and Macroharder facility. At the time, SpaceX was reportedly gunning to have its Gun Range and Project SPAM centers ready in short order. Judging by the photos, they appear to be progressing at a rapid pace, as there are visible facilities where there was nothing but loose dirt a few months ago — though nothing says the racks of GPUs are in there yet.
Semianalysis' team remarks that SpaceX's builds have become so fast that they kick off well before it decides how the facility will be powered, and the respective power supplies come in. We've all seen the news about the scarcity of GPUs and RAM, but for a data center, just having enough power is problem enough.
If SpaceX can keep its stream of gas turbines coming along, that's quite the achievement by itself. The analysts think that Tesla may be manufacturing mechanical and electrical equipment in modules, presumably ready to install directly from the factory, or even trucks. Heck, the aforementioned temporary turbines are mounted on truck flatbeds as "mobile" power generation, seemingly in a bid to skirt regulations.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
In the hyperscaler world, speed is the name of the game, particularly in these trying times when there are mounting suspicions that not all players will even make it to the finish line. Compute capacity being built and eventually becoming available is enticing for AI players, yes, but they're willing to pay through the nose for anything they can get their hands on right now, as current demand far outstrips supply.
Having facilities built doesn't mean that they're actually working, however, or that they're functioning at their expected rate. Zoning, permits, grid connections, power generation constraints, water supply, and public opposition are some of the few problems that have plagued builds most everywhere, none of which relate to the existence and installation of computing hardware.
Microsoft's Satya Nadella put it clearly: "You may actually have a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that I can’t plug in. In fact, that is my problem today." That's far from the only report that a significant percentage of AI accelerators are still stuck in warehouses, on hold until they can go fulfill their duties in a server rack somewhere.
Since building a datacenter involves many moving parts, even assuming that Colossus 2 wraps up as quickly as it appears to be, that doesn't necessarily mean that SpaceX will be able to replicate its success across its other sites. There is no luck involved in engineering, yes, but some factors like availability of hardware and materials, changes in legal winds, and public opposition are hard to predict, even for someone with resources as extensive as Elon Musk.
And yet, the folks at Semianalysis note that two data centers at Starbase are undergoing rapid construction, suggesting that SpaceX can indeed replicate Colossus' success. They attribute the speed to SpaceX having most of the infrastructure and power generation hardware effectively in-house, via Tesla's manufacturing ability. If that assessment holds, the firm could be bypassing supplier lead times that other hyperscalers have to contend with.
Even if SpaceX doesn't reach its "10 GW in a year" target, if the Colossus buildouts are anything to go by, the company may well be moving faster than anyone else in this space. Metrics aside, in the AI gold rush, coming first is all that's needed to win.

articles.title: 'I think we could do it on a technical level' — Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director says RTS games on console are 'always a big challenge' due to the multiple controls, but suggests it could be achieved
articles.text:
Could Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 come to console? Its creative director says RTS games on console are 'always a big challenge,' but 'I think we could do it on a technical level'
King Art is already planning for the game's future
- Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director Jan Theysen suggests a console version could be achieved on a "technical level"
- Theysen says bringing RTS games to console "is always a big challenge" because of the many key prompts on PC
- He adds that King Art would ideally make adjustments so that it "actually works well on controller"
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director Jan Theysen has suggested the upcoming real-time strategy (RTS) game could eventually come to consoles, as King Art plans for its future.
In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the creative director confirmed that the studio borrowed hero mechanics and UI features from Dawn of War 2 and 3 for inspiration, Theysen said that while nothing has been announced at the moment, he believes a console edition of Dawn of War 4 isn't out of the realm of possibility.
"I mean, I think we could do it on a technical level," Theysen said. "We are also looking, of course, into what else might come in the future."
The King Art co-founder explained that since RTS games generally have a wide selection of keyboard and mouse prompts, it can be difficult to cohesively translate the controls to a gamepad. However, King Art has achieved this in the past with games like Iron Harvest and Battle Worlds: Kronos.
"RTS on consoles is always a big challenge when it comes to the controls, right?" he said. "And so if we did it, I think our goal would not be to try to get the exact same controls mapped on a gamepad because that's not really working. I think we literally have something like 40 keys on the keyboard for different things."
He added that King Art would ideally look at how it could change the gameplay in places and make adjustments so that it "actually works well on controller."
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 launches on PC on December 3. In the same discussion, Theysen also described how the game manifests the classic RTS experience of the 2004 game and how the game's advanced animation system, Combat Director, initially sounded like an impossible challenge.

articles.title: WoW Forever : Blizzard officialise sa toute première arme légendaire inédite pour son « nouveau » MMORPG
articles.text:
La scène avait quelque chose d’un peu émouvant pour qui a connu les premiers jours de World of Warcraft, il y a plus de vingt ans. Pour accompagner le lancement de WoW Forever, et montrer l’engouement de la communauté autour de ce « troisième » WoW, le studio a partagé une animation assez hypnotisante à regarder.
Selon Blizzard, cette animation en forme de carte montrait les joueurs et les joueuses se connectant à WoW Forever depuis les différentes régions de départ, côté Alliance ou côté Horde. Un point clignotant par brave rejoignant le serveur, d’après le studio. Mais ce n’était pas là la seule animation que l’entreprise avait prévue autour de la sortie de WoW Forever.
Une autre surprise a également été conservée pour le jour J : alors que le jeu a fait ses débuts dans la nuit de ce mercredi 4 à ce jeudi 5 novembre (les serveurs ont ouvert à minuit, heure de Paris), le compte officiel de Warcraft sur X a présenté vers 23h… la toute première arme légendaire inédite propre à World of Warcraft Forever.
Et l’item en question est un bâton à deux mains appelé Taldramir, aussi surnommé The Whispering Wood (qu’on traduirait par Le Bois Murmurant). Juste avant, lors d’un direct sur Twitch, l’atelier néo-zélandais Wētā Workshop (à qui l’on doit les armes et armures du film Warcraft de 2016) en avait assemblé une réplique grandeur nature.
L’officialisation de Taldramir comme arme légendaire dans WoW Forever est triplement notable.
D’abord parce qu’un tel équipement est accompagné, dans l’immense majorité des cas, de statistiques exceptionnelles, et bénéficie au passage d’une direction artistique très souvent admirable. Deux critères qui attisent, forcément, bien des convoitises.
Ensuite parce que dans le WoW d’origine, ces armes se comptent sur les doigts d’une main (Sulfuras, Lame-tonnerre ou Atiesh, qui était déjà un bâton…). Qui plus est, leur obtention demandait des semaines, voire des mois de jeu, et passait par des activités de haut niveau en groupe, comme les raids. Et il valait mieux avoir l’appui de toute une guilde pour y parvenir.
Enfin, et surtout, le bâton est la première arme légendaire pensée spécialement pour Forever. Blizzard avait évidemment prévu d’ajouter du contenu pour ce troisième WoW, comme de nouvelles quêtes, des régions inédites et des items supplémentaires. Celui-ci est le premier de très haut niveau à être mis en avant.
On notera au passage que ce bâton apparaît dans une illustration du jeu publiée dès le 29 octobre, dans l’actualité annonçant la sortie du MMORPG.
Taldramir, un bâton légendaire pour… druide ?
Compte tenu du design de l’arme (tout en branches noueuses et en bourgeons naissants) et de son nom (qui rappelle l’ambiance des elfes de la nuit), on présume que la classe druide sera capable de se servir du bâton. Cela étant, Blizzard n’a rien dit des classes qui pourront le porter ni de ses effets, rappelle le site spécialisé Wowhead.
Du côté du data mining, c’est-à-dire l’extraction des données cachées dans les fichiers du jeu, des pistes ont été trouvées. D’après Icy Veins, ce bâton serait tourné vers les soins, et sa quête passerait par le raid du sommet d’Hyjal, le cratère d’Un’Goro (deux zones où la présence des druides peut se justifier) et le Cercle cénarien, la faction des druides.
Des indices de cette quête étaient déjà apparus dans les fichiers de la bêta en septembre, au moment où Blizzard promettait une nouvelle suite de quêtes légendaire pour le printemps 2027. Ces étapes restent non confirmées.

articles.title: Transformer de la ferraille « sale » en super-métal : l'incroyable trouvaille de l'IA
articles.text:
Des chercheurs utilisent les impuretés du métal recyclé pour améliorer ses propriétés. Sur 17 variantes de fonte proposées par leur méthode d’apprentissage automatique, puis fabriquées et testées, 14 offrent un meilleur compromis entre résistance et capacité à se déformer avant de casser.
Pour obtenir un bon alliage recyclé, les industriels diluent souvent les impuretés de la ferraille avec du métal neuf. Une équipe réunissant plusieurs universités chinoises et l’Institut Max-Planck pour les matériaux durables a choisi de tirer parti de ces éléments indésirables. Ses travaux, publiés dans Science Advances, utilisent l’IA pour trouver les compositions et les traitements qui leur donneront un rôle utile.
Composer avec les impuretés plutôt que les diluer
Ajouter du métal primaire aide à retrouver les propriétés recherchées, mais sa production consomme de l’énergie et émet du CO2. Une partie de l’intérêt environnemental du recyclage se perd donc dans l’opération. Avec leurs « dirty alloys », ou alliages « sales », les chercheurs veulent conserver davantage de ferraille dans le mélange et utiliser certains éléments qu’elle contient pour renforcer le matériau.
Mais comment trouver les bonnes proportions ? Avec l’IA, pardi ! Pour faire ses calculs, l’IA s’appuie sur deux bases de données : une première de 330 entrées détaillées et une seconde d’environ 2 400 entrées associant compositions et propriétés mécaniques. Un algorithme explore différentes compositions et fait aussi varier les paramètres de fabrication, notamment les températures du métal et les durées des opérations de fonderie. Des réseaux de neurones prédisent ensuite la résistance à la traction et l’allongement à la rupture, qui mesure la capacité du matériau à s’étirer avant de casser. La recherche vise un équilibre entre les deux propriétés.
Un second modèle, entraîné sur davantage de données, affine la sélection. Les candidats retenus sont alors fabriqués et soumis à des essais mécaniques. Les mesures rejoignent ensuite la base de données pour améliorer les prédictions au tour suivant. Le laboratoire fournit ainsi de nouveaux résultats à l’IA qui s’en sert pour proposer les prochaines compositions.
Jusqu’à 15,2 % de résistance en plus
L’équipe a commencé par une fonte à graphite sphéroïdal, aussi appelée fonte ductile, déjà connue pour sa tolérance aux impuretés. Parmi les 17 variantes testées, 14 améliorent les compromis entre résistance et déformabilité par rapport aux fontes recyclées de référence recensées dans les données.
À allongement comparable, la résistance à la traction progresse jusqu’à 15,2%. À résistance comparable, l’allongement avant rupture augmente jusqu’à 73,2%. Ces maxima correspondent donc à des compromis différents selon les alliages. Les auteurs annoncent également un coût de fabrication inférieur de 8,1% à celui du procédé conventionnel mêlant ferraille et fer primaire.
Ces résultats concernent pour l’instant une seule famille de fonte. Les chercheurs envisagent d’étendre leur méthode aux aciers recyclés ainsi qu’aux alliages d’aluminium et de cuivre.
Pour une fonderie, la perspective serait de fabriquer des pièces de qualité avec les lots de ferraille disponibles en ajoutant moins de métal neuf pour les corriger. Ou comment faire des économies en obtenant un bien meilleur alliage.
Source : Institut Max-Planck pour les matériaux durables via Heise

articles.title: Las gafas inteligentes de Amazon fotografiarán hogares, sin opción de exclusión.
articles.text:
Amazon está preparando un despliegue de gafas inteligentes para sus repartidores que prometen facilitar las entregas, pero también pueden convertir cada recorrido hasta la puerta de una vivienda en una sucesión de fotografías. Según una investigación de Bloomberg, los dispositivos capturan imágenes cada pocos segundos mientras los trabajadores caminan, algo que podría traducirse en miles de fotografías durante una sola jornada.
El problema es que los clientes no disponen de una opción para impedir esa recopilación, consultar las fotografías o solicitar su eliminación. Las gafas, presentadas por Amazon en octubre de 2025, servirán para ayudar a los repartidores a identificar paquetes, seguir indicaciones y fotografiar las entregas sin utilizar el móvil, pero irán un poco más allá.
Las imágenes también sirven para alimentar Wellspring, una herramienta de IA que permite elaborar mapas más precisos de los barrios. Viraj Chatterjee (directivo responsable del proyecto) reconoció ante Bloomberg que la compañía ni siquiera había contemplado ofrecer a los clientes la posibilidad de rechazar las fotografías. Por ello, su intención es desplegar 5.000 dispositivos durante 2026 y superar los 20.000 a finales de 2027.
Amazon defiende las medidas de privacidad, pero quedan preguntas por resolver
La compañía asegura que su intención principal es mejorar las entregas y no vigilar a los clientes, así que aplica sistemas que difuminan rostros y matrículas antes de que las fotografías puedan ser revisadas por personal autorizado. Además, también han confirmado que las gafas no graban vídeo ni sonido y que los repartidores pueden desactivar la cámara con un interruptor físico.
Amazon, por su parte, afirma que las imágenes se eliminan de forma automática tras un periodo breve, pero no concreta cuánto dura exactamente ese almacenamiento. Así, la cuestión es que esa protección depende de las decisiones de la empresa y de quienes utilizan los dispositivos, mientras que las personas fotografiadas siguen sin contar con un mecanismo específico de exclusión.
Según Bloomberg, las autoridades también podrían acceder a las imágenes mediante una orden judicial. Amazon defiende que la tecnología permitirá trabajar con mayor rapidez y reducir errores, pero su despliegue abre un debate que va más allá de las entregas: ¿hasta qué punto puede una empresa recopilar imágenes de viviendas y personas para mejorar un servicio sin darles la posibilidad de negarse?

articles.title: MediaMarkt agota la solución para instalar los 212 GB de 'GTA VI' en Xbox Series sin borrar otros juegos, pero aquí hay otra opción aún mejor
articles.text:
El 19 de noviembre sale a la venta 'GTA VI', uno de los videojuegos más esperados de los últimos años, en consolas PS5 y Xbox Series. Pero unos días antes, el 10 de este mismo mes, los usuarios de ambas plataformas podrán comenzar su predescarga, tal y como ha confirmado la propia Rockstar. Predescarga para la que necesitaremos nada menos que 212 GB libres, una capacidad difícil de alcanzar en modelos como Series S sobre todo si contamos con Game Pass y somos de acumular títulos.
SANDISK Optimus GX C50 512 GB
Por este motivo, muchos usuarios probablemente tendrán que desinstalar alguno de sus actuales videojuegos para hacer hueco a 'GTA VI'. Pero para los de Series X|S hay una estupenda y relativamente económica solución: las tarjetas de expansión oficiales de Seagate y SanDisk.
En este sentido, hoy mismo MediaMarkt rebajó bastante (215,65 euros) el modelo de Seagate en su versión de 1 TB en su outlet, pero rápidamente se agotó. Sin embargo, el SanDisk de 512 GB (132,98 euros), que además viene con un mes de regalo de Xbox Game Pass, está disponible en Amazon a un precio aún mejor y es la opción ideal para instalar el lanzamiento de Rockstar (y varios juegos más) sin eliminar otros títulos.
512 GB de capacidad adicional para Xbox Series, con instalación rápida y sencilla
Tanto el modelo agotado en el outlet de MediaMarkt como este otro de SanDisk, aún disponible en Amazon, son dos de las mejores formas de ampliar la capacidad con que vienen de serie Xbox Series X|S sin complejas instalaciones ni configuraciones. Este último, además, también se puede comprar en versión de 1 TB, aunque su precio no resulta tan interesante (257,99 euros) y tiene un tiempo de envío muy elevado.
Estos SSD oficiales para las consolas de Microsoft se instalan en segundos, gracias al puerto que incluyen Series X y Series S en su zona trasera. Y hacen las veces del almacenamiento interno, permitiendo así seguir disfrutando de tecnologías como Quick Resume o instalaciones de videojuegos rápidas.
Este es precisamente una de sus mayores ventajas frente a otros SSD y HDD externos: la posibilidad de instalar títulos en el propio SSD manteniendo el rendimiento. Un aspecto clave si pensamos jugar a 'GTA VI' en Series X o Series S (sobre todo en esta última) y no queremos eliminar otros juegos para hacer sitio a esos 212 GB para los que no todas las consola están preparadas.

articles.title: WhatsApp : comment libérer de l'espace de stockage sans supprimer vos discussions
articles.text:
WhatsApp : comment libérer de l'espace de stockage sans supprimer vos discussions
WhatsApp dévore la mémoire de votre téléphone ? Pas de panique : en deux étapes simples, vous pouvez freiner son appétit numérique et libérer de l’espace sans tout supprimer.
Cet article a été initialement publié en mai 2026. Nous le republions aujourd'hui car la saturation de la mémoire des smartphones, très souvent causée par l'accumulation de photos et de vidéos sur WhatsApp, reste un problème universel et récurrent pour nos lecteurs.
Photos, vidéos, messages vocaux... Au fil des conversations, WhatsApp peut rapidement saturer la mémoire de votre smartphone et devenir une véritable mine d'or pour les gigaoctets superflus. Heureusement, il n'est pas nécessaire de désinstaller l'application pour retrouver du souffle. Qu'il s'agisse de configurer l'application pour bloquer proactivement l'accumulation de fichiers volumineux ou de procéder à un grand nettoyage chirurgical de vos conversations existantes, voici un guide complet et pratique pour maîtriser et réduire efficacement l'espace de stockage occupé par WhatsApp sur votre appareil.
Comment limiter l'espace de stockage utilisé par WhatsApp
Avant de supprimer des fichiers dans WhatsApp sur votre smartphone, il est possible de régler quelques options dans l'application pour que les fichiers y occupent un peu moins d'espace à l'avenir. Cette astuce est pratique pour justement ne pas avoir à opérer des suppressions trop régulièrement.
WhatsApp est une messagerie gratuite pour échanger des messages, des fichiers et passer des appels audio ou vidéo. Elle se télécharge sur Android, iPhone, Windows et macOS, et s’utilise également dans un navigateur avec WhatsApp Web.
- Licence : Licence gratuite
- Auteur : WhatsApp
- Systèmes d'exploitation : Windows 10 / 11, macOS, Service en ligne, Android, iOS iPhone
- Catégorie : Communication
- Direction les Paramètres de WhatsApp. Sur Android, appuyez sur les trois points en haut à droite, puis pointez Paramètres.
- Descendez et validez l'entrée Stockage et données.
Là, plusieurs options s'offrent à vous. La première se trouve dans Qualité de chargement des médias et permet de choisir entre Standard et HD pour envoyer et recevoir par défaut les photos en deux formats dont la taille varie.
La seconde, en dessous, permet de sélectionner quels types de données (photos, audio, vidéos ou documents) l'app va télécharger automatiquement ou non en fonction du type de connexion (wifi, données mobiles ou itinérance). Pratique, par exemple, pour télécharger une vidéo manuellement uniquement quand vous disposez d'assez d'espace de stockage sur votre terminal.
Comment récupérer de l'espace de stockage utilisé par WhatsApp
Passons au vrai gros morceau, à savoir le nettoyage actif de l'espace de stockage utilisé par WhatsApp sur votre smartphone.
- Direction les Paramètres de WhatsApp. Sur Android, appuyez sur les trois points en haut à droite, puis pointez Paramètres.
- Descendez et validez l'entrée Stockage et données.
- Appuyez sur Gérer le stockage. Après quelques secondes, la quantité de stockage utilisée s'affiche.
Ici aussi, plusieurs fonctionnalités sont proposées pour récupérer de la place.
Tout d'abord, la section Passer en revue et supprimer les éléments permet d'afficher, triés par taille par défaut, les fichiers envoyés ou reçus dans WhatsApp. Ne reste plus qu'à sélectionner tout ou certains fichiers, puis de les supprimer avec l'icône de poubelle en haut à droite.
Ensuite, deux outils supplémentaires sont disponibles :
- Activer les messages éphémères rentre plutôt dans la première catégorie de ce tutoriel afin de limiter proactivement la place prise par WhatsApp en limitant le nombre de messages stockés.
- Gérer les téléchargements propose de supprimer les téléchargements opérés directement par l'application, comme les transcriptions de messages vocaux.
Enfin, tout en bas sont listées toutes vos discussions par contacts, rangées par espaces que vos conversations avec eux occupent. Là aussi, vous pouvez supprimer tout ou partie des éléments multimédias pour récupérer de l'espace de stockage.
Suivez toute l'actualité des Numériques sur Google Actualités et sur la chaîne WhatsApp des Numériques
