articles.title: Canada to implement QSBS-style tax incentive and ‘level playing field’ with US | BetaKit
articles.text:
The federal government announced a new tax incentive for entrepreneurs in Budget 2026, rewarding a priority ask from the Canadian tech sector.
Budget 2026 outlines the Canada Growth Incentive, which includes two measures: a new tax exemption on up to $15 million CAD in capital gains earned from successful eligible investments, and an expansion of a capital gains tax rollover for small businesses.
The budget document calls the double-measure “one of the most significant incentives to attract and retain builders here in Canada” because it will encourage founders to build companies, early employees to accept equity, and investors to back Canadian companies.
“This is how you create this circle of investment so that innovators, employees, reinvest.”
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne
“By allowing builders to keep more of the benefits when a business succeeds, these measures will help level the playing field with the United States, encourage more capital to flow to Canadian businesses, and enable successful entrepreneurs to reinvest their proceeds into Canada,” the budget reads.
“We’re gonna be very competitive [for] people who want to grow companies, reinvest in Canadian companies,” Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said at a press conference on Thursday.
The changes come after demands from several Canadian tech and investor groups. The Council of Canadian Innovators, the Canadian Venture Capital & Private Equity Association (CVCA), the National Angel Capital Organization (NACO), and other industry associations launched a campaign last month asking the feds to create a tax incentive similar to the US Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) regime.
The QSBS rules in the US allow early investors to shield up to 100 percent of their federal capital gains when a company sells, with a value of up to $10 million USD or 10 times the original investment.
Canada’s new exemption would shield up to $15 million CAD of exit value from capital gains taxes. For instance, a founder with a $15-million gain from selling their business would keep nearly 96 percent of that exit value, compared to 71 percent before.
In practice, that means immediately before and after shares are issued, the combined value of the corporation’s assets can’t exceed $100 million. The business must also be a Canadian-controlled private corporation. For at least two years after shares are issued, the company must be “carried on primarily in Canada.” When the shares are sold, the business can be a Canadian-resident corporation that is either private or publicly listed on a stock exchange located in Canada.
Canada’s tech advocates saw the tax changes as a way to de-risk initial investment in Canadian companies—amid a difficult environment for early-stage fundraising—and to make it easier for the eventual profit to be reinvested into other domestic ventures.
The groups involved in “Bet on Canada” welcomed the federal announcement. CVCA CEO Ben Bergen called it an “important step towards rewarding investors who put capital into Canadian companies,” and NACO CEO Claudio Rojas said it was “the strongest signal in a decade that risk-takers and builders at the earliest stages of growth are a national priority.”
“Bet on Canada” also proposed a broader capital gains rollover that would allow more entrepreneurs and investors, including those investing through corporations or funds, to defer capital gains taxes when they reinvest proceeds into another qualifying Canadian business. A small-business rollover currently exists under the Income Tax Act, allowing individuals to defer capital gains taxes when they reinvest proceeds into another eligible small business by the following year.
The feds did not expand on the eligibility of who can use the small business rollover, but did extend the time period to reinvest shares into another Canadian small business. An individual who has realized capital gains will have three years after the year they sold shares to reinvest them in a qualifying Canadian business. There’s also a provision for individuals who enter into simple agreement for future equity (SAFE) agreements—a common investment structure for early-stage startups—where the capital gain could be deferred for another two years.
The “Bet on Canada” campaign noted that the measures should cover sectors like advanced manufacturing and mining. But the new measures exclude companies operating as consultancies, or those in agricultural, fishing, forestry, mining, financial, insurance, utilities, real estate, food and accommodation, arts, recreation, or entertainment sectors.
RELATED: Canadian tech and investor groups call for tax incentives, capital gains rollover
The new capital gains exemption is immediately coming into effect and is applicable to shares issued before 2037. The expansion of the capital gains rollover will start on Jan. 1, 2027.
The measure represents a complete policy turnaround for the federal Liberals, who, under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau in 2024, butted heads with the tech industry over a controversial capital-gains inclusion rate increase. That measure was axed by then-Prime Minister-designate Mark Carney the evening he won Liberal party leadership.
In Budget 2026, the feds framed the Canada Growth Incentive as a measure to make the country’s tax system more competitive, alongside the previously announced Productivity Mega-Deduction. This measure allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of most new capital investments, such as software, computer hardware, and patents.
The government estimates this will result in a $715-million tax revenue drop by 2031. The budget’s annex also says the measure will benefit the founders, early-stage employees, and shareholders in eligible Canadian corporations, over 80 percent of whom would likely have an adjusted gross income of more than $200,000.
In response to media questions about how this tax break for tech squares with the federal government’s affordability focus, Minister Champagne said he was thinking about supporting Canada’s startups.
“If you want to grow, there’s this kind of valley where you have to go to the United States—you cannot find capital here,” Champagne said. He added that the tax incentive was modelled to be competitive with the US QSBS measure.
“This is how you create this circle of investment so that innovators, employees, reinvest,” the minister said. “We want more Shopifys.”
Feature image courtesy Francois-Philippe Champagne via X.

articles.title: Nicolas Cage rompe su silencio por el fichaje de Ryan Gosling como nuevo 'Ghost Rider' de Marvel
articles.text:
Marvel ya prepara su próxima gran película de Ghost Rider con Ryan Gosling como protagonista. El actor de La La Land y Barbie se pondrá en la piel del Motorista Fantasma para una entrega que llegará en 2028, después de Avengers: Secret Wars, con la intención de abrir camino a una nueva era marvelita. Pero si de alguien queríamos saber su opinión, ese era Nicolas Cage.
Aunque este mismo año hemos podido verle en Marvel en el papel de Ben Reilly /Spider-Noir, en realidad Nicolas Cage interpretó a Ghost Rider en dos películas estrenadas en 2007 y 2012. Por ello, muchos de los fans de La Casa de las Ideas ya asocian irremediablemente su rostro al del Johnny Blaze. Ahora, el intérprete ha revelado al fin qué piensa sobre este nuevo reboot.
"Ryan va a darle su toque personal y tengo muchas ganas de verla. Ryan sabe lo que pienso de él como actor. Hemos tenido conversaciones muy agradables y seguimos en contacto. Me alegré por él, le deseé mucha suerte en sus aventuras y estoy deseando ver la película", asegura en una entrevista concedida a The Hollywood Reporter. En definitiva, Nicolas Cage ha dado su bendición a Ryan Gosling como Ghost Rider.
Qué sabemos de Ghost Rider
De Ghost Rider se sabe es que fue el propio Ryan Gosling, muy fan de sus cómics, quien les presentó la idea a los ejecutivos de Marvel. El filme estará dirigido por Shawn Levy, cineasta responsable de Deadpool y Lobezno. Y es que actor y director ya saben lo que es trabajar juntos, pues están desarrollando actualmente Star Wars: Starfighter, la nueva película de la franquicia galáctica.
También tenemos la fecha de estreno. Ghost Rider se estrenará en cines el 28 de julio de 2028. Esto quiere decir que llegará después de la película de X-Men, que se estrena en mayo de ese mismo año y será la primera entrega de la nueva era de Marvel después de cerrar el multiverso con Avengers: Secret Wars. Lo cierto es que, con la compañía desarrollando abiertamente toda una Saga Mutante, se desconoce exactamente cómo encajará el filme del Motorista Fantasma en esos planes.

articles.title: Dropbox ditched AWS S3 for its own in-house system. Now it’s buying Tigris to sell S3-compatible storage to AI developers.
articles.text:
Dropbox ditched AWS S3 for its own in-house system. Now it’s buying Tigris to sell S3-compatible storage to AI developers.
Dropbox is entering the AI infrastructure space in a big way, announcing plans on Thursday to acquire Tigris, a startup that provides object storage for AI applications.
The cloud-storage giant tells The New Stack that it’s paying $350 million for Tigris, a move designed to accelerate Dropbox’s own ambitions in selling storage infrastructure to developers and businesses. Indeed, alongside the acquisition news, Dropbox also announced DBX Agent Cloud, an upcoming offering that will initially let developers purchase object storage directly from Dropbox.
Dropbox, it’s worth noting, is no stranger to building storage infrastructure itself. Kicking off in 2015, the company moved more than 90% of its user data off Amazon’s S3 cloud storage service onto an in-house system dubbed Magic Pocket, in a bid to improve performance and reduce costs. But as Dropbox chief business officer Eric Webster explains, selling storage infrastructure to external customers presents an entirely different set of challenges.
“Operating infrastructure for Dropbox and offering a storage product to developers involve different requirements,” Webster tells The New Stack. “Tigris brings a working commercial product, an experienced team, developer relationships and early customer traction.”
“Tigris brings a working commercial product, an experienced team, developer relationships and early customer traction.”
That “customer traction” includes a slew of companies such as Amplified, Railway, Runpod, and Replicate, spanning everything from developer hosting platforms to GPU infrastructure and AI model deployment. Precisely the kinds of businesses that need fast, reliable access to large volumes of data, often while running applications and AI models across different environments.
Eye of the Tigris
Founded in 2022 by former Uber engineers Ovais Tariq (CEO), Himank Chaudhary (CTO), and chief architect Yevgeniy Firsov, Tigris has built an S3-compatible storage platform that allows developers to keep their data accessible across different cloud and compute environments.
For developers training AI models, that could mean storing large datasets in one place while renting computing power from multiple providers. Using Amazon S3 in such situations can incur additional data-transfer costs, known as egress fees, and delays, particularly when the computing happens outside AWS. Tigris addresses this by automatically keeping data close to where it’s needed, while charging no egress fees for transfers out of its storage service.
The company announced a $25 million Series A round of funding in October 2025, with investors including Spark Capital and existing backer Andreessen Horowitz.
While much of Tigris’s appeal lies in its existing product, customers and developer relationships, Dropbox sees an opportunity to turn that foothold into a much bigger business in the commercial storage infrastructure market.
“Combining those strengths with Dropbox’s experience operating storage at scale would give us a faster path into this market,” Webster says. “The acquisition lets us build on what both teams have already developed and learned from their customers.”
And so one of the clearest expressions of that ambition is DBX Agent Cloud, a service through which Dropbox plans to sell storage infrastructure to developers building AI applications, with Tigris expected to provide the underlying object-storage technology if the acquisition passes the usual array of regulatory approvals.
But why is Dropbox making this push into AI infrastructure? And why now?
“AI applications are creating and working with growing volumes of content, from images and video to training datasets and model artifacts,” Webster says. “As models and compute providers change, that content needs a consistent home.”
“AI applications are creating and working with growing volumes of content, from images and video to training datasets and model artifacts.”
Founded in 2007, Dropbox has spent the best part of two decades dealing with the challenges of storing and managing vast amounts of customer data, from consumers through the enterprise. And it now hopes to put that experience to work for developers building their own applications.
“DBX Agent Cloud extends that expertise to companies and developers building applications, starting with standalone object storage,” Webster says.
The plan, ultimately, is to add filesystem and content-processing capabilities next, allowing AI applications to work with different types of content, track files, and pick up where they left off across sessions.
Dropbox has yet to provide a launch date for DBX Agent Cloud, or explain exactly how the two companies’ technologies will be integrated.
“We’ll share more about the technical integration and availability as those plans develop,” Webster says.
As for existing Tigris customers, well, Dropbox is promising business as usual, at least initially. Webster says they won’t “need to migrate or change how they use the service” when the acquisition closes, and will “continue to receive support for the Tigris product.”
What happens further down the line is less certain, particularly as Dropbox builds out its own filesystem and content-processing capabilities around Tigris’s foundation.
“As the product evolves, we’ll communicate directly with customers before any changes that affect them,” Webster adds.
Dropbox puts AI to work on files
Alongside the acquisition news on Thursday, Dropbox also announced what it’s calling a “major evolution” of its main product, one that “brings AI-powered capabilities directly to customers’ existing files and workflows,” the company says.
Back in 2023, Dropbox debuted Dash, an AI-powered search tool that allowed users to find information scattered across services such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Dropbox itself. Now, the company is taking things further, allowing users to instruct AI to work directly on their files, from editing PDFs and images, to reorganising folders, transcribing recordings, and completing multi-step tasks.
“Customers told us they wanted these AI-powered features directly in the product where their content and workflows already live,” Mike Torres, Dropbox’s chief product officer, tells The New Stack.
The company had already begun integrating Dash into Dropbox last year, bringing AI-powered search, document summaries, and the ability to ask questions about stored content into the core product.
“The new experience builds on that foundation and what we’ve learned from customers, helping them move from finding and understanding information to organizing files, editing content, and completing supported multi-step tasks,” Torres continues.
“We want customers to have the freedom to use the AI tools that work best for them.”
Dropbox says more than 70,000 teams have received access to the new capabilities, although it hasn’t disclosed how many are actively using them. As for pricing, Torres says that eligible Standard and Advanced plans include a certain allocation of AI credits, with customers able to purchase more as needed.
The company is also giving users a choice of AI models within Dropbox, alongside integrations with third-party tools including ChatGPT and Claude. These connections allow customers to work with their Dropbox files through external AI services without repeatedly uploading them, with the resulting content saved back to Dropbox.
“We want customers to have the freedom to use the AI tools that work best for them,” Torres says.
Behind that, perhaps, lies a similar philosophy to the Tigris acquisition: allowing developers to choose where they run their AI applications while keeping the underlying data accessible. Dropbox is betting it can turn that proposition into a substantial new infrastructure business, although with the acquisition still to close and no launch date for DBX Agent Cloud, it remains to be seen how that ambition translates into a product developers actually want to use.
Learning Path

articles.title: Smart appliances need power and Wi-Fi. A look at who in Africa has both
articles.text:
LG leads South Korea’s laundry and refrigeration markets, and is now pushing connected appliances in the Middle East and Africa, where it already sells other products like home entertainment devices. But where power cuts are common, internet access is patchy, and budgets are tight, paying extra for a smart fridge is a hard sell. Wealthier urban households, hotels and developers are the likely first buyers. In this edition of Delve into AI, Kenn Abuya toured LG’s model home in Seoul and its factory in Busan, and asks what manufacturers must prove before the connected home becomes an everyday purchase on the continent.
The curtains opened as I walked into the model home at LG Electronics’ headquarters in Seoul, South Korea’s capital. The lights came on a beat later. Someone from the LG team said a command and the room changed mood, while a washing machine hummed away in the background, doing its thing. The fridge, dishwasher, and air conditioner were all hooked into the same system, and one interface ran the lot.
It’s a neat party trick, and a serious bet. Appliance makers want to be the software layer in your home, not just the thing that keeps your milk cold. Euromonitor puts LG’s 2025 share of home laundry appliances at 44%, ahead of Samsung’s 37%. In refrigeration, it’s 39% to Samsung’s 34%. Both are now fighting over whose platform you’ll use to run it all.
LG wants to sell its connected appliances across the Middle East and Africa, where the conditions look very different. Power can be unreliable, internet access patchy and household incomes tight. Even people who can afford a connected appliance may find half its features useless without a stable connection. Asking customers to pay extra for smart features is a tough sell where a fridge that simply stays on can’t always be taken for granted.
LG’s regional headquarters in Dubai oversees 75 markets across the Middle East and Africa. Its East African operation, based in Nairobi, covers 16 countries across East and Central Africa, according to LG Electronics East Africa.
The company sells everything from basic household appliances to connected models in the region, but does not disclose how many African customers use its ThinQ app, which controls its connected appliances, or how much it earns from them.
World Bank data for 2024 show that 62.5% of Nigeria’s population had access to electricity, compared with 90.2% in South Africa. In Nigeria, Afrobarometer found in 2024 that only 13% of respondents had reliable electricity from the national grid.
A smart home powered by LG ThinQ services. Image: TechCabal
The model home also raised a question I kept coming back to: what do manufacturers actually mean when they call an appliance AI-powered? Connected appliances can be monitored remotely, switched on or adjusted through an app, and set to send alerts. Some also use data, such as the weight of a laundry load or a household’s usage habits, to suggest settings and tweak how they run.
But connected isn’t the same as intelligent. Curtains that open when you walk in can run on a motion sensor and a pre-programmed routine. A washing machine you can start from your phone is connected, and that’s about it. Even one that weighs the load and picks a cycle may just be working from sensors and preset rules.
Manufacturers charge a premium for the AI label, yet buyers may see little reason to pay extra for features that only work online. In homes that deal with power cuts, the priority is an appliance that keeps food cold or washes clothes once the electricity comes back. Remote controls and automated settings matter less if the machine can’t do its job reliably. Internet access is the same story. A connected appliance can still do its basic work offline, but much of what’s sold as the smart-home experience goes missing.
Juhyun Liu, marketing communications lead at LG’s Home Appliance Solutions, told me the appliances run without an internet connection and work with home automation systems from other manufacturers. Lose connectivity, though, and users lose remote controls, alerts, and data-based settings. The machines can still wash clothes and chill drinks, but they stop being smart.
The limits of the African market
Mobile connectivity is far more common than fixed broadband across much of Africa, while data costs and network quality vary widely by market. For appliances that rely on Wi-Fi, that gap could limit how often people use connected features after they buy the device. Their appeal will depend partly on how well they cope with patchy connections.
Connected features require a compatible appliance and a Wi-Fi connection. Owners can control supported devices remotely, receive notifications, and monitor operation through an app. Much of that is lost in homes that cannot keep a steady connection. Power cuts hit the appliances themselves, whether or not the owner can reach them through the app.
Cost is another hurdle, since smart appliances typically cost more than basic models, and the extra features may not justify the premium. A household buying a fridge is paying, first of all, to keep food cold. Remote temperature monitoring and maintenance alerts come second, especially where budgets are tight.
Some of the smart home appliances need a reliable internet connection and power supply to work well. Image: TechCabal
South Africa offers a glimpse of the market available to manufacturers. Statistics South Africa’s 2024 General Household Survey found that 80.9% of households owned a refrigerator, while 88.3% had an electric stove. Internet access reached 82.1% of households. The figures suggest a consumer market with the basic infrastructure and appliance ownership needed to support connected products, although they do not measure smart-appliance adoption.
Nigeria presents a different proposition. About 61% of Nigerians had access to electricity in 2023, according to the World Bank, compared with 87.7% in South Africa, and supply remains unreliable even for those connected. Internet use stands at 45.5% of the population, compared with 79.6% in South Africa, according to DataReportal. Buyers of connected appliances are likely to be concentrated among wealthier urban households and businesses with dependable power and internet.
Hotels, serviced apartments and property developers could also provide a market. Connected appliances can be useful in properties where operators manage several units and want to monitor equipment, schedule maintenance or control energy use. Such customers may find a stronger business case than households buying individual devices.
The factory behind the appliances
LG’s AI push goes beyond what it sells in shops. In Busan, South Korea’s second-largest city, the company showed the visiting media team the factory floor where its appliances are made.
Photography was not allowed on the tour, but the automation was hard to miss. Machines moved parts between stations, took on the repetitive jobs, and kept watch over the line, with few people on the floor.
LG is now selling that technology and skill. In 2024, the company set up a smart factory division that sells factory planning, automation and operations software to other manufacturers, built on the systems it runs in its own plants.
For African countries courting manufacturers, that cuts both ways. Automated plants can lift output and quality, but they need fewer hands and different skills. Kenya, Nigeria, Egypt and South Africa will have to decide what they’re willing to trade for investment.
Copying Busan also takes more than buying machines. It needs steady electricity, workers who can run and repair the kit, and the data infrastructure behind it. Across much of Africa, those are still missing.
Selling a practical benefit
LG must show African consumers that connected appliances are worth the extra cost. Voice-controlled lighting and appliances that communicate with one another may appeal to wealthier households, but lower electricity bills, reduced water consumption and cheaper repairs offer more concrete benefits.
A washing machine that adjusts its cycle to the laundry load could use less water and electricity. A refrigerator that detects faults early could prevent food spoilage and expensive repairs. These are benefits consumers can measure, unlike the convenience of controlling appliances through a phone.
Some home appliance products at a store in Seoul. Image: TechCabal
ThinQ also depends on Wi-Fi for its connected features. Power interruptions, internet costs, and limited support for African languages could restrict its appeal. Pricing will be another factor, particularly where conventional appliances already stretch household budgets.
Early buyers are likely to be wealthier urban households, hotels, and property developers. Reaching beyond them will take lower prices and products that cut bills under local conditions. That isn’t an African problem alone; a fully connected home still isn’t an everyday purchase anywhere. But with shakier grids and tighter budgets, the gap between premium and mainstream could take longer to close here.

articles.title: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscriptsclaiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.
Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.
On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.
Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.
The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.
Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.
Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.
For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.
That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.
“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”
The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.
“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.
To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”
Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.
The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan said.
Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.”
Axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”
Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.
Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.
“We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan said. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”
The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.
“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong said. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”
Hong is confident enough in that approach to issue a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”

articles.title: Canada’s drone ambitions put domestic manufacturers to the test | BetaKit
articles.text:
To anyone pitching themselves as a Canadian drone manufacturer, Josh Ogden has a question: If you’ve assembled IKEA furniture, are you a manufacturer?
“If we’re going to build, let’s be honest about what that means. Building means building our own product.”
Josh Ogden, AVSS
It may sound like a joke, but the co-founder and CEO of AVSS is making a serious point as Ottawa looks to expand its drone fleet and build a domestic supply chain to support it. If Canada wants control over the technology it needs to defend itself, Ogden says, it needs people who know how it was built and can change and adapt it quickly when required. Just being the people who put a drone together from someone else’s design doesn’t give the country that sovereign control.
“If we’re going to build, let’s be honest about what that means. Building means building our own products,” Ogden said in an interview with BetaKit.
His comments come as federal spending opens new opportunities for the sector. In September, Ottawa announced its Defence Drone Initiative Marketplace, a digital procurement platform for the Canadian Armed Forces and Coast Guard to acquire drones and counter-drone systems. AVSS, which operates in Ottawa and New Brunswick, was among six Canadian companies awarded initial contracts collectively worth up to $50 million.
Now, with nearly 400 suppliers qualified for the marketplace and further requests for proposals expected, Ogden sees an opportunity for those purchases to strengthen Canadian engineering and manufacturing. He wants buyers to consider who owns the technology, where the expertise is, and whether a supplier can make changes without turning to a foreign partner for permission or advice.
“If there’s a shortage in one chip, you should be able to go and have your designs done so that you can modify that chip without talking to anybody,” he said.
Designing for disruption
Ogden doesn’t have to look far for an example of why sovereign capability matters; his own company had to learn how to keep manufacturing through the supply-chain disruptions of COVID-19.
AVSS brought its first product to market in 2020, after three years developing and testing parachute safety technology that helps drones meet strict aviation requirements to fly over people. As the pandemic took hold, the company ran into chip shortages, unpredictable component prices, and injection-moulding suppliers laying off staff.
AVSS began stockpiling parts, but the experience also changed how its engineers learned how to design future products. Modular design, for instance, became a priority, giving the team room to swap components as supplies and costs shifted.
“What COVID taught us was how to design for potential shortages, price increases, and making modifications,” said Ogden.
He sees that experience as a vital part of what established Canadian manufacturers bring to defence work. “Any company that existed before COVID—and made it through COVID—is already tougher. They’ve already got the calluses.”
Owning the innovation
The same ability to make changes proved useful when AVSS received a request from the avalanche industry.
The company had become the first in Canada approved to drop explosives from drones for avalanche mitigation, carrying out demonstrations in Alberta’s Jasper National Park. Its system dropped five pounds, but the feedback was to develop a way to release a 50-pound bag of explosive material.
AVSS received the request in March, and, over the following months, its engineers redesigned the new release system. Ogden said the company has now produced three product lines ready for testing in the mountains.
Making those changes quickly and accurately required detailed knowledge of the hardware, including the strength of attachment points and the forces acting on them.
“You can’t do that when you don’t own the IP, and you don’t know how it was built and how you can modify it,” said Ogden.
A company licensing foreign technology may have to pay ongoing fees and accept limits on where it can sell. Owning the technology gives Canadian manufacturers more freedom to reach customers abroad and keep more of each sale to invest in products and jobs at home.
Building domestic expertise
AVSS is ready for a busy 2027, with the recent expansion activities finalized and new contracts to deliver more than 1,000 drones and associated equipment to the federal government over the year. That’s on top of a commercial business that sold more than 2,500 units of its parachute safety technology, avalanche tech, and integrated systems worldwide this year.
The company is increasing its workforce to support its growth. AVSS currently has approximately 50 staff in Ottawa and five in New Brunswick, with plans to reach 70 by December. An expansion that triples its facility space is also nearly complete, and Ogden is already planning to grow it fivefold next year.
AVSS is also developing the engineers it will need. Junior staff spend two years working on technology alongside senior colleagues and without the commercial deadlines handled by more experienced team members.
“That is what it takes to build a sustainable company,” he noted.
For him, every purchase is a chance to build up Canadian expertise so the country can develop, produce, and adapt the technology it needs without depending on anyone else.
“We’re building capability so that when someone comes to me and says, ‘Can you modify this drone?’ The answer is yes, and I could do it that day.”

articles.title: Klimaanpassung, jetzt! So steht es um Deutschlands Kampf gegen den Klimawandel
articles.text:
Plan B für Deutschland: Wie weit sind wir bei Strategien zur Klimaanpassung?
„Es ging nicht mehr“, sagt Markus Funke. Seit über 20 Jahren wohnt er am nordwestlichen Stadtrand von Frankfurt am Main. Ende Juni lagen die Temperaturen dort bei über 40 Grad, begleitet von hoher Luftfeuchtigkeit. Klimaanlagen waren ausverkauft. Nach ein paar Tagen kapitulierte er und zog für zwei Nächte in ein klimatisiertes Hotel. Das hat den 57-Jährigen nachdenklich gemacht, denn er erwägt schon länger aus privaten Gründen einen Umzug nach Norddeutschland. Nun kommt auch noch der Klimawandel dazu. „Ich hätte früher nie vermutet, dass die Hitze bei der Entscheidung mal eine Rolle spielen könnte“, sagt er.
Fast 16.000 Menschen aus Deutschland haben diese Option nicht mehr. Sie sind tot, gestorben während der Hitzewelle im Sommer 2026. Das Robert Koch-Institut hat ermittelt, dass viele von ihnen statistisch gesehen noch lange hätten leben können. Das Problem betrifft auch junge und gesunde Menschen. „In den letzten 24 Stunden haben wir sieben Menschen bewusstlos in ihren Wohnungen aufgefunden“, schrieb die Feuerwehr Köln im Juni auf Instagram. „Und nein, auch Menschen ohne Vorerkrankungen, fit und mitten im Leben, befanden sich mit 42 Grad Körpertemperatur in Lebensgefahr.“
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 8/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns mit den Folgen des Klimawandels und wie wir uns an Hitze, Dürre und Überschwemmungen anpassen sollten. Das Heft erscheint am 06.11.2026 im Zeitschriftenhandel und ist auch in unserem Online-Shop bestellbar.
Viele Europäer glaubten lange, der Klimawandel betreffe vor allem ferne Gegenden wie Südseeinseln, afrikanische Farmen oder asiatische Küsten. Doch nun zeigt sich: Er bedroht auch Leib und Leben in vermeintlich gut gewappneten Industriestaaten. Trockenheit und Hitze bedrohen Felder und Wälder, Niedrigwasser den Warenverkehr, Überflutungen die Küsten und Täler, überhitzte Arbeitsplätze die Produktivität, vertrocknete Feuchtgebiete die Artenvielfalt. Mehr noch: Europa erwärmt sich seit den 1980er-Jahren doppelt so schnell wie der Rest der Welt, wie das EU-Programm Copernicus festgestellt hat. Zu den Ursachen zählen die dichte Besiedlung Europas sowie seine Nähe zu den abschmelzenden Eismassen des Nordpolarmeers.
Gut gefüllte Tatenbank
Die wirksamste (und zugleich wirtschaftlichste) Gegenmaßnahme wäre natürlich eine Senkung der Treibhausgase. Sich stattdessen an die Folgen anzupassen – etwa durch höhere Dämme, schattigere Städte, robustere Wälder – gilt vielen Klimaschützern als ein Herumdoktern an den Symptomen, als eine Ausrede, sich nicht um die wirklichen Ursachen zu kümmern. Doch es hilft nichts: Seit Jahrzehnten steigt die CO₂-Konzentration in der Atmosphäre. Plan A darf damit als gescheitert gelten. Aber vielleicht läuft es mit Plan B, der Anpassung, ja besser?
In anderen Ländern machen spektakuläre Großprojekte Schlagzeilen: Niederländische Ingenieure schlagen beispielsweise vor, einen 80 Kilometer langen Damm durch die Beringstraße zu bauen, um das arktische Eis vor warmem Pazifikwasser zu schützen. In Venedig ist seit 2021 ein sechs Milliarden Euro teures Sperrwerk aus 78 beweglichen Toren im Einsatz. London plant, die seit den 1980er Jahren bestehende Thames Barrier ab 2030 durch ein neues, noch größeres Sperrwerk zu ersetzen.
In Deutschland listet die „Tatenbank“ des Umweltbundesamts derzeit 481 Anpassungsprojekte auf. Allerdings liest sich diese Liste in Teilen recht beliebig: Da werden Megaprojekte zum Küstenschutz oder schon seit Jahren laufende Flussumbauten ebenso aufgeführt wie ein paar kümmerliche Bäumchen in einer Wohnstraße; ein begrünter Schulhof hier, eine Projektwoche da und eine Fortbildung dort.
Solche Kleinteiligkeit liegt einerseits in der Natur der Sache, schließlich wirkt sich der Klimawandel von Ort zu Ort und von Branche zu Branche sehr unterschiedlich aus. Andererseits führt diese Zersplitterung auch zu vielen verpassten Chancen.

articles.title: Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
articles.text:
Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use.
Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
Like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet, Perplexity’s Teammates can perform an array of tasks while running 24/7.
Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer, an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet. Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan.
Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X.

articles.title: Why Integrated Gate Drive Regulation Matters For High Reliability Space GaN Designs
articles.text:
Eliminating the need for a separate bias regulator dedicated to the gate driver for a more streamlined power architecture.
As Gallium Nitride (GaN) technology becomes increasingly prevalent in space power systems, designers are leveraging its inherent capabilities to deliver higher efficiency, faster switching speeds, and greater power density. These advantages help designers support the growing demands of modern satellite platforms.
While GaN devices are central to many modern power architectures, achieving their full efficiency and switching performance depends on the gate driver that controls them. Infineon HiRel’s new, rad hard single-channel gate driver for GaN delivers the precise drive conditions that GaN devices require. Designed specifically for extreme environment applications, the device incorporates an integrated low dropout regulator (LDO). The LDO simplifies gate-drive implementation while providing a tightly regulated voltage optimized for GaN operation, while also reducing the total bill of materials (BOM).
The switching advantages of GaN stem from device characteristics such as low gate charge, reduced output capacitance, and fast transition times. These attributes enable lower switching losses and support operation at higher frequencies than traditional silicon MOSFET (Si) technologies.
Designers must provide stable and controlled gate-drive voltages to achieve optimal switching behavior. Even relatively small variations in gate voltage can affect switching losses, power-stage efficiency, electromagnetic interference (EMI), device stress, and long-term reliability. GaN devices have extremely high slew rates (dv/dt) when switching. As a result, maintaining a stable and well-controlled gate-drive voltage is critical for predictable system performance across operating conditions.
Traditionally, designers generate the gate-drive supply rail using external regulators, bias circuits, or dedicated auxiliary power supplies. While effective, these approaches add components, consume board area, and create additional design considerations related to regulation accuracy, startup behavior, and power sequencing. In space systems, every additional component increases design complexity. It can also drive up qualification and testing costs, add weight, and extend development timelines. Infineon HiRel’s new RIC70115 gate driver simplifies this architecture with many integrated features, such as an integrated LDO that generates a tightly regulated 4.8 V gate-drive rail from input voltages ranging from 4.75 V to 15 V.
By regulating the gate-drive supply internally, the RIC70115 helps ensure that GaN transistors receive a consistent drive voltage, even as upstream supply rails vary during normal operations. This approach aligns directly with recommendations outlined in the application note, which emphasizes the importance of maintaining tightly controlled gate-drive conditions to support efficient and reliable GaN HEMT operation in space environments. Even better is that no additional external components are needed to deliver this regulated drive voltage, helping customers meet their SWaP-C needs. For space programs operating under tight development timelines, this reduction in design complexity can support faster qualification efforts and lower implementation risk.
Space power systems present unique challenges beyond those encountered in terrestrial applications. Every additional component introduces potential reliability considerations, increases PCB area requirements, and compromises qualification and system-level verification efforts.
The integrated LDO within the RIC70115 eliminates the need for a separate bias regulator dedicated to the gate driver. This results in a more streamlined power architecture that supports the industry’s ongoing pursuit of reduced size, weight, and power (SWaP) advantages. By consolidating gate-drive regulation within the controller itself, designers can reduce component count without sacrificing the precision required for high-performance GaN operation.
As designers transition from Si to GaN, solutions that simplify implementation without sacrificing performance stand out.
The RIC70115 does just that. With high-speed gate driving and integrated voltage regulation, the device helps optimize GaN operation. Rather than developing and validating a separate regulated gate-drive supply, designers can rely on the device to provide a controlled and consistent bias environment directly within the gate-driver architecture. The integrated approach helps reduce design complexity while enabling the efficiency, switching speed, and power density advantages that drive GaN adoption in next-generation satellite power systems.
Evaluate RIC70115 with Infineon HiRel’s companion evaluation board, the RIC70115EVAL1. Prepopulated with two RIC70115 gate driver ICs and two IG1NT052N10R GaN HEMTs in a half-bridge configuration, the evaluation board highlights RIC70115’s ability to operate in both high- and low-side configurations.
When paired with the right gate driver, GaN can enable a more power-dense spacecraft power architecture. Through its integrated LDO, the RIC70115 helps designers reduce complexity, streamline development, and take full advantage of GaN’s efficiency and performance benefits. Take the next step in next-generation space exploration: download the RIC70115 datasheet and the application note to learn more.

articles.title: La DGA a conçu son propre drone naval kamikaze en six mois, et elle veut maintenant le produire en série
articles.text:
En à peine six mois, la Direction générale de l'armement a conçu SMOKERS, une munition navale télé-opérée, une sorte de drone kamikaze à bas coût destiné à la Marine nationale, qui vient d'être présenté.
Avec SMOKERS, la Direction générale de l'armement (DGA) a dévoilé cette semaine un drone naval kamikaze entièrement développé par ses propres ingénieurs, sans passer par un industriel de l’armement. Testée par la Marine nationale lors de l'exercice Wildfire, ce qui est à considérer comme une munition navale télé-opérée mise sur une conception volontairement simple, et surtout un coût unitaire réduit. Un appel d'offres vient d’être lancé pour confier sa fabrication en série à l'industrie, avec un premier jalon fixé à la mi-2027.
Six mois chrono pour la munition navale télé-opérée de la DGA
L'ingénieur principal de l'armement Quentin, chef de projet SMOKERS au centre DGA Techniques hydrodynamiques, résume très bien ce qu'est cet engin. Il s'agit d'« un objet qui flotte, qui transporte une charge explosive et qui la met à feu contre sa cible ». Avec un garde-fou de taille, car il y a « en permanence un homme dans la boucle ». Un opérateur pilote en effet l'appareil à distance, à l'aide d'une liaison satellite, en gardant les yeux rivés sur une vidéo en temps réel. Ce cordon ombilical est aussi un point sensible, car le ministère des Armées reconnaît lui-même que garder le contact sous brouillage reste l'un des grands défis des drones navals.
SMOKERS, c'est à peine cinq mètres de long, 500 kilos, une coque en résine et fibre de verre, ainsi qu'un moteur hors-bord ordinaire, cousin de ceux des semi-rigides. Cela suffit pour atteindre 40 nœuds, environ 74 km/h, sur une cinquantaine de milles nautiques, soit un peu plus de 90 km. Une boule optronique, sorte de tourelle à caméras munie d'un capteur thermique, lui permet d'y voir la nuit. Son système pyrotechnique est même imprimé en 3D. Le tout pour un coût visé de quelques dizaines de milliers d'euros pièce.
Cela peut prêter à sourire, mais l'acronyme SMOKERS signifie « Système maritime opérationnel kamikaze évolutif en réalisation souveraine »). Il faut savoir qu'il n'aura fallu que six mois à l'engin pour passer du statut de l'idée à la mer. Plutôt que de passer commande à un industriel, la DGA a fait travailler ses propres équipes, coordonnées par le CERDAN, son centre expert des drones navals, avec l'appui de l'Agence de l'innovation de défense (AID) au lancement. Le centre DGA Techniques navales, à Toulon, a signé l'électronique et le logiciel. DGA Techniques hydrodynamiques s'est occupé de la coque et de la navigation. Le tout nourri des leçons de l'Ukraine et du golfe Arabo-Persique.
Éprouvé en mer, le drone kamikaze se cherche des missions… et des chantiers
Un exemplaire est exposé cette semaine à Euronaval, sur le stand du ministère des Armées et des Anciens combattants, et ce n'est pas une maquette. C'est « le vrai drone tel qu'il a navigué lors des exercices Wildfire et Typhoon », insiste Quentin. Après plusieurs campagnes d'essais à Toulon et à Cherbourg, trois unités ont rejoint fin septembre Wildfire, un exercice de lutte anti-drones. Ils ont été mis en œuvre depuis une frégate, un porte-hélicoptères amphibie et un ravitailleur, et au moins l'un d'eux était configuré en cible. On mesure bien le chemin parcouru depuis avril 2025, quand la Marine testait une simple motomarine chargée d'explosifs. L'autre belle trouvaille de SMOKERS, c'est l'étrave, la pointe avant de la coque, qui se démonte, ce qui permet de stocker la charge à part.
Le drone pourrait frapper une flotte adverse « comme on se servirait d'un missile naval ». Il pourrait aussi attaquer par surprise un port défendu, lors d'une opération spéciale menée avec des moyens commandos par exemple. Et enfin, il pourrait s'inscrire dans une logique de dissuasion, « pour remplacer des missiles ». L'idée semble être de menacer l'adversaire sans avoir à puiser dans des stocks de missiles bien plus coûteux.
Désormais, il faut envisager une production à la chaîne. La DGA, qui est propriétaire des plans, a lancé un appel d'offres de 36 millions d'euros TTC. Un industriel (Naval Group ?) devra ajuster la conception, monter l'outil de production et fabriquer SMOKERS en série, pendant quatre ans, avec deux années en prolongation envisagées. Conçu sans vraie complication, l'engin pourrait même sortir des petits chantiers du littoral, plaisance comprise, imagine-t-on à la DGA. Son industrialisation fait partie du premier volet du programme « drones navals », lancé en juin 2026, volet qui doit entrer en réalisation mi-2027.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 05, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 05, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, November 05, 2026.
From how KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand, began as a college project and became a full-time venture in 202, to how PhysicsWallah and Lenskart's doubled their profit in the second quarter of FY27, here are the latest developments across sectors.
Featured Stories
How KumaonKhand is building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand
KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand, began as a college project and became a full-time venture in 2021 with his mother, Sangeeta and Anuj Sharma, the founder and CEO of Alsisar Impact, a social impact incubator and investment firm.
A problem-mapping exercise through an environmental and social lens pointed toward hemp as a solution.
Latest News
altM raises $10.3M in Series A funding
Specialty chemicals startup altM has raised $10.3 million in a Series A funding round, with Rainmatter by Zerodha and Mela Ventures joining as new investors. Existing backers Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact also participated in the round, along with strategic angel investors.
The Bengaluru-based company said it will use the funds to expand its manufacturing capacity, strengthen research and development, support customer qualification programmes, and grow its engineering and commercial teams. The investment will help altM transition from pilot-scale production to commercial manufacturing.
Funding News
Venomics AI raises $2.7M pre-seed round led by Speciale Invest, South Park Commons
Bengaluru-based Venomics AI, a biotechnology startup spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), has raised $2.7 million in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. Co-founded by Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, the company uses artificial intelligence, venom biology and laboratory screening to identify venom-derived molecules with therapeutic potential.
The funding will be used to expand its Venom Atlas molecular dataset, strengthen AI and experimental screening capabilities, hire across research and computational science, and validate promising molecules. The startup aims to build a drug discovery platform for global markets.
Other News
Zoho launches restaurant POS platform in India
Zoho has launched a point-of-sale (POS) platform for restaurants in India, with Kolkata-based sweet shop Asha Sweets becoming its first customer. The product is being offered free of charge to restaurants with annual billing of up to Rs 12 lakh, as part of Zoho’s push to bring smaller food businesses onto digital platforms.
In a post on X, Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu said Asha Sweets began using Zoho POS for Restaurants during the festive rush. Zoho’s team visited the outlet to observe how the platform was being used during one of its busiest periods.
Prodigi Connect partners with Indonesia's Lokanima to develop AI-powered animation for Fun Cican
Dubai-headquartered AI video production company Prodigi Connect has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Lokanima, a creative venture of Indonesia's Singhasari Special Economic Zone, to develop animated content based on Indonesian children's entertainment property Fun Cican.
The partnership will combine Prodigi Connect's AI-native production capabilities and India-based operations with Lokanima's intellectual property access, local creative direction and Indonesian production talent. Prodigi Connect has already produced an approximately one-minute animation sequence as an initial demonstration. The collaboration aims to reduce the cost and time associated with conventional animation production while expanding the company's presence in international character-based intellectual property development.
75% of Gen Z and Millennials more likely to travel across generations, finds Airbnb survey
Airbnb's 2026 intergenerational travel survey found that 75% of Gen Z and Millennial respondents are more likely to travel with family members across generations. The findings highlight a growing preference for holidays centred on shared experiences, with 55% citing creating memories and 51% strengthening family bonds as key motivations.
Airbnb reported a more than 55% year-on-year increase in domestic searches for stays by groups of five or more travelling with children or infants. The survey also found that 63% of respondents prioritise relaxing together at their accommodation over sightseeing. Bangalore, Goa, Hyderabad, The Nilgiris and Pondicherry feature among popular domestic destinations.
This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.

Au tour de Dreame de sortir son styler. Polyvalent, l'AirStyle Pro permet de sécher, coiffer, lisser et boucler les cheveux d’un tour de main. Avec ses six embouts, il part à l’assaut d’un Dyson Airwrap de plus en plus concurrencé.

articles.title: Anthropic toma medidas drásticas contra los clones de videojuegos de IA hechos con Claude
articles.text:
El mundo de los videojuegos está viviendo una revolución debido a la IA. Muchos grandes estudios la usan, con exponentes tan extremos como una Epic Games que hasta se ha vibecodeado la tienda, pero lo que las grandes productoras ven como una herramienta, en el mundo independiente es visto como una bomba. La muestra es el último festival de demos de Steam, donde la idea era dar a conocer demos de juegos futuros para que los usuarios los tengan en el radar y añadan a la lista de deseados que tanto ayuda a estos desarrolladores.
En la última edición, la cantidad de contenido hecho con IA eclipsaba a los lanzamientos desarrollados por personas, pero lo peor no es eso: lo peor es que hay desarrolladores que no quieren subir demos por miedo a que alguien con IA copie todo su trabajo antes de que el juego legítimo salga a la venta. Anthropic va a tomar medidas, pero el problema es que es complicado que sirva para algo.
En corto. A través de The Verge, vemos que Anthropic ha actualizado el sistema de Claude Code para que las instrucciones internas que orientan al modelo antes de cada conversación no deje recrear videojuegos existentes. Ha sido un usuario de Twitter el que señaló este cambio de condiciones hacia el 27 de octubre, localizando las nuevas reglas de la herramienta bajo el identificador "tengu_heron_brook".
Esta regla permite crear juegos originales, juegos pertenecientes a un género y juegos basados tanto en diseños como en recursos propios del usuario. Lo que no deja es reconstruir un juego específico, aunque se le cambie el nombre o se presente como algo original. Este usuario afirma que es una regla que no se puede desactivar y la propia Anthropic ha confirmado el cambio.
¿Y si se equivoca? También en Twitter, Addy Osmani, que es miembro del equipo técnico de Anthropic, explicó que añadieron dos frases al prompt de Claude Code sobre Opus 5.5 para que no pueda recrear el juego concreto de otra persona. Es algo que va contra sus propias políticas de uso, pero deja ver que puede haber fallos en el programa y que rechace algo propio. En ese caso, Osmani afirma que pueden escribir al soporte.
El porqué. La razón ya la hemos dicho: propiedad intelectual. Y el problema es que, como apuntan en PC Gamer, Opus 5.5 es extremadamente bueno en hacer ingeniería inversa de código. Esto ha alimentado varias cosas, desde una ola de juegos de consolas recompilados (reconstruidos para que sean ejecutados en PC de forma nativa) hasta clones descarados que roban el contenido original de juegos. Incluso aquellos que no se han lanzado.
Problema. Antes hablaba del festival de demos de Steam, algo conocido como Steam Next. Se trata de un evento que estaba pensado para que los desarrolladores (tanto grandes como pequeños) lanzaran demos de sus juegos con la esperanza de que destacaran y llamaran la atención de los jugadores. Si alguien jugaba una demo de tu juego y le gustaba, había probabilidades de que lo añadiera a la lista de deseados, lo que podría convertirse en una futura venta cuando el juego se acabara.
Y el problema de la última edición no es la cantidad de basura hecha con IA, sino que hay desarrolladores que trabajan "a mano" que no han lanzado demos por miedo a que llegue otro con la IA y les copie el juego. No es un temor a la ligera:
- Alliance Arts canceló la demo de 'Drunken Goddess Reflux'por miedo a que aparecieran copias hechas con IA antes del lanzamiento del juego. Lo sustituyó por un periodo de beta cerrada por sorteo.
- Digital Sun Games canceló la prueba de 'ReVamp' por el mismo motivo, alegando que una demo pública es un riesgo demasiado alto.
- Studio Bitdot tiene 'Needle in a Haystack Simulator' y han aparecido una cantidad obscena de clones, hasta el punto de que en la ficha de Steam, el original ha puesto una etiqueta de "original".
Puertas al campo. Hay desarrolladores que se están planteando incluso retrasar tráileres para no mostrar esa mecánica, estilo artístico o idea que hacen que sus juegos sean especiales por el miedo a que alguien con IA lo clone sin pudor, y este es un problema mayúsculo porque las demos y la promoción intensa son claves para que los estudios pequeños logren hacerse un hueco. 'GTA VI' no necesitó ni un gameplay para que las reservas explotaran, pero 'Cairn', por poner un ejemplo, necesitaba toda la carne en el asador para ser atractivo.
La propia Valve, responsable de Steam, reconoció que esto es un problema y dos de los responsables del equipo de negocio apuntaron que los clones existían desde antes de la IA y que no querían ser los guardianes. ¿La recomendación? Que los juegos no dependan sólo de una mecánica fácil de copiar, algo mucho más fácil de decir que de hacer.
Y el problema es que esto cubre Claude Code sobre Opus 5.5, una sola herramienta que sí, puede ser la más capaz en estos momentos, pero el resto de grandes empresas de la IA tienen su propio brazo de programación y, a medida que se hagan más y más capaces, más clones descarados y 'slop' aparecerán en las tiendas digitales. Y luego está por ver si, realmente, cambiar esas líneas de código servirá para algo... o quien quiera copiar algo podrá dar la vuelta a la petición para seguir haciéndolo.

articles.title: El gasto anual de los británicos en inteligencia artificial supera los 1.400 millones de dólares y sigue en alza
articles.text:
Los consumidores del Reino Unido gastan más de 1.000 millones de libras al año (USD 1.400 millones) en suscripciones de IA. Claude, de Anthropic, concentró el 29,4% del gasto directo en julio, frente al 7,4% de diciembre de 2025, según un estudio de tres universidades.
La investigación es un documento de trabajo de Nikhil Datta, Peter John Lambert y Patrick Schneider, de la Universidad de Warwick, la London School of Economics y el Imperial College de Londres. Analizó registros anonimizados de 14,2 millones de cuentas bancarias y de tarjetas del país, y cuenta con apoyo del centro CAGE y del consejo de investigación ESRC.
ChatGPT, de OpenAI, sigue primero, pero su parte bajó del 73,5% al 52,5% en esos siete meses. Gemini, de Google, pasó del 5,8% al 5,1%, y el resto de los proveedores se mantuvo en torno al 13%. El estudio mide el gasto en pagos directos a los proveedores y excluye las compras hechas a través de las tiendas de aplicaciones.
El total de mercado sí incluye una estimación de esas compras: a la tasa de julio de 2026, el gasto de los adultos británicos en productos de IA equivale a 1.070 millones de libras al año, según el sitio del estudio.
Uno de cada 20 adultos paga por un asistente de IA
En junio de 2026, el 5,1% de los adultos del Reino Unido pagaba por un asistente de IA, unos 2,8 millones de personas. Un año antes, la proporción era del 2,3%. El sitio del estudio publica una actualización cada mes.
El perfil de quienes pagan es desigual. Entre los adultos de 20 a 29 años, el 17,9% ha pagado alguna vez por IA, frente al 3,0% de los mayores de 60. En el tramo de ingresos mensuales superior a 4.000 libras, la cifra es del 18,8%, y en el inferior a 1.500 libras, del 10,0%.
Por profesión, los trabajadores de tecnología de la información encabezan la lista, con el 20,3%. Les siguen los profesores universitarios, con el 16,0%, y los profesionales de finanzas y seguros, con el 15,8%. En julio, los hombres pagaban 28% más que las mujeres: 62,2 por cada 1.000 adultos, contra 48,6.
Los planes que explican el salto de Claude
Según el estudio, ChatGPT aún lidera por amplio margen en suscriptores activos de asistentes: 71,2% frente a 27,1% de Claude en julio de 2026. La brecha es menor en dinero que en usuarios. El documento atribuye parte de la diferencia a que el 6,2% de los suscriptores de Claude paga planes de más de 80 libras al mes, contra el 0,3% en ChatGPT.
Esa mejora de plan explica cerca de una cuarta parte del aumento de la cuota de gasto de Claude entre diciembre y julio. El resto proviene de usuarios nuevos, según el documento. Los autores fechan el cambio tras el lanzamiento de Claude Opus 4.5 y la difusión de la herramienta de programación Claude Code.
El estudio también rastrea el origen de los nuevos suscriptores de Claude: cerca de una quinta parte había sido cliente de ChatGPT y había cancelado. Además, los lanzamientos importantes de Anthropic se asocian con un aumento de 39,5% en nuevas altas, frente al 10% de un período al azar.
Peter Lambert, de Warwick, dijo que le sorprendió “el puro volumen” de gasto. Según el estudio, que ChatGPT Go, el plan de entrada de OpenAI de 7 a 8 libras mensuales, atrajo sobre todo a quienes no habían pagado nunca: el 70,2% de sus compradores británicos.

articles.title: Shigeru Miyamoto (73 años), sobre la inteligencia artificial generativa: “Si la IA llegara a encargarse de todo, siempre habrá un papel para nosotros”
articles.text:
Shigeru Miyamoto cree que, aunque la inteligencia artificial tome más funciones, los creadores tienen algo que ofrecer. “Si la IA llegara a encargarse de todo, siempre habrá un papel para nosotros”, ha dicho el diseñador de Nintendo. Para ello, hace referencia a cómo se concibe una obra y cómo se desarrolla.
El creador de Mario y The Legend of Zelda ha comentado este tema en una comparecencia relacionada con la concesión de la Orden de la Cultura de Japón. Cuando le han preguntado sobre la IA generativa y el desarrollo de videojuegos, ha hecho referencia a los cambios tecnológicos que ha vivido su generación.
La evolución de las herramientas
Por ejemplo, recuerda cómo pasaron de las máquinas de escribir a los procesadores de texto. En aquella época, las herramientas estaban en constante evolución. Cree que el avance de los ordenadores les ha ayudado a entender mejor la capacidad de los diseñadores. En este sentido, considera que la IA generativa puede suponer un cambio similar.
Ha explicado que hay un aspecto que es el de la estructura global. Es decir, cómo se concibe algo. Y otro que es el de rellenar los huecos o de pulir detalles. Estos pueden ser trabajos agradables. Pero existe el riesgo de confusión entre la satisfacción de hacer el trabajo y el hecho de tener una obra de calidad.
La intención del creador
Por ello cree que cuanto más deleguen en la inteligencia artificial, más oportunidades de reflexionar sobre lo que realmente importa de su obra tendrán los creadores. También ve aquí un potencial beneficio de la herramienta, que es que te hace repensar qué es lo que tú aportas.
Además, también recuerda que los diseños de copia y pega raramente sobreviven. Lo que les falta es la intención personal. Aquí sigue siendo el creador el que tiene la intención y el ordenador es una herramienta para realizar el trabajo.

articles.title: Kia n'avait visiblement pas assez de SUV électriques et préparerait un EV7
articles.text:
La gamme électrique de Kia ressemble déjà à un catalogue de SUV. En Europe, la marque coréenne vend le petit SUV urbain EV2, le crossover EV3, le SUV compact EV5, la berline crossover EV6 et le grand SUV EV9, sans compter la berline compacte EV4 et le van PV5. Bref, une gamme déjà bien complète.
Mais cela ne semble pas suffire pour la marque coréenne puisqu’un nouveau nom viendrait s’y ajouter : l’EV7, un SUV électrique de taille « moyenne » qui serait produit dans l’usine de Gwangju, en Corée du Sud. L’information a fuité d’un document interne publié ce mardi 3 novembre par Korean Car Blog. En revanche aucune date de sortie ni de fiche technique n’a filtré.
Un document de la future production de Kia
Ce document viendrait du comité de stabilité de l’emploi de Kia, une instance où la direction et le syndicat négocient ce que chaque usine coréenne va produire. Il liste les projets site par site : un Carnival hybride entièrement nouveau en 2028 à Gwangmyeong, un Carnival à hydrogène d’ici 2029 et un nouveau Sorento hybride en 2028 à Hwaseong. L’EV7 n’y a droit qu’à une ligne, selon laquelle sa production à Gwangju serait actée. C’est dans cette même usine qu’est déjà assemblé l’EV5 vendu en Europe.
Le document a l’air crédible, car il indique aussi que l’usine de Hanam, rattachée à Gwangju, arrêterait les grands autobus pour se consacrer aux véhicules militaires. Or, en juin 2026, la direction de Kia avait bien annoncé au syndicat la fin de la production de son bus Granbird. Pour autant, un plan de production peut encore bouger d’ici 2028. Il faut donc prendre l’EV7 avec des pincettes tant que Kia n’a pas officialisé son arrivée.
Près de 40 centimètres de vide entre l’EV5 et l’EV9
Sur le papier, la place existe dans la gamme. L’EV5 mesure 4,61 m de long et l’EV6 4,68 m. Au-dessus, l’EV9 passe directement à 5,01 m et peut accueillir sept occupants. On pourrait donc supposer que l’EV7 s’intercale entre les deux avec une longueur autour des 4,80 m. Un gabarit semblable à celui du SUV hybride Sorento (le haut de gamme thermique de la marque), accessoirement le modèle le plus vendu en Corée du Sud en 2025.
Côté technique, il y aura fort à parier qu’une architecture 800 volts soit de la partie à ce niveau de gamme. On pourrait également imaginer que l’EV7 reprenne la batterie de 84 kWh de l’EV6, ce qui serait en adéquation avec le format du SUV.
Neuf SUV électriques prévus d’ici 2030
Kia ne cache pas son goût pour les SUV. Lors de sa journée investisseurs du 9 avril 2026, la marque avait annoncé vouloir passer de 11 modèles électriques en 2026 à 14 en 2030, dont neuf SUV, deux voitures qui n’en sont pas et trois utilitaires. L’EV7 entrerait donc sans mal dans ce plan. Kia a aussi promis une nouvelle plateforme électrique, avec jusqu’à 40 % de capacité de batterie en plus, sans dire quels modèles en profiteront.
Mais entre un EV5, un EV7 et un EV9 un peu plus grand, un acheteur de SUV familial électrique aurait le choix entre trois Kia séparés de quelques dizaines de centimètres, et la marque risquerait de cannibaliser sa gamme.
