articles.title: Web3Bridge expands into startup incubation as Web3 funding shrinks
articles.text:
Web3Bridge, the Nigerian developer training organisation that has trained blockchain engineers since 2019, is expanding into startup incubation and plans to charge entrepreneurs for its new founder residency programme.
The shift is a bet that Africa’s Web3 and broader tech industry needs more businesses that can hire developers, not just more skilled engineers. It also allows Web3Bridge to build a sustainable revenue model as grants become harder to secure after Lisk, one of its major ecosystem funders, shut down and early-stage startup funding remains selective.
In an email to users on Thursday, Web3Bridge said it is opening a new training cohort, capped at 150 participants, alongside a founder residency programme that will help entrepreneurs develop products, attract customers, understand business models, and raise capital, with registrations to close on November 28.
“Training developers alone is not enough,” Awosika said in the email seen by TechCabal. “We need builders who understand how products are created, how businesses operate and how technology can solve real-world problems.”
The new cohort will cover conventional software engineering (Web2), blockchain development and Rust programming, and Zero Knowledge (ZK) development, used to build secure digital payment and identity verification systems that protect users’ private information. The cohort will also feature on-site learning options across all tracks, according to the email.
Web3Bridge is expanding beyond technical training into startup incubation, entering a market where CV Labs, the accelerator arm of Swiss blockchain venture capital firm Crypto Valley VC, already operates.
The expansion comes after seven years of training developers amid blockchain project closures, declining funding, and limited job opportunities for skilled engineers. Lisk, one of Web3Bridge’s funding partners, shut down its blockchain network in October and closed its investment fund as it shifted focus to financial software.
In October, Awosika told local publication Technext that the organisation had invested nearly ₦700 million ($520,630) in physical infrastructure without recovering that expense, while its reliance on grants had become difficult to sustain.
The residency will introduce participation fees for eligible founders and is expected to kick off on November 12.
African Web3 startups raised $90.1 million across 28 deals in 2025, down 26.6% from the previous year, according to CV VC’s African Blockchain Report. The five largest deals accounted for 58.3% of the funding, underscoring how investment remains concentrated among a handful of startups and the challenge facing emerging founders seeking capital to turn their ideas into viable businesses.

articles.title: Google's Quick Share can now back up your Android photos to a Windows PC automatically
articles.text:
In a nutshell: While there are plenty of free and paid-for cloud backup services for your phone's media, an option to automatically back up photos and videos to a PC with ease would be a welcome one. Now, Google has revealed its version of a tool that performs this function for Android users.
The addition appears in Google's November system services release notes, under Google Play services version 26.43, dated November 2. The company confirms that Quick Share is gaining automatic photo and video backups from Android to Windows.
Quick Share already lets users wirelessly move files between Android devices and Windows PCs. Automating the process should make it more useful for anyone who wants a local copy of their camera roll without remembering to transfer everything manually.
The setup is expected to involve using the Quick Share Windows app, a nearby Android phone, and the same Google account signed in on both devices. Google still hasn't published detailed instructions, so we don't know the exact process just yet.
Reports also point to a shared Wi-Fi network, daily camera roll backups, and a "Back up now" option for starting transfers manually. The feature will likely appeal to those who don't want to rely on cloud backups or have eaten through Google's 15GB of free storage, which is shared across Photos, Gmail, and Drive.
Samsung owners might not get the feature when it first rolls out. Android Authority's earlier examinations of unreleased app code suggested that Samsung phones would be excluded, with a later discovery pointing to Samsung PCs being left out, too. Google's release notes don't mention either restriction, but the automatic backup option could initially be limited to Pixel devices.
The update marks the latest expansion of Quick Share's capabilities. There was the arrival of AirDrop interoperability on the Pixel 10 family, followed by Samsung bringing the functionality to its Galaxy S26 series earlier this year.
As is usually the case with Google Play services updates, availability is rolling out gradually. Having the latest version installed doesn't necessarily mean the backup option will appear immediately, and users should also keep Quick Share for Windows updated. Google hasn't provided a date for when everyone with eligible hardware will receive it.

articles.title: CISO Conversations: Ryan Davis – The Unknown Is Where Security Meets Reality
articles.text:
Starting as a young hacker provides a solid grounding in how to defend. Ryan Davis, now CISO at New Charter Technologies, successfully made the transition.
The journey
Ryan Davis became interested in computers at an early age, before the internet changed the world. As a child, his mother ran a secretarial college from the family home in the 1980s. “We had six personal computers in the house, and I had plenty of time to tinker with them at a formative age. There was no internet, so I had to learn what to do by trial and error. As I grew older, that desire for tinkering grew into a desire to explore beyond the intended confines of the system and make it do something that was never intended.”
Davis is now a CISO, but he started as a hacker. “I did some things that, in retrospect, would probably be considered illegal,” he admits. But he never did anything with malice or malintent. “It was always to see how far I could go. Could I get the system to do something that wasn’t intended? Could I gain access to something that was supposedly a secure system or supposedly isolated in some way?”
As the internet became available, he began spending time on forums and message boards, learning how systems worked or could be reworked. “But never,” he says, “with any personal gain in mind. It wasn’t to get something to sell, to dox somebody, or gain some advantage; it was always just to see how far I could get. It was more like a personal competition.”
He could have done stuff to benefit himself, but he didn’t. He thinks the defining moment in this was while still in high school. He found vulnerabilities in the school network. He took the moral high ground and reported these findings to the school’s sys admin. “I said, ‘Hey, you probably want to lock these things down because here’s all of the things that I can do.’ I was met with shock that turned to gratitude, and I got a high off that gratitude.”
But he doesn’t think he turned to the light; he just doesn’t think he deviated from his natural path. He believes that people are born with a natural morality: “We have a desire to seek the approval of other people, although bad habits can be learned in our upbringing. We see this in different parts of society where kids learn a dubious set of values; but I think we are innately born with a good moral compass.”
A career in cybersecurity was the natural step: from a child who learned about computers to a youth who knew how to hack into them, to the young adult who wished to stop them from being hacked.
After high school, Davis went to Champlain College in Burlington, Vermont. “I chose it because it offered the closest thing I could find to a security degree. It was a course in computer networking but with elements that included firewalls and securing Windows 2000. While I was there, the college introduced a new program: something called Information Security. I ended up doing a dual bachelor’s program and graduated in four years with two degrees. From there, I was recruited directly out of school into MIT.”
The career
Ryan Davis started his professional career with MIT Lincoln Laboratory at Lexington, Massachusetts. Its core purpose is to apply advanced technology to solve critical national security problems, and cybersecurity is one of its focuses. In his own words, “developing new technologies and prototypes that we think we might need in a couple of decades from now.” There he got immersed in the world of information assurance and internal audit, and stayed with MIT for five years.
“Then I pivoted to the software security company Veracode, starting in 2012 as a security program manager working in application security and managing enterprise programs.” He was the senior security program manager by 2014, and was promoted to security program architect in the same year.
“As my career matured, I sat down and had conversations with our internal CISO at Veracode. I told him, ‘I want to be sitting where you’re sitting one day.’ He said, ‘Well, what are you doing about it?’ and I thought, ‘Yeah, what am I doing about it?’ Those conversations ultimately led to me managing the information security program at Veracode in 2016. I started with a team of one and built it into a team of 15. From there, following a series of separate events that were well beyond my control, including two acquisitions and a divestiture, I ended up in the CISO seat at Veracode in 2019.”
He was with Veracode for almost a decade and grew its cybersecurity during that time.
He moved on from Veracode to be CISO at NS1 in 2020, where he stayed for five years. (During this time, NS1 was acquired by IBM in 2023 and rebranded as NS1, an IBM Company.) In 2025 he moved on to be CISO at New Charter Technologies, where he remains today.
New Charter is a Denver-based group, backed by private equity, that acquires managed service providers across North America and runs them as semi-autonomous operating companies.
The CISO
The title of chief information security officer is a misnomer. The function is less to protect information per se, and more to protect the business that owns and uses the information. Protecting the business can be achieved even if some of the data is damaged or lost, provided the business can be made resilient to that loss. The role is closer to protecting business continuity than protecting information.
So, is it more important for the head of security today to be a technician or a businessperson? “I think you have to be both,” says Davis. “A CISO who doesn’t understand the business and the business drivers will have a harder time than the CISO who is well-versed in the business.”
This aligns with the modern view that a CISO is a business enabler rather than simply an information protector and needs to be both tech- and business-savvy to achieve this. CISOs must be technicians to know how to protect data, and businesspeople to know what data to protect most heavily. It also requires that the CISO can explain the technical issues to the business leaders in a way they can understand.
“In the ten years I’ve been a CISO,” he says, “I have learned that if you can’t speak the business language, you’re going to end up speaking over the heads of the rest of the executive team”
Being a leader
The CISO must be a leader, but there is no pre-packaged definition of leadership suitable for all individuals across all organizations. The most common view is that it’s a quality that can be learned while doing the job. Davis, however, believes people either have a natural disposition toward leading or they don’t. But he also has his own view of leadership and believes people can be successful managers or executives without being traditional leaders. It’s all down to style. 
“When I talk about a leader,” he explains, “I think about somebody who has the ability to influence without being overpowering – somebody who can affect the will of others in a way that makes them feel they’re joining something bigger than themselves, and want to align with that bigger purpose for the benefit of everyone. To me, a leader is somebody who invests in their people more than they invest in themselves, and ultimately everyone gains from that investment.”
This somewhat unusual idea of what makes a leader is what explains his view that leadership is a quality more inherent to the person than learnable from the environment. It is more personality- than rules-driven.
The team
It’s a common axiom that leaders are only as good as the team around them. Even those CISOs who inherit a security team will need to replace team member churn with new members. So, whether a CISO builds a new team or simply reshapes an existing one, team building is an essential aspect of being a successful CISO.
“A team is the sum of all its parts,” suggests Davis. “So, when I’m building a team, I’m trying to find a group of individuals with a complementary skill set, where each one brings something to the table that will benefit the whole. If you have a team with a high proportion of introverts who just want to code all day, it’s going to be hard to get that team to interact with other parts of the company.”
Instead, he continues, “What I try to do when I’m building a team is to find individuals that have skills – not just the technical skills, but also the soft skills – that complement one another. Some may have those outgoing extrovert qualities of natural leadership, while others may be more technical, and you know they are perfectly fine diving in for four hours and coding when it’s necessary.”
He also stresses that he is a great believer in diversity. “Having both men and women and people with different backgrounds on the team is important. People approach problems differently, and that can be beneficial; especially in the world of security, where there is rarely simply a single answer. There are many answers, and having people approach problems from different perspectives is highly beneficial. You can iterate on a number of possible solutions, and potentially even start actioning multiple to see which might be best for any given circumstance.”
For Davis, synergy is a synonym for team. “Because that’s where the magic happens.” He’s still the leader, but he aims for consensus decisions where possible. He seeks a balance between his team having been selected for their individual expertise and his own access to the company C-Suite leaders and information unavailable to the team.
“I try really hard to be transparent in such circumstances, so that we’re always building trust. Trust can very quickly erode; and if you erode trust, you erode the sense of team.” So, while the ability to speak security to the business is essential for a CISO, so too is the ability to speak business to security.
It is perhaps no surprise that he considers diplomacy to be a CISO’s most important personality trait.
Burnout
“Any leaders who claim they are not affected by burnout in security are lying to themselves,” he comments. “It’s a very real thing.”
This is the machine age. We have to think and react in terms of machine speed, and that’s incredibly difficult for the human brain to handle – and the result is often burnout.
“I’ve experienced being truly burned out,” he comments. “I was working 80 to 100 hours every week, not sleeping well and not eating right. And this always affects personal relationships outside of work. It’s an incredibly difficult place to be in.” It’s a form of self-perpetuating spiral where the spiral always goes downward.
The prevention and possible cure is, he suggests, ’balance’. “Achieving balance is different every single day. But it’s making sure that you get time with your family and kids and dog and eat well. And time for yourself with decent exercise. But at the same time, you have to stay on top of your work and know what’s going on in your industry.” Balancing your life and staying professional in a stressful job is not easy.
“But if I’ve learned nothing else in my career, it’s that you must strive for some sense of balance because if you don’t, then what are we all doing here? It’s easy to go all-in in a career. It’s not just security, but security is one that is constantly demanding. If I responded to every alert that happened throughout the night, I wouldn’t ever sleep. You have to trust in the systems and the architecture and the team that you put in place, so you don’t need to be in a constantly heightened sense of, oh my gosh, the sky is falling. Ultimately, if you do that, then you’re putting burnout into high gear.”
Mentoring
Mentoring, in the form of advice, is an important part of all CISOs’ careers. On their own journey, they are likely recipients of advice from others who have already trod the same path. If that journey leads to being a CISO, the new CISOs then become mentors for the next generation of travelers, especially from within the team they created.
The best career advice Davis personally received was via the conversation he had with Veracode’s CISO before he became Veracode’s CISO: what are you doing about it; that is, how do you intend to achieve what you want? “It was short for ‘you need a plan to achieve what you want’.” It’s similar to planning a road trip on a map: you need to know the next town you’re aiming at, but you also need to know the town after that, and after that, and each town you need to achieve before you can arrive at the destination you seek.
“For me, that journey isn’t just what is the next job I want on the journey, but what must I do to keep moving forward and growing. Personally, it’s continuous learning, going to conferences, networking, speaking about those things I’m passionate about and having in-depth discussions and debates about key topics. The day you stop learning is the day you become obsolete.” And if you’re obsolete, you no longer have a career.
Now a CISO, the advice he gives his own team members is similar: ‘invest in yourself and never stop learning’. “My core belief, backed by personal experience,” he explains, “is that if you invest in yourself, you’ll reap the rewards. The investment will be different for different people. It may be taking a professional speaking course, or getting a different certification or speaking at a public event. That investment is different for everybody because we’re all different individuals – but personal investment will always pay dividends in the end.”
For Davis this included developing new skills and getting exposure to new technologies and new and unfamiliar disciplines. He doesn’t believe any single process was defining, but that success is the synergistic result of wide experience.
“Constant investment in yourself and finding new ways to grow is the best advice I could give anyone.”
This CISO’s biggest security concern
It’s a cliché, but also a truism, that people have things that keep them awake at night. For Davis, it is the unknown. “It is the unknown that worries me. What I know about, I can secure; but there are always things that are unknowable. The state of shadow AI in my environment. What is the individual who used his own LLM based on an unknown Chinese model being told to do? Those unknowns are so hard to defend against.”
And it’s an ongoing unknowing. “Because as soon as you have a grasp on one set of technologies, there’s always another set of technologies right behind it that becomes the next new thing that proliferates. You cannot secure what you don’t know about, so I spend a part of every day concentrating on getting better visibility into the environment.”
This field of the unknown goes in all directions. It can be not knowing what internal staff are doing, what shadow AI exists where, and even what is novel and different. “Because the unknown,” he says, “is the place where security really meets reality.”

articles.title: CPPIB takes $50-million USD stake in AI holding firm Beacon Software | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB) is taking an equity stake in Toronto AI company Beacon Software, contributing to an upsizing of the company’s previously announced Series C fundraising round.
The news: Beacon Software, a holding company that acquires software companies and integrates AI into their operations, announced an investment from CPPIB of $50 million USD ($69 million CAD) on Thursday. The investment comes from CPPIB’s Growth Equity Unit, and will be used to further accelerate Beacon’s acquisitions and hire “frontier AI engineers” to build out the company’s shared AI operating system.
From the source: Beacon’s portfolio boasts 45 companies, primarily serving sectors like logistics, education, finance, manufacturing, and utilities. It now reports more than $200 million USD in consolidated annual revenue and is valued at $1.75 billion USD ($2.4 billion CAD), according to The Globe and Mail.
The context: CPPIB’s investment is one part of a larger expansion to Beacon’s Series C raise. Announced last June, that raise netted Beacon $225 million USD and was led by Silicon Valley-based investor General Catalyst and Boston’s HarbourVest Partners, as well as Toronto’s Intrepid Growth Partners. This recent upsizing, which includes CPPIB’s $50 million investment, brings Beacon Software’s Series C to $425 million USD.
Beacon’s rollup strategy—sometimes compared to the celebrated Canadian software firm Constellation Software—not only brings AI integration into already established operations, it also provides portfolio companies with a shared tech platform and advisors from tech heavyweights like Instacart (of which CEO and co-founder Nilam Ganenthiran is an alumnus), Meta, OpenAI, and Shopify.
Final thought: Founded just two years ago, Beacon has seen remarkably quick growth, raising more than $750 million, according to The Globe and Mail, and opening offices in New York and San Francisco. The company claimed last June to be acquiring new portfolio companies on a near-weekly basis. That success likely contributed to the CPPBI’s interest in taking an equity stake at such an early point in the startup’s career, particularly on the heels of other, later-stage investments in Canadian success stories like Cohere and Wealthsimple.

articles.title: Redditor fudges DLSS 5 to work on GTA 6 trailer — and full console game could be run this way in a hook-up with a gaming PC, with the input lag being 'completely acceptable'
articles.text:
Want to play GTA 6 with DLSS 5 at launch? It's possible to pipe your console through a gaming PC to do this, and we've just caught a glimpse of what it'd look like
Courtesy of a DLSS 5 makeover for GTA 6's 'extended look' trailer
- A gamer took the GTA 6 'extended look' trailer and fudged it to work with DLSS 5 and Frame Generation
- The results posted on YouTube look impressive, albeit with some notable glitches
- It'll actually be possible to run the game on console, piped through a PC with an Nvidia GPU to add DLSS 5 and other visual trickery, at the cost of some input lag
- …and some believe that trade-off might be worth it
Will the best way to play GTA 6 at launch be to pipe it from your PS5 to your PC with an Nvidia GPU and then back out to your TV?
No, it absolutely won't, but a convoluted setup along these lines could be the optimal way to experience the game visually (with some major caveats) — before the PC version arrives — given that you can fudge the addition of DLSS 5 this way.
How does this work? Wccftech picked up the story of the Redditor who proposed this experiment, and actually applied DLSS 5 to the GTA 6 'extended look' trailer that Rockstar brought out a couple of months ago.
To be specific, this gamer gave the trailer a DLSS 5 makeover with 3x Frame Generation tripling the frame rate from 30 fps to 90 fps, via an app called Veyra, which is a GPU video enhancement tool for Windows on GitHub.
The Redditor explains: "I used Veyra 2.1.1, a tool that can take a video source (video files, capture cards, Remote Play) and apply Neural Rendering [DLSS 5], upscaling, and Frame Generation in real time. I also integrated MFG Unlocker into it so I can unlock Multi Frame Generation on my RTX 4080 and experiment with 3x/4x FG on 40-series cards."
MFG Unlocker is an experimental tool (again on GitHub) which the Redditor is using for getting Multi Frame Generation on their RTX 4080, in case you were wondering. (As ever, download any third-party software entirely at your own risk).
As you can see in the YouTube clip below, the results of this polishing of the official trailer are very impressive in some ways. That said, there are clear issues with artifacts and glitching in terms of the characters and lighting, with the best results seen in the background environment details.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It's pretty remarkable given that this is a fairly aggressive implementation of DLSS 5 by all accounts, fudged on top of a video with no relevant game data (the likes of vector and geometry data) to guide the neural rendering.
The Redditor's plan is to use a console-to-PC pipeline to play GTA 6 on the PS5, with the PC effectively sitting between the console and final output on the TV, adding DLSS 5 and jazzing up the visuals.
This means taking the PS5 and hooking it up to a 4K HDR capture card in the PC, running it through Veyra with the RTX 4080, then outputting to the 4K TV. It's a roundabout way of using the Nvidia GPU as an external graphics card for the console, except all the GeForce GPU is doing is applying DLSS and/or MFG to the image the PS5 has rendered — although there is a price to pay in terms of input lag, of course.
Analysis: capture capers
The Redditor doesn't actually have their PS5 yet (although they've ordered it) to try out this setup fully, but others on Reddit have run such a setup, and in fact it's not that uncommon (albeit still far from a mainstream concept).
One gamer says that they've played GTA 5 using an Elgato capture card with NitLink software, and "the gameplay was 100 times better", and while "there is a noticeable input lag" they claim that "it's completely acceptable — around 1-2 milliseconds."
That little input lag seems a stretch (to say the least), and overall, there's some dispute on whether this way of gaming is viable. Some gamers say that such a setup is just too laggy, while others claim it provides a decently playable experience. Of course, it will depend on what type of game you're playing — a fast-reaction shooter, for example, isn't going to do well with any extra lag being introduced, and you're certainly going to get some.
Really, the success of this kind of console to PC capture card to TV setup is going to heavily depend on a number of factors. The quality of the capture card (a PCIe board would be best, rather than one connected via USB) and the related software are the primary factors, and by all accounts, a higher-end Elgato with NitLink gives you a good chance of enjoying your PS5 games with an Nvidia GPU souping them up using DLSS 5 and Frame Generation.
I'm betting there will also be an element of subjectivity here, too, with some people likely to feel any latency more keenly than others.
Some gamers use this setup to play PS5 games on their PC monitor (in other words, without piping the image back out of the PC to the living room TV, which would cut down on some of the input lag), and there are guides to running this kind of setup on YouTube, like this one. Others recommend Zanit's tutorials on YouTube, but those videos are in Portuguese, so you'll need to translate them if you're not a native speaker. It's pretty cool stuff, if rather convoluted — and a good capture card doesn't come cheap (neither does a high-end RTX 5000 GPU).
Meanwhile, as far as GTA 6 on the PC goes, we may see this happen a lot sooner than expected, due to the way the emulation scene is going right now (in turbo mode thanks to AI). In other words, Rockstar may want to get the PC port on sale before PC gamers start playing it via emulation.

Ben Stockton is a deals writer at Tom’s Hardware. He's been writing about technology since 2018, with bylines at PCGamesN, How-To Geek, and Tom’s Guide, among others. When he’s not hunting down the best bargains, he’s busy tinkering with his homelab or watching old Star Trek episodes.

articles.title: Bluesky hit peak usage for the year on election night | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The blue wave swept Bluesky on Tuesday night as the microblogging platform recorded its highest daily number of posts, replies, and likes in 2026.
“We’re seeing a wave of new people joining and old friends coming back,” Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider posted.
According to Schneider, posts and likes doubled during the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.
COO Rose Wang told TechCrunch that usage began to peak between 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. PT, when many election results were rolling in. Daily posts and likes increased 30% and 70%, respectively, compared to the previous 30-day averages; clicks on links also spiked 20%.
According to open source data, Bluesky reached 44 million likes, 4.8 million posts, and 2 million new follows on November 4. This nearly eclipsed Bluesky’s all-time record 45 million likes in a single day, set in November 2024.
This jump was especially visible in Bluesky’s data traffic, which was 200% higher than usual, reaching up to 35.8 GB/s.
Bluesky is — sometimes snidely — referred to as “Twitter for the left,” given that its user base seems to skew that way politically. This isn’t a coincidence; Bluesky’s most concentrated period of user growth occurred after Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, so it makes sense that those users would post actively during a night of overwhelming victories for the Democratic party.

articles.title: Google, Meta e TikTok processam Califórnia para barrar lei de proteção a menores
articles.text:
Google, Meta e TikTok entraram com ações judiciais contra uma lei da Califórnia (EUA) que restringe o uso de recursos considerados potencialmente viciantes em redes sociais por crianças e adolescentes. As empresas querem impedir que a legislação entre em vigor em janeiro de 2027.
As ações foram apresentadas separadamente em tribunais federais da Califórnia nesta quinta-feira (5). As companhias argumentam que a lei viola direitos de liberdade de expressão e entra em conflito com a Seção 230 da Lei de Decência nas Comunicações dos Estados Unidos, que protege plataformas de responsabilidade pelo conteúdo publicado por usuários.
Assinada pelo governador Gavin Newsom em setembro, a legislação proíbe empresas de oferecer determinados recursos a usuários com menos de 16 anos. Entre eles estão a reprodução automática de vídeos e os sistemas de recomendação personalizada.
O texto considera que essas ferramentas podem ser psicologicamente exploratórias e estimular menores a consultar compulsivamente as redes sociais. Empresas que não cumprirem as exigências poderão receber multas.
Empresas alegam violação à liberdade de expressão
- A Meta afirma que a legislação interfere na maneira como conteúdos são organizados, exibidos e compartilhados com os usuários. Segundo Edward Patterson, porta-voz da companhia, a medida também prejudicaria a capacidade da empresa de recomendar conteúdos apropriados para cada faixa etária;
- O Google, por sua vez, argumenta que já oferece mecanismos de proteção para menores no YouTube. A plataforma impede que vídeos sejam reproduzidos automaticamente em contas infantis e permite que responsáveis desativem o Shorts, seu feed de vídeos curtos;
- “ Acreditamos que os pais estão mais bem posicionados para tomar as decisões certas para suas famílias. Por isso, oferecemos uma variedade de proteções e ferramentas que colocam os pais no controle”, afirmou José Castañeda, porta-voz do Google;
- O TikTok não falou sobre o assunto ainda, mas afirmou na ação judicial que exerce “poder de decisão editorial” sobre os vídeos apresentados aos usuários. Para a empresa, a legislação restringe esse direito.
Leia mais:
- Musk gastou mais de US$ 400 milhões, mas republicanos perderam
- Pioneiro da IA diz que mundo estaria melhor sem inteligência artificial
- EUA: eleitores dão recado à indústria de IA e ameaçam expansão de data centers
Lei chega em meio a processos sobre vício em redes sociais
As ações acontecem em momento em que as plataformas enfrentam uma série de processos relacionados aos possíveis efeitos do uso excessivo de redes sociais por crianças e adolescentes.
Em março, Meta e YouTube perderam processo em Los Angeles (EUA) movido por uma jovem que afirmou ter desenvolvido dependência dos serviços. As empresas foram condenadas a pagar US$ 6 milhões (cerca de R$ 32,8 milhões) em indenização.
No mês passado, a Meta também fechou acordo em processo semelhante movido por uma jovem de 18 anos do Mississippi (EUA). A autora da ação havia firmado acordos com TikTok e YouTube.
Defensores da nova legislação afirmam que as empresas estão tentando preservar seus modelos de negócio, em vez de proteger os direitos dos usuários.
“Os modelos de negócio da Meta, do Google e do TikTok dependem de manter crianças e adolescentes rolando as telas. Agora, eles alegam que proteger esses recursos é uma questão de liberdade de expressão”, disse Brooke Istook, diretora-executiva da Heat Initiative, organização que atua pela responsabilização do setor de tecnologia.
A entidade argumenta que o ponto central da disputa é a possibilidade de as plataformas continuarem lucrando com mecanismos de design que podem colocar menores em risco.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Tokenmaxxing war gestern: Apple-Mitarbeiter sollen ihre KI-Ausgaben jetzt drastisch reduzieren
articles.text:
Modelmaxxing: So stark kürzt Apple jetzt die KI-Budgets seiner Teams
Tech-Konzerne haben ihre Teams lange ermutigt, KI-Tools für möglichst viele Aufgaben einzusetzen. Damit wollten sie die Effizienz steigern und Kosten senken. Jetzt zeigt sich immer öfter: Diese Rechnung geht nicht auf. Wie Bloomberg unter Berufung auf Insider:innen berichtet, will auch Apple seine KI-Ausgaben im Rahmen von Kosteneinsparungsmaßnahmen deutlich reduzieren. So sei das Limit für Entwickler:innen von 300 auf 200 Dollar pro Tag gesenkt worden. Weitere Kürzungen könnten folgen.
Von hohen KI-Ausgaben überrascht
Der sogenannte Tokenmaxxing-Trend könnte Unternehmen Millionen gekostet haben. Tech-Konzerne wie Meta und Amazon haben den Begriff maßgeblich geprägt. Sie drängten ihre Mitarbeiter:innen dazu, ihren Tokenverbrauch massiv zu erhöhen. Anfang April 2026 deckte The Information daraufhin einen internen Wettbewerb auf, bei dem Meta-Mitarbeiter:innen versuchten, sich gegenseitig zu übertreffen.
In nur 30 Tagen sollen so rund 60 Billionen Token zusammengekommen sein – je nach API-Preis mit Kosten von bis zu einigen Millionen Dollar. Zu mehr Produktivität hat das allerdings nicht zwangsläufig geführt. Zwar erzeugen KI-Tools Code schneller als menschliche Entwickler:innen. Dieser muss aber häufiger überarbeitet werden, was oft Mehrarbeit verursacht.
Immer häufiger wird KI deshalb als Kostenfaktor betrachtet, der die Margen belastet. Laut einer Bitkom-Umfrage waren auch in Deutschland rund ein Drittel der befragten Unternehmen von ihren hohen KI-Kosten überrascht. Jetzt suchen sie verstärkt nach Wegen, ihre Ausgaben wieder unter Kontrolle zu bringen.
Einige setzen auf Modelmaxxing und nutzen je nach Aufgabe unterschiedliche KI‑Modelle, statt pauschal auf teure Spitzenmodelle zu setzen. Daraus sind schon erste Startups entstanden, die mit ihrer Software jeder Aufgabe automatisch das passende Modell zuordnen. Auch bei Apple sollen Teams dazu angewiesen worden sein, günstigere KI-Modelle zu verwenden.
Apple-Teams sollen jetzt modelmaxxen
Eine weitere Konsequenz scheint darin zu bestehen, die Limits drastisch zu senken. Laut den Informant:innen von Bloomberg unterliegen viele Apple-Abteilungen schon jetzt einer täglichen Obergrenze von 100 Dollar pro Person. Der Konzern soll sogar erwägen, sie auf bis zu 25 Dollar zu reduzieren. Mitarbeiter:innen, die einen höheren Bedarf haben, können bei der Geschäftsleitung eine Ausnahmegenehmigung beantragen.
Die Reaktionen auf die Änderungen sollen laut Bloomberg gemischt ausfallen. Einige Mitarbeiter:innen geben an, dass nur wenige Kolleg:innen in den Technologie-Abteilungen ihre täglichen Pauschalen in Höhe von 300 Dollar vollständig ausgeschöpft hätten. Die Kürzung mache für sie also keinen großen Unterschied. Andere sehen in der Entscheidung ein Zeichen für umfassendere Kosteneinsparungen – und befürchten Entlassungen.
Neuer Apple-CEO will Ausgaben senken
Zuletzt waren Apples Gesamtausgaben deutlich gestiegen. Laut dem Bericht für das Geschäftsjahr 2026 lagen die Forschungs- und Entwicklungsausgaben 32 Prozent höher als im Vorjahr – vor allem wegen höherer Infrastruktur- und KI-Kosten. Die unternehmensweiten Betriebsausgaben stiegen um 22 Prozent auf insgesamt 75,5 Milliarden Dollar. Das entspricht rund 16 Prozent des Gesamtnettoumsatzes. Laut Bloomberg wolle der neue CEO John Ternus die Ausgaben wieder reduzieren und das Unternehmen dazu bringen, schneller und schlanker zu arbeiten und die Zahl der Führungsebenen zu reduzieren.

articles.title: Salon is shutting down after 31 years
articles.text:
Salon launched 31 years ago as one of the first online-only news magazine outlets, and it announced today in an unsigned post that it’s ceasing publication.
Salon is shutting down after 31 years
Salon says its publishing model is ‘no longer sustainable.’
The company said that the “business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years,” and it decided that its publishing model is “no longer sustainable.” It didn’t go into detail about why, but many websites are grappling with “Google Zero” and the impact of AI tools. When reached for comment, Salon general manager Amanda Wolfe pointed The Verge to today’s announcement post.
“Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them,” Salon said in its post. “Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.”
On Bluesky, Salon chief content officer Erin Keane says that the editorial archive will “stay live for now.”
Current Salon owner Find.co acquired Salon in 2023 and describes itself as a “Performance Marketing Ecosystem transforming crypto marketing with performance and precision.”

articles.title: IA soberana: la apuesta de las grandes empresas para ocultar sus datos a los tecnoligarcas estadounidenses
articles.text:
IA soberana: la apuesta de las grandes empresas para ocultar sus datos a los tecnoligarcas estadounidenses
Compañías europeas como Airbus, TotalEnergies y BMW buscan inteligencias artificiales privadas para esconderse de la vista de las tecnológicas
Desde la Comisión Europea se rema por impulsar una soberanía tecnológica que brilla por su ausencia. En los últimos años este movimiento se ha intensificado con la irrupción de la inteligencia artificial (IA) como un elefante en una cacharrería. La UE ha redoblado sus esfuerzos para intentar fabricar chips avanzados, al tiempo que promociona la construcción de centros de datos y el desarrollo de una IA propia.
Aumenta la premura, pero no tanto las opciones. En realidad es imposible tener una IA exclusivamente con tecnología hecha en Europa. Solo con los chips, de la empresa estadounidense Nvidia, ya se trunca cualquier aspiración en ese sentido. Pero en la soberanía tecnológica, como en todo, hay grados. Y uno de los más críticos es el sistema donde se introducen los datos.
El uso creciente de la inteligencia artificial en las empresas hace que los datos internos cobren cada vez mayor importancia. Y algunas compañías se muestran reticentes a que su información viaje a los servidores de OpenAI, Anthropic, Google o Microsoft para poder utilizar su inteligencia artificial.
Recurrir a los servicios de estas compañías directamente implica enviar datos confidenciales del negocio de la empresa a la nube. “La gente ha empezado a reaccionar negativamente ante estos modelos de IA. Les generan preocupación porque las empresas pierden control de sus datos, que abandonan su perímetro, ya sea este tecnológico o geográfico”, explica Charles Sansbury, director ejecutivo de la multinacional estadounidense Cloudera.
La compañía de Sansbury cubre la trastienda de las empresas, allá donde los sistemas informáticos almacenan los datos y tratan de exprimirlos. A día de hoy, parte de su negocio pasa por facilitar la aplicación de la IA a estos grandes volúmenes de información interna. Durante el evento EVOLVE 2026, organizado por Cloudera el 27 de octubre en Nueva York y al que EL PAÍS acudió invitado, la firma destacó cómo las empresas son cada vez más celosas de sus datos. Muchas de ellas prefieren ejecutar los modelos de IA en una nube privada o en sus servidores locales.
Algunas empresas llegan al extremo de aplicar esta IA a su información en equipos sin conexión a internet, para reforzar la protección de este activo tan valioso, el llamado oro del siglo XXI. “El término IA soberana tiene un matiz más geopolítico”, comenta Sansbury. “Pero en realidad se trata de controlar hacia dónde van tus datos, quién los procesa y con qué sistemas se procesan. Al final se trata de dar a los clientes las herramientas para que operen cualquier aplicación en un contexto de control que han definido previamente”.
La desconfianza creciente entre ambos lados del Atlántico y la voluntad europea de sacudirse el dominio digital de las grandes tecnológicas estadounidenses han tensado el escenario geopolítico. Y de esto se nutren las ambiciones de IA soberana. Una de las compañías mejor colocadas para aprovechar esta necesidad es la francesa Mistral.
“Es absolutamente esencial para las empresas inyectar sus datos, protegidos con su propiedad intelectual, en modelos de IA. Hay una correlación directa entre hacer esto y obtener valor de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial. Hay señales claras de que si no enriqueces los modelos con tu propiedad intelectual pierdes una ventaja competitiva respecto a otras empresas”, apunta Marjorie Janiewicz, directora de Ingresos de Mistral.
La empresa emergente francesa, asociada recientemente con Cloudera ―que ofrece sus modelos en su sistema de gestión de datos―, trabaja con grandes paladines empresariales europeos. La holandesa ASML, TotalEnergies o Airbus se cuentan entre las compañías que han introducido su información en los modelos de Mistral. Todas ellas operan en sectores altamente regulados, donde la protección de la información es aún más crítica.
Garantizar que los datos se queden en casa
La Comisión Europea ha diseñado específicamente una hoja de ruta para la digitalización y la introducción de IA en el sector energético. Este ámbito, sometido a una exhaustiva regulación, ha adquirido cada vez más importancia estratégica ante la guerra de Ucrania y el creciente aumento de los precios de la electricidad. La UE no quiere dejar la implementación de la inteligencia artificial en este sector en manos extranjeras.
Algo similar ocurre en otros ámbitos, también considerados críticos para el funcionamiento de un Estado. “Para las empresas en sectores regulados de Europa, ya sea en España, Francia, Alemania o los países escandinavos, están surgiendo normativas nacionales que previenen la salida de datos del perímetro geográfico del país”, apunta Sansbury, cuya compañía trabaja en España con gran parte del sector bancario y de telecomunicaciones.
En este escenario, para garantizar que los datos no salen de los sistemas propios de una compañía, se impone el uso de los llamados modelos de pesos abiertos. Se denominan así porque se pueden descargar —a diferencia de los de OpenAI o Anthropic— y modificar algunos de sus parámetros. Así, las empresas crean una IA ajustada a su contexto y a sus necesidades.
Pero para las compañías europeas no existen tantas opciones. “Si necesitas un modelo de IA [abierto] de calidad y necesitas que se ejecute en tus servidores, puedes recurrir a los modelos de Nvidia, pero son de Estados Unidos. Y la mitad de los modelos [abiertos] disponibles en el mercado son chinos, por lo que acarrean sus propios resquemores a nivel geopolítico”, señala Sansbury.
Es irónico que Cloudera, una compañía estadounidense aunque con presencia global, actúe como llave para impulsar la IA soberana entre las empresas europeas. Sus sistemas, basados en una estructura de código abierto, permiten introducir datos de forma privada y procesarlos con modelos de IA de diferentes proveedores. Aunque la opción preferida son los sistemas de Mistral, especialmente de cara al territorio de la UE.
Janiewicz, de la compañía francesa, ilustra con un ejemplo la utilidad de sus sistemas para las empresas: “Aplicar la inteligencia artificial es hoy muy diferente a cómo era hace solo unos años. Hoy podemos tener listos casos de uso reales en tres meses. Trabajando en pruebas de accidentes con BMW construimos muy rápido un modelo de pruebas con el que BMW acelera la evaluación de sus vehículos”.
En este caso, los datos que BMW utiliza para generar este modelo de pruebas de accidentes son demasiado valiosos como para volcarlos en los servidores de un OpenAI o Anthropic. Por muchas garantías que las políticas de estas compañías concedan sobre el papel, siempre queda un poso de inquietud. ¿Terminarán por filtrarse datos confidenciales?, ¿servirán para entrenar nuevos modelos de IA?, ¿qué ocurre si las condiciones del servicio cambian y, por tanto, el tratamiento de los datos?
Las empresas buscan evitar este tipo de incertidumbres cuando ejecutan los modelos de IA en sus propios sistemas, sin que la información viaje a la nube. Un informe de Cloudera, basado en encuestas a más de 1.500 responsables de departamentos de estas tecnologías a nivel global, indica que casi la mitad de las empresas ya ha trasladado parte de sus procesos a sistemas privados.
“Un banco, que tiene sus datos de transacciones, de depósitos y de inversiones de todos sus clientes, no quiere subir toda esta información a un sistema en la nube. No quiere poner todos esos datos, que son suyos, en un sitio fuera de su terreno”, explica Sansbury. “Lo que podemos hacer con nuestras herramientas y los modelos de IA a los que damos acceso es permitir que las empresas construyan su IA en un entorno que controlan, sin que la información salga de su perímetro de seguridad”.
En realidad, tener una IA soberana no es otra cosa que tener una IA privada. En el contexto europeo, se ha impuesto el primer término, pero el concepto alude a una preocupación básica entre las empresas: evitar el riesgo de que su información confidencial pase por manos ajenas.

articles.title: WhatsApp : cette nouveauté majeure va changer la façon dont vous organisez vos soirées — Frandroid

Jusqu’ici, un événement WhatsApp restait dans une discussion de groupe, donc seules les personnes avec un compte pouvaient le voir. Le 14 octobre, l’application avait déjà permis d’inviter à un appel quelqu’un qui n’a pas WhatsApp, grâce à un lien qui s’ouvre dans un navigateur.
