articles.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit - Microsoft Research
Zipline hits $21.5B valuation as Walmart expands bet on drone delivery | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.
Zipline and Walmart reached a new multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.
On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.
The company, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, said it plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.
Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based company began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.
But it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.
Zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.
The company said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

articles.title: Wealthsimple unveils AI assistant and major product expansion in latest showcase | BetaKit
articles.text:
Wealthsimple announced a dozen new banking, investing, and AI products and features today at the Toronto FinTech company’s latest showcase.
The most significant is Penny, an AI assistant that any Wealthsimple user will soon be able to leverage to not only better understand their financial situation, but also to make moving their money around and placing trades easier. Wealthsimple senior director and head of AI products Sam Newman-Bremang and vice-president of investing products Swapnil Parikh revealed the news to BetaKit in a joint interview ahead of Thursday’s event.
“We’re expanding our product suite across every line.”
Swapnil Parikh, Wealthsimple
Wealthsimple revealed Penny and other offerings Thursday at Toronto’s Massey Hall during the fourth edition of its biannual Wealthsimple Presents series, titled “Something Good Is Going to Happen,” to reflect the company’s belief in the future it can deliver using technology.
“This is a step in showing that we’re working on everything,” Parikh said. “We’re expanding our product suite across every line.”
Last week, Wealthsimple announced a $425-million CAD Series F round from existing backers at a whopping $13.8-billion valuation on the back of some major growth. The profitable firm now serves more than four million Canadians and oversees more than $169 billion in total assets under administration.
“Today, people can live their whole financial lives on Wealthsimple, and we’re seeing more and more Canadians choose us,” Wealthsimple co-founder and CEO Michael Katchen told BetaKit at the time.
Parikh said yesterday that this fundraise reflects the firm’s desire to grow and bring new products to market faster, and will provide the fuel it needs to deliver the banking, investing, and AI offerings and functionality its users demand.
RELATED: Wealthsimple announces $425-million Series F at $13.8-billion valuation
Penny’s launch comes as personal AI agents become increasingly popular and raise heightened security concerns. With Penny, Wealthsimple aims to provide its clients with an in-app chatbot they can ask questions about their finances to and use to complete many of the steps associated with transferring and investing their money, from sending e-transfers to paying bills and planning contributions to various accounts. Penny stops just short of actioning these decisions without manual sign-off. The AI assistant will be broadly available by late 2026 or early 2027.
“It’s really the first time we’ve been able to meet Canadians and have that one-to-one conversation with them, in a way,” Newman-Bremang said. He noted that Penny will also help Wealthsimple clients “remove a lot of the overhead around actually doing things with your money.” Both are capabilities that Newman-Bremang said advance Wealthsimple’s quest to make managing your finances “simpler, easier, and more accessible” for Canadians.
Canada’s largest banks recently committed to blocking AI agents from directly accessing their customers’ online banking information, but while Wealthsimple shares the sentiment, it isn’t quite following suit. “Just like the big banks are saying, we don’t think clients should give their ID [and credentials] out to [a third-party] agent,” Newman-Bremang said.
However, for customers who aren’t satisfied with Penny alone, Wealthsimple is working to help them more securely connect with outside AI systems like Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT by ensuring they keep greater control over what accounts, information, and money those agents can access, plus retain ultimate sign-off. These integrations will become broadly available early next year, with more to come over time.
“It’s really the first time we’ve been able to meet Canadians and have that one-to-one conversation with them.”
Sam Newman-Bremang, Wealthsimple
“One of the biggest issues with AI is that you’re just handing over a login to some chatbot, [and] now it can do anything with your money,” Parikh said. “We built this from a security lens. Customers actually approve every action.”
These AI moves come as one of Wealthsimple’s biggest Canadian competitors, fellow Toronto firm Questrade, also looks to remake its platform for the age of AI.
“Optimism is believing that things will get better,” Wealthsimple co-founder and CPO Brett Huneycutt said on stage. “Agency is believing that you can make them better. You need both, and we’re living in a moment where those two traits are more accessible than ever before. With new tools, especially AI, it has never been easier to go out and build the world that you want to see.”
Wealthsimple said 1,000 people gathered in-person and 700,000 registered to tune in virtually for Thursday’s showcase. The event, which was prefaced by a live band, was the largest and flashiest Wealthsimple Presents to date, and saw the company gift cash to help its clients meet their financial goals throughout the presentation.
While the inaugural Wealthsimple Presents in June 2025 took aim at the country’s big banks with the firm’s first credit card, an expanded chequing account, and line of credit, the company’s second event that October targeted investing with more advanced tools. Both were held at Toronto’s Evergreen Brick Works. The third edition, held this May in Calgary, followed that up with more banking offerings for families and businesses.
Newman-Bremang said those three events were “about launching all of the things that Canadians wanted.” While today’s showcase also brings more of the same, this time around, Wealthsimple put more attention on how its users interact with all of its products.
One of the core ways Wealthsimple aims to do that is with its revamped mobile app, which the firm claims it rebuilt “from scratch” with the help of the Fey team, and will be available in early 2027 for iOS and Android users. “It’s extremely customizable,” Parikh said. “It’s super fast.”
Wealthsimple has also promised Wealthsimple Pro, a new, advanced trading suite for active investors that’s separate from its core platform and can execute faster. Parikh characterized it as the firm’s first foray into “technical trading.” That desktop product will be released in beta by the end of November.
“We have historically focused on simplicity and ease of use, but as we’ve grown our sophisticated trader base, they demanded this product, and so we’ve introduced a lot of complexity,” Parikh said.
The company is also expanding its offerings to reach more companies, a particularly fast-growing client segment, with a Wealthsimple Business credit card that has no foreign exchange fees and a one-percent cashback planned to be released by early 2027.
RELATED: Wealthsimple unveils new family and business products as it broadens banking push
Wealthsimple also shared plans to make a Canadian-dollar stablecoin, CADD, available through cryptocurrency accounts on its platform (pending final regulatory approval) and launch perpetual futures, commission-free CAD options, and temporary virtual cards with prescribed limits, which could help users ensure their AI agents access their money in a more controlled fashion.
On Wednesday, the Government of Canada also released draft regulations to ban banks from charging transfer fees, typically $150, for switching providers. This marks the first step towards fulfilling a promise the feds made in Budget 2025, and a change Wealthsimple had spent years advocating for given that it has been an obstacle for challengers to the country’s large banks.
“We’re incredibly grateful to the government for making this change,” Parikh said. “It’s going to be so helpful for people that signed up for an institution 10 [or] 15 years ago and want something better.”
Disclosure: Wealthsimple vice-president of payments strategy and chief compliance officer, Hanna Zaidi, sits on BetaKit’s board of directors.
Feature image courtesy Josh Scott for BetaKit.

articles.title: The midterms proved once and for all that X is not real life
articles.text:
A week before the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance hosted a town hall in Texas with Fox News host Jesse Watters. It was a friendly event with a friendly audience in what should have been a friendly state, and maybe that’s why Vance couldn’t help himself. When a college student earnestly asked how the right expected young people like her to settle down and have kids, given the ever-growing cost of living, Vance replied with a quip about Jon Husted’s ass.
The midterms proved once and for all that X is not real life
The student, Kate White, introduced herself as the vice president of the Texas Christian University chapter of Turning Point USA, the conservative group started by Donald Trump ally Charlie Kirk. She was offering Vance an opportunity to explain how MAGA could work for young people, and he turned it into a joke. Vance did eventually answer the question, saying Republicans don’t pay enough attention to the issue of affordability and blaming rising housing costs on institutional investors and the “20 million illegal aliens” supposedly living in the United States. But the order of operations revealed the fatal flaw of Republicans’ 2026 strategy: Everything is a gag to them, and they’re way too online.
For the past decade, Republicans have adhered to Steve Bannon’s maxim that politics is downstream from culture. This fixation with liberals’ alleged capture of elite institutions has animated the right’s war against Big Tech and in particular social media platforms — which the right claims actively silenced conservative voices — and its crusade against diversity, equity, and inclusion. With his purchase of X, Elon Musk finally succeeded in building a conservative platform where right-wing voices not only had real influence but also a direct line to those in power. More recently, some people have claimed that Musk’s X is the only social media that really represents the people, unlike platforms like Bluesky, which have more left-leaning user bases.
Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise. They ignored their base’s valid concerns about affordability and served them nonsensical memes instead. And they failed spectacularly in the realm where it actually mattered: politics. X, we can now declare once and for all, is not real life. Republicans not only lost historically red states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina, but barely managed to win Florida. The Senate race in Mississippi, of all places, is still too close to call.
Vance, especially, is a creature of X, where his following list includes such illustrious accounts as Raw Egg Nationalist, Bronze Age Pervert, Howling Mutant, and Captive Dreamer. But White House aides, department employees, and Hill staffers are stewing in the same ecosystem. Writer John Ganz has termed this phenomenon “groyperfication,” after followers of influencer Nick Fuentes, who call themselves groypers. This is a useful shorthand, though Fuentes’ fans are mostly too NEET-pilled to land jobs on the Hill. American Moment, a boot camp for young conservative up-and-comers, reportedly screens out groypers. There’s a real need for such protective measures. Kingsley Wilson, the hard-right press secretary for the Department of War (or per its legal name, Defense), has posted antisemitic conspiracy theories about Leo Frank, a Jewish man who was lynched in Georgia 1915 for allegedly raping a teenage girl. (Historians largely believe Frank was innocent.) The Department of Homeland Security regularly posts fascist fancams and wink-wink references to white supremacist memes.
Republicans saw their 2024 victory as a mandate. Having clawed the White House and Congress back from Democrats, they assumed the public was on board with MAGA’s cultural project when in fact people were largely mad about the price of eggs. And with two years of dominance under their belt, they decided to go even harder on culture, not realizing — or maybe just not caring — that people are still mad about gas prices and groceries.
Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise.
In the run-up to the midterms, the Department of Education was posting about “Malfoid” — a gender-swapped version of Draco Malfoy from Harry Potter that far-right influencers claimed would save Western literature from the scourge of wokeness. The Department of Homeland Security was bragging about record lows in legal immigration, which outside white nationalist circles is typically not considered a negative thing. Pseudonymous shitposters like Howling Mutant were posting memes comparing themselves to noted child murderer Anakin Skywalker, the new avatar for the online right. Musk, a Republican megadonor, got in on the fun, as did Katie Miller, wife of ultranationalist White House adviser Stephen Miller, who dressed up as Anakin’s wife Padmé Amidala for Halloween. (Katie Miller’s last government role was advising Elon Musk’s failed Department of Government Efficiency; now she devotes her time to throwing lavish parties and hosting a podcast no one listens to.)
Most of the American public isn’t on X, but the conversations conservatives have there do bleed out into the mainstream — often with disastrous results. Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas railroad commissioner, lost his election by a huge margin after posting anti-Indian memes on X. (Asian American voters, including Indian Americans, moved to the left in Texas elections down the ballot.) Musk did his part to drive turnout, spending nearly half a billion dollars on Republican candidates and PACs. But even Musk’s money failed to make up for voters’ dissatisfaction with Republicans’ performance, perhaps because the ads he funded focused largely on culture war issues that were out of step with voters’ concerns about the cost of living.
And Miller, it turns out, didn’t even vote, telling CBS Newsshe feared doing so would put her safety at risk, since Virginia law makes voters’ home addresses public. (The Millers, like other members of the Trump administration, live on a military installation with tight security; it’s unlikely intruders would be able to get to their home.) Republican myopia may have contributed to their poor performance across the board, including with groups that were touted as their new base. One poll found that a majority of young men of all races — including young white men — voted for Democrats in the midterms.
In a long postmortem on X — reportedly posted without input or permission from White House officials — Vance said he asked “the smartest data guy” he knows for insight on the electorate ahead of the midterms. Vance claims several pollsters told him that voters’ main concerns were the war against Iran, the cost of living, and America’s relationship to Israel. So why didn’t Republicans listen?
The answer lies in the algorithmic nature of social media, X especially. If you interact with even one post about a relatively niche topic — say, genderbent Harry Potter fanfiction — the algorithm will feed you post after post after post about the same thing. Just like Trump spent the early years of his first term obsessing over Fox News, the single mainstream network that would reflect his biases back to him, MAGA is now all in on X. And if you’re the kind of person who spends a lot of time scrolling, you may even delude yourself into thinking the issue clogging up your feed is something people just can’t stop talking about.

articles.title: Kurz vor historischem Meilenstein: Kontakt zu Voyager 1 steht wieder
articles.text:
Kurz vor historischem Meilenstein: Kontakt zu Voyager 1 steht wieder
Aufatmen bei der Nasa: Voyager 1 hat sich zurückgemeldet. Die Raumsonde, die seit 49 Jahren im Weltall unterwegs ist, hatte kurzzeitig nicht auf Kommunikationsversuche des Deep Space Network auf der Erde reagiert.
Voyager 1 reagierte zweimal nicht auf Kontaktversuche
Das Funk- und Kommunikationsnetzwerk der Nasa hatte am 18. und 19. Oktober Voyager 1 kontaktiert. Doch die Raumsonde blieb bei beiden Kontaktversuchen stumm.
Wie die US-Raumfahrtbehörde kürzlich bekannt gab, löste sich das Problem aber von selbst. Am 20. Oktober meldete sich Voyager zurück. Seitdem ist die Kommunikation stabil. Die Nasa versucht nun herauszufinden, was zu dem Ausfall geführt hatte. Es handelte sich schließlich um den ersten Vorfall dieser Art.
Als erstes menschengemachtes Objekt ein Lichttag von Erde entfernt
Der Wackler kam zur Unzeit, denn bald erreicht Voyager 1 einen Meilenstein, der die Kommunikation noch schwerer macht. Die Raumsonde wird als erstes menschengemachtes Objekt einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein. Dies entspricht etwa 25,9 Milliarden Kilometern.
Wie das Wort Lichttag schon sagt: Das Licht, das von einem Objekt in dieser Distanz ausgestrahlt wird, benötigt 24 Stunden, um die Erde zu erreichen.
„Wartet zwei Tage, bis man endlich eine Antwort bekommt“
Ein Radiosignal, das die Kontrollstation auf der Erde in Richtung Voyager abschickt, ist dann ebenfalls einen ganzen Tag unterwegs. Das sorgt für massive Delays in der Kommunikation.
„Wenn man ‚Voyager ‚Hallo‘ sagen will, schickt man seine Nachricht ab, geht nach Hause und wartet zwei Tage, bis man endlich eine Antwort bekommt“, sagte Suzanne Dodd vom Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) der Nasa in der Mitteilung.
An diesem Tag erreicht Voyager 1 den historischen Meilenstein
Die Nasa hat den Moment, an dem Voyager 1 einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein wird, bereits exakt berechnet. Demnach ist es am 18. November um 5.16 Uhr US-Ostküstenzeit so weit.
Zu diesem Zeitpunkt wird die Distanz der Sonde zur Erde exakt 25.902.068.356 Kilometer betragen.
Voyager 1: Seit fast 50 Jahren im Einsatz
Voyager 1 startete am 5. September 1977 von Cape Canaveral aus. Seitdem bewegt sie sich mit einer Geschwindigkeit von über 60.000 Kilometern pro Stunde durchs All.
Voyager 1 erforschte zunächst Jupiter und Saturn. Im Sommer 2012 trat sie als erstes von Menschen geschaffene Objekt in den interstellaren Raum ein.
Zahn der Zeit nagt an Voyager 1: Nur noch zwei Intrumente aktiv
Doch ein Jahr vor ihrem 50. Geburtstag nagt der Zahn der Zeit an der Sonde. Deswegen musste die Nasa im Frühjahr 2026 ein weiteres Instrument abschalten, den Teilchenmesser LECP. (Low-energy Charged Particles).
Die Abschaltung spart Energie, die der Sonde ein Jahr weiterer Lebensdauer verschaffen soll. Von ursprünglich elf Instrumenten an Bord der Voyager 1 sind damit nur noch zwei aktiv.
Interessant! Aber… die NASA Kontaktiert am 18.10. und die Sonde blieb still…
2 Tage auf eine Antwort warten, dann am 20.10. eine Antwort.
also, nicht still geblieben, oder? Aber genug für einen spannenden Artikel… denke ich!

articles.title: Physical AI Pushes The Limits Of Hardware
articles.text:
Autonomous machines promise to transform industries, but memory bottlenecks, power constraints, specialized architectures, and safety requirements are forcing chip designers to rethink the entire system.
Key Takeaways:
The race is on to develop physical AI fit for widespread use, but building these sensor-powered systems will require engineering teams to address a variety of technical challenges concurrently and continuously.
Analysts predict significant market growth for physical AI, with the promise that autonomous systems will fundamentally reshape industries spanning transportation, manufacturing, medicine, energy, and more. PwC’s Strategy& projects that the global physical AI market could reach approximately €430 billion by 2030, reflecting the potential commercial impact of autonomous systems across multiple industries.
“Physical AI systems are expanding beyond automotive to robotics and drones, and the bottlenecks for development of these applications cover the entire system,” said Licinio Sousa, senior director of Interface IP for Automotive and Physical AI at Synopsys. “AI is expanding from the data center to the edge, and with machines such as robots, drones, and vehicles, all driven by the need for autonomy, privacy, personalization, faster response, and less reliance on the cloud.”
The list of technical challenges that need to be addressed is long and intertwined. Memory capacity and bandwidth need to be increased, latency and power consumption need to be decreased, product lifespans need to be stretched, and safety needs to be verified. And if that isn’t hard enough, addressing any one of these can create problems elsewhere.
Specialized architectures
Solving these system-wide bottlenecks requires highly specialized hardware and software that are optimized for specific use cases.
“We need to start talking about optimized, more tailored compute that you build for the specific workload, and this is where physical AI gets more interesting,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president and chief product and marketing officer, and general manager for Security Solutions at Arteris. “That workload needs to be highly optimized for the hardware. We’re basically going back to ASICs in the traditional sense of what ASICs were supposed to be — very application-specific, extremely optimized, versus more generic. Some of that is already starting. It will be interesting to see how the more nimble systems evolve for very specific applications between the software and the hardware and the workload, and keep evolving because the models are moving way faster.”
Autonomous robotics systems share some of the same technology found in self-driving vehicles, particularly in perception and control, but each physical AI use case adds unique challenges.
“Robotics is not a new AI stack,” Vasanthan Karunanithy, staff systems architect for Automotive at Micron Technology, said at the recent JEDEC Automotive Forum. “From an ADAS system, the robot inherits real-time perception, path planning, and motion control. From an intelligent cabinet, robotics inherits natural language understanding, contextual reasoning, and personal interaction. In embodied intelligence, the bigger challenge is running these two workloads together and then exchanging information at the end. So that is the commonality between these two segments. But there is also a difference that tells the scale of the channel. An autonomous vehicle operates in a relatively structured road environment and draws power from a larger source — the vehicle battery. But when you look at robots, they operate in an unstructured 3D environment. [A robot] also needs to maintain multiple degrees of freedom. It has to manipulate objects and maintain balance, and it has to understand the commands in the instructions. It has to do all this with a limited power source compared to automotive.”
Those distinctions vary considerably across applications. Autonomous vehicles operate within established transportation infrastructure, but they must respond to unpredictable road conditions. Mobile and humanoid robots, in contrast, may need to navigate less structured environments, coordinate manipulation and balance, and operate within much more restrictive power budgets. Meanwhile, industrial robots may operate in controlled environments with fixed electrical power. These differences make it hard to optimize a single architecture for every form of physical AI.
Fig. 1: Robotic system. Source: Synopsys.
Designers must build system architecture with these requirements in mind from the start.
“As workloads and models evolve, we are already seeing purpose-built silicon designed to meet the specific needs of each class of machine,” Sousa said. “Our customers continue to address the need for advanced VLA (vision-language-action) models. In the hardware world, this translates to more intensive compute and AI engines. At the same time, the spectrum of use cases makes it harder for a single monolithic architecture, leading to a transition to chiplets where compute, AI, memory, and I/Os can be scaled using a UCIe interface based on specific use cases.”
Chiplets offer one potential path to scalable physical AI platforms, particularly when heterogeneous compute, memory, and I/O requirements justify advanced packaging. However, they also can ratchet up costs and complexity due to customized packaging, thermal management, and die-to-die communication. Monolithic SoCs may be preferable for smaller, highly integrated systems where power, size, and cost are constrained.
Those constraints apply to both hardware and software. “The sensors are going to be much more focused on use cases, and you need to make sure that you have good use cases, and it’s customized, and you need to have a software layer on top of it as well,” said Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI & Solido at Siemens EDA. “I always joke that everything involved in the real world is analog and we are trying to abstract it to digital, so one of the most important things is redundancy. Sensors have gotten pretty good. We can sense in terms of visual, thermal, pressure, anything. We have gotten good in terms of radar and everything else. What’s more important is making sure that the sensors can operate in the environment, and that environment needs to be captured in a way that it doesn’t make it doesn’t really degrade, or you have redundancy built in.”
Still, the effectiveness of redundancy can vary, depending on whether components can fail independently and whether the system can identify and respond to faults. Adding sensors alone doesn’t guarantee reliable operation, especially when environmental conditions can affect multiple sensors at once.
Tailoring the compute architecture to the workload or use case introduces tradeoffs, as well. “There is the question of how close the intelligence needs to be to the actual origination of where the sensing is happening, and there’s a push-pull,” said Yasmine King, corporate vice president and head of Automotive at Analog Devices. “If you have intelligence distributed throughout a system, that makes it more complicated to update. Centralizing allows one point of over-the-air updates, easy to patch and fix, but it can create latency issues when you need to react quickly to this data. In a vehicle, if a pedestrian runs out in front of your car, you need to be able to respond extremely quickly. So where you locate your intelligence is based on what sensory information you’re trying to gather, and how quickly you need to respond.”
Fig. 2 Analog Devices’ Yasmine King speaks at Reuters Automotive 2026 Oct. 27, 2026. Source: Semiconductor Engineering
The placement of intelligence is an architectural decision involving more than compute performance. It requires balancing response time, communication bandwidth, power consumption, updateability, as well as coordination of distributed components. Centralized compute may simplify management, while local processing can reduce communication delays and preserve essential functionality when connectivity is interrupted.
Physical AI’s memory wall
Memory capacity, bandwidth, latency, and energy consumption stand out as key chokepoints for physical AI, alongside potential supply constraints for some memory technologies. The challenge is designing a memory subsystem capable of feeding increasingly demanding AI workloads within tight power and thermal limits, not just adding a sufficient number of memory components.
“The billions of associated model parameters also need to be stored and transported across storage, memory, and processing elements,” Sousa said. “Today, this is referred to as the memory wall. As memory footprint continues to grow, DRAM needs an ultra-fast interface, such as LPDDR6, to no longer be a bottleneck to processing.”
Performance also depends on access patterns, latency, data reuse, cache capacity, memory-controller efficiency, and the energy required to move data. Increasing raw bandwidth may provide limited benefit if workloads are constrained by other parts of the memory hierarchy.
Workload-specific system design can help offset some memory burdens. “Coming up with right-sized memory, right-sized compute and redundancy, everything that needs to fit into your thermal and power envelope is going to be very key,” said Balasubramanian. “The most important thing is that size matters. You don’t need a 100-gallon tank in your Prius. You need a 10-gallon tank. That’s the analogy I use in terms of memory. You can manage it in a way that you don’t need a huge DRAM, but you have a pretty good cache and an SRAM built in. It can always store critical requirements in DRAM, but you can move everything else to flash or SRAM when needed. The memory path, in terms of cache coherency from DRAM to SRAM, to the actual compute, and to making the actual physical AI, is going to be very key.”
The trade-offs between these memory technologies are significant. On-chip SRAM and caches can provide fast access to frequently used data, but their capacity is limited by silicon area and cost. External DRAM offers greater capacity, while flash provides nonvolatile storage for models, software, and other information that doesn’t need to remain in active memory.
Moving information among these tiers can reduce some capacity requirements, but it adds transfer overhead and latency. Cache coherency, meanwhile, focuses on keeping copies of data consistent across caches and memory, rather than simply moving information between storage technologies, but that adds more overhead. So engineers must consider the working set, data locality, and access frequency when determining how much memory belongs at each level.
Automotive memory innovations will likely loom large in how the issue is addressed for physical AI.
“It’s very closely coupled to our automotive range at the moment, and we see the majority of requirements from the robotics side coming directly from the automotive side,” said Rob Fisher, senior director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “A lot of automotive players will now present their chips as automotive and robotics platforms, so the 4-, 6-, and 8-bit support are really going to benefit memory bandwidth and memory footprint of embedded edge-type applications. It’s less of a concern in data centers, but the impact is different. You can probably have a bigger model in a data center by using a smaller bit width on your words. In an automotive application and a robotics application, you’ll probably take the other side of that benefit, which is a smaller memory footprint. You’ll constrain your model to do exactly what you need it to do, and then you’ll reduce the amount of memory and bandwidth you have available to contain it.”
Lower-precision representations can reduce model storage and memory bandwidth requirements, making them particularly attractive for embedded AI. But the benefits depend on whether the accelerator efficiently supports the chosen numerical format and whether quantization preserves the application’s required accuracy. Formats such as 6-bit representations can also introduce packing or implementation overhead, limiting the gains achievable on hardware not designed for them.
Flash storage also plays a critical role in managing memory for autonomous systems.
“DRAM is constrained in capacity, power, and availability,” Sousa said. “Faster storage bandwidth shortens load time, so the same DRAM budget can support larger models. These systems run continuously on batteries and often without active cooling, so every data transfer costs power and adds delay, making it necessary for each component — mechanical, electronic, and software — to limit power consumption and improve efficiency. Interfaces such as MIPI, UFS, LPDDR, PCIe, etc., have techniques built in to ensure fast transmission of bursty data and then transitioning to long low-power idle modes.”
Faster non-volatile storage can shorten model-loading delays and, when paired with appropriate model partitioning or weight-streaming techniques, allow systems with limited DRAM to execute workloads whose total model footprint exceeds available active memory. However, storage bandwidth alone does not increase the amount of data that can be kept in DRAM at any point in time.
The interfaces used to move that data also differ in their power-management mechanisms and operating characteristics. Their efficiency depends on the particular specification, implementation, transfer patterns, and opportunities to enter low-power states.
Physical AI’s memory demands could eventually justify new memory technologies or variants of existing ones, provided the market becomes large enough to support the investment.
“Memory is a critical technology, and it’s going to be needed in all the physical AI that’s out there,” said Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus. “What’s different about these markets is some of them are going to just leverage the memories that are out there, but it’s possible some of them could become so big in terms of market sizes that they may warrant their own type of memory or some variant of an existing memory. We saw that with HBM, for example. People were using other kinds of memories, and suddenly the market got big. And if you go back before LPDDR, phones were just using binned, carefully selected DDR parts that just happened to be low power. The market got big enough, and people said, ‘Well, let’s just make a special part.’ Physical AI has the potential to become a big enough market on its own, so that if the requirements vary enough, there could be another kind of memory.”
Whether such specialization occurs will depend on the scale and consistency of demand. Unlike data centers, physical AI spans applications with widely differing requirements for cost, capacity, endurance, bandwidth, temperature, and energy efficiency. That diversity may favor adaptations of existing memory technologies in some markets and purpose-built solutions in others.
Validating the edge cases
Ensuring a system behaves safely, including under rare and unexpected conditions, is another major challenge. Solving the validation problem is especially important as physical AI developers target integration into heavy machinery, medical devices, and other safety-critical technologies.
“The validation loop that we need to bring physical AI into before we get into any production is paramount, and I would say is the most important thing we need to do,” said Siemens’ Balasubramanian. “What happens if there is a huge power cut or there’s an earthquake, and your fiber optic cable is cut from the outside world, or there’s a power cut? How do you manage that kind of a scenario on the edge? Having some kind of compute, some kind of memory, and some kind of intelligence close to the sensor is going to be very key, and the way people do that is by coming up with what they determine is the most important thing given use-case needs. In an industrial environment, when do I need to stop the assembly line? When do I need to know that I need to phone back or start the siren or anything else? Those are some of the things that need to be handled within a given sensor.”
These scenarios illustrate why safety-critical functions cannot always depend on continuous cloud connectivity or centralized decision-making. Local processing may be necessary to recognize faults, trigger protective actions, or place equipment into a defined safe state when communications or power systems fail.
But verification and validation address different parts of the problem. Verification establishes whether a design satisfies specified requirements, while validation examines whether the system behaves appropriately in its intended operating environment. Safety assurance may additionally require hazard analysis, fault-injection testing, evaluation of common-cause failures, and evidence of compliance with applicable standards.
Systems must therefore be designed to establish and verify trust throughout the relevant hardware and software stack, with assurance requirements matched to each use case.
“When we’re designing something for a wheelchair, we have specific needs, like any physical AI application,” said Owen Kent, co-founder of assistive robotics startup ATDev. “You have to be able to really put this hardware through the wringer in your quality management system and your third-party electromagnetic compatibility testing. Whatever hardware you use, whether it’s custom or not, you have to be able to verify safety.”
For developers, that means evaluating whether components function correctly in normal operation, as well as how the complete system responds to degraded sensors, communication failures, unexpected inputs, and other foreseeable hazards. Passing component-level tests is necessary in many applications, but it does not by itself establish system-level safety.
Conclusion
Physical AI’s practical limits extend across the entire path from sensing to action. Designers must match models and hardware to the task, move data within available energy and thermal budgets, and validate how machines behave when conditions or connections change. Increasing compute capacity only helps when the rest of the system can support it.
“Start with standards-based, low-power and proven interfaces along the whole path, from sensor to processor to actuator,” said Balasubramanian. “They give designers predictable behavior, ecosystem interoperability, and silicon-proven building blocks.”
A relevant example is the MIPI Camera Security Framework, which combines the Camera Service Extensions (CSE) 2.0 specification with complementary security specifications. CSE 2.0 supports data-integrity protection and optional encryption of CSI-2 camera data, while the broader framework addresses authentication of imaging-system components and secure-session establishment.
“It provides end-to-end security for camera data, covering integrity, authentication, and confidentiality from the image sensor to the SoC,” he said. “It also gives designers flexible options to minimize compute and traffic overhead, power, and latency, so security can be matched to the application rather than designed for the worst case.”
The distinction matters because confidentiality is optional, and the level of protection depends on the security services and configurations implemented. The broader framework lets developers balance protection against processing overhead, power consumption, and latency, rather than applying identical protections to every data stream.
It’s not enough to make autonomous machines more capable. They also must be dependable within real-world constraints. For physical AI, the architecture choices that conserve memory, power, and bandwidth must also support predictable behavior, resilience, and the safety assurance that widespread deployment demands.

articles.title: Bambu Lab releases the H3C printer to take 3D printing to an all-new level - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Bambu Lab has unveiled its first third-generation 3D printer – the H3C – which is capable of multi-material printing to take the category to an all-new level and produce prints we could have only dreamed about just a few short years ago.
The H3C has new Swaptek architecture, which includes nine print tools, each with its own filament path and heating.
A material switch can now be achieved in as little as six seconds which speeds up print time and reduces waste.
To achieve multi-material printing it required a machine that can handle such a capability.
And that’s how Bambu Lab conceived the idea for the H3C.
The company brought all its engineering experience to the table to come up with a machine that could handle more than one material and overcome the limitations experienced with older models.
As a result the new H3C has three new major parts – the Swaptek to handle the tool changes, FlexFeed Extruder to deal with flexible materials, and the AMS 3H, which can store and dry and feed the material to the printer.
When they work together it makes bringing nine materials together as effortless as it is to reach for one.
Each of the nine print tools has its own filament path and its own heating so the filament stays loaded and ready to go.
This means it’s ready to go in an instant and can be preheated ahead of the switch.
This means there’s no need to retract one material to feed the next, resulting in faster more efficient printing.
Swaptek also introduces capabilities like mixing colours and mixing nozzle sizes within a single print.
The FlexFeed Extruder makes printing with soft TPU easier than ever before.
The issue with softer filament was that it would bend and buckle before it reaches the nozzle so regular extruders had to slow down to remain stable and reliable.
But FlexFeed can handle both 1.75 and 2.85 mm filament and switch them on the fly.
The larger 2.85 mm TPU can now stay rigid under pressure, melt in greater volume, and push through with more force.
The result is being able to print at up to three times the flow rate of a regular printer.
This softer TPU is used to print comfortable wearables like shoes which is now easier to print than ever before with the H3C.
AMS 3H integrated filament management system is fully enclosed and has been designed to work seamlessly with Swaptek.
Each spool sits in a sealed airtight chamber to protect it from moisture and filament feeds into the print tool automatically.
Alongside the multi-material system is a motion platform built from scratch.
The toolhead and X-axis assembly are 40 per cent lighter, which means they can operate smoother and faster.
Prints can be finished, on average, more than 10 per cent faster than on the previous models without reducing any detail.
The new Bambu Lab H3C is available now and is priced at $3,999.
Stay tuned to Tech Guide for a full review of the Bambu Lab H3C in the coming weeks.

articles.title: CERT-In warns NBFCs and fintech firms of AI-driven attacks
articles.text:
CERT-In warns NBFCs and fintech firms of AI-driven attacks
An advisory from the government body said the AI-assisted financial threat is still active and warns BFSI entities to treat it as an “immediate and continuing threat”.
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has issued an advisory warning that hackers are attacking non-banking financial corporations with the help of artificial intelligence.
Terming the threat campaign "CRAFTY FALCON", the government body describes it as an “AI-assisted financial threat actor that surveys its targets with machine intelligence, operates at machine speed and strikes by invoking the victim's own payment and disbursement APIs.”
CERT-In is the national nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents.
“Continued analysis of incidents reported by affected entities including non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment aggregators, payment service providers and cryptocurrency exchanges / virtual digital asset service providers has revealed a significant escalation of this campaign.”
The advisory further said the threat is still active and has warned BFSI (banking, financial services, and insurance) entities to treat it as an “immediate and continuing threat”.
Outlining some of the reported attacks, the advisory said merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators were exploited or abused to move funds. Cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers were also targeted, with wallet keys stolen and funds siphoned from cryptocurrency wallets.
The advisory mentioned that the same companies have faced repeated attacks.
The body also revealed that its analysis has shown the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools. These include the ARTEX family of LLM-based, the PentAGI autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system, the Cairn attack search engine, and the CyberStrikeAI framework.
Last month, CERT-In had flagged incidents involving AI agents exceeding their authorised tasks and accessing live systems of Indian organisations, alongside financially motivated attacks using open-source agentic AI tools.
Globally too, such attacks have been on the rise. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported observing AI offensive security tools being used in real-world intrusions, including attacks on organisations across the United States and Europe.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: La Nasa n'a pas pu le sauver : le télescope Swift s'est désintégré dans l'atmosphère (vidéo)
articles.text:
C’était son dernier plongeon. Ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, le télescope Swift de la Nasa est retombé sur Terre, mettant fin à près de 22 ans de mission. Selon l’US Space Force, l’observatoire est rentré dans l’atmosphère à 13h39 (heure de Paris). Il s’est enflammé dans le ciel, « au-dessus de la région de Sumatra du Nord, en Indonésie », détaille l’agence spatiale dans un communiqué.
Cette désintégration, qui a donné lieu à un spectaculaire bolide (une grosse étoile filante), a pu être filmée depuis la surface de la Terre.
L’Aerospace Corporation, un centre de recherche qui travaille pour l’armée américaine et suit les rentrées atmosphériques des satellites, a publié de son côté une carte sur X montrant l’endroit où Swift est retombé.
Swift se désintègre après une tentative de sauvetage ratée
Officiellement, la mission de Swift était déjà terminée depuis quelques jours. Sa dernière observation du ciel a eu lieu le 20 octobre, alors que le télescope évoluait à 275 km au-dessus de la surface terrestre. À cette altitude, Swift ne parvenait plus à compenser le freinage de l’atmosphère et s’est mis en mode sans échec. Trois jours plus tard, la Nasa a expliqué avoir « fermé les yeux » de Swift, en coupant ses instruments.
Quelques mois plus tôt, la Nasa avait tenté de sauver Swift à l’aide de LINK, un remorqueur de l’entreprise américaine Katalyst Space. Lancé le 3 juillet, l’engin n’a pas pu remplir sa mission, et la Nasa a renoncé au sauvetage. LINK devait essayer de placer Swift sur une orbite plus adaptée, à 600 km de la surface de la Terre, mais des problèmes techniques l’ont empêché de mener à bien cette mission (LINK s’étant mis à tourner de façon incontrôlée).
« La Nasa s’attendait à ce que la majeure partie du vaisseau se consume lors de son passage dans l’atmosphère, mais certains composants pourraient avoir survécu à la rentrée », précise la publication de blog de l’agence spatiale.
Le satellite pesait environ 1 450 kg. Avant sa chute, la Nasa estimait à environ 1 sur 2 100 le risque qu’une personne soit touchée par un débris. Comme l’orbite de Swift était peu inclinée, les fragments éventuels ne pouvaient retomber qu’entre 20,6 degrés de latitude sud et 20,6 degrés de latitude nord.
Une mission de la Nasa prévue pour 2 ans, qui en a duré près de 22
Swift a largement dépassé les attentes de la Nasa. À l’origine, il avait été envoyé dans l’espace en 2004 pour une mission principale de 2 ans. Il devait étudier les sursauts gamma, les explosions les plus puissantes connues dans l’Univers.
L’observatoire a finalement servi pendant plus de 2 décennies, comme « outil polyvalent pour explorer l’Univers », résume la Nasa. Swift a ainsi permis d’étudier des galaxies alimentées par des trous noirs supermassifs, des supernovae, ou les comètes et astéroïdes de notre système solaire.

articles.title: Aspiration, lavage et entretien du rouleau : le Dreame H15 Pro passe sous les 250 €
articles.text:
L’aspirateur laveur Dreame H15 Pro est à 249,16 € (-45 %)
Avec son format inclinable à plat et son rouleau autonettoyant, le Dreame H15 Pro passe à 249,16 € chez Amazon, soit 45 % sous le prix conseillé.
Vendu et expédié par Amazon, ce modèle neuf bénéficie de la livraison gratuite. L’économie atteint 199,84 € face au prix conseillé de 449 €. Le tarif est également inférieur de 48,83 € au plus bas des 30 derniers jours indiqué par le marchand, de 297,99 €.
Un nettoyage jusque sous les meubles
Le H15 Pro aspire les poussières et lave les sols durs avec son rouleau humide. Sa conception inclinable à 180° permet d’atteindre le dessous des meubles bas. Une raclette mobile accompagne les mouvements pour récupérer les petites saletés et limiter l’eau laissée au sol.
Sur sa base, le rouleau bénéficie d’un autonettoyage avec de l’eau chauffée jusqu’à 100 °C, suivi d’un séchage à l’air chaud. Ces températures concernent l’entretien de la brosse sur la station. Les réservoirs séparés permettent de conserver l’eau propre à l’écart de l’eau récupérée.
Une bonne autonomie, mais un poids sensible
Lors de notre test, nous avons mesuré près de 44 minutes d’autonomie. Les réservoirs ont permis environ 39 minutes de nettoyage avant de nécessiter une intervention. Nous avons également apprécié l’efficacité de l’autonettoyage du rouleau et le ramassage des petites poussières le long des murs.
Ses 5,8 kg restent toutefois sensibles malgré les roues motorisées, particulièrement dans les virages serrés. La raclette peut aussi repousser les gros déchets. Ce modèle convient donc surtout à l’entretien régulier des sols durs, avec une bonne endurance entre deux charges.

articles.title: Supermicro Super AI Station Review: The AI Server That Doubles as a Workstation
articles.text:
With several partners in its DGX Station initiative, NVIDIA’s project to bring its server-grade Grace Blackwell GB300 hardware to desktop workstations has no shortage of hardware suppliers. Or system designs, for that matter. Of all of these, Supermicro is a clear frontrunner for the most interesting workstation, thanks to its unique, convertible design.
Today we are taking a look at our latest DGX Station system with Supermicro’s Super AI Station (ARS-511GD-NB-LCC). By squeezing in as much compute hardware as a 1.6kW power supply can sustain, NVIDIA and its partners are positioning these systems as the ultimate desk-side AI boxes for local AI work.
| Supermicro Super AI Station (ARS-511GD-NB-LCC) Key Specs |  | 
| CPU | NVIDIA Grace 72-Core Neoverse V2 (72C/72T) | 
| GPU | NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra | 
| Operating System | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS with NVIDIA AI Developer Tools | 
| Memory | CPU: 496GB LPDDR5X (396GB/s) GPU: 252GB HBM3E (7.1TB/s) | 
| Storage | 2x M.2 2280 (PCIe Gen6 x4) 2x M.2 2280 (PCIe Gen5 x4) | 
| Video Card | Optional: NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell 2000/4000/6000 | 
| PSU | 1600W (80 PLUS Titanium) | 
| Form Factor | Tower Workstation (5U) 218 x 455 x 701 mm (8.6 x 17.9 x 27.6 in) | 
| Networking | 2x 400Gbps (QSFP112, ConnectX-8) 10Gb Ethernet (RJ45, Marvell) 1Gb Ethernet (BMC) | 
| Ports | Front: 2x USB-A 5Gbps Rear: 4x USB-A 10Gbps, 1x USB Micro-B UART (BMC), 2x 400GbE (QSFP112), 1x 10GbE LAN (RJ45, Marvell), 1x 1GbE LAN (RJ45, BMC), 3x 3.5mm Audio, 1x Mini DisplayPort (BMC) | 
Meanwhile, every DGX Station vendor is putting their own spin on how a GB300 desktop should be built, and Supermicro is no different. For Supermicro, that means taking the “server at your desk” motif a little more literally than most, by developing a system that can either be set up as a full-size desktop tower or placed in a rack as a 5U system. It is, without a doubt, quintessentially Supermicro and a great example of how the company has applied its server expertise to the workstation market. It also makes a lot of sense given what we have learned with the networking on these systems.
Without further ado, let us dive right in.
Supermicro Super AI Station External Hardware Overview
The first time you see Supermicro’s Super AI Server, it is immediately obvious that it is different from the full-tower PCs other DGX Station vendors offer. For their own DGX Station system, Supermicro has done the most Supermicro thing possible by putting the system inside of a convertible chassis. This system can be set up as a desktop workstation, or it can be put on rails and rack-mounted as a 5U server.
That kind of convertible design has a huge impact on the system design, as we will see. Both the system’s form factor and internal layout have been optimized to fulfill both roles, which at times makes this a very different system from other DGX Station systems.
One immediate impact of that design is that the Super AI Station is a bit shorter and much deeper than a typical PC tower workstation. At 455mm tall, the Super AI Station is skinny enough to fit between a pair of rack posts. The trade-off is that it is 701mm (or nearly 28 inches) long.
With 1600 watts of hardware to cool, the Super AI Station is best described as a high-airflow system. Almost every square millimeter of space on the front of the system is dedicated to drawing in air to cool the system.
The sole exception to that is a small front I/O panel, which, despite the heavy airflow emphasis, marks the first time we have seen an actual front I/O panel on a DGX Station. Supermicro’s server roots make themselves apparent here once again, as the port collection is a simple pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports. Compared with other systems, we have seen other vendors put 10Gbps USB-A and USB-C ports here, underscoring the server roots of this design once more. The ports themselves are adequately labeled, but it feels a bit more like a server in this respect.
Otherwise, the front I/O panel is rounded out with the power button, a smaller reset button, and finally a drive activity LED. The system status LED is embedded in the power button and can illuminate red or blue, depending on the system status.
To the left of the front I/O panel is a locked cage, which hides the system’s service tag information. This area could also theoretically house front panel storage expansion.
As for the sides of the Super AI Station, both sides are unremarkable. Unlike Supermicro’s fun demo unit back at Computex, the production hardware does not come with a plexiglass window. If you want to see inside, you will have to take the side panels off. Since the system is convertible, Supermicro doesn’t rely on the sides for significant ventilation, so these panels are little more than simple steel sheets.
Flipping over to the rear of the system, we finally get a better idea of just how different the Super AI Station is from more standard workstations: this is not a standard EEB/E-ATX chassis. The power supply is on its own side of the system, there is an obvious coolant tank, and, though not obvious in this shot, the motherboard is installed upside-down. The PCIe slot brackets are at the top of the system.
Because NVIDIA provides the motherboards for all these DGX Station systems, the port layout is standardized, so Supermicro’s matches the other vendors.
Starting on the left, the system’s two QSFP112 ports are fed by the powerful NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC. Each port offers 400Gbps networking and is the primary way the system connects to high-speed storage and/or other DGX Station-based systems. We have shown that these systems can push 800Gbps through the NIC in certain circumstances. The ConnectX-8 SuperNIC driving these ports does a lot of heavy lifting beyond networking, and the capabilities and limitations of these QSFP ports are somewhat complex as a result (more on this in a bit). Meanwhile, there is a grate above the QSFP cages to allow for a bit more airflow for cooling.
For more mundane networking use cases, the system also has a pair of RJ45 Ethernet jacks. The left 1G port connects to the BMC and is for system management. OpenBMC handles management via an HTML5 iKVM. The RJ45 jack on the right side is a 10Gb Ethernet port powered by Marvell’s tried-and-true 10GbE controller. The system topology is fascinating. Marvell’s 10Gbase-T controller is attached to the NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC’s built-in PCIe switch, then to the CPU. It does not connect directly to the CPU.
Below are the remaining USB ports. These four ports all run at 10Gbps, making these the fastest USB ports on the system. This also means that since NVIDIA did not include USB-C ports in its motherboard design, you will not find any USB-C ports on the Super AI Station.
To the right, we have a trio of audio jacks for two-channel audio out, plus separate mic and line-in jacks.
At the end of the rear I/O panel, two more ports connect to the BMC. On the left is a serial UART in a micro-USB form factor. To the right is a Mini DisplayPort output from the BMC for system management and configuration. DGX Station systems do not have a true integrated display GPU (Blackwell Ultra is more of a compute accelerator), so the BMC provides the only out-of-the-box graphics output. For a full-featured graphics solution, you can pair DGX Station systems with a compatible NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell video card. In this case, Supermicro has included an RTX PRO 2000 Blackwell card.
Notably, no port is labeled on the rear of the system. Supermicro has seemingly opted not to print anything on its I/O shield, at least in this example. For a server, this is par for the course, but as the Super AI Station is meant to double as a workstation, it would have been nice to see. We have an early system, so sometimes those early systems miss details like that.
Like all DGX Station systems, the Super AI Station is liquid-cooled. Supermicro’s design makes this obvious. The company uses an externally accessible coolant tank mounted toward the top of the system. Because the system comes completely pre-built, the Super AI Station is designed for minimal maintenance, so the externally accessible tank seems like a holdover from data center systems that can require more active maintenance. Regardless, if the system starts running low on coolant, the liquid level indicator makes it easy to see, and there are ports for filling and draining the system.
Elsewhere, near the bottom of the system, we have the Super AI Station’s 1600 Watt power supply. While the wattage is standardized across DGX Station systems, the actual power supply model is not. This benefits Supermicro, as theirs is the first DGX Station system to cross our labs with an 80 Plus Titanium-rated power supply, one step higher than the Platinum units we have seen in other systems.
Because Supermicro put all of their front I/O and buttons on the front of the system, there is no need for the top of the system to be anything special. Coupled with the fact that it has no ventilation here, since that would not work in a rackmount scenario, Supermicro is keeping things simple on top. This top can be popped off to expose mounting points for rackmount rails.
The bottom, for that matter. Here it is much more obvious, even in a workstation configuration, that this chassis can be rack-mounted, as you can easily see where the rails would go.
This also means that for workstation mode, the chassis needs a pair of feet attached to properly support the system and its copious 88lb weight.
That wraps things up for our outside look at the Super AI Station. For the rest of the story, let us dive into the system’s chassis, where this gets very different.

articles.title: Las escuelas de EEUU quieren un Google sin IA, pero se enfrentan a un dilema: o aceptan sus resúmenes con IA o se quedan sin buscador
articles.text:
Estos días ha habido cierta polémica en Estados Unidos acerca de una serie de cambios que Google quiere introducir en torno al uso de su IA en los centros educativos del país. Y es que tal y como compartía la compañía, desactivará por defecto sus herramientas de IA para las cuentas de estudiantes de educación obligatoria el año que viene. Sin embargo, se ha generado controversia precisamente porque los colegios que no quieran nada de IA también perderían Google Search.
El dominio de Google en las escuelas. Sus Chromebooks son los dispositivos para estudiantes que más se ven en las aulas de EEUU, según The New York Times, y son más de 150 millones de profesores y estudiantes en todo el mundo los que utilizan su plataforma Classroom. En Estados Unidos ahora mismo hay un debate político bastante profundo en torno al uso de la IA en las escuelas, y hay distritos que quieren prohibir su uso. El tema es que se enfrentan a un dilema, pues tal y como están las cosas, o aceptan los resúmenes de IA (AI Overviews) o dejan a los alumnos sin el motor de búsqueda de Google.
Lo que anuncia Google. En una publicación en su blog el pasado 3 de noviembre, la compañía indicaba que Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini en Classroom y Google Search quedarían "totalmente desactivados" para las cuentas de estudiantes de K-12 (desde infantil hasta el último curso de secundaria) hasta que los administradores quieran activarlos. Los encargados de gestionar estas apps en los colegios podrán habilitar cada servicio de forma individual. Google afirma que esto ofrece a los colegios "más opciones, y no menos", y que responde a las quejas de los profesores que pedían un mayor control sobre el uso de la IA por parte de los alumnos.
El problema. No hay un interruptor separado para AI Overviews, los resúmenes generados por IA en la parte superior de los resultados. Chris Phillips, vicepresidente de educación de Google, declaraba al Times que "la búsqueda y la IA están profundamente integradas". Las escuelas que opten por rechazar la IA, señalaba, no tendrán acceso a las búsquedas, y los estudiantes verán un mensaje indicando que no está disponible. Los cambios entrarán en vigor a principios de 2027, y Google afirma que compartirá los detalles con los colegios en los próximos meses.
Qué ha cambiado desde agosto. La compañía había activado las funciones de Gemini por defecto dentro de Classroom para los centros escolares que ya permitían a los alumnos acceder al chatbot, pero esta medida molestó a algunos directivos de las escuelas, según el Times. Google está ahora dando marcha atrás a esa configuración por defecto.
La preocupación en el aula. Algunos profesores afirman que los resúmenes pueden disuadir a los alumnos de comparar fuentes y llegar a sus propias conclusiones. Un administrador de sistemas escolares escribía en un foro de soporte de Google que los estudiantes necesitan oportunidades para examinar fuentes "antes de haber empezado siquiera" con una síntesis de IA, tal y como cuentan desde Wired. El medio también cita un estudio de la Universidad de Washington en St. Louis que descubrió que solo alrededor del 42 % de los resúmenes de IA podían verificarse por completo a través de sus propias citas. Desde Google afirman que los resúmenes se someten a “rigurosas pruebas y siguen mejorando”.
La respuesta de Google. La compañía afirma que está integrando su función de Aprendizaje Guiado (Guided Learning) en la Búsqueda y en los Resúmenes de IA para las cuentas de estudiantes. En lugar de dar una respuesta rápida, su objetivo es guiar al estudiante a través de un problema paso a paso, un diseño que, según Google, fomenta el "esfuerzo productivo". Está prevista una prueba piloto en determinados colegios de EEUU este mes, extendiéndose en los próximos meses.
Reacción política. La decisión de la compañía ha sido uno de los temas centrales de la agenda de varias figuras políticas. El senador Bernie Sanders calificaba la medida de "extorsión" en X. El senador Richard Blumenthal afirmaba que “Google parece más preocupado por imponer Gemini en las escuelas que por el éxito de los estudiantes”. La ex presidenta de la FTC Lina Khan decía que Google está utilizando su "monopolio de búsquedas para coaccionar a los colegios", y el alcalde de la ciudad de Nueva York, Zohran Mamdani, aseguraba que ninguna corporación “debería dictar cómo se enseña a los niños”.
Qué pueden hacer los colegios. Algunos han optado por soluciones alternativas como URLs de búsqueda modificadas y extensiones de navegador, pero estas podrían dejar de funcionar si Google cambia la forma en que se muestran los resultados. Y cambiar de motor de búsqueda también es difícil para los estudiantes vinculados a los Chromebooks y a las herramientas educativas de Google. Es un filón que puede aprovechar DuckDuckGo, aunque un portavoz de la compañía contaba a Wired que no hay intenciones de lanzar pronto una versión para aulas.
Por otro lado, Microsoft ofrece una extensión de Chrome para desactivar los resúmenes de IA en Bing. Pero claro, Bing.
Y ahora qué. Google no ha aclarado si añadirá una forma de desactivar los resúmenes por sí solos, y la ex jefa de producto de Google Search, Nicole Kerson, contaba a Wired que el obstáculo puede ser el coste de mantener una versión separada de la Búsqueda.
Imagen de portada | Nathana Rebouças
En Xataka | Google por fin te da la respuesta que buscas a la primera. Y ese es exactamente el origen de sus problemas
