articles.title: Nokia 1100 vs el primer iPhone de Apple: cuánto duraba la batería de cada modelo
articles.text:
El Nokia 1100 y el primer iPhone de Apple expusieron dos formas opuestas de entender la telefonía, con diferencias visibles en diseño, funciones y duración de batería.
El celular de Nokia priorizó la comunicación básica, los controles físicos y la resistencia; el dispositivo presentado por Steve Jobs en 2007 concentró herramientas digitales en una pantalla táctil.
Los dos modelos respondieron a las condiciones técnicas y a los hábitos de sus respectivas épocas. Mientras el Nokia 1100 buscaba mantenerse operativo durante varios días con llamadas y mensajes, el primer iPhone incorporó navegación web, reproducción multimedia, correo y una interfaz que demandaba recargas más frecuentes.
Cuánto tiempo duraba la batería del Nokia 1100
El Nokia 1100, lanzado en 2003, utilizaba una batería de iones de litio BL-5C con capacidad de 850 mAh. Tenía una autonomía de hasta 4,5 horas de conversación continua y entre 10 y 16 días en espera, con un máximo de 400 horas. La cifra variaba según la señal de la red y la frecuencia de uso.
En la práctica, el teléfono podía funcionar entre cinco y siete días con una sola carga en un uso cotidiano. La pantalla monocromática, de bajo consumo, y la nula cantidad de aplicaciones explicaban ese rendimiento. El aparato se concentraba en llamadas, mensajes de texto, agenda, alarma, calculadora y, en algunas versiones, linterna.
Qué autonomía ofrecía el primer iPhone de Apple
El primer iPhone de Apple tenía una batería no extraíble de 1.400 mAh, una capacidad superior a la del Nokia 1100. El aumento respondía a la necesidad de alimentar una pantalla táctil a color de 3,5 pulgadas, el procesador, la conexión WiFi, las redes EDGE y las funciones multimedia incluidas en el dispositivo.
Según las especificaciones de Apple, el modelo alcanzaba hasta ocho horas de conversación, seis horas de navegación por internet mediante WiFi, siete horas de video y cerca de 250 horas, equivalentes a unos 10 días, en modo de espera.
Con navegación, música, correo y llamadas, su batería solía durar entre 12 y 24 horas, así que la recarga diaria se convirtió en una práctica habitual.
Por qué el Nokia 1100 consumía menos recursos
La autonomía del Nokia 1100 estaba ligada a un diseño sin grandes exigencias de procesamiento. Su pantalla pequeña y monocromática requería menos energía que los paneles a color, mientras que sus funciones no dependían de una conexión permanente a internet ni de aplicaciones que operaran en segundo plano.
El teléfono tampoco incluía cámara, reproducción de video, navegador web avanzado ni una pantalla que debiera permanecer activa durante períodos prolongados. La combinación entre funciones limitadas y batería de 850 mAh permitía varios días de uso, incluso con una capacidad menor a la del iPhone.
Cómo cambió el teclado la relación con el celular
El Nokia 1100 tenía un teclado numérico de plástico, con teclas separadas para marcar números y escribir mensajes. Cada número reunía varias letras, así que redactar un SMS requería pulsar la misma tecla varias veces hasta seleccionar el carácter. El sistema era habitual en los teléfonos de comienzos de los años 2000.
Esa estructura permitía usar el aparato con una mano y sin mirar de forma continua la pantalla. El teclado ocupaba una parte importante del frente y dejaba poco espacio para visualizar información.
Qué trajo el iPhone con su pantalla táctil
El primer iPhone eliminó el teclado físico y reservó la mayor parte de la parte frontal para su pantalla de 3,5 pulgadas. Apple sostuvo que los botones permanentes limitaban el espacio y fijaban una misma distribución para tareas distintas. El teclado virtual aparecía solo cuando el usuario debía escribir y desaparecía al abrir otras funciones.
El cambio modificó la interacción con el celular. Los controles podían adaptarse a cada aplicación, desde el correo hasta las notas, la búsqueda de contactos o la navegación.
El dispositivo mantuvo un botón principal y botones laterales para volumen y encendido. La pantalla multitáctil permitió ampliar o reducir páginas web mediante gestos.

articles.title: Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede urges better use of Africa's capital
articles.text:
Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede, chairman of Nigerian tier-1 lender Access Bank Group and financial services holding company Coronation Group, argues that African financial institutions must move beyond financial stability to productive finance, unlock capital tied up in commercial transactions and build banking systems capable of operating across borders.
Africa’s financial institutions have spent years debating the availability and cost of capital. However, Aig-Imoukhuede believes the continent is asking the wrong question.
Rather than focusing primarily on how much capital Africa can attract, he wants policymakers and financial institutions to examine how effectively the money already available is being deployed.
“At this particular moment in Africa’s development, I believe the more important question is: How do we make better use of the capital we already have?” he said during the closing session of the Africa Financial Industry Summit (AFIS) in Luanda, Angola.
His argument is that the continent’s financial systems must become better at connecting existing capital to businesses, productive economic activity and long-term investments. Without that shift, financial stability and stronger banking institutions may not translate into the broader economic prosperity Africa needs.
Aig-Imoukhuede outlined three priorities for achieving this: unlocking capital trapped in commercial transactions, mobilising long-term savings for long-term investments, and addressing government borrowing that limits the private sector’s access to financing.
The money trapped in commercial transactions
One of the biggest opportunities, in his view, lies in the financing of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
Across Africa, businesses generate significant economic value through production and commercial activities, often in cycles lasting 90 to 120 days. Yet smaller businesses that supply goods and services to larger companies frequently struggle to access financing.
A supplier may fulfil an order for a large corporation and record a credible commercial transaction on its books, yet still face liquidity constraints because its own credit profile is weaker than the buyer’s.
Aig-Imoukhuede believes financial institutions should change how they assess such transactions.
“When an SME supplies goods or services to a creditworthy buyer, that transaction should enable the SME to access financing at a rate that reflects the creditworthiness of the buyer, rather than the weaker credit profile of the small supplier,” he said.
In effect, the commercial transaction itself could become the basis for accessing credit, allowing smaller businesses to benefit from the financial strength of the larger companies they supply.
He pointed to digital invoicing as an example of the infrastructure that could make this possible, citing more than three billion registered invoices in India, following the introduction of digital invoicing a decade ago, and approximately 60 billion in Brazil.
He argued that Africa could unlock significant economic value by developing similar systems, particularly given the continent’s large population of SMEs and sole traders.
The proposal requires central banks, commercial banks and other financial institutions to reconsider how they assess creditworthiness. Instead of relying primarily on the financial standing of individual small businesses, lenders could use verified commercial transactions and the buyer’s strength to support financing.
That would address a persistent constraint for smaller suppliers: the gap between generating revenue and receiving payment.
Why long-term projects need long-term money
A second priority is mobilising savings for investments that require longer financing terms.
Aig-Imoukhuede argued that banks cannot continue to rely heavily on deposits that customers can withdraw at short notice to finance projects requiring capital over 20 years.
“We cannot continue to rely on bank deposits, which can be withdrawn tomorrow, to finance long-term projects that require 20-year money,” he said.
He believes there is an appetite among Africans for longer-term economic opportunities, but the financial channels linking their savings to such investments need to be developed.
He cited the Dangote Refinery as evidence that investors are willing to participate in major real-sector projects and earn returns from economic activity.
The challenge, therefore, is not simply encouraging people to save, but creating investment structures that enable their savings to finance productive assets over appropriate time horizons.
This would require financial institutions and markets to provide avenues for ordinary investors to participate in major projects, rather than leaving such opportunities to a relatively small pool of investors.
His argument also raises a broader question about the role of African pension funds and other institutional investors. These pools of capital could play a greater role in financing infrastructure and productive assets instead of remaining heavily concentrated in government securities.
Government borrowing and the private sector
A third constraint is the extent to which government borrowing competes with private businesses for available financing.
Aig-Imoukhuede acknowledged that governments have legitimate funding requirements, but warned that public borrowing can limit the capital available to businesses.
He argued that central banks cannot address this challenge in isolation. Collaboration among monetary authorities, fiscal policymakers, and the private sector is necessary to achieve a more sustainable balance between government financing needs and private-sector investment.
He suggested that central bank governors and finance ministers should work together more deliberately on the issue.
The underlying concern is that a financial system can remain stable while failing to provide sufficient financing for businesses capable of expanding production, creating jobs and supporting economic growth.
As he put it, a banking system can be safe and profitable but still serve an economy that is fundamentally unproductive.
African banks must compete beyond their home markets
Aig-Imoukhuede also challenged African banks to look beyond the growing presence of locally owned institutions and focus on their ability to compete internationally.
The departure of several international banks from African markets has created opportunities for domestic and regional financial institutions. But he argued that African ownership alone should not be treated as evidence of progress.
“Is it enough that an international bank has exited Africa and an African bank has taken its place? No, it is not,” he said.
The next challenge, he argued, is to translate the scale of African banks into globally competitive institutions capable of serving customers across multiple markets.
He said African banks must develop stronger regional strategies and cross-border operations, while establishing the infrastructure needed to connect African businesses and individuals to the global financial system.
“We must be present in the G7 countries. We must have clearing status and establish clearing infrastructure, whether digital or through other channels, that allows African businesses and citizens to remain connected to the global economy,” he said.
His comments point to a distinction between having African-owned banks operating in individual countries and building institutions capable of supporting businesses across borders and competing with international financial groups.
For Aig-Imoukhuede, the latter is the more consequential ambition.
Financial integration cannot happen without the movement of people
The argument for stronger African banking institutions is closely linked to his broader call for continental integration.
Aig-Imoukhuede said the discussion about African integration should not be limited to the prospect of a common currency. Before a monetary union can become meaningful, countries must address the practical barriers that restrict the movement of goods, services, capital and people.
He illustrated the problem with his own experience at the summit. His chief of staff could not travel with him to Angola because he was unable to obtain a visa in time.
The experience, he said, exposed the contradiction in discussing continental integration while movement between African countries remains difficult.
“We cannot build an integrated African banking industry or financial system without integrating the movement of goods, services and people,” he said.
He argued that integration must precede monetary union, requiring countries to establish the practical conditions for businesses, investors and individuals to operate across borders.
That includes functioning financial infrastructure, more effective settlement arrangements and cooperation between regulators.
Without these systems, African banks may expand into more countries without delivering the full benefits of an integrated market.
Making capital count
Aig-Imoukhuede’s proposals ultimately return to one central issue: Africa must improve the connection between its available capital and the economic activities that need it.
He called for a more productive financial system, the integration of African financial markets, and greater macroeconomic convergence, including improved alignment of inflation and economic stability across countries.
He also challenged the continent to reconsider who benefits from financing major investments. The Dangote Refinery, in his illustration, should not remain an isolated example of large-scale capital mobilisation. More Africans should be able to invest in and benefit from transformative projects.
He framed the test of progress over the next 10 to 20 years around whether African businesses can raise capital efficiently across borders, whether pension funds can make more meaningful investments in infrastructure and productive assets, and whether the continent can finally make its available capital count.
For Africa’s financial institutions, the implication is clear: attracting more money will not, on its own, resolve the continent’s financing constraints. The greater task is to build the systems that enable existing savings, commercial transactions, and institutional capital to reach productive businesses and investments.

articles.title: Stop Letting Your Hard Work Stay Invisible At Review Time
articles.text:
This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!
Hard work rarely speaks for itself.
When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).
That plan stalled my career for about five years.
I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.
So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”
Honestly, it never occurred to me.
I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).
Today, I would take a different approach.
Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.
Now is a great time to start the conversation.
Hard work is invisible by default
Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.
Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.
A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.
Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.
Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)
The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.
Just ask
Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.
If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”
A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)
When the answer is “no”
Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.
Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.
Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.
Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.
—Brian

articles.title: A third of acquired game studios have closed since 2000, and Arkane Lyon could be next
articles.text:
The takeaway: Layoffs and game studio closures have surged in recent years, largely due to the hangover from pandemic-era overinvestment. As Microsoft continues its layoffs and closures and Arkane Lyon fights for its life, a new analysis suggests that most studios are worse off after being acquired. However, those game studios that have thrived under certain publishers show a consistent pattern.
Game industry veteran Sebastian Cardoso recently investigated the fates of more than 300 studios bought by large companies over the past quarter century, finding that roughly 61% sold fewer games, earned lower review scores, or faced closure post-acquisition.
Arkane Lyon risks becoming the latest example if it doesn't find a buyer by mid-December, but Ubisoft and at least two other companies have made offers for the Dishonored and Deathloop developer.
Cardoso's lengthy breakdown shows changes in output and staffing for hundreds of developers since 2000, as well as post-acquisition lifespans. Although closures and layoffs have spiked since 2023, the acquiring company's identity is easily the biggest predictor of a studio's well-being.
The consequences are final, the stats show: a third of acquired studios were shut down, half of those closures coming within five years of the deal. Closures were also rarity until recently: only one acquired studio in Cardoso's dataset closed between 2019 and 2022, compared with 33 from 2023 through October.
Studios that managed to buy themselves back from their owners fared far better, with none of the 18 such cases ending in decline or closure, though Cardoso cautions those studios were probably healthy enough to fund a buyout in the first place.
Activision Blizzard is the worst offender, having either shuttered or hollowed out every single studio it acquired. Developers under Disney and Midway have a 0% survival rate, while Square Enix and EA, which recently closed BioWare, aren't much better.
Cardoso found that these publishers tend to buy studios to boost existing intellectual properties, and that debt-financed buying sprees, like Embracer's, end badly too.
At the other end of the spectrum, Nintendo, Sumo Group, Krafton, and Kadokawa have each acquired only a handful of studios since 2000 and closed none of them.
These publishers tend to buy developers only after working with them, and leave the original studio heads in charge. Kadokawa, in particular, hit the jackpot with FromSoftware, which has since released Bloodborne, Sekiro, and Elden Ring.
Meanwhile, Microsoft, Ubisoft, Take-Two, Epic Games, Sony, and Sega occupy the middle of the road. However, Microsoft recently began one of the worst rounds of layoffs, affecting 3,200 employees and the sale or closure of several studios. Fortunately, Double Fine and Compulsion escaped without shutting their doors, but Ninja Theory wasn't so lucky.
It remains unclear which camp Arkane Lyon will fall into. Sources recently told Bloomberg that Microsoft might sell it back to management, and that closure is still on the table if no deal comes together.
The French game development union representing Arkane, STJV, recently accused Microsoft of sabotaging Blade to justify a closure. The union claims development of Marvel's Blade is going fine, but a forced 19-month hiring freeze prolonged it. STJV claimed that Arkane is profitable, just not profitable enough for Microsoft.

articles.title: Zyxel Switch Hacks Blamed on Patched Flaw Actually Exploited a Zero-Day
articles.text:
A recently patched vulnerability in Zyxel GS1900 series switches was exploited in the wild as a zero-day to hack almost 1,000 devices, cybersecurity firm Binarly reports.
The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-107441 (CVSS score of 8.8) and is described as an out-of-bounds write issue in the CGI program of the Zyxel GS1900 series switch firmware.
According to Zyxel, an unauthenticated attacker could exploit the security defect via crafted HTTP requests to achieve OS command execution.
The vulnerability impacts 10 GS1900 switch models. Zyxel rolled out fixes for it on October 23 and published an advisory on November 3.
On the same day, Binarly warned that attackers had exploited CVE-2026-107441 in attacks previously attributed to a Chinese hacking group.
The previous report came from GreyNoise, which warned on September 21 that the hackers exploited CVE-2026-7273, a Zyxel bug patched in June, to compromise roughly 1,000 devices in August.
GreyNoise linked the attacks to Red Heron, a Chinese threat actor that Acronis caught targeting Gitea instances in a large-scale hacking campaign, and CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its KEV catalog.
Now, Binarly says that the attackers did not target CVE-2026-7273. They deployed variants of the Jitterly and Sixzut malware analyzed by Acronis, but their exploit targeted a previously unknown vulnerability.
“Because the threat actor was exploiting a different vulnerability, and the patch for CVE-2026-7273 remained ineffective, this had no effect on protecting devices from being exploited by this threat actor,” the cybersecurity firm notes.
Binarly notified Zyxel of the findings on September 29, and the vendor confirmed the new vulnerability, now tracked as CVE-2026-107441, two weeks later.
“Cases such as this highlight the urgency for a more reliable way of checking vulnerabilities in software. Advisories and version numbers certainly help, but they cannot be blindly trusted. We truly believe the definitive way to assess whether software components contain vulnerabilities is by looking at their binary code,” the company notes.

articles.title: Bluetooth 7 gets a massive speed boost that brings hi-res audio and better battery life to your wireless earbuds and headphones
articles.text:
Bluetooth 7 will bring a major hi-res audio upgrade in 2027 — HDT support almost quadruples bit-rates for wireless headphones and speakers
A massive speed boost for hi-res audio and better battery life
- Bluetooth LE gets support for High Data Throughput (HDT)
- It boosts the standard's maximum supported bit-rate by almost four times
- That means support for hi-res audio, spatial audio and multi-channel audio
Good news for the best headphones of 2027 and beyond: the latest Bluetooth technology includes High Data Throughput technology, HDT for short, which gives Bluetooth LE a huge performance boost. It can transmit almost four times as much data as the current version, enabling it to send hi-res audio, spatial audio and multi-channel audio to other devices.
The fact that HDT is part of Bluetooth is important, because that means you aren't reliant on a proprietary technology for your hi-res music: if manufacturers choose to use HDT, which we'd expect them to do, then you'll have compatibility across a huge range of headphones, Bluetooth speakers and other home entertainment hardware.
There are other benefits too, as many current hi-res audio streams are sent via Wi-Fi rather than Bluetooth. Sending them over Bluetooth LE removes that traffic from your home network, potentially cutting down on congestion, and it is likely to boost your headphones' battery life, too.
Faster data transfer means less work for your Bluetooth radio, whether you're listening to hi-res audio or lower-res streams.
What's new in the blue
HDT is an optional feature in the newly published Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard, and it ups the bitrate of Bluetooth LE connections from 2.5Mbps to 7.5Mbps. Those are headline speeds, and as ever you'll get a bit less in the real world. But it's still a huge boost.
The benefits aren't just limited to headphones and other audio equipment. Anything that currently transmits or receives data via Bluetooth could benefit from the improved throughput of HDT, whether that's a smartwatch, smart glasses or a smart home device. If HDT can make updating my Apple Watch software take less time than forever, I'm sold on it already.
The downside is that you can't buy an HDT device yet. That's because there's always a lag between a new version of Bluetooth being published and products with the latest version appearing on shelves.

Bluetooth 6.0 was released in September 2024 and the first Bluetooth 6.0 headphones arrived in June 2026, with major headphone brands such as Sennheiser updating their flagships mid-year. You can expect a similar time frame with Bluetooth 7.0, so that's a summer to look forward to.

articles.title: TikTok quietly launches a stand-alone TikTok Shop app | TechCrunch
articles.text:
TikTok has quietly launched a stand-alone TikTok Shop app in select markets as it continues to expand its e-commerce ambitions. The app will offer personalized product recommendations, the ability to shop through livestreams and short-form videos, app-exclusive deals, in-app checkout, order tracking, and customer support.
The app, which was first spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra, is available in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines on iOS and Android.
The launch of a stand-alone app gives TikTok Shop a chance to reach shoppers beyond the main TikTok platform and compete more directly with established e-commerce apps like Amazon and Temu. It also suggests that TikTok is prepared to invest more heavily in social commerce by giving Shop its own dedicated destination rather than simply keeping it within the main app.
TikTok did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment regarding the rollout.
It’s unknown whether TikTok plans to release the app more widely and bring it to the United States. If TikTok does bring the app to the U.S., it would be competing not only with Amazon and Temu but also with big-box retailers like Walmart and Target, whose customers have grown accustomed to routinely ordering through the stores’ apps.
According to the app’s description, users will be able to access free shipping offers and exclusive first-order benefits, along with “secure payments for safe checkout.” By offering users app-exclusive deals, the company is incentivizing them to shop in the app rather than the main TikTok app.
Interestingly, the launch creates something of a full-circle moment in the rivalry between TikTok and Amazon. While Amazon previously introduced a TikTok-like short-form video feed called Inspire to draw consumers’ attention away from apps like TikTok and drive sales on its platform instead, TikTok is now making a similar play in reverse. With its new stand-alone commerce app, TikTok is looking to draw consumers away from platforms like Amazon and fuel more purchases within its own ecosystem.
The launch marks another step in TikTok’s efforts to branch out beyond social media. Although the company was once primarily focused on social networking and entertainment, TikTok has gradually ventured into new areas.
Beyond TikTok Shop, the company has added games, restaurant guides, sports hubs, hotel booking, and microdramas, and is also exploring payments.

articles.title: Lightspeed meets revenue expectations, but stock drops on Q2 earnings | BetaKit
articles.text:
Montréal retail technology firm Lightspeed Commerce met its earnings outlook for fiscal Q2, but investors were still unimpressed.
The news: The point-of-sale and commerce tech company published its second-quarter financial results this morning, which showed that the company generated nearly $324 million USD ($454 CAD) in revenue. It posted a net loss of $4.2 million USD ($0.03 per share) in Q2—a far cry from the $32.7 million USD ($0.24 per share) it lost during the same period last year—while recording adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) of $22.7 million USD during the three-month period ending Sept. 30.
While Lightspeed’s Q2 sales represent year-over-year growth of just two percent, this figure and other comparisons to the same period last year were impacted by its April 2026 divestiture of Upserve’s US hospitality line to Skyview Equity for up to $81 million USD (a steep discount compared to the price it paid to purchase it back in 2020). Lightspeed’s stock ($LSPD) dropped nearly 15 percent on the day on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
From the source: Given that Upserve exit, Lightspeed pointed to the 15 percent year-over-year organic revenue growth it posted in fiscal Q2 as a more representative measure of the company’s health. Meanwhile, sales in Lightspeed’s two priority markets, retail in North America and hospitality in Europe, were up 17 percent. Lightspeed CFO Asha Bakshani said the firm remains focused on scaling in both and “translating that growth into sustained profitability and cash generation.”
RELATED: Lightspeed stock sinks despite narrower net loss, revenue beat in fiscal Q1
The context: Lightspeed’s stock price soared in 2021 during the early days of the pandemic, plummeted following a short-seller report, and has since struggled to regain its previous heights. Its transformation plan has the company refocusing on particular regions and verticals, divesting from non-core areas (it remains open to more such deals), and shedding staff. Last month, Lightspeed laid off employees and closed vacant positions, impacting 250 total roles; this restructuring followed other cuts earlier this year.
Final thought: Investors have not reacted favourably to the company’s latest earnings: as of publication time, Lightspeed’s stock had dropped to $13.77 CAD per share on the Toronto Stock Exchange, erasing all of its gains so far this year. That performance may be in part due to the broader rout in tech stocks; the Nasdaq is down more than 11 percent so far this month.
Feature image courtesy Lightspeed Commerce.

articles.title: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
articles.text:
AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action.
Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task.
As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power.
What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt.
Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity.
The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.
- Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU.
- Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.
Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests:
- Perplexity: Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system.
- DeepInfra: Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested.
- ClickHouse: Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard.
- DuckLabs: Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline.
- Daytona: Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86.
- Modal: Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load.
Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU.

articles.title: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
articles.text:
Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space.
Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
Blue Origin had been aiming for a launch at the end of this year after a launchpad explosion in May, but now it’s reportedly targeting January.
In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process.
“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

articles.title: iOS 27.3: Diese Funktionen könnten mit dem nächsten Update aufs iPhone kommen
articles.text:
iOS 27.3: Diese Funktionen könnten mit dem nächsten Update aufs iPhone kommen
Seit Mitte September können iPhone-Besitzer:innen iOS 27 installieren. Allerdings enthält das Betriebssystem noch nicht alle Funktionen, die Apple im Sommer auf der WWDC versprochen hat. Diese reicht das Unternehmen in kleinen Schritten nach. iOS 27.2 enthält etwa ein Feature für die Nachrichten-App, das Daten direkt zu Kalendereinträgen machen kann.
Ein Feature entfernte Apple allerdings aus der finalen Version wieder: Die neu gestaltete Health-App war Teil der Beta-Version, hat es schlussendlich aber doch noch nicht aufs iPhone geschafft. In der ersten Beta zu iOS 27.3 hat Apple sie nun wieder integriert, wie 9to5Mac berichtet. Diesmal ist sie offenbar gekommen, um zu bleiben.
iOS 27.3 bringt die neue Health-App zurück
Die neu designte App bietet demnach drei zentrale Features: Der Insights-Tab liefert Informationen zu Herz-, Fitness- und Schlafdaten und schlüsselt sie auf einer “For you”-Seite passend zu euren Gewohnheiten auf. Im Longevity-Tab sollt ihr euer “Gesundheitsalter” vorfinden, das sich laut 9to5Mac aus Apple-Watch-Daten wie der geschätzten VO2Max-Leistung oder der Herzruhefrequenz zusammensetzt. Mit der dritten Funktion sollen Nutzer:innen mithilfe von iPhone und Apple Watch Werte zu Flexibilität, Kraft oder Balance selbst zu Hause messen könen.
Ein großes Update gibt es zudem für den Safari-Browser. Der bekommt eine neue, optionale Ansicht, bei der Tabs vertikal neben dem eigentlichen Inhalt erscheinen. Das dürfte vor allem auf dem großen Bildschirm des iPhone Duo und auf iPads ein Vorteil sein, weniger aber auf normalen iPhones. Alle profitieren dann aber von einem neuen, adaptiven Dark-Mode. Der soll Webseiten auf Knopfdruck im dunklen Design erscheinen lassen, auch wenn diese das gar nicht unterstützen.
Weitere Neuheiten betreffen den Standby-Modus normaler iPhones. Er lässt sich mit dem Update auch auf normalen iPhones besser an die eigenen Wünsche anpassen, indem sie ihn etwa um Wetter- oder Kalender-Compilations erweitern oder die Hintergrundfarbe wechseln.
Für das iPhone Duo kommt außerdem eine neue Bedienungshilfe: der Einhandmodus. Auf normalen iPhones sorgt er dafür, dass die obere Bildschirmhälfte per Swipe nach unten wandert, damit man bequem Bedienelemente erreichen kann. Das iPhone Duo ist allerdings schon kompakt. Deswegen funktioniert der Modus hier etwas anders. Per Swipe schiebt ihr die Inhalte vom linken auf den rechten Bildschirmbereich – oder andersherum.
Neue Siri-Funktionen leider nicht für uns
Vorerst nicht für deutsche iPhones vorgesehen sind neue Siri-AI-Funktionen. Im Stile eines KI-Agenten kann Siri für Nutzer:innen künftig Aktionen in Apps ausführen. So ist es möglich, den Versand einer iMessage mithilfe der Sprachassistenz zu timen, oder Fotos per Sprachbefehl in der Fotos-App zu bearbeiten. Außerdem kann Siri Tab-Gruppen in Safari oder Playlists in Apple Music erstellen.
Die Beta zu iOS 27.3 legt außerdem den Grundstein für die kontroverse “Audio Intelligence”-Funktion auf der Apple Watch. Dabei kann Siri über den Tag hinweg aufgenommene Unterhaltungen zusammenfassen oder auf Wunsch ein Transkript der vergangenen 15 Sekunden in einer Unterhaltung erstellen.
Dass alle Features in der fertigen Version von iOS 27.3 landen, ist nicht gesagt. Apple kann sie jederzeit wieder aus den nachfolgenden Versionen entfernen. Wann genau das Update erscheint, bleibt vorerst offen. Apple will die neue Health-App aber noch 2026 aufs iPhone bringen. Zunächst wird das Unternehmen einige Folge-Betas veröffentlichen, inklusive der öffentlichen Beta, die neugierige Nutzer:innen installieren können.

articles.title: Inside GitHub's new Git storage architecture
articles.text:
Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
GitHub’s new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here’s how it works.
Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.
Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.
We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.
The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.
Building for agent scale
We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:
- Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few.
- Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis.
Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.
We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.
We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:
- Accept thousands of writes per second.
- Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this:
  - Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly.
  - Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails.
- Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step.
- Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading only the data it needs to serve the incoming request.
- Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio.
- Let each component scale independently.
On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.
Introducing “Project Rubicon”
In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.
Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.
Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.
Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.
When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.
Durable state lives in two places:
- Git objects, in the form of packs and auxiliary read acceleration data, live in Azure Blob Storage.
- References and the list of packs that make up the repository (the pack manifest) live in a separate replicated log service we call Ref-CAS (for “Reference Compare-and-Swap”).
Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:
- Write: a virtual replica indexes the incoming pack and uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one transaction to Ref-CAS that lists the pack in the manifest and updates the references. Later, a compaction node merges that pack with others to keep reads fast.
- Read: a virtual replica checks its reference version with Ref-CAS, pulls the packs it needs from Blob Storage into its cache, and serves the read from there.
There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.
Minimizing coordination: mutating reference state at high throughput
Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:
- Packs and indexes written by pushes, compaction, and garbage collection.
- Various read accelerators (like multi-pack indexes, reachability bitmaps, and some custom formats) that our maintenance process builds from those packs.
- Records that let compaction and garbage collection resume or audit their work, along with the leases that compaction nodes use to claim work.
- Cached responses for frequently repeated fetches.
- Checkpoints for the reference state of the repository, though not the authoritative state used to serve requests.
Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.
References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.
Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.
Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:
Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.
Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.
Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.
Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.
These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.
But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.
Decoupling storage from compute: compaction at thousands of writes per second
Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.
Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:
The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.
To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:
Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.
Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.
What comes next
The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.
This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.
Improving the architecture
We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:
- Read only what’s needed. Fetch a single object from Blob Storage instead of the whole pack that holds it.
- Organize packs by type. Group commits, trees, and blobs into their own packs. Many requests then touch less data.
- Partial replicas. Serve requests without every pack on local disk.
- Materialized views. Keep repository data in ready-to-use forms, like prepared archives, a near-live shallow copy of the default branch, and agent session context stored alongside each commit.
- Global replicas. Place replicas in any region, close to the workloads that use them. Reads stay within bounded staleness of the latest write.
- Scale to zero. Grow and shrink the fleet with the repositories that are actually active.
Efficient agent operations on GitHub
Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:
- Work without a clone. Many agent tasks never need a full working tree. They need a handful of files and enough context to make a change. They can read both straight from the server.
- Atomic commit API. Land a multi-file change in one operation. The whole change commits, or it’s rejected cleanly on conflict.
- Event streams. Agents and the systems around them work best with real-time information. A generic event stream lets them subscribe to changes and react as they happen.
Improving Git for agents
We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:
- Lightweight clones. Partial clone, shallow clone, and sparse checkout each let an agent fetch less. Each one has gaps. They don’t always work well together, either. We want to improve each piece and make them fit.
- Remove hidden scaling costs. Git still has code paths that slow down much faster than the repository grows. Recent releases fixed several of them, but we expect to find more.
- Faster history walks. Metadata like the commit-graph can answer merge-base and reachability questions without walking every commit. That matters most when an agent’s API call turns into Git work on the server.
- Avoid common gotchas. Agents make the same mistakes developers do. Git can catch more of the common ones and warn before they cause damage.
Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.

articles.title: What’s in Budget 2026 for Canadian tech? | BetaKit
articles.text:
What does a federal budget “about entrepreneurs” look like? Today, Canadian tech received the answer.
While Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first budget set an ambitious vision (with massive spending commitments—or investment, depending on who you ask), Budget 2026 gets into the gritty implementation details. Twenty months into office, Carney’s government has evolved its plan to spur investment, support economic growth, and enhance Canada’s sovereignty and resilience.
“We’re gonna be very competitive [for] people who want to grow companies, reinvest in Canadian companies.”
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne
“We’re gonna be very competitive [for] people who want to grow companies, reinvest in Canadian companies,” Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said at a press conference on Thursday.
Refinements to Canada’s defence and dual-use strategy—including aerospace, quantum, and drones—and globally competitive tax incentives all appeared as expected. Continuing on recent sovereign AI investments, the feds also committed to supplying 500 MW worth of compute for Canadian tech companies.
That’s not to say Budget 2026 is without surprises. It introduced a massive reorganization of the nation’s Crown corporations, including the planned merger of the two most familiar to Canadian tech: BDC and EDC. While the decision has been publicly welcomed, BetaKit was told that BDC employees attending SAAS NORTH collectively gasped upon learning the news.
Budget 2026 also featured a few high-profile omissions and controversial decisions. An effective replacement for the failed Start-up Visa program is still MIA, and CFIB president and CEO Dan Kelly did not mince words about the feds’ ongoing approach to the trade war. “I find it appalling that, a year and a half into the trade war, the government hasn’t even bothered to fix the failing tariff relief measures,” he tweeted.
Still, buoyed by higher tax revenues from restated economic growth figures and higher oil prices, the federal government was able to announce $151.1 billion in new investments, while largely keeping the deficit track unchanged from the Spring Economic Update.
But, as always, the devil is in the details. Here’s a look at what Canadian tech expected, what it got, and how it’s reacting.
Crown Corps
Taxes and IP
AI
Defence & Dual-Use
Financial Innovation
Energy & Cleantech
Executive Summary
Crown Corp. Changes
- BDC & EDC to consolidate under a single federal development bank
- Canadian Commercial Corporation to become a subsidiary of Export Development Canada (EDC)
- Minister of Finance now responsible for Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB)
- Canada Strong Fund to become Crown corp.
- Canada Growth Fund mandate to be expanded
- $3.5 million over two years to the Department of Finance to oversee new Crown corp. functions & support consolidation
Taxes & IP
- A new Canada Growth Incentive tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains earnings, starting in 2027-28
- $930 million over five years for SR&ED expansion to cover commercialization expenses ($235 million ongoing)
- Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits extended to end of 2040
- Patent Act amendments for greater visibility on Canadian patent ownership
- Additional IP modernization measures to be announced spring 2027
- Simplified business tax rules, including dividend exemptions and increasing dividend allowance to $1.5M
AI
- Access to 500 MW of sovereign AI compute through new financial tools
- Exploring creation of a Technology Stability Board to assess whether advanced AI models are safe and remain under human control
- $6.2 million over four years to ISED for Canada’s continued participation in the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence
- $100 million over three years towards Federation of Canadian Municipalities partnership to support AI adoption & e-permitting
Defence & Dual-use (Quantum & Aerospace)
- $2.7 billion (previously committed) from the Defence Industrial Strategy to:
  - Canadian Quantum Champions Program Phase 2
  - Expand Launch the North initiative to establish sovereign medium-launch space capability
  - Further develop space technology through CSA’s Space Technology Development Program
  - Extend BOREALIS, Defence Industry Assist, and the Regional Defence Investment Initiative
  - Recapitalize the Canadian Defence Industry Resilience Program
  - Defence production and artillery manufacturing capacity funding
  - Fully operationalize the National Research Council’s drone innovation hubs
- Provide $2.3 billion over five years (a portion from existing funding) to the Department of National Defence for the Defence Drone Initiative
Financial Innovation
- Real-Time Rail Phase 1 launch Nov.9
- Public consultation on payments modernization in early 2027
- Amendments to the RPAA to strengthen Bank of Canada’s oversight of payment service providers
- Require regulated financial institutions to issue stablecoins through non-financial institution subsidiaries regulated under the Stablecoin Act
- Extend Stablecoin Act to foreign financial institutions not prudentially regulated in Canada
- Introduce a Multi-Sector Anti-Fraud Framework as cornerstone of National Anti-Fraud Strategy
- Establish new Financial Crimes Agency (operations beginning fall 2027)
- Competition objective to instruct OSFI regulations
- One-year timeline on application decisions for prospective regulated financial institutions
- Greater flexibility on foreign ownership structures to encourage entry of mid-sized challenger banks
Energy & Clean Technologies

- $45 million to Natural Resources Canada over five years for charging infrastructure R&D
Other Priorities
Tariffs

- Minimum revenue requirement to access BDC’s tariff programs lowered to $1 million
Competition

- Competition objective to instruct OSFI regulations
Natural Resources

- Renewed $2.3-billion critical minerals strategy
Investment

Digital Transformation

- $176.3 million over five years to establish a new, arm’s-length Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada
