The breakdown
Crown Corp. changes
The two Crown corporations most familiar to Canadian tech will become one.
The dollars: $3.5 million
The ask: When the Canada Strong Fund was initially announced in the spring, some critics had questions about how the sovereign wealth fund would work and urged the government to put a greater emphasis on the digital economy.
When laying out plans for the fund, the Spring Economic Update also contained a note that proved to be consequential on budget day: to avoid duplication, the government would be undertaking “comprehensive mandate reviews” of each Crown corporation in the federal financing ecosystem. But there weren’t specific asks from the innovation sector about significant changes to the main Crown corporations that invest in Canadian tech made in Budget 2026.
What the feds did: Surprise! Following said review, Budget 2026 revealed that the feds would launch a transition process to combine the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) and Export Development Canada (EDC), effectively putting two of the most important financing bodies for Canadian businesses under one roof.
The major restructuring notice came alongside a number of other Crown corporation changes. The Canadian Commercial Corporation will become a subsidiary of EDC, and the Minister of Finance will take over responsibility for the Canada Infrastructure Bank. The Canada Growth Fund’s mandate will expand, too, though Budget 2026 was unclear on how. The Department of Finance will get $3.5 million over two years to support and oversee these structural changes.
The budget also confirmed the $25-billion Canada Strong Fund will operate as a Crown corporation that will invest in Canadian companies on behalf of Canadians on a “fully commercial basis” with the private sector. Launching in early 2027, the fund will have an associated retail investment product called Canada Strong Notes, which Canadians will be able to purchase through participating financial institutions.
The changes come as the federal government seems to be broadly reimagining its relationship with Crown corporations, having recently introduced a bill to turn the Defence Investment Agency into one to make it “more fleet-footed.” Budget 2026 says the federal government now “expects financing Crown corporations to have a greater risk tolerance than private sector peers.” It also stresses that government-backed financing should complement, rather than replicate, private investments.
The reaction: In a LinkedIn post, the BDC stated that it welcomed the merger. “Our two organizations have complementary mandates and a shared ambition: to simplify and accelerate access to the support and financing entrepreneurs need to grow their businesses,” BDC stated.
“Between them, BDC and EDC have historically large scopes and impact many stakeholders across Canadian markets, so their merger will have lasting implications for not only those stakeholders but for the new players that Budget 2026 is seeking to activate,” TJ Misra, interim executive director of the Canadian Startup Capital Association, told BetaKit. She said she looks forward to further details as to how the merger will impact the deployment of Growth VCCI and the Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy.
Gideon Hayden, co-founder and managing partner of Leaders Fund, told BetaKit that he’s always in favour of simplifying organizational structures. “In the past six years we’ve seen the tech industry try to unwind the overhiring and layers of management they’ve implemented … I’d like to see the same effort be applied in government,” he said.
Taxes & IP
Budget 2026 is “about entrepreneurs,” which means tax breaks for entrepreneurs.
The dollars: ~$1.6 billion
The ask: Business and tech groups wanted tax changes to make Canada a more compelling place to invest. CCI, CVCA, NACO, and other investor groups launched a campaign asking the feds to create a tax incentive similar to the US Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) regime, and a capital gains tax deferral when proceeds are reinvested in another Canadian company. Build Canada went a step further, suggesting a corporate tax change that only taxed profits, not reinvested earnings. CFIB asked to cut the small-business rate from nine to six percent and to extend the preferred tax rate for small businesses to a company’s first $700,000 of income, rather than $500,000.
What the feds did: Canada’s answer to QSBS is here. The budget outlines a new Canada Growth Incentive tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains earnings, providing $715 million in tax relief over four years, starting in 2027-28. The feds say a founder with a $15-million capital gain would now retain nearly 96 percent of the value when they exit, compared with 71 percent before Budget 2026.
Read our breakdown on the Canada Growth Incentive here.
The feds are also giving the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax credit a $930-million expansion, setting it up to cover certain commercialization expenses, like obtaining regulatory approvals and intellectual property protection. Budget 2026 says the CRA will work to provide sector-specific guidance on SR&ED eligibility for commercialization expenses.
The government has also extended the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits to the end of 2040 and simplified business tax rules, including dividend exemptions and increased dividend allowance to $1.5 million. The Patent Act is also set to be amended to allow for greater visibility on Canadian patent ownership and establish minimum requirements for written patent demand letters, with additional IP modernization measures to be announced in Spring 2027.
The reaction: Investors and investor advocacy groups welcomed the QSBS-style incentive. “Credit to Minister Champagne and this government definitely is deserved for listening and acting on what the innovation and entrepreneurship community really needs,” CCI CEO Patrick Searle told BetaKit.
NACO CEO Claudio Rojas said that capital will come with “mentorship, access to networks, and the expertise needed to scale.” Joe Canavan, principal at Canavan Capital, said that the government’s move to put investors and entrepreneurs first will unlock a “powerful period” of growth for the country. John Ruffolo, founder and managing partner of Maverix Private Equity, also told BetaKit he was pleased to see the incentive.
However, Dan Kelly, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), said in a statement that while the capital gains exemption is helpful, the government has a “blind spot” when it comes specifically to small business. For those facing rising costs and tariffs, “the budget will provide you with no help whatsoever,” he argued.
AI
The feds follow their AI for All strategy with more compute, cash for digital transformation, and the concepts of a plan to keep advanced AI models safe.
The dollars: $1.1 billion
The ask: The tech sector wanted AI infrastructure built in Canada. CCI recommended that the feds build a “sovereign industrial base” of Canadian firms by providing domestic compute capacity, better access to high-quality data, and procurement rules that prioritize buying Canadian. Similarly, the Canadian Shield Institute called for a “strategic sovereign compute entity” that Canadian companies can tap for computing power.
Meanwhile, other groups were focused on adoption. Accountant group CPA Canada asked for more responsible AI adoption and stronger governance, while Sage Canada suggested an AI and digital investment tax credit to encourage small businesses to integrate the technology. Academics, including Canadian AI godfathers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, have called for the creation of an international AI regulator, an idea AI Minister Evan Solomon has already floated.
What the feds did: Crank the juice. The government said it will enable Canadian AI companies to access 500 MW of sovereign AI compute through financial tools like backstops and offtake agreements, giving domestic firms a chance to secure space in Canadian data centres at a time when hyperscalers like Anthropic and Meta take that capacity, and more, for themselves. The government will also supply $100 million over three years towards a partnership with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities to support AI adoption and e-permitting.
Building on the launch of Digital Transformation Canada, which looks to improve how the feds develop, buy, and use AI and other tech, the budget has committed $1 billion over five years to establish a Government Transformation Fund for such “transformative IT projects.”
At the international level, the budget committed $6.2 million over four years to support Canada’s continued participation in the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence. The feds will also work with international partners to explore the creation of a new “Technology Stability Board,” which would assess whether advanced AI models are safe and remain under human control.
The reaction: Ali Asaria, co-founder of AI research firm Transformer Lab, told BetaKit that “right now, getting GPUs in Canada is close to impossible,” adding that the lengthy and unpredictable waits for startups to access hardware are not feasible. “Ottawa helping data centres finance those purchases might sound crazy, but it might be crazy enough to work. Demand is so high that the government’s risk is close to zero,” he said.
Defence & Dual-use
The dollars: $5 billion (over $2.7 billion previously committed)
Space is the place for the next phase of Canada’s revitalized defence and dual-use strategy.
The ask: Canadian defence tech firms wanted clearer and faster-moving procurement rules. Aspiring neoprime Dominion Dynamics asked the feds to lower the threshold for contracts awarded through the Defence Investment Agency to $25 million and to create “agile procurement models” for software and other advanced defence tech. The Canadian Strategic Mission Corporation advocated for funding toward its own nuclear micro-reactors and asked for increased investment in dual-use technologies.
Similar procurement asks came from the spacetech sector. Satellite company Kepler Communications wanted the government to apply the defence Build-Partner-Buy framework to the space sector, and more clarity on how to be selected as a strategic partner. A coalition of space companies, including Maritime Launch Services and Reaction Dynamics, called for a new national space industrial strategy and for the feds to commit to being the first customers for domestic space companies.
What the feds did: There was nothing new on procurement and relatively little new funding committed for defence tech in Budget 2026. Instead, this year’s budget established where some of last year’s $81.8-billion commitment to reinvest in the Canadian Armed Forces is going.
This includes $2.7 billion from the Defence Industrial Strategy being divvied up to a smorgasbord of dual-use initiatives, such as Phase 2 of the Canadian Quantum Champions Program, expanding the Launch the North initiative to establish sovereign medium-launch space capability (to support Canadian firms no longer able to hitch a ride on SpaceX), further developing space technology through the Canada Space Agency’s Space Technology Development Program, and extending other initiatives like BOREALIS, Defence Industry Assist, export promotion, and the Regional Defence Investment Initiative.
Some of that funding will also be used to recapitalize the Canadian Defence Industry Resilience Program, fund munitions production facilities in Québec and Ontario, and to “fully operationalize” the National Research Council’s drone innovation hubs.
Some net new funding will be applied within the $2.3-billion commitment to the Department of National Defence over five years for the Defence Drone Initiative (DDI), starting in 2027-28. The DDI was established earlier this year to create a pool of drone suppliers for Canada and its allies.
The reaction: Matthew Lombardi, co-founder of defence innovation network The Icebreaker, told BetaKit the funding for the DDI is a “positive signal,” but suggested it’s one that will need to be followed by ongoing, timely procurement. He said that if Ottawa can back that funding with ongoing orders, it will support Canadian companies to build factories here, but “otherwise, they’ll keep selling prototypes while our allies buy the full production runs.”
Meanwhile, Xanadu founder and CEO Christian Weedbrook celebrated the government’s commitment to quantum funding, adding that it helps his company resist pressures to move to the US to access capital.
Financial Innovation
A tech sector tired of waiting sees incremental progress and a few new fig leaves to financial competition.
The dollars: N/A
The ask: Canada’s financial disruptors continued to bang the drum for long-awaited competition-boosting measures to finally come into effect.
Industry group Fintechs Canada, FinTech startup Neo Financial, and EQ Bank asked for the feds to follow through on (and, in some cases, speed up delivery of) an open banking system. Fintechs Canada and EQ Bank also asked for an accelerated rollout of Real-Time Rail (RTR); Payments Canada, the organization responsible for delivering it, wanted the government’s continued support for the launch.
Wealthsimple wanted the feds to implement a ban on investment and registered account transfer fees that was announced last year. On crypto, the Canadian Web3 Council and Shakepay recommended the government loosen its language around a ban on stablecoin interest and yields.
What the feds did: The wait is almost over: the first phase of Canada’s Real-Time Rail payment system launches Monday, Nov. 9 (likely without any banks initially participating). The government said the next phase will be guided by a public consultation it expects to hold in early 2027. There was no meaningful mention of open banking outside of the government’s intention to expand data portability beyond banking. In a press conference prior to tabling the budget, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said “there’s regulation, which is going to be published soon.”
Read more about the upcoming Real-Time Rail payments system launch here.
Budget 2026 does forward a number of other measures to boost FinTech competition. This includes streamlining the process for becoming a federally regulated financial institution by establishing a one-year timeline for application decisions, and encouraging challenger banks to enter the country by loosening ownership structure requirements. This means foreign bank subsidiaries with less than $8 billion in equity will be exempted from a requirement to have public holdings, so long as their foreign parent is listed on a recognized foreign stock exchange. Canada will also raise the threshold at which banks must transition to widely held ownership (meaning they must have no single major shareholder) from $12 billion to $25 billion in equity.
The government is also looking to introduce a secondary competition objective for OSFI, introduce a Multi-Sector Anti-Fraud Framework to increase protections across the financial sector and digital platforms, establish a new Financial Crimes Agency to investigate serious financial crime by fall 2027, and strengthen the Bank of Canada’s oversight of payment service providers.
On stablecoins, the government intends to require federally regulated financial institutions to issue stablecoins through non-financial institution subsidiaries regulated under the Stablecoin Act, as well as extend the Stablecoin Act to foreign financial institutions that are not prudentially regulated in Canada.
The reaction: Abraham Tachjian, managing director of payments and open banking for Accenture, said in a post on LinkedIn that he’s left with an open question—”how stablecoins will fit alongside Real-Time Rail and the broader payments modernization agenda.”
Feature image courtesy François-Philippe Champagne via LinkedIn.

articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.text:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗
Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance.
In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering.
Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training.
Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools.
These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications.
Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill.
Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗
Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation.
PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model.
Explore the Onshape importer guide.
Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.
Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗
With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.
Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.
Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗
In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.
Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable.
Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.
The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.
Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab.
Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗
Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.
Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.
Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial.
Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗
Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.
Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.
DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.
Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗
Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.
Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.
Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗
Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.
To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.
Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.
Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.
Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗
Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.
Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.
Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗
Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.
The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.
Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.
Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗
A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.
The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect.
Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

articles.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves.
If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart.
The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent.
What Web Answer does
Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result.
Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back:
- A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available.
- Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information.
- Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer.
- Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards.
Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer
How it differs from Web Search
Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model:
- Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed.
- Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it.
Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer.
Set up and invoke Web Answer
Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent.
Getting started
Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through tools/list and tools/call.
Prerequisites
- An AWS account with AgentCore Gateway access.
- An AgentCore Gateway in us-east-1 that uses IAM (AWS_IAM) inbound authentication. To create one, see Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway in the Developer Guide.
- AWS credentials for an identity that has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock access to the model your agent uses.
- Python 3.10 or later, with the required packages:
Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”).
Step 1: Grant the Gateway service role access to Web Answer
The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs:
- bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer, to call Web Answer. The Gateway checks this permission on every request against the ARN that AWS owns, arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1.
Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy:
The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need bedrock:InvokeModel: your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity.
Step 2: Create the Web Answer target
Add Web Answer as a connector target. The connectorId tells the Gateway which managed integration to provision: in this case, an agent that searches the web and writes a cited answer.
Outbound authentication is automatic for connectors. With GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE, the Gateway calls the Web Answer backend with the service role from Step 1, so you don’t create or store any credentials for the tool. Wait until get_gateway_target reports the target status as READY before you call it.
As the Gateway administrator, you can also set a domain filter on the target. The filter applies to every call that goes through the target. To limit the target to a set of domains, set parameterValues to {"domainFilter": {"include": ["bis.org"], "exclude": ["unreliable-source.net"]}}.
Step 3: Invoke Web Answer from a Strands agent
Your agent discovers Web Answer through the Gateway’s tools/list and calls it with tools/call, like any other MCP tool. This works with Strands Agents, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or any other MCP-compatible client.
When a question needs current information, your agent calls the Web Answer tool (web-answer-tool___WebAnswer). Web Answer runs the agentic search and returns a finished answer with citations.
Besides the question, the Web Answer tool takes optional arguments that your agent can set on each call: a domain filter to include or exclude sites, a published-date range, and a country to localize results. The agent’s domain filter is combined with the target’s filter. The agent can exclude more domains, or limit results to some of the target’s included domains, but it can’t add a domain that the target’s filter blocks.
Response format
Web Answer returns an MCP tool result with both content and structuredContent fields. The answer is markdown text with inline citation markers like [1], and structuredContent.answer carries the same text alongside a structured citations list:
structuredContent.answer normally holds a single block. Each citation carries the source url and, when available, the domain.
Clean up resources
Delete the Web Answer target when you no longer need it:
If you created the Gateway only for this walkthrough, delete its targets first, then the Gateway (delete_gateway), and then the service role and its policy. There is no persistent infrastructure on the AWS side beyond these resources. After they are removed, you stop incurring charges.
Enterprise controls, built in
Web Answer inherits the same enterprise controls as other AgentCore tools:
- Gateway authentication. No separate API key to provision, rotate, or manage for Web Answer. Callers authenticate to the gateway with the inbound method you configure, such as AWS IAM (SigV4) or a JSON Web Token from your identity provider. The gateway then calls Web Answer with its own service role, which needs the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer permission.
- VPC and AWS PrivateLink. Your agents can call the gateway through an interface virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint (com.amazonaws.us-east-1.bedrock-agentcore.gateway), so traffic stays off the public internet.
- Zero data egress. Your queries and results stay within your AWS environment.
- Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Operational metrics publish to CloudWatch from the first call.
- Per-account rate limits. Enforced from launch, with 10 transactions per second per account in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1). To request an increase, contact AWS Support.
- Admin-time policy bounds. The Gateway administrator sets domain filter bounds at target setup. Agents can narrow the filter bounds on each call but can’t widen them.
- Queries stay within AWS. Web Answer searches an Amazon-operated web index and Amazon’s knowledge graph, and doesn’t send your question to third-party search engines or external websites.
Use cases
Web Answer helps agents retrieve current, cited information to support a range of knowledge-intensive workflows. Example scenarios include:
- Financial services. Regulatory Q&A agents answering questions about compliance requirements, market regulations, and policy changes, where every answer must trace to an authoritative source.
- Healthcare. Clinical support agents grounding responses in current medical literature and treatment guidelines published on the web.
- Customer service. Support agents answering product and policy questions in real time, where ten ranked links are not useful and a cited answer is.
- Legal and compliance. Research assistants answering questions about case law, regulatory filings, and policy interpretations with auditable citations.
- Enterprise knowledge workers. Internal copilots that answer questions from current public information without requiring employees to build their own search and synthesis workflow.
Availability
Web Answer is available in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), with more AWS Regions coming soon.
Pricing
Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is priced at $10 per 1,000 tool calls.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how Web Answer gives your agents current, cited answers through agentic search, with no search pipeline for you to build or maintain. We granted a Gateway service role access to Web Answer, added a Web Answer target, called it from a Strands agent, and read the answer and its citations from the response. Use Web Search on AgentCore when your own model should reason over raw results, and Web Answer when your agent needs a finished, cited answer.
To get started, see:
- Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation
- Web Answer structured output schema
- Adding Web Answer to an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
- Supported regions

articles.title: Menaces envoyées par mail, décollage d’un Rafale : ce que l’on sait de la vague d’alertes à la bombe qui frappe les vols européens
articles.text:
La menace se répand comme une traînée de poudre chez les compagnies aériennes européennes.
Ce jeudi 5 novembre 2026, un Airbus A320 d’Aer Lingus qui reliait Dublin à Rome a dû quitter sa route au-dessus de la France pour rejoindre la base aérienne d’Évreux, dans l’Eure, à la suite d’une alerte à la bombe.
C’est l’un des 14 vols au moins concernés ce jour-là, selon le décompte de Libération, après une dizaine mardi et un appareil de Wizz Air lundi. Jeudi à la mi-journée, aucune inspection dont le résultat a été rendu public n’avait permis de trouver un explosif.
Un Rafale et un Mirage 2000 ont escorté l’avion jusqu’à Évreux
Matignon a annoncé le déroutement vers 9h30, et l’armée de l’Air et de l’Espace a indiqué à l’AFP avoir fait décoller ses avions de permanence pour intercepter l’A320. Un Rafale serait parti de Saint-Dizier, en Haute-Marne, avant d’être rejoint par un Mirage 2000. L’appareil a atterri à Évreux vers 10h avec 151 passagers et 6 membres d’équipage, mis à l’abri pendant l’intervention des démineurs.
6 autres pays au moins ont été touchés dans la matinée. En Bulgarie, 3 avions se sont posés en urgence à Sofia ou à Plovdiv, et le ministère des Transports a indiqué que leur inspection n’avait révélé aucun engin explosif. 4 vols à destination de Prague ont aussi été menacés, tout comme un avion parti de Varsovie vers Bruxelles.
En Italie, un vol Finnair venu d’Helsinki a été accompagné par des avions de chasse jusqu’à Rome-Fiumicino, tandis qu’un appareil de Wizz Air reliant Milan à Varsovie a été redirigé vers Vienne. 2 vols à destination de Milan Malpensa et un autre à destination de Bucarest ont également été visés.
Des mails à Prague et à Sofia
Le mode de transmission des alertes n’est connu que pour une partie des vols. À Prague, un représentant de l’aéroport a expliqué à CNN que les menaces contre les 4 avions de jeudi étaient arrivées via un mail anonyme, dont la police tchèque a jugé la crédibilité faible tout en déclenchant les mesures de sécurité prévues. Le même canal avait déjà été utilisé mardi en Bulgarie, où des alertes ont été envoyées au ministère de l’Intérieur selon la police des frontières, et à Rome, d’après un responsable de l’aéroport de Fiumicino cité par l’agence AP.
Pour la plupart des avions visés jeudi, dont celui d’Aer Lingus, aucune précision n’a été donnée à ce stade sur la manière dont l’alerte a été transmise.

articles.title: Qui a donné à l’IA l’accès aux données sensibles ? Seuls 36 % des décideurs IT peuvent l’affirmer avec certitude
articles.text:
Selon une étude de Delinea, spécialiste de la sécurité des identités, presque tous les responsables IT affirment que leur entreprise a une politique formelle sur les données auxquelles l’IA peut accéder (99,7 %). Pourtant, seuls 36 % peuvent toujours retrouver qui a autorisé un accès sensible à un chatbot.
Delinea a interrogé 2 254 responsables IT et sécurité, ainsi que 2 250 salariés hors IT, dans des entreprises d’au moins 500 personnes. Huit pays sont couverts, dont la France, mais le rapport ne détaille pas de résultats propres à l’Hexagone.
Des règles écrites, mais peu de moyens de savoir qui a validé quoi
En théorie, tout est en place et les entreprises sont fin prêtes. Mais en pratique, ce n’est pas vraiment la même chose. Seules 51 % des organisations comparent les accès de l’IA à cette politique en temps réel, et moins d’une organisation sur cinq (19 %) remarque sur le moment qu’un agent a accédé à des données qu’il n’était pas censé consulter. 87 % des responsables IT affirment qu’un outil ou un agent IA est sorti de son périmètre au cours de l’année écoulée. Pour trois quarts de ces derniers, cela s’est d’ailleurs confirmé. Concernant les accès à des données sensibles, seuls 36 % des personnes interrogée sont en mesure de remonter systématiquement jusqu’à la personne ayant accordé l’autorisation. Pourtant, presque tous disent que leur entreprise exige l’accord d’une personne nommée avant qu’une IA accède à une nouvelle source confidentielle, au moins pour certains usages.
Côté salariés, 60 % disent avoir déjà ressenti une pression pour utiliser l’IA sur des données sensibles ou confidentielles, sans pour autant être sûrs que cela soit permis par leur employeur. Près de la moitié (48 %) affirment accéder toujours ou régulièrement à des données de l’entreprise via l’IA sans approbation formelle. Côté IT, 34 % reconnaissent que le dernier accès donné à une IA est passé par une équipe métier sans supervision ou par un salarié sans validation formelle.
Dans la moitié des cas, l’entreprise ne donne pas à l’agent des droits d’accès propres et limités. Elle le laisse agir avec les droits de la personne qui l’a lancé. La “limite” de ce que l’agent peut consulter est donc en théorie celle de son utilisateur. 42 % des organisations n’ont aucun moyen automatique de couper l’accès d’un agent à la fin d’une session.
L’étude distingue six environnements :
- Le stockage cloud ;
- les applications en ligne ;
- les bases de données internes ;
- les serveurs de fichiers internes ;
- les chaînes de déploiement automatique du code (CI/CD) et
- Kubernetes, l’outil qui gère les applications sur les serveurs.
47 % des organisations n’ont pas de contrôle au moment de l’action dans au moins deux de ces six environnements
Delinea rappelle l’incident ayant touché PocketOS en avril dernier. Dans un environnement de test, un agent de programmation a rencontré une erreur d’identifiants, puis trouvé une clé d’API sans rapport avec sa tâche. Il s’en est servi pour supprimer en neuf secondes la base de production et les sauvegardes de l’entreprise.
En décembre 2027, l’AI Act rendra obligatoire l’audit des actions menées par l’IA.
Source : étude Delinea

articles.title: « La pire interface jamais conçue par Google » : le nouveau YouTube sur mobile fait déjà polémique — Frandroid
articles.text:
YouTube n’en finit pas d’évoluer ces derniers et mêmes ces dernières semaines. Récemment, la plateforme a lancé Ask YouTube, sa recherche conversationnelle par IA, sur smartphone en octobre, puis a testé une interface qui range le bouton « Je n’aime pas », et elle préparerait même un réseau social à part, baptisé Tamba. Et désormais, elle s’apprête à changer l’ergonomie principale de son application mobile.
Depuis une dizaine d’années, l’application mobile de YouTube s’organise autour d’une barre de cinq boutons en bas de l’écran. L’un d’eux, l’onglet Abonnements, rassemble les vidéos des chaînes qu’on suit. Google avait annoncé sa disparition en octobre, et c’est désormais fait : ce jeudi 5 novembre, 9to5Google a vu la nouvelle interface arriver sur Android, et de nombreux utilisateurs l’ont aussi vu débarquer sur iOS. Les vidéos des abonnements restent accessibles, mais il faut maintenant aller les chercher dans l’onglet Accueil, elles n’ont plus d’onglet dédié via le menu principal en bas de la fenêtre.
Une nouvelle interface déjà controversée
YouTube abandonne ainsi sa barre à cinq boutons pour une navigation qui met en avant les Shorts, ses vidéos verticales façon TikTok, et la création de vidéos. Le nouvel onglet Accueil regroupe les recommandations et une section consacrée aux abonnements, qu’on ouvre en swipant sur la droite.
Sur le fond, l’accès ne change donc pas beaucoup, mais comme le mentionne 9to5Google, ce sont des années de mémoire musculaire qui sont mises à mal. Surtout, le changement passe par les serveurs de Google, sans mise à jour à installer : la nouvelle interface peut apparaître du jour au lendemain.
Sur r/youtube, le forum Reddit consacré à la plateforme, des internautes qualifient la nouvelle interface de « bâclée », de « dégoûtante », voire de « pire interface jamais conçue par Google ». Des réactions quelque peu disproportionnés si vous voulez notre avis, surtout qu’un simple swipe du doigts permet d’accéder à ses abonnements.
Beaucoup reprochent à YouTube d’avoir pensé son application pour ce que la plateforme veut leur faire faire, alors que nombre d’entre eux ouvrent surtout YouTube pour retrouver les chaînes auxquelles ils sont abonnés, et non pour créer du contenu.

articles.title: Sarampo: bebê morre nos EUA em meio a surto com mais de 400 casos
articles.text:
Um bebê morreu após contrair sarampo no estado de Wisconsin, nos Estados Unidos. A morte foi confirmada nesta quinta-feira (5) pelo Departamento de Serviços de Saúde local e está relacionada a um surto da doença no sudoeste do Estado. É o primeiro óbito por sarampo registrado na região desde 1990.
As autoridades não divulgaram a idade exata da criança nem outros detalhes sobre o caso. Segundo o departamento de saúde, a decisão busca preservar a privacidade da família. O legista responsável apontou o sarampo como causa imediata da morte.
O caso ocorre em meio ao avanço da doença em Wisconsin. Até 3 de novembro, o Estado havia registrado 431 infecções em 13 condados, o maior número em mais de 35 anos. Nove pessoas precisaram ser hospitalizadas por complicações.
Um dado chama a atenção: 428 dos 431 casos foram identificados em pessoas não vacinadas. A Secretaria Estadual de Saúde também alertou que os números podem não representar toda a extensão da circulação do vírus, já que nem todos os infectados procuram atendimento médico ou realizam testes.
Sarampo avança nos Estados Unidos
- O surto de Wisconsin faz parte de cenário mais amplo de aumento de casos nos Estados Unidos. A doença voltou a ganhar força no país depois de décadas de controle, com registros de surtos em diferentes estados;
- Em Wisconsin, a maior parte das infecções está concentrada em surto que envolve os condados de Grant, Iowa, Lafayette e Vernon. Até 3 de novembro, essas localidades somavam 362 casos confirmados e outros seis prováveis;
- O condado de Chippewa também enfrenta surto separado, com 44 casos confirmados. Outras infecções foram identificadas em diferentes regiões do Estado, algumas relacionadas a viagens para fora de Wisconsin;
- A morte do bebê é um dos óbitos associados ao sarampo registrados nos Estados Unidos em 2026. O número divulgado pelas autoridades estaduais é maior que a contagem oficial do Centro de Controle e Prevenção de Doenças (CDC, na sigla em inglês), que utiliza critérios próprios para incluir mortes em seus levantamentos.
Leia mais:
- Casos de sarampo disparam e geram alerta internacional
- EUA: Nova York declara estado de emergência por surto de sarampo
- Nenhum estado brasileiro atinge meta de vacinação contra o sarampo
Vacina é principal forma de prevenção
O sarampo é doença viral altamente contagiosa, transmitida pelo ar e por partículas respiratórias. A infecção pode provocar febre, tosse, coriza, conjuntivite e manchas vermelhas na pele. Em casos graves, pode causar pneumonia e inflamação do cérebro, com risco de morte.
Crianças pequenas, gestantes e pessoas com o sistema imunológico enfraquecido estão entre os grupos mais vulneráveis a complicações.
A principal forma de prevenção é a vacina tríplice viral, conhecida pela sigla MMR nos Estados Unidos, que protege contra sarampo, caxumba e rubéola. Duas doses oferecem aproximadamente 97% de proteção contra o sarampo.
O Departamento de Serviços de Saúde de Wisconsin informou que distribuiu duas mil doses da vacina a departamentos locais de saúde desde 1º de agosto. No mesmo período, mais de 42 mil doses foram aplicadas por profissionais de saúde em todo o Estado.
As autoridades recomendam que moradores verifiquem se estão com a vacinação em dia. Pessoas que tiveram contato com alguém infectado devem permanecer em casa e procurar orientação médica. Quem apresentar febre e manchas na pele, especialmente após possível exposição ao vírus, deve telefonar antes de ir a uma clínica ou hospital, para evitar expor outras pessoas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
