articles.title: How a car-importing problem led Sheriff Adedokun to build Clea
articles.text:
In car importing, business owners must find the vehicle and pay the auction house, which could be in another country. This proved harder than expected for Sheriff Adedokun, a serial entrepreneur who founded Clea, a cross-border payments platform for African businesses.
Africa’s fragmented cross-border payments landscape was not new. Businesses trading internationally had relied on banks or other financial intermediaries to move money between markets. By 2022, when Adedokun started importing vehicles from the United States, Nigerian fintechs were building products to make international payments easier. However, the available options did not always work for the transactions he needed.
“I tried to use some of the fintech platforms in Nigeria, but it didn’t work because most of my payments were rejected,” Adedokun told TechCabal in an interview. “Then I had to go to the bank, fill a form, and try to do the transfer. There was also a limit on sending international transfers from Nigerian banks.”
He explained that US vehicle auction platforms required payments to come directly from the person or business buying the car, as third-party transfers could be rejected.
Car importation was one example of a deluge of businesses that had to pay suppliers before their orders could be shipped. Total imports stood at over ₦15 billion ($11.1 million) in the first quarter of 2025, according to National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data.
In 2024, Adedokun founded Autoclear, a business that helped customers source vehicles and pay US auction platforms. While working with importers, he noticed they also had to pay shipping companies, freight forwarders, and brokers, each with its own payment requirements and separate from the auction houses where they buy the cars.
So, he teamed up with his longtime friend Sidney Egwuatu to build Clea, a cross-border payments platform to serve African businesses importing goods from overseas. The company developed the product in stealth before publicly launching in December 2025.
How Clea moves money across borders
Clea allows businesses to manage international supplier payments from a single platform. After signing up and completing verification, a business can fund its account in naira from a Nigerian bank account, convert the funds into the required currency, and add its overseas supplier as a beneficiary. During a live product demonstration, Adedokun showed that the platform supports currencies including the US dollar, British pound, euro, and Chinese yuan.
To add a new supplier, a customer provides details such as the recipient’s address, country, and the nature of their relationship with the beneficiary. After adding the beneficiary, the customer can initiate a payment using the available payment routes for that destination. Adedokun said payments to US beneficiaries could go through ACH, Fedwire or the Real-Time Payments (RTP) network, while payments to other destinations could be routed through SWIFT.
Stablecoins form part of the infrastructure Clea uses to move value between the different parts of this payment process. Adedokun said the platform is designed to keep this complexity out of sight, allowing customers to focus on funding their accounts in naira and ensuring suppliers receive the agreed foreign currency. Customers can also fund their dollar wallets directly with stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, through supported blockchain networks.
Africa’s cross-border payments ecosystem has seen growing stablecoin use for remittances and business settlements. Flutterwave, a Nigerian payments infrastructure company, has begun exploring an integration of USDC settlement into its payments infrastructure. In February, Onafriq partnered with Conduit to use USDC for cross-border payments and payouts to international partners.
“Stablecoins are also part of our settlement infrastructure,” Adedokun explained. “They allow value to move efficiently between parts of the payment stack, but our customers don’t need to understand stablecoins or interact with crypto. They simply know that they were funded in naira and their supplier received dollars, pounds, euros or yuan.”
In August, Clea launched a Vendor Payments feature for businesses that regularly pay the same overseas companies. Adedokun said the product emerged from a deeper understanding of customer needs, shaped by observing how businesses used the platform. Clea serves wholesalers, manufacturers, electronics distributors, fashion businesses, machinery importers and African businesses that depend on international suppliers.
“Initially, we thought speed and FX access were the biggest problems,” he said. “ They are still very important, but once customers started using Clea repeatedly, we realised that trust, payment identity, reconciliation and supplier management are equally important.”
With Vendor Payments, customers can select the supplier from a list of preconfigured vendors whose payment information the platform maintains. They still need to provide the transaction-specific reference the supplier requires, such as a buyer number or lot number, before authorising the payment.
According to Adedokun, Vendor Payments supports US-dollar payments to selected suppliers in the United States, including vehicle auction platforms Copart and IAA.
“If thousands of importers are paying the same shippers, auction companies and suppliers, it doesn’t make sense for every importer to establish that relationship independently every time,” he said. “Once the vendor already exists on Clea, we can simplify the transaction for both sides: fewer incorrect account details, faster reconciliation, better visibility and potentially much faster settlement.”
Clea is betting on importers
Clea makes money primarily from transaction fees and the margin between the exchange rate it sources foreign currency at and the rate it offers customers. Adedokun said the company is building a transaction-driven business, where higher payment volumes and more efficient infrastructure can help lower its underlying costs and improve pricing over time. Since its launch, Clea says it has processed more than $50 million in payments.
“We have to be very disciplined about pricing because our customers understand FX extremely well. These are businesses moving significant amounts of money, so even a small difference in the exchange rate matters,” Adedokun said.
Clea is competing with fintechs such as Verto, Raenest and Grey, which offer businesses multi-currency accounts and international payments. In February, Olayemi Cardoso, Nigeria’s Central Bank (CBN) governor, stated that the country’s average monthly diaspora remittance inflows are about $600 million, showing the scale of cross-border money movement in Nigeria. Adedokun argued that Clea’s focus is narrower: it is building around the specific needs of importers, rather than offering a general-purpose international payments product.
“We don’t think of Clea as another generic international money-transfer product. We are building specifically around the workflow of an importer,” he said. “Our objective is to stay competitive on FX and fees while giving customers speed, reliability, transparency and proper payment documentation.”
When asked about regional expansion, Adedokun said the company is prioritising growth in Nigeria. Its immediate plans include expanding the vendor network, strengthening its payment infrastructure, improving transaction efficiency and reducing the underlying cost of payments.
“There’s a temptation with an African fintech company to announce ten countries very quickly, but there is still a huge amount of market for us to capture in Nigeria,” Adedokun said. “Our immediate priority is to deepen our presence in Nigeria, where we still see considerable opportunities to serve businesses involved in international trade. Ultimately, we want Clea to become the preferred financial infrastructure partner for African businesses trading globally.”

articles.title: “Mes lasers spatiaux n’ont pas marché cette fois” : humilié chez lui au Texas, Elon Musk voit désormais ses centres de données IA menacés
articles.text:
Un demi-milliard de dollars pour rien : Elon Musk humilié aux élections américaines, et c’est son empire IA qui trinque
Un demi-milliard de dollars pour les républicains, dont 168 millions pour un seul siège de sénateur dans l'État qui abrite Tesla et SpaceX. Mardi soir, les électeurs texans ont pourtant tout renversé et le patron de X espère s'en tirer par une blague. Le vrai problème pour lui se trouve ailleurs : ses projets dans l’IA.
Au lendemain des élections de mi-mandat étasuniennes du 3 novembre, Elon Musk a commenté sa défaite avec un sarcasme appuyé. L'homme le plus riche du monde avait en effet engagé près d'un demi-milliard de dollars de sa fortune pour le parti républicain et, selon OpenSecrets cité par l'AFP, aucun donateur individuel n'avait autant donné dans une campagne fédérale depuis la levée des plafonds de dépenses en 2010. Une bonne part de cet argent visait le Texas, où le magnat a installé Tesla, SpaceX et X. Malheureusement pour lui, le démocrate James Talarico y a battu Ken Paxton, procureur général de l'État, tandis que Gina Hinojosa, elle aussi du parti à l'âne, a délogé le gouverneur conservateur sortant Greg Abbott.
Le 4 novembre, il a ironisé sur son réseau social : "J'imagine que mes lasers spatiaux d'ingérence électorale n'ont pas marché cette fois". La pique visait une théorie du complot jamais étayée, selon laquelle les satellites Starlink auraient truqué l'élection présidentielle de 2024.
Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷♂️
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 4, 2026
Le pari d'une sénatoriale à 168 millions de dollars perdu au Texas
En septembre, l'engagement politique d'Elon Musk avait franchi un cap. Il avait versé 158 millions de dollars au Senate Leadership Fund, un comité de financement républicain qui avait aussitôt reversé cette somme au principal groupe de soutien à Paxton. Musk avait ajouté 10 millions à un autre comité pro-Paxton, puis 5 millions à la campagne d'Abbott dans la dernière ligne droite. Las, ses deux candidats ont perdu dans les urnes.
La sénatoriale texane a été la course la plus chère de ces élections, avec plus de 500 millions de dollars de dépenses au total. Déjouant moult pronostics, Talarico est devenu le premier démocrate élu sénateur au Texas depuis 1988, et sa victoire a contribué à la reprise du Sénat fédéral par les démocrates. Dans son discours de victoire à Austin, rapporté par l'AFP, le nouvel élu a résumé l'enjeu : "Dans cette course, nous avons affronté nos propres Goliath. L'homme le plus riche du monde, l'homme le plus puissant du monde et toute la classe politique de Washington".
	
Dans cette course, nous avons affronté nos propres Goliath.
Centres de données IA : le Texas sonnera-t-il la fin de la récréation pour Musk ?
Si Elon Musk s'est autant impliqué financièrement, c'est que Talarico et Hinojosa ont tous deux fait campagne pour encadrer plus strictement les centres de données dédiés à l'IA. Les Texans s'inquiètent de la hausse des factures d'électricité, de la consommation d'eau et de la pression sur un réseau électrique déjà fragile. Pour l'homme d'affaires, la menace avait déjà pris corps avant les urnes, des habitants se plaignant du bruit occasionné par son centre de données IA.
Or Gina Hinojosa a promis un moratoire sur les nouveaux projets jusqu'à ce que le Parlement texan fixe des règles. Elle veut aussi supprimer les avantages fiscaux accordés aux centres de données. Sous la pression, Abbott avait lui-même gelé certaines autorisations à la fin de l'été.
Le Texas est le marché des centres de données qui croît le plus vite aux États-Unis, et Tesla y fait déjà tourner Cortex, son supercalculateur dédié à l'IA, dans sa Gigafactory d'Austin. Musk a répondu sur X que "les centres de données dans l'espace semblent plutôt séduisants en ce moment". SpaceX promet depuis des mois des datacenters IA dans l'espace, mais la Deutsche Bank estime que l'orbite ne deviendra compétitive face aux installations au sol qu'au cours des années 2030. D'ici là, Musk devra composer avec une gouverneure élue sur la promesse d'un moratoire. Bad for business…

articles.title: El Pentágono dará a conocer qué leyes rigen a los laboratorios de IA en Estados Unidos
articles.text:
El gobierno de Estados Unidos dará a conocer en una o dos semanas el conjunto de leyes y regulaciones que ya se aplican a los laboratorios nacionales de inteligencia artificial. Lo anunció el miércoles 4 de noviembre Emil Michael, director de tecnología del Pentágono, en una conferencia de The Wall Street Journal en Napa, California, según Reuters.
Michael es vicepresidente del Super Intelligence Task Force (grupo de trabajo de superinteligencia), un organismo interinstitucional que creó el presidente Donald Trump para definir la política del país en materia de IA. Reuters informó que el funcionario no ofreció más detalles sobre el contenido del documento.
“Lo que intentamos es crear un marco que haga que los estadounidenses tengan confianza en que estas empresas van a hacer lo correcto”, dijo Michael. Si no, añadió, “lo que se obtiene son 535 legisladores escribiendo una norma que podría matar a la industria”. La cifra corresponde a los miembros del Congreso de Estados Unidos.
Con ese argumento, el funcionario planteó el documento como una alternativa a una ley nueva del Congreso. No precisó qué organismos participarán en la publicación ni en qué formato se difundirá.
Una revisión de las leyes vigentes, no una norma nueva
La declaración en Napa coincide con lo que Michael dijo semanas antes a The Information, medio especializado en tecnología. En esa entrevista, según el resumen que publicó The Next Web, el funcionario aseguró que las leyes existentes son “más que suficientes” para los laboratorios de IA.
Michael explicó que esa conclusión se basa en su propia lectura y en lo que le comentó Andrew Ferguson, presidente de la Comisión Federal de Comercio, el organismo que vigila la competencia y la protección del consumidor en Estados Unidos.
El trabajo del grupo incluye un marco de respuesta ante incidentes, planes para proteger la infraestructura crítica y una revisión de las leyes que ya alcanzan a las empresas de IA.
Controles de exportación y el caso de Anthropic
En esa entrevista, Michael afirmó que el gobierno puede usar controles de exportación contra las empresas de IA que no cooperen, y que el Departamento de Justicia puede hacer cumplir las normas. Aseguró que Anthropic quedó bajo esos controles dos horas después de negarse a retirar un modelo que, según el gobierno, había sido vulnerado. The Next Web recogió esa versión sin confirmación independiente.
El Pentágono clasificó a Anthropic como riesgo para la cadena de suministro y la empresa pidió que el tribunal de apelaciones en pleno revise su caso. Michael dijo que espera que el gobierno gane. También señaló que prevé tratar a Anthropic de manera equitativa, como al resto de los laboratorios, dentro del grupo de trabajo.
Michael dijo que el Departamento de Guerra, nombre con el que el gobierno designa hoy al Pentágono, es también un gran usuario de IA: unos 1,7 millones de sus 3,5 millones de empleados la usan, frente a 80.000 hace un año. Afirmó que prefiere modelos de código abierto estadounidenses, como Nemotron, de Nvidia, aunque ninguno está todavía en la frontera tecnológica.
El plazo anunciado, una o dos semanas desde el 4 de noviembre, es el único compromiso concreto de Michael. Hasta ahora no se informó una fecha exacta ni los organismos que firmarán el documento.

articles.title: Russia-Linked Hackers Hit iOS, Android Devices With Exploit Chains via Watering Holes
articles.text:
Russian state-sponsored threat actor Midnight Blizzard is believed to have targeted iOS and Android users in Europe and the US with zero-click exploits targeting n-day vulnerabilities, cybersecurity firm Sekoia reports.
Also known as APT29, Cozy Bear, The Dukes, Nobelium, and Yttrium, and believed to be sponsored by the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), Midnight Blizzard is known for targeting government organizations, diplomats, IT services providers, and NGOs for intelligence gathering.
The attacks uncovered by Sekoia, mounted as part of a large-scale watering hole campaign, involved compromised or cloned high-profile websites of organizations in the US, Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria.
Midnight Blizzard injected malicious JavaScript code in the websites of a Ukrainian gas production company, a major industry trade association, and a far-right European political party, and modified legitimate files on the site of a Bulgarian military-related website.
The code was designed to fingerprint visitors, harvesting browser and device configuration data and sending it in JSON format before the exploit is delivered.
In an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) setup, the APT registered two lookalike domains that acted as reverse proxies for high-profile sites, injecting malicious code into copies of america250.org, the site of the 250th anniversary of American independence, and the website of the Raffles London at The OWO hotel near sensitive UK government institutions.
“By doing this watering hole impersonation of the Raffles London at The OWO, the intrusion set may have sought to target diplomatic delegations and high-profile guests through targeted spear-phishing campaigns. Recent open-source reporting, for example, indicates that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stayed at Raffles London during a visit on 14 October,” Sekoia notes.
The hackers also targeted Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy in a supply chain attack, adding their malicious code to the tracker file. This exposed hundreds of websites to the exploit kit for one week, including army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) sites.
Sekoia identified three exploit chains (two targeting iOS and one targeting Android) used across the campaign. All three target previously patched vulnerabilities, and the iOS chains rely heavily on the DarkSword exploit kit that was uncovered earlier this year.
The first reimplements the initial remote code execution (RCE) code from DarkSword for arbitrary read/write access, and then exploits CVE-2024-27834 to bypass Apple’s Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC) protection and execute code that steals cookies outside of Safari.
CVE-2024-27834 was patched in May 2024 in iOS 17.5 and iPadOS 17.5, iOS 16.7.8 and iPadOS 16.7.8, macOS Sonoma 14.5, Safari 17.5, tvOS 17.5, watchOS 10.5. On Wednesday, CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog, telling federal agencies to patch it within two weeks.
The second chain relies solely on DarkSword for initial access, code execution, and privilege escalation. The final payload was designed to fully harvest the device: messages, emails, voicemails, credentials, tokens, contacts, calls, calendar entries, browser cookies and history, photos, and iCloud Drive content.
Midnight Blizzard’s last exploit chain targets Android users via CVE-2026-3910, a Chrome vulnerability patched in March as a zero-day, and CVE-2025-27038, a Qualcomm bug patched with Android’s August 2025 security update.
The final payload, AndroSnitch, targets data stored in Chrome, including cookies, account information, passwords, browser history, and Wi-Fi passwords. It is similar to AndroSnatch, a Chrome cookie stealer Google TAG observed in Midnight Blizzard attacks mounted between 2023 and 2024.
“The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation. Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendor] exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent,” Sekoia notes.

articles.title: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M to bolster its AI infrastructure | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Dropbox is making a big push into AI infrastructure with a $350 million acquisition of cloud technology company Tigris Data, marking what appears to be its largest acquisition to date.
Announced Thursday, the deal is expected to strengthen Dropbox’s AI infrastructure capabilities and support the development of DBX Agent Cloud, a new storage platform aimed at businesses and developers building AI models and agents.
Dropbox told TechCrunch via email that the transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. The company also said it currently has no plans to reduce headcount as part of the acquisition. The company already cut 9% of its global workforce last month, WSJ reported.
DBX Agent Cloud will initially offer object storage as a stand-alone product, allowing businesses to purchase storage independently and use it with existing tools and applications built for Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), which is a cloud storage service that enables businesses to store and retrieve large volumes of data.
Beyond its infrastructure ambitions, Dropbox is also bringing more AI capabilities to its core product. Users will be able to ask AI to perform supported tasks using their files, choose between different AI models, and connect their Dropbox content to third-party tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse.
The company also plans to expand DBX Agent Cloud with additional capabilities designed to help AI systems work with different types of content, including documents, images, audio, and video. Other planned additions include filesystem features that will allow AI agents to manage files and maintain continuity across tasks and sessions.
Dropbox says the updated experience has already reached more than 70,000 teams. The initial rollout is available to eligible Standard and Advanced customers in the U.S., U.K., and Australia, with broader availability planned for 2027.
Tigris Data was founded by former Uber engineers who helped develop the ride-hailing company’s storage infrastructure. The company provides cloud storage technology that helps businesses store and access data across different regions. Its platform automatically positions data closer to the users and computing resources that need it, helping reduce access times and improve performance.
Tigris Data raised $25 million in a Series A funding round last year.
While the Tigris deal appears to be Dropbox’s largest acquisition, it is not the company’s first move to expand its AI capabilities through M&A. Dropbox has previously acquired several AI-focused companies, including Reclaim.ai, Promoted.ai, and Mobius Labs.

articles.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is $300 off ahead of Black Friday
articles.text:
Android fans with a bit of iPhone Duo envy, take note: The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is discounted to $1,599.99 at both Amazon and Best Buy, a hefty $300 markdown from its usual price, and just $50 higher than the lowest we’ve seen. Considering the device only launched a few months ago, you’re saving a significant amount of cash on the unlocked device, and you can also opt for the 512GB model, doubling the storage, for just $200 more (Amazon, Best Buy). Best Buy currently has all three colors in stock, while the 256GB model is currently sold out on Amazon in cream.
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is $300 off ahead of Black Friday
You can also save on the Beats Pill Bluetooth speaker, a battery-powered Ring doorbell, and a Lego Star Wars droid.
The shorter and wider passport-style shape (similar to the iPhone Duo) quickly became natural and comfortable to handle, according to our reviewer Dominic Preston’s experience with the Z Fold 8. Despite its thin and light construction, it doesn’t skimp on battery life, with a 4,800mAh battery that still had 40 percent charge remaining after a full day of use. The interior 4:3 screen has the same ratio as most Apple iPads, which is great for watching movies or TV, but even better for reading. There’s no telephoto lens on this model (it’s present on the pricier Z Fold 8 Ultra), and it only has an IP48 rating, so you’ll want to be careful near the beach, but those are small compromises to make given the discounted price.
Other deals to consider
- Both Amazon and Best Buy are selling the Beats Pill for a discounted $99.95 and $99.99 respectively, a sizable break from the usual $149.99 price point. The 2024 edition of this iconic Bluetooth speaker adds in lossless audio over USB-C, as well as native feature support for both iOS and Android devices. It’s rated IP67 for dust and water resistance, and comes in three different colors to match your other Beats devices. Read our review.
- The Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is on sale for $39.99 at Amazon, over half off its $99.99 list price. This battery-powered doorbell camera is easy to install, and shoots clear 2K resolution video with a 140-degree field of view and up to 6X digital zoom. You’ll get real-time notifications on your phone for any activity the camera spots, with live view and two-way talk in case you need to have a chat with your neighbors or delivery folks without coming to the front door.
- You can pick up the Lego Star Wars: Ahsoka Chopper set for just $66.99 at Amazon, the lowest price we’ve seen yet for this 1,039-piece building kit. This brick-based droid has great play features, like detachable arms and center wheel for different display positions, and a head that spins and bobs realistically. It stands at over 8.5 inches when fully built, making it a fun addition to your existing Lego display or bookshelf.

articles.title: CoolIT, PurposeMed among companies honoured at Start Alberta Tech Awards | BetaKit
articles.text:
Two of the Calgary tech ecosystem’s most high-profile exits, CoolIT Systems and PurposeMed, received accolades on Wednesday night as they landed among the companies honoured at the Start Alberta Tech Awards.
“You can build a real company in Alberta without burning through capital.”
Start Alberta is an Alberta-focused database on startups and funding that is operated by The A100, a community of tech and innovation leaders, founders, and investors founded in 2010 and serving Western Canada. Now in its ninth year, the Start Alberta Tech Awards celebrate “outstanding achievements” in Alberta’s tech sector.
“These award honourees are building technology that meets real needs for people around the world,” Tamara Woolgar, the executive director with The A100, said in a press release. “Together, they show what’s possible when we build in Alberta.”
Held at Calgary’s National Music Centre, recipients were honoured across 10 categories. CoolIT Systems took home the Deal of the Year award for its $4.75-billion USD ($6.6 billion CAD) exit to Ecolab. Announced last March and closed in July, the exit secured by the advanced liquid cooling company is the largest disclosed acquisition price for an Alberta-based company in history.
CoolIT’s win was mirrored by another historic exit in the Calgary scene this year: PurposeMed. The company behind telehealth startups Freddie, Frida, and Foria took home the Anchor of the Year award, honouring a “flagship company that supports the foundation upon which others build in Alberta.” PurposeMed and Freddie were recently acquired by dating platform Grindr in another high-value acquisition, netting $250 million USD.
RELATED: Platform Calgary unveils 10 most promising startups ahead of Calgary Innovation Week
“You can build a real company in Alberta without burning through capital,” said PurposeMed co-founder and CEO, Pete MacLeod, in a statement. “I’d love to see more founders realize you can do big things and keep talent here.”
Helcim, the Calgary-based FinTech and payment processing platform, took home Scaleup of the Year for more than doubling its team since 2021. Last August, the company closed a $53-million CAD Series C round at a valuation of $250 million with more than $150 million in annual recurring revenue.
The remaining list of winners and award categories include:
- Most Promising Founder: Cheng (Jack) Su, EnerNode AI. EnerNode uses AI to manage oil and gas operations. Founded in 2026, it has already seen industry adoption in Western Canada, and was selected for the Plug and Play Canada and NVIDIA Inception programs.
- Investor of the Year: Graphite Ventures. Graphite Ventures boasts teams in Calgary and Edmonton, leading early investment in companies like PataBid, WaitWell, Black Owl, ResolvMD, and Ontopical. It was also selected to manage the University of Alberta Innovation Fund.
- A100 One to Watch: NiaHealth. Edmonton-based NiaHealth is a medtech company offering blood testing, medical consultations, and personalized health metrics. It has raised more than $8 million since founding in 2023.
- VCAA Rod Charko Service Award: Jade Alberts. Longtime Calgary ecosystem builder Jade Alberts received the award for his decade of work with Peer Guidance, a fractional support network for founders, as well as hosting Founders’ Coffee, a weekly meetup for entrepreneurs. He has been a mentor at Innovate Calgary and has made more than 30 angel investments.
- Ecosystem Support of the Year: Kristina Milke, Sprout Fund. A general partner at Sprout Fund, Milke is a founding member of the University of Alberta’s Thresholdimpact Venture Mentoring Service and has spent more than a decade working with, investing in, and supporting Alberta founders. She also co-founded Sprout, Valhalla Private Capital, and Valhalla Angels, one of the largest angel networks in Western Canada.
- Woman in Tech: Dr. Christy Lane, Flora Fertility. Lane is the co-founder and co-CEO of Flora Fertility, a fertility insurance startup. The company closed a $5-million USD seed round in April, and is now expanding into Canada. Flora Fertility is Lane’s third venture, after Vivametrica, which she exited in 2020.
- Leader of the Year: Dr. Caley Shukalek, PurposeMed. Shukalek was chief medical officer of PurposeMed. Under his leadership, Freddie expanded to all 50 US states, and expanded HIV care in Canada.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Kyler Nixon.

articles.title: 18 Millionen Domains und ein Wertverfall: Was von der .de-Goldgräberzeit übrig ist
articles.text:
Im Internet ist fast alles beliebig oft verfügbar. Nur die Adresse nicht: Jede Domain gibt es bloß ein einziges Mal. Für shopping.des wurden 2008 fast zwei Millionen Euro gezahlt, für kredit.de fast 900.000 Euro. Der Handel mit solchen Namen zeigt, dass digitale Adressen ein knappes und mitunter kostspieliges Gut sind – und das seit nunmehr vier Jahrzehnten: Am 5. November wird die deutsche Länderkennung .de 40 Jahre alt.
Die Verwaltung übernahm 1986 zunächst das US-amerikanische Forschungsnetzwerk CSNET. 1988 ging sie an die Universität Dortmund – zu diesem Zeitpunkt waren gerade einmal sechs .de-Domains registriert. Mit der Verbreitung des Internets wuchsen die Anforderungen. 1993 entstand der Interessenverbund IV-DENIC, am 17. Dezember 1996 gründeten 37 Internet-Service-Provider die DENIC eG als genossenschaftlich organisierte Registrierungsstelle.
Heute zählt .de mehr als 18 Millionen registrierte Domains und gehört damit zu den größten Länderendungen weltweit. Die technische Infrastruktur bewältigt nach Angaben der DENIC rund 3,5 Milliarden Nameservice-Anfragen täglich. Sie sorgt dafür, dass Internetadressen weltweit erreichbar sind. „Aus den frühen, überschaubaren Netzstrukturen ist eine leistungsfähige digitale Infrastruktur geworden“, sagt DENIC-Vorstand Tom Keller zum Jubiläum.
Digitales Gold: Hunderttausende Euro für Top-Adressen
Nach den akademischen Anfangszeiten entdeckten auch Geschäftemacher die Internetdomains. Dass Internetadressen als digitale Immobilien gehandelt werden, zeigt der florierende Zweitmarkt. Zwar kostet eine Neuregistrierung einer .de-Domain meist nur wenige Euro im Jahr, doch für kurze, einprägsame Alltagsbegriffe werden weiterhin hohe Summen gezahlt.
Wie wertvoll begehrte Begriffe unter .de nach wie vor sind, belegen die Zahlen der Domainpreisdatenbank: So wechselte zuletzt die Adresse ferienhaus.de über den Kölner Marktplatz Sedo für 357.000 Euro den Besitzer – der teuerste öffentlich dokumentierte Verkauf einer deutschen Domain im Jahr 2025. An die schwindelerregenden Rekordwerte aus den Boomjahren 2007 und 2008 reicht das heutige Preisniveau allerdings nicht mehr heran. Der Markt hat sich im Vergleich zur damaligen Hochphase spürbar abgekühlt.
Geopolitische Kuriosität: Der Hype um .si
Wie stark die Abkürzungen am Ende einer Webadresse die Spekulationen befeuern können, zeigte jüngst eine Posse um die slowenische Länderendung .si. Nachdem US-Präsident Donald Trump gefordert hatte, Künstliche Intelligenz (KI beziehungsweise AI) in „Super Intelligence“ (SI) umzubenennen, stürmten Domain-Händler und Tech-Unternehmen plötzlich das slowenische Register. Binnen kürzester Zeit explodierten die Registrierungszahlen für Adressen mit der Endung des kleinen EU-Landes – pikanterweise die Heimat von Trumps Ehefrau Melania. Der Fall verdeutlichte schlaglichtartig, dass Top-Level-Domains selbst im Zeitalter von Apps und Social Media nichts von ihrer Wucht verloren haben.
Neue Welle von Endungen: Von .agent bis .taylorswift
Trotz der ungebrochenen Anziehungskraft bewährter Adressen wächst die Vielfalt im Namensraum. Pünktlich zum runden Geburtstag von .de kündigt sich ein neuer globaler Vergabeschub an. Wie der Branchenverband Eco mitteilte, hat die weltweite Internet-Verwaltung ICANN soeben die Bewerbungsliste für eine neue Runde generischer Endungen (gTLDs) vorgelegt. Insgesamt gingen 1.615 Bewerbungen von 481 Antragstellern ein, darunter 333 direkte Markenbewerbungen.
Der Trend spiegelt aktuelle technologische und kulturelle Entwicklungen wider: Neben Adressen aus dem KI-Umfeld wie .agent oder .api sowie Tech-Marken wie .openai und .chatgpt bewerben sich Interessenten auch um prominente Namen wie .taylorswift. Sport- und Finanzbegriffe wie .olympic, .euro und .bitcoin stehen ebenfalls auf der Liste. Ob all diese Endungen tatsächlich an den Start gehen, entscheidet sich in den kommenden Prüfverfahren.
„Verbundenheit mit Deutschland“
Zum runden Geburtstag der deutschen Länderkennung blickt die Branche geschlossen mit Stolz auf die heimische Erfolgsgeschichte: „Vierzig Jahre .de sind eine echte Erfolgsgeschichte“, sagt Thomas Rickert, Director Names & Numbers beim Verband der Internetwirtschaft Eco. Der Namensraum des Internets werde zunehmend auch zu einem wirtschaftlichen Wettbewerbsfaktor. Und auch DENIC-Vorständin Barbara Stolz zeigt sich überzeugt, dass die Traditionskennung das verlässliche Fundament der deutschen Netzwelt bleibt: „.de steht wie kaum eine andere Länderkennung für die Verbundenheit mit Deutschland.“
Apps, KI-Assistenten und der Bedeutungsverlust der Adresszeile
Gleichzeitig wächst unter Experten die Skepsis, ob klassische Domainadressen ihre einstige Dominanz dauerhaft behaupten können. Längst tippen nur noch die wenigsten Internetnutzer eine vollständige Webadresse per Hand in die Browserzeile ein. Auf Smartphones dominieren App-Ökosysteme, in denen Internetadressen unsichtbar im Hintergrund bleiben.
Zudem leiten KI-gestützte Suchsysteme und Chatbots eine fundamentale Trendwende ein: Anstatt wie klassische Suchmaschinen auf eine Liste verlinkter Webseiten zu verweisen, fassen moderne Sprachmodelle und KI-Agenten die gesuchten Informationen direkt zusammen. Wer im Netz gefunden oder gekauft werden will, muss nicht mehr zwingend über eine einprägsame Domain verfügen, sondern vielmehr in den Trainingsdaten und Datenquellen der KI-Modelle optimal auffindbar sein.

articles.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
articles.text:
Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it.
“We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.
Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube, where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents.
“I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.”
Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere
Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it.
“Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.”
That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents.
“I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.”
It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand.
It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains.
“You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.”
In non-wizard terms?
“There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks.
“I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.”
From Birding to Model-Building
Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada.
“After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions.
“Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.”
Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community.
“To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.”
And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan?
“It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.”
Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.

articles.title: A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush
articles.text:
About a dozen workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taoyuan in Taiwan went on strike in October, the first in the island’s semiconductor industry, after their union and the chipmaker failed to reach an agreement on salaries and bonuses. Their one-day action, while largely symbolic, is a reflection of the growing discontent among laborers in the artificial intelligence industry over how profits are distributed.
The leading American memory chipmaker has posted record profits this year on the back of surging demand for AI chips. Unions representing workers at Micron’s facilities in Taoyuan and Taichung have been negotiating with the company for months for a profit-sharing agreement similar to those reached by employees at rivals Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in South Korea.
“Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit instead of this unequal distribution between high-level executives and the rank and file,” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union, told Rest of World.
The global tech industry is heavily reliant on Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. Idaho-based Micron, the world’s third-biggest memory chipmaker, employs more than 15,000 workers in Taiwan. They produce over 60% of the company’s dynamic random access memory chips, used in AI servers. A prolonged workers’ strike could severely disrupt already strained supplies of memory chips worldwide.
Micron on October 22 said it had reached an agreement with the Taichung union for higher salaries and quarterly bonuses, and bigger contributions to the pension accounts of all workers at its Taiwan operations. But many union members rejected the deal, which they said was made in secret, while the majority of members of the Taoyuan union said they were dissatisfied with the terms of the agreement.
“We do not accept the deal. None of our demands were fulfilled,” a Taoyuan union member, who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak to the media, told Rest of World. “We are surprised that the Taichung union representatives signed the deal.”
The Taoyuan union, which is registered as a separate entity with more than 2,300 members, can still go on strike.
Micron respects the workers’ “lawful rights and the applicable legal process,” a spokesperson for the company told Rest of World. “We are committed to constructive engagement with the Taoyuan and Taichung unions to reach a solution that works for all parties.”
Heightened consumer concern
Labor disputes and strikes in Taiwan have historically been associated with traditional industries. The actions by the Micron workers’ unions signal a broader shift as semiconductor workers increasingly organize to demand greater transparency and a fairer share of the value they help create, Wu Yu-ren, a labor relations professor at National Chung Cheng University, told Rest of World.
Over the past few months, membership in Micron’s two worker unions has surged from around 440 to more than 13,000. Earlier this year, employees of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. — which makes about 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors and 99% of the chips used to train frontier AI models — also discussed unionizing and striking over pay.
Taiwan’s high-tech companies have traditionally used generous benefits and bonuses to discourage workers from forming unions. White-collar tech workers have tended to change jobs instead of seeking collective action.
Now, “soaring demand for high-end memory has driven up share prices and corporate profits, making workers question how those gains are distributed,” Wu said. “The labor actions of Samsung and SK Hynix have also influenced the unionization of Taiwan tech workers.”
Across the world, policymakers, economists, and civil society groups are grappling with the widening gap between those who are benefiting from the AI boom and those who are being left behind. U.S. startups alone have created 19 billionaires worth a combined $59 billion over the past year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
The Micron workers’ actions come as American frontier AI company Anthropic prepares to launch what could be the world’s biggest initial public offering, valuing the company at nearly $2 trillion. Its founders, investors, and some employees stand to become very wealthy.
In Taiwan, negotiations between Micron’s Taoyuan union and the company are continuing. In the event of another strike, the impact of a brief stop in production would likely be limited if backup personnel are available for equipment maintenance, process monitoring, and troubleshooting, Ellie Wang, an analyst at consulting firm TrendForce, told Rest of World.
“The main consequence would be heightened customer concern over delivery reliability,” she said.
But if worker discontent spreads to other facilities or if there are prolonged strikes, it could disrupt supplies to downstream AI hardware makers such as Nvidia, and drive up prices. It would also hurt Taiwan’s wider economy, with the semiconductor sector making up more than a fifth of gross domestic product.
The stakes are high. Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, attended Micron’s opening ceremony for its new plant in Taichung last month, and urged the company and its workers to reach an agreement. “Corporations and employees should help each other like fish and water,” he said.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Labor said it would provide assistance and facilitate further dialogue between Micron and the Taoyuan union. “We hope that both parties will be willing to negotiate, reach a consensus as soon as possible and bring the dispute to an end,” it said in a statement.
Building a constructive labor-management relationship before disputes escalate will be a challenge for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, Pan Shih-wei, a former labor minister and adjunct labor relations professor, told Rest of World. “Taiwan has traditionally relied on government intervention for labor disputes, and companies lack established channels for dialogue with workers.”
The Micron dispute could lead to a wider labor movement as younger workers become more conscious of their rights, Pan said.
“High-tech companies really need to take a closer look at how they manage labor relations,” he said. “Discussions about strikes and the distribution of profits will become increasingly common. … Ultimately, determining the profit-sharing ratio requires negotiations and engagement between the parties.”

articles.title: Chasse aux mines : la France dévoile sa solution pour déployer rapidement ses drones en haute mer
articles.text:
La Marine nationale dispose déjà de drones de surface capables de repérer des mines marines. Problème, il leur manque un navire pour les emmener loin des côtes.
Début août 2026, la Direction générale de l’armement (DGA) avait annoncé la commande de 12 drones supplémentaires et l’affrètement de navires pour les porter, sans préciser lesquels. Elle a présenté sa solution le 5 novembre, en marge du salon Euronaval, avec deux plateformes civiles baptisées « Protée », fournies par les Chantiers de l’Atlantique et Les Abeilles International et affrétées pour 10 ans au maximum.
Une nouvelle avancée pour le programme SLAM-F (système de lutte anti-mines du futur), lancé en 2020 pour remplacer tous les moyens de guerre des mines de la Marine.
Des navires de guerre qui se font attendre
Les Protée doivent permettre de mettre en œuvre plus rapidement les drones au large, notamment pour soutenir les forces stratégiques, mais ils ne seront qu’une étape.
Dans un billet publié le 5 novembre, le ministère des Armées rappelle en effet que d’autres navires sont prévus. La DGA prépare l’acquisition de bâtiments de guerre des mines (BGDM) qui permettront « d’aller loin et partout, tant en métropole qu’en projection ».
Reste que ces bâtiments se font attendre. Le rapport annexé au projet d’actualisation de la loi de programmation militaire prévoit leur acquisition « dès 2032 », et 4 exemplaires au lieu de 6 à l’horizon 2035.
D’ici là, la Marine doit réduire sa flotte de chasseurs de mines, de 8 navires fin 2024 à 2 fin 2030. Les Protée et leurs drones devront assurer la relève en attendant les BGDM.
Des navires civils pour embarquer les drones de la Marine
D’après les éléments fournis par la DGA, chaque Protée mesurera 80 mètres pour 4 000 tonnes de déplacement. Un équipage civil conduira le navire, tandis qu’un détachement de la Marine se chargera des opérations.
Pour répondre aux besoins de la Marine, ce navire civil pourra recevoir, sous forme de modules, un poste de commandement, deux drones de surface, deux drones sous-marins, des moyens de neutralisation des mines ou une équipe de plongeurs démineurs.
L’intérêt des drones tient d’abord à la distance qu’ils mettent entre les équipages et le danger. Ils descendent aussi plus bas que les chasseurs de mines, jusqu’à 300 mètres de profondeur contre 100 mètres. Leurs sonars sont épaulés par des algorithmes qui aident l’opérateur à trier les échos, mais la décision de neutraliser une mine « reste toujours humaine », précise le ministère dans son billet.
D’autres drones, commandés à Thales et Exail, sont par ailleurs attendus à partir du premier semestre 2028.
