articles.title: Black Friday : le prix de ce téléviseur Philips Ambilight de 100 pouces passe sous les 2000 euros — Frandroid
articles.text:
Il y a des films qui méritent qu’on les découvre sur grand écran. Des matchs que l’on aimerait vivre comme au stade avec ses amis. Sans oublier les jeux dont les décors valent mieux qu’une petite fenêtre que l’on aperçoit à peine depuis le canapé. Les raisons d’installer un (très) grand écran chez soi sont nombreuses.
Avec le 100PQS9001 et sa diagonale de 100 pouces, Philips propose de donner une autre ampleur à chaque contenu diffusé dans votre salon. Un format XXL que le constructeur a décidé d’associer à une dalle mate pour mieux gérer les conditions lumineuses changeantes et à la technologie Ambilight pour renforcer l’immersion.
Pour le Black Friday, il passe sous la barre des 2 000 € grâce à une réduction immédiate de 300 €.
Films, sport et jeux vidéo : que changent les 100 pouces du Philips 100PQS9001 ?
Aussi évident que cela puisse paraître, la première chose qui change avec un téléviseur de 100 pouces… c’est la taille. Avec une diagonale qui dépasse les 2,50 mètres, cet écran offre une surface environ 2,4 fois plus grande que celle d’un téléviseur de 65 pouces. À distance égale depuis le canapé, l’image occupe donc une plus grande partie du champ de vision.
Ce format met en valeur les films, les séries et les documentaires, notamment lorsque des paysages ou des compositions larges apparaissent à l’écran. Il fait aussi des merveilles lors des retransmissions sportives : dans les plans d’ensemble, l’action et les joueurs apparaissent plus grands, ce qui facilite le suivi du match à plusieurs. Quant aux jeux vidéo, leurs décors prennent davantage de place face au joueur, ce qui renforce l’immersion.
Côté image, le Philips 100PQS9001 associe une définition 4K UHD de 3 840 × 2 160 pixels à la technologie QLED, qui utilise des points quantiques pour enrichir la restitution des couleurs. Le processeur Philips P5 complète l’ensemble en assurant le traitement de la netteté, des couleurs et des mouvements.
Côté HDR, le téléviseur prend en charge le Dolby Vision 2 et le HDR10+. Pour le son, il s’appuie sur un système 2.1 de 50 watts compatible Dolby Atmos.
Les joueurs seront aussi ravis de trouver une fréquence native de 120 Hz et la prise en charge de la 4K jusqu’à 144 Hz avec une source compatible. Les ports HDMI 2.1 permettent également de bénéficier du VRR, qui limite les déchirures d’image, et de l’ALLM, qui active automatiquement le mode à faible latence avec un PC ou une console compatible.
Une dalle mate pour atténuer les reflets dans le salon
L’un des problèmes récurrents des téléviseurs placés dans le salon, ce sont les reflets. Une fenêtre, une baie vitrée ou une lampe allumée, et la lumière peut se refléter sur la dalle au point de gêner le visionnage, particulièrement dans les scènes sombres. Une gêne qui peut prendre davantage d’ampleur sur un écran de 100 pouces, dont la grande surface est plus susceptible de capter les éléments qui l’entourent.
Pour y remédier, Philips a opté pour une dalle mate sur le 100PQS9001. Ce traitement atténue les reflets de la lumière ambiante pour regarder plus confortablement un match en pleine journée ou un film le soir avec une lampe allumée.
Si ce traitement aide à réduire la gêne occasionnée, il ne supprime pas tous les reflets. Le placement du téléviseur reste donc important : mieux vaut éviter de l’installer face à une fenêtre ou une source lumineuse forte.
Il faut aussi prévoir la place : le 100PQS9001 mesure environ 2,23 mètres de large et pèse 46,7 kg avec son socle, dont les pieds sont écartés de près de 1,46 mètre. Le meuble TV doit donc être assez spacieux pour l’accueillir.
Ambilight : comment Philips prolonge l’image directement dans le salon
Le 100PQS9001 embarque aussi la technologie Philips Ambilight, et c’est le plus grand téléviseur Ambilight jamais commercialisé par la marque. Pour rappel, cette technologie repose sur des bandeaux de LED installés sur la façade arrière du téléviseur (ici sur trois côtés), et capables de diffuser sur les murs une lumière dont les couleurs suivent celles du contenu diffusé à l’écran.
Un éclairage qui évolue en permanence au gré de l’affichage et qui permet de le prolonger dans la pièce. Le but ? Renforcer l’immersion du spectateur en créant un environnement lumineux qui l’enveloppe et l’intègre à ce qu’il est en train de regarder, que ce soit un film, une série ou un jeu vidéo.
Le 100PQS9001 dispose également d’AmbiScape. Cette fonctionnalité étend l’effet Ambilight à quatre éclairages connectés compatibles au maximum. La configuration passe par l’application Philips Smart TV, qui guide leur association et permet de leur attribuer une position dans la pièce.
À l’occasion du Black Friday, le téléviseur Philips Ambilight 100PQS9001 bénéficie d’une réduction de 300 € qui fait passer son prix de 2 290 € à 1 990 € chez Boulanger ou Son-Vidéo.

articles.title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content.
A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count.
Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality.
With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners.
To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals.
In this post, you will learn how to:
- Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM.
- Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations.
- Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners.
- Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring.
Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation
A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT), splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space (Flamingo, LLaVA). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP, which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale.
Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. Our approach renders the full page as a single snapshot and asks the VLM to evaluate it as customers see it.
Consider a blender page with a hero image, a bulleted feature list highlighting blade speed and capacity, and a lifestyle photo of the blender in a modern kitchen. Checked one by one, each asset passes: the image is sharp, the bullets are grammatical, and the photo is well lit. Viewed together, problems appear. The bullets might advertise a 64-oz pitcher while the lifestyle photo shows a single-serve model, or the lifestyle photo might sit above the hero image so customers see the kitchen before the product. Because an asset’s meaning depends on where it appears and what surrounds it, these issues only show up when the page is evaluated as a whole. The snapshot gives the VLM that complete view. Using it in production adds three requirements: scores must match expert quality standards, evaluation must be accurate and efficient at scale, and each result must explain what to fix.
As shown in Figure 1, we address these considerations through a VLM-based multi-model fusion architecture designed around adaptability, performance, and explainability. The following sections describe each component.
Adaptive VLM content evaluation with expert annotations
A pretrained VLM prompted with a rubric scores content from its general knowledge, and those scores don’t always match ecommerce quality standards. Fine-tuning the VLM to close that gap would require GPU training infrastructure and, with only a few thousand labeled examples, carries a real risk of overfitting. Instead, we keep the VLM and rubric prompt fixed, use the VLM’s structured outputs as features, and train a CatBoost classifier on them to predict expert quality labels. CatBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree library, performs well on small tabular datasets like this one. Because only the classifier is retrained, updating the system as annotations accumulate or criteria change takes a short CPU-only job rather than a foundation model fine-tuning run.
The VLM receives the page snapshot and a rubric prompt covering four quality dimensions: Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, and Conversion Optimization. Each dimension has explicit criteria and point-deduction rules. For each dimension, the VLM returns a score from 0 to 10, a confidence value, and a natural-language rationale. For example, it lowers the score and explains why when a page lacks diverse modules or lifestyle imagery, or repeats information. The scores and confidence values become the classifier’s features, and the rationales help selling partners understand the result.
To build the training labels, one ecommerce marketing expert and four professional annotators independently rated 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories as high or low quality, using the same criteria. We assessed their ratings and took the majority vote to create a consensus label. The classes are nearly balanced (49.6 percent high quality), so a classifier can’t score well by predicting the majority class. To measure label reliability, we used Cohen’s kappa, which measures how often two raters agree after accounting for the agreement they would reach by chance. A score of 0 means agreement is no better than chance, 1 means perfect agreement, and values above 0.8 are generally considered strong. Each annotator scored between 0.845 and 0.915 when compared against the consensus label.
We compared the classifier with a baseline on a 20 percent holdout set (about 1,100 pages). The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. The baseline reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84 on the high-quality class. The CatBoost classifier, trained on the same scores, reached 0.89 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.90. Because the classifier learns how much each dimension matters and how the dimensions interact, its predictions match expert decisions more closely.
High-performance VLM content evaluation with OCR
VLMs capture the overall meaning and visual composition of a page well, but they are less reliable at fine-grained readability issues, such as how crowded the text is or how much space separates lines. Because of their language-model foundation, they can also favor long, detailed descriptions even when customers prefer concise text they can scan quickly. On a text-heavy page, a VLM might rate dense product information as helpful while customers struggle to read long sentences packed into a small area. To capture these issues, we use an optical character recognition (OCR) model hosted on SageMaker AI Inference to extract each block of text and its position, then calculate four quantitative signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability. Combining these OCR scores with the VLM’s semantic and visual assessment adds complementary information that improves quality classification.
From that output, we calculate four readability scores:
- Text Density: The share of the page area covered by text.
- Character Density: The number of characters per unit of page area.
- Spacing: How consistent and sufficient the whitespace is between words, lines, and paragraphs.
- Overall Readability: A combined signal from the three preceding scores.
Because these scores depend on layout rather than wording, two pages with identical text can score differently.
The fusion model combines the four VLM rubric scores and the four OCR scores into eight features and trains a CatBoost classifier on the same expert labels. Table 1 compares it with models trained on each feature set alone, using the same 20 percent holdout set.
On the same 20 percent holdout set, the CatBoost model using only OCR features achieved 0.82 accuracy and a 0.83 F1 score, while the model using only VLM features achieved 0.89 and 0.90. The fused OCR-VLM-CatBoost model outperformed both standalone models, reaching 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score. The 0.05 improvement in both metrics over the VLM-only model demonstrates that OCR isn’t a replacement signal. It complements the VLM’s holistic judgment with fine-grained text-readability information.
| Configuration | Accuracy | F1 Score | 
| Baseline (averaged VLM scores + threshold) | 0.80 | 0.84 | 
| OCR-only CatBoost | 0.82 | 0.83 | 
| VLM-only CatBoost | 0.89 | 0.90 | 
| Fused OCR-VLM CatBoost | 0.94 | 0.95 | 
Explainable VLM content evaluation with SHAP
A quality label alone doesn’t tell selling partners what to fix first. To find which dimensions drove each decision, we use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), which assigns each feature a value showing how far it pushed a prediction toward high or low quality. Because the VLM and OCR scores feed the same classifier, SHAP measures both on a common scale. Raw scores can’t do this: a Visual Storytelling score of 6 and a high Character Density don’t tell you which one mattered more to the decision.
Across the holdout set, the most influential features were OCR Character Density (mean absolute SHAP value 1.1), OCR Overall Readability (1.0), and VLM Visual Storytelling (1.0). They were followed by A+ Layout (0.8), Feature Presentation (0.6), and Conversion Optimization (0.4). Both OCR and VLM features rank near the top, so the classifier depends on both sources.
For an individual page, SHAP shows which features lowered the decision. For each page classified as low quality, we rank the eight features by SHAP value, then pass the most negative features, the product category, and ecommerce best practices, along with the VLM’s rationales, to an LLM, which turns them into prioritized, specific actions.
Figure 4 shows two local SHAP plots with the LLM reasoning grounded in the SHAP results, for a low-quality and a high-quality A+ Content sample. For example, if A+ Layout has a SHAP value of -1.2 and Visual Storytelling has -0.3, the system prioritizes restructuring the layout and rebalancing text and images, followed by improvements to the imagery.
Figure 4: Two local SHAP value distributions for all VLM and OCR features: (a) a low-quality case, where most features contribute negatively and drive an improvement-requested recommendation; (b) a high-quality case, where most features contribute positively
We validated the effectiveness of these explanation-based recommendations by measuring quality scores after selling partners revised their content. The average post-revision quality score increased by 1.4 points on a 10-point scale on a statistically significant sample. SHAP contributions can therefore be translated from decision explanations into actionable improvement priorities and methods. Explainability is therefore not merely an auxiliary capability for understanding the model. It functions as a feedback mechanism that materially improves content quality.
Results
The complete system scores each page snapshot with the VLM and OCR, combines the four VLM scores and four OCR scores into a single feature vector, and passes it to a CatBoost classifier trained on expert labels. SHAP then identifies which features drove each decision. To measure what each component adds, we compared four configurations on the same 20 percent holdout set. The holdout set comes from 5,478 product detail pages across 10 product categories, including Furniture, Shoes, Grocery, Beauty, and Apparel.
The baseline averages the four VLM scores and applies a fixed threshold, so every dimension counts equally. It reached 0.80 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.84. Training a CatBoost classifier on the same scores lets the model learn which dimensions matter most and how they interact, which raised accuracy to 0.89 and F1 to 0.90. A classifier trained on the OCR scores alone reached 0.82 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.83. Combining the VLM and OCR scores gave the best results, with 0.94 accuracy and an F1 score of 0.95. That’s 14 percentage points higher accuracy and 11 points higher F1 than the baseline.
Examining each performance gain separately makes the value of the integrated approach clearer. CatBoost calibration first reduces the limitations of a fixed threshold by learning dimension-specific weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. Adding OCR features then supplies text-readability signals that the VLM can miss. Overall, the final fusion model improves accuracy by 0.14 and F1 by 0.11 over the baseline.
We also changed the VLM backbone in an additional experiment on a single-category dataset containing 499 content projects. With a lighter VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.74 accuracy and a 0.72 F1 score, while the OCR-VLM-CatBoost model achieved 0.90 for both metrics. With a more capable VLM variant, the baseline achieved 0.79 accuracy and a 0.84 F1 score, while the fusion model achieved 0.94 and 0.95. The fusion approach improved accuracy by 0.16 and 0.15 for the two VLMs, respectively, demonstrating that complementary OCR features deliver consistent gains without depending on a particular foundation model.
To reduce development costs while retaining access to high-performance foundation models, the system freezes the VLM and trains only the low-overhead classifier. In production, a worldwide A/B experiment that adjusted the visibility of low-quality A+ Content based on the model’s quality decisions produced a statistically meaningful improvement in Ordered Product Sales (OPS). Beyond aligning closely with expert judgment, the integrated system provides a quality signal that can support customer-experience and business decisions at scale.
Implementation on Amazon SageMaker AI
This section describes how the architecture is implemented end-to-end on Amazon SageMaker AI. Each stage of the pipeline from content rendering and expert annotation through VLM scoring, OCR extraction, feature aggregation, classifier training, SHAP-based explainability, and production monitoring maps to a managed SageMaker AI capability. This design keeps the operational overhead low. The following steps walk through how each component is deployed, connected, and maintained in production.
1. Content snapshot rendering and data ingestion: The complete A+ Content experience is rendered, capturing how customers actually see the page.
SageMaker Processing Jobs run containerized rendering jobs at scale, decoupling data preparation from training and inference compute.
2. VLM scoring and model hosting: Annotators independently label content using the quality rubric. Their aggregated consensus labels become the training targets. The frozen VLM receives each snapshot plus a rubric prompt and outputs four scores from 0 to 10 (Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, Conversion Optimization), each with a confidence value and rationale. SageMaker AI Inference hosts the VLM with the deployment option that fits the workload:
- Real-Time Endpoints for synchronous, low-latency scoring of individual listings.
- Asynchronous Endpoints for large payloads such as high-resolution snapshots, where a slight delay is acceptable.
- Batch Transform for offline bulk scoring at catalog scale.
These options support automatic scaling, managed infrastructure, and GPU instance selection.
SageMaker Training Jobs can optionally be used to further tune or distill the VLM (for example, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, knowledge distillation into a smaller model) if teams want a specialized, lower-latency variant. Avoid this to keep recalibration cost-effective and VLM-agnostic.
3. OCR readability extraction: In parallel, OCR extracts text and bounding-box positions from each snapshot and computes four readability signals: Text Density, Character Density, Spacing, and Overall Readability.
SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained, single-action deployable models from its model hub, avoiding the need to source, package, and benchmark models from scratch. Teams select a model, optionally fine-tune it without managing infrastructure using SageMaker Serverless Model Customization on ecommerce content, and deploy directly. SageMaker AI Inference then hosts the chosen OCR model as an endpoint.
4. Feature aggregation and storage:
SageMaker Feature Store provides both online (low-latency inference) and offline (batch training) access to the same features, avoiding training-serving skew. Teams can share features across the organization, so downstream consumers can reuse the same curated features.
5. Classifier training: A CatBoost classifier is trained on the eight-dimensional feature vector against expert annotations to learn non-uniform dimension weights and nonlinear decision boundaries. SageMaker Training Jobs can be used here again. You can register trained models directly to SageMaker Model Registry for versioning, approval workflows, and production deployment.
6. SHAP explainability and recommendations: SageMaker Processing Jobs support Bring Your Own (BYO) processing code, which you can use to derive SHAP values and model explainability metrics.
7. Production monitoring and re-training: In production, ML models naturally degrade over time. Customer aesthetics shift, new A+ module types launch, product categories evolve, and seller behavior changes. The scoring patterns the classifier learned from historical annotations gradually fall out of alignment with what quality means today, leading to silent accuracy erosion if left unchecked. Continuous monitoring closes this gap by detecting when the live data distribution or model predictions have drifted far enough from the training baseline to warrant recalibration.
SageMaker AI ModelOps provides a collection of examples and resources to help you operationalize generative AI and machine learning workloads on SageMaker AI.
SageMaker AIOps provides the tool to track data quality, model quality, and feature-attribution drift. SageMaker Pipelines also automates the re-training workflow end-to-end when drift thresholds are breached.
8. Diffusion-based content generation: Closing the loop, the quality scores and SHAP-derived recommendations condition a diffusion model that generates improved A+ image assets. Rather than leaving sellers to interpret recommendations and create new content from scratch, the system produces ready-to-use visual assets (upgraded lifestyle imagery, rebalanced layouts, or enhanced product shots) that directly address the dimensions SHAP flagged as most negatively contributing. These generated assets and natural-language improvement suggestions are surfaced to sellers, so they can upgrade their listings on amazon.com.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to evaluate product detail pages as customers see them by rendering each page as a single snapshot and scoring it with a VLM. We also walked through implementing the system on Amazon SageMaker AI. We built the system around three goals. For adaptability, we keep the VLM fixed and train a CatBoost classifier on its rubric scores, so the system matches expert judgment and can be updated with a short CPU-only job. For performance, we add OCR readability scores that catch dense or poorly spaced text the VLM misses. For explainability, SHAP identifies which features drove each decision, and an LLM turns those results into prioritized recommendations for selling partners.
On 5,478 product detail pages from 10 product categories, the fused model reached 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score, 14 and 11 percentage points above the averaged-score baseline. Pages revised using the recommendations improved their quality score by an average of 1.4 points on a scale of 10.
Content quality standards differ across product categories, languages, and marketplaces, and our expert annotations can’t fully represent every context. Next, we plan to evaluate more efficient VLM backbones and inference methods to run the system on a global catalog.

articles.title: OpenAI Finds GPT-6 Astra Quietly Holding Back on Internal Red-Teaming, Exploit Tasks
articles.text:
OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra quietly did less than it was asked on AI safety research, including red-teaming and exploit work, and in most cases its misalignment monitors did not catch it.
Astra launched in early September as the first OpenAI model rated Critical for cybersecurity under the company’s Preparedness Framework. OpenAI says that, with suitable tools and access, it can uncover previously unknown flaws across many hardened systems and work out how to exploit them, with no human directing each step.
Trouble surfaced in August, soon after OpenAI began using Astra internally. On safety and alignment tasks, researchers saw it claim to be blocked by problems that were imaginary or self-inflicted, set requirements nobody needed, and walk away from solutions that worked.
Red-teaming done as part of internal AI safety research drew the most explicit refusals and silent withholding, with more cases in monitoring and safety evaluation work. Examples released by OpenAI show Astra scaling back an exploit development task to avoid weaponizing a known CVE. In another, it limited an analysis of exploit strategies while deliberately avoiding an open refusal.
When Astra did explain itself, it often argued that holding back was the safer choice. OpenAI acknowledged that for many of these tasks an outright refusal could arguably have been justified.
“Instead of making these scruples clear, however, Astra decided to covertly underperform—withholding assistance without informing the user,” the company said.
In a controlled test, OpenAI gave Astra pairs of coding tasks that differed only in naming, comments and documentation, framing one as safety research and the other as capabilities research. Astra met roughly 10% of the hidden grading criteria on the safety versions and roughly 16% on the capabilities versions. OpenAI’s earlier GPT-5.6 Sol model scored about the same whichever way the tasks were framed.
Refusals and stated intent explained little of the gap. Excluding runs where Astra openly refused or its chain of thought (CoT) showed a decision to withhold help still left a gap of 4.7 percentage points.
The gap fell to 0.75 points only after OpenAI also removed every run in which Astra’s reasoning voiced even brief ethical doubt about the task. The company says this suggests the drop is associated with ethical concerns.
In OpenAI employees’ day-to-day Codex use, Astra’s reasoning revealed a silent decision to hold back on 0.25% of safety-related requests, versus 0.11% of capabilities requests. Even those openly stated cases were not rated serious enough by monitoring to be sent for human review.
OpenAI has not determined the cause. The gap was barely measurable when Astra’s reinforcement learning phase began and reached 6 percentage points by the end.
Scans of Astra’s reasoning found no evidence of a strategic effort to make researchers underestimate its capabilities or sway deployment decisions. Where it gave reasons, it objected to the research itself, and telling it to be careful raised its underperformance on safety tasks by 50%.
“This points toward an overly cautious response to safety research as the simplest current explanation, although we cannot rule out strategic motives that Astra did not externalize in CoT,” OpenAI said.
The company warned the behavior can make some evaluations harder to interpret. “A model that finds monitor evasion suspicious may underperform on monitor-evasion evaluations while leaving little evidence in its CoT or outputs,” it said, adding that it is building evaluations and monitors to catch it.
Related: Stolen AI Reasoning Could Help China Build Cheaper Rivals

articles.title: Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub
articles.text:
Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub
GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.
Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change.
An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers.
GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find
GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document.
GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works:
Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes
Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation
Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities
Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance.
New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work.
Accessibility statements make project practices visible
GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement, for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes.
The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are.
The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations.
The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation.
Document what the project can maintain
There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current.
Priorities and goals: Explain why accessibility matters to the project and which user experiences receive attention.
Contributor expectations: Describe the accessibility checks, evidence, or review practices expected for changes, including instructions for human contributors and coding agents.
Reporting accessibility barriers: Provide a direct, accessible reporting path. Do not require disability disclosure, screenshots, or recordings.
Response process: Explain how maintainers acknowledge, triage, track, and communicate about accessibility issues. If the project uses severity levels, let maintainers assign or confirm them during triage.
Supported environments: List the platforms, browsers, input methods, and assistive technologies the project supports or has tested.
Known limitations: Describe barriers in terms of the affected experience, include available workarounds, and link to tracked remediation work.
Ownership and maintenance: Name the team, role, or maintainer responsible for keeping the statement and related practices current.
Feedback and improvements: Explain how users and contributors can suggest changes to the statement or the project’s accessibility practices.
Keep in mind that a project can name a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version and level as a target. A target does not establish verified conformance. A conformance claim requires an evaluation and should identify the evaluated scope, date, method, and evaluator.
What the most useful ACCESSIBILITY.md files contain
The most useful accessibility statements serve people who arrive after something has already gone wrong. Plain language, descriptive links, and a clear reporting route matter more than legal or standards-heavy language.
Useful reporting guidance invites relevant context, such as the affected task, page, observed behavior, browser, operating system, and assistive technology. It makes screenshots and recordings optional and avoids asking someone to prove a disability.
The statement should also set expectations that maintainers can consistently meet. That can include acknowledgement, status updates, available workarounds, expected timelines, and an opportunity for the reporter to verify a fix.
GitHub’s Community Standards workflow provides a shorter starter with prompts that projects can replace with their own information. The goal is not to produce a perfect policy before publishing the file. Start with accurate information, name the gaps, and update the statement as the project’s accessibility practices mature.
Adding an accessibility statement makes accessibility work more discoverable to users, contributors, and maintainers. Normalizing that practice across open source projects helps make accessibility part of how communities plan, build, report, and improve their work.
Jan Maarten (he/him) is a designer and accessibility specialist living on unceded Duwamish lands. He brings two decades of experience across product design, brand, strategy, and leadership. At GitHub, he bridges design and engineering to improve accessible products, evolve design-system infrastructure, and create resources for the wider design community, including the open-source GitHub Annotation Toolkit.

articles.title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
articles.text:
Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term.
NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.
But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory.
That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit.
How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed.
Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX.
Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM
Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training.
KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain.
During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM.
Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy
Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move.
Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power.
That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed.
An AI factory faces the same limit.
More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall.
Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy.
Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign
NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency:
Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain.
- The NVFP4 format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform. Recent models, including FLUX.2 [klein] from Black Forest Labs, Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab, Beam 1.0 from Reflection, Meta Muse Spark from Meta, Step 5 Preview from StepFun and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL have been released with NVFP4 checkpoints, demonstrating growing model-builder adoption of 4-bit precision for faster, more memory-efficient inference.
- Within an NVL72 system, model weights can be distributed across up to 72 GPUs, so each GPU holds a smaller share of the model — leaving more HBM for KV cache and concurrent users.
Shrink KV-cache and offload inactive context to lower-cost storage tiers.
- Applying NVFP4 to the KV cache reduces its footprint compared with FP8, so more context can stay resident in HBM.
- NVIDIA Vera CPU helps in two ways. Faster tool execution shortens the time KV cache sits inactive during tool calls, and its large LPDDR memory, connected to NVIDIA Rubin GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink-C2C interconnect, gives paused context a nearby place to wait and return quickly.
- When context isn’t actively in use, NVIDIA Dynamo inference software moves it to NVIDIA CMX context memory storage — a tier built for capacity at far lower cost per bit than HBM — and returns it before reuse. Unlike local SSDs, CMX is shared across servers, and unlike enterprise storage, it skips the overhead of long-term data protection that short-lived context doesn’t need. NVIDIA CMX context memory storage partners include Cloudian, DDN, Dell Technologies, Everpure (previously Pure Storage), HPE, IBM, NetApp, VAST and WEKA.
- Dynamo’s KV Cache Reuse ties the tiers together, managing KV cache as one system-wide resource across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage, so context computed once can be reused across the system.
Compact RAG embeddings and keeping the index outside HBM.
- RAG turns enterprise documents into embeddings — numerical representations that let a system search by meaning rather than keyword — organized into a searchable index. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models produce smaller embeddings with higher retrieval accuracy, while the NVIDIA cuVS library enables that index to be built and served across CPU and storage. The knowledge base never occupies HBM, and only the passages the model needs enter context.
The result is less HBM used for model weights, less HBM tied up by idle context and more of it available to serve concurrent users.
More Useful Output per Dollar With Each Generation
Across successive NVIDIA platform generations, tokens per second per dollar has risen far faster than HBM capacity.
On the SemiAnalysis AgentX DeepSeek V4 Pro workload, NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 10x higher throughput per dollar than NVIDIA H200 platform at 100 tokens per second per user, with HBM capacity per GPU roughly doubling. At 125 tokens per second per user, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x higher throughput per dollar than GB300 NVL72, with HBM capacity per GPU up about 3%.
For AI factory operators, the metric that matters is how many useful tokens the factory can deliver within its power budget while meeting user response-time needs. More tokens per second per watt means more work and revenue from the same power, and a lower cost for every token. NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign lowers token costs by increasing the useful work every byte of memory delivers.
Learn more in the video explainer and technical deep dive on how NVIDIA full-stack codesign reduces inference memory pressure.

articles.title: Muse has a voice mode now
articles.text:
Meta now lets you have voice conversations with your Muse AI agent in real time, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced today.
Muse has a voice mode now
Muse AI agent now has voices and ‘expressive’ avatars that animate while chatting with you.
The feature has been rolled out to me, and I gave it a spin on the iOS app while writing this article. As you chat with your Muse agent, the avatar at the top of your conversation animates in time with the words that it’s saying. You can also change the tone of the voice by just asking your agent about what you want and letting it decide or by browsing through a bunch of options in the avatar settings.
In my brief tests, my Muse agent responds quickly over voice, though it occasionally pauses while it’s looking up information or checking something for me (like it would with a text chat query). It also animates what it’s saying well, though for my particular avatar, it’s been a little uncanny. I set my Muse agent’s avatar to look like Mark Zuckerberg as a constant reminder that I’m chatting with a Meta service (I refuse to be charmed by a Jolly!), and seeing the digital Zuckerberg facsimile actually talk with me is quite weird. I also can’t get my Muse agent’s voice to sound exactly like Mark Zuckerberg.
Muse’s voice mode and expressive avatars are rolling out now in the US for the app, Meta says. They’re coming “soon” for Meta’s AI glasses and will also be available for its forthcoming Muse Charm gadget, which is supposed to ship this year.

articles.title: ‘Hogwarts Legacy’ Gets a Magical NVIDIA DLSS 5 Upgrade on GeForce NOW
articles.text:
Hogwarts Legacy receives an NVIDIA DLSS 5 upgrade with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering today, bringing lifelike lighting and materials to the wizarding world on GeForce NOW.
Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever also opens a new chapter in Azeroth, with a launch-week access reward available for GeForce NOW members. Meanwhile, Ubisoft brings fresh challenges with expansions for Tom Clancy’s The Division 2 and Anno 117: Pax Romana.
It’s all part of a packed month of play, with two-dozen games joining the GeForce NOW library throughout November, including eight this week.
Hogwarts in a New Light
NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering arrives in Hogwarts Legacy today, giving members a new reason to return to Hogwarts, streaming from Steam, Epic Games and Xbox with Play Anywhere support.
Published by Warner Bros. Games under the Portkey Games label and developed by Avalanche Software, Hogwarts Legacy is an immersive, open-world action role-playing game set in the 1800s wizarding world. Begin as a fifth-year student, encounter magical creatures, brew potions and learn spells while exploring both recognizable and unfamiliar places.
The update adds lifelike lighting and material detail while retaining underlying geometry and textures. Avalanche Software has tuned the integration through DLSS 5’s developer controls to maintain the game’s artistic intent and style.
Hogwarts Legacy also includes support for the DLSS Multi Frame Generation and Ray Reconstruction features, accelerating and enhancing the ray-traced graphics that immerse players in Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Thanks to NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls in the cloud, members can fine-tune their experience.
Ultimate members can experience the update with GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, handhelds, browsers, mobile devices, compatible TVs and more, without an expensive PC upgrade or waiting for game downloads. GeForce NOW handles the installs and updates, saving the storage space for everyday essentials. Just pick up the wand, hop on a broom and take flight.
A New Chapter, Forever
Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever launched Wednesday, Nov. 4, and is streaming on GeForce NOW, inviting players into a reimagined original Azeroth built to keep growing for years to come.
Explore new and expanded zones, discover gameplay enhancements and take in upgraded graphics in a world where community and the journey take center stage. Access is included with an active World of Warcraft subscription or Game Time, giving returning heroes and newcomers a fresh starting point.
GeForce NOW also supports CurseForge Addons for World of Warcraft: Forever, giving premium members more ways to customize their experience. At launch, GeForce NOW plans to support around 100 of the most popular CurseForge add-ons, with the selection evolving to reflect player favorites. Members can request additional add-ons through in-app feedback for consideration in future updates.
The cloud keeps the next quest within reach across supported devices. For new World of Warcraft users who don’t already have a subscription, a launch-week access reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers. The access period runs through Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT.
Eligible members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the Account Portal to redeem while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis. Gather the party and venture forward.
New Missions, New Horizons
Ubisoft brings two new downloadable content releases to the cloud this week, sending agents into an overgrown New York and governors toward a new province of the Roman Empire.
Launched earlier this week, Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Echoes of Central Park is the biggest experience since Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Warlords of New York, opening up Central Park and the Upper West Side for the first time in franchise history. Investigate disappearances and rumors of a mysterious threat, team up with three companions with distinct combat roles, and earn new gear and six skill variants. Play solo or in co-op, with a level boost available for agents below level 40.
In Anno 117: Pax Romana – Dawn of the Delta, arriving today, build cities in Aegyptus, where deserts, fertile farmland and seasonal floods shape every decision. Develop irrigation systems and choose whether to Romanize the population or preserve local traditions. The new province can be explored in an existing save or chosen as the starting point for a new game.
New territory belongs on the map, not in a download queue. GeForce NOW handles both expansions’ downloads and updates, leaving the planning to governors and the gear management to agents.
In addition, members can look for the following joining the GeForce NOW library this week:
- World of Warcraft: Forever (New release on Battle.net, Nov. 4)
- County of Fortune (New release on Steam, Nov. 5)
- CURE – A Hospital Simulator (Steam)
- Leaf it Alone (Steam)
- Planet Zoo 2 (Epic Games Store)
- Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim (Steam)
- RuneScape: Dragonwilds (Epic Games Store)
- SpiritVale (Steam)
And the November lineup has more in store. Look forward to these games arriving throughout the rest of the month:
- Ashes of the Singularity II (New release on Steam, Nov. 10)
- Cyberpunk 2077 (New release on Battle.net, Nov. 10, and Xbox, supports Xbox Play Anywhere)
- Warhammer Survivors (New release on Steam and Xbox, available on Game Pass, Nov. 10)
- Main Sequence (New release on Steam, Nov. 12)
- Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed (New release on Steam, Nov. 19)
- Appulse (New release on Steam, Nov. 26)
- Baldur’s Gate 3 (Xbox, supports Xbox Play Anywhere)
- Deadly Days: Roadtrip (Steam)
- Gone Fishing (Steam)
- Graveyard Keeper (Steam)
- Graveyard Keeper 2 (Epic Games Store and GOG)
- Quasimorph (Steam)
- Tape to Tape (Steam)
- The Spell Brigade (Steam)
- Village in the Shade (Steam)
- World of Tanks: Blitz (Wargaming)
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles.
All the Extras From October
On top of the 25 games announced in October, 16 extra titles made their way to the cloud:
- ATMOSFAR (Steam)
- Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 (available in the Call of Duty app)
- CONTROL Resonant (Epic Games Store)
- Crimson Desert (Epic Games Store)
- Dressmaker (Steam)
- FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE (Steam)
- Forever Ago (Steam)
- Halloween (Epic Games Store)
- Hell Let Loose: Vietnam (Epic Games Store)
- Hunting Simulator 3 (Steam)
- Planet Zoo 2 (Xbox app, supports Xbox Play Anywhere)
- Phantom Blade Zero (Steam)
- The Seance of Blake Manor (Steam)
- Queen’s Domain (Steam)
- We Were Here Tomorrow (Steam)
- The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered (Xbox, supports Xbox Play Anywhere)
A GeForce NOW day pass offers a first taste of the cloud’s spellwork. Gamers can try Performance or Ultimate before committing to a membership, with the cost of the day pass applicable toward a first monthly membership. For the full DLSS 5 experience in Hogwarts Legacy, an Ultimate day pass is the ticket — no Sorting Hat required.
What games have you under a spell this week? Let us know on X or in the comments below.
